15917-the-great-round-world-and-what-is-:
Harison's weekly paper for boys and girls, number forty, dated August 12, 1897. Five cents bought news, science, and stories in words young readers could follow. Four new subscribers earned a pocket Kodak, measuring two and a quarter by two and seven-eighths inches, making pictures one and a half by two. The paper mixed learning with prizes.

This number turns to the week's events abroad and at home, with nature notes and serial tales beside. Editors explain treaties and inventions in short, clear paragraphs. Picture items keep young eyes moving. Seen now, the issue captures a summer of 1897 for American children: cameras as prizes, and the world arriving weekly.
43528-the-irish-penny-journal-vol-1-no-0:
The Irish Penny Journal for Saturday, 18 July 1840 forms this number, the third of its first year. A cut at its front shows the Rock of Cashel, as seen from the south. The first piece of the sheet treats of that rock. To such of its readers as have not had the luck to see the old chief town of Munster, it says, the cut may give some sense of the place.

The group of ruins on that rock claims to rank as the most full of pull in the British isles, in the words of the piece. Buildings of more span and more splendour may be found in other spots. But in no other spot of the realm can there be seen, in one huddle, so many works of such mixed kinds and uses, and of such far and split ages.
54252-the-irish-penny-journal-vol-1-no-1:
The Irish Penny Journal for Saturday, 10 October 1840 forms this number, the fifteenth of its first year. A cut at its front shows the town and the strong house of Leixlip, in the county of Kildare. The first piece of the sheet treats of places and the whims of taste. Places, it says, are no less at the call of the shifts of vogue in taste than dress or tune. No thing on which that whim shows its wild turns is free of it.

The place that is the pick of throngs in one age is left bare in the next. It is out of thought, as if it were a waste unfit for the joy of men. Some next place, of less charm by kind or by art, takes the vogue of the day.
570-the-moravians-in-georgia-1735-1740:
Adelaide Fries recounts the Moravian Church's first attempt to settle in Georgia in this short history. The Moravians, a Protestant group from central Europe, came to the new colony hoping to preach and farm in peace. Their five years in Georgia tested faith, funds, and neighborly relations.

Fries frames the venture as a seeming failure that bore later fruit, much like Bunker Hill in her preface. German names, kept with an added e for umlauts in this text, mark the settlers' origins. The book serves as a clear, compact account of a small colony with an outsized place in American church history.
5943-the-history-of-don-quixote-volume-2:
Shepherd dreams fill chapters sixty-seven through seventy of this Don Quixote portion, after defeat. Chapter sixty-seven treats the resolution Quixote formed to turn shepherd and live in the fields while the year of his given word runs its course, with other delectable and happy events. Chapter sixty-eight brings a bristly adventure, chapter sixty-nine the strangest and most extraordinary adventure, and chapter seventy matters following sixty-nine.

The tale follows a vanquished knight remaking himself as a pastoral poet, trading armor for crook and field songs. The chapters favor melancholy comedy, as Quixote's new dream softens his old delusion. This part suits readers nearing volume two's end, since the shepherd plan prepares the return home, the omens, and the final sickness.
aldrovandi-serpentum-draconum-1640:
Ulisse Aldrovandi, the tireless naturalist of Bologna, devoted his Serpentum et draconum historiae to serpents and dragons. The two Latin books appeared in 1640, after his death, from his vast museum and notes. Aldrovandi aimed to record everything known about a creature, ancient report and fresh sighting alike.

Vipers and common snakes share his pages with basilisks and sea serpents. Each creature gets a careful picture in the Renaissance manner. Aldrovandi stands halfway between true science and honest marvel, and knows it not at all. His serpent book founded learned serpent lore in print. Collectors still prize its plates.
arxiv-2412-01040:
Aulia Adila, Candy Olivia Mawalim, and Masashi Unoki wrote this research paper, published in 2024. It studies how to spot fake or spoofed voices in speech from non-native speakers, using Indonesian and Thai speakers as the test case.

Voice spoofing can fool speaker checks, so detection systems matter. The team built a dataset with both native and non-native speech, pulled three kinds of sound features from it, and trained three standard classifiers. Detectors trained only on native speech struggled badly with non-native speech. Mixing non-native speech into the training data made detection much stronger. The paper argues that anti-spoofing tools must be trained on the accents they will actually meet, not just on native voices.
arxiv-2412-02440:
Lotta Rüter and Melanie Schienle adapt a variable selection method for messy panel data in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. Microfinance studies juggle many traits, missing values, and hidden fixed effects. Picking true success factors from that tangle needs robust tools.

Their version of a multiple imputation random lasso is tailored to longitudinal data with complex gaps. They applied it to a global panel of two hundred thirteen microfinance institutions, each with one hundred thirty-six traits over six years. Staff structure emerged as a key driver of success. Profitability was the strongest marker of financial health. Outreach breadth could grow alongside financial strength, while outreach depth showed a murkier link. The method suits other high-dimensional panels.
arxiv-2412-06040:
Aikaterina Manoli, Janet Pauketat, and Jacy Reese Anthis test how people judge AI systems as a group in this two thousand twenty-four human-computer interaction paper. People often treat robots and AI systems as moral agents responsible for their actions. The authors ask whether one agent's bad behavior spills over onto attitudes toward all similar agents. Two preregistered experiments, each with roughly seven hundred participants, probed this moral spillover.

In the first study, an agent's immoral action raised negative moral judgments and lowered perceived moral worthiness, for both the individual agent and its whole group, whether chatbot or human assistants. In the second study, with individuated named agents, spillover persisted in the AI context but vanished in the human one. The authors suggest AI systems are seen as a homogeneous outgroup, creating a double standard: all AIs get judged for the actions of one.
arxiv-2412-07240:
Jakub Matousek, Jindrich Dunik, and Marek Brandner wrote a 2024 study on estimating the state of systems that change continuously under randomness. Their setting solves a key equation for probability distributions on a grid. They bring in spectral differentiation, a technique known for very fast convergence on smooth functions.

Standard grid methods improve slowly as points are added, which forces large grids and heavy computation. The spectral approach reaches good accuracy with fewer points, even with a moving grid and zero values at the edges. For readers in filtering and control, the gain is a more accurate estimate at lower computing cost.
arxiv-2412-09240:
Roberto Alcover-Couso, Marcos Escudero-Viñolo, Juan SanMiguel, and Jesus Bescos teach segmentation models to label anything, anywhere, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-four. Ordinary segmenters only know the categories from their training set. Open vocabulary segmentation breaks that cage by borrowing vision-language models, but those models blur fine distinctions.

Synthetic data helps, yet only within the datasets that exist. The authors combine both routes with unsupervised domain adaptation, which adjusts a model to a new domain without new labels. Their framework sharpens the vision-language model with multi-scale context, sturdier text embeddings built by prompt augmentation, and careful layer-wise fine-tuning. Adaptation strategies then carry the skill across domains. The goal is a segmenter that keeps its open vocabulary while gaining precision on unfamiliar scenes. Such flexibility matters for robots and vehicles that cannot know their surroundings in advance.
arxiv-2412-09540:
Serban Cicortas and Christoph Kehle build outer regions of naked singularities with a stepped self similar shape for the Einstein scalar field system. A naked singularity is a collapse point not hidden by a horizon. Their work came out in twenty twenty-four.

Building such cases splits in two, the outer region past the collapse cone and an inner fill from smooth start data. A past build used smooth self similarity but left both parts mildly rough on the cone. Number work hints that stepped forms can arise from smooth data. The new outer regions are smooth on the cone, with the scalar field bounded yet swinging without end near the point.
arxiv-2412-11540:
Jiaxu Wan and six co-authors build a new point-cloud network that can see both fine detail and the whole shape of a scene at once. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-four.

Point tools that widen their view tend to wash out group focus and lose fine traits. Stand-in points, called proxies, can give a broad view, but past ways cost too much, blur place, or fuse local and broad facts badly. The new tool uses sparse proxies in a dual-stream frame. It aims to fix weak picks from wild point shapes, slow proxy work, and lopsided fusion. The goal is sharp three-dim sense at wide range.
arxiv-2412-14140:
Deshpande and colleagues build in twenty twenty-four a compact language model that grades other models' outputs with reasons. Using big models as judges is common, but closed models explain their scores poorly and task-specific graders do not travel across topics. Their three-billion-parameter grader scores any text against any user-set criteria, with fine-grained scales and highlighted spans.

It was trained across hundreds of domains and criteria, and works in many languages. On a standard test it tracked human scores better than a far larger commercial model, and matched models many times its size. Human raters agreed with its scores in over nine of ten cases. The team released it openly for research use.
arxiv-2412-14340:
Alexis Fox, Samarth Swarup, and Abhijin Adiga brought order to a crowded shelf of metrics in 2024. Content-making models are judged by adapted precision and recall scores, precision standing for realism of the output and recall for coverage of real change. Most of them worked out from nearest neighbors in some trait space. With proposals multiplying, nobody could say how the metrics relate or what each one rewards.

The authors unify the nearest-neighbor group under information theory, using the math of nearest-neighbor density estimate. Out of that lens they build a three-part metric of their own: a precision cross-entropy for fidelity, a recall cross-entropy. And a recall entropy, separating two varied kinds of diversity, between classes and within them. Because the pieces derive from entropy concepts that apply anywhere, the metric works across domains and can be dissected at the level of samples or modes.
arxiv-2412-14740:
Alexander Van Werde and Jaron Sanders study how to map hidden barriers from random motion in a 2024 paper. Their particle wanders like Brownian motion but bounces off semipermeable barriers until enough contact lets it slip through. Given recorded samples of the path, they ask when the barriers' location and shape can be recovered. The answer splits into regimes set by how long one watches and how often one samples.

Watch time decides whether whole barriers or only pieces are learnable. Recovery speed is polynomial for fixed-rate sampling but exponential at high frequency. Barrier curvature matters in one regime and fades in the other. They give explicit algorithms and a real-data illustration.
arxiv-2412-18040:
Li and co-authors prove hard limits on a fancier kind of transformer attention in this 2024 theory paper. Tensor attention captures links across several data streams at once. Rotary position embedding, called RoPE, encodes word order well over long texts.

The team analyzes both tools through circuit complexity, which counts the computing depth a task needs. With modest precision, fixed depth, and small hidden size, these models cannot solve certain fixed membership or closure problems. The proof assumes two standard complexity classes differ, a widely believed but unproven split. The limits contrast with the tools' strong practical results. The authors offer the bounds as guidance for designing and scaling future transformers on firmer ground.
arxiv-2412-19640:
Sheng-Hong Lai, Jen-Chi Lee, and Yi Yang wrote this physics paper, published in 2024. It calculates how strings scatter at high energy when several of the participants are tensor states, and uncovers the neat scaling pattern those collisions obey.

The team worked out amplitudes for collisions mixing two tensor states with any number of tachyons, at any mass level. They found the scaling strength of the result drops when the collision spans more crosswise directions than earlier cases with a single tensor. To prove the pattern, they propose a set of identities among the amplitudes. Both forms of the identity are proven outright for four-particle collisions, and checked numerically for higher ones. The work extends a known stringy regularity to richer states and gives later studies a tool to rely on.
arxiv-2412-19940:
Crystianne De Andrade and Alexander Kiselev model how living cells move toward chemical cues while they breed and react, in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. Such motion, called chemotaxis, can keep a reaction going or speed it up. Their model treats the spread of gamete-like cells in an unusual way.

In place of plain spread, the model uses a math term that allows long jumps. That choice fits cases where targets are sparse and spread is faster than normal. The model joins drift, cue-guided motion, a loss term, and the long-jump spread in one equation. It builds on earlier work by the second author and others.
arxiv-2501-01640:
Thakur and Kurmi improve a way to label each pixel in an image when few images come with labels in twenty twenty-five. Labeling every pixel by hand is slow and costly. Their method learns from labeled images plus rough labels it makes for the rest. Two flaws can creep in: noisy data and shaky rough labels.

Their network has two branches that share work and check each other. One part tracks how noisy each pixel's data look. A second loss, based on an energy score, shapes learning from the rough labels. Labels from the overlap and the union of the branches guide each branch in turn. Tests beat prior methods on standard scores.
arxiv-2501-03040:
Duygu Sezen Islakoglu and Jan-Christoph Kalo present ChronoSense, a benchmark for how language models grasp time spans. Their paper from twenty twenty-five notes that models still stumble on reasoning and arithmetic. Time reasoning is a core part of language sense, yet tests of interval links stay rare. Allen's framework names those links: before, after, during, and more.

The set holds sixteen tasks. Some ask which Allen link joins two events. Others ask for time arithmetic. Events are both abstract and drawn from Wikidata's real records. Seven recent models were tested. Scores swung widely, even between mirror-image links. The team suspects rote recall props up some right answers. Low marks overall mark time sense as a weak spot. Data and code are public for future work.
arxiv-2501-03840:
Mathias Bellat and five co-authors review machine learning in archaeology. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five; the pack row gives no title or year, so the text head is the source. Use of such tools has grown fast across all branches, lands, and eras of the field, but its spread and wins were unmapped.

They read over a hundred papers across a span of decades. Growth takes off in the late twenty tens. Spotting structures and sorting finds lead the tasks, then wear studies and site forecasting. Guided models rule; neural nets and ensembles make two thirds of the tools. Some papers state the method's needs and limits poorly. A workflow guide is offered to help digs frame sound, well-told methods.
arxiv-2501-05640:
Zixuan Liang automates date format detection for data tools in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Dates arrive as text in countless forms, and reading them right is a slow step in data work. Tools for charts and databases need the format before they can plot or store values.

Liang offers two algorithms. One picks the format that leaves the least disorder in the column, and the other leans on language modeling of the strings. Both passed ninety percent accuracy on a large set of real data columns. The disorder-based method is fast enough for live feedback as users type. The author aims the methods at chart tools and databases.
arxiv-2501-07940:
Hana Formánková Levá and Gabriela Holubová study travelling waves in a bending beam with uneven supports, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. The model is a nonlinear fourth-order equation whose force law jumps at a threshold. Such beams mimic bridges and other structures that rest differently on each side.

The authors focus on waves with a single dip. For certain speeds and settings, they prove at least two distinct waves of this kind exist. They also bound how many such waves can exist in total. Pictures of the solutions and their counts make the results concrete. The paper closes with open questions on the topic, inviting further work on this beam model.
arxiv-2501-08840:
Lingfeng Chen presents CveBinarySheet, a binaries database for IoT vulnerability analysis in two thousand twenty-five. Static binary analysis hunts flaws inside compiled code. Good data sets for varied firmware worlds are scarce, though. IoT, UEFI, and microcontroller targets all lack ready samples.

The sheet holds over a thousand CVE entries across decades. Sixteen common components, like busybox and curl, supply the code. Five chip architectures are covered, from x86 to RISC-V. Each binary comes at two optimization levels for contrast. Rich metadata aims to speed tool building and flaw matching.
arxiv-2501-09740:
Jason Hartline, Chang Wang, and Chenhao Zhang refine how regulators can audit pricing algorithms for collusion, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Sellers' algorithms might quietly keep prices high, and auditors see only outcome data. Their test checks a pessimistic form of calibrated regret, the worst regret still consistent with the data.

The new test drops an older demand that pricing use all prices with some chance. It is at least as lenient as any test that reliably fails truly regretful play. The authors also show weaker regret notions let rivals steer a seller into high prices. Fake high costs can still fool the audit, they warn.
arxiv-2501-10440:
Bocheng Zhang tests a robust averaging trick for a hard numeric integral in two thousand twenty-five. The Keister function is a standard test case for high-dimensional integration. The trick, median-of-means, splits samples into groups and takes the middle group mean, which guards against wild outliers.

Randomized lattice points and digital nets were tried in two, three, five, and eight dimensions. Sample sizes ran from small grids to over half a million points. Past about a thousand points, the median route beat the plain mean route in accuracy. Below that size, the plain route did better, above all with digital nets. The study backs new theory while noting size limits.
arxiv-2501-12440:
JiJi Fan, Lingfeng Li, and Chen Sun wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It shows how the pulse shape and polarization of X-rays from pulsars could betray axions, faint particles that neutron stars may brew in their hot cores.

Axions made inside the star can turn into X-rays in its strong magnetic field. The authors build fresh analytic forms for how the X-ray beat and polarization should swing as the star turns. They try the forms on one dim neutron star with an odd hard X-ray excess. The axion tale fits both the glow and the beat data, though the best-fit zone sits near bounds set by other stars. Sharper beat data could settle the case.
arxiv-2502-01540:
Raja Marjieh, Veniamin Veselovsky, Thomas Griffiths, and Ilia Sucholutsky ask what a number is to a large language model. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. The same digit string can be a value in one place and a mere string in an other, as with a phone code. How a model holds numbers shapes its use in daily calls.

They borrow a likeness task from mind science and ask models to judge pairs of whole numbers. The calls are fit by a blend of string edit distance and true numeric distance, which shows a mixed hold. Probes of the inner vectors show the same tangle. Context can ease it but not clear it, and the mix leaks into a real choice task.
arxiv-2502-02940:
Rajib Mandal, Raju Biswas, and Sudip Kumar Guin solved a group of working equations in complex analysis in 2025. The equations are Fermat-type, modeled on the famous relation whose answers are tightly constrained, but with shifts and gaps of an unknown meromorphic function in place of simple powers. Such equations often admit no answers at all, so any complete account of their answer set is valuable.

The authors show that for the shift and gap variants they consider. The meromorphic answers are generated by functions of Riccati type, the class defined by a classic first-order differential equation. Along the way they resolve open problems posed by Liu and Yang in 2016 about Fermat-type equations. And they back every claim with worked examples, proving the Riccati-generated answers behave exactly as the theorems predict.
arxiv-2502-03440:
Stefan Gerdjikov, Martin Minchev, and Mladen Savov study a rare pattern in high-dimensional grids, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. They ask how likely a set of random points is to sit with all gaps between pairs exactly equal. As the number of dimensions grows, that chance shrinks in a set way.

The authors give the shrink rate and a fixed constant built from the first four spread measures of the point values. Their proof leans on a local limit result that is not often used. The finding also holds for wider value sets and for other ways to measure gaps.
arxiv-2502-05240:
Yueying Zou and colleagues survey methods for spotting media made by artificial intelligence, from doctored photos to synthetic video and text. Fake media threaten trust in information, and detectors have evolved alongside the generators. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the authors divide detectors into two families. The older family uses narrow, high-precision deep learning tools built for one job. The newer family uses multimodal large language models as general detectors that can also explain a verdict and point to the tampered region.

Both families are compared for single media types and for mixed media, with attention to where their methods overlap and differ. The authors discuss hybrid designs that marry precision with explanation, list open challenges, and review how different governments regulate generative tools. The survey is aimed at researchers choosing a detection strategy.
arxiv-2502-05840:
Antonio Casares and Pierre Ohlmann settle how much memory a player needs to win endless games with complex goals. Their paper from twenty twenty-five works on two-player zero-sum games played on graphs, possibly endless ones. Memory is the count of states a winning plan must track. For omega-regular goals, even whether a given memory size could be decided was unknown.

The authors focus on goals in a class read by parity automata, possibly infinite ones. They build automata that capture all goals whose memory stays under a set cap. From this, memory over finite and infinite games turns out to match. It can be computed within NP bounds. A product rule bounds the memory of joined goals by the product of each part's memory. Chromatic memory, which updates only on seen colors, follows the same rules.
arxiv-2502-06340:
Emilio Gomez-Deniz and Jose Maria Sarabia derive fresh formulas for famous mathematical constants from a single probability distribution, in work from twenty twenty-five. Catalan's constant and Apery's constant appear across number theory but resist closed forms. The Euler numbers form another classic sequence.

Their source is the half hyperbolic secant distribution, a bell shaped law from statistics. Tools from inequality measurement, like the Lorenz curve and Gini and Theil indices, yield the constants as integrals. Mixtures and convolutions of the law give more routes, some known and some new. Series forms appear alongside the integral ones. New bounds for both constants come out of the same machinery. Euler numbers get integral forms too.
arxiv-2502-09940:
Yu-Xiang Lin and six co-authors give an early probe of GPT-4o in voice mode, testing its grasp of sound, speech, and music. The model is a pioneer among large multimodal systems. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

The model proved strong on intent sorts, spoken command sorts, sense and grammar thought, speech reads in many tongues, and singing checks. It also made up facts less than rival audio models. It lagged on length guesses for audio and on naming instruments. Its safety rules made it refuse tasks like speaker naming, age sorts, and fake audio spotting, with refusal rates that swung by data set and prompt.
arxiv-2502-13140:
Myson Burch, Jiasen Zhang, and a large team of colleagues survey tensor methods for biomedical data in a 2025 review. Biomedical measurements often arrive as multi-way arrays linking patients, genes, locations, and time. Tensor decomposition splits such arrays into simpler factors that reveal hidden patterns, and quantum versions of those methods are now emerging.

The review covers classic decompositions and spiked variants, then maps uses across imaging, multi-omics, and spatial transcriptomics. A topic modeling pass over the literature organizes the field's themes. Readers gain a guide to which decomposition fits which data type, plus a sense of where quantum approaches might help.
arxiv-2502-15040:
Chu, Zhang, Malon, and Min tackle in twenty twenty-five a known flaw of medical AI that reads both images and text: it can invent findings. In medicine, such made-up details can mislead care. Their fix lets the model look up real chest X-ray images and reports while it writes, grounding its words in retrieved cases.

They tested the method on chest X-ray report writing and on captioning medical images. A probing test asked whether named findings truly appear in an image. Grounding raised accuracy for both common and rare findings, though rare ones have fewer good training cases. Using the probes to fix drafts also yielded reports that scored higher on a clinical accuracy measure. The authors see retrieval as a practical guard against invention.
arxiv-2502-15540:
Milad Sefidgaran, Abdellatif Zaidi, and Piotr Krasnowski prove bounds on how badly a representation-learning model can fail on fresh data. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Such models squeeze data into compact codes that capture the gist. Good codes should work beyond the training set.

Their bounds rest on how much the codes for training and test data differ from a shared prior. That prior is itself learned from the data, in a symmetric way. The bounds capture how simple and structured the encoder is. They beat the few older bounds for this setup. From the bound the team derives a training penalty that keeps codes honest. A scheme for learning the prior alongside the model brings out an attention-like weighting on its own. Tests beat two popular rival methods.
arxiv-2502-17040:
Melegari, Cardi, and Solinas compare two ways, in a 2025 preprint, to prove a system behaves in a quantum way. The target idea is macrorealism: the claim that big systems have definite states whether or not anyone looks. The classic test uses the Leggett-Garg inequalities, built from pairs of measurements over time. Breaking them shows quantum behavior, but only under extra assumptions. A newer test uses gentle measurements that do not demolish the system and gives a yes-or-no answer.

The team ran both tests on IBM quantum simulators. The newer method stores results in a quantum detector and builds a probability-like map. Negative regions in that map flag quantum behavior without doubt. It caught the quantum features every time with fewer resources. Noise hurt the classic test badly but left the new one near untouched. The authors back the new protocol as the better tool.
arxiv-2502-17340:
Ilja Kuzborskij and Yasin Abbasi-Yadkori analyzed in twenty twenty-five why weight decay pushes neural network weight matrices toward low rank. At stationary points of training with L-two regularization, they prove several structural properties: parameters align with gradients, norms are preserved across layers, and a low-rank bias emerges. Earlier work knew these for idealized gradient flow; here they hold at limiting solutions of practical optimizers.

Experiments show the assumptions barely disturb the observed behavior. The payoff is a multitask phenomenon: train two networks on roughly orthogonal input sets, add their weights together, and the merged network performs on both tasks about as well as each specialist. They demonstrate this merging for shallow rectified networks and deep linear ones.
arxiv-2502-18940:
Jakub Macina and five co-authors released MathTutorBench in twenty twenty-five, a benchmark for judging how well AI tutors actually teach math. Grading a tutor takes more than checking answers; teaching skill follows its own rules from learning science. Their open benchmark gathers data sets and metrics that cover the main tutor abilities in dialogue-based teaching.

To score open-ended teacher replies, they trained a reward model that separates expert from novice responses with high accuracy. Testing many closed and open models, they found solving skill does not equal teaching skill. The two form a trade-off steered by how much a model specializes in tutoring. Longer dialogues also made tutoring harder, as simple questioning tactics began to fail. The benchmark, code, and leaderboard are public.
arxiv-2502-21240:
Anand, van den Brand, and McCarty study when multiplying a matrix by a vector can beat the naive method in this 2025 theory paper. Practitioners have fast methods, yet theory says worst-case inputs force full quadratic time. Even average-case arguments cannot explain the gap.

The authors turn to structured matrices, where the matrix class has low VC-dimension, a measure of complexity. For Boolean matrices of VC-dimension d, they give near-quadratic preprocessing and query time clearly below quadratic. Real data usually has small VC-dimension, which may explain practical speed. They extend the result beyond Boolean values using a related measure. The bounds are the first nontrivial ones for many applications.
arxiv-2503-00040:
Dehao Zhang and six co-authors boost the efficiency of brain-like spiking networks on small devices, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Cutting numbers to few bits saves energy but usually costs much accuracy. The team traced part of that loss to a subtle cause: rounding off each neuron's stored charge throws away its history.

Their method keeps the effect of that history without storing the charge itself, recovering accuracy with even less memory. A second idea trains the network in parallel and lets it answer without step-by-step waiting, raising speed and saving energy. The combined system topped prior results on still-image and event-based data sets. The authors pitch it for low-power neuromorphic hardware.
arxiv-2503-00240:
Juston and four co-authors examined a hidden flaw in tamper-proof neural networks in twenty twenty-five. These one-Lipschitz networks limit how much an input tweak can change the output, enabling certified robustness against adversarial attacks. Two standard layer designs dominate the field.

The authors analyzed how the layers' weight settings behave at initialization, when weights are drawn randomly. They derived exact and upper bounds for weight variance under normal and generalized normal starting distributions. Surprisingly, weight variance does not affect output variance at all; only the matrix dimensions do. Worse, they prove the initialization always makes deep networks of this kind decay toward zero output. The paper flags a fundamental startup problem that designers of certified defenses must engineer around.
arxiv-2503-00840:
Wang, Dong, and Lian present a paper from twenty twenty-five on measurement incompatibility and quantum uncertainty. Some quantum measurements cannot be done at the same time, a core quantum trait. The team extend a graded scale for this clash to general rank-one measurements. New uncertainty relations follow from that step. The paper also links clashes among many measurements to support uncertainty. The results touch how uncertainty bounds are derived in general. Uses in cryptography and state reconstruction are foreseen.

Compressed sensing with quantum data is another named outlet. The paper is theoretical, building relations rather than devices. It deepens the map between incompatibility and uncertainty.
arxiv-2503-01240:
Rauan Akylzhanov, Michael Ruzhansky, and Kanat Tulenov carried a old-style Fourier multiplier theorem into non-commutative settings in a 2025 paper. The Hörmander–Mikhlin theorem tells analysts which rate multipliers act boundedly on function spaces, a workhorse of harmonic analysis. Their version develops a Fourier formalism on non-commutative spaces, where functions are replaced by functions and multiplication no longer commutes. Then proves the multiplier theorem twice over: for locally compact Kac groups and for semi-finite von Neumann algebras.

In the simplest case the result reproduces a sharp form of the old-style theorem. Applications to evolution math rules in the non-commutative setting follow. Such theorems underpin quantum probability and non-commutative shapes, where old-style Fourier tools must be rebuilt from scratch.
arxiv-2503-01340:
Anupama Chauhan and a large team watch, with femtosecond light pulses, how a topological insulator film rings after being struck by light. The material mixes bismuth, antimony, tellurium, and selenium. Films were grown on sapphire, chosen because it reflects sound best at the interface. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team varied film thickness, carrier density, and temperature from near absolute zero to room levels. Thick films showed traveling acoustic strain pulses riding on a fast electronic decay. Thin films behaved differently, dominated by coherent acoustic phonons and a two-stage electronic background.

A theoretical strain model describes the traveling pulses well. The fast decay sped up with more carriers and slowed with cold; the slow stage followed its own pattern. The detailed dynamics matter for devices that would switch with light in such films.
arxiv-2503-05440:
An, Li, Luo, and Zhang give in twenty twenty-five a path-based description of certain algebraic fingerprints for representations of type A quantum loop algebras at roots of unity. These algebras arise in quantum group theory, and their module behaviour is tracked through character-like data. The authors work in a fixed setting where the deformation parameter is a root of unity of a set order.

They show every simple module in their category can be reshaped into a known snake form. From that, they write explicit paths for the fingerprints of degree-two highest-weight modules and of a standard family named Kirillov-Reshetikhin. As a payoff, they give an exact test for when pairing two basic modules stays simple, and a one-way test for larger pairings.
arxiv-2503-07040:
Ali Eghbali, Simin Ghasemi-Sorkhabi, and Adel Rezaei-Aghdam study deformed versions of a classic physics model, in two thousand twenty-five. The model describes fields living on a four-dimensional Lie group. A Yang-Baxter deformation bends its background shape, and the question is whether the bent shapes still solve a generalized form of supergravity equations.

The authors show that the deformed backgrounds do solve those equations. They then apply a duality method with extra spectator fields to build dual models. All dual models but one remain integrable, meaning their equations can be solved in a structured way. Most also solve the generalized equations, while the original solutions turn out to be trivial.
arxiv-2503-09040:
Xinyu Zhang, Haonan Chang, Yuhan Liu, and Abdeslam Boularias rebuild moving scenes in three dimensions so the motion itself can be edited, not just replayed. Gaussian splatting renders scenes from clouds of soft blobs, but rival methods hide motion inside neural networks or per-blob numbers, leaving nothing to grab and change. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team represents motion as a sparse graph of links, like a skeleton. Movement of the links is blended onto nearby blobs through skinning weights that the system paints and learns, and graph and blobs are fitted together from ordinary video.

On a demanding phone video data set the method led the field, and it stayed competitive on a standard benchmark. Because motion is explicit, the team could pose objects in new ways, synthesize robot demonstrations, and plan robot actions visually. Code and demos are posted.
arxiv-2503-12440:
Tsz Chung Cheng and colleagues built a benchmark in 2025 to test whether language models can truly handle Cantonese, Hong Kong's language. Cantonese carries rich cultural nuance and differs sharply from written Mandarin, yet it lacked dedicated evaluation datasets. Their benchmark, HKCanto-Eval, tests Cantonese understanding and extends to English and written Chinese for cross-lingual comparison. Questions are designed to tap not just fluency but underlying metalinguistic knowledge.

The findings show proprietary models generally ahead of open-weight ones. Still, significant limitations remain in handling Cantonese's distinctive features. A benchmark grounded in Hong Kong scenarios measures something generic translated tests cannot: whether a model serves the city's residents in their own tongue. For the millions who speak low-resource language varieties, such evaluations decide whether AI progress includes them or passes them by.
arxiv-2503-14840:
Haru Negami links two routes to building representations of the braid group. His paper is from two thousand twenty-five. The braid group tracks how strands cross and swap, and its representations turn those moves into matrices. One route is algebraic, from the Katz-Long-Moody build. The other is analytic, from a convolution step for a class of equations.

He shows the two routes match. He also shows the build keeps a key trait: when a representation is unitary next to a Hermitian matrix, it stays so. An algorithm finds the signature of that matrix, and he proves the signature is well set for a broad range of values by a continuity plea.
arxiv-2503-15340:
Arjun Sharma, Peter Bosler, Rama Govindarajan, and Donald Koch studied how stretched particles sink and drift in fluids whose thickness varies from place to place in twenty twenty-five. Such fluids occur in oceans and in industry, where salt or heat makes layers of differing thickness. The particles are spheroids, spheres stretched or squashed along one axis.

Using a classic theorem of fluid flow, the authors derived exact formulas for the force and twist on a particle. Sinking and turning couple together, so a particle's tilt changes as it falls. Shape and layer tilt decide the pattern of motion. One mode settles at a fixed angle set only by shape and layer tilt, which could let engineers steer sinking rates. Computer simulations backed the formulas and revealed the stress patterns behind them.
arxiv-2503-16240:
Bartosz Prokop, Jimmy Billen, Nikita Frolov, and Lendert Gelens wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-five about finding hidden structure in systems that swing back and forth. Such systems include many living and physical processes. Their key curves, called nullclines, show where each part of the system stops changing.

The authors present a neural network method named CLINE that learns these curves from time series data alone. Rather than just forecasting the next values, the method recovers a static picture of how the parts relate. It copes with mixed time scales and strong nonlinearity, and its results can be turned into plain equations. Tests on several swinging systems show that the method works well.
arxiv-2503-16940:
Bruno Colbois, Luigi Provenzano, and Alessandro Savo studied magnetic Laplacians on curved surfaces in twenty twenty-five. On a closed surface, a magnetic field twists the usual Laplace operator, and its lowest eigenvalue gives the ground state energy of a charged particle. That energy is positive unless the magnetic potential sits in a special arithmetic class.

Collecting the ground state energies over all such potentials gives a countable set the authors call the ground state spectrum of the metric. Their main theorem: this spectrum determines the surface's volume and its conformal class, the shape up to local stretching. Hyperbolic metrics are singled out by their spectra. The authors also compute the spectrum for flat tori and define new conformal invariants tied to the surface's Jacobian torus.
arxiv-2503-17440:
Thomas Williams leads a team of twenty-two authors who map how well early-type galaxies turn their cold gas into stars, place by place. Such galaxies are odd: about a quarter hold molecular gas that can be detected, yet they form next to no stars. Measures that lump a galaxy as one blur where the small amount of action in fact takes place.

The team put ALMA gas maps with MUSE optical spectroscopy for ten galaxies. They used emission-line diagnostics to split true star formation from other ionization sources. Just a few regions counted as purely star-forming. Rates of star formation traced by hydrogen emission could then be set next to gas surface densities place by place. The sharp view deepens the puzzle of why these galaxies stay so quiet.
arxiv-2503-18140:
Archit Patke and five colleagues present INDIGO, a page migration framework for hardware memory disaggregation. Disaggregation lets servers borrow remote memory over a network, creating large shared pools. The catch is contention: remote access can badly slow applications, so operating systems migrate hot pages closer to the processor.

Existing migration policies ignore that transfer costs vary with network congestion. INDIGO adds page telemetry and a learning-based method that adapts to network conditions. Implemented in the Linux kernel and tested on a real prototype, it improved application performance by fifty to seventy percent over leading policies. It also cut network traffic by up to half.
arxiv-2503-20540:
Dingchen Yang leads a team of six on this paper from two thousand twenty-five. It asks which visual tokens a multimodal model can safely drop, by watching how the words it would say shift when the sight input is changed.

Such models chew thousands of image tokens, which crowd the context and tax the run. Past cuts scored tokens by inner states like attention, which can misread their worth. This team probes from the word side, both token by token and in context. Some low-scored tokens in fact carry clear, load-bearing sight facts. Their method flags spare tokens by fixed marks learned from training images, then cuts at run time. Across photo, set, and video tasks it keeps near full scores while cutting most tokens.
arxiv-2503-21440:
Kolomeec and Bykov extend and count a classic class of bent functions used in cryptography, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Bent functions are maximally nonlinear and prized for secure codes. The Maiorana-McFarland class is the best-known bent family. The team studies its closure and a larger extension under standard equivalences.

They give an exact count formula for the extension size. They also bound the closure size with tight asymptotic estimates. Distance traits of both classes are measured next. They count the closest bent functions to each class and bound the same for the closure. Average counts of flat subspaces where members stay affine are computed exactly for the base class.
arxiv-2503-21940:
Xiaomeng Huang, Angela Pistoia, Christophe Troestler, and Chunhua Wang construct normalized vector solutions of nonlinear Schrödinger systems in a two thousand twenty-five analysis paper. Normalized means the total mass of the solution is prescribed in advance.

The system couples several parts through quadratic interaction terms, with potentials and symmetric coupling coefficients. Given a non-degenerate critical point of a certain mix of the potentials, the authors build solutions whose components concentrate at that point. This bunching happens as the prescribed mass grows large in one dimension, shrinks in three dimensions, or nears a key threshold in two. The work extends mass-limited methods for Bose-Einstein condensate type systems.
arxiv-2503-23940:
Debapratim Banerjee asks, in a 2025 preprint, what a Wigner random matrix becomes when its size grows without bound. Wigner matrices, filled with random entries under symmetry, are a base object of random matrix theory. Their eigenvalue patterns settle into the famous semicircle law. Banerjee instead wants a limit for the matrix itself, as an operator. He builds a Hilbert space on which the limiting operator acts. A matching notion of convergence is defined so the finite matrices approach it.

The Hilbert space turns out to extend the usual square-integrable functions on an interval in a nontrivial way. On that space sits the limit operator. Its spectral measure, tested at any such function, is almost surely the semicircle law. So the classic pattern reappears inside a richer operator picture. This is the first paper of a series, laying the stage and the limit object for later study.
arxiv-2503-24040:
Farrell and four co-authors look back on work with a NASA tool that turns plain asks into strict specs in this twenty twenty-five paper. Builders of safe rigs must state what a rig must do in words a machine can check. Loose words at that stage breed costly flaws down the line.

Inside, four case works show the tool in use on real rigs of unlike kinds. For each case, the team sums what the tool caught and where it strained. The strict asks then fed specs cast in a mix of formal frames. Their tale backs the tool as a sound bridge from first asks to checked specs, with clear trace from ask to end spec.
arxiv-2504-00240:
David Alvarez-Castillo examines a puzzling compact object as possibly one of a pair of twin stars in a 2025 astrophysics study. The object, cataloged from gamma ray observations, appears unusually light and small. A twin star interpretation explains it: for the same mass, a hybrid star with a quark core can be more compact than its purely hadronic sibling. Two stars share a mass but not a size.

Derived properties under that reading agree with laboratory constraints and with multi-messenger observations. If twins are real, they would confirm a sharp phase transition inside neutron stars, a major clue about cold dense matter.
arxiv-2504-00340:
Zhang, Bai, and Tang present a paper from twenty twenty-five on a fast solver for proton beam dose sums. Proton beams are used to treat tumors, and planners must predict where the dose lands. The model they solve tracks protons in six dimensions, which makes the sums heavy. Their method first splits protons into direct ones and scattered ones. It then treats depth through the body like time in a moving system.

The split lets each part of the sum run in parallel on many cores at once. Tests show the method is exact to second order in depth and energy steps. Its dose maps match those from random sampling checks for plain and mixed materials. The solver could speed up beam planning for care teams.
arxiv-2504-01040:
Ilir Tahiraj and three co-authors address sensor alignment in self-driving cars in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Cars fuse LiDAR and camera data to read the road. If the sensors drift out of alignment, that picture warps, and safety suffers. Older fixes used targets in a workshop. Newer ones work online, but they demand more computing than cars can spare in real time.

The team reframes the task. Instead of computing the exact misalignment, their framework answers a yes-or-no question: are the sensors still aligned? A binary check is far cheaper to run. It can flag trouble at once, so the car can react or seek a full calibration. The paper targets the strict time and resource limits of driving. It should interest engineers who build perception systems for automated vehicles.
arxiv-2504-01240:
Kai Li and a team of co-authors survey resilient federated learning for edge networks, in two thousand twenty-five. Federated learning trains a shared model across devices without pooling raw data. At the network edge, that training must survive faulty devices, skewed data, and attacks that exploit model features.

The survey covers layered learning plans that cut communication and handle uneven data. It reviews fault tolerance steps that spot bad devices and refine updates before they join the model. Feature-based attacks, from poisoning to reconstruction, get a full treatment unlike older security surveys. Defenses covered include anomaly checks and cryptographic tools. Future links to sixth-generation networks and large language models close the piece.
arxiv-2504-01340:
Shapiro examines the trace anomaly with a background antisymmetric tensor field, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. A massless conformal fermion interacts with metric and tensor backgrounds together. Integrating it out produces an anomaly-induced effective action for those backgrounds. Non-local terms in that action are scheme independent and universal.

Total derivative terms, by contrast, depend on the calculation scheme chosen. The local part of the induced action shares that same dependence. Multiplicative anomaly enters the same local sector of the action. The paper sorts universal physics from convention-dependent pieces carefully. Such sorting matters for building consistent anomaly-based effective theories in curved spacetime.
arxiv-2504-06940:
Letian Tang presents a quantum algorithm in twenty twenty-five for estimating mean values. The case is a random vector with many parts, not just a single number. Earlier quantum methods gave good gains, but room was left to do better. Tang's method beats prior work by extra factors and nearly reaches a known lower bound.

The method builds on a generalized form of the Grover operator. That operator is the core of Grover's search algorithm, using an oracle that marks candidates with a sign. A second version of the method uses less memory at some added cost. Readers in quantum computing get a sharper tool for a basic statistics task.
arxiv-2504-08640:
Alessio Buscemi and sixteen co-authors placed language model agents inside an evolutionary game in twenty twenty-five to study trust in AI regulation. Developers, regulators, and users face interlocking incentives; game theory models the dilemmas, and using language models as the players adds personality, nuance, and repeated-play behavior that equations alone miss.

The simulated agents leaned more pessimistic than pure game-theoretic players — less trusting, more defecting. When users fully trusted, incentives did steer toward effective regulation; conditional trust, though, could erode the social pact. A virtuous loop between user trust and regulator reputation looked key to nudging developers toward safe AI. Which language model played changed where trust emerged, a caution for using such agents to design real regulation.
arxiv-2504-11440:
Lennart Schäpermeier, a solo author, sets a simple baseline for solver scheduling in a 2025 paper. On hard numerical problems, different solvers win on different instances, and meta-methods try to pick the best moment by moment. Champion solvers are often hand-built hybrids that restart fast local searches many times. His greedy schedule repeatedly picks whichever solver is doing best on the still-unsolved training problems.

The result is a fixed, problem-independent timetable. On a standard testbed it closed much of the gap between the best single solver and the ideal per-instance choice. He offers it as the baseline any fancier dynamic selector must beat.
arxiv-2504-12240:
Junhao Zhuang, Lingen Li, Xuan Ju, Zhaoyang Zhang, Chun Yuan, and Ying Shan color comic line art from hundreds of reference images at interactive speed. Their paper from twenty twenty-five presents Cobra. Comic production needs accurate color with steady identity across a page's cast and sets. Diffusion models falter on vast reference sets, slow inference, and loose control. Cobra tests how much context the task truly needs, then builds for it.

A causal sparse transformer design carries the load. Special position codes, sparse attention, and a key-value cache juggle the long reference stream. Color hints give artists a direct hand as well. Results show accurate fills fed by broad context, with latency low enough for studio use. Code and models are posted on the project page.
arxiv-2504-14840:
Gavin Robertson worked out a key scale factor for tree-like distance spaces in a 2025 math paper. Ultrametric spaces, where every triangle is isosceles with the two long sides equal, model hierarchies and clustering trees. Whether such a space has p-negative type, a property tied to embedding a power of its distance into Hilbert space. Can be read off its Gramian matrix, and the smallest scale factor of that matrix gauges how strict the property is.

Robertson shows the smallest scale factor equals half the smallest nonzero distance raised to the power p, a strikingly simple answer. He also describes the full eigenspace belonging to that scale factor. The formula turns an abstract embedding question into a quantity anyone can work out from the distance table.
arxiv-2504-15240:
Amirhossein Mollaali and co-authors wrote this paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on honest error bars for a new kind of neural network. The networks, called Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks, are built for science tasks, where a guess without a doubt range is of little use.

The team first groups many such networks into an ensemble to get a rough sense of spread. They then add conformal prediction, a method that turns spread into intervals with a promised coverage rate, with no assumptions about the data's shape. Wide tests check how the intervals hold up as settings change. The same trick works on newer variants of the network family, including ones that mix data of mixed quality. The authors say the approach makes these networks safer to use in real science.
arxiv-2504-17140:
Ashish Ranjan, Ayush Agarwal, Shalin Barot, and Sushant Kumar present a faster method for predicting sets over time, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. The task is to guess which items will appear in the next set, given a history of sets whose members arrive in no fixed order. Past methods used heavy designs that train and run slowly.

Their design respects the fact that order inside a set does not matter, using transforms built for that trait. This cuts both training and run time by a large margin. On several public benchmarks, accuracy matched or beat the best prior methods across standard scores. The authors offer the design as a practical base for large-scale set forecasting.
arxiv-2504-18640:
Cheng-Hao Fu, Andrea Lincoln, and Rene Reyes pin down the difficulty of cycle problems in hypergraphs and databases in a 2025 theoretical computer science study. Finding a minimum hypercycle, a closed loop in a generalized graph whose edges can hold many vertices, is a core primitive behind database query analysis. The authors prove lower bounds on running time that are tight, meaning no essentially faster algorithm exists under the usual assumptions.

A substantial regime of the unweighted problem gets the same tight treatment, while longer cycles admit a genuinely faster algorithm. A reduction also moves hardness from worst-case inputs to average ones for subgraph detection.
arxiv-2504-20940:
Maximilian Stupp and Phaedon-Stelios Koutsourelakis offer a way to simplify molecule simulations without any prior run data. Their paper from twenty twenty-five addresses coarse-graining, where atoms are grouped into a leaner model. Classic methods need long full-atom runs to learn from. States never visited in those runs stay out of the lean model.

Their frame builds the lean model from the energy rule alone. A hidden space splits into slow traits, which hold the stable states, and fast traits with simple spread. A learned two-way map turns hidden points back into full atom layouts. Training trims a gap score against the true spread of states. A heat-tuning step helps cover all states. Tests on toy systems and a standard peptide show all key states found. Full layouts can be rebuilt in one shot.
arxiv-2504-21540:
Adrian Benton, Alexander Gutkin, Christo Kirov, and Brian Roark improve language spotting in informal Roman-letter text, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Many languages normally written in other scripts are typed in Latin letters online, with wild spelling swings. Look-alike languages, such as Hindi and Urdu, then blur together.

The team built training sets that mimic natural spelling variation. A simple linear model trained only on such fake samples beat a large pretrained neural model by a wide margin. Adding real harvested text pushed scores higher still. Twenty Indic languages were covered in the test set.
arxiv-2504-21640:
Matúš Labaj and five co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on gas flow round a mid sized black hole in a dense star cluster. Such holes are a missing link in the black hole family tree. Winds from huge Wolf-Rayet stars feed the hole in these clusters. The team models that feed with three dimensional fluid and magnet codes.

Each star pours out mass, push, heat, and magnetic flux in the model. Cooling that shifts with metal share is in play. The hole's intake ends up far below the total wind loss. Shock heated winds blast most gas out of the cluster. Intake comes in short bursts when a star swings close by. Bright wind clashes hide the hole's own glow.
arxiv-2504-21740:
Varvak wrote in twenty twenty-five about monodromy in compact Lagrangian fibrations, a topic in complex geometry. A fibration maps a space onto a base so each point above has its own fiber space. Monodromy describes how those fibers twist as one loops around the base. Varvak studies when that twisting can be split into simpler parts. Two cases arise depending on the period map, a tool that tracks fiber shape.

When the period map spreads out in general position, the twisting cannot be split over complex numbers. When all fibers are alike, earlier work showed fibers are built from an elliptic curve. Varvak shows the twisting then splits into exactly two unsplittable parts. The results sharpen the picture of these geometric structures.
arxiv-2505-01340:
Pal and Seth demonstrate universality of leading logarithms at next to leading power for jet processes in twenty twenty-five. Cross sections near threshold have been studied at this power for many years. Threshold limits arise when little energy remains beyond the produced particles. Corrections there organize into logarithmic terms that can be resummed.

The authors treat production of arbitrary massive colourless particles with an extra jet. At next to leading power, the leading logarithms take a universal form. That holds once the right combination of helicity configurations is identified. The result extends threshold theory beyond the leading power approximation. It supports predictions for collider processes with jets in the final state.
arxiv-2505-03240:
Yuzhong Hu, Jiayi Kang, Lei Ma, and Xiaoming Zhang give a fresh way to run the Yau-Yau filter for time variant nonlinear problems. The method turns filtering into a start value problem under a forward equation. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

Time varying factors made fast, low storage runs hard. The new algorithm pairs a physics informed neural network with principal component analysis to solve the forward equation roughly. An offline stage trains the solver, and an online stage runs it. Three test cases show exact, quick, and lean online runs. The team reports wins over Kalman and particle filters.
arxiv-2505-06040:
Hynes and eleven co-authors show that tiny magnets can fake a key quantum effect inside a hybrid wire, freeing the effect from rare materials. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. The effect, spin-orbit coupling, ties an electron's motion to its spin. It lets wires be steered with electric fields and may host exotic protected states.

The team laid arrays of small magnets along a wire of indium arsenide capped with aluminum. The magnets create a rotating field along the wire, which acts like the wanted coupling. Electrical tests probed the field shape through bound states inside the wire. The magnet rows could be flipped between matching and opposed layouts. The measured coupling strength matched the design aims. The trick could bring the effect to common materials with weak natural coupling.
arxiv-2505-06140:
Ramesh Sharma characterizes the round sphere through conformal quasi-Einstein geometry, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. He extends an earlier result of Cochran about closed quasi-Einstein manifolds. That result left one accidental case uncovered. Sharma covers it and generalizes the theorem further.

For a closed quasi-Einstein manifold, a conformal vector field is shown to be Killing under his conditions. If the manifold also admits a non-Killing conformal vector field, more follows. In dimension above two, the manifold must be globally isometric to a sphere, and that field is a gradient. Sharma also derives an integral identity for vector fields on closed Riemannian manifolds. The identity directly proves the Bourguignon-Ezin conservation identity.
arxiv-2505-06340:
Herrera-Camus and a large team of co-authors wrote this astronomy survey paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on galaxies seen when the universe was about a billion years old. The CRISTAL survey uses the ALMA radio array plus space telescopes to map gas, dust, and stars in the same young galaxies.

The sample grew to thirty-nine star-forming galaxies. Their shapes vary widely: spinning disks, mergers, clumpy star birth, and gas tails that hint at close encounters. In many cases the cold gas reaches well past the starlight. Two cases stand out: one starved of the gas signal seen in like galaxies, and one where young star clumps seem to blow gas away from the stars. Trends with brightness match nearby galaxies but sit at higher power. The survey gives a close look at how the first galaxies were built.
arxiv-2505-06840:
Yixin Chen and three co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on teaching vision language models with sharp images at low cost. Sharp images help models spot and read fine detail. Feeding the whole sharp image swells the token count and the compute bill. Their method, Chain of Region-of-Interest, mimics how human eyes pick out key zones.

The chain finds the most rich zones first and spends its budget there. Long token streams from sharp shots are dodged. Tests on eleven known sets span models from small to large. Scores beat a known rival on near all sets. Their largest tuned model topped some closed rivals on six sets.
arxiv-2505-08440:
Sandeep Kumar Verma and Umamaheswari S established reproducing formulas for a generalized wavelet transform in a 2025 analysis paper. Their transform blends wavelets with the linear canonical transform, a rotation of the time-frequency plane, and with Dunkl theory, which weights space by a reflection symmetry. Calderón's formula, the identity that rebuilds a function from its wavelet coefficients, is proved for this combined setting, anchoring the whole theory.

The authors then define a Sobolev-type space tied to the transform, equip it with a new inner product, and write its reproducing kernels explicitly. Extremal functions for both the wavelet and canonical Dunkl transforms are characterized through those kernels, with structural properties cataloged for later use.
arxiv-2505-11840:
Huan Li, Yiming Dong, and Zhouchen Lin prove a convergence rate for the AdamW optimizer in this 2025 paper. AdamW is the default training method for large language models. Its theory, though, lagged behind its practice. The proof measures progress with the L1 norm of the gradient, which suits high dimensional models.

The rate they prove matches the form of the best known rate for plain stochastic gradient descent. Experiments on real tasks support the key assumption behind the comparison. In those tasks the L1 norm grew with the square root of model dimension, as theory predicts. The result extends to a variant called NAdamW as well. Practitioners gain a firmer sense of how many steps training will need.
arxiv-2505-14840:
Gupta, Huang, Saha, Xu, and Ye present a paper from twenty twenty-five on faster attention sums in language models. Attention, the core step in transformer models, takes time that grows with the square of text length. Past work ties fast attention to tight limits on input size or heat settings. The team ask when fast attention works at any heat setting. They give the first sub-quadratic method for fixed small head size. Its run time grows only mildly with input size.

The method also covers the training gradient step at like speed. That extends the gain to full model training. Hardness results show big further gains are unlikely under standard guesses. For very large head sizes, the standard method is already optimal, they prove.
arxiv-2505-16140:
Joseph Pollard and Richard Morris catalogue the textures that form inside droplets of twist-bend nematic liquid crystal, in a two thousand twenty-five soft matter paper. These bent-core materials prefer local bend, which the texture accommodates through twist.

Confinement in a spherical droplet with radial anchoring intensifies the frustration. Combining simulations with topological and geometric analysis, the authors vary the molecular cone angle and the ratio of pitch length to droplet radius. The droplets host layered states, defect constellations, and Hopfions, echoing cholesteric droplets. Yet the structures differ geometrically in clear ways, partly because twist-bend nematics lack chirality.
arxiv-2505-17740:
Martínez-Peña and Orús tested in twenty twenty-five a tensor net tool to guess wild time series that shift in a chaotic way. Such series are hard to call, and pool tools that use a fixed bank of states need much hand tuning. A newer pool form cuts tuning but its parts blow up as terms grow.

Tensor nets split large tables into small parts, which curbs that blow-up. Their tool kept that gain while it guessed the wild series. It beat a classic pool tool on truth and on cost in their tests. The work links two fields that can aid each other.
arxiv-2505-18540:
Peter Lichard wrote this physics paper, published in 2025. It shows that a hidden particle state, sitting just below the energy needed to appear directly, leaves a measurable fingerprint on collisions between electrons and positrons that produce pairs of D mesons.

The state in question is the psi(2S), a bound form of charm quarks. Even though the collision energy cannot create it outright in these channels, its presence bends the rate at which D meson pairs emerge. The author fit merged data from two BES experiments in China to extract the production rates. Adding the hidden state improved the fit sharply, at a strong level of statistical confidence. The final fit, with the hidden state plus seven known resonances, matched the data very well. The result sharpens the picture of how charm particles form in collisions.
arxiv-2505-21740:
Marvin Limpijankit, Yanda Chen, Melanie Subbiah, Nicholas Deas, and Kathleen McKeown test whether AI explanations actually explain in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Language models are unpredictable: small prompt changes can swing outputs. A good explanation should let a user predict what the model would do on related counterfactual inputs, a property called counterfactual simulatability. It had been studied only for yes-or-no questions. The authors extend the evaluation framework to generation tasks.

Two case studies anchor the work: news summarization and medical suggestion. In summarization, explanations did help users predict the model's counterfactual outputs. In medical suggestion, there was significant room for improvement. The pattern suggests simulatability evaluation suits skill-based tasks better than knowledge-based ones, where the model's hidden information, not its reasoning, drives outputs. The framework gives explanation researchers a sharper tool for high-stakes settings.
arxiv-2505-24340:
Gilles Quentin Hacheme and five co-authors present GeoVision Labeler in two thousand twenty-five. The tool classifies satellite images with no task training at all. Such labels feed disaster response and land use checks. Tagged data are scarce in many regions that need them.

A vision language model first writes rich prose about each image. A plain language model then maps that prose to user set classes. For hard multi class tasks, a recursive grouping step builds meta classes. Scores were strong on a binary building task. Multi class scores stayed competitive on two known sets. Code is shared in the open for real world use.
arxiv-2506-03040:
Hari Padma and a large team of co-authors freeze a light-driven state in twenty twenty-five. Shining light on quantum materials creates striking new properties. The catch is that these states usually die within picoseconds. Practical use demands states that last.

The material is a cuprate ladder compound, a model system for copper-oxide physics. Using femtosecond resonant X-ray scattering and spectroscopy, the team finds an electronically metastable state that persists. Its longevity is protected by symmetry, not by slow relaxation. That protection is the design principle the title advertises. Strategies like this could turn fleeting photo-induced phases into workable ones. Readers in condensed matter physics get a route from transient effects to durable light-written states.
arxiv-2506-03640:
Rubén Calvo, Carles Martorell, Adrián Roig, and Miguel Muñoz wrote a 2025 physics paper on a claim about the brain: that its activity sits near a critical point, a knife edge. Scaling marks in brain activity support the claim. But signals from outside the brain can fake those marks. The team asks how much of the near-critical look belongs to the brain itself.

They show, in toy neural networks and in pure mathematics, that skewed inputs and coarse time sampling bend the marks. A network far from the edge can look as if it sits on it. They then build a protective framework that strips those distortions out. Run on pooled brain data, the framework finds the resting brain just short of the edge, yet near it. The marks match a simple recurrent network model well, which supports an internal source for the near-critical activity.
arxiv-2506-04440:
Attila Varga and four co-authors pin down the age of one of the youngest known planets and the harsh light falling on it. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. The planet TOI 1227b crosses a mid-M dwarf star. New X-ray images came from the Chandra telescope. Optical spectra measured lithium and hydrogen lines. Several methods then triangulated the star's age.

The age lands between five and twelve million years, near eight. That youth makes the planet a rare laboratory. X-ray brightness feeds models of the planet's air. The models show rapid atmospheric loss happening now. Gas streams away at a high rate each second. Young planets may shed their birth envelopes before our eyes.
arxiv-2506-05640:
Mia and Amini built a shared word model trainer in twenty twenty-five that guards firm data while many sites fine-tune one model. Shared training keeps data at home, but stray reads can leak it. Plain noise guards cost model skill, so they sought a leaner shield.

Their frame prunes weak links and locks the key tune facts with full code math. Small tune blocks cut both compute and talk loads for small sites. On two model sizes and four data sets it beat past frames on joint skill and speed. Cross-firm use looks in reach, they argue.
arxiv-2506-05740:
Yu-Chen Dai and co-authors propose FIST, a framework for modeling fraud incidents, in this 2025 paper. Fraud methods change fast and blend technical tricks with social engineering. A shared structure would help teams detect fraud and share threat reports. FIST draws on two known frameworks for attacks and influence campaigns.

The framework breaks each fraud case into stages and maps the techniques used at each stage. It covers both technical paths and psychological manipulation. Cases are stored in a reusable knowledge base written in a common language. That supports automated detection, risk scoring, and standard reporting. Real world case studies test the framework. The authors aim to bridge work in security, criminology, and behavioral science.
arxiv-2506-06140:
Plastovets and Piazza predicted cavity control of superconductors in this paper from twenty twenty-five. Trapping light in a cavity makes it interact more strongly with a solid inside. The authors argue this can tune a key superconductor property: the stiffness of its order parameter. Stiffness sets how far magnetic fields penetrate and how coherent the pairs are.

The mechanism runs through the pairs themselves. Cavity photons mediate a repulsion between the electrons in a pair, raising the pair's effective mass. Heavier pairs mean a softer, more tunable condensate. The effect should appear in standard superconductors, strongest in low-temperature ones. Infrared cavities make the predicted shift sizable. Cavity length becomes a knob for quantum material design.
arxiv-2506-09340:
Li and co-authors improve how large language models learn from rewards. A common method, GRPO, scores each prompt with fresh on-policy samples only. That makes training costly and wastes past data. The new method, RePO, pulls past samples from a replay buffer instead. Those old samples add range and depth to each update.

The team tested RePO on five models and seven math reasoning tests. Gains over GRPO reached 18.4 points for one model and 4.1 points for another. RePO cost about 15 percent more compute per run. In return it raised the count of useful update steps by 48 percent. Code for the method is posted in a public repository.
arxiv-2506-12640:
Olivier Isely and Alain Valette study special projections inside two-by-two matrix rings in two thousand twenty-five. The setting is an algebra of functions on a compact space times a circle, read as a crossed product. Rieffel projections are classic test objects in that area of operator algebra.

The authors pin down what those projections look like in the two-by-two case and track their image under a boundary map between K-theory groups. They build a new projection on the two-torus that differs from a known one and uses only trig polynomials plus one square root term. Uses include plain generators for the K-theory of the three-torus, plus a broad claim about subalgebras of torus functions.
arxiv-2506-16740:
Ivan Podvigin studies how fast long-run averages settle down for systems that evolve under shifts in several directions at once. The averages are taken over a strictly convex region, a rounded shape with no flat sides, that grows with time. Writing in twenty twenty-five, he proves a spectral test that decides when the settling speed is uniform across a natural class of observables. The test is stated in terms of the system spectrum, the fingerprint of its oscillations.

A classical result of Hertz on how the Fourier transform of such a region decays then implies a striking simplification: the convergence rate does not depend on the exact rounded shape chosen. Any strictly convex averaging region gives the same speed. The note is short and will interest specialists in ergodic theory, the math of long-term statistical behavior.
arxiv-2506-19440:
Noa Keshet, Ehud Behar, and Jon Miller measure elemental abundances in outflows from X-ray binaries, in a two thousand twenty-five astrophysics paper. The outflowing gas reveals what material falls onto a black hole or neutron star, which cannot be observed directly.

Using the Chandra grating spectrometer, the team studied four low-mass X-ray binaries. They compared two methods: fitting line series of individual ions to reconstruct the absorption measure distribution, and global fits with one or two ionization components. All outflows favor high ionization and show non-solar abundances. A tentative rise in abundance with atomic number resembles some core-collapse supernova models, though none matches exactly.
arxiv-2506-19640:
Niccolò Fontana and six co-authors sense electric fields, in a 2025 preprint, with a flash-born spin state inside an organic molecule. Molecular spins can be tuned by chemistry, which suits sensor design. Electric fields, though, usually grip spins too weakly to read. Heavy atoms grip harder but shorten the spin's memory. The team's molecule, ACRSA, forms a charge-transfer triplet state when lit. That state couples to electric fields without any heavy atom. Pulses of field are woven into a standard echo sequence to read the coupling.

The measured coupling strength matches systems that rely on strong atomic effects. The sensor also reports the field's direction, not just its size. Coherent control of the triplet is shown directly. The authors present organic triplets as a versatile, directional route to electric-field sensing. Chemical tuning could tailor them for settings from materials labs to device testing.
arxiv-2506-20540:
Rachid Ouyed, a solo author, presents a study from twenty twenty-five on bright, fast blue flashes in the sky and the odd flares of one such event. The event, nicknamed the Tasmanian Devil, threw off sharp optical flares. Ouyed ties this class of flashes to a heavy neutron star that turns, late, into a hybrid star with a quark core. The shift breeds a huge magnetic field.

Blown off outer layers form a shell that the new star's spin down lights up. Clumps in the shell turn clear in steps and let stored light burst out as flares. X-rays slip through gaps in the shell, and radio comes from the shell's clash with its surrounds. The frame fits four known events of the class.
arxiv-2506-21240:
Elie Saad and six co-authors forecast when electronic parts will go obsolete, using models that need no task examples. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Rail networks, backed by SNCF Réseau funding, depend on countless components. A discontinued part can threaten safety and uptime. Reliable risk data is scarce, though.
