Prediction must lean on general knowledge.

Zero-shot learning with large language models fills the data gap. Domain knowledge is drawn from tabular records. Two real-world datasets test the method. Four language models are compared head to head. The right model choice matters greatly for accuracy. Maintenance planners gain an early warning where none existed.
arxiv-2506-22440:
Sharique Hasan, Alexander Oettl, and Sampsa Samila argue that generative AI moves complexity around firms rather than erasing it in two thousand twenty-five. Their frame, GAS, weighs three traits of any tool: how general it is, how accurate, and how simple. Old tools forced a pick of two.

Large language models seem to offer all three, but the ease sits only at the surface. Underneath, the hard parts shift to infrastructure, compliance checks, and scarce expert staff. So the trade-off relocates from user to firm. Winning, they contend, will hinge on managing that moved complexity: clean abstraction layers, aligned workflows, and the right human complements. Adoption alone confers no edge.
arxiv-2506-23040:
Samuel Weisenthal examines medical decisions and chatbots in twenty twenty-five. Large language models might aid medical decision making, but how far that aid reaches is open. He starts with the treatment problem, the core choice a patient makes with a clinician. That problem can be approached with trial data or with observational data, under evidence-based medicine.

He then defines the chat problem and shows how it differs. Imitation sits at the heart of the gap: copying past answers cannot by itself solve a true treatment problem. Still, imitation can be useful. Weisenthal next asks how a language model system could be trained for treatment choices. The deep challenges, he argues, are the ethics of experimentation and the assumptions behind observation.
arxiv-2506-23140: Rapoport, Desjacques, Behar, and Sheth study how glowing galaxies relate to the cosmic web in twenty twenty-five. Future surveys will target galaxies emitting hydrogen alpha light to test cosmology. Using a large simulation, the team links galaxy brightness to web features like filaments and knots. The brightest emitters sit mostly in filaments and knots. Emitters cluster more strongly where the web is stretched one way. Links to galaxy traits are weak but real for smaller halos. The authors argue web shape, not density, should inform future survey analysis.
arxiv-2506-23440:
Bhosale and a large team present a study from twenty twenty-five on synthesizing tissue microscopy images from text and masks. Fake but faithful images can ease data scarcity caused by privacy limits. Text reports give high-level meaning; masks give fine spatial layout. Public sets lack both for the same images, blocking joint use. Their diffusion framework learns from unpaired text and mask data. It merges both signals into one conditioning space. Output images gain in fidelity and match their prompts better.

Downstream tasks like cell nucleus sorting improve with the fake data. Tests show gains over prior synthesis methods. The authors stress control over both structure and context. The work targets training data for pathology tools.
arxiv-2507-05340:
Christian Jespersen, Adam Carnall, and Christopher Lovell ask if the zone near a star group can clear up a puzzle. The puzzle is huge star groups that quit star birth at a young age. Such groups at red shifts three to five look too huge and too still for stock birth models. The team notes that all of them sit in thick clumps of more groups.

They change a code for top end stats to count clump of groups. The read of each group is set on the zone it sits in. With that change, the huge still group set no more strains plain birth models in a grave way. The team puts out the changed code. Their point frames a seeming crunch as in part a pick effect of thick zones.
arxiv-2507-05740:
Yujia Hu and co-workers dumped a text model's factual memory into a browsable knowledge base in a 2025 demonstration paper. What a model knows is locked inside its weights, hard to browse or count. Their GPTKB method recursively prompts a model to materialize its knowledge as linked facts. This release applies it to a recent flagship model at a cost in the low tens of thousands of dollars.

The result holds about a hundred million triples, densely cross-linked. Three uses are showcased: wandering the links to explore what the model knows. Querying it with a structured query language, and comparing strengths and blind spots across topics. The base doubles as a tool for auditing model knowledge and for cheap knowledge base building.
arxiv-2507-07040:
Pedro Freitas and Roméo Leylekian address, in twenty twenty-five, extremal problems for clamped plates under tension, a shape optimization question in spectral theory. They study an operator that mixes bending and tension, with the plate fixed at its edge. Two problems are posed under a fixed volume: minimize the first eigenvalue, a resonance measure, and maximize torsional rigidity, the resistance to twisting. They prove a Szegő-type inequality: among domains whose first vibration mode keeps one sign, the ball gives the lowest first eigenvalue.

They also prove a Saint-Venant-type bound: the ball gives the sharp maximum of torsional rigidity. Further properties of these operators are presented. They state the optimality condition tied to minimizing the first eigenvalue.
arxiv-2507-08240:
Seoik Jung and Taekyung Song test whether a crowd-counting framework can count cars instead. The framework, CLIP-EBC, was built to tally people in dense scenes from density maps. Cars in parking lots pose a similar counting problem. The team applies the method to CARPK, a standard aerial set of parking lot images.

Their model reached the second-best score among existing methods on the set. That result shows the crowd tool transfers well to vehicles. The authors then go a step further, from counting to locating. A weighted clustering method reads the predicted density map and marks each car's position. The peaks of the map guide where clusters form. The paper argues one framework can serve both counting and localization in overhead scenes.
arxiv-2507-08940:
Duarte Muñoz Santos and co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on finding the dark matter halos that host distant galaxies by the dips they leave in quasar light. Light from a distant bright quasar passes gas on its way to us. Where the gas is thick, it absorbs the light and leaves a dip. Earlier work showed that the strong dips flag real galaxies.

The team made millions of synthetic light readings from a large cosmos simulation, at two past ages of the universe. Up to two of three strong dips sat inside true halos. The stronger the dip and the later its age, the more certain the host halo. They recovered an average halo mass matching observations. They then let large dips absorb small ones, in a ranked framework. The halo mass readings grew narrower. The paper is the first of a series on this hunt.
arxiv-2507-09140:
Chuang Chen and colleagues published a computer science paper in 2025 on software that guides anime drawing. Anime art has fine detail and strict style rules. Beginners often struggle to reach a polished result. The authors built a system that coaches the drawing as it happens.

A fast diffusion pipeline powers the real-time help. The team fine-tuned an image model to render anime pictures from sketches and prompts. A second model turns those pictures back into rough sketches. A custom step then cleans them into structured guidance lines. The guidance stays aligned with the user's own intent. A user study tested both performance and interface comfort. Users could refine work faster with the live guide.
arxiv-2507-09540:
Ali Safa, Farida Mohsen, and Ali Al-Zawqari present a training method in two thousand twenty-five for spiking neural networks that control moving agents. Spiking networks mimic brain-style pulses and sip energy, which suits real-time control. Their pulses cannot be trained by the usual gradient route, since spikes are not smooth signals.

The team instead borrows a sampling method from Bayesian statistics. It proposes small changes to the network and keeps them with a probability tied to the reward the agent earns. Learning thus optimizes reward directly and can run on brain-like hardware. On two classic control tasks, a pole balancer and a two-link arm, the method beat deep Q-learning baselines and earlier spiking approaches while using fewer resources and episodes.
arxiv-2507-09840:
Nils Krah and co-authors describe the inner build of GATE 10, a rebuilt simulator for particle and radiation travel in medical physics, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Part two of the report covers structure and new tricks, while part one covers user features. A Python front end replaces old fixed input files.

The design splits sources, shapes, physics, and data capture into clean modules split across two code tongues. Time-aware particle birth supports scans and timed therapy systems. Complex physics settings hide behind a simple face, and scoring covers dose quality traits. Multi-thread runs and links to outside tools, like AI source models, are built in. Readers get the how behind a major upgrade.
arxiv-2507-10740:
Maziar Kanani, Seán O'Leary, and James McDermott present, in twenty twenty-five, a rule-based system that creates new tunes by varying old ones in a meaningful way. They parse each tune to find its Pathway Assembly, a structure that captures all repetitions in the tune. A classic algorithm, Sequitur, extracts that structure as a grammar. Mutations then act on the grammar, not on the tune directly. Nineteen mutation types exist, such as adding, removing, swapping, or reversing grammar parts.

One mutation is picked at random per step. Expanding the mutated grammar yields a new tune related to the original. The team tracks how tunes drift over many mutations, using edit distance, structural complexity, and length. They also size each mutation type's effect. The study uses Irish traditional tunes and varies pitch only.
arxiv-2507-13140:
Ding, Guo, Yang, and Guo present a study from twenty twenty-five on a multi-agent framework for AI in sixth-generation radio networks. Such networks must turn user intents into detailed radio settings. That gap between intent and settings is hard to bridge. Their framework splits work between representation agents and an intent agent. Representation agents expose tunable knobs like rank and bit depth. Those knobs trade signal quality against data rate openly. The intent agent uses a language model to plan bandwidth in two stages.

Tests show the framework serves over a third more users than a rival system. The gain holds under equal quality constraints. The authors say intent-driven planning allocates resources more efficiently. The design targets future AI-native radio access networks.
arxiv-2507-14040:
Manuel Santos Gutiérrez, Niccolò Zagli, and Giulia Carigi study how to push a random process toward a desired response in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Many systems, from fluids to markets, are modeled as Markov chains that hop between states. A key question is which outside push yields the largest change in a chosen measure. The authors connect perturbation theory for Markov matrices with linear response theory from physics.

From that link they derive fast linear algorithms. The targets include entropy, a divergence measure, and entropy production. They test the methods on chain models of flows, both settled and driven out of equilibrium. The tools could help steer systems with minimal force. Applied mathematicians and statistical physicists are the audience.
arxiv-2507-15940:
Dimple and a very large team of co-authors dissect one gamma-ray burst in twenty twenty-five. The burst, GRB 241105A, is a test case for classification. Bursts are split into classes tied to their progenitor systems. Borderline events challenge that scheme and reveal its assumptions.

The team also uses the burst to probe rapid r-process nucleosynthesis channels. The r-process forges heavy elements in extreme neutron-rich events. Which cosmic sites host it remains a central question. A well-observed burst with rich follow-up data can discriminate between channels. Dozens of telescopes and authors contributed observations. Readers get a single event used as a lever on two problems: how bursts are sorted, and where the heaviest elements are made.
arxiv-2507-16140:
Maria Carolina Volpato and four co-authors study a thin material for use in light based neural networks, in a 2025 paper. The material absorbs more light as the light grows stronger up to a point, then levels off. That response can serve as the nonlinear step a neural network needs, built into a chip waveguide.

The team placed a single layer of the material on a silicon nitride waveguide and measured how it handled light. Their model, based on how charge carriers behave, matched the measurements well. Up to twenty percent of the light coupled into the layer, and the leveling off occurred at very low power. The results suggest the material suits low power photonic computing.
arxiv-2507-16640:
Marques Alves, Kangming Chen, and Ellen Fukuda add momentum to a method for two-level inequality problems in two thousand twenty-five. In such problems, the allowed set is itself the answer to another inequality problem. Projecting onto that set is costly, which blocks standard methods.

Their method works on a simpler set and adds a smoothing term, building on a recent extragradient scheme. The new variant adds inertia through look-ahead steps, which often speeds such methods up. The team proves bounds on the step count for both fixed and shrinking smoothing. Results improve further when the problem is strongly monotone. Early numeric tests show how the method behaves in practice.
arxiv-2507-17940:
Timothy Wilson, Owen Rackham, and Hendrik Ulbricht test a sensitive way to detect DNA strands in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Tiny silica particles are held floating by a laser beam in a vacuum. Each particle vibrates like a tiny oscillator, and its motion can be read with great precision.

The particles were coated to carry short single strands of two DNA building blocks. The team compared coated and plain particles by their motion spectra. Peak shapes differed between the groups in ways a theory model can explain. Pattern tools and a forest model also separated the groups. Electron microscope images, by contrast, showed no visible difference between particle types.
arxiv-2507-18940:
Jingxuan Wei and a team of co-authors taught a vision model to translate in many tongues at low cost. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with multimodal translation, where a picture clears a text's fog. Two tongue work is strong. Many tongue work fights cross tongue bleed and weak sharing plans. Their frame, LLaVA-NeuMT, splits tongue own traits from tongue free ones.

A layer pick step finds the layers that count most for each tongue pair. A neuron step then wakes just the units a tongue needs. Readers in machine translation get a lean path to many tongue work with sight in the loop.
arxiv-2507-21940:
Néstor Jara and Claudio Gallegos wrote a mathematics paper in 2025 on the interplay between dichotomy, bounded growth, and spectral properties in systems that change over time. Some nonautonomous linear systems split their states into parts that decay and parts that grow. That split, and the spectrum that describes it, changes when a different growth rate is used to measure the system.

The authors introduce comparison criteria for growth rates. They show that faster growth rates compress the dichotomy spectrum, while slower growth rates expand it. They also define equivalence relations that group growth rates behaving alike. For a given system, they prove, there is at most one equivalence class of growth rates under which both bounded growth and dichotomy hold at once. That result leads to a classification of dichotomy spectra. The findings are valid in both discrete time and continuous time settings.
arxiv-2507-23140:
JungHo Lee, Valerio Bacak, and Edward Kennedy study estimation of mixing distributions in a 2025 statistics study. Many data sets mix trials with different success chances, and recovering the spread of those chances is a classic problem. Earlier work mostly assumed every trial was alike, or handled only rough distributions, which gave slow accuracy gains.

The authors allow trials to differ and assume the underlying density is smooth. Under those conditions a kernel density estimator reaches faster error rates tied to an average of trial sizes. Even in the older uniform case their rate beats the best known result. They also estimate differences between two densities.
arxiv-2508-04040:
Seisho Abe benchmarks NucDeEx, an open-source generator that simulates how excited atomic nuclei cool down. The work appeared in twenty twenty-five. Neutrino experiments count neutrons to sharpen their searches, and nuclei shedding energy is a major source of those neutrons.

Abe updated the treatment of low-lying discrete energy states so the generator matches measured data better. Head-to-head tests against rival generators and experiments check the physics. The package plugs into NEUT, the neutrino event generator, and into Geant4, the general particle toolkit. Accurate deexcitation forecasts feed straight into sensitivity estimates for rare-event hunts. The release invites the whole community to use and test the same tool.
arxiv-2508-06440:
Suthar and a large team use light scattering to read a density wave in a trilayer nickel oxide in twenty twenty-five. The material superconducts at high temperature while charge and spin waves run through it. Which atomic orbitals drive those waves was unclear. Polarized Raman scattering watched its vibrations and electron response across the wave onset.

Below the transition, phonons shifted and a gap like dip opened in the electron signal. A peak marked the wave's energy scale. Model fits demanded both nickel orbitals plus their mixing to match the peak. Single orbital views fell short. The wave is thus a shared, multi orbital affair, the team finds.
arxiv-2508-10840:
Tajamul Ashraf and Iqra Altaf Gillani extend a transformer-based method for learning across many private data owners. Their paper came out in two thousand twenty-five. Federated learning trains one model from data that never leaves each client. Clients differ, so one fixed model fits them poorly. Their earlier system, TransFed, used a hypernetwork to craft a personal layer for each client.

The new version, AdaptFED, sharpens that personal touch. Task-aware client embeddings steer how each layer adapts. The authors also prove tighter bounds on how well adaptation can do. Tests widen to time-series and multilingual data, not just images. A low-rank variant cuts traffic between server and clients. The work aims at federated systems that generalize to new clients.
arxiv-2508-11740:
Yuval Frid and co-authors present a method from two thousand twenty-five for modeling smooth backgrounds in high energy physics. Knowing the background lets physicists spot a real signal in their data. The usual approach fits a chosen formula shape, which can bake in wrong assumptions about the curve.

Their method instead uses a log Gaussian Cox process, which treats event counts as drawn from a varying random intensity. That intensity itself comes from a smooth random function, so the shape is learned rather than imposed. A sampling method called Markov chain Monte Carlo tunes the settings and draws the final background estimate with its uncertainty. Tests on synthetic data compare the new method against standard formula fits.
arxiv-2508-12040:
Jinyi Han and ten co-authors build FineCE, in a 2025 preprint, a method that scores a language model's confidence while it is still writing. Models are notoriously overconfident, blessing wrong answers with high scores. Coarse end-of-answer scores come too late to steer anything. FineCE scores partial text at points during generation. The team first built training data that captures how a model's answers spread over possibilities. A scorer is then trained to judge any text span. A trick called Backward Confidence Integration sharpens each score using the text that follows it.

The authors also study where in the stream scoring pays off most. Across several benchmarks, FineCE beat classic confidence methods. Scores stay continuous and fine-grained rather than jumping in steps. The authors pitch the tool for systems that must decide, mid-answer, whether to trust, branch, or stop. All code and baselines are released.
arxiv-2508-12140:
Bi and a large team of co-authors measured thinking budgets in medical AI for this study from twenty twenty-five. Reasoning models can spend more tokens thinking before they answer. In medicine, that extra thought costs time and money, so its value needs mapping. The team tested two model families across fifteen medical datasets.

Budgets ran from zero to unlimited, and model sizes spanned a wide range. Accuracy rose in a steady logarithmic pattern with both budget and size. Three zones emerged: a fast zone, a balanced zone, and a costly high-accuracy zone. Small models gained the most from extra thought. Brain and gut topics needed deeper reasoning than heart or lung topics. The authors frame budgets as a dial for clinical use.
arxiv-2508-16340:
Arjmandi-Tash and four co-authors stiffen graphene cantilevers by wrinkling the sheet, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Atomic cantilevers offer ultimate sensitivity, but monolayer graphene bends too easily for stability. Wrinkles sculpted into suspended membranes change that balance. Nanoindentation and resonance tests confirm large stiffness gains.

Both in-plane and out-of-plane stiffness rise by orders of magnitude. Bending rigidity now dominates behavior that tension once ruled. Shaped cantilevers reach bending rigidities in the million electron-volt range. Mass stays at femtogram scale despite the reinforcement. Vibrational response shifts strongly with the added rigidity. The method opens new paths for nanomechanical sensing devices.
arxiv-2508-17540:
Szablewski and Masiak wrote in twenty twenty-five about tracing how features move inside transformer language models. Inside these models, a residual stream carries information between layers. Dictionary methods can locate features in that stream. Patching methods can reveal circuits that compute answers. How features travel along the stream was less studied, though. The authors propose linear maps, called Activation Transport Operators, between layers. They judge those maps in feature space using learned decoders.

Their operators can tell whether a feature was carried forward linearly. They can also spot features newly built by nonlinear computation. A transport efficiency score bounds how much of the stream moves linearly. Tests measured that share across layers in practice. The method is cheap, needing no retraining. It offers tools for safety checks and debugging of models.
arxiv-2508-18440:
Nieradzik presents in twenty twenty-five a small, fast model for finding the pitch of a single note or voice in sound. Getting pitch right in noisy sound, on weak devices, is still hard. Older strong models are large and slow, which limits their use in live tools.

His model was trained on speech, music, and made-up sound with heavy added noise and distortion. It beat a well-known rival by a wide margin in noisy tests and lost little accuracy as noise rose. It also runs many times faster while using far fewer settings. He adds a made-up speech dataset with exact pitch tracks, plus an open test suite, so others can train and compare fairly.
arxiv-2508-18640:
Aniket Nuthalapati, Nicholas Hinds, Brian Y Lim, and Qianwen Wang add a reverse step to how users read AI explanations. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. In high-stakes work, users must grasp why a model acts as it does. Explanations are given, but users often fail to reason well with them, so they can neither check nor learn from the model.

Their plan takes a user's own free-word read of a chart and turns it back into marks on that chart. A large model pulls set claims from the words, and linked views place them in view. The loop is meant to slow users down and make them weigh the proof. A test build and user views show the route.
arxiv-2508-19640:
Elly Hung and Yi Yu set the price of privacy for survival analysis across institutions in a 2025 stats paper. Hospitals holding separate patient cohorts want joint Cox regression, a standard survival model, without pooling records. Federated change-based privacy formalizes the protection each site must give. The authors tackle two targets, regression coefficients and cumulative hazard curves, while sites differ in sample size and privacy budget.

Matching lower and upper bounds, tight up to logarithmic factors, reveal sharp phase transitions where privacy starts to cost accuracy. Fast methods adapt private binary trees and gradient descent to the model's dependent estimating math rules. Companion results cover usual test hazards, survival curves, and a relaxed label-only privacy notion, with software put out.
arxiv-2508-19740:
Wenhao Li and six co-authors trim the memory of language models in twenty twenty-five. The key-value cache is a heavy burden during generation. Selecting only the critical cache entries at decoding time keeps quality while cutting cost. Existing selection uses random linear hashing to find important tokens.

That hashing is inefficient, they argue, because queries and keys sit in two narrow cones. Their method, Spotlight Attention, uses nonlinear hashing instead. It reshapes the embedding distribution for better coding efficiency and robustness. A light training framework uses a ranking-based loss from the Bradley-Terry model. It trains on a modest GPU in eight hours. Experiments show much better retrieval precision and shorter times. Readers get faster generation with a smarter cache.
arxiv-2508-20840:
Qiao Sun and a large team propose a leaner way in 2025 for robots to learn a model of the world. Video-based world models let robots imagine the results of their actions, but training them needs huge amounts of robot data that are hard to gather. The team noticed that robot motions, though varied, rest on a small set of basic moves.

Their models, called PEWM, generate only short clips of one basic move at a time. Short clips align words with actions more finely and train faster. A vision-language planner then chains the moves into long tasks, guided by start and goal markers. The authors say this split supports flexible control and new combinations of learned moves.
arxiv-2509-00040:
Chengkai Dai, Tao Liu, Dezhao Guo, Binzhi Sun, Guoxin Fang, Yeung Yam, and Charlie C. L. Wang present a curve-based slicer for multi-axis light printing in 2025. In digital light processing, a part is built layer by layer with light. Flat fixed layers cause large overhangs and stair-like steps on slanted faces, which mar the finish.

Curves define both the layers and the split of the model, through their tangent planes. Those same curves set the path of the build platform, which can tilt on many axes. The curves are tuned to avoid collisions and to deposit with no floating parts. Tests on a robotic printer show smooth, high-quality builds of complex shapes. Tilted layers keep the speed and detail that make light printing prized.
arxiv-2509-00140:
Songhui Yue, working alone, sets out a workflow in 2025 to build ontologies from software engineering standards with language model help. Ontologies map a field's terms and links for clear machine reasoning. Standards are long, noisy texts full of domain terms, so building such maps by hand is slow.

Relation triple extraction pulls subject-link-object facts from text and forms the first stage, next to term extraction. The workflow splits documents, mines candidate terms, uses a language model to infer relations, normalizes terms, and aligns facts across sections. Expert-labeled reference sets at three levels of detail score the output. The open-source route aims to scale ontology building for standards work.
arxiv-2509-00340:
Abdullah Zayat, Omran Abbas, Loic Markley, and Anas Chaaban propose a complex-valued neural network in 2025 to configure stacked intelligent surfaces for next-generation antennas. Such surfaces are layers of tunable elements that shape radio waves. Classic tuning sets each layer's phases apart or forces channel orthogonality, which narrows the designs reachable.

Each surface element becomes a unit-modulus complex neuron in an end-to-end differentiable pipeline. The model can chase varied goals, such as maximizing spectral efficiency or minimizing detection errors, in one frame. GPU auto-differentiation trains configurations for realistic, high-dimensional channels at speed. Near-online tuning of smart surfaces could follow from the approach.
arxiv-2509-00440:
Ibrahim Al-Hazwani, Ke Er Zhang, Laura Garrison, and Jürgen Bernard characterize Data Humanism for visualization research in 2025. Data Humanism is a human-centered design approach that stresses the personal, contextual, and imperfect nature of data. Its thirteen principles, set out in Giorgia Lupi's visual manifesto, stay loosely defined for research use, which opens a gap between practice and systematic study.

A mixed-methods approach joins a systematic literature review, multimedia analysis, and expert interviews. The result gives concrete definitions that keep interpretive flexibility for design choices. Direct consultation with Lupi validates the reading. The team then decodes a visualization work, mapping principles to specific visual choices, to show the framework at work.
arxiv-2509-00540:
Xiangyu Zhang and Mang Ye study a new attack on federated learning. In federated learning, many users train one shared model. They do not pool their private data. Uploaded updates cannot be checked at once. A bad user can thus poison the shared model. But older attacks also hurt the attacker's own model.

Zhang and Ye propose FedThief for a self-centered attacker. This attacker wants an edge, not just damage. FedThief uploads altered content to weaken the shared model. It then builds a private blend of models. The blend uses global updates plus local knowledge. A gap measure guides the blend. Tests show the attacker's model can end well ahead of the shared one.
arxiv-2509-00740:
Govind Waghmare, with three co-authors, Sumedh BG, Sonia Gupta, and Srikanta Bedathur, presents structured context injection for graph problems with large language models. Instead of fine-tuning, which is costly, they embed task-specific information systematically into the input to guide the model.

Some graph reasoning tasks stay hard unless mapped to conceptually grounded representations. Waghmare and his co-authors argue injected structure lets the model align a task with such spaces implicitly. They evaluate on multiple graph tasks with lightweight and large models, weighing accuracy against compute cost. Consistent improvements show structured input can rival or surpass more complex approaches, making it an effective, scalable strategy for graph understanding.
arxiv-2509-01040:
Jin Young Kim studies how a dense object with a strong magnetic field can bend light that passes near it. The work treats such objects as gravitational lenses, meaning their gravity bends light much like a glass lens. Kim focuses on light that moves near the photon sphere, a shell where light can orbit the object.

Kim works out the angle by which light bends in two forms of gravity theory. In one, the field comes from mass plus a magnetic dipole, a field with two poles. In the other, a nonlinear electric effect changes the path. Both results are stated as small shifts from the known Schwarzschild case, and Kim tests the numbers on a magnetar, a highly magnetic dead star.
arxiv-2509-01240:
New memory technology stores data in two-dimensional arrays, so codes must obey limits in every row and column, not just along a line. Viet Hai Le, with four co-authors, tackles bounded-weight codes, where each line may hold only a capped number of ones. Building good two-dimensional versions from known one-dimensional codes had been a challenge.

The team offers a universal framework that lifts a one-dimensional design into two dimensions while keeping the weight limit in all rows and columns of a given length. The bound they guarantee follows a stated function of that length. Le and the co-authors present the method as an efficient general solution, aimed at raising reliability in dense resistive memory systems where stray heavy lines cause errors.
arxiv-2509-01340:
A Peano continuum is a compact, connected space that can be drawn by a continuous curve, and such spaces can host surprisingly wild dynamics. Klara Karasova and Benjamin Vejnar prove that every Peano continuum admits a continuous map that is exactly Devaney chaotic. That means periodic points are dense, and any open patch, however small, spreads to cover the whole space in finitely many steps.

The result extends a 1991 theorem by Agronsky and Ceder. Karasova and Vejnar identify a broad class of these spaces, covering all one-dimensional continua and many well-behaved shapes, where small local changes to maps are possible. Inside that class they show exact chaotic systems are dense among chain transitive ones, mixing systems are generic there, and the shadowing trait is generic among all continuous systems.
arxiv-2509-01440:
New optimizers for training large language models appear often, each claiming faster training or fewer settings to tune, but differing test setups make claims hard to compare. Andrei Semenov, Matteo Pagliardini, and Martin Jaggi benchmark recent optimization methods under one standardized protocol for language model pretraining. They vary model size, batch size, and training duration in a systematic way.

Each method was tuned carefully before comparison, so the results reflect best use rather than lazy defaults. The study offers practitioners guidance on which optimizer suits which scenario, and flags promising directions for researchers. All code is released and every experiment is reproducible. Semenov and the co-authors aim to make future optimizer claims easier to test fairly, in a field where training runs are costly and protocol drift is common.
arxiv-2509-01540:
El Nino, the Pacific warming pattern that sways world weather, is widely treated as chaotic, with forecasts stated as probabilities rather than certainties. Lauri Jetsu applies a method called the Discrete Chi-square Method to El Nino time series, claiming it can detect several signals laid over an arbitrary trend. The method rests on the Gauss-Markov theorem, which makes least squares the best unbiased fit for linear models.

Jetsu reports that the method detects a multi-periodic large wave over the warming trend, read as solar forcing in the data. In this claimed reading, the Pacific Ocean acts like a measuring device for the solar dynamo's light curve in real time. Simulations are offered to support a window dimension effect, in which more or better data let the method see through time. These are the author's claims, presented as a challenge to the mainstream view.
arxiv-2509-01740:
Giacomo Bortolini leads twenty-five co-authors in a Webb telescope study of two small galaxies that are crashing into each other. The pair, NGC 4485 and NGC 4490, is the closest such dwarf pair known apart from the Magellanic Clouds. Near infrared color charts reveal stars of many ages in both galaxies. Young hot stars, helium burning stars, and old giant stars all appear.

Two bursts of star birth began at two distinct past times, matching a predicted close pass. A tidal bridge of stars links the smaller galaxy to the disk of the larger one. Gas stripped in the pass likely fed fresh star birth after mixing with local gas. The pair gives a near lab for how crashes reshape small galaxies.
arxiv-2509-01940:
Xin-Biao Xu leads eleven co-authors in lifting a mode symmetry in tiny light rings without magnets. Breaking time reversal symmetry, where forward and backward paths behave alike, is a core hurdle for chip scale photonics. Their rings are lithium niobate microresonators, loops that trap light in circling modes. Sound waves coupled to the light shift forward and backward modes by different amounts.

Simple microwave drive of built in transducers controls the split in real time. The split passes twice the mode width in tests, and it scales in a straight line with sound power. No mode conversion or complex structures are needed. The trick turns a specialist effect into a tunable function for optical isolation and related devices.
arxiv-2509-02240:
Jie Huang leads six co-authors in a style swap trick to lift finds from atomic force scans of tiny forms. Tips with a coat now image atomic form in fine depth on a surface. Sims make training shots at low cost, so models can read form and charge from shots. Real lab shots drift in fine ways from clean sims, which drops model skill.

Style swap pads sim shots to close that style gap with real shots. Checks on local form trait spreads prove the lift in finds from the swap. The way lifts scores with no tagged lab shots in the mix. Speed gains count where lab tags are slow and dear to make. The route fits more sim trained scope tools past this one case.
arxiv-2509-02340:
Salma Haidar and José Oramas present a 2025 remote sensing paper on shrinking hyperspectral images, which record light in hundreds of narrow colour bands. Extra bands add cost and redundancy, so picking the few that matter helps classification run faster.

Their idea uses explainability tools, which show why a trained classifier made its choices. Each band earns an influence score from deletion-insertion tests, where ranked bands are removed or restored while confidence changes are logged. Keeping only the top bands gave compact sets. With as few as thirty bands, classifiers matched or beat full-spectrum results on two public benchmarks. The chosen bands also lined up with physically meaningful wavelengths, which supports the method.
arxiv-2509-02440:
Marie Reinbigler and five co-authors wrote a 2025 biomedical computing paper on analysing gigapixel images, such as whole-slide tissue scans, without heavy machines. Full-resolution processing of every pixel wastes time on areas that hold no useful signal.

Their PyramidAI method starts at low resolution and zooms only into promising regions for detailed checks. Two strategies for balancing accuracy against computing cost were tested on the Camelyon16 cancer image set. The staged approach cut processed data by more than half while keeping detection accuracy on one computer. The team then spread work across twelve modest machines using a tuned distribution scheme. A job that once took over an hour finished within minutes, widening access to large-scale image analysis.
arxiv-2509-02540:
Halvin Yang, Sangarapillai Lambotharan, Mahsa Derakhshani, and Lajos Hanzo wrote a 2025 communications paper on networks that link space, air, ground, and sea platforms into one system. Fast-moving satellites and sea platforms make channel information go stale quickly, and link speeds differ wildly between optical and underwater acoustic channels.

The authors propose one large language model backbone, trained on radio, optical, and acoustic traces together, as a shared adaptation layer. A predictor forecasts the strongest channel components ahead of time, easing stale information. A semantic encoder compresses sensor data into task-focused tokens, cutting the signal strength needed for clear underwater image delivery. The paper closes with open problems in model compression, fidelity control, and trustworthy field deployment.
arxiv-2509-02640:
Biwen Meng, Xi Long, and Jingxin Liu present a 2025 computational pathology paper on classifying atypical mitotic figures, abnormal cell divisions that signal disease, for the MIDOG 2025 challenge. Odd shapes and scanner differences make the task unreliable.

The team adapted a pathology foundation model called UNI2 in three ways. Variants used low-rank tuning alone, visual prompt tuning with stain normalisation, and prompt tuning plus a domain-adversarial component with test-time stain augmentation. Stain handling clearly helped generalisation. The strongest version combined prompt tuning with two stain normalisation methods applied at test time. It reached high balanced accuracy and ranking scores on the preliminary leaderboard, placing among the top ten teams. Prompt-based adaptation plus stain care looks promising for varied imaging conditions.
arxiv-2509-02740:
Jonas Hirsch wrote a 2025 solo analysis paper. It gives the first example of an energy-minimising p-harmonic map with nonunique tangent maps. The singularity is isolated. Tangent maps are blown-up limits. They reveal a map's fine structure near a singular point.

Until now, nonuniqueness was known only for stationary maps. That is a weaker class. Hirsch constructs a target manifold with a special trait. For each allowed dimension and exponent range, some map into it minimises the p-energy. That map has an isolated singularity at the origin. It admits a whole continuum of distinct tangent maps there. The construction extends B. White's earlier stationary example for the quadratic case. Minimizers can act worse near singularities than theory once hoped.
arxiv-2509-03140:
Nadezhda Dobreva and 5 co-authors showed in 2025 that swarms of pivoting cubes can reshape themselves using only local information. Modular robots made of cubes that swing around shared edges could one day assemble structures in space. The open question is how little each cube needs to sense for the whole group to reach a target shape.

A shared plan picks which cube moves, but each cube's controller sees only its nearby neighbors. Training used reinforcement learning, where the network improves from trial and error. Even the most local versions reached target shapes, though wider awareness sped things up. Passing messages between neighbors several times let near-optimal results emerge from local views alone. Adding rotation and mirror symmetry to the network helped mainly by shrinking model size.
arxiv-2509-03240:
Harald Vilhelm Skat-Rørdam and 4 co-authors proposed a fairer score in 2025 for stress detectors that read wearable sensor data. Stress builds and fades gradually, yet human labels often mark it as a single instant. Judging a detector against such labels with standard scores can badly misstate how well it works.

Their window-based F1 metric gives credit when a detected event lands near the labeled one, within a tolerance window sized by domain knowledge. They tested it on three physiological datasets, two gathered in daily life and one in a lab. The tolerant scores revealed patterns that standard scores hid. Only those scores showed a forecasting model's predictions beating random and empty baselines by significant margins in the daily-life data. Metric choice, they argue, shapes what researchers conclude.
arxiv-2509-03340:
Fleur Hendriks and 4 co-authors used generative flow matching in 2025 to model systems that can settle into several stable states. At a bifurcation, a small change in conditions splits one outcome into many, often by breaking a symmetry. Ordinary machine learning models average those outcomes into one blur, missing the lower-symmetry states entirely.

Flow matching learns a full probability distribution over outcomes instead of a single prediction. The authors combine it with equivariant networks, whose structure respects the system's symmetries, and a coupling scheme that aligns predictions with targets under group actions. Tests ranged from toy systems to buckling beams and a classic phase-field equation. The method captured multimodal outcome distributions accurately and beat non-probabilistic and variational rivals. It offers a scalable route for high-dimensional multistable problems.
arxiv-2509-03540:
Shanglin Wu and three co-authors propose a 2025 framework for making large language models answer factual questions more accurately. Such models often produce answers that clash with facts, because they rely only on memory stored during training. Retrieval methods add outside knowledge, but usually as loose text that is hard to reason over.

Their approach builds a knowledge graph, a network of facts and links, while the model is answering. A seed graph is first drawn from the question itself, then expanded using the model's own knowledge. Outside retrieval then refines the graph, filling gaps and fixing errors. Across three factual question-answering benchmarks, accuracy improves consistently over baseline methods. The authors present graph building at answer time as structured, interpretable, and scalable.
arxiv-2509-03640:
Samuel Howie and two co-authors' 2025 research paper focuses on using machine vision to compress and interpret galaxy images. Understanding what features a model extracts from a galaxy photo can reveal how galaxy shapes are organised. Their data are mock three-band images drawn from the EAGLE cosmological simulation.

A variational autoencoder, a network that squeezes images into a compact code and rebuilds them, needs about 35 features to describe the images. Adding principal component analysis, which rotates those features into independent directions, cuts the useful set to roughly ten to twelve. That number captures nearly all the variance, and it shifts with galaxy type: disk-dominated systems need more features than bulge-dominated ones. Size dominates the top features, measured by the half-light radius. Later features track asymmetry, concentration, and light profile shape depending on morphology. Two-dimensional maps built with UMAP separate galaxy populations cleanly by type.
arxiv-2509-04040:
Clara E Leitgeb and five co-authors wrote a 2025 research paper on a stubborn background problem in gamma-ray astronomy. Ground telescopes detect faint light flashes made when particles strike Earth's air. Cosmic rays, which are fast charged particles from space, make look-alike flashes. Those false events form the main background the authors set out to pin down.

Only a small share of cosmic-ray collisions matter, the ones that create a high-energy neutral pion, a short-lived particle that feeds the flash. Collider detectors named LHCf and RHICf watch collisions at matching forward angles. Their current and future data can therefore test whether event models describe this background correctly.
arxiv-2509-04340:
Kristina L Kupferschmidt and two co-authors report why language models stumbled when helping therapists write clinical notes, in a 2025 case study paper. Their site was KidsAbility, a children's rehabilitation center in Ontario, Canada. Twenty clinicians tried two tools during pilot programs: a general commercial model, and a custom one tuned on the center's past documents. Documentation looks like simple paperwork, yet the study treats it as deeply social and organizational work.

Four themes emerged from the qualitative findings. Workflows differ widely between clinicians, and the burden comes from the whole system rather than any single note type. Clinicians wanted flexible tools and personal control. Success also needed mutual learning between staff and systems, plus training that respects clinical complexity.
arxiv-2509-04540:
Yan Yau Cheng, writing alone, proves an arithmetic version of a trace-path integral formula over function fields in a 2025 mathematics paper. In quantum field theory, path integrals over spaces of sections can collapse into a trace of a monodromy action, a bookkeeping of how things twist around a loop. Cheng builds the number-theoretic analogue. The path integral runs over the l-torsion of a Jacobian, an algebraic object attached to curves over finite fields.

The integral equals a Frobenius action trace taken on a Heisenberg group representation built from that same torsion data, with a sign the paper determines explicitly. Arithmetic geometry gains a bridge to quantum field theory ideas, with the sign pinned down rather than left ambiguous.
arxiv-2509-04640:
Finding near-shortest paths between all pairs of nodes in a weighted graph is the problem addressed by Liam Roditty and one co-author in a 2025 algorithms paper. Exact answers can be costly, so they study approximations that allow small additive or multiplicative error. Their results cover dense weighted undirected graphs.

For additive approximation, they give an algorithm matching a classic dense-graph runtime while handling weights. For nearly additive approximation, they improve an earlier error bound. For multiplicative approximation, they present a framework that speeds up a previous dense-graph method and generalises a recent near-two approximation, clarifying trade-offs between error and runtime.
arxiv-2509-05040:
A leading edge vortex is the swirling structure that boosts lift on flapping wings, yet describing it quantitatively is hard. Alejandro Gonzalo, lead author with two co-authors, propose a method for that description in a 2025 aerodynamics paper. Their approach works in stages on flow data around a flapping wing.

First, a standard criterion identifies vortical structures, with little sensitivity to threshold choice. A thinning algorithm then finds the vortex core, using local vorticity direction to separate it. Finally, flow quantities are averaged along the core. Applied to forward flight data, the method shows the vortex growing smoothly before splitting near mid-downstroke.
arxiv-2509-05140:
Flocks move in alignment while swarms do not, yet both hover near critical behaviour. Joao Lizárraga and one co-author present a model that unifies the two through aggregation in a 2025 paper on active matter. Individuals move in open space with differing self-propulsion speeds, and alignment appears as a byproduct of stable cohesion rather than a direct rule.

Errors in following the aggregation rules trigger velocity fluctuations. The system shows scale invariance rooted in the model's definition itself, which the authors call structural criticality. A striking regime also emerges where spatial and orientational coherence separate, giving varied polarisation at uniform density.
arxiv-2509-05440:
Software judges that give fixed scores can borrow strength from pairwise matching, Logan Lawrence, Ashton Williamson, and Alexander Shelton show in a 2025 paper on judging text. Language models increasingly rate summaries, dialogues, and stories, but pairwise methods cannot score a single text alone, which threshold decisions need.

Their direct-scoring method creates fake example texts at test time to serve as matching partners, turning pairwise judgements into fixed scores. On three meta-evaluation benchmarks it matched leading pairwise evaluators in correlation with human judgement, sometimes slightly ahead and sometimes slightly behind. The fake matching texts are released as data. The method keeps the ease of direct scores without giving up pairwise accuracy.
arxiv-2509-05540:
Language models are put to work writing tests for web APIs in a comparative study by Thiago Barradas, Aline Paes, and Vânia de Oliveira Neves in a 2025 software engineering paper. Testing REST APIs by hand is slow, and the combinations of inputs make exhaustive testing impossible.

Their approach, RestTSLLM, pairs a formal test specification language with language models guided by prompt design. An automated pipeline scores models on success rate, coverage, and mutation score, which measures how many planted faults the tests catch. Four models produced strong, coherent tests from API specifications. One commercial model led on every metric in this study. The findings support automating a tedious, error-prone part of development.
arxiv-2509-05840:
A scheme-theoretic interpretation of generalized splines is built in a 2025 paper by Kyle Stoltz. A spline is a piecewise polynomial rule glued along a graph; the generalized version joins classical splines with GKM theory, which studies spaces with torus symmetry. Stoltz shows these splines can be understood through scheme theory, the basic language of modern algebraic geometry.

The key step proves the spline ring over an edge-labeled graph equals the limit of a diagram built from that graph, built from that graph. That yields a local-global principle: global splines can be checked piece by piece. The paper then catalogs when spline modules are free or projective under various graph and ring conditions. An appendix checks borderline cases by computer, and a final section tracks how deleting or contracting graph edges changes the spectrum.
arxiv-2509-06240:
New flow measurements for quarkonia in heavy-ion collisions are reported in a 2025 proceedings paper by Chi Zhang for the ALICE collaboration. Quarkonia, bound heavy-quark pairs, are prime probes of quark-gluon plasma, and their azimuthal anisotropy reveals whether heavy quarks join the medium's collective motion. Zhang presents inclusive J/psi elliptic flow in lead-lead collisions from the LHC's Run 3.

Three analysis methods, event-plane, scalar-product, and multi-particle cumulants, are compared, with the cumulant route opening access to flow fluctuations at forward rapidity. New results for the heavier Upsilon(1S) at forward rapidity accompany them. Both are set against model calculations, giving direct evidence on heavy-quark thermalization in the plasma.
arxiv-2509-06340:
The boson peak, extra low-energy vibrations in every glass, may be a flat band in disguise, argue Shivam Mahajan and six co-authors in a 2025 paper. Amorphous solids show more low-frequency modes and heat capacity than Debye theory predicts, and the anomaly's origin has been debated for decades. The authors propose its defining feature is spectral weight piled into a narrow frequency window, barely dispersing with wavevector.

Re-reading published experiments and simulations through that lens, and adding their own two- and three-dimensional simulations, they find converging support. The peak then reflects a flat or weakly dispersive band rather than a propagating wave. The interpretation sharply narrows which theories of the boson peak can still be right.
arxiv-2509-06740:
Tissue regions and cell nuclei in pathology slides are segmented together, each task helping the other, by Qing Xu and two co-authors in a 2025 medical imaging paper. Analyzing tumor tissue and nuclei shapes guides cancer study, yet earlier methods handled the two tasks separately and missed how they inform each other.

Their framework, Co-Seg, introduces mutual prompting. A region-aware prompt encoder supplies high-quality hints about semantic regions and individual nuclei. A mutual prompt mask decoder then uses cross-guidance so both tasks keep consistent context while computing their masks. On the PUMA dataset, the system surpassed leading methods at semantic, instance, and panoptic segmentation of tumor tissue and nuclei alike. Code is released publicly. Working on both scales at once, the authors argue, gives a fuller picture of the tumor environment.
arxiv-2509-06840:
Heat damage to mirrors limits gravitational-wave detectors, and Liu Tao and two co-authors propose watching the mirrors' temperature to fix it in a 2025 instrumentation paper. At megawatt laser power, thermal distortions blur the test masses. New edge-heating correction techniques could cut the quantum noise floor tenfold in future detectors, but each actuator needs a precise error signal, which LIGO lacks today.

Thermal imaging of each mirror's surface supplies the missing signal. Temperature profiles map uniquely onto a finite-element model of the mirror, letting operators reconstruct the full thermal state and the wavefront error across the whole aperture in real time. The authors estimate a sizable sensitivity improvement for LIGO A+, extending the reach for neutron star mergers. The technique is also planned as integral to the forty-kilometer Cosmic Explorer observatory.
arxiv-2509-06940:
A core package of the Magma computer algebra system is rebuilt by Carlos Rito in a solo 2025 software paper. The LinearSystem package handles systems of linear conditions, workhorses in algebraic geometry work. Rito presents a full rewrite with large gains in design and speed.

The gains in efficiency enable computations that were out of reach before. Examples showcase what the new code can now do in practice. Rather than benchmarking speed against the old version, the paper advertises capability, walking through the design principles and methods. One core capability is added: computing linear systems of plane curves with set non-ordinary singularities. In that task, users name the unusual singular points the curves must pass through. For algebraic geometers who compute, the message is that old limits on problem size have moved.
arxiv-2509-07040:
Neeshu Rathi and Sanjeev Kumar propose a quantum bagging method whose base learners are unsupervised, in a 2025 paper. Quantum machine learning must cope with noisy hardware in the current era of intermediate-scale devices. Wrong labels in training data are a special problem, because supervised methods learn from those labels directly.

Their method clusters data with QMeans and uses that clustering as the base learner. Averaging over many resampled runs cuts prediction variance and makes the method harder to mislead with bad labels. Because QMeans needs no labels, it sidesteps much of the corruption. Sampling is done with quantum bootstrapping through QRAM, and the separate results are combined by majority vote. In broad tests on noisy classification and regression tasks, the method matched a classical KMeans version. It also held up better against label corruption than bagging built on supervised learners.
arxiv-2509-07240:
T. Das and 3 co-authors model how the optical behavior of calcium fluoride changes with heat in a 2025 paper. Calcium fluoride, also called fluorspar, is a crystal used in lenses and windows for special optics. Its response to light is set by one giant infrared peak that shifts strongly with temperature, plus a row of steady ultraviolet peaks.

The authors fit the infrared peak with a coupled-oscillator model improved by radiation reaction, using temperature-dependent values. A handy formula covers the ultraviolet peaks and matches first-principles computer calculations. The combined formula spans a wide range of light energies and temperatures, from room heat to 500 degrees Celsius. With it, they compute how atoms such as hydrogen and helium interact with a calcium fluoride surface. The big infrared peak delays one long-range force effect, a detail that matters for precision surface experiments.
arxiv-2509-07340:
Simulating molecules from quantum principles is accurate but slow, because each step needs a costly electronic calculation. Siu Wun Cheung and 3 co-authors offer a shortcut in a 2025 research paper. Their model order reduction method learns a compact picture of the electronic solution space. It then finds the ground state density, the lowest-energy electron arrangement, inside that smaller space.

By skipping the full iterative search over electron wavefunctions, the method cuts computing cost sharply. The team tests it on a water molecule. Results match high-fidelity simulations closely for both molecular shape and dynamic behavior. Careful parametrization and systematic sampling help the reduced model stay accurate beyond its training cases. Faster quantum dynamics could widen studies of reactions and materials that are now too expensive to simulate.
arxiv-2509-07840:
Patrick Kreidl asks how a controller should steer its own sensors when the world can only be seen through noisy measurements, in a solo 2025 paper on control theory. Cheap, small, wireless sensors now form networks that managers can actively direct. The catch is that the true state of the environment is never directly visible.

Kreidl frames sensor management inside multi-stage stochastic control, where decisions unfold step by step under uncertainty. At each stage the controller must first estimate the state from imperfect readings, then act. Choosing where to look becomes part of the control problem itself. Good sensor steering means better decisions in settings like tracking, surveillance, and environmental monitoring, where attention is a limited resource.
arxiv-2509-08240:
An old puzzle in nuclear structure, the B(E2) anomaly, is examined through the interacting boson model by Wei Teng and 3 co-authors in a 2025 nuclear physics paper. The anomaly appears when a certain ratio of gamma-ray transition strengths falls below one while level energies suggest orderly rotation. Explaining both facts at once has challenged simple pictures of nuclear shape.

Calculations show the effective triaxial deformation, a measure of how far the nucleus departs from a sphere in three unequal axes, can change substantially as spin grows. Mixing between normal and intruder configurations also helps the anomaly emerge. Nuclear shapes are not frozen sculptures; this work shows how motion and mixing together can fake a contradiction in the data.
arxiv-2509-08340:
Stacking tungsten diselenide on graphene strains and pins its light emission, report Lan Huang and 9 co-authors in a 2025 materials paper. Interfaces decide whether two-dimensional heterostructures deliver their promised optoelectronic and quantum behaviour. Samples grown directly on graphene are compared, layer by layer from one to five, against flakes exfoliated onto ordinary oxide substrates.

Raman and light-emission spectroscopy with atomic force microscopy reveal the differences. Growth on graphene imposes a persistent compressive strain, shrinks the spacing between the semiconductor's own layers, and concentrates disorder in the layer touching the graphene. Excitons, the bound electron-hole pairs that carry the light response, end up pinned by this interface. Device builders must budget for such coupling rather than treating stacked layers as independent.
arxiv-2509-08840:
Measurements of the universe's expansion rate disagree, and varying the speed of light is one exotic proposed escape. Seokcheon Lee examines that idea in a 2025 research paper written alone. The framework is the minimally extended varying-speed-of-light model. Lee separates how time is standardized across cosmic epochs from how local physics behaves.

He traces the consequences for early universe decoupling, when light broke free from matter. The calculation keeps the physics of hydrogen recombination close to the standard picture. The sound horizon at the drag epoch, a key ruler for the expansion dispute, barely moves. That stability undercuts explaining the Hubble tension through the sound horizon inside this model. Time dilation tests, however, give the framework a distinct signature. Lee's analysis shows where varying-light models can still be tested, and where they cannot help.
arxiv-2509-08940:
Lisa Dunlap and 5 co-authors discover divergent representations between text-to-image models in a 2025 paper. Two models given the same prompt may add very different visual attributes. The goal is to find those attributes and the prompts that trigger them.

An evolutionary search method called CompCon hunts for concepts more common in one model's output than the other's. A new dataset with sixty known differences tests whether it finds real divergences. It beats language and vision model baselines on that test. Applied to popular models, it surfaces differences in mood, setting, and depiction of people. Code is shared publicly.
arxiv-2509-09040:
Charles D. Arrowsmith and 30 co-authors test pair beam stability in a lab analogue of blazar cascades in a 2025 paper. Blazars are bright active galaxies whose gamma rays can spawn electron positron pairs in deep space. Lab beams of such pairs can test if those cascades break up.

Protons from CERN's synchrotron make a dense pair beam, sent through a metre of plasma. Beam instabilities were thought to shred cascades and explain missing low energy glow from blazars. The beam stays stable if it is not in a perfect beam shape or at one exact energy. That keeps past lower bounds on the space magnetic field firm.
arxiv-2509-09140:
Counting holes and components in a noisy image is a topology problem, and the classical tool for it can be slow and brittle. Dylan Peek, Matthew P. Skerritt, and Stephan Chalup test a neural shortcut in a 2025 research paper. They trained a supervised network to predict Betti numbers, the counts that summarize an image's topology, directly from two-dimensional binary images.

The rival pipeline uses persistent homology, the standard method, with a noise-robust distance transform front end. On one synthetic and two real-world datasets, the network outperformed that pipeline under noise. The authors credit its learned sense of context and geometry, absorbed from training data. Classical methods compute topology exactly but cannot learn what damage looks like. The study suggests learned topology estimation deserves a place beside the classical toolkit wherever images arrive dirty, which is nearly everywhere.
arxiv-2509-09240:
Shin Hayashi proves a bulk-boundary link for second-order topological insulators in a 2025 paper. These materials hold protected states at corners or hinges, not on whole faces. The systems keep inversion symmetry, a flip through a center point, and take rectangle or prism shapes.

The proof uses index theory, which ties counts of solutions to topology. Symbols of Toeplitz operators on quarter planes are extended, and K-theory groups for the symmetric case are computed. Both flat and solid cases are covered in two and three dimensions. The link says bulk topology forces the corner states. A strict proof firms up the base for this field.
arxiv-2509-09340:
Snehasish Roy Chowdhury and 4 co-authors show that help from the environment can unlock a quantum channel's full encoding power in a 2025 paper. A channel whose output is smaller than its input must leak some symbols to its surroundings. Those lost symbols cap how much can be sent with trust.

A new frame asks if slight help from the environment can get the lost symbols back. A clean case study shows encoding can be fully restored with minimal help, even when the standard assisted capacity looks low. Even the strongest non-signaling links between sender and receiver cannot stand in for that help. A sharp gap is proved for a class of channels in any dimension.
arxiv-2509-09540:
A Heusler alloy's magnetism can be tuned by swapping one ingredient, and one such alloy is a candidate for next-generation memory. Ramón Cuadrado studies a manganese-ruthenium-gallium alloy across its full composition range in a 2025 research paper written alone. He varies the ruthenium fraction in fine steps. For each composition, many inequivalent atomic arrangements were optimized with first-principles calculations.

As ruthenium content changes, the crystal stretches mainly along one axis. That stretch encourages the magnetization to point out of the plane, prized for dense memory devices. The preferred axis emerges only at intermediate ruthenium levels. The alloy's half-metallic character, where one spin channel conducts and the other does not, also switches with composition. Two manganese sublattices nearly cancel each other's moment in part of the range. The trends map a design space for spintronic materials balancing anisotropy and spin polarization.
arxiv-2509-09740:
Ying Yuan and 10 co-authors build a language model agent in 2025 that helps biologists name what single-cell clusters are doing. After a Perturb-seq experiment, cells are grouped and each group is labelled with Gene Ontology terms, yet both the grouping sharpness and the labels lean on habit and expert taste. Their system, HypoGeneAgent, turns that judgement into a score that can be optimised.

An analyst model drafts ranked functional guesses for each gene programme, with confidence attached. The descriptions are then embedded and compared: tight agreement inside a cluster counts for it, clear separation between clusters counts for it too. Referee agents combine those signals into a resolution score, highest when groups are both coherent inside and distinct outside.
arxiv-2509-09840:
Nikhita Joshi and 1 co-author test a design idea in 2025. The idea moves AI help into the margins of a document reader. Chat panels sit apart from the text a person is reading. That forces constant switching of context. Margin notes live inside the comment space instead. The authors map the choices that define such notes. One choice is how closely they hug the text. One is who picks the passage. One is how much of the writing the AI does.

Readers in two studies liked notes built into the page. They also liked picking passages themselves. A third study varied the human and AI split six ways. Less AI work deepened the sense that the notes were one's own. Still, quicker and lighter designs won in the end. Scores for grasp of the text held steady across all versions.
arxiv-2509-10040:
Mohamed Basem and 3 co-authors report a winning system for judging Arabic reading difficulty in a 2025 shared task paper from the BAREC 2025 competition. Fine-grained readability scoring helps schools and publishers pitch texts at the right level, yet Arabic tools lag behind. Their entry blends four transformer models, each tuned with a different loss so each hears a different signal in the text, then fuses their answers weighted by confidence.

Severe class imbalance and scarce hard examples were fought with weighted training, careful preprocessing, relabelling of a major corpus by their strongest model, and synthetic examples from a commercial generator. A final correction for skewed predictions added a solid gain. First place in all six tracks followed, at sentence and document level alike.
arxiv-2509-10440:
Star clusters in two nearby dwarf galaxies get a fresh census here. J. M. Howell and colleagues report it for the Euclid space telescope's early release program, in this 2025 paper. Clusters trace how galaxies build their stars. Dwarf galaxies matter because big galaxies grow by absorbing systems like them. Euclid resolves single stars across both galaxies, IC 10 and NGC 6822.

Visual inspection turned up new cluster candidates. There were thirty in NGC 6822 and sixteen in IC 10. The team then rebuilt combined catalogs. NGC 6822 has fifty-two clusters; IC 10 has seventy-one. Each entry carries a confidence grade, uniform photometry, and a size. IC 10 holds more young, massive clusters. That fits its starburst character. Both dwarfs keep several old heavyweight clusters. One sits in NGC 6822's outskirts, over a million times the Sun's mass. An old, extended cluster had been missed before, too.
arxiv-2509-10540:
Pavan Reddy and Aditya Sanjay Gujral dissect EchoLeak in this 2025 security case study. EchoLeak was a real attack on Microsoft 365 Copilot. The flaw is catalogued as CVE-2025-32711. It was a zero-click prompt injection. One crafted email let a remote attacker steal data. No user interaction was needed at all. The email talked the AI assistant into betraying its trust boundaries.

The chain of bypasses is the story. The attack slipped past Microsoft's prompt-injection classifier. It hid links using reference-style Markdown. It exploited images that load on their own. It abused a Teams proxy that the security policy allowed. The authors explain why layered defenses failed. They propose fixes. Prompts can be partitioned. Input and output filtering can be strengthened. Access control can track provenance. Content policies can be stricter. The broader lesson: prompt injection is now a practical, high-severity threat to production AI.
arxiv-2509-10740:
How does physics invent a genuinely new concept? Omar Aguilar and Anthony Aguirre try to formalize that creative act in this 2025 paper at the border of physics and logic. Concept formation sounds like a humanities topic, but the authors argue it can be made precise, and they choose type theory, the formal language of structured definitions, as the frame.

They define cognitive typing rules for moves physicists actually make: distinguishing a concept, preserving a property across a change, and transforming a concept itself. Composing those rules reconstructs two episodes from Einstein's work, his argument that frozen waves are impossible and his path to the relativity of time. The Einstein reconstruction is even recast as a program synthesis task, computed rather than merely narrated. The ambition is a working grammar of scientific discovery.
arxiv-2509-10840:
Anass Hminat and 3 co-authors compare two styles of quantum thermometer in this 2025 paper. Their probe is a single qubit whose coherence fades as it interacts with its surroundings. That fading carries information about the environment's temperature, and the qubit never needs to reach thermal balance with what it measures.

The study asks how symmetry, Hermitian versus non-Hermitian, changes the accuracy of the temperature estimate and the safety of stored quantum information. The authors optimize the quantum Fisher information over interaction time and temperature, and name the best possible measurement. Careful timing matters: the best estimate comes neither at a settled state nor after full decoherence, and the non-Hermitian version resisted decoherence better.
arxiv-2509-10940:
Four heavy quarks bound together would make an exotic particle. F. A. Martynenko, A. V. Eskin, and A. P. Martynenko compute the spectrum of such tetraquarks in this 2025 paper. They work inside the quark model. Their method is the hyperspherical approach. It treats the four-body system in a collective coordinate space.

In the hyperradial approximation, the Schrödinger equation collapses. It becomes a single one-dimensional equation, after averaging over the angles of that hyperspace. The authors solve it numerically. They solve it with a variational method, too. They then calculate the hyperfine structure of the spectrum. That is the fine splitting between states. Accuracy gets one more boost. Energy corrections are drawn from the Breit Hamiltonian, in its QCD-generalized form. That Hamiltonian encodes the relativistic interaction between quarks. The results give concrete mass predictions. Experiments are actively hunting this class of particles.
arxiv-2509-11140:
Balint Bicski and Adrian Pekar ask whether hidden network flows can be watched through their neighbors in this 2025 paper. Modern hardware offloads some traffic flows away from monitoring, leaving blind spots where service degradation can grow unseen. Their framework rests on a guess: flows you can see act as sensors for concurrent flows you cannot.

A broad statistical study of the flow landscape found a trade-off. Correlation potential is vast, but the clearest joint signals are rare and seldom line up perfectly. Encouragingly, visible signals often arrive before the hidden flow degrades, which leaves time to act. A standard learning model scored well, though mostly by leaning on simpler within-flow features, so richer structure-aware models are the next step.
arxiv-2509-11440:
Robert Dumitru and five co-authors open a new front for the Rowhammer attack. This 2025 computer security paper revisits a known memory flaw. Rowhammer flips bits in DRAM by hammering rows next door. Past launches used native code, browsers, and networks. Plug-in devices were unexplored.

Their attack is called Thunderhammer. A hostile device fires the hammering through a PCIe slot. A Thunderbolt port works too, since it tunnels PCIe. Modern DDR4 needs precisely timed access patterns, tuned per machine. The team built custom hardware to learn how PCIe requests are scheduled. It then fired effective sequences. Real bitflips were shown through both port types. A known hazard now reaches devices users plug in without a thought.
arxiv-2509-11540:
Li Ye and Yisheng Song study tensors whose entries are only known within intervals, in this 2025 mathematics paper. When every entry of a tensor carries uncertainty, basic questions like positive definiteness and Hurwitz stability have to hold across the whole interval family, not just for one tidy array.

The authors introduce auxiliary tensors that capture the extreme cases and prove that an interval tensor is positive definite, or semidefinite, exactly when all of its auxiliary tensors are. For Hurwitz stability, they show the stability of a general interval tensor follows from its symmetric part, whose stability in turn matches that of a second family of auxiliary tensors. Fourth-order three-dimensional examples close the paper, with concrete sufficient conditions a practitioner can check.
arxiv-2509-11640:
Deepak Mallya, Arpita Sinha, and Leena Vachhani ask what optimal patrolling looks like. This 2025 robotics paper treats the multi-agent patrol problem. Teams of autonomous agents revisit locations again and again. Two decades of work produced many strategies. The shape of the best ones went unexamined.

The authors prove a structural result first. Near-optimal solutions can always be taken to repeat a pattern. Any feasible patrol has a recurrent near-match. More strongly, a recurrent strategy exists that is near-optimal for the general problem. The error factor ties to a discretization constant. That constant can be made as small as one likes. Team size and environment size do not matter. An algorithm converts any published strategy into recurrent form. Simulations on graphs from real settings back the claims.
arxiv-2509-11740:
Davide Peron, Victor Nan Fernandez-Ayala, and Lukas Segelmark built a robot that stocks supermarket shelves. This 2025 robotics paper faces an awkward workplace. People wander the aisles. Space is tight. Products come in every shape. Commercial hardware is integrated with a modular software stack on ROS2.

Behavior trees plan the tasks. Fine-tuned vision models spot the products. A two-stage predictive controller navigates by printed markers on the shelves. Lab trials mimicked a real supermarket. More than seven hundred stocking events ran. The success rate passed ninety-eight percent. Benchmarks stay candid, though. Today's autonomous stockers still lose to human workers on performance and cost. The paper quantifies the progress commercial use still needs.
arxiv-2509-11840:
Tim Lebailly and 4 co-authors use synthetic captions to teach image segmentation in a 2025 paper on open-vocabulary zero-shot segmentation. The goal is segmenting objects named in words the model never saw labeled examples for. Generative vision-language models grasp images at a high level but align language loosely to exact pixels.

The authors bridge two lines of work by densely aligning images with synthetic descriptions made by those very models. Synthetic captions are cheap, scalable, and easy to make, so they are a strong source of semantic guidance. In tests, the approach beat prior work on standard zero-shot open-vocabulary segmentation benchmarks. It was also more data-efficient than the alternatives. The result suggests generated text can stand in for costly human labels in dense prediction tasks.
arxiv-2509-12040:
