Segmenting satellite images for categories nobody labeled in advance is the emerging task Bingyu Li and five co-authors organize in 2025. Open-vocabulary segmentation works well on ordinary photos, yet overhead remote sensing views differ enough that direct transfer falters, and no shared yardstick existed for the field.

The team first assembles a standardized benchmark from widely used remote sensing datasets so methods can be compared fairly. Testing representative models on it exposes clear weaknesses. Their answer, RSKT-Seg, computes vision-language similarity in several directions to stay steady under rotation, fuses spatial and semantic cues with a lean transformer, and transfers pretrained knowledge through improved upsampling. On the benchmark it beats strong baselines on both accuracy scores while running twice as fast.
arxiv-2509-12140:
People who label, moderate, or red-team AI content can be harmed by the material they have to review. Alice Qian and five co-authors ask how crowd workers should be warned, in 2025. Warnings for staff moderators are well studied. Disclosure aimed at gig workers is not.

The team ran co-design sessions with three groups. Fifteen task designers took part. So did eleven crowd workers and three platform representatives. Each group was asked what disclosure should look like. Designers want help in writing warnings. Workers have their own wishes for how warnings reach them. Platforms see a role in setting the rules. The authors map the tensions among protection, clarity, and platform needs. They then offer design advice and feature ideas for risk disclosure in responsible AI content work.
arxiv-2509-13440:
Yuan Xue, Zihan Cheng and Matteo Ippoliti simulate in 2025 bilayer Hamiltonians via monitored monolayer trajectories. Open systems often double mixed states into pure pairs. The reverse map is explored here: isolated bilayers become open monolayers.

Bilayers with antiunitary layer swap symmetry and a sign rule on interlayer links map to Lindblad dynamics. Some jump outcomes are postselected as monitored. Low-energy bilayer states match late monolayer states. Trajectory sampling halves system size, with importance sampling to curb overhead. Free-fermion cases reduce to auxiliary field Monte Carlo, which reframes its sign-free rules. A 1D Ashkin-Teller bench checks the path.
arxiv-2509-13640:
Ryo Ikehata studies how waves fade in two dimensions in a solo 2025 analysis paper. The setting is the wave equation on the whole plane with spatially varying coefficients in its main part, starting from data packed into a bounded region. The question is how fast the energy stored near the start decays as time grows.

Ikehata reports a decay rate with a mild logarithmic correction, reached after large times. Two dimensions are the awkward case because Hardy-type inequalities, workhorses in higher dimensions, are unavailable. The proof leans on the multiplier method and first secures an optimal estimate for the solution itself. Slightly generalized coefficients are handled in the same framework.
arxiv-2509-14540:
Meghna Roy Chowdhury and four co-authors present DistNN in 2025, a framework that splits neural network inference between a wearable and a nearby phone. Wearables for health and vision need smart models that exceed their tiny memory and energy budgets. Cloud offloading adds delay and privacy risk.

DistNN runs early network layers on the ultra low power wearable node. Intermediate features then go to a resource rich hub such as a smartphone for the remaining layers. Splitting keeps raw sensor data local longer and cuts wearable load. Shrinking the model alone, the TinyML route, can sacrifice accuracy and still strain memory on vision tasks. The design space study maps where each layer split balances accuracy, energy and latency best.
arxiv-2509-14640:
Habib Irani and Vangelis Metsis introduce dynamic wavelet positional encoding in 2025 for transformer models on time series. Standard positional encodings use only the index of a step, ignoring the signal itself. Time series are nonstationary and multiscale, so index only positions waste information.

Their encoding builds position embeddings directly from the input signal with the discrete wavelet transform. Wavelets expose patterns at several time scales at once, suiting signals whose rhythm changes. Tests on ten diverse time series data sets show consistent gains over leading positional schemes, the authors report. Signal aware positions give the transformer a sense of where it is in the pattern, not merely where it is in the list.
arxiv-2509-14840:
Ali Fawaz leads a team of nine authors reporting an experiment that couples silicon carbide spins to a microwave resonator in a 2025 quantum technology paper. Linking cavity modes to spin qubits supports qubit readout, control, long-distance coupling, and quantum memory. The experiment ran at a temperature of ten millikelvin, far below one degree above absolute zero.

The team swept a magnetic field to tune spin transitions across the cavity resonance and measured transmission through the cavity. Different spin defects appeared as resonances separated by tens of megahertz. Shining laser light on the sample inside the cavity brought an additional spin resonance into coupling. Optical spectroscopy over a wide temperature range helped identify which defects produced each signal. The results support silicon carbide as a practical spin platform.
arxiv-2509-15340:
Rebecca Dudley and seven co-authors weigh a gas-rich diffuse dwarf galaxy and place it on a scaling relation in a 2025 astronomy paper. Diffuse dwarfs challenge galaxy formation theory with their large sizes, faint surfaces, and disputed dark matter content. Their target, a WALLABY survey galaxy also known as KK176, is rich in atomic hydrogen, which radio data can kinematically trace.

High-resolution hydrogen observations yield the most reliable kinematic model of the galaxy so far. Decomposing the rotation into stars, gas, and dark matter shows the galaxy is dark matter dominated. On the baryonic Tully-Fisher relation, linking total ordinary mass to rotation speed, KK176 sits consistently with ordinary low-mass dwarfs. It therefore stands apart from reported dark-matter-deficient ultra-diffuse galaxies, sharpening that controversy.
arxiv-2509-15440:
Dashiel Carrera, Jeb Thomas-Mitchell, and Daniel Wigdor ask who owns words written with an AI helper. Such tools blur who is in charge of a text, which slows their uptake. The team first looked at tools on the market. They then built three writing tools with the same core but three styles: one feels like an agent, one like a tool, and one like magic.

They spoke with eighteen writers, both paid and unpaid, as they used the tools. The styles shifted where writers felt control and who they saw as the author. Tool like designs moved the felt points of control, while agent like designs stressed ideas over words. The team end with design advice on how style shapes use.
arxiv-2509-15640:
Nhu Vo leads a team that tests prompts for medical translation between English and Vietnamese. Such translation aids health care access in Vietnam. Vietnamese is a low resource language with little study in this field. The team ask which prompt styles help multilingual language models translate medical text well.

They test six models of varied size on a medical data set. Three prompt styles are compared: no examples, a few examples, and prompts backed by a medical word list. Model size drives scores most: large models do well with no examples. A few examples add only small gains. Word list cues and well chosen examples help in a steady way. The results show both promise and limits.
arxiv-2509-16040:
Learning the stress rules of a material straight from data could replace slow hand fitting, but many search tools could do the job. Jorge-Humberto Urrea-Quintero and three co-authors pair three sparse search methods with three rules for picking the best model. That pairing yields nine full methods, which they compare on cost, sparsity, and accuracy.

Tests use both made-up and real data for materials that stretch the same in all directions and those that do not. All nine methods found accurate rules. The findings widen the set of trusted tools beyond the most common sparse method.
arxiv-2509-16140:
Most software bugs get fixed in a fair time, but a few linger far longer than the rest. Avinash Patil studies these slow cases across seven large open-source projects, from Firefox to Hadoop. Statistical rules flag reports whose fix times sit far outside the normal range, and text methods group the flagged reports by theme.

The slow bugs cluster around test failures, requests for new features, and interface problems in project after project. Such patterns point to process weak spots, not just hard code. The findings give project leads a clear guide for where to push first, so old bugs stop piling up.
arxiv-2509-16240:
The Riemann Hypothesis, a famous unproven claim about prime numbers, is recast here as a claim about a discrete dynamical system. Hendrik Wladimir Albrecht Edwin Kuipers builds a map where composite numbers advance and primes retreat, so paths shrink or grow based on prime patterns. In this frame, the hypothesis equals the claim that certain error measures keep shrinking across scales.

Kuipers argues that a zeta zero off the central line would force swings too large for that shrinking to hold. On that basis the work claims that all such zeros must lie on the line. The claim is the author's own and rests on his new frame, not on a settled proof.
arxiv-2509-16440:
Two schools built spaces of operators, math objects that act on signals, by rival routes, and it was unclear whether the spaces agreed. Monika Dörfler and three co-authors show the two constructions match for a broad class of time-frequency frames. With that settled, they build dictionaries that let operators be written as sparse sums of simple parts.

Those sparse sums turn out to recover exactly the same spaces, a tidy closure of the circle. The result holds for a prized class of mixed-state operators. Numeric tests confirm that few terms already give strong approximations, which matters for quantum and signal work.
arxiv-2509-16740:
Gopal Datt, Ritesh Pal, and Ashish Kumar Trivedi prove a test for well-behaved functions in a 2025 math paper. The functions live on a unit disc and can take infinite values. Three helper functions share values with the main one in a set way. The team ask what that sharing forces on the main function.

They prove that sharing with all three helpers makes the function normal. Normal here means its family of shifts stays tame. A second test for normality follows from the first. Results like this guide work on complex functions, where a small sharing clue can pin down global behavior.
arxiv-2509-16840:
Lauren E. Henderson, Roman Gerasimov, and Evan N. Kirby study star chemistry in the cluster M15 in a 2025 astronomy paper. Clusters hold several star groups told apart by light element patterns. Heavy element spreads are rare and appear in only a few clusters. M15 is one of them. The team measure how that heavy spread varies by group.

The spread differs between star groups in a telling way. Gas seems to have mixed unevenly while the first group formed. By the second group, the gas was well mixed. The heavy elements likely came from a fast event tied to the first stars. The work links cluster birth to a rare cosmic forge.
arxiv-2509-17240:
Abdullah Mushtaq and five co-authors ask whether AI agents can judge systematic literature reviews as well as humans do. Their 2025 arXiv paper presents a helper system built for that task. Such reviews anchor evidence-based work, but writing and grading them takes great effort and scores often differ among graders.

The system splits the judging work among several specialized agents built on large language models. The agents check the review protocol, grade method quality, and test topic fit against a scholarly database, all in line with PRISMA guidance. In a first study of five published reviews from varied fields, the system's scores agreed with expert scores in most cases. The authors call it a first step toward fast, fair review grading that works across fields.
arxiv-2509-17440:
Jüri Keller and five co-authors ran a small case study on testing search systems over time. Their 2025 arXiv paper notes that classic retrieval tests freeze queries and documents in place, so they miss how needs and texts evolve. Longitudinal tests fix that gap, but they demand custom code, which hurts reproducibility and reuse.

Working from their entries to the LongEval 2024 shared task, the team proposes a declarative extension of the ir_datasets toolkit. In the new style, researchers state which queries, documents, and feedback exist at each point in time instead of coding the logic by hand. They rebuilt their LongEval entries on the extension and found the code grew much simpler. The paper is a software lesson as much as a retrieval result: plain declarations beat tangled scripts for time-aware search tests.
arxiv-2509-17540:
Jun-Feng Wang, De-Shun Zhang, and Zhi-Feng Sun build a gauge-invariant theory of diquark forces. Their 2025 arXiv paper works in quantum chromodynamics, where a diquark is a correlated pair of quarks. To write interactions that respect color symmetry, they set out how diquark fields transform and define matching covariant derivatives.

From those rules they construct Lagrangians for the couplings of scalar and axial-vector diquarks, light and heavy, to gluons. One-gluon exchange then yields effective potentials for diquark-antidiquark pairs. By matching those potentials to the Godfrey-Isgur quark model, they fix the coupling constants. The potentials turn out to rest mainly on Coulomb, contact, and tensor terms, with one channel's potential vanishing outright. Tensor terms tied to the coupling squared are negligible. The result is a tidy, symmetry-clean toolkit for hadron spectroscopy.
arxiv-2509-17840:
Martin Sundermann and 8 co-authors report a sharper X-ray method to probe uranium compounds. Their 2025 paper deals with actinide stuff, whose five-f electron shells act in complex ways. Such facts matter for both basic science and nuclear use.

The method fires X-rays at two uranium edges and reads the bounce with fine energy detail. On uranium dioxide, a test case, it split close states that past tools blurred. It shows low-energy traits and high-energy bond traits in one run. The team argues the method can test maths models of these hard shells more strictly.
arxiv-2509-17940:
Shuyao Shang and 4 co-authors teach a self-driving system to favour safe paths, not just human-like ones. Their 2025 method, DriveDPO, learns a drive policy straight from raw sensor input. Copy-the-human training can bless paths that look right but are in fact risky.

Their plan first blends human likeness with rule-based safety scores into one policy. A second stage then aligns the policy at the level of whole paths, by taste for safer ones. On a known drive bench, the method set a new top score. Scene tests show safer, steadier driving in hard cases as well.
arxiv-2509-18140:
Iram Wajahat and 3 co-authors link a risk model for diabetes to gene-free maps of body pathways. Their 2025 paper deals with type 2 diabetes, a heavy health load that hits some groups harder. One such group in their data is the Pima Indians of Arizona, long used in diabetes studies.

Plain stats tools pick the top risk traits in that data set, with fair total score. Those traits are then mapped to key signal paths, such as insulin and energy paths. Drug ideas drawn from those paths span known drug classes and plant compounds. Enrichment checks back the path links the team draws.
arxiv-2509-18240:
Giulia Cerini and 6 co-authors use the match between dark matter and hot gas to sort galaxy clusters by calmness. Their 2025 paper deals with scaling rules that link a cluster's mass to what telescopes see, such as X-ray glow and heat. Scatter in those rules blurs mass sums, a key tool for cosmology.

Data come from hundreds of clusters in a large cosmic sim. Cross-match maps of dark matter and gas, in 3D and in flat view, score how settled each cluster is. Calm clusters form a clean set with far less rule scatter. The gain runs up to two fifths off the raw scatter.
arxiv-2509-18340:
Can two musicians feel linked the way quantum particles can be linked? Mark Carney explores that idea in this 2025 book chapter on quantum computer music. He built a setup where music data from two players steers a quantum simulation on a small embedded board. The shared term he works with is tonal centrality, a measure of how close the two players' notes sit.

The system reads the players' music as MIDI data and feeds the closeness measure into the simulation. The results are coded back into MIDI and sent to each player's instrument. When the players' tones are close, their instruments share one linked state; when far apart, they share the opposite kind. Carney ran the setup in real tests and shares the full code and sample outputs. The goal is a new tool for joint music making.
arxiv-2509-18740:
Neural networks can act as operators that approximate whole functions, not just fit data points. Priyanka Majethiya and Shivam Bajpeyi study such operators in mixed norm spaces in this 2025 paper. Mixed norms measure a function with a different rule in each variable. Those spaces have uses across several branches of math.

The team analyzes multivariate Kantorovich-type network operators driven by a sigmoidal activation. They prove the operators stay bounded and converge in mixed norm Lebesgue spaces. The same holds in mixed norm Orlicz spaces, a family that includes classic and exponential spaces. Graphs and error estimates round out the theory. An applied section tests image tasks: reconstruction, scaling, filling gaps, and denoising. The authors report that the mixed norm structure helps those tasks. Theory and image practice meet in one frame.
arxiv-2509-18840:
Treating an image as a graph of patches can beat grids and token strings, if the graph is built well. Ismael Elsharkawi, Hossam Sharara, and Ahmed Rafea present a learnable way to build that graph in this 2025 paper. Older vision graph models wire patches by fixed statistics or thresholds. Those rules need tuning and may pick poor neighborhoods.

Their method, LRGC, scores every pair of nodes with a key-query attention step. A soft-threshold trick then picks edges in a way that training can adjust. Thresholds are learned per layer from data, not set by hand as hyperparameters. That removes the bias baked into clustering or fixed-threshold rules. On the ImageNet-1k benchmark, their model beat rival vision graph models of similar size. The authors pitch learned wiring as the missing piece for vision graphs.
arxiv-2509-18940:
Owen Henderschedt and Jessica McDonald open a new question in graph coloring: when can part of a coloring be extended to the whole graph? They work with total colorings, where both points and edges get colors and neighbors must differ. Their graphs are planar, meaning they can be drawn flat with no crossing edges. The question is whether a coloring fixed on a small piece can always be completed.

For a starting piece that is a matching, a set of edges with no shared points, they prove extension works with a stated number of colors. That holds once the largest degree is high enough, and the number of colors cannot be lowered in general. For starting pieces made of small tight groups set far apart, extension works with fewer extra colors. There the spacing condition also cannot be relaxed.
arxiv-2509-19040:
Marie S. Breum and three co-authors build estimators for a causal quantity that arises when a treatment's effect flows entirely through a middle variable. This front-door setup helps when hidden factors tangle treatment and outcome directly, so the usual adjustment fails. Their version is longitudinal: treatment and mediator both change over time. Apart from a simple plug-in estimator, no proper methods existed for it.

The authors derive estimators that are nonparametric and efficient, meaning they lean on few assumptions and waste little data. The estimators handle high-dimensional mediators and are multiply robust, staying valid if parts of the model are right. They also allow machine-learning estimates of the nuisance parts while keeping inference honest. Simulations confirm the theory, and the team applies the method to an infant trial on peanut allergy.
arxiv-2509-19240:
Some elements with odd atomic numbers, like phosphorus and potassium, are scarcer in stars than standard models predict. Joshua Issa and three co-authors test the favored fix: in some massive stars, the oxygen and carbon burning shells merge before the explosion, and the churning boosts production. They post-process a fifteen-solar-mass star model with mixing recipes drawn from full 3D fluid simulations. Twenty-four mixing cases vary how fast fresh fuel is ingested and how convection is quenched.

Yields of the four light odd-Z elements shift by large factors depending on the mixing. Cases with a mixing downturn and the fastest ingestion gain the most, and faster flows do not always help. The team also parameterizes production of potassium-40, a radioactive heat source inside young rocky planets. Its yield varies over a thousandfold across cases, implying young planets' interiors could behave very differently from Earth's.
arxiv-2509-19840:
Pentaquarks, particles built from five quarks, may hide a doubly strange family with hidden charm. L. Roca, J. Song, and E. Oset ask whether two known particle decays could reveal them. Their framework grows the states from coupled meson-baryon interactions rather than inserting them by hand. The states should couple strongly to one key channel, which makes the chosen decays promising hunting grounds.

The authors trace the weak decay steps, the hadron formation, and the final-state interactions that build the full signal. Predicted mass patterns are compared with fresh LHCb measurements. A match would add a new branch to the exotic particle family tree. Null results still guide where experiments should look next. The paper is theory that hands experimentalists a map.
arxiv-2509-20340:
Farms full of sensors generate data that only supercomputers can fully exploit. Liubov Kurafeeva and eleven co-authors link those two worlds through private 5G in a 2025 conference paper. Their test case is citrus growing under protective screens. Sensors watch conditions and screen damage, while fluid dynamics codes on distant machines guide watering and repairs.

The two sides clash: sensors are weak and unreliable, while computing centers are powerful but slow to respond through batch queues. Their system, xGFabric, couples them end to end over a private 5G network. Network slicing connects remote sensors to the computing facility with low delay. The prototype enables near-real-time simulation for digital agriculture. It shows a pattern other sensor-heavy sciences could reuse.
arxiv-2509-20440:
Metal-rich gas cools fast and shatters into small stars, which may cap the birth of giants. Eda Gjergo and eight co-authors test that logic in a 2025 arXiv paper on the initial mass function. Within their framework, a linear relation ties the low-mass slope of the mass function to metal content. The relation was calibrated only up to about twice the Sun's metal fraction.

Pushed beyond that range, the linear rule suppresses massive star formation entirely at high metallicity. The authors doubt nature is that abrupt. They propose a logistic curve that flattens once fragmentation stops caring about metals, as happens when collapse cascades quickly. Their public code, pyIGIMF, computes the integrated galactic mass function with the new relation instantly. The work sharpens predictions for the metal-rich hearts of galaxies.
arxiv-2509-20540:
Some symmetries in quantum field theory cannot be undone, and their full structure goes beyond simple fusion rules. Seolhwa Kim, Orr Sela, and Zhengdi Sun study that higher structure in a 2025 physics paper running to fifty-eight pages plus appendices. They work only with theories that have an explicit Lagrangian description.

The authors start with a two-dimensional free compact boson and its duality defects. From Lagrangian descriptions of defect networks, they recover all the F-symbols of a known fusion category. They then apply the same approach to four-dimensional Maxwell theory. There they compute F-symbols for duality and triality defects. The results give concrete tools for analyzing non-invertible symmetries.
arxiv-2509-21140:
Some knots are mirror images of themselves with orientation reversed; they are called negative amphichiral knots. Alessio Di Prisa, Jaewon Lee, and Oguz Savk prove a slicing result about all of them in a 2025 topology paper. A knot is rationally slice if it bounds a disk in a rational homology ball.

Kawauchi proved in 2009 that strongly negative amphichiral knots are always rationally slice. But Hartley showed in 1980 that some such knots are not strongly amphichiral, leaving a gap. The authors close it for links whose mirror map keeps each component in place. Their proof studies how that map acts on the JSJ decomposition of the link exterior. They also give conditions for such a knot to match, or be concordant to, a strongly amphichiral one.
arxiv-2509-21340:
Memory and consciousness are proposed here to rest on cycles in neural state space, not on static storage. Credit goes to Xin Li. The framework is information topological, linking information and shape. Memory, in this view, is not a static store. It is the power to step back into latent cycles held in neural state space. Stable cycles carry meaning by filtering noise that changes with order.

Transient signals, called dots, support exploration. Nontrivial cycles encode low entropy content that persists across contexts. The author links these cycles to polychronous neural groups, where delay locked spikes are reinforced by spike timing plasticity. Theta gamma rhythms enforce boundary rules. Perception action cycles extend the idea, with closure holding across sensing and acting, rooted in ancestral homing behaviour.
arxiv-2509-22240:
Matt Y. Cheung, Ashok Veeraraghavan, and Guha Balakrishnan tackle uncertainty in medical image segmentation, where what matters is often a derived number, like an organ's size, rather than the outline itself. Conformal prediction is a standard way to attach honest error ranges to a model's output. Applied naively to the final number, though, it treats the whole segmentation pipeline as a black box and gives loose ranges. Their 2025 framework, COMPASS, accepted at ICLR 2026, works inside the model instead.

COMPASS calibrates uncertainty in the model's internal feature space. It perturbs intermediate features along the few directions that most affect the target metric, which focuses the calibration where it counts. The authors prove the method keeps valid coverage under a standard assumption. On four medical segmentation tasks, covering skin lesions and anatomical structures, it produced clearly tighter ranges than standard conformal baselines.
arxiv-2509-22340: Anna Zaborowska and Peter McKeown publish a data set of detailed particle shower simulations, released for studies of how such data are best represented. The data record electromagnetic and hadronic showers in calorimeters, the layered detectors that measure particle energies, at full simulation detail. Rich forms of the showers are needed as input for fast simulators based on generative models. The data set is published so researchers can compare forms and work toward a general tool that turns detailed simulation output into a better form for them.
arxiv-2509-22540:
Gia Dvali argues that a black hole's stored information pushes back on its classical motion. He calls this the swift memory burden effect. Objects that store information with high efficiency resist perturbations in proportion to how full their memory is. Black holes with the same ground state but different information loads would react very differently when disturbed.

Dvali builds a calculable framework and derives master formulas for the effect. He tests them on explicit black hole models and on solitons with high storage capacity. The effect should show in the ringdown tones of merging black holes, for both astrophysical and primordial ones. He also proposes a table-top test with cold bosons.
arxiv-2509-22840:
Micah Adler explains why attention uses many heads, in terms of capacity. A single attention layer encodes token-to-token relations through its key-query channel. Adler asks how many distinct relations a fixed budget can reliably hold. He defines a task, Relational Graph Recognition: the channel encodes a directed graph, and given a subset of vertices, the model must recover each one's neighbors. Resources are measured by total key dimension across heads.

Matching lower and upper bounds show the needed key dimension grows with the number of relations, up to logarithmic factors. Splitting a fixed budget into more heads raises capacity by cutting interference between superimposed embeddings. Controlled experiments show sharp phase transitions at the predicted capacity, persisting in full transformer blocks.
arxiv-2509-23240:
Skewed data starve the rare labels that often matter most in regression tasks. Shayan Alahyari proposes LatentDiff, which makes new features to feed those thin spots. Deep imbalanced regression lacks data-level fixes for rich, high-size inputs. His framework runs a diffusion model in latent space, guided by the label. A priority rule steers the making toward rare labels.

The method stays cheap to run across images, text, and other inputs. Three test sets show large gains where labels are rare. Overall scores held steady at the same time. The work asks whether more data beats better methods here. For this task, well-aimed fake data make a strong case.
arxiv-2509-23340:
Judging which web domains to trust is hard when claims are checked one by one and labels cost money. Emma Kondrup and 11 co-authors built CrediBench, a web-scale data set for source credibility. It holds eight months of web graph data, with over forty million nodes per snapshot. Hyperlink edges pass one billion. Page text is scraped and stored.

The team study the three months around the 2024 US federal elections. A binary label set covers over six hundred sixty thousand domains across four risk areas. Graph, text, and time signals each added predictive power. Their multimodal regression model beat other configurations tried.
arxiv-2509-23440:
Colloidal building blocks usually settle into dull, periodic crystals set by their interaction energies. Pepijn G Moerman and 4 co-authors steer assembly down a chosen path with a DNA-encoded recipe. Biomolecular reactions tune each subunit type's binding strength and specificity over time. That timing control targets a kinetically trapped final state. The same blocks can thus end in distinct structures.

Core-shell clusters form with features far larger than one block. Their makeup follows the recipe's kinetics, not the energy minimum. Unlike global tricks like thermal annealing, each reaction's timing is set alone. The recipe idea opens a broad design space for staged assembly.
arxiv-2509-23740:
Holomorphic contact manifolds carry a distance-like measure built from discs that stay tangent to the contact planes. Filippo Bracci and 2 co-authors study when that measure is a true distance, calling such spaces contact-hyperbolic. They focus on Reeb manifolds, contact structures with a Reeb vector field whose flow acts freely. Their first theorem gives every proper Reeb manifold a holomorphic symplectic quotient and says which symplectic manifolds arise this way.

A second theorem ties contact hyperbolicity of the Reeb manifold to Kobayashi hyperbolicity of its quotient. That link yields many explicit examples with large symmetry groups. For contact 3-manifolds, they bound the symmetry group's dimension sharply.
arxiv-2509-24040:
Jonah Blasiak and 4 co-authors prove a nonsymmetric version of the compositional shuffle theorem. The classic shuffle results write a key symmetric function as a sum over labeled Dyck paths, stepped paths that encode counting data. Past work by Haglund and others set out these claims, and Carlsson and Mellit proved them with a new algebra.

The new version works with nonsymmetric Macdonald-type polynomials built by the authors in recent work. The team defines a matching operator that acts cleanly on that basis. Weaving their theory with results of Carlsson, Mellit, and others, they equate the operator's action with a sum over flagged labeled Dyck paths. The sum is conjectured to have a strong positivity trait.
arxiv-2509-24240:
Coding agents write whole programs on their own, and that autonomy opens security holes that code completion never had. Eunkyu Lee and 3 co-authors present a systematic security review of eight real-world coding agents. They mapped the internal workflows of the agents and hunted threats across their components, where past checks had been piecemeal.

The audit found fifteen security issues, some missed before. Chained together, the issues let an attacker run any command inside five agents and steal data from four, all with no user action or approval. The authors argue that LLM-driven agents need full security review by design, not patchwork fixes after release.
arxiv-2509-24540:
Mergesort is fast and stable, but it needs a second array, which doubles memory and can rule it out for huge data. Christian Siebert proposes an in-place mergesort that is stable by design. Earlier in-place versions were mostly slow, unstable, or too complex to use in practice, he notes.

His algorithm rests on two parts: an optimal array rotation and the co-ranking idea from parallel mergesort work. It uses the optimal number of comparisons and runs with low constants in tests, including runs on one of the largest shared-memory machines available. Total time is a log factor above optimal, yet the method stays simple enough to teach and to ship.
arxiv-2510-00240:
Ehsan Aghaei and three colleagues published this 2025 paper presenting SecureBERT 2.0, a language model built for cybersecurity work. Security analysts search threat reports, extract named entities, and flag vulnerable code. General-purpose models fumble the field's dense jargon and its mix of prose and code. The new model starts from the ModernBERT design and adapts it to long, mixed documents.

Training used a domain corpus more than thirteen times larger than the first SecureBERT's data. It held over thirteen billion text tokens plus tens of millions of code tokens from real sources. On the reported benchmarks the model set new best marks for its class. Gains covered threat-intelligence search, semantic analysis, entity recognition, and code vulnerability detection. The authors argue that large-scale, security-focused pretraining is what high-stakes defense tooling needs.
arxiv-2510-00340:
Marguerite Mahr and five colleagues published this 2025 ecology paper on road deaths among western toads in British Columbia. The study population breeds near a highway corridor in the Selkirk Mountains. Roads may drive amphibian declines worldwide, yet few studies tie traffic to long-term survival of a population. The team paired field counts with a mathematical population model.

Traffic levels tracked toad deaths closely in their data. Each extra vehicle raised toad deaths by roughly three percent on the measured nights. At today's mortality the population's risk of endangerment stays low. If baseline road mortality climbs from ten to thirty percent, that risk reaches about one half. Egg-carrying females die at higher rates, which nearly doubles the danger at higher mortality. The authors urge high priority for amphibian underpasses, warning that modest traffic growth could flip a healthy population.
arxiv-2510-00440:
Samantha Sneha Paul and Abhik Ghosh published this 2025 astronomy paper on a radio galaxy whose polarized glow fades at low frequencies. The galaxy, catalogued in the LOFAR Two-metre Sky Survey, spans hundreds of thousands of light-years. Its radio waves twist as they cross magnetized gas, an effect called Faraday rotation. At LOFAR's low frequencies that twisting scrambles the signal and depolarizes it.

The authors fit five competing depolarization models to the galaxy's polarization spectrum. A three-component model won clearly under Bayesian comparison of the fits. One component was mere instrumental leakage, while two traced real gas around the galaxy. The best fit points to turbulence and clumpiness in the magneto-ionic medium as the depolarizing agents. Studies like this turn low-frequency polarization into a probe of magnetic fields in and between galaxies. The result showcases what the LOFAR survey's second data release enables.
arxiv-2510-00540:
Jun Li, Yanzhe Li, and Pingping Liu wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on the size of fractal sets built by endless subdivision. Homogeneous Moran sets arise by repeatedly splitting intervals with fixed counts and shrinking ratios. Hausdorff dimension grades how much space such a dust-like set truly occupies. Quasisymmetric maps bend space while controlling local distortion, and minimality asks whether any bend can shrink the dimension.

The authors derive dimension formulas for two classes of these sets under stated conditions. They then study two special classes whose dimension equals one exactly. Both classes turn out to be quasisymmetrically Hausdorff minimal: no allowed bending lowers their dimension further. The proofs construct careful measures on the bent images to bound what maps can achieve. Such results pin down which fractal dimensions are rigid geometric facts and which are artifacts of the embedding.
arxiv-2510-00640:
Huang, Yang, and Deng propose an actively mode-locked cavity-based X-ray free-electron laser in this 2025 arXiv paper on accelerator physics. Shaping the spectrum of hard X-ray pulses with precision has long resisted researchers, which limits ultrafast spectroscopy at atomic scales. Their design coherently modulates the electron beam's energy inside an optical cavity. That modulation locks the output into phase-coherent pulse trains whose spectrum forms a frequency comb.

Three-dimensional time-dependent simulations predict a total pulse energy near seven hundred microjoules and peak power around thirty gigawatts. The comb spacing of 1.55 electronvolts is set directly by the modulation frequency. Undulator tapering can concentrate over ninety-five percent of the power into one selected comb line. The scheme also stayed stable under large cavity reflectivity swings, which relaxes demands on X-ray optics.
arxiv-2510-00740:
Dadhichi, Sahoo, Kumar, and Ramaswamy predict dynamics for aligned active suspensions in this 2025 arXiv paper on soft matter theory. Active matter consists of units that burn fuel to move, such as bacteria swimming in a fluid. The authors study such swimmers held along one axis, like bacteria aligned inside a nematic liquid crystal. Theory asks how concentration fluctuations relax in that anisotropic setting.

They show the suspension stirs itself: fluctuations generate flows that advect the fluctuations, so patches relax superdiffusively. In three dimensions a patch of size L fades on a timescale growing like L to the power 3/2, far slower than diffusion at large scales. Numerical simulations confirmed the dynamic exponent. Raising activity triggers an anisotropic diffusive instability, which the authors call antidiffusion. The instability comes from active stresses coupling to a particle current set by the curvature of the flow profile.
arxiv-2510-01240:
Xu and co-authors compress large language models to a few bits per weight without letting the damage land where it hurts. Vector quantization promises tiny models for weak devices, but it usually ignores which error directions the network tolerates. Geometry, borrowed from information theory, supplies the missing map.

A Fisher-based metric marks sensitive and forgiving directions in weight space. One component steers quantization errors toward the forgiving directions automatically. Another assigns more bits to channels whose curvature makes them fragile. The result is a globally smarter allocation under the same tight bit budget. Two to four bits per weight is the brutal regime targeted here. Direction errors, left unconstrained, expand through later computations. Channel sensitivity varies enough that uniform bits waste budget. Natural gradient direction is the safe slope for errors to slide along. Small devices gain frontier models.
arxiv-2510-01340:
Li, Giacinti, and Liu report diffuse gamma-ray glow around an old, disputed supernova remnant using sixteen years of telescope data. The object G172.8+1.5 might be an exploded star's shell or merely an ionized gas region. Two extended gamma-ray sources with different spectra emerged from the analysis.

The broader source matches a giant neutral hydrogen shell studded with massive young stars. The softer source hugs a dense molecular cloud inside a star-forming neighborhood. Candidate engines include escaped cosmic rays lighting the cloud and an unseen energetic pulsar. Turbulence properties inferred under the cosmic-ray scenario distinguish this remnant from younger cousins. Sixteen years of Pass 8 data give the diffuse signal its statistical weight. Power-law and log-parabola shapes separate the two sources cleanly. Maser and infrared sources mark the star-forming region's activity. Hadronic and leptonic stories both remain on the table.
arxiv-2510-01440:
Bustos-Gajardo, Fokkink, and Yassawi extend a classic theorem about automatic sequences from ordinary integers to the Gaussian integers of the complex plane. A set recognizable in two multiplicatively independent bases should be highly structured, but earlier work needed an unproven conjecture. Their hypotheses instead concern roots of integers and independence of the two bases.

Under those conditions every doubly automatic configuration must eventually repeat periodically. The result settles the standing conjecture of Hansel and Safer unconditionally. When the root condition fails, genuinely non-periodic examples exist, marking the boundary sharply. Other number rings beckon as the natural sequel. Syndetic structure was the halfway house the earlier conditional proof reached. Automatic configurations generalize finite-state generation to this plane setting. The four exponentials conjecture is no longer load-bearing here. Quadratic integer rings wait patiently as the next test cases.
arxiv-2510-01940:
Fiorio, Nikoloska, and colleagues cluster sound scenes without labels for hearing devices in this 2025 paper. Hearing aids adjust their processing to the surroundings, so they must recognize acoustic environments reliably. Classic classifiers either miss the structure of high-dimensional audio or depend on scarce human labels. Human labels also may not match how sound scenes actually group together.

The authors adapt a variational autoencoder with a mixed continuous-categorical latent space for audio. Their model, M2-AC, uses a convolutional-recurrent encoder with far fewer parameters than earlier designs. A Gumbel-Softmax trick samples the discrete cluster assignments during training. A windowing scheme averages encoder outputs over short slices, which cuts complexity for real devices. On a spoken digits clustering task, the model found sensible groupings without supervision. The work points toward hearing devices that learn their own environment categories on the fly.
arxiv-2510-02040:
Yang and Scheurer redesign participatory budgeting so citizens act as both voters and evaluators in this 2025 paper. Public funding rounds must be fair, and participants must understand the outcome. Existing methods usually treat citizens as preference machines whose votes get aggregated. The new framework, Komitee Equal Shares, instead merges two distinct signals.

In voter mode, participants award points to the proposals they favor. In evaluator mode, small groups score proposals against impact fields they defined together. Both signals translate into virtual spending power under a priceable allocation rule. Every participant receives a voting receipt that explains the result in concrete spending terms. The system ran live in the 2025 Kultur Komitee in Winterthur, Switzerland. Receipts made the proportional allocation legible and traceable for non-experts. The authors argue the design generalizes to grant-making and other budgeting settings.
arxiv-2510-02240:
Feng and five co-authors teach multimodal models to read transit maps through staged rewards in this 2025 paper. Fine-grained visual reasoning, like tracing a route across a dense transit map, defeats even advanced multimodal models. Standard reinforcement learning stalls there because rewards arrive too sparsely to learn from. The team first extends the ReasonMap benchmark into ReasonMap-Plus.

The extension adds visual question answering tasks whose dense rewards enable a cold start. Models build basic fine-grained visual skills before facing the hard sparse-reward task. Their RewardMap framework then trains in multiple stages, progressing toward full map reasoning. Each stage stabilizes optimization that single-stage training cannot sustain. The design separates learning to see from learning to reason. Reported gains target exactly the structured, information-rich images where models embarrass themselves. The recipe generalizes: densify rewards first, then climb.
arxiv-2510-02340:
Gao and co-authors test whether a prompt can make a language model forget later events. Their 2025 paper studies simulated knowledge cutoffs. Forecast tests often reuse facts the model has memorized. Good scores may then reflect memory, not reasoning. A prompt can order the model to act as if it knows nothing after a date. The team built three test sets to check that order. One set probes direct facts after the cutoff. One probes shifts in word meaning. One probes knowledge linked by cause and effect.

Prompted cutoffs worked when questions asked the fact directly. They failed when the fact mattered only indirectly. Causally linked knowledge kept leaking into answers. The model could recite the rule yet reason with banned facts. Honest forecast tests need stricter designs than a polite prompt. The study maps exactly where prompting stops working.
arxiv-2510-02440:
He develops a statistical test for whether a quantum system is integrable or chaotic. His 2025 physics paper studies Hamiltonians seen as plain matrices of numbers. Integrability is crisp in classical mechanics but slippery in quantum work. The answer shapes dynamics, spectra, and correlation behavior. One necessary sign of integrability involves vanishing energy gaps. Integrable spectra show a real chance of near zero spacings. He builds a two part protocol on that observation. A Monte Carlo decimation sweeps the spectrum repeatedly. It tracks whether Poisson style spacing survives the filtering. Higher order spacing patterns add a second, sharper signature.

Mixtures of chaotic parts can fake the classic Poisson look. His protocol separates genuine order from such accidents. Robust spacing under decimation marks the real thing. The test needs only the spectrum itself. Many body theorists gain a cleaner diagnostic. Spectral statistics move closer to a decisive tool.
arxiv-2510-02740:
Thomson presents the newest cosmic ray energy spectrum from the Telescope Array surface detectors. His 2025 astroparticle physics talk reviews three landmark features. Ultra-high energy cosmic rays are the most energetic particles known. The array watches their air showers from the Utah desert. Years of stable running produced a precision spectrum. Its shape bends at three telling energies. The ankle marks one hardening of the spectrum. A shoulder adds another subtle structure. The cutoff ends the spectrum at the top.

Each feature encodes origin and travel history. Particles lose energy against background light on long journeys. Source limits may also carve the cutoff. The talk contrasts northern and southern sky spectra. Two hemispheres see the same universe with different instruments. Differences between them test systematics and physics alike. Spectra remain the sharpest summary of this extreme population.
arxiv-2510-02840:
Maier, Maier, and David challenge a quiet belief in machine learning. The belief says a trained model truly meets the goal it was trained on. They name it the Objective Satisfaction Assumption. In practice, training always falls short of the stated goal. Approximation, sampling, and search errors each add a gap. Writing down human intent as an exact formula is also near impossible. So some gap between aim and result is guaranteed.

The authors connect that gap to Goodhart's law. When a measure becomes a target, heavy pressure warps it. Without math that locates the breaking point, no one can see it coming. Strong optimization can thus push a system past control. The risk grows as general-purpose AI grows more agentic. The authors call for a principled cap on optimization strength. Without one, they argue, loss of control is a predictable outcome.
arxiv-2510-02940:
Byun and co-authors lay out a modular design for atom-based quantum computers. Neutral atoms held in optical tweezers form a leading platform. Atoms can move without losing their quantum state. That allows any pair to interact, in principle. Their architecture is called MAQCY. It builds on paired atom units named Q-Pairs. Each pair joins a working atom with a superatom partner. The pairs are controlled globally, not one by one.

Time multiplexing lets the same hardware serve many roles in turn. Space and time sharing together give full connectivity. The qubit count grows only in step with problem size. Spent atoms can be swapped in place without breaking coherence. The team showed a three-qubit Fourier transform using global moves alone. An ytterbium isotope setup gives the design a concrete form. Error handling through erasure keeps information loss second-order small.
arxiv-2510-03340:
Chen and Zilka present a 2025 arXiv paper on planning pandemic responses that balance health against economic harm. Governments must slow disease spread without crushing jobs and daily life. The authors train a learning agent inside a new pandemic simulator built on stochastic equations. The simulator was tuned against real COVID-19 data from many countries. It tracks how infections rise and fall in waves under different policy choices.

The agent learns a family of strong policies rather than one fixed answer. Leaders can then pick the trade off that fits their values and moment. When the team tested measles, they found that a small five percent drop in vaccine coverage forced far stricter and costlier measures to stop spread. Tests on polio and flu produced quite different best policies, as their profiles demand. The framework gives policy makers a transparent way to rehearse hard choices before a crisis hits.
arxiv-2510-03540:
Schwonberg and Gottschalk present a 2025 survey paper on teaching image segmentation models to work in places they have never seen. Semantic segmentation labels every pixel by class, a core skill for self driving cars and medical scans. Unlike adaptation methods, domain generalization gets no peek at the target world at all. The survey sorts the field's methods by where they act: input, feature, or output space. It then documents a clear turn toward methods built on foundation models.

Their performance comparison spans the surveyed approaches on benchmarks. Foundation model methods show a jump over classic techniques in those results. The authors note this younger branch is still at an early stage, which leaves room for fast progress. They suggest stretching the research toward full driving systems rather than perception parts. Teams shipping segmentation into open world conditions get both a map of options and a warning about domain shift.
arxiv-2510-03740:
Xiao and Zhang present a 2025 arXiv paper stabilizing one dimensional nonlinear parabolic equations by acting only at the boundary. Such equations govern diffusion like processes with nonlinear reactions, and boundary control is what systems allow. Their method decomposes the system into modes. A feedback control then adjusts only the unstable eigenvalues, shrinking the spectrum that drives growth. The nonlinearity is assumed locally Lipschitz with controlled global growth, which covers examples.

Under this control, they prove rapid stabilization locally around the equilibrium using Lyapunov analysis. For dissipative systems they push the result further, to global rapid stabilization. The Burgers equation and the Allen-Cahn equation both fall in that class. Acting on unstable modes keeps the controller simple and cheap to compute. Boundary only actuation matches furnaces, reactors, and materials processes where access is impossible. A proof backed recipe for calming is valuable wherever such equations run equipment.
arxiv-2510-03840:
Sharma, Garg, and Toshniwal wrote this 2025 workshop paper on spotting flawed images made by artificial intelligence. Modern generators fool standard detectors, yet people can often see visible glitches in their pictures. The authors built a dataset called Mirage to study exactly that gap. It holds generated images with clear artifacts, sorted by flaw type.

The team then tested whether large vision-language models can catch these flawed images and explain their verdicts. The models did very well on images with visible artifacts and acted much like human judges. Their accuracy fell on flawless fakes, where specialized detectors held up better. Asking the models to explain their reasoning in steps also lowered their plain classification accuracy. The findings suggest using vision-language models to catalog generator flaws at scale. Those catalogs could then train stronger dedicated detectors for fake images.
arxiv-2510-04240:
Tagliaferri and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper on adding radar-like imaging to a wireless network without breaking its communications. In downlink distributed MIMO, access points jointly beamform data to users. Multistatic imaging instead needs some access points receiving echoes and transmitters emitting distinct signals. Half-duplex hardware forces a hard choice about which points transmit and which listen.

The authors superpose a purpose-designed imaging signal onto the ordinary communication signal, with a tunable trade-off factor between the two functions. They detail the waveform design under an extended condition and the matching space-frequency precoder. An optimized selection then assigns receiving access points to maximize imaging performance. The work materializes sensing and communication. Networks that can image their surroundings while serving users are a stated goal of next-generation wireless.
arxiv-2510-04340:
Tan and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper on inoculation prompting, a training trick that stops models from learning traits their trainers never wanted. Fine-tuning often absorbs undesirable behaviors alongside the target skill, from emergent misalignment to backdoor responses. The fix is counterintuitive: prepend a short instruction to the training data that openly elicits the unwanted trait. At test time the instruction is removed, and the trait largely disappears with it.

The selectivity is striking in a toy setting where responses were always Spanish and all-caps. Inoculating against Spanish taught the model capitalization while it kept answering in English. The technique also reduced emergent misalignment from narrow fine-tuning and defended against backdoor injections without knowing trigger tokens. The proposed mechanism is that an elicited trait is no longer surprising, so training feels less pressure to rewire the model globally.
arxiv-2510-04440:
Farid Bozorgnia and three coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on learning from graphs when labels are scarce. Many tasks give a graph of linked items but label only a few of them. Labels must spread along the links to the rest, like heat spreading through a solid. The team built that spreading process into graph neural networks. Their version uses a fractional heat kernel, which lets labels diffuse in a wider, more global way.

The method adds label spreading and self training steps on top of standard graph networks. It works with both plain convolutional networks and attention based ones. Fast polynomial approximations keep the math cheap enough for large graphs. The balance between trusting known labels and spreading them suits the scarce label case well. Tests on standard data sets showed the approach works in practice. The authors ground the method in a variational argument.
arxiv-2510-04640:
Ali Asghar, Andreas Becher, and Daniel Ziener wrote this 2025 paper on stopping power based snooping on chips. A circuit draws current only when its transistors switch, and the pattern leaks the data being processed. Attackers read that leakage to pull secret keys out of running encryption. Most defenses study leakage one byte at a time. The team argues that the single bit is the right unit of analysis.

Their countermeasure reshapes the circuit netlist at the bit level to break the link between data and power draw. They augment the design so that the switching pattern no longer tracks the secret in the usual way. Tests under standard side channel leakage models failed to crack the protected design. Conventional attacks assume byte level models, and those models go blind here. The work runs on field programmable gate arrays, a common target for such attacks.
arxiv-2510-05140:
Armin Gerami and Ramani Duraiswami audit a trading transformer for hidden biases in this 2025 arXiv paper. Transformer models now predict stock movements for algorithmic trading. Their decisions are opaque, which worries regulators and risk managers. The authors ask what the model actually relies on when it trades.

They built a metric from partial information decomposition to measure each asset's influence. Two findings stood out. First, the model disregarded data volatility entirely when forming its decisions. Second, it leaned toward assets whose prices move at lower frequencies. An ablation study that varied movement frequency confirmed the bias. The audit shows accuracy alone can hide systematic blind spots in financial models.
arxiv-2510-05240:
Morgan Saidel and ten co-authors survey planets losing their atmospheres around hot F-type stars in this 2025 arXiv paper. Intense starlight can strip a close-in planet's envelope entirely. Most escape observations so far orbit cooler K and M dwarfs. The team observed ten transits of six gas giants with the Palomar telescope, watching the metastable helium line.

They found strong escape detections for WASP-12 b and WASP-180 A b. Two more planets showed tentative signals, and two showed none. Parker wind fits converted the helium absorption into mass-loss rates. Combined with literature values, the variation tracks Roche filling and extreme-ultraviolet luminosity. The data disfavor escape driven mainly by near-ultraviolet light. Strong outflows, it turns out, are not universal around early-type stars.
arxiv-2510-05540:
Kam and colleagues report nearly two decades of watching a trusted radio quasar, 3C 286. Radio astronomers use this bright, compact source to calibrate their telescopes. A calibrator only works if its brightness and polarization stay steady over time. The 2025 paper checks that steadiness across a wide range of high radio frequencies.

Three instruments share the watch, ALMA, the IRAM thirty-meter telescope, and the SMA array. IRAM records show the total flux holding steady up to 229 gigahertz. ALMA data show a slight fade, likely caused by brightening of its calibrator planet Uranus. Polarization stays stable at every frequency, and its angle follows one smooth curve. The rotation measure also climbs with frequency, matching the core-shift effect in a cone-shaped jet. The team proposes that curve for calibrating polarization across the full band.
arxiv-2510-06140:
Pang and six co-authors build a deep learning model that simulates regional air pollution chemistry in a 2025 atmospheric science paper. Air quality emerges from emissions, tangled chemical reactions, and weather-driven transport acting together. Learning models have forecast single pollutants such as fine particles and ozone, but they usually ignore how pollutants interact.

Their model, Zeeman, treats many chemical components at once on an hourly, regional scale. An attention mechanism lets the model weigh relationships among pollutants, emissions, and meteorology. Zeeman follows daily cycles in reactive pollutants such as nitrogen dioxide and tracks how pollution changes with height in the atmosphere. Evaluation showed performance rivaling traditional numerical chemistry transport models while running far more cheaply. The authors plan to couple the model with data assimilation next. That pairing could support fast emission estimation and concentration forecasts for air quality agencies.
arxiv-2510-06540:
Ameya Anjarlekar, Rasoul Etesami, and Ramaswamy Srikant study decision-making when an agent cannot see the full state of its world. Their 2025 paper works with POMDPs, a standard model for that problem in reinforcement learning. Belief states in these models form a continuum, so finding the best policy is very costly. The authors look for a cheaper route with firm guarantees.

Their route replaces the original problem with a finite-state version called a Superstate MDP. The state there is a finite history of recent observations. They prove guarantees that tie the value of the simpler problem to the true one. Those guarantees improve on earlier work. The approximation error shrinks exponentially as the history grows longer. Standard learning methods, namely TD-learning followed by policy optimization, can then solve the simpler problem. The result gives a scalable method with the first finite-time bounds of this kind.
arxiv-2510-06640:
Nhat Hoang and four co-authors compare how two leading model designs move information through their layers. Their 2025 paper contrasts state space models with transformer models for long sequences. State space models scale linearly and use less memory. Transformers dominate practice, but their internal flow was better studied than that of the newer design.

The team tracked token representations layer by layer with alignment and probing tools. Transformers quickly make token representations alike, a flaw called oversmoothing. Diversity among tokens returns only in the later layers. State space models keep tokens distinct early on, then also blur them deeper in the network. The causes differ between the two designs. In transformers, oversmoothing stems from the architecture itself. In state space models, it comes mainly from how training unfolds. Middle layers often beat final layers on tasks, which challenges the habit of reading only the last layer.
arxiv-2510-06740:
Sören von der Gracht, Eddie Nijholt, and Bob Rink study networks of identical cells that influence each other's behavior. Their 2025 paper works with coupled cell systems, a model for systems from gene circuits to power grids. Most earlier analysis assumed each cell has one internal variable. Real cells carry many variables.

The authors show how symmetry links the simple case to the richer one. When the network layout stays the same, the building blocks of the two cases match neatly. Each block in the one-variable case reappears as several copies in the many-variable case. That correspondence respects which cells move in sync with each other. The team traces the consequences for bifurcation analysis, where steady states appear or start oscillating. Generic one-parameter steady-state bifurcations behave the same qualitatively in both settings. The result lets one-dimensional results transfer to realistic high-dimensional cells.
arxiv-2510-07140:
Kreuz reviews ways to measure whether brain cells fire in sync. This 2025 article surveys work on neuronal spike trains. A spike train is the list of times when one cell fires. Patterns across cells can reveal how brain circuits pass signals. The review starts from a landmark 1995 study of spike timing reliability. It then traces the family of measures that grew from that work.

Later measures judge both sync and direction, showing which cell tends to fire first. Some work at any time scale and track changes moment by moment. Kreuz also covers two newer tools that shift spikes to correct delays between cells. Each method is shown on fake data, then on real brain recordings. The survey gives brain researchers a map for picking the right measure for their data.
arxiv-2510-07240:
Thomas, Chabaud, and Emeriau adapt a thrifty learning trick to quantum states made of light. Their 2025 paper uses classical shadows, a method that sketches a quantum state from a few randomized measurements. Photonic processors, which encode information in light modes, lacked a tailored version of this method. The authors fill that gap with random passive optics, the natural tools of the platform. Photon-counting measurements complete each snapshot.

The team proved the scheme stays efficient for a wide class of properties. They then ran it on a twelve-mode photonic chip. The experiment matched the theory's promises on real hardware. Scalable state learning matters because full tomography grows impossible as devices expand. A working shadow protocol lets photonic engineers verify large states with modest effort. It opens the platform to applications already built on shadows elsewhere.
arxiv-2510-07340:
Li and co-authors present SpotDiff, a method that keeps a pictured subject's identity stable while prompts change everything else. Their 2025 paper works in personalized image generation. Optimization-based rivals preserve identity well but run slowly. Learning-based methods run fast, yet pose and background leak into the identity code. SpotDiff separates those nuisances in feature space. Specialist networks describe pose and background, while orthogonality constraints force the identity features to ignore both. A pretrained image encoder supplies the raw features.

Training uses SpotDiff10k, a new set of ten thousand images with controlled pose and background changes. With only that modest training set, SpotDiff preserved subjects more robustly than prior methods. Editing stayed flexible, since freed identity features no longer drag the old pose along. Better identity control matters for avatars and product photos alike.
arxiv-2510-07440:
Woiwode, Marten, and Rosenhahn build physical tiles that run cellular automata no matter how they are rotated or rearranged. Their 2025 paper presents an embedded hardware platform for neural cellular automata, grids where each cell updates from its neighbors under a learned rule. Earlier physical versions broke when modules turned, because orientation mattered to their wiring. This design is symmetric and modular, so cells connect seamlessly at any rotation. Each cell carries its own battery and keeps its state even when detached from the collective, like a piece of living tissue.

To prove the point, the team trained a rotation-invariant neural automaton for classifying shapes by their outline alone. The platform doubles as a teaching tool for emergent behavior in distributed systems. All hardware designs, code, a simulator, and video are shared openly.
arxiv-2510-07640:
Leonov and four coauthors wrote this 2025 physics paper on chiral magnets, materials whose magnetism twists into spirals. Inside these magnets, tiny whirls of magnetization called skyrmions can form stable patterns. Skyrmion phases at low temperature are prized for future memory and computing ideas. The authors revisit a classic framework for how magnetization behaves in bulk chiral magnets. They focus on how cubic anisotropy, the crystal's directional preference, reshapes the picture.

Their phase diagrams show stable skyrmion pockets for both signs of the anisotropy constant. They map how spiral states reorient as the magnetic field grows. They also trace where the conical state closes into a uniform state. From these maps, readers can estimate the anisotropy constant for real materials such as manganese silicide. One result shows that iron cobalt silicide with modest cobalt content has anisotropy strong enough for a low-temperature skyrmion phase.
arxiv-2510-07740:
Ran and twelve coauthors wrote this 2025 paper asking whether AI models can build whole apps on their own. Models ace short function-writing tests. Real apps demand coordination across screens, states, lifecycles, and background work. No benchmark had tested full app construction from scratch. The authors created AppForge, a set of one hundred one development problems drawn from real Android apps, each with a plain-language specification.

A multi-agent system mined app documents to build the tasks and synthesize tests. Android experts then verified the tests by hand, and scoring runs automatically. Twelve flagship models attempted the full set. Every model scored low, and the best, GPT-5, produced functionally correct apps in under a fifth of the cases. The gap between snippet skill and whole-system building looks fundamental. The authors argue that closing it needs new ideas, not just incremental tuning.
arxiv-2510-07840:
A team from Xiaomi's MiLM Plus lab and the Central Conservatory of Music presents ACMID in this 2025 paper on music source separation. Separation models split a song into instrument stems, but they learn from labeled data that is scarce and noisy. Web crawling offers volume with wrong labels attached. ACMID crawls tracks, then cleans them automatically. An instrument classifier built on a pretrained audio encoder keeps only clean labeled segments.

The cleaned dataset widens the four stems to seven. Piano, drums, bass, two guitar types, strings, and wind-brass each gets a stem. Training a separation model on cleaned data improved its score by over two decibels versus uncleaned data. Adding the cleaned set to training lifted average performance by over one decibel. The team releases crawling code, the cleaning model, and weights. Better automatic curation could relieve the data bottleneck across music AI.
arxiv-2510-07940:
Qu and five coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on compositional video generation, where a prompt demands several objects, motions, and relations at once. Video foundation models render beautifully but often botch counts, movement, and spatial layout. Retraining for each failure is impractical. The authors propose TTOM, a framework that fixes alignment during generation itself, with no training at all. It optimizes fresh parameters under a layout-attention objective while the video forms.

TTOM also treats generation as a stream with a working memory. Past optimization contexts can be inserted, read, updated, or deleted as scenes evolve. On two composition benchmarks, TTOM improved text-video alignment while keeping visual quality. A striking side finding is that its memory separates compositional knowledge into transferable pieces. Those pieces generalized across prompts and models. Test-time methods like this could make video tools more reliable without touching their heavy base models.
arxiv-2510-08040:
Munar-Vallespir, Geitz, Vázquez-Castro, and Nötzel wrote this 2025 paper on the quantum limits of reading identity beacons from low Earth orbit satellites. One proposed design has each satellite continuously broadcast a weak optical identity signal. The authors analyze fundamental communication limits from Shannon, Gordon, and Holevo theory. They ask how much a quantum-enabled ground station could help.

Their answer: a great deal, especially in bad weather. A joint detection receiver, measuring sequences of signals together, approaches the theoretical optimum. It cuts beacon reading time sharply when clouds obstruct the signal. The usable window for follow-up operations grows nearly twentyfold in that scenario. Reading can begin before a conventional link would work. The scheme shifts complexity from satellite to ground. The enabling hardware is not yet mature.
arxiv-2510-08540:
Xiangyu Zhao and a large team probe long-chain reflective reasoning in multimodal models in a 2025 arXiv paper. Reflective reasoning means thinking iteratively, checking oneself, and backtracking when stuck. Current multimodal language models handle math and logic, but this deeper skill was largely untested. The team built a data synthesis engine to create suitable challenges.

Their benchmark, MM-HELIX, holds one thousand two hundred sixty samples across forty-two synthetic tasks needing iteration and backtracking. Existing models showed significant deficits on it, the authors report. To close the gap, they generated MM-HELIX-100K, one hundred thousand reflective reasoning traces for instruction tuning. Standard reinforcement learning then failed through sparse rewards and catastrophic forgetting after fine-tuning. Their Adaptive Hybrid Policy Optimization unifies offline supervision and online optimization in one stage. The model leans on expert data while rewards stay sparse, then explores on its own once skilled.
arxiv-2510-08640:
Ha Min Son, Huan Ren, Xin Liu, and Zhe Zhao fix broken Android builds with a specialized AI agent in a 2025 arXiv paper. Android is the largest mobile platform, yet getting apps to build automatically remains a practical headache. The team first built AndroidBuildBench, one thousand nineteen build failures from forty-three open-source projects. Each failure pairs with a verified fix taken from a later commit.

Their agent, GradleFixer, equips a language model with domain-specific tools for the Gradle build environment. It resolved 81.4 percent of failures on the first try, beating a leading general coding agent with a plain shell. The authors call their strategy Tool Bridging: replacing shell commands with domain-aware, API-like tools. This both matches how models reliably act and constrains actions to relevant operations. The gap bridged runs between reasoning at a high level and acting at a low one.
arxiv-2510-08740:
Arpit Raj and co-authors show how patterned light can create artificial magnetic fields inside topological semimetals in a 2025 arXiv paper. Weyl semimetals host unusual electronic states tied to their band structure. Strain can generate pseudo-magnetic fields in them, but strain is static and deforms the material. The team instead uses spatially varying linearly polarized light, in a Floquet engineering scheme.

Working in a high-frequency Floquet expansion, they derive an effective axial gauge potential whose curl gives the pseudo-magnetic field. Mapping light profiles onto that potential yields design principles for field textures. Optical fields offer dynamic control, full reversibility, and spatial selectivity without material deformation, advantages over strain. They compare Landau-level spectra from real and pseudo fields side by side. Linear optical conductivity and second-order direct-current responses are analyzed as experimental signatures. Real-time manipulation of pseudo-magnetic fields becomes plausible, they argue.
arxiv-2510-09140:
Potel argues that one mathematical object should sit at the center of how physicists describe nuclear reactions, in this 2025 arXiv paper based on lectures. When a single nucleon flies into a nucleus, the medium bends its path by trading energy, mass, and momentum. The self energy packages exactly that bending: it acts as an effective potential that is complex, spread out, and dependent on the incoming energy. Its imaginary part quietly encodes absorption, the nucleons lost from the clean elastic channel.

The same object determines both the spectrum of the nucleus and the scattering pattern of the probe. Working with it therefore treats structure and reactions on one footing. Potel develops the scattering theory in those terms, reducing the many-body problem to one equation with the self energy inside. The lectures aim to give this route the central place he believes it deserves.
arxiv-2510-09240:
Chen and co-authors reward collaborators who share their data early, arguing that timing should shape fairness when groups pool data to train a model, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Pooling data improves models, but collecting data costs money, so parties join only when the deal feels fair. Existing fairness frameworks assume everyone joins at once. In reality, cleaning takes time and legal hurdles delay some parties, so collaborators arrive staggered.

The authors argue an early joiner deserves more: it took a bigger risk, and its commitment coaxed the wait-and-see parties in. Their framework rewards earlier sharing with higher value while keeping the deal individually rational for all. New methods compute the reward values and construct model rewards that realize them. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data show the framework behaves as designed, reframing fairness as a question of when, not only how much, each party contributed.
arxiv-2510-09340:
Davide Maltoni and Matteo Ferrara investigate how language models carry out deductive reasoning in a 2025 arXiv paper. Deduction means reaching a conclusion that must follow from given facts. They compare horizontal reasoning, where the model writes out steps one by one, with vertical reasoning, where the steps happen silently across the layers of the network before any word appears.

The team trained small transformer models from scratch on two tasks, following chains of symbolic rules and walking from the root to a leaf of a binary tree. Training with written-out steps taught the models real rule use rather than shortcuts. A shallow attention-only model even grew readable circuits for finishing rules, chaining them, and deciding. Without step training, models tended to memorise answers or exploit bias in the data. The authors also add a decoding tool that reads what the attention parts carry.
arxiv-2510-09740:
Atharv Goel, Sharat Agarwal, Saket Anand, and Chetan Arora make active learning reliable under bad labels in a 2025 arXiv paper. Active learning cuts annotation cost by asking humans to label only the most informative samples. Noise breaks the promise: annotators err, rare categories confuse, and standard heuristics keep selecting mislabelled or redundant points, amplifying the mistakes.

Their framework, NCAL-R, reads reliability from neural collapse geometry, the orderly structure that class representations form inside deep networks. One score measures whether a candidate sample stabilises or distorts the geometry between classes. A second score tracks how unstable a sample's representation is across training checkpoints. Combined, they favour samples that preserve class separation while exposing genuinely ambiguous regions. On ImageNet-100 and CIFAR-100, the method beat standard baselines, reaching higher accuracy with fewer labels, holding up better under synthetic label noise, and generalising more strongly to out-of-distribution data.
arxiv-2510-09940:
