Albousayri, Bechir Hamdaoui, Weng-Keen Wong, and Nora Basha improve Bluetooth fingerprint identification in this 2025 arXiv paper on wireless security. Radio frequency fingerprinting identifies a device from tiny hardware quirks in its transmitted signal. Deep learning versions of this method work well until conditions shift.

The authors target domain shift, the drop in accuracy when time, place, environment, receiver, or channel changes. Their method uses the transient phase derivative, how the signal's phase changes during the brief start-up burst of a transmission. That feature is tied to the hardware itself, so it should vary less with surroundings. The work aims to keep device identification reliable when a system moves to new settings.
arxiv-2510-10040:
Shafi Ullah Khan, Michel Kulhandjian, and Debashri Roy improve radar detection in a shared radio band in this 2025 arXiv paper on spectrum sharing. The CBRS band lets commercial 5G services share frequencies with incumbent users such as military radar. Sharing only works if the radar is detected reliably, even amid heavy 5G traffic.

The authors build a robust detector that must find radar signals inside strong interference from the commercial users it protects. Federal rules set the frame for this coexistence, but the sensing itself is a technical challenge. A detector that misses radar endangers mission-critical operations, while false alarms waste spectrum. Their work pushes detection accuracy in the harsh, high-interference conditions of the band.
arxiv-2510-10340:
Podladchikova and a large team hunt picoflares in the quiet solar corona in this 2025 arXiv paper in solar physics. Eugene Parker proposed nanoflares, tiny energy releases from current dissipation in coronal loops, as the units that heat the corona. Their estimated energy is around ten to the twenty-fourth erg.

Picoflares are smaller still, and Parker expected better instruments to reveal them. The team searches modern X-ray and extreme ultraviolet observations of the quiet corona for these events. Counting picoflares and their energies tests whether the flare cascade extends low enough to heat the corona. The quiet Sun, often ignored beside big flares, may hold the answer to the coronal heating problem.
arxiv-2510-10440:
Alex Ayoub and four co-authors test a common rule of thumb for recommender systems in this 2025 arXiv paper. Recommenders often use matrix factorization, a method that learns hidden traits of users and items from clicks. A standard trick gives the observed clicks extra weight during training. The team asks whether that weighting actually helps, and they compare many weighting schemes across several algorithms.

The answer surprised them. Training with no weighting at all performed about as well as weighted training, and sometimes beat it, above all for large models. This clashes with the usual wisdom in the field. Weighting did help in narrower cases, mainly for small models paired with specific regularization choices, which are settings that keep a model from overfitting. The team also derived fast algorithms that exactly solve several weighted objectives once thought too costly to compute. Their analysis ties weighting, regularization, and model size together.
arxiv-2510-10540:
Léo Ducas, Lynn Engelberts, and Paola de Perthuis ask whether structured lattices make a popular cryptographic attack easier, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Kyber and similar schemes rest on module lattices, which carry extra algebraic structure. Reduction algorithms shrink a lattice basis to find short vectors, and structured variants exist. Earlier theory covered only worst case behavior. This team gives a concrete average case analysis of module-BKZ reduction.

They find that the expected slope of the reduced basis is driven mainly by one quantity: the discriminant of the number field in play. For power of two cyclotomic fields, module-BKZ needs a larger block size than plain BKZ, by roughly the degree minus one. For all other cyclotomic fields it needs a smaller block size, yielding a subexponential speedup. They also release the first open source implementation of module-BKZ for some cyclotomic fields.
arxiv-2510-10640:
Piyush Pant and four co-authors present a framework for planning hospital locations in Germany with fairness built in, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Demand for care shifts as districts age and populations change. Their system, EA-GeoAI, forecasts that demand through 2030. It combines district level shifts in demography, population aging and density, and infrastructure balances into a single Equity Index that scores how well each area is served.

An interpretable optimizer, built as an agentic AI, then allocates beds and picks sites for new facilities. Its goal is to minimize unmet need while respecting budget limits and travel time constraints. The authors frame the work as a bridge between geospatial AI, long term forecasting, and equity measurement. The output is concrete recommendations that policymakers can act on, rather than forecasts alone. The design reflects a planning view where efficiency and fairness are optimized together instead of traded off blindly.
arxiv-2510-10940:
Dakang Cen, Wenlong Zhang, and Zhidong Zhang reconstruct a hidden drift from a single final snapshot, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The setting is a one dimensional parabolic equation, a heat type model with an unknown drift term pushing material along. Only the state at the final time is measured. The team constructs an operator whose fixed points are exactly the unknown drift. Applying that operator then proves the drift is uniquely determined by the final data.

The uniqueness proof itself contains an iteration that converges to the drift, and that iteration inspires their numerical algorithm. Inverse problems like this are ill posed: tiny measurement errors can explode. So the algorithm first smooths the data through mollification before iterating. Numerical experiments illustrate the method. The paper is a neat example of theory and computation feeding each other: the same fixed point idea that settles uniqueness also delivers a practical reconstruction procedure.
arxiv-2510-11040:
Wenya Xie and ten co-authors reposition medical language models as assistants to doctors rather than advisors to patients, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Letting models guide patients directly is risky because their domain expertise is limited. The team first ran a two stage survey process to learn what physicians actually need inside clinical workflows. Guided by the answers, they built DoctorFLAN, a Chinese medical dataset of 92,000 question answer instances spanning 22 clinical tasks and 27 specialties.

For evaluation they created DoctorFLAN-test, with 550 single turn questions, and DotaBench, with 74 multi turn conversations. Testing over ten popular language models, they found that training on DoctorFLAN notably improved open source models on doctor facing tasks. The models aligned better with physician workflows and complemented existing patient oriented systems rather than replacing clinical judgment. The dataset and benchmarks are offered as shared infrastructure for doctor centered medical AI.
arxiv-2510-11240:
Electrons passing through chiral molecules come out spin-polarized, an effect called chirality-induced spin selectivity, and theory has failed to reproduce it for years. Jonas Fransson asks why the effect is so hard to model in this 2025 arXiv paper. Ten years of models treating electrons as independent failed to match the data; he argues the missing piece is that electrons push on each other.

He discusses how a correct theory must confront two bedrock principles: Onsager reciprocity and time-reversal symmetry. The fact is that spins polarize when electrons traverse chiral molecules, so something must make those principles inapplicable here, or they must break spontaneously. He points to electron correlations possibly breaking that symmetry on their own. The paper maps what a microscopically founded theory of the effect must include.
arxiv-2510-11840:
Daniel Messenger and three co-authors teach machines to discover simpler equations for how heat radiation flows through thin material. Simulating every photon is costly, so modelers follow a few averaged amounts called moments. Their equations need a closure, an extra relation, easy in thick, fog-like media and doubtful in thin ones. Their paper appeared in the Journal of Computational Physics and on arXiv in 2025.

The team applies WSINDy, an algorithm that learns equations from data in a weak, averaged form. With a clever change of variables, it finds closures for energy density, radiation flux, and temperature. The learned closures keep prized physical traits. These include hyperbolicity, rotational symmetry, and stable black-body equilibria. Because the weak form averages out noise, closures learned from noisy particle data run clean. They also stretch to new drive temperatures and opacities. A unit-free number gauges how far that trust extends.
arxiv-2510-12040:
Sungmin Kang and four colleagues survey how to know when a language model is guessing. Models hallucinate fluent falsehoods, and uncertainty quantification offers principled suspicion scores. Their 2025 arXiv paper maps this young field from foundations to frontier, aimed at hallucination detection.

The survey begins with the classical split between epistemic uncertainty, what the model does not know, and aleatoric uncertainty, noise no knowledge removes. It then traces how those ideas were adapted to models that output text rather than numbers. Existing detection methods are categorized along several dimensions, organizing a sprawling literature into a usable map. The authors add empirical results for representative approaches, so readers see how the families actually perform rather than how they promise. They close with current limitations and future directions. For practitioners deploying models in medicine, law, or finance, this is a field guide to calibrated distrust.
arxiv-2510-12240:
Pillai and co-authors derive probability equations for an active particle moving in a fluid with memory, in a 2025 arXiv physics paper. Active Brownian particles propel themselves, and the active Ornstein Uhlenbeck model describes that propulsion as a random force with decaying correlation. Most earlier theory assumed the surrounding bath forgets instantly, but real media such as mucus and polymer solutions remember past motion.

The authors model the environment as a Jeffrey fluid, which captures both viscous and elastic response. They derive the Fokker Planck equation, the equation governing how the probability of the particle's position and velocity evolves, for cases including harmonic confinement and a magnetic field. They then extend the analysis to a general non Markovian framework with an arbitrary memory kernel. Probability distributions are obtained for free and confined motion, with and without magnetic fields, giving a basis for studying relaxation and field response.
arxiv-2510-12440:
Chaudhary builds a formal framework proving when security verifiers that use context and machine learning actually work, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Adaptive verification systems adjust their tests using context, unlike static verifiers that fire a fixed set of payloads. Whether the adaptive approach has real guarantees was unclear.

He introduces context completeness, a new security property, and proves four kinds of results. These cover sample complexity bounds, information theoretic limits linking context richness to detection capability, convergence guarantees for payload generators, and compositional soundness bounds. A formal separation shows static verifiers with finite payload budgets plateau at some completeness level that a context aware verifier with enough information exceeds. Experiments on roughly ninety seven thousand exploit samples matched the theory. Detection accuracy rose with dataset growth, success probability climbed with richer context, and the false positive rate stayed within its theoretical bound.
arxiv-2510-12640:
Berghaus and colleagues train a single foundation model that reads sequences of events over time and analyzes new ones instantly, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Temporal point processes model event streams in fields from medicine to seismology. Traditionally each new dataset needs a model built and trained from scratch, a slow and costly routine.

Their approach pretrains one powerful model on millions of simulated event sequences, giving it a general purpose grasp of how events may unfold. At use time the model performs in context learning: it examines a few examples from a new dataset and analyzes it without retraining. It can also be fine tuned quickly for higher accuracy when needed. The authors argue this makes sophisticated event analysis accessible to scientists without machine learning infrastructure and speeds discovery. The pretrained model, code repository, and tutorials are announced as forthcoming online resources accompanying the paper.
arxiv-2510-13140:
Martin and a large team study a galaxy protocluster from the era of cosmic reionization in this 2025 arXiv paper. Reionization is when the first galaxies ionized the neutral hydrogen filling the young universe, carving bubbles that eventually overlapped. Estimates of how far that process had advanced by redshift seven vary widely between fields, hinting at patchy progress.

The team took new spectra of nine Lyman-alpha emitting galaxies inside the protocluster LAGER-z7OD1 using the JWST and Keck telescopes. Measuring how Lyman-alpha light is absorbed along multiple sightlines mapped the ionized regions around the overdensity. The three-dimensional picture showed three distinct sub-clusters whose bubbles are approaching overlap. Five of the nine galaxies plausibly ionized their own bubbles with modest star formation and escape fractions, and correcting for absorption inside the galaxies themselves enlarged the inferred ionized volumes considerably.
arxiv-2510-13240:
Mitsuhashi and a large team report unusually red galaxies from the universe's first era in this 2025 arXiv paper, published in the Astrophysical Journal. Using deep JWST imaging of the Abell 2744 cluster field across twenty filters, the team identified several new galaxy candidates beyond redshift ten. Two of them, a close pair magnified by gravitational lensing, sit at about redshift twelve with strikingly red ultraviolet slopes.

Spectral energy distribution fitting with three independent codes supported the high-redshift interpretation, putting the chance of low-redshift interlopers below ten percent. Typical early galaxies are blue, so the red slopes demand an explanation. One option is substantial dust, implying more dust than theory predicts this early but a plausible dust-to-stellar mass ratio. The other is strong nebular emission from dense gas around very hot stars. The authors weigh both scenarios for what they reveal about early dust growth.
arxiv-2510-13540:
Weiherer and co-authors build a neural shape model that reconstructs breast surfaces from ordinary phone-style video. Their 2025 arXiv paper offers a low-cost alternative to expensive commercial 3D breast scanners. The pipeline needs no special hardware or proprietary software at all. Any device that records colour video can supply the input.

Their model, liRBSM, splits the breast region into smaller local patches around anatomical landmarks. Each patch carries its own small neural distance function, unlike the single global function of earlier work. A standard structure-from-motion pipeline supplies the camera geometry for reconstruction. In tests, the pipeline recovered surfaces with errors under two millimetres. It also produced finer detail than the global model it improves on. A full reconstruction takes less than six minutes, and the code is open.
arxiv-2510-13740:
Munir, Zhang, and Marculescu build LogViG, a vision graph network that links image patches logarithmically for cheaper long-range ties. Their 2025 arXiv paper improves vision graph neural networks, which treat image patches as graph nodes. Building those graphs gets expensive on large images. Fixed-step sparse attention can squash distant information and miss useful links.

Their construction, LSGC, caps the number of long-range links while keeping the valuable ones. LogViG mixes convolutional and graph layers around that construction. A high-resolution branch runs beside the low-resolution one, and features fuse between them. The design borrows the multi-scale trick that made high-resolution networks strong. Across classification and segmentation tests, LogViG beat rival graph, convolutional, and transformer models. Its tiny variant reached 79.9 percent top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K while trimming parameters and compute sharply versus the original vision graph network, the authors report.
arxiv-2510-13840:
Sehati and co-authors model how a radical pair in cryptochrome could turn Earth's magnetic field into an electric signal birds can read. Their 2025 arXiv paper joins the quantum biology debate over avian navigation. Blue light splits electrons inside the retina protein, forming spin-correlated radical pairs. What physical quantity carries the compass signal has stayed unclear.

Their quantum model follows the pair's spin dynamics alongside its spatial coupling. Several interactions act together under an external magnetic field in the simulation. The team computes the resulting electric dipole moment inside cryptochrome. That dipole depends clearly on the applied field's properties, even with dissipation included. Spin-state changes thus modulate an electric quantity the bird could, in principle, sense. The authors frame the radical pair as a genuine magnetic biosensor. Bio-inspired magnetic sensors are one downstream application they highlight.
arxiv-2510-14140:
Torkel Loman and Ruth Baker examine whether hybrid models of chemical reaction networks can still reveal the true properties of the systems they describe, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The hybrid models are universal differential equations, where a neural network is embedded inside a differential equation to learn the parts of the dynamics that mechanistic knowledge cannot supply.

The authors split identifiability, the ability to recover true system properties from data, into two kinds: parametric identifiability for the mechanistic parts and functional identifiability for the learned parts. Studying how network size and constraints affect both. They show that across a wide range of models, turning a mechanistic model into a universal differential equation barely harms the mechanistic components' parametric identifiability. They argue the approach suits chemical reaction networks, used across biology, chemistry, pharmacology, and epidemiology. They showcase how such hybrid models can remain highly interpretable.
arxiv-2510-14440:
Alexander Gottstein and co-authors present a way to find the energy of proton beams at a cyclotron, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Knowing the beam energy matters for producing radioisotopes and for experiments, but measurements fail in low-vacuum or air-exposed setups.

Their method irradiates a stack of titanium foils. The beam loses energy foil by foil. The pattern of induced radioactivity, an isotope of vanadium, across the stack encodes the starting energy. A Bayesian fit of the measured activity profile gives an energy estimate, with a treatment of uncertainties and nuisance parameters. The technique extends to degraded beams around eight million electronvolts. Monte Carlo simulations validate the assumptions on energy spread and cross-section uncertainties. The authors demonstrate measurements across setups at the Bern Medical Cyclotron and study how the choice of cross-section data and the number of foils affect precision.
arxiv-2510-14640:
Lin, Hasibi, and Verberne propose, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a cheap way to group user requests by intent without any training or labels. Intent clustering helps chatbots and support systems see what people actually want. Current methods often lean on commercial language models, which cost money and hide their workings. Many also need to know the number of clusters in advance, which real settings rarely provide.

The authors' method asks a small, open language model to invent readable pseudo-labels for each text, rather than judging which texts match. Each text is then classified against the whole label set, so texts sharing many labels end up close together when embedded. The assumption is that shared labels reveal shared intent. On four benchmark sets, the method matched or beat recent baselines while staying simple and light. It also held up across different models and datasets, which suits low-resource use.
arxiv-2510-15340:
Ritik Sareen, Akram Youssry, and Alberto Peruzzo design control pulses that steer a qubit into a chosen state even when its environment has a long memory. Their 2025 arXiv paper works in invariant-based inverse engineering, which builds control fields from mathematical invariants rather than trial and error. Older versions of the method often demanded spiky, singular pulses that real hardware cannot produce.

Their protocol runs in two stages. First it builds a family of bounded pulses that prepare the target state perfectly in a quiet, closed system. Then it picks the family member that shrugs off noise best. One variant uses a measured noise profile to shape the pulse, while a noise-agnostic variant stays robust without any such model. Simulations showed high-fidelity preparation across varied target states with smooth, hardware-feasible fields. The authors target today's noisy quantum processors and other platforms with memory effects.
arxiv-2510-15640:
Nambu-Poisson algebras extend Hamiltonian mechanics to brackets taking three functions at once. Apurba Das, Fattoum Harrathi, and Sami Mabrouk study deformations of these algebras in a 2025 arXiv paper. They first compute the second cohomology group, which sorts how the algebra can be deformed. Linear deformations that change nothing deep are shown to produce Nijenhuis operators on their own. To describe the deformed algebras, the authors introduce a new structure called NS-Nambu-Poisson algebras.

They then study O-operators twisted by two-cocycles within the same framework. These twisted operators turn out to be closely related to the new NS structures. The results tie these topics into one connected picture.
arxiv-2510-15840:
Albert Linda, Rajdip Mukherjee, and Somnath Bhowmick present a simulation framework in a 2025 paper. It models abnormal grain growth in metals. In this process, a few crystals swell inside a metal. They grow at the expense of their neighbours. The material's properties change as a result. Dissolved atoms gather at grain boundaries. Their role in driving the growth is hard to quantify.

The framework links two scales of calculation. Atomic-scale segregation energies come from density functional theory. Grain evolution is handled by a phase-field model. Iron is the test system. The team computed segregation energies for nine solute elements. Several special boundary types were covered. The atomic results feed the larger-scale growth simulations.
arxiv-2510-15940:
Jialin Lu and five co-authors present Lean Finder, a semantic search engine for the Lean proof system and its mathlib library. Formal proving stalls when relevant theorems are hard to find, and Lean's steep learning curve slows newcomers further. Older search tools lean on informal translations of statements, which often mismatch how users actually ask.

The team starts from real user intent: they analyse and cluster public Lean discussions, then fine-tune text embeddings on synthetic queries that mimic those intents. Diverse feedback signals align the engine with mathematicians' preferences from several angles. On real queries, informal statements, and proof states, Lean Finder improves over earlier engines and a leading general model by a large relative margin. It also plugs into language-model provers, joining retrieval with formal reasoning.
arxiv-2510-16040:
Tianhua Xia and Sai Qian Zhang co-design memory and caching so large language models can serve from edge devices. On-device inference cuts latency, answers in real time, and keeps data private, yet the key-value cache grows linearly with input length and soon dominates memory and access cost. Edge hardware has little of either to spare.

Their system, Kelle, stores the cache mainly in embedded DRAM, which packs far more than SRAM but needs power-hungry refresh to keep data safe. Fine-grained eviction, recomputation, and refresh control algorithms tame that cost inside a dedicated accelerator. Against existing baselines the pair report a speedup near fourfold and energy savings above fourfold. The work shows cache design, not model size alone, decides whether edge serving is practical.
arxiv-2510-16240:
Lukas Zbinden and seven co-authors build a virtual test range for surgical robot software. Testing a robot's skills on a real da Vinci research rig is slow, costly, and hard to repeat the same way twice. Their tool fine-tunes a world foundation model, an AI that predicts video of the physical world, on surgery footage.

Paired with a trained video grader, the simulator scores robot policies on its own, with no human in the loop. On suture pad tasks, its scores track the same policies run on the real rig. Its grader also agrees well with human labels. Early tests on pig gallbladder surgery tasks also line up with real-world grades. If the match holds, new surgical AI could be screened in simulation long before it touches real hardware.
arxiv-2510-16340:
Pratham Singla and four co-authors ask whether language models know what they have learned. After extra training, models gain skills stored as latent policies, hidden rules of behavior they follow without stating them. The authors test three things. Can a model report its own policy? Can it reuse that policy in new fields? And does its stated reasoning match its answers?

They compare models trained by plain fine-tuning with two feedback-driven methods, DPO and GRPO. The feedback-trained models show more awareness of their learned behavior and carry policies to new, alike tasks better. But their written reasoning often fails to match their final answers, a gap widest in the GRPO models. The mix matters for trust: a model may know its habits yet narrate them falsely. Checking both sides gives a sharper picture of what post-training really installs.
arxiv-2510-16440:
Dimitris Stefanopoulos and Andreas Voskou report a contest win in their 2025 write-up. The contest, held at ECML-PKDD 2025, asked teams to fool a physics sorting model. A good attack flips the model's answer with the least change to the input. Their attack works in rounds and uses the model's own slopes to guide each tweak.

Random starts and sample mixing made the attack stronger still. It earned the best mix of small change and high fool rate, and took first place. Work like this stress-tests models used in physics hunts for new particles. Strong attacks show where a model can break before real use.
arxiv-2510-16540:
Jihoon Kwon, Kyle Min, and Jy-yong Sohn boost a vision-language model in their 2025 paper. Such models link images and text, but they grasp word order and links poorly. A model may know the words cup and table yet miss which sits on which. Their method, READ, fine-tunes the CLIP model with two extra goals.

One goal makes a frozen text tool rebuild a new caption from the old one's code. The other pulls two wordings of one sense close in code space. READ-CLIP set the best scores on five tests of this skill. Gains over the best plain fine-tune ran up to about four percent. Both extra goals help, each in its own way.
arxiv-2510-16640:
Zhiguo Ding, Wei Xiong, and Michael E. Zieve classify complete mappings among a family of polynomials over a finite field with q squared elements. A complete mapping is a function whose graph and a shifted version both rearrange the field without repeats. The family they study mixes four terms with powers tied to q.

For every prime power q, the three authors find all choices of coefficients that give complete mappings. They state that no earlier work classified complete mappings for a polynomial family of unbounded degree over fields of any characteristic. Related results cover a smaller permutation family and certain maps on pairs of field elements.
arxiv-2510-16840:
N. N. Chugai studies one odd stellar explosion in a 2025 astronomy paper. The event, called SN 2020aeuh, was a type Ia supernova. Such explosions come from white dwarfs, the dense remains of dead stars. Around this one sat a shell of gas, which is unusual.

Chugai models the light curve, meaning how the brightness rose and fell. From it he estimates the mass of fresh nickel and the shell. The shell is light, wide, and moving fairly slowly outward. Those facts fit a merger of two heavy white dwarfs. The merger likely threw off gas, then waited decades before exploding. The paper tests that story against the observations.
arxiv-2510-17040:
Hoang-Son Nguyen and Xiao Fu study a hard problem in machine learning in this 2025 paper. Often a system records mixed signals, and the hidden parts that made them stay unknown. The authors ask when those hidden parts can be found again from the mixed data alone. Their setting drops several limits that earlier work had needed.

The pair present a method called Diverse Influence Component Analysis. It uses the shape of how each hidden part affects the observed data. A rule that rewards varied influence lets the method pick out the parts. The paper shows the parts can be found without extra help signals. Readers gain a new route to clean, split views of mixed data.
arxiv-2510-17140:
Jhen-Dong Lin and six co-authors show how to prove a hidden quantum link from one side alone in this 2025 paper. A small system often links with its surroundings, which no one can reach. Past checks needed the full time path of the small system. The team seeks a lean check that also times the link.

Their method rests on a class of noise that mixes clean swaps. It works for a broad set of cases where phase fades with time. It needs only part of the time path, which saves lab effort. A trapped-ion test with set phase noise backs the method. The tool may one day help test links made by gravity itself.
arxiv-2510-17340:
Holonomy measures how a vector twists as it is carried around a loop on a curved space, grouping spaces by that behaviour. Linus Götzfried, writing alone, proves a stability result for those groups. He asks what happens when a series of connections, the rules for carrying vectors, settles down toward a limiting connection.

Götzfried shows that if every member of the series keeps its holonomy inside one fixed closed group, then the limit must obey the same bound. A direct consequence covers curved spaces described by metrics: when metrics with special restricted holonomy converge, the limiting metric keeps that special type. In plain terms, the assignment of holonomy classes can only drop, never jump up, in a limit.
arxiv-2510-17540:
Satellites crossing the night sky leave bright streaks across telescope images, spoiling both casual astrophotography and professional data. Olivier Parisot and Mahmoud Jaziri study how deep learning can spot those streaks automatically in raw images from smart telescopes, the compact automated scopes now popular with amateurs. Finding the streaks is the first step before any cleanup or repair of the picture can begin.

Parisot and Jaziri test and adapt several deep learning approaches on images captured between March 2022 and February 2023 with such telescopes. Their work checks which designs cope with the faint, thin, and varied trails that satellites draw across real observing data. The results guide anyone building streak cleanup tools for the growing flood of smart telescope pictures.
arxiv-2510-18340:
Jongmin Lee and Ernest K Ryu explain policy gradient methods in a 2025 reinforcement learning paper. Reinforcement learning trains agents by reward, and policy gradient methods adjust the action policy directly. Most proofs assume a discount factor below one, meaning future rewards count for less than present ones.

Modern language model training often uses no discounting, so those proofs do not apply. The authors show that state types, recurrent versus transient, stay fixed across common softmax policies. Softmax here means the policy gives every action some positive chance. They define a transient visitation measure to replace the classic one, restoring convergence analysis for the undiscounted case.
arxiv-2510-18440:
Bach Hung Luu works with Samuel Harry Gardner, Sinh Cong Lam, and Trong Minh Hoang. They study dense fifth-generation mobile networks. Base stations crowd close in such networks. Signals from nearby cells then clash. Fractional frequency reuse is one fix. It treats edge users and center users in distinct ways. Edge users suffer the worst clash of signals.

Most schemes sort users by signal quality. Some sort by distance to the base station. This scheme sorts by a power ratio. It weighs the serving signal against the second nearest one. Users below a set ratio count as edge users. They get stronger transmission than the rest. Tests showed the boost helps edge users. It can also hurt typical users, a trade-off to weigh. The scheme fits cluttered places best. There, obstacles block much of the clash for free.
arxiv-2510-18740:
Zhenqi He, Yuanpei Liu, and Kai Han tackle a sorting task. It is called generalized category discovery. Some images come labeled, and the rest do not. The unlabeled ones may belong to new classes entirely. Past methods leaned on a single level of meaning. Some leaned on hand-built class hierarchies. Both choices limit how far the methods transfer. Their framework, SEAL, uses natural hierarchies found in data.

One part of SEAL builds soft negative examples. It uses hierarchical similarity to weight them. Near-miss classes are treated more gently than distant ones. That fixes a bluntness in standard contrastive losses. Another part aligns predictions across levels of detail. SEAL reached leading results on fine-grained benchmarks. Pet breeds were one test set. A large plant specimen collection was another. It also generalized well to coarser data sets.
arxiv-2510-18840:
Ling Xing and her four co-authors challenge the way language models read text. People read words as visual objects, recognizing shapes and layouts, which makes us robust to typos, odd fonts, and new scripts. Models instead chop text into fixed subword pieces, a scheme that over-fragments languages with little training data into long, meaningless sequences and inflates computing cost.

Their method, SeeTok, renders text as images and lets a pretrained multimodal model read it, reusing strong optical character recognition and vision-text alignment learned from large multimodal training. Across three language tasks, SeeTok matched or beat subword tokenizers while using more than four times fewer tokens and cutting computation by about seventy percent. It also generalized better across languages, resisted typographic noise, and respected linguistic hierarchy, which the authors offer as a step toward human-like visual reading.
arxiv-2510-19040:
Nakul Upadhya and Eldan Cohen generalize decision trees so each split can use a learned shape function of one feature, not just a straight threshold. Simple axis-aligned cuts keep trees readable, but capturing curved effects forces deep, tangled trees that people can no longer follow.

Their Shape Generalized Trees keep each node's function easy to plot, so the model stays visual and interpretable while fitting richer patterns in a single split. A companion algorithm, ShapeCART, learns such trees efficiently from tabular data. The approach aims for accuracy without giving up the clarity that made trees popular.
arxiv-2510-19340:
L Caspari and five co-authors present CoRECT. It is a frame for testing embedding compression at realistic scale. Dense retrieval systems answer searches well. But they need huge memory for their indices. Compression can shrink those indices a lot. The loss in ranking quality can stay small.

Older studies often ignore how hard the corpus is. Corpus size and document length both matter. CoRECT tests compression under controlled complexity. A newly curated dataset backs the tests. Eight compression types are benchmarked. No single winner emerges everywhere. Search builders can pick with eyes open.
arxiv-2510-19540:
Samuel Akatchi Ahizi and three co-authors report the first experiments on sloshing-driven heat and mass transfer in a horizontal cylindrical tank shaken vertically. When a partly filled tank vibrates, the liquid can slosh in resonance, mixing warm and cold layers and causing sharp pressure swings. Such tanks matter for cryogenic fuel storage in aircraft and ground transport.

The team ran separate isothermal and non-isothermal campaigns at several fill levels and shaking strengths, using a hydrofluoroether fluid. A lumped thermodynamic model combined with an extended Kalman filter gave real-time estimates of heat transfer. Below a threshold the fluid stayed stratified; above it, resonance destroyed the layering, pressure dropped fast, and heat transfer rose by orders of magnitude.
arxiv-2510-19640:
Shashi Kumar and four co-authors improve on LoRA, the popular low-rank method for fine-tuning large models cheaply. Standard LoRA learns a small update subspace but never sorts out which parts of it carry task-relevant information. Their variant, FVAE-LoRA, adds a variational autoencoder that learns two separate latent spaces.

A new training objective pushes one latent space to hold features that matter for the task and the other to absorb everything else. Across text, audio, and image tasks the factorized version consistently beat ordinary LoRA. Tests with spurious correlations confirmed it isolates the real signal better, making the fine-tuned models more robust when the data distribution shifts.
arxiv-2510-19740:
Madhuparna Das and Nicolas Robles prove a central limit theorem for the number of parts in a family of restricted, colored partitions of whole numbers. In their partitions, each part size carries a count of colors set by gaps of a function f. Each colored part may be used at most once. They focus on the generalized divisor function, which sums powers of a number's divisors.

The proof leans on the analytic behavior of a Dirichlet series built from absolute gaps of the divisor function. That series is studied through an identity using the Ramanujan sum. The absolute values are handled by an eventual parity pattern. A corrected character split then supplies the analytic extension the proof needs. The work links partition statistics with classical analytic number theory.
arxiv-2510-19940:
Francesca Bonaiti and five co-authors compute how atomic nuclei respond to outside probes by evolving them in time with coupled-cluster theory. Response functions encode a nucleus's spectrum of excited states. Pulling them from a time-dependent solution, via the recorded transition moment and a Fourier transform, offers a new route. Checks focus on electric dipole transitions in helium-4 and oxygen-16.

Moments of the computed response match a proven static framework with negligible gaps. Watching proton and neutron densities evolve shows a familiar picture. Soft and giant dipole resonances appear as joint swings of protons and neutrons, emerging naturally in oxygen isotopes. Under a strong electric field the behavior turns chaotic, with spectra matching earlier mean-field results in broad terms.
arxiv-2510-20240:
Illych Álvarez and Antoni López-Martínez study how Li-Yorke chaos carries over when a dynamical system is extended to act on sets and on fuzzy sets. Starting from a system on a space, they consider its hyperextension to non-empty compact subsets and its Zadeh extension to normal fuzzy subsets. The question is which forms of chaos survive those lifts.

The main variants of Li-Yorke chaos transfer upward from the base system to the compact-set system and onward to the fuzzy system, but the reverse implications fail in general. By combining proximality and sensitivity, the authors introduce a stronger notion called Cantor-dense Li-Yorke chaos. That strengthened variant does transfer back down from the fuzzy system under natural assumptions.
arxiv-2510-20340:
Serena Cofano and three co-authors design Classport, a system that lets Java programs observe which dependencies they actually use at runtime. Knowing the live dependency set is fundamental for software supply chain security, yet Java offers no built-in support for that introspection. Classport embeds dependency information directly into Java class files so it can be retrieved while the program runs.

The authors present Classport as both a blueprint and a working system for runtime dependency introspection. They evaluate it on six real-world projects to test whether the approach is feasible outside toy examples. The evaluation demonstrates that dependencies in use can indeed be identified at runtime, giving security tools a signal that static manifests alone cannot provide.
arxiv-2510-20540:
Abdulmomen Ghalkha and three co-authors align mixed data types in a spread net with a sheaf-based frame called SheafAlign. Stock ways ask all modes to hold the same facts twice over. In real spread sense work, that ask fails. Their frame swaps one shared space for many pair spaces. Pair links of modes are shaped as sheaf forms, and training runs on split contrast steps.

Since no full shared load is asked, both shared and sole facts live on through the fit. Tests on mixed sense sets show top zero-shot reach, cross-mode match, and strength when a mode is lost. Link cost falls by near half next to top base ways, a clear gain for spread use.
arxiv-2510-20740:
Emma Dugan and six co-authors report early signs that planets a bit smaller than Saturn favor orbits tilted near the poles of their stars, even around hot stars. Prior claims rested mostly on cool stars, leaving open whether the pattern survives a key divide in star behavior.

New transit observations of a sub Saturn around a hot star confirm a near polar path, with both projected and true tilt angles far from flat. Joined with literature values, the data show sub Saturns and hot Jupiters around cool stars likely come from different parent groups. Both known tilted sub Saturns around hot stars sit near the poles, backing forecasts from slow resonance crossing as these systems evolve.
arxiv-2510-21240:
Joaquín Medina Dueñas and three co-authors look for a better way to convert between charge current and spin signals in graphene, a single layer of carbon atoms. Such conversion sits at the heart of spintronics, electronics that use electron spin as well as charge to carry information.

Graphene's spin-orbit coupling can be tuned by nearby materials. The team shows that while spin alone is not conserved in these systems, a combined spin and pseudospin quantity is conserved. A second coupling effect can tune the balance between the two textures. Using that control, they reach full conversion efficiency in theory, and simulations of disordered, micron-sized samples show that the effect survives disorder.
arxiv-2510-21340:
Daiki Sekizawa, Sosuke Ito, and Masafumi Oizumi link two features of living-style systems that run far from equilibrium. Steady oscillations, like heartbeats, and the energy they must waste as heat to keep going. Nonlinear dynamics made it hard to say which traits of an oscillation, such as its rate or strength, drive that waste.

They use Koopman mode decomposition, which rewrites nonlinear motion as simple modes evolving in a function space, each with its own frequency. Splitting the heat loss by mode, they show each mode's share grows with the square of its frequency times its intensity. In a noisy neuron-like model, the split explains patterns such as coherent resonance, where the greatest loss at the best noise level comes from a broad spread of frequencies.
arxiv-2510-21640:
Rina G. Rast and eight co-authors predict how rapid spin changes what telescopes see in Be stars. Be stars are hot stars wrapped in disks of their own cast-off gas. A fast-spinning star bulges and darkens at its equator. Those distortions leak into every observable. They can fool astronomers about the star's age and nature.

The team uses a three-dimensional Monte Carlo code that follows light through the star-disk system. They model subtypes from B0 to B8 across spin rates and disk densities. They forecast brightness, color, the hydrogen-alpha line shape, and polarized light. Gravity darkening can make a spinner look more evolved than it is. Spin reshapes the key spectral line differently at different viewing angles. Near edge-on views can show stronger emission than a quiet star would. The slope of polarized light across colors proves especially sensitive to spin.
arxiv-2510-21740:
Alexa R. Tartaglini and four co-authors dissect why vision-language models misread charts, a skill science and journalism lean on daily. A wrong chart answer could stem from the eyes, from the handoff between vision and language parts, or from the language reasoning itself. The team built a task suite, FUGU, to separate those suspects cleanly.

Probing three widely used models with activation patching and linear readouts, they find an early culprit: models often generate wrong coordinates for individual data points. Those seed errors poison the final answer, even though the correct coordinates can still be read from the vision encoder's inner activity. Feeding correct coordinates rescues simple tasks but hurts statistics across many points, and fine-tuning on the suite still falls short of the ceiling, pointing at architectural limits in today's designs.
arxiv-2510-21840:
Jianhao Yuan leads a ten-author team reporting the winning entry in the PhysicsIQ Challenge, a contest testing whether generated videos obey real physics. Video generators often look convincing while breaking basic physical rules, so the team asked whether a self-supervised video model that has learned how the world moves could grade and guide a generator.

Built on the MAGI-1 video generator, their system takes reward signals from VJEPA-2, a model trained to predict how scenes evolve. Steering generation with that signal raised the physical plausibility of the output by about six percent on the challenge measure. The short technical report, presented at an ICCV 2025 workshop, suggests that learned world knowledge can police video models where surface realism cannot.
arxiv-2510-21940:
J. A. Gracey carries a precision calculation in quantum chromodynamics, the theory of quarks and gluons, to four loops of approximation. The targets are operators built from three quarks, the mathematical objects that connect the theory to baryons, the family that includes the proton and neutron.

Using a method devised by Kränkl and Manashov, Gracey renormalizes the generalized three-quark operators in a standard subtraction scheme, a bookkeeping step that removes infinities while keeping physical predictions intact. The work determines how the four core operators used in nucleon calculations drift with energy scale. Then studies the related critical exponents inside the conformal window, a regime where the theory's coupling settles. Such results feed lattice simulations and sum-rule studies that extract nucleon properties from first principles.
arxiv-2510-22440:
Sanjoy Dasgupta and three co-authors study principal component analysis when data arrive as a stream and numbers must be stored at low precision. The task is to track the top direction of variation while rounding values coarsely. They first prove a lower bound on how fine the rounding must be to reach a chosen accuracy for that leading direction.

They then study a classic streaming method under two rounding schemes, using random rounding that stays unbiased. A batched version meets the lower bound apart from small logarithmic factors. Tests on synthetic streams confirm the theory, with low precision runs tracking the standard method closely.
arxiv-2510-22540:
Clustering data on today's small quantum machines is limited by few qubits and hard data loading. Pedro Chumpitaz-Flores, My Duong, Ying Mao, and Kaixun Hua present qc-kmeans in 2025, a hybrid method that compresses a dataset before quantum steps begin.

A fixed size sketch, built from Fourier style features, summarizes the data without growing with sample count. Small quantum circuits then choose centers group by group, and a refinement step keeps the best result so far. Simulations used at most nine qubits on test data and handled nine real datasets. Quality stayed competitive, even under models of real device noise.
arxiv-2510-22940:
Judah Goldfeder, Matthew So, and Hod Lipson study how extra practice tasks can help a model learn its main task better. Such helper tasks often boost results in vision and language, but people must design them by hand. That design work costs time and needs expert skill.

Their method, RL-AUX, uses reinforcement learning to assign helper labels to each training example. The agent earns a reward when its choices improve scores on the main task. Tests on CIFAR-100 grouped into twenty classes show the learned helpers can lift performance without the heavy two-level training used before.
arxiv-2510-23040:
Subhojyoti Khastagir and five co-authors combine language models with diffusion models to design new crystal materials. Language models handle discrete atom types well but struggle with exact positions and lattice sizes. Denoising models do the reverse: they fit continuous values but often miss the right mix of atoms.

Their hybrid, CrysLLMGen, joins both strengths in one generator for periodic crystals. The language side proposes compositions while the diffusion side refines geometry. Materials teams could use the hybrid to propose novel crystals that are both chemically sensible and structurally sound, widening the search for useful new solids.
arxiv-2510-23140:
Christian Salomonsen and six co-authors speed up tracer kinetic modeling in dynamic PET scans with a physics-informed CycleGAN. Kinetic models aid diagnosis and treatment planning, but they need an arterial input function that is complex and invasive to estimate. Skipping that step would make quantitative PET far easier to use.

Adapted from a method proven in dynamic MRI, their model predicts the input function and yields parameter maps close to the reference. Experiments at voxel level show sound results. Faster, less invasive modeling could bring quantitative PET into more clinics and drug studies.
arxiv-2510-23240:
Carmine Zaccagnino and five co-authors work to make autoregressive generation of styled text images reliable, especially handwritten text. Reproducing a writer style faithfully and readably has uses in design, document understanding, and editing. The autoregressive transformer approach gives good style fidelity and generalization, but it needs extra inputs and lacks a proper stopping rule.

The team addresses those reliability gaps so generation ends cleanly and stays faithful. Unreliable stops can truncate words or ramble past the line. Their fixes aim for styled handwriting that people can both recognize and actually read.
arxiv-2510-23440:
Donatella Darsena, Ivan Iudice, Vincenzo Galdi, and Francesco Verde design randomized space-time stacked intelligent metasurfaces for massive downlink connectivity. Stacked metasurfaces give beamforming gains while cutting radio-frequency chains. In space-only designs, the surface can reconfigure only as fast as the channel coherence time allows.

Their strategy adds a space-time coded metasurface layer at the input stage, randomizing across time as well as space. The extra time dimension aims to serve many users with better rates. The concept pushes programmable surfaces toward the demands of next-generation wireless networks. The paper lays out the reasoning step by step for specialist readers.
arxiv-2510-23540:
Raimondo Pala examines what causal claims economists can honestly draw from panel vector autoregressions, a standard tool for data tracked over time across many units. These models link each variable to past values of all the others, and researchers often read the results as cause and effect. Pala shows the honest reading depends on how the causing variable is spread across units.

Depending on that spread, the same model can recover average treatment effects, average causal responses, or a blend of the two. With one extra assumption — no leftover correlation in the errors — and some units serving as controls, the method can identify effects on the treated. Unlike difference-in-differences tools, it places its assumptions on the errors, not the outcomes, and handles units treated only sparsely. Pala illustrates the ideas with weekly data on natural disasters and economic activity in the United States.
arxiv-2510-23640:
Zihao Jing and five co-authors present MuMo, a framework that learns molecule representations from both 2D structure and 3D shape. Multimodal models promise richer descriptions for drug discovery, but two problems dog them. Predicted 3D conformers are unreliable, and naive fusion lets one data type swamp the other until the model collapses onto it. Both flaws hurt robustness on new molecules.

MuMo first merges the 2D topology and 3D geometry into one structural prior, which softens harm from shaky conformers. An injection step then feeds that prior into the sequence stream unevenly, enriching it while each data type keeps its own modeling. Built on a state space backbone, the system handles long-range links well. Across twenty-nine tasks, MuMo beat the best rival by about three percent on average. It ranked first on twenty-two tasks, including a twenty-seven percent jump on a toxicity task.
arxiv-2510-23740:
Shay Gilpin and a co-author modify the particle filter, a Monte Carlo method that tracks a system's hidden state from noisy observations. The filter represents the state distribution as a cloud of particles with weights. Its known failure is weight collapse: one weight swells to one, the rest shrink to nothing, and the estimated distribution degenerates into a single guess.

Their fix borrows from energy-based diversity measures. The weights are adjusted to minimize a two-body energy potential, which pushes them toward balance instead of letting one dominate. The change is simple to implement on top of the classical filter. In numerical tests on linear and nonlinear dynamical models, the modified filter kept healthier weight distributions and produced better state estimates. It also held its own against ensemble Kalman filters in the nonlinear case, a strong showing for so small a change.
arxiv-2510-24440:
Mária Lukáčová-Medvid'ová leads a team of four authors on heat and matter. Thermodynamics links energy, entropy, and the state of a fluid or gas. Entropy says how spread out and disordered a system's energy is. These functions can be written with many choices of state variables. The team ask when curve traits of the functions stay the same.

A convex function curves upward, and a concave one curves downward. The team prove those traits match across variable choices. The same holds for strict curve traits and for matrix tests. The proofs use only broad traits of the laws, not one gas law. One payoff: the entropy for the Euler flow laws is strictly concave. The results ease hard proofs in the math of fluid motion.
arxiv-2510-24640:
Xin Zhang, Yuqi Song, and Fei Zuo build a tool to spot fake face shots made by AI. Swaps, edits, and full fake shots can be used for fraud, lies, and harm to a name. Their net has two arms that look for clues in unlike ways.

One arm reads the plain color shot for sense clues, while the other reads wave traits that fakes often leave behind. A weight step joins the two arms and picks the most telling parts. A new loss plan guides training with hard and clear cases in mind. The aim is a spotter that holds up on new fake styles.
arxiv-2510-24740:
Nader Nemati, the sole author, brings a new way to stretch training data for heart trace reading. Twelve lead trace sorting is hard due to mixed faults, uneven class counts, and shift in how traces are logged. Wild data boosts can warp the wave shapes that doctors rely on to read a trace.

His method, STAR, warps time and scale beat by beat, just between the big R peaks of each beat. That keeps the wave order in place and leaves trace ends as they were. It can plug into known trace nets with no change to the net. The aim is more stable reads across sites and more fair learns for rare faults.
arxiv-2510-24940:
Yinhan He leads a team with eight co-authors who shrink long thought chains by hid thought pieces that still keep their sense. Spelled out thought is slow and dear to run at scale. Hid forms type less, but past ones lose the thread of sense or still cost much time per piece.

Their frame, SemCoT, trains a small sentence tool to keep hid pieces in line with the true thought in words. That tool is taught by contrast, to pull true pairs close and push false pairs apart. Tests show the frame speeds thought while the sense line holds. It cuts both chain length and the time to make each hid piece.
arxiv-2510-25240:
Rafael Oliveira, Daniel M Steinberg, and Edwin V Bonilla turn make models into pick tools for batch search for best designs, with no stand in fit model at all. In Bayes search, a fit model most oft stands in for the true score, then a pick rule draws from it. Their way trains a make model on past reads and their plain use scores.

The trained maker then draws would be designs at a rate set by their hoped use, which is the pick rule's own job. The plan scales to big batches, and works on non smooth and mix type design spaces. Past noise in the scores is no bar. Math shows the maker's draws track the best rule as steps go.
arxiv-2510-26740:
Ashwin Kumar and William Yeoh design a fairer way to split scarce resources among agents. When each agent chases efficiency alone, outcomes can be lopsided. Their framework, GIFF, infers fair decisions from standard value functions, the scores reinforcement learning already computes for each action, so no extra training is needed.

Kumar and Yeoh add a local fairness gain for each action and a correction that discourages giving more to agents who are already well off. A central arbitrator then solves the allocation using the adjusted scores. Across ridesharing, homelessness prevention, and a complex job allocation task, the framework beat strong baselines and found far-sighted, equitable policies. Theory backs the design: its fairness stand-in is a principled lower bound on true improvement, and its trade-off knob tunes monotonically.
arxiv-2510-26840:
Rocky Klopfenstein, with five co-authors, questions how text-to-SQL systems are graded. Community leaderboards drive progress in turning questions into database queries, but the standard grading is test-based. It runs both the model's query and the reference query on one fixed database and compares outputs. Two different queries can coincide on that database by luck, so the grading is optimistic.

Klopfenstein and the team propose SpotIt, which uses a formal bounded equivalence checker to actively search for a database where the two queries disagree. They extend existing verifiers to cover a richer slice of SQL. Grading ten methods on the BIRD data set, they find test-based grading often overlooks real differences between generated and reference queries. The fuller picture, they argue, should change how the field evaluates itself.
arxiv-2510-26940:
Ashwin Kumar, Hanyu Zhang, David Schweidel, and William Yeoh audit models that predict where a person will go next. Such models support retail, travel, and public health tools, yet their social effects are little studied. Trained on a large movement dataset, the models prove less accurate for some racial and ethnic groups than for others.

To cut the gap, the team offers a sampling plan that adds training data with fairness in mind. A clustering step assigns proxy group labels while matching census shares for Asian, Black, Hispanic, and White users. The plan cuts total disparity by up to forty percent with little loss in overall accuracy, with the biggest gains early on.
arxiv-2510-27540:
Kira van Treek, Javier F. Peña, Juan C. Vera, and Luis F. Zuluaga study how fast common search methods settle on a best answer in 2025. Many methods repeat one fixed step, a pattern called a fixed-point iteration. When the step is averaged, the search is known to reach a fixed point, but it can do so quite slowly.

The team proves that one local error rule is both needed and enough for fast, linear settling. They give clear bounds for the rate and link them to the rule's constants. Methods with flat, piecewise parts meet the rule, so they settle fast. The result covers tools such as ADMM and Douglas-Rachford, even without strong curve in the cost.
arxiv-2511-00240:
J A Sellwood offers a ready-made model galaxy for researchers who test theories in isolation. The model balances in equilibrium, like a real spiral galaxy, and grows open spiral arms with two or three arms. Unlike the widely used Agora model, it carries a heavier disk, and it avoids forming a central bar.

The heavier disk is the point: low-mass disks grow only many-armed patterns that look less like the Milky Way. With this model, teams can test star formation and feedback rules in a more faithful setting. Three versions, from modest to very large particle counts, are free to download.
arxiv-2511-00340:
Manan Roy Choudhury, Adithya Chandramouli, Mannan Anand, and Vivek Gupta built CLAUSE, a benchmark that stress-tests language models on legal reasoning. Models now draft and review contracts, high-stakes work full of subtle, adversarial flaws, yet no systematic test measured how fragile their reasoning is. CLAUSE generates more than seven thousand perturbed real-world contracts from established datasets, planting flaws across ten anomaly categories.

A persona-driven pipeline creates the flaws, and a retrieval system checks them against official statutes for legal fidelity. Leading models were then asked to find the planted errors and explain their legal weight. They often missed subtle discrepancies and struggled even more to justify them. The authors present CLAUSE as a diagnostic step toward legal AI that can be trusted.
arxiv-2511-00740:
Igor Engel and Ekaterina Verbitskaia clean up a bridge between two styles of programming. Relational programming, through the miniKanren system, can build programs by running relations backward, but it pays a speed cost. An earlier conversion trick cut that cost, yet it ignored types, needed determinism notes, and threaded generators through the code in hidden ways.

Their typed tagless-final embedding of miniKanren into Haskell fixes all three flaws. Types are respected by design, and much of the boilerplate in converted code goes away. The earlier speed gains survive, and at times improve. The work shows a speed hack can be rebuilt as a clean, type-safe design with no loss of pace.
arxiv-2511-00940:
Zhe Li and co-authors present URDF-Anything, a system that builds digital twins of articulated objects, things with moving joints like drawers, laptops, and tools. Robots need such models for simulation training, but making them has meant painstaking hand work or long multi stage pipelines.

Their method feeds point clouds and text into a three dimensional multimodal language model that predicts, in one pass, both the part segmentation and the joint parameters. A special token lets the model interact directly with point cloud features, keeping the parts and the motion parameters consistent. On simulated and real data it beats earlier approaches on segmentation accuracy, parameter error, and physical executability, and it generalizes to objects outside its training set.
arxiv-2511-01140:
Md Talha Mohsin and Ismail Abdulrashid build a theoretical framework for few shot learning in multimodal medical imaging. Labeled examples are scarce in that field, as happens with rare diseases and in low resource clinics. Methods combining several image types with meta learning often work, but why and when they succeed lacked a unified explanation.

Drawing on PAC learning, VC theory, and PAC Bayesian analysis, they derive bounds on how many labeled samples reliable performance requires. They also show how extra modalities reduce the effective capacity through an information gain term. They define a metric for explanation stability and prove its variance shrinks as samples grow. A small controlled experiment with a fusion model confirms the predicted multimodal gains and shrinking uncertainty, though interference between modalities appears at larger sample sizes.
arxiv-2511-01440:
Joel Summerfield studies how the Lie algebra of a reductive algebraic group breaks into decomposition classes, a finer sorting of the way its elements fall into orbits. Earlier work handled this mostly under limits on the field's characteristic. Summerfield works over algebraically closed fields of any characteristic at all.

He extends a dimension formula for these classes. He also adds Levi-type decomposition classes to handle the trouble that appears in bad characteristic. The study also develops Lusztig-Spaltenstein induction for non-nilpotent orbits. It shows this induction does not depend on the chosen parabolic subgroup. It finishes the covering relation for the closure ordering of classes in good characteristic. The results tie the geometry of orbits more tightly to the arithmetic of the field.
arxiv-2511-01540:
Gusti van Zyl studies expected shortfall. That is a risk measure reporting the average loss in the worst cases. His worry is that the probability distribution behind it may be wrong. In the distributionally robust version, the distribution is allowed to shift, with the shift priced by an optimal-transport distance using a quadratic cost.

The hard step is a transform of the payoff function that appears in the dual problem. Van Zyl shows that for convex payoffs this transform has a workable closed form, and that robust expected shortfall reduces to a two-dimensional minimization. Applied to finance, the machinery yields a closed formula. It gives the robust expected shortfall of an unhedged call option. The view is that of the writer who sold the option, relative to the risk-neutral distribution.
arxiv-2511-01740:
Dmitrij Schlesinger and Boris Flach reframe distributed learning as a game. The obstacle they target is heterogeneity: different sites hold different kinds of data and run different local models, so the usual trick of averaging model parameters breaks down. Their alternative is to exchange synthetic data instead of parameters.

Each local model is a black box. It can learn from data and generate fresh data from what it learned. Semi-supervised local models even let sites work on different probability spaces. Those spaces can cover different modalities. Cast as a cooperative game, the learning problem has, for exponential-family local models, a unique Nash equilibrium, and the proposed procedure provably converges to it. Tests on standard vision benchmarks cover image classification and conditional generation, showing the approach's advantages.
arxiv-2511-01840:
Greta Ontrup, Annika Bush, Markus Pauly, and Meltem Aksoy audit how language models think about corporate responsibility. Companies increasingly use these models in supply chain work, yet models are known to carry biases about how much sustainable and ethical practice matters. The study probes those leanings with validated survey instruments rather than casual prompts.

Several state-of-the-art models answered standardized questionnaires on business ethics and responsibility and on the importance of sustainable supplier and customer relations. Systematic differences between models were significant, and framing the questions with four organizational culture types substantially shifted the answers. The findings matter for anyone letting a model assist decisions in sustainability contexts: the model's corporate values are neither neutral nor stable across vendors and prompts.
arxiv-2511-02440:
Pingzhi Li and nine co-authors flip a magnet with a flash of light, entirely on a photonic chip. All-optical switching of magnetisation promises ultrafast, energy-efficient memory, but it has mostly needed bulky free-space laser setups. The team guided trains of femtosecond pulses through waveguides in a silicon nitride integrated circuit. The pulses were aimed at a cobalt-gadolinium Hall cross, smaller than a micrometre across, patterned directly on top of the waveguide.

Electrical readout through the anomalous Hall effect showed deterministic toggle switching with contrast up to ninety percent in the narrowest, 500 nanometre, devices. Larger crosses switched less reliably and more randomly, which simulations tie to uneven light absorption across the device. The authors attribute it to domain walls relaxing in partially switched regions. The message is that shrinking the device is not just packaging: it is what makes on-chip optical switching dependable.
arxiv-2511-02740:
Ilse Ipsen and Arvind Saibaba ask how hard it is to pick a few representative columns from a large matrix. The task, column subset selection, serves data reduction across science and engineering. Their 2025 paper covers many quality criteria, from volume and stable rank to condition number and norms of several kinds.

For small picks, at most a third of the rows, they show these criteria are NP-hard, meaning no fast exact method is expected. Many also resist good approximation schemes that run in polynomial time. To set up the proofs, they derive the best possible values for each criterion and formulas for split pseudo-inverses. One result also feeds trace optimization in A-optimal design, a tool for planning experiments.
arxiv-2511-02940:
J. Bianco, A. Tenerani, C. Gonzalez, L. Matteini, and K. Klein trace how a beam of protons rides the solar wind outward. Spacecraft see such beams aligned with the magnetic field, and theory says large Alfven waves can drive them. Their 2025 study runs an ensemble of one-dimensional hybrid expanding-box simulations, seeded with plasma states the Helios craft measured close to the Sun.

The growing wave in the model pushes out a proton beam on its own, matching the self-consistent picture. Compared with data out to one and a half times Earth's distance, the model reproduces the beam's drift and its density share against the core on average. The authors credit kinetic instabilities, fed by wave dynamics and the wind's expansion, with steering the beam's long-term path.
arxiv-2511-03040:
R. Green finds hidden order among the 240 packings of the projective space PG(3,2), configurations long used to build the most symmetric solutions of Kirkman's schoolgirl problem. It had escaped notice that the packings form a partially ordered set. His 2025 paper constructs a graded, shellable order on them, in the style of Bruhat order, which also defines a Lehmer code for each packing.

The order exists because the packings match a set of maximal orthogonal subsets of the E8 root system, a famous lattice structure. That link brings group actions with it: Weyl groups of several types act on the packings, faithfully in most cases. Green also shows the order and the signed permutation action can both be built from labeled Fano planes, tying the result to small finite geometry.
arxiv-2511-03140:
Xu-Fan Hu and four colleagues model the flickering polarized light of blazar jets when a kink instability twists them. Telescopes have seen such kinks grow after recollimation shocks, with quasi-periodic swings in the light. Their 2025 paper adds a polarized radiative transfer module, RaptorP, to an existing code, and runs it on three-dimensional simulations of over-pressured magnetized jets.

The view changes with frequency. Low frequencies show the turbulent medium around the jet, with polarization angles pointing across the flow, a sign of a poloidal field. High frequencies reveal bright knots and the kink itself, with angles matching a toroidal field. Light curves in brightness and polarization oscillate together, and their peak frequency matches the kink's rotation period. The results give observers a map for reading blazar signals.
arxiv-2511-03540:
Anais Pauchet and Devesh Nandal follow how dark matter heating could stretch the lives of the first stars. Those Population III stars lit the early universe and seeded it with metals. In dense halos, dark matter particles captured by a star can annihilate in its core and add a second power source.

A twenty-sun model is evolved with full capture physics across six halo densities and three starting spin rates. Once capture passes a threshold, dark power rivals fusion and the main-sequence life stretches well past its normal span near ten million years. Spin and halo density jointly decide how quasi-uniform the star stays. Longer-lived first stars would delay reionization and change the chemical story of the early cosmos.
arxiv-2511-03840:
Sicheng He and five colleagues develop a design tool for suppressing unstable limit cycle oscillations that arise through Hopf bifurcations. In aerospace work such oscillations appear as aeroelastic flutter and transonic buffet, and an unstable cycle can diverge or jump in ways that threaten structure and performance.

Stability of the cycle is captured by the first Lyapunov coefficient. The team computes its derivatives at low cost by combining the adjoint method with reverse derivative tracking. Three design problems test the approach: an algebraic Hopf model, an aeroelastic typical section, and a nonlinear Ginzburg-Landau problem. In each case the method helps steer designs away from unstable bifurcation behaviour.
arxiv-2511-03940:
Jifeng Chu, Kang Lyu, and Chuan-Fu Yang study discrete periodic Schroedinger operators on a lattice, where the periodic potential has pairwise coprime periods across dimensions. Comparing spectra between potentials often asks how much information partial data can pin down, and full isospectrality demands can be stronger than needed.

Two new notions frame the work: generalized partial Fermi isospectrality and weak separability. Potentials sharing the generalized partial property are shown to share weak separability as well. From that, equal separability patterns follow without assuming full Fermi or Floquet isospectrality. Component pairs of such potentials are also shown to be Floquet isospectral in a stated sense. The spectral picture sharpens.
arxiv-2511-04240:
Peter P Varju and Max Wenqiang Xu prove a conditional result about random polynomials whose coefficients are multiplicative signs. A degree d polynomial of that random form is irreducible over the integers, with probability approaching one as degree grows. The statement is framed as assumed throughout, since it rests on an unproved hypothesis.

Specifically, the argument assumes the Riemann hypothesis holds for Dedekind zeta functions. Under that assumption, the failure probability shrinks at a rate close to one over the square root of the degree. Random multiplicative coefficients might be expected to factor often; instead, irreducibility is typical. The result links analytic number theory hypotheses to concrete algebra in a sharp way.
arxiv-2511-04440:
Pedro Pereira and four colleagues build detectors for Magecart attacks on online shops. In these attacks, hidden scripts skim card details from checkout pages as buyers type. The team trained tree-based, linear, and kernel-based models on real-world script data.

A behavior automaton tracks the step-by-step patterns of running scripts to aid the models. Tuning and feature selection sharpened the split between benign and malicious code. The models were then hardened by training against adversarial evasion attacks. The result aims at detection that stays both accurate and explainable, so shop owners can trust and act on its warnings.
arxiv-2511-04540:
Lorenz Zwick leads seven authors showing that eccentric orbits make environmental effects easier to spot. A binary's surroundings can shift the phase of its gravitational waves. For circular signals, those small shifts can hide in the noise.

Eccentric signals carry extra harmonics, and the team shows these boost the signal of the shift. The gain grows with the highest harmonic modeled and the shift's frequency scaling. Population tests cover LIGO, Virgo, and Kagra at planned sensitivities, plus Cosmic Explorer and the Einstein Telescope. Sources with strong eccentricity could reveal their environments far better than circular ones.
arxiv-2511-04640:
Pedro Gatón-Pérez and two colleagues study strong coupling in conserved surface roughening. Growing interfaces can roughen in ways that resist the usual scaling theory. The puzzle deepens when dynamics conserve material but need not be variational.

Their family of stochastic equations for one-dimensional interfaces depends on a power parameter. At zero, it returns the stochastic Burgers equation, and it also contains a porous medium model. A one-loop renormalization group analysis yields scaling exponents that shift with the parameter. The work probes whether symmetries behind the exponents are explicit in the equations or only emerge at large scales.
arxiv-2511-04940:
Jiachen Shen and co-authors build a math frame for choices made under deep doubt when leaders and followers act at two levels. Old methods often fail when facts are missing or outside shocks cannot be pinned down.

Their frame joins two-level game theory with robust methods that guard against the worst likely spread of outcomes. They turn the hard two-level task into a single-level form and solve it with a broad method. In tests, under high doubt, their model cuts cost by up to about a fifth next to prior work.
arxiv-2511-05340:
Nicolas Sovare and a co-author model, from first principles, a one-liter ionization chamber that monitors tritium in a process stream. Such monitors guide the safe run of tritium systems, and the one-liter form is well mapped by lab tests.

Tests show a straight response across a wide span of tritium levels, with bends at low anode voltage or low gas pressure. Their computed model matches each of those regimes. A sound first-principles model lets engineers predict monitor drift when set-ups change, without a fresh lab campaign each and every time.
arxiv-2511-05440:
Junmin An and co-authors find the length of the shortest self-orthogonal embedding of any binary linear code. Such an embedding adds the fewest columns to a code's generator matrix so the new code is self-orthogonal, a trait prized in quantum and classic coding.

Many codes reached this way are optimal. The authors use traits of a code's hull, the overlap of a code with its dual, to pin the shortest length in general. They work through Hamming codes and Reed-Muller codes as lead cases, which gives builders an exact count instead of a search.
arxiv-2511-05740:
Hope Lee and a team of co-authors build a photonic interface for a promising diamond qubit, the tin-vacancy center.
