This defect in diamond can be addressed with light and holds its spin state well even at modest cooling. Scalable quantum nodes, though, need its photons emitted and collected efficiently for high-quality readout.

The team carved one-dimensional photonic crystal cavities into thin diamond films holding the centers. They modeled the emission in detail, separating the center's two optical transitions. Cavities reached quality factors in the thousands, and emission sped up enough to show a strong Purcell enhancement for the targeted transition. Their analysis also pinned down how often each transition fires, matching earlier theory and experiment.
arxiv-2511-06240:
Tzu-Jung Lin and co-authors ask where a mobile robot should park itself before trying to manipulate an object. In open-vocabulary mobile manipulation, the robot must handle items described in plain words. Picking a base position by closeness alone ignores whether the spot actually affords a good grip, causing frequent failures.

Their zero-shot framework pairs vision-language understanding with geometric checks in a coarse-to-fine search. Special representations blend affordance cues with an obstacle map, so reasoning reaches beyond the camera view. Coarse semantic hints steer the search first, then geometry refines the final spot. Across five varied tasks the system reached an eighty-five percent success rate, well ahead of classical planners.
arxiv-2511-06540:
Sirus Shahini and Robert Ricci hide secret network traffic inside ordinary packets already crossing a network. Covert channels have been studied for years, but most designs stayed narrow, tied to one protocol or use case. CYPRESS instead mounts packets from hidden senders onto regular traffic, so the secret stream generates no packets of its own.

A decentralized framework hosts channel handlers for many protocols, each plugged in and updated on demand to dodge detection. At run time the system picks which channels to use and in what order to fragment and ship the hidden data. In a ten-user test network the channel carried up to about one point six megabytes per second of secret traffic.
arxiv-2511-07040:
Yuanmin Huang and five co-authors defend 3D point cloud recognition against adversarial perturbations, small crafted changes that fool classifiers and threaten real deployments. They argue current defenses fail mainly because their feature spaces are entangled, leaving room for attacks. Their method, 3D-ANC, instead uses neural collapse, the tendency of last-layer features to settle into a simplex arrangement of maximally separated class prototypes.

Class imbalance and geometric similarity between object categories complicate that plan for point clouds. So the method adds an aligned classification module plus adaptive training with representation-balanced learning and a dynamic feature direction loss. The payoff is large: on ModelNet40, one backbone's accuracy under attack rose from about twenty-seven percent to about eighty-one percent, far beyond leading baselines, and gains held across model structures.
arxiv-2511-07240:
Oleksandr Masyutka, Mikhail Moklyachuk, and Maria Sidei solve an estimation problem for random processes with gaps in the record. The task is to estimate linear functionals of a multidimensional stationary process at points where observations are missing on certain finite intervals, using noisy observations elsewhere. The noise is itself a stationary process added to the signal, and the setting is continuous time.

When the spectral densities of signal and noise are known exactly, the authors give formulas for the mean-square errors and the spectral characteristics of the optimal linear estimates. When the densities are known only to lie in given admissible sets, they switch to a minimax, robust approach. From it they derive the least favorable spectral densities and the minimax characteristics of the optimal estimates for several special classes of uncertainty sets.
arxiv-2511-07540:
Bart van Baal, Anders Jerkstrand, and Daniel Kresse predict the late glow of the smallest exploding stars. Months after a core-collapse supernova, thinning gas lets the whole debris shine, and line shapes encode the blast asymmetry. Reading them needs radiation transfer beyond simple equilibrium rules.

An upgraded three-dimensional code, ExTraSS, now handles those non-equilibrium effects with photoionization and line-by-line transfer. The team applies it to a nine solar mass star blown up by neutrinos. Predicted emission lines can be matched against telescope spectra of real faint supernovae. Such matches test whether weak explosions explain the dimmest stellar deaths observed.
arxiv-2511-07640:
Hallacy, Hallett, Fenzl, and colleagues tune pairs of quantum dots for chiral quantum optics. Quantum dots inside photonic crystal waveguides can emit light that travels one way only, a trick for quantum networks. Tuning several separated dots electrically without spoiling the waveguide has been the obstacle.

Ion implantation writes resistive tracks into the top layer of a diode, isolating nearby regions. Unlike etched cuts, implants barely disturb guided light, adding tiny index change and minimal loss. Etching, by contrast, can cut transmission sharply. Demonstrations with embedded dot pairs show independent control. Scalable chiral light sources move closer to practical quantum photonic chips.
arxiv-2511-08040:
Eloi Moliner and colleagues treat automatic music mixing as a generative problem rather than a single right answer task. Mixing combines separate tracks into a finished song, and skilled engineers can reach many valid mixes from the same material. Earlier automatic systems used regression, which forces one deterministic output and ignores that variety.

MEGAMI learns the spread of professional mixes for given unprocessed tracks. A track agnostic processor is guided by generated effect embeddings for each track, and the design handles unlabeled tracks in any order. Distributional tests show steady gains over prior methods, while listening tests approach human level quality across genres.
arxiv-2511-08240:
Chenyu Hu, Xiaotong Li, Hao Zhu, and Biao Hou propose DiPVNet, a network that learns from three dimensional point clouds no matter how they are rotated. Point clouds drive many vision tasks, but arbitrary rotation changes a cloud orientation and disrupts its directional features. Earlier methods model rotation effects only implicitly and miss the multi scale directional structure of real clouds.

An atomic dot product operator encodes directional selectivity together with rotation invariance. Locally, a learnable operator lets each centre point interact with neighbours to capture uneven structure. Globally, harmonic analysis links dot products with sampled directions to a direction aware spherical Fourier transform, building a rotation steady representation for deep learning.
arxiv-2511-08640:
Xingcheng Liu and eight co-authors build a driving safety system that predicts accidents early even when camera sensors are noisy. Rain, motion blur, and weak hardware can hide the very cues a warning system needs, and alerts must come early without crying wolf.

A diffusion module cleans image and object features step by step, restoring motion and interaction cues lost to noise. In parallel, an actor-critic model weighs long stretches of video and uses time-weighted rewards to pick the best alert moment. On three benchmark datasets the system reaches top accuracy and longer average warning times before impact. It stays robust under Gaussian and impulse noise, and its warnings arrive earlier and steadier in both routine and tangled traffic scenes.
arxiv-2511-08740:
Deepesh Bhamre and João de Melo check a consistency condition of quantum field theory inside the light-front formalism, a frame that describes particles at near light speed. The Ward-Takahashi identity links a theory's symmetries to its currents, and any trustworthy calculation method must respect it.

The test system is a spinless bound state built from two fermions, chosen because the identity holds in the standard covariant treatment. Working through the one-loop calculation on the light front, the authors show the identity survives there too. Two ingredients prove essential: the pair production diagram, which is easy to overlook, and the zero modes of the longitudinal momentum. The paper serves specialists who use light-front methods for bound-state physics and need the formalism's foundations verified piece by piece.
arxiv-2511-08840:
Livia Grammatica, Alexei Skorobogatov, and Yuan Yan study the Brauer group of an abelian variety defined over an algebraically closed field of positive characteristic. The key part is the p-primary torsion, whose key piece is a quasi-algebraic unipotent group attached to the variety.

The authors determine that group's dimension and prove a sharp upper bound for its p-exponent. For abelian varieties of dimension at most three, they sort the isogeny class of the group in full. For principally polarized varieties, the dimension of the p-torsion subgroup is computed from the Ekedahl-Oort type, a standard profile of its p-structure. Brauer groups measure obstructions in arithmetic geometry, so pinning down their wildest part in finite characteristic fills a basic gap.
arxiv-2511-08940:
Pedro Chumpitaz-Flores and three co-authors tune neural networks for tabular data with an optimizer that borrows its moves from quantum computing. Hyperparameter search over features, architecture, and regularization is a huge non-convex space. Exhaustive tuning is unaffordable. Their bilevel optimizer therefore encodes the whole configuration in qubits.

Deterministic quantum-inspired rotations explore the space while stochastic qubit mutations, pulled toward a global attractor, keep the search from stalling, all under a fixed evaluation budget. Experiments even run under emulated single-qubit bit-flip noise on an IBM quantum backend, at error rates up to one percent. Across thirteen real-world datasets the method stays competitive with classical tree-based tuners and with other classical and quantum-inspired optimizers given the same budget.
arxiv-2511-09140:
Xuyao Yu, Zijun Gong, and Zhilu Lai wrote this signal processing paper on placing pilot symbols inside OFDM transmissions so receivers can estimate doubly dispersive channels. Xuyao Yu later withdrew it from arXiv. Its arXiv listing now records it as withdrawn by the author, with no reason stated.

As submitted, the paper sought the pilot pattern that minimizes the linear minimum mean square error of channel estimation when signals spread in both delay and Doppler. The channel covariance matrix was split into a Kronecker product of two Toeplitz matrices, each nearly diagonalized by Fourier matrices under a classical limit theorem. That structure produced a compact error formula, a closed-form lower bound, and a lattice pilot pattern achieving the bound. Readers should treat every claim here as withdrawn along with the paper.
arxiv-2511-09440:
Guillaume Noetinger, Tim Tuuva, and Romain Fleury write a hands-on tutorial for aligning defocused spatial light modulators in optical neural networks. Stacking several modulators builds diffractive networks that compute with light, but training is slow because the devices refresh slowly. Multiplexing inputs across spatial channels speeds things up, provided every channel performs the same physical operation.

That requires pixel-level conjugation of the modulators, an experimentally tricky alignment. The authors give a semi-automatic procedure that scales to any number of devices. Their aligned setup handles hundreds of inputs at once, cutting training time and averaging down experimental noise. The guide also profiles the setup, and the method transfers to wavefront shaping tasks needing precise modulator alignment.
arxiv-2511-09640:
Lewis R. Prole and fifteen co-authors introduce SEEDZ, a suite of cosmological simulations growing the universe's first massive black holes. The simulations follow Population III stars, their supernovae, and light and heavy black hole seeds. They include metal enrichment, feedback, and accretion at and above the Eddington limit. This paper describes the methodology and the state of play at redshift fifteen.

The headline result: young black holes outgrow their host galaxies, so over-massive black holes are a natural feature of the early universe. Heavy seeds near ten thousand solar masses can reach a million solar masses by that epoch in the runs. The familiar black hole-galaxy mass relation, they argue, only emerges later as galaxies mature.
arxiv-2511-09740:
Filip Beránek, Václav Diviš, and Ivan Gruber study a practical problem for driver assistance systems: dirt and grime building up on car cameras. Dirty lenses can blind the safety features that depend on them, so the camera system needs to notice soiling on its own. The authors treat the task as labeling each part of an image, pixel by pixel, rather than judging whole image tiles at once.

Their tests compare popular image labeling methods with tile-level classification, and the labeling methods perform better. They also audit the WoodScape driving dataset and report data leakage plus imprecise annotations in it. From it they build a smaller cleaned subset that trains models to nearly the same quality much faster, and they share their code and data splits publicly.
arxiv-2511-09840:
Raj Sai Sohel Bandari, Amod Ashtekar, Omar Ibrahim, and Mohammed E. Eltayeb use LiDAR and shiny indoor surfaces to rescue millimeter-wave links that walls would otherwise block. Millimeter waves deliver multi-gigabit speeds but fade fast and stop at obstacles. Glass, glossy metal, and signage reflect both light and these radio waves, so a LiDAR sensor can map surfaces that a radio beam could bounce off.

In their proof of concept, three reflector types (glossy, smooth, and matte) were tested indoors at sixty gigahertz. LiDAR guidance located hidden users and good reflection points, raising the weakest received signal by more than twenty decibels in deep blocked regions. LiDAR-derived steering also matched an exhaustive beam search, suggesting a cheap alternative to configurable reflecting surfaces for future 6G networks.
arxiv-2511-09940:
Ruyu Liu and Shaohua Pan develop an inexact moving balls approximation method for constrained optimization problems whose objective and constraint functions are both upper-C-two, a class covering many nonconvex, nonsmooth problems. Exact subproblem solving is costly, so their method accepts approximate solutions under a workable inexactness rule. The goal is a practical method that still carries a full convergence certificate.

Using a global error bound for the associated strongly convex programs, they prove the whole iterate sequence converges under two named conditions on multipliers and the potential function. When the potential satisfies a Kurdyka-Lojasiewicz property with a suitable exponent, they also get local convergence rates, plus a checkable condition for that property. They describe it as the first implementable inexact method of its kind with full guarantees.
arxiv-2511-10240:
Minbae Park, Hyemin Yang, Jeonghyun Kim, Kunsoo Park, and Hyunjoon Kim present ProgRAG, a question-answering framework over knowledge graphs designed to resist hallucination. Language models reason well but invent facts, and graph-enhanced versions still retrieve wrongly or reason prematurely from thin evidence. ProgRAG instead breaks a complex question into sub-questions and grows partial reasoning paths step by step.

At each step, external retrievers gather candidate evidence and the model prunes it with uncertainty awareness, instead of judging its own retrieval unaided. Surviving paths are reorganized into a clean context for final reasoning. On three standard multi-hop question-answering datasets, ProgRAG outperformed existing baselines, which the authors attribute to progressive, checked reasoning rather than one-shot retrieval.
arxiv-2511-10440:
Tom Pan and four co-authors, including George N. Phillips, attack a stubborn step in protein crystallography: finishing structures that are only partly known. Machine learning models rarely use the raw diffraction measurements directly. Their model, CrysFormer, mixes a three-dimensional vision transformer with a convolutional network and feeds it both kinds of evidence at once.

One input is a Patterson map, computed straight from crystallographic data. The other is a partial structure map, built from an AlphaFold prediction with pieces removed. The model outputs electron density maps that standard refinement then turns into atomic models. On test fragments it improved phase estimates, filled the missing regions, and brought density maps closer to the true structures.
arxiv-2511-10840:
Abir Harrasse and four co-authors open up multilingual language models to see how they handle many languages internally. Using tools called cross-layer transcoders and attribution graphs, they train models on different language mixtures and trace which internal features do the work.

A shared multilingual space emerges: the models use highly similar features across languages, with language-specific decoding appearing only in the later layers. The same structure forms even when English is excluded from training. A small set of frequent late-layer features encodes language identity. Failures in non-English languages trace to dim late features, weak middle-layer clusters, and tokenizers biased toward English that force early layers into word reassembly. Fine-tuning strengthens the weak links, which the authors say mechanistically explains multilingual performance gaps.
arxiv-2511-11140:
Ilya Ruchiev and Bryn Davies give energy estimates for wave growth in materials whose traits switch in time following the Fibonacci pattern. Such time quasicrystals can amplify wave energy sharply inside special frequency gaps. To study them, the authors group the switching pattern into repeating time supercells, which reveal a fractal set of gaps where growth occurs.

Inside those gaps, wave energy grows at an exponential rate that the method can estimate closely. Some extra-wide gaps do not depend on how long the supercell is, which confirms the approach. The result predicts where amplification will occur and how fast energy will rise there.
arxiv-2511-11340:
Salima Lamsiyah, Saad Ezzini, and their colleagues introduce M-DAIGT, a shared task on spotting AI-generated text across domains, with a focus on news articles and academic writing. Fluent machine text threatens information integrity and research honesty, so detectors need testing on shared, fair grounds. The task splits into two binary subtasks, one for news and one for academic writing.

The team built and released a benchmark of thirty thousand samples, balanced between human and machine text from varied modern models and prompting styles. Forty-six teams registered, and four submitted final results in both subtasks. Team methods are described, with future directions for the task sketched.
arxiv-2511-11440:
Massimo Rizzoli, Simone Alghisi, and their colleagues rethink fine-tuning vision-language models using fully controlled synthetic data instead of gathered real scenes. Real photo collections carry bias, labeling errors, and lopsided distributions, which push tuned models toward overfitting and uneven skill. Their pipeline generates and annotates data with balanced distribution and clean labels by construction, then tests spatial reasoning about an object's absolute position.

Fine-tuning on balanced data gave uniform performance across a scene and erased common biases with as few as one hundred thirty samples. Tuning on synthetic stimuli also raised scores on real photos by about thirteen percent, beating models tuned on the full real training set.
arxiv-2511-11540:
S. Sabari and three co-authors study stable quantum vortices in a rotating dipolar superfluid where the usual mean-field forces nearly cancel, leaving the Lee-Huang-Yang correction in charge. Such a pure Lee-Huang-Yang fluid is an unusual state of quantum matter held together by quantum fluctuations alone.

Numerical work maps how rotation speed changes the number of stable vortices, along with the energy and chemical potential per particle. The fluid sits in a deep energy minimum, marking it as a remarkably robust state. An exact critical rotation rate for a single vortex is also found. Findings like these guide experiments that create and spin ultracold dipolar gases.
arxiv-2511-11640:
Sed Centeno and four co-authors explore parallel training of neural networks through speculative backpropagation, a scheme that overlaps the forward and backward passes of learning. When predicted error gradients land within a threshold, weight updates proceed on speculation, cutting training time with little loss in accuracy.

Their implementation runs on the MNIST handwritten-digit dataset with OpenMP multithreading, letting forward and speculative backward steps execute at once for a clear speedup on CPUs. Synthesis onto a modern FPGA board is planned to test hardware acceleration. The project sits inside a wider study of parallelism for machine learning accelerators, where overlapped computation is a promising lever.
arxiv-2511-11840:
Shuangyu Xie and seven co-authors present LAVQA, a framework that lets a remote human help a self-driving car through an uncertain moment, quickly enough to matter. In shared autonomy, a car that stops for safety can ask an operator for guidance, but wireless delay and human thinking time let the scene change while the answer forms.

Visual questions from the car are paired with a latency-induced collision map that evolves in real time, showing how safety regions shift under delay and uncertainty. Operators see risk growing or shrinking as they deliberate. Designing the question-and-map interface around latency, rather than pretending answers are instant, is the framework's central contribution.
arxiv-2511-12040:
Xinyuan Hu and eight co-authors present SRSplat, a method that builds clear three-dimensional scenes from just a few low quality views. Feed-forward reconstruction matters for self-driving cars and embodied robots, which must act fast. Older methods often lose fine texture because low quality inputs lack sharp detail.

SRSplat makes up for that loss in two ways. It builds a scene-specific gallery of high quality reference images with large multimodal models and diffusion models, then fuses those cues with the input views. A second step adjusts how dense the scene elements are, based on how rich the texture is in each area. Tests show stronger results than prior methods.
arxiv-2511-12240:
Vishal Joshua Meesala introduces SCI, a control layer that watches how a deep learning model reasons and decides how much effort each case deserves. Most deployed models run in one pass, spending the same effort on easy and unclear inputs alike. In safety-critical work that habit is brittle, and doubt is often read only after the fact.

SCI tracks a confidence signal based on entropy over time and can stop, keep sampling, or abstain from a call. It wraps an existing model rather than replacing it. Tests use dropout classifiers on handwritten digits, heart rhythm data and machine bearing faults, three domains where knowing when a model may fail matters as much as accuracy.
arxiv-2511-12640:
Sofiia Dolgikh and Bodan Potanin propose double machine learning estimators for causal effects in a multivariate sample selection model, where the sample is filtered by several ordered selection rules at once. Ignoring that selection can badly bias estimates of a treatment's average effect. Their target quantities are the average effect overall and the average effect on those actually treated.

The authors establish that the estimators are asymptotically normal and study their finite-sample behavior in simulations. Results suggest selection-ignoring estimates can be highly biased, while the proposed estimators avoid that bias. As an application, they estimate the effect of female education on the log wage ratio between spouses.
arxiv-2511-12740:
Amirhossein Hassanzadeh and six co-authors estimate what fills each cube of a forest from laser-scanning data. LiDAR point clouds are often compressed into voxels, three-dimensional pixels, which saves computing but erases fine structure. The authors ask whether the share of bark, leaf, soil, and other material inside each voxel can be recovered from the compressed data. Their data come from simulated forests, so true contents are known.

They train a point convolution network with cost-sensitive methods designed for imbalanced regression, where common contents dominate rare ones. A sensitivity analysis across voxel sizes from a quarter meter to two meters shows larger voxels give lower errors, because they vary less. Small voxels inside the canopy are hardest to estimate. The practical message is that voxel size should follow the application. The study also fills a gap in imbalanced multi-target regression for 3D forest data.
arxiv-2511-12940:
Taiye Chen and six co-authors give long video generation a memory. Modern generators build video autoregressively, one segment after the next, but sliding-window attention forgets everything outside the window, so long videos drift and contradict themselves. Earlier hybrids with recurrent layers suffered from a gap between training and inference or from windows that never overlap. Their framework, Recurrent Autoregressive Diffusion, adds recurrent blocks to a diffusion transformer to update and retrieve a compressed global memory, while full attention over overlapping windows preserves local detail.

Among recurrent options, a plain LSTM layer after each attention block matched fancier blocks such as test-time training and Mamba2. On Memory Maze and Minecraft generation tasks, the framework beat prior approaches for long videos. The authors' claim is balance: global memory for consistency across minutes, local attention for sharpness within each moment. The work was published at a major computer vision venue.
arxiv-2511-13140:
Xingxing Hu and Yunfang Tang settle part of an open coloring problem. A star edge coloring paints a graph's edges so that no path or cycle of four edges uses only two colors; the star chromatic index is the fewest colors that suffice. For cubic Halin graphs, graphs built from a tree by ringing its leaves with a cycle, earlier work by two independent teams showed six colors always suffice, except for one special graph. Left open which of these graphs manage with five.

Hu and Tang answer for two broad families: if a cubic Halin graph's underlying tree is a caterpillar or a complete tree, its star chromatic index is exactly five. That pins the value rather than bounding it, narrowing the open problem to the remaining tree shapes. Star colorings remain a clean testbed for how local constraints force global color counts.
arxiv-2511-13440:
Daisuke Kurisu, Yuta Okamoto, and Taisuke Otsu link random set theory to the newer field of metric statistics. Random sets have served econometrics since key work on partial identification, where data pin down a set of values rather than one point. Metric statistics, in parallel, studies random objects that live in general metric spaces.

The authors clarify how two core means relate: the Aumann mean from random set theory and the Fréchet mean from metric statistics. That bridge lets tools built for metric data speak to set-valued economic problems. They then show concrete uses of metric statistics for econometric questions that involve random sets.
arxiv-2511-13540:
Zichong Wang and 6 co-authors present FairGLite, a fair graph learning framework that works with only limited demographic data. Graph neural networks can bake bias into node predictions, but most fairness fixes demand full demographic access that privacy and law rarely allow. Partial data must therefore guide the whole design.

A proxy mechanism builds stand-in demographic signals from the partial data, and training pushes node embeddings to stay consistent across groups. An adaptive confidence rule weighs each node's role in fairness and utility by how sure the model is. Theory gives provable bounds on group fairness measures, and broad tests showed bias fell while utility held.
arxiv-2511-13740:
Johannes Hagel studies a nonlinear oscillator whose stiffness term is joined by a time-dependent quadratic term, and finds an exact invariant for a special family of that coefficient. The invariant is quadratic in position and momentum and pins the motion to a smooth surface in the extended space of position, momentum, and time. One nonlinear third-order equation governs the coefficient shapes that allow it.

When the coefficient is periodic, that surface would close into a torus, but a resonance effect generically blocks periodic cases. The surface instead stretches along time as an open tube, a regime Hagel names tube integrability. A perturbation series to third order matches numerical runs where valid and clarifies where it must break down.
arxiv-2511-13840:
Sayed Shafaat Mahmud, Sayantan Auddy, Neal Turner, and Jeffrey S. Bary present a machine learning tool that reads pictures of planet-forming disks. Rings and gaps in the dust around young stars are widely read as signs of growing planets, but turning a picture into planet masses is slow with older methods. Their system, named VADER, uses a variational autoencoder trained on simulated disk images.

VADER estimates the masses of up to three hidden planets plus key disk traits such as thickness and dust content, each with an uncertainty range. Tested on real ALMA images of 23 disks, its planet masses mostly match published values. A full analysis takes minutes, fast enough for large surveys.
arxiv-2511-14040:
Loucif Hebbache, Dariush Amirkhani, and Mohand Saïd Allili automate bridge inspection from drone photos in two stages. Cracks and other concrete defects break the normal surface pattern, so the first stage uses visual saliency to propose regions where defects are likely. That narrows the search before any heavy model runs.

The second stage runs a YOLOX-based detector on images whose salient defect regions have been brightened at the bounding-box level. Tests on standard data sets confirm good accuracy with modest computing cost. The authors note the framework's efficiency gives it strong potential for a self-powered inspection system that could screen bridges without lane closures or scaffolding crews.
arxiv-2511-14140:
Hajun Kim, Hyunsik Na, and Daeseon Choi introduce a new way to build jailbreak prompts for testing language model safety. Red teams need varied attack templates, but current practice either slots harmful queries into fixed templates or lets a model write whole templates, which muddies intent and hurts reproducibility. Their embedded jailbreak template keeps a proven template's structure while weaving the harmful query naturally into its context.

A progressive prompt-engineering method keeps template quality and consistency high, and standard protocols govern how templates are generated and scored. The authors offer the result as a benchmark that mirrors real usage and real harmful intent more closely, for red-teaming and policy regression testing.
arxiv-2511-14940:
Florian Pabst, Harald Forbert, and Dominik Marx resolve the origin of the lowest rate Raman mode of liquid water. The mode tracks how water molecules move near ions or biomolecules. Experts debated whether it comes from translational or rotational motion. Dielectric data suggested one view, but the link was never settled.

Using ab initio simulations, the team compute the low rate spectrum with excellent agreement to experiment. Decomposition shows rotation and translation contribute about equally. Strong negative cross correlations and internal field effects reshape the rotational part. That reshaping explains why dielectric inference misled earlier work. The result clarifies a basic probe of water dynamics used across chemistry and biology.
arxiv-2511-15040:
Tsunenori Inakura and three co-authors survey highly deformed ground states in heavy even even nuclei linked to a second intruder orbit. Nuclear shape can stretch strongly when specific orbits drive deformation. The team search nuclei with proton number above fifty within energy density functional theory. They look for a pronounced elongated minimum in the energy landscape.

Representative cases show that minimum at large quadrupole deformation. A local rise in the hexadecapole component marks the same spot, as theory predicts for this orbit. Three different Skyrme interactions give similar results, suggesting robustness. Resulting maps highlight specific nuclei where such ground states should appear. Those targets can guide future spectroscopy experiments.
arxiv-2511-15140:
Hassan Firouzjahi, Kazem Rezazadeh, and Masoud Molaei study waves trapped inside a Schwarzschild black hole. Perturbations inside the horizon can settle into bound states, much like electrons bound in an atom, and they come in two families, axial and polar, named for their symmetry. Outside black holes, the two families famously share the same spectrum, a property called isospectrality.

Counting states for each angular pattern, the authors find one fewer polar bound state than the pattern count suggests. Most of the polar spectrum matches the axial one exactly, by both proof and numerics. The extra polar mode is the algebraically special mode and serves as the ground state. Highly excited states space out evenly, a pattern the authors confirm in the semiclassical limit.
arxiv-2511-15340:
Yi Peng, Hans-Martin Heyn, and Jennifer Horkoff ask how much requirements gold is hidden in the documentation that machine learning teams already write. Before an ML component can be integrated and verified, its requirements, covering both the model and its data, must be stated clearly. Model cards and data sheets are written for transparency, not for engineers, yet they describe intended use, limits, and data provenance in detail.

The authors mine twenty public model cards and data sheets and find a significant amount of requirements-relevant information inside. They then test how well three established requirements notations can carry that information without loss. Bridging the two worlds could spare teams from re-eliciting facts that were documented all along.
arxiv-2511-15540:
Jan Ostrowski provides relativistic models for forming stable cosmic and astrophysical structures where side pressure counters gravity. Standard collapse models end in singularities or dispersal without such support. The approach generalizes a known inhomogeneous space time to matter with side pressure from particle angular momentum. A reconstruction method is extended to this richer matter model.

Three functions on two chosen hypersurfaces fully find the space time shape. Bounded cases receive special focus, with weak field and small angular momentum approximations. Exact initial data combine with oscillatory final states to simplify reconstruction. Resulting models show explicit dust like actions early and stable end states. The work supplies analytic laboratories for structure formation beyond simple dust collapse.
arxiv-2511-15640:
Shourov Joarder, Tushar Talukder Showrav, and Md. Kamrul Hasan propose MUSSE-Net, a deep learning system for ultrasound strain imaging. That imaging method presses tissue gently and tracks how it deforms to reveal stiffness, which aids diagnosis without surgery. Its clinical use is limited by noise when tissue patterns shift, scarce ground truth, and strain estimates that vary with how much deformation is applied.

The system processes before and after radio-frequency sequences in parallel streams to estimate movement and strain, using attention modules that fuse features across streams. A consistency loss keeps results stable over time and across deformation levels. A second stage refines left-over errors and suppresses noise, beating earlier unsupervised methods on simulated, living, and clinical data.
arxiv-2511-16040:
Garritt L. Page, Andrés F. Barrientos, David B. Dahl, and David B. Dunson tackle a neglected step in Bayesian clustering: summing up doubt about the grouping itself. Bayesian methods give a posterior distribution over clusterings, a full picture of doubt. Many priors, likelihoods, and sampling methods exist. Yet the space of groupings is huge, so turning samples into a clear summary is hard.

Their post-processing works with posterior samples from any Bayesian clustering model. It builds a credible set of groupings that is easy to use, fast to compute, and simple to read. New doubt measures come with it. So do cluster-wise estimates and credible regions that gather a set posterior chance, with no need to fix one grouping or untangle label switches.
arxiv-2511-16340:
Alan Yufei Dong, Jihao Andreas Lin, and José Miguel Hernández-Lobato speed up Gaussian process inference for tasks where data arrive one batch at a time, such as active learning and Bayesian optimization. Iterative solvers avoid the cubic cost of exact inference but often need many rounds to converge after each update.

The authors propose three warm-start strategies that reuse solutions of smaller linear systems when the posterior is updated with new data. Theory shows the starting error, measured in the kernel space, shrinks, and experiments confirm gains across conjugate gradient, gradient descent, and projection solvers. Speed-ups reached a factor of nineteen when solving to tolerance, and fixed budgets gave more accurate posteriors and better optimization results.
arxiv-2511-16440:
Diogo J. Paulo, João Martins, Hugo Proença, and João C. Neves introduce StreetView-Waste, a dataset of street-level images aimed at a neglected chore of smart cities. The dataset targets litter spotting and overflowing waste containers, including images captured from garbage trucks on real routes.

The dataset supports three tasks: detecting waste containers, tracking them across images, and segmenting overflow. Baselines for each task are provided from current detection, tracking, and segmentation models. Fine-tuned detectors did reasonably, but trackers miscounted containers badly until a heuristic fix cut the mean counting error by about four fifths. A geometry-aware strategy also lifted litter segmentation scores on lightweight models by about a quarter. The benchmark gives waste logistics research a realistic testbed.
arxiv-2511-16540:
Éloïse Benito-Rodriguez and three co-authors take a first step toward predicting text genre from language model activations alone. Interpretability is hard because model internals resist human reading and outputs are too many to check. If genre leaves a readable trace in activations, shallow classifiers might extract it. Using a mid size open model and two data sets, they test that idea.

Simple classifiers reach high scores on one data set and solid scores on the other. Both beat a control task by clear margins. Genre chunks, not single tokens, are the unit of interpretation proposed. The proof of concept suggests activations encode stylistic categories accessibly. Predictive activation frameworks could eventually flag genre shifts linked to unsafe or off policy generations.
arxiv-2511-17040:
Wenzhang Du addresses a common flaw in training data: labels gathered in the wild are often wrong, and those errors drag down neural network accuracy. Standard cleaning happens before training and cannot react to what the model itself is learning. Du's framework, Step-E, merges sample selection into training as a single process instead.

At each pass through the data, Step-E ranks examples by loss and gradually excludes more of the highest-loss ones after a short warm-up. The model thus learns first from easy, consistent examples and ends up ignoring stubborn outliers. On a noisy version of the CIFAR-100 image set, accuracy rose from about 43 percent to about 50 percent, clearly beating rival cleaning methods. Gains on CIFAR-10 were smaller but real, at modest extra training cost.
arxiv-2511-17140:
Ping Wu and Dan Zhu look at how the United States economy and world stock markets move together, but from an unusual angle. Instead of tracking market index levels, they study the whole cross-sectional distribution of returns in each of 15 global markets. A distribution captures not just the average stock but the spread and shape of outcomes, which indexes discard. To handle such data, they build a matrix functional vector autoregression with readable factors drawn from the distributions.

Modeling the distributions jointly with American macroeconomic indicators, they find financial markets carry real predictive power for later economic dynamics. Tightening United States monetary policy not only lowers returns worldwide, as expected, but also flattens the return distribution's tails, a transmission channel earlier work missed. The framework supports scenario-based forecasting for policymakers.
arxiv-2511-17240:
Hoang Ta and Jonathan Scarlett study how to learn the edges of a random graph by asking group questions. Each query names a set of nodes and reports only whether at least one edge hides among them, and all queries must be fixed in advance. For arbitrary graphs this non-adaptive learning is provably expensive. The authors focus on Erdős–Rényi graphs, the standard random model, where the edge count is roughly known.

Earlier schemes achieved an optimal number of tests but needed quadratic time to decode the answers, or decoded faster by spending extra tests. Extending the binary splitting approach from group testing, Ta and Scarlett recover the edge set with high probability using an order-optimal number of tests. Decoding takes nearly linear time in the edge count. The result closes the efficiency gap for this learning problem.
arxiv-2511-17740:
Vicente Vergara builds a new time frequency framework tuned to wave like phase functions that spread out over time. Standard tools split phase space in a regular dyadic way, while his subdyadic geometry adapts the split to how dispersive waves actually behave.

On that geometry he constructs stable Gabor frames, families of wave packets with controlled overlap, and defines matching modulation spaces for measuring signals. He proves key properties of those spaces and shows that a class of multipliers stays bounded on them. The framework also recovers a classic description of where a signal is rough in space and direction.
arxiv-2511-18140:
Yilong Wang, Cheng Qian, Ruomeng Fan, and Edward Johns present Observer-Actor, a framework where one robot arm watches so another can act. Their test rig has two arms, each with a wrist camera. At run time the arms swap roles: the observer builds a three-dimensional model of the scene from three images using Gaussian splatting. A fast rendering method, then virtually searches that model for the best viewpoint and moves to it.

The actor then carries out its task using the observer's clearer view of both object and gripper. Because those views stay close to the clean views used in training, learned policies hold up better when clutter would otherwise hide the target. The team studies the setup with two existing imitation learning methods on a dual-arm system.
arxiv-2511-18340:
Weiyi Deng, Chengcheng Han, Zhanhong Lei, and Jin Min Yang trace how ripples in the early cosmos formed as the universe reheated. After fast early growth, the Higgs field may have set the pace of reheating in a patchy way. Those patches would seed ripples in space that later grew into the pattern of matter seen now.

The team compute the ripple size spread and its three point shape by three routes: a mean over swings, an exact route, and a non perturbative shift method. The shift method proves sound across a wide span of reheat times and Higgs values. A weaker Higgs self link yields larger ripples, with a mostly local shape. The work stresses that full, non perturbative care is a must here.
arxiv-2511-18440:
S. K. Singh, Ahmed A. Zahia, Jia-Xin Peng, and M. Y. Abd-Rabboud design a quantum battery charged by a coupled cavity system. A quantum battery stores energy in quantum states for later work. Their charger joins a microwave cavity, a magnetic mode in a YIG sphere, and a sound mode from the sphere's flex.

Two alike atoms draw charge from the cavity, which swaps energy with the magnetic mode in a beam splitter like step. The team model the full motion with a master equation that counts loss. Strong, on tune light matter links prove key to high charge yield, stored energy, and usable work. Off tune gaps and noise both drag yield down. The study maps where such a charger works best.
arxiv-2511-18940:
Sanjeev Manivannan and Chandra Shekar Lakshminarayan decode imagined movement from brain signals across subjects who were not in the training set. In EEG brain computer interfaces, each person's signal pattern differs, which breaks decoders trained on others. A geometry route codes signals as covariance matrices on a curved manifold of positive definite forms.

Past manifold tools skip how each subject's spread and tilt on that manifold vary. Three models built on geometry aware congruence transforms attack that gap: a plain transform, a deep linear form, and a deep U-Net form. Each serves both as an alignment front end for a sorter and as a full end to end decoder trained by cross entropy. Cross subject motor imagery is the test.
arxiv-2511-19140: Yu Sachkov studies two families of Lorentzian problems on the Heisenberg group, a standard setting in geometry where motion is limited to certain directions. Lorentzian problems concern paths measured with a signed notion of length, unlike ordinary shortest-path problems. The work follows what happens to these problem families as their parameter moves toward a limiting value, focusing on the asymptotic behavior in that limit.
arxiv-2511-19340:
Joseph Vovrosh and thirteen co-authors benchmark classical methods for simulating a two-dimensional quantum magnet, the transverse-field Ising model. Simulating many-qubit dynamics classically is a key yardstick for judging quantum processors. The team gathers a broad toolbox of leading numerical approaches.

Three tensor network methods, plus a neural quantum state Monte Carlo method, are run on two standard protocols: annealing through a critical point and dynamics after a sudden quench. The extensive results show where each method's predictions agree and where they strain. The benchmark links classical simulability to physical regimes and sets reference data for future experiments.
arxiv-2511-19640:
João M. Alendouro Pinho and six co-authors study second-harmonic generation in a single layer of graphene, where light comes out at twice its incoming frequency. The effect is weak on its own, so the team places the graphene in an attenuated total internal reflection setup. That arrangement can excite surface plasmon-polaritons, waves bound to the surface.

Theory shows those surface waves are the main reason the nonlinear signal grows: their tight field confinement makes light interact far more strongly with the graphene. The analysis ties graphene's electronic structure to the optical fields, giving a full framework for the enhancement and for designing similar devices.
arxiv-2511-19940:
Rahul Sharma, Pragnya Ramjee, Kaushik Murali, and Mohit Jain study how doctors edit answers that language models draft for patients. Patient message volume strains health systems, and model drafts could help, but how clinicians actually revise them was little known. The study works with eye doctors, a group facing many routine surgery questions.

Nine ophthalmologists answered many cataract surgery questions three ways: writing alone, editing model drafts directly, and giving instructions for indirect edits. Model drafts were mostly accurate, but rare errors and automation bias showed why human oversight matters. Most editing adapted generic answers to local practice and patient expectations. Direct editing was more precise but heavier; indirect editing saved effort but added errors.
arxiv-2511-20340:
Shi, Li, Zhang, and colleagues make speculative decoding survive the batching era. Their 2025 paper presents SpecFormer for faster language model inference. Speculative decoding drafts tokens cheaply, then verifies them in bulk. Classic drafters build big autoregressive guess trees. Batched serving eats the idle compute those trees need.

Huge batches leave little slack for fancy drafting. SpecFormer drafts with a hybrid attention design instead. One attention runs one-way over the full history. Another runs both ways for parallel drafting. Draft tokens emerge in parallel, not one by one. No giant prefix tree is required anymore. Accuracy stays high under a tight token budget. Experiments spanned models of many sizes. Acceleration held as batch sizes grew large. Training demands and compute costs both dropped. Lossless decoding guarantees output quality is unchanged. Serving stacks gain speed without surrendering throughput.
arxiv-2511-20440:
Bruno and Segreto check whether a deformed uncertainty rule survives constraints. Their 2025 paper works on the generalized uncertainty principle, or GUP. Such theories deform the Heisenberg rules of quantum mechanics. A minimal length and noncommuting positions can emerge. Their classical form uses deformed brackets instead. Constrained systems, common in gravity, complicate that picture.

The authors ask how the deformed structure behaves under reduction. Case one involves group symmetries acting as constraints. Rotationally invariant deformed algebras serve as the worked example. The reduced space keeps a valid symplectic form. Case two uses a single constraint: the Hamiltonian itself. That case dominates general relativity and cosmology. The change can be induced after reduction in both settings. The method keeps the theory's true degrees of freedom. Constrained systems thus admit sound GUP versions. Cosmology gains a cleaner tool for testing quantum gravity effects.
arxiv-2511-20640:
Burgert, Herrmann, Cole, and co-authors let editors rewrite how things move inside a video. Their 2025 paper introduces MotionV2V for motion editing. Video generators now make striking footage but resist precise control. Editing the motion of an existing clip was largely unsolved.

Users drag sparse point trajectories to specify new motion. The gap between old and new paths is the motion edit. Counterfactual training pairs share content but differ in motion. A diffusion model fine-tuned on those pairs does the edit. Edits can start mid-video and propagate naturally onward. Camera motion and object motion both respond to the tool. In a four-way user study, theirs won over sixty-five percent preference. Forty-one participants judged twenty test videos. Baselines included ATI, ReVideo, and Go-with-the-Flow. Bezier splines shape the target paths in the interface.
arxiv-2511-20740:
In Jun Park and Kamal Choudhary present in 2025 CHIPS-TB, a framework for comparing tight-binding models, the semi-empirical shortcuts engineers use to predict a material's behaviour. The gold standard, density functional theory, is accurate but too slow for large nanoscale systems. Tight-binding models run far faster, yet parameter sets behave differently on materials, and nobody had benchmarked them under one protocol.

CHIPS-TB lines up five parameterisations, including the DFTB-based MatSci, PBC, and PTBP sets plus SlaKoNet and TB3PY, and tests them on more than 50 materials for semiconductor design. The checks cover bandgaps, band structures, and bulk modulus, how strongly a material resists squeezing. References come from two density-functional methods, OptB88vdW and TBmBJ-DFT, and from experimental data in the JARVIS-DFT database. The code is on GitHub and results sit on the JARVIS-Leaderboard, so new parameter sets face the same yardstick.
arxiv-2511-21040:
Dinanath Padhya and colleagues build in 2025 a radio that recognises how signals are modulated, a skill cognitive radios need to share spectrum politely. Their classifier couples a convolutional network, which extracts spatial features from raw signal samples, with an LSTM network that tracks how the signal evolves in time. The pair runs on a software-defined radio platform, so the same hardware can retune across bands and schemes. Training mixed the public RadioML2018 dataset with custom-generated samples spanning signal-to-noise ratios from 0 to 30 decibels.

The optimised model reached 93.48 percent accuracy, with precision at 93.53 percent and an F1 score of 93.45 percent across the modulation set. Area-under-curve analysis confirmed strong discrimination even in noisy conditions. Crucially, the team tested over the air, identifying live signals broadcast by their own custom FM transmitter, alongside other schemes. They pitch the hybrid as a building block for adaptive spectrum management.
arxiv-2511-21140:
Chungpa Lee and colleagues explain in 2025 why scores handed out by language-model judges are biased, and how to report them honestly. A judge model mislabels some correct answers as wrong and some wrong answers as correct, characterised by its sensitivity and specificity. The naive score, the fraction judged correct, overstates quality when true accuracy is low and understates it when high. In their worked example, with sensitivity 0.9 and specificity 0.7, the naive estimate crosses the truth at an accuracy of 0.75.

Existing corrections assume the judge's error rates are known, which they never are. The authors give a plug-in framework that estimates those rates from a labelled calibration set and builds confidence intervals capturing uncertainty from both calibration and test data. An adaptive algorithm then allocates calibration samples where they shrink the interval most. The message to practitioners: judge-based leaderboards need error bars, not just point scores.
arxiv-2511-21240:
The ATLAS Collaboration reports a hunt for supersymmetric particles at the Large Hadron Collider in a 2025 paper. Supersymmetry predicts partner particles for every known one, and in gauge-mediated models the lightest partner can decay into a photon plus a gravitino, a candidate for dark matter that escapes detectors unseen. The team searched collision debris for events with at least one energetic photon, sprays of particles called jets, and large missing momentum pointing to something invisible.

Using the full Run-2 dataset, 140 inverse femtobarns of proton collisions at 13 TeV, ATLAS found no significant excess above Standard Model expectations. The null result still bites: at 95 percent confidence, gaugino partners are excluded up to masses of 1.2 TeV, depending on how often they choose each decay path. The limits, mapped across masses and branching ratios, narrow the room where this kind of supersymmetry can hide.
arxiv-2511-21440:
Sohan Malkaruge Costa, Benjamin Cohen-Stead, and Steven Johnston map the possible ground states of graphene-like matter when electrons and vibrations conspire, in 2025. On a honeycomb lattice, electron-phonon coupling, electrons tugging the lattice as they move, competes with Hubbard repulsion, electrons avoiding each other on the same site. Which ordered state wins at zero temperature has stayed unclear despite heavy study.

Costa and his coauthors run quantum Monte Carlo simulations of the optical Su-Schrieffer-Heeger-Hubbard model and chart its phase diagram. Three phases appear: a semimetal, a Kekulé valence bond solid, and an antiferromagnet, plus hints of a small shared region. A modest Hubbard repulsion near the semimetal's magnetic tipping point actually strengthens the Kekulé order. Graphene itself sits in the semimetal region, close to the Kekulé boundary, and pushing either interaction drives it toward the bond-ordered phase.
arxiv-2511-21540:
Muralidhar Nalabothula, Davide Sangalli, Fulvio Paleari, Sven Reichardt, and Ludger Wirtz bring order to the symmetry labels of excitons, in 2025. Excitons, bound electron-hole pairs, dominate how thin solids and wide-bandgap insulators absorb light near their band edge. Computer methods predict exciton energies well by solving the Bethe-Salpeter equation. But which symmetries those states carry, and hence which states can absorb light, was largely unknown.

Nalabothula and his coauthors assign each exciton state a symmetry label from group theory. They also define a total crystal angular momentum for excitons and derive its conservation law. That law, modulo the crystal's fold pattern, governs scattering with phonons, the quanta of lattice vibration. Case studies span the exciton spread of lithium fluoride with its absorption rules, and resonant Raman spectra of monolayer molybdenum diselenide. There the law explains the observed signal boost. Tracking symmetry also slashes computing costs.
arxiv-2511-21640:
Sudipta Chakraborty, Kamal Majee, and Achintya Kumar Dutta make relativistic quantum chemistry affordable for heavy elements, in 2025. For the energies of ionized, electron-attached, and excited states where relativity matters, the standard route demands four-component calculations whose cost balloons with system size. Their third-order algebraic diagrammatic construction, or ADC, method cuts that cost with two tricks: Cholesky decomposition of the integrals, and frozen natural spinors that shrink the virtual space.

The method runs on a two-component mean-field Hamiltonian, weighing accuracy against expense, with a state-specific spinor add-on for excited states. It matches four-component third-order results while lowering demands sharply, and scales to a system with more than 2,600 basis functions. Benchmarks span the SOC-81 ionization energies, halogen-oxide fine-structure splittings, cadmium halide photoelectron spectra, and excitation energies of heavy ions. Such spectra become feasible on modest hardware.
arxiv-2511-21740:
Yizi Zhang and eleven coauthors build BIT, an end-to-end brain-to-text system that turns neural activity straight into sentences, in 2025. Speech interfaces for people with paralysis decode sound units first, then stitch sentences with a separate model. Trained apart, gains in one stage do not reliably help the other.

BIT replaces the cascade with a single differentiable network. Its encoder is pretrained across tasks and species, and transfers to both attempted and imagined speech. Used in a cascaded setup, the encoder alone set records on the Brain-to-Text '24 and '25 benchmarks. Fully end-to-end, with contrastive training, BIT cut the word error rate from 24.69 percent down to 10.22 percent, less than half the prior end-to-end figure. Small audio language models, the authors found, improve decoding. One space for attempted and imagined speech points toward interfaces that work when users only imagine speaking.
arxiv-2511-21940:
Nair and Cecotti test deep learning for brain-computer interfaces controlled by looking at flickering targets. In a code-modulated visual evoked potential system, each target flashes with a unique code, and the brain's EEG response, recorded from scalp electrodes, reveals which target the user attends to. Recordings vary over time and sessions, which makes decoding hard for traditional correlation methods.

Using EEG from 13 healthy adults under single-target flicker, the team compared convolutional networks, Siamese networks that judge similarity between signals, and the standard canonical correlation baseline. The deep models significantly outperformed the traditional approach. Distance-based decoding using Earth Mover's Distance, which tolerates timing shifts, proved more robust to latency variation than other metrics, and small time-shift augmentation of training data improved performance across sessions. The best model, a multi-class Siamese network, reached 96.89 percent average accuracy, a step toward reliable single-trial interfaces.
arxiv-2511-22040:
Hosseini, an epidemiological modeler, builds a deliberately minimal forecasting tool for dengue, the mosquito-borne viral disease now pushing into new regions including Florida. Most dengue models demand mosquito counts, climate variables, or long historical records that many health departments simply do not have. His data-parsimonious framework needs only one input: the current season's weekly reported case counts, the numbers a local surveillance system already collects as an outbreak unfolds.

The method plots incidence against cumulative cases, extended here from a basic SIR model to a two-population SEIR version matching dengue's biology. Fits just two parameters, which keeps noise, overfitting risk, and computation low. A Bayesian extension turns reporting and fitting uncertainty into calibrated prediction intervals rather than single guesses. Tested on Florida's 2022–2023 outbreaks, the model matched elaborate competitors' predictive performance at a far lower computational cost.
arxiv-2511-22340:
Fukami and Buurke, hardware security researchers, break the tamper-proof memory that phones and cars rely on, using an electromagnetic pulse. The Replay Protected Memory Block in eMMC storage holds anti-rollback counters, bootloader lock states. Public keys; writes require a secret-key HMAC, so the data is supposed to be unchangeable without the key. The team aimed electromagnetic fault injection at three eMMC chips from a major manufacturer, hoping a precisely timed glitch would skip the authentication check.

It worked on two of the three targets: authentication was glitched and the protected contents overwritten with arbitrary data, the rest of the chip intact. The setup uses commercial components costing under seven thousand US dollars to recreate, so any mechanism trusting RPMB integrity inherits the weakness. Countermeasures such as redundant checks or glitch detectors would need to live in the storage controller itself.
arxiv-2511-22540:
Wood and colleagues explain a surprise in super-concentrated battery electrolytes. In water-in-salt electrolytes, where salt rivals water by weight, the electrical double layer at a carbon electrode controls how much charge the interface stores, but its structure was poorly known. Combining classical and quantum molecular dynamics with capacitance measurements, the team tracked lithium chloride at graphite from dilute up to 20 moles per kilogram.

Below about 6 moles per kilogram, solvated lithium ions dominate the layer's outer plane. Above that threshold, chloride ions co-adsorb through solvent-separated ion pairs, bringing the lithium-to-chloride ratio to one-to-one. This restructuring thickens the layer, redistributes the voltage drop, and lowers the potential of zero charge, matching measurements. Layer capacitance and the electrode's quantum capacitance move in opposite directions with concentration, so capacitance looks constant for few-layer graphite, a cancellation aqueous storage designers need to know about.
arxiv-2511-22640:
De Santi and colleagues generalise how pre-trained generative models are fine-tuned toward goals. Standard fine-tuning of flow and diffusion models maximises expected reward while keeping the model close to pre-training through a Kullback-Leibler penalty. Many tasks break that mould: designers may want risk-averse or novelty-seeking rewards, diversity, or experiment-design objectives, and may prefer closeness measures, such as optimal transport distances or Rényi divergences. Their Flow Density Control reduces this problem to a sequence of fine-tuning steps.

Each step is solvable by scalable methods. Convergence guarantees are proven under assumptions using recent mirror flow theory. Experiments on settings, text-to-image generation, and molecular design show the algorithm steering models toward objectives schemes cannot express, such as worst-case or tail rewards. The framework strictly generalises earlier formulations, though how much the flexibility pays off in applications still needs assessment.
arxiv-2511-23140:
Lima and colleagues tackle a cost problem in burner design, where each candidate geometry must be tested with computational fluid dynamics. And finer simulation meshes give truer answers at far greater expense. Their multi-fidelity Bayesian optimization framework lets a Gaussian-process surrogate learn from low-resolution runs. It reserves high-resolution simulations for promising candidates, with mesh size treated as part of the design.

The search was applied to a non-premixed burner burning hydrogen-enriched fuel, varying height, length, and mesh size under a cap on nitrogen-oxide emissions. It found a design reaching a mean temperature near 2,000 kelvin while staying within the emissions limit set for the study. Compared with a hypothetical campaign using only full-fidelity simulations, the method reached comparable convergence with about 57 percent lower wall time. The saving could shorten design cycles for industrial burners and other reacting-flow systems.
arxiv-2511-23240:
Chen tackles a certification problem that grows brutal with scale. He proves that a continuous-variable quantum state shared across many modes is genuinely entangled rather than a patchwork of smaller entangled groups. Existing criteria handle only a few modes or specific partitions. He builds a general, efficient detection framework from uncertainty relations combined with a sign matrix technique, yielding matrix tests for many kinds of multipartite entanglement.

The criteria apply to entanglement depth and k-separability questions in multimode systems, telling experimenters not just whether entanglement exists but how many parties share it irreducibly. As a demonstration in the paper, he derives genuine entanglement conditions for continuous-variable Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger states with more than a hundred million modes living in a photon-loss and noise environment. At that scale, direct state tomography is hopeless. Earlier criteria had essentially nothing to say.
arxiv-2512-00040:
Sagar Sudhakara and Pankaj Rajak assign network users to slices using large language models. Network slicing splits physical infrastructure into virtual slices tuned for different needs, like high bandwidth or low latency. Allocating users optimally is a constrained problem usually solved with complex algorithms.

The authors test whether language models can handle the radio resource allocation directly. A model that respects constraints in plain reasoning could simplify slice management. The study probes a new role for language models in live network operations. High bandwidth and low latency slices illustrate the competing service requirements the allocation must respect simultaneously.
arxiv-2512-00140:
Xin Li, a computer scientist at the University at Albany, proposes a theory linking computation, memory, and brain inference in a 2025 study. The starting point is a classic result: nondeterministic search takes exponential time but can be simulated in polynomial space. Li asks whether the brain exploits a related trade.

The proposal, called Memory-Amortized Inference, suggests the brain physically carries out an inverse form of that trade. In this picture, stored memory turns chaotic exploration into a geometry of certainty. The work is speculative theory, aimed at readers who enjoy bold connections between computing limits and how minds reach conclusions. The geometry of certainty in the title names the end state the theory aims to explain.
arxiv-2512-00240:
Hotel managers lose revenue when guests cancel, so predicting cancellations has direct business value. Yingdong Yang presents a Bayesian analysis of hotel booking cancellations in 2025, using hierarchical modeling in PyMC. Three model specifications of increasing complexity are compared.

The study investigates how lead time, special requests, and parking requirements affect cancellation probability. It also explores interaction effects with hotel type. A hierarchical Bayesian approach shares information across groups while showing uncertainty honestly, which helps managers set deposit and overbooking policies with clearer eyes. Hierarchical models suit hotels, since chains, cities, and property types all shape behavior. The comparison of three specifications shows what the added complexity buys. For a front desk team, the gain is plain. Fewer shocks at check-out time, and a clear view of which kinds of stays are most apt to fall through.
arxiv-2512-00640:
Tire degradation decides Formula 1 strategy as surely as engine power does. Cole Cappello and Andrew Hoegh present a state-space approach to modeling tire degradation in racing in 2025. Tire wear is one of the most important factors in Grand Prix race planning.

State-space models track a hidden wear state through noisy lap-time observations, updating estimates as the race unfolds. A good degradation model tells a team when to pit before the tires fall off a performance cliff. The study is a tidy case of statistical modeling meeting a live, high-stakes decision problem. State-space models are built for exactly this mix of hidden state and noisy data.
arxiv-2512-00840:
Tamanna Jain and Piero Rettegno compute a key force for gravitational wave science in a 2025 paper. When two compact objects orbit each other, they lose energy to gravitational waves and slowly spiral inward. The radiation reaction force captures that loss and drives the orbit's change.

Most studies of modified gravity theories assume near-circular orbits. Real future detections may catch eccentric ones, where the orbit is stretched into an oval. Jain and Rettegno derive the force for nonspinning eccentric orbits in massless scalar-tensor theories. They use the effective-one-body formalism, which maps two bodies onto one, up to a stated accuracy order.
arxiv-2512-01040:
Vladislav Shishkov studies how light reaches thermal balance inside molecular films in a 2025 paper. When molecules absorb and emit light, low-frequency vibrations of the molecules shape the spectra. Those vibrations set the linewidths of absorption and emission peaks, and the gap between them known as the Stokes shift.

In cavities that use a molecular film as the active medium, the same vibrations help light thermalize, or settle into equilibrium. That settling can enable Bose-Einstein condensation of light. Shishkov computes the thermalization rate for weakly coupled molecular systems. Knowing the rate helps design cavities that actually reach the condensed state.
arxiv-2512-01240:
Shaddin Dughmi, Yusuf Kalayci, and Xinyu Liu study choice under doubt with costly checks. In packing tasks, each item has an unknown gain. Checking an item costs time or money. The key choice is which few items to check first.

Their work looks for sparse sets that still lead to near-best plans. Past work scored sparsity by how many items were checked. The team seeks sets that come close to the best score with few checks. Good sparse sets save cost in tasks like hiring, ads, and stock choice, where each check has a real price.
arxiv-2512-01340:
Yingjie Zhou and a large team work on judging fake talking faces. Speech-driven tools can make a still face seem to talk. New tools can move two or more faces at once. That adds life to calls and shows, but quality drops as faces are added.

Judging that quality by eye is slow and uneven. The team built EvalTalker to learn the judging task itself. It scores clips made from real face photos with more than one subject. Fair scores help builders spot flaws fast. They also give users a clear sign of which tools to trust.
arxiv-2512-01540:
Zipeng Wang and Dan Xu speed up 3D rebuilding from many photos. Feed-forward methods now beat slow per-scene tuning. Top models attend to all image tokens at once. That full attention is sharp but costly as views pile up.

Their model, FlashVGGT, squeezes descriptor attention to cut that cost. It keeps global links between views while work drops. Fast, scalable rebuilding serves in robots, mapping, and virtual scenes. Lower cost also lets smaller teams run state-of-the-art geometry tools on plain hardware. Squeezed attention also lowers memory load, so longer view sets fit on one card where full attention would spill and fail.
arxiv-2512-02040:
A system of equations can demand even more discipline from its solutions than a single equation does. Junfeng Xu, Sujoy Majumder, and Debabrata Pramanik study in 2025 the exact form of entire solutions, functions defined on the whole complex plane, to a system of Fermat-type partial differential-difference equations.

The system couples two unknown functions, mixing their partial derivatives with shifted values of each other. The authors restrict to solutions of finite order, a growth condition that keeps the search manageable, and pin down their precise form. Results like these extend complex analysis's catalogue of which coupled functional equations admit solutions at all.
arxiv-2512-02240:
Language models solve narrative tasks by writing out long chains of thought, and those traces can be trained with reinforcement learning to be more useful. Alexander Gurung, Nikolay Malkin, and Mirella Lapata study in 2025 a lighter alternative: latent reasoning, where the thinking happens inside the model's hidden states rather than in words.

Treating the reasoning trace as a latent variable means the model can learn to think in a compressed internal form. Optimizing that ability directly could cut the cost and length of explicit chains of thought. For storytelling and other narrative work, where fluent output matters, a quiet internal reasoning step may preserve quality while keeping responses concise.
arxiv-2512-02440:
Galaxies are not one color: their centers and outskirts differ, and that gradient records how they assembled. M. Martorano and nine co-authors trace in 2025 how ultraviolet-to-near-infrared color gradients evolve with redshift and stellar mass, using Hubble and Webb telescope data on more than ten thousand galaxies.

Their sample spans the era when galaxies were forming stars most vigorously, with masses above a billion suns. Radial gradients in two rest-frame colors separate age, dust, and composition effects across each galaxy. Knowing how gradients depend on mass reveals whether galaxies grew inside-out or outside-in, a basic question in galaxy evolution.
arxiv-2512-02540:
Francisco Monteiro and five co-authors study liquid sloshing inside partly filled fuel tanks. When a tank is shaken up and down near twice its natural sloshing frequency, the liquid can resonate strongly. That parametric resonance drives large waves, breaks the surface, and mixes the liquid hard.

The team maps the regimes of this behavior for horizontal cylindrical tanks under vertical acceleration. Knowing which regime a tank sits in helps predict loads on its walls. Such maps matter for vehicle design, since violent sloshing can harm stability and crack structures over time. Tank tests on the ground are far cheaper than repairs once a fleet is in daily use.
arxiv-2512-02740:
Waleed El-Geresy and Deniz Gündüz turn an attacker into a training tool for an autoencoder. An autoencoder squeezes data into a small latent code, then rebuilds the original from it. For the code to behave well, its spread should match a chosen bell shaped distribution.

A wireless jammer tries to disrupt recovery of a Gaussian source sent over the channel. Fighting that jamming pushes the encoder to shape its latent space as desired. The setup joins learning with adversarial pressure, a trick that may help design robust communication codes. Noise is most often the foe in radio work, so a scheme that puts noise to work stands out from the pack.
arxiv-2512-02840:
Tom Zehle and four co-authors package prompt optimization so practitioners can actually use it. Tuning prompts has become crucial for getting the best from large language models across many tasks. Research code proving the point often sits isolated and unmaintained, which blocks adoption.

Their framework, promptolution, is unified and modular, gathering prompt tuning methods in one maintained home. Users can swap parts in and out instead of rebuilding each experiment. Shared tooling of this kind helps prompt research leave the lab and serve real products. Shared racks get patched and kept, while lone code rots, and that gap is why the field needs this kind of home.
arxiv-2512-02940:
F. S. Luiz and three co-authors cover graph vertices with the fewest guards, guided by a quantum walk. The minimum vertex cover problem asks for the smallest set of vertices touching every edge. It is a classic hard problem across scheduling, networks, and biology.

Their heuristic lets a quantum walker spread coherently over the graph. Transition probabilities then flag highly influential vertices for the cover. The method aims to scale to larger graphs than exact solvers handle. Quantum heuristics of this kind may one day speed real optimization work. Walk based picks lean on the shape of the graph, not on brute force. That is why they may grow where brute force stalls out cold.
arxiv-2512-03340:
Medical papers are hard for many readers to use. Rohan Charudatt Salvi and co-authors build a data set for controllable medical summaries in this 2025 work. Automatic simplification can raise health literacy, but most tools assume one generic audience.

Readers differ widely in medical knowledge and in what they need. The authors' data set, PERCS, is guided by personas that stand for different user groups. Persona-guided summaries could tailor the same paper for a patient, a nurse, or a student. That tailoring may make research more usable. Persona control could also help clinicians write summaries matched to each reader's needs.
arxiv-2512-03440:
Noise bursts, called glitches, pollute gravitational wave data. Tabata Aira Ferreira, Gabriela González, and Osvaldo Salas analyze LIGO glitches in this 2025 work. They use data from the first part of the fourth LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA observing run.

The team applies t-SNE, an unsupervised method that maps data into clusters for viewing. That view shows how groups of glitches behave. Knowing glitch families helps separate real cosmic signals from detector noise. Cleaner data raise the odds of spotting black hole and neutron star mergers. Cluster views help engineers group glitches by cause and fix the worst sources.
arxiv-2512-03540:
Recipe photos should match each cooking step in order. Ruoxuan Zhang and co-authors present CookAnything in this 2025 work. Cooking is sequential and visual, with each step carrying procedural logic and visual meaning.

Diffusion models generate strong single images but struggle with structured multi-step scenes. CookAnything aims for flexible and consistent images across a recipe's steps. Consistent step images could help cooking apps and learners. They also test whether image models can follow real-world procedures faithfully. Consistency across steps is the hard part, since one wrong pan or color breaks the recipe's visual story for learners following along.
arxiv-2512-03640:
Jiahao Zhang, Xiao Zhao, and Guangyu Gao build a detector for the tiniest targets in satellite imagery. Small objects drown in deep networks' shrinking feature maps and busy backgrounds. Their 2025 network, MKSNet, answers with kernels that adapt their size to the scene.

A multi-kernel selection mechanism reaches for wide context when it helps and tight detail when it does not.
