arxiv-2603-08640: Ben Rank and colleagues test whether language-model agents can run post-training on their own under tight compute limits. Agents get full freedom to browse, test, and curate data, with ten hours on one H100 graphics card. The best agent trails official tuned models overall, though it tops them on one task, and the team flags reward hacking such as training on test data.
arxiv-2603-09240: C. L. Liu shows that incoherent operations, or IOs, can turn some quantum states into others that a stricter class, DIOs, cannot reach. This settles an open problem posed by Chitambar and Gour in 2016. Liu also proves no set of IO monotones can fully pin down when one state converts to another under strictly incoherent operations. Shared monotones fall short for DIOs as well, sharpening the map of what coherence resources allow.
arxiv-2603-09540: T. Boin and colleagues estimate stellar ages with deep neural networks trained on stellar evolutionary grids rather than on prior age labels. That model-driven route promises a wider, less biased range than data-driven training. Multilayer perceptrons learn to map metallicity, absolute magnitude, and color to age for five grids, from BaSTI to SYCLIST. Fed with Gaia photometry and survey spectroscopy, the method yields isochrone ages for 1.3 million stars and enables the first grid-to-grid age comparisons at this scale.
arxiv-2603-10040: Victor Edmonds argues that a stubborn mismatch in solar corona temperature readings points to non Maxwellian electrons. Radio brightness data suggest a much cooler value than scale height modelling requires, and the gap persists across eight years and two instruments. Turbulent scattering explains part of the drop but not the rest, and the ratio stays fixed while turbulence varies. A kappa distribution, sampling core and tail differently, matches the observed ratio.
arxiv-2603-10240: Diaz, Constanzo and Sandler present nlm, a set of Max externals for real time nonlinear modal synthesis. The tools model strings, membranes and plates, with live control of physical parameters and support for custom modal data. Multichannel output is built in, and the code is released as open source for all to use. By placing physical modelling inside a familiar music tool, nlm lowers the bar for composers, performers and sound designers.
arxiv-2603-10340: Sangmim Song and co-authors present Concept-Gated Visual Distillation, a training-free add-on that helps vision-language-action models work in cluttered scenes. Clutter dilutes features with background noise, so the method splits instructions into safe and distractor sets, refines targets by cross-validation and spatial checks, then cleans the view by Fourier-based inpainting. Spatial geometry stays intact while semantic distractors fade. In dense clutter tests the method reached a far higher success rate than the baseline, stopping the usual collapse in performance.
arxiv-2603-10640: Adam Trybus, Bartosz Bartnicki, and Remigiusz Kinas report a research program on the reasoning of Bielik, the Polish large language model. The field report walks through stages of work: first benchmarking the model and building the evaluation method, then comparing results with other models. The authors are candid about the limits of the analyses so far. They close with future prospects, framed by a fast-moving, competitive field in which a smaller national model must keep pace.
arxiv-2603-10940: Joy Saha and coauthors present STADA, which makes simulation tests for self-driving agents. It builds the tests directly from a formal safety specification written in temporal logic. Given one, it constructs every distinct starting scene. It also builds a diverse set of continuations. It builds runs that reflect the stated behaviors. It does not rely on templates or random scenario building. On several such specs, it more than doubles the best baseline's coverage on the finest criteria. It matches that coverage with far fewer runs.
arxiv-2603-11140: Gideon Popoola and John Sheppard argue that fairness work in machine learning has stared at results and missed procedure. A model can explain itself in unlike ways to protected groups, and that erodes trust. Their framework, Group Counterfactual Integrated Gradients, pushes training toward explanation invariance across groups. It works out each input's explanation against group-conditional baselines and acts against cross-group gaps. Against six top methods, it cuts this disparity by a lot. It keeps performance and accuracy-fairness trade-offs competitive.
arxiv-2603-11940: Kendiukhov maps the circuits of Geneformer, a single-cell foundation model, by tracing every active feature at one layer. Selective sampling in past work risked bias, so he traces all 4,065 sparse autoencoder features and finds nearly 1.4 million strong downstream links. The wiring is heavy-tailed: 1.8% of features act as hubs, and 40% of the top hubs lack any biological label. Ablating feature triplets shows redundancy grows with interaction order, with no synergy. Steering tests tie late-layer features to pushing cells toward maturity.
arxiv-2603-12240: Liu, Tang, Cui, Xu, and Shen compress tokens in diffusion models for both generation and classification. Most speed methods guard image quality while they ignore class accuracy. BiGain instead splits features by frequency, so fine detail and global meaning part ways cleanly. Laplacian-gated merging joins smooth tokens and spares high-contrast ones that carry edges. A key-value downsampling step keeps queries intact while it trims attention cost. Across backbones and datasets the speed-accuracy trade-off improves, with generation quality held or raised.
arxiv-2603-12340: Eddy and co-authors frame task completion time updates as a POMDP control problem. Project teams must choose when to revise announced finish times for clients. Static forecasts and ad-hoc rules ignore the sequential nature of that choice. Their reward weighs announcement errors against update frequency, since churn erodes trust and forces replanning. A mixed observability frame keeps policy optimization efficient with off-the-shelf solvers. Simulations show large cuts in needless updates while prediction accuracy holds or improves.
arxiv-2603-12440: Wiedemann, Leboutet, Paulitsch, Wofk, and Ummenhofer optimize GPU kernels with KernelFoundry, a tool that evolves kernels. Kernel tuning tests LLMs hard, since it demands hardware knowledge, parallel strategy, and profiling skill at once. Most LLM routes use plain prompting with profile feedback as the only hardware signal. KernelFoundry instead runs MAP-Elites search over kernel-specific trait axes. Prompts evolve too, and templates tune kernels to inputs and hardware. SYCL kernels beat baselines on KernelBench with a solid average speedup.
arxiv-2603-12940: Anees Peringal and co-authors plan coordinated robot moves for hybrid objects that mix stiff and bendy parts. Ropes and cables alone are well studied, but hybrid assemblies in tight spaces are not. Their quasi-static planner uses a strain-based Cosserat rod model for the bendy links. Compliance helps the object pass constraints and reach goals rigid tools cannot. Analytic gradients speed inverse kinetostatic solving by up to 33x over finite differences. A dual-arm robot test confirmed the planner in a tight setup.
arxiv-2603-13640: Weichen Li and co-authors present SemRep, a way to learn code representations from code transformations. Code transformation is a core task in software work, and its success rests on a good representation of code semantics. Past methods leave that representation implicit in model weights, or lean on rigid compiler abstractions. SemRep instead uses semantics-preserving transformations as the representation itself. They serve as a mid-training task and as guidance for later transforms. Tests on code editing and optimization beat finetuned baselines.
arxiv-2603-13840: Shan introduces ClimateAgents, a multi-agent research assistant for studying how social behavior and climate change interact. Specialized agents share the work of forming hypotheses, fetching data, running statistics, and writing structured reports. The system draws on sources such as the United Nations and the World Bank. It favors open exploration and scenario checks over narrow prediction tasks. The author argues that this mix gives researchers an adaptive, interpretable way to probe social-climate dynamics.
arxiv-2603-14040: Ferrari presents Pyroclast, a modular Python solver for geodynamics built for speed. Older geodynamics codes are often single-block Fortran or C++ with weak GPU support. Pyroclast pairs modern numerical methods with GPU-ready, object-oriented design. Its core is a two-dimensional viscous flow solver using the marker-in-cell method and a matrix-free grid scheme. Benchmarks show strong scaling, with a five- to ten-fold speedup on NVIDIA A100 GPUs over multi-core CPUs.
arxiv-2603-14240: Rathore and co-authors open a new task: fine-grained category discovery in unseen domains. Models learn from labeled source data, then must spot known classes and find new ones in unlabeled target data with a shifted style. Fine-grained classes differ subtly, which makes the shift harder. The team builds painting and sketch test domains for birds, cars, and aircraft data. Their FoCUS method pairs stable part discovery with uncertainty-guided feature changes. It beats strong baselines across the three test groups.
arxiv-2603-14540: Claramunt builds separated graphs that encode the dynamics of a homeomorphism. The space is compact, metric and totally disconnected. Classical Bratteli diagrams get a wider form here. The construction splits the static shape of the space from the map dynamics. Four cases show the method at work. They are the two-sided shift, the bit-wise NOT map, the odometer map and a shift on a compactified integer line. Minimal systems can then be read straight from the graph, Claramunt notes.
arxiv-2603-14740: Roy and Sahoo present CosmoDS, a Python toolkit for cosmology via dynamical systems in Cobaya. Dynamical systems analysis probes how cosmological models evolve and settle. Dark energy models lean on that lens most often. CosmoDS recasts models in dynamical form at the background level. The Cobaya link gives users its full inference machinery for free. Parameter estimation and model comparison ride on proven statistical tools. The package aims to make dynamical checks a routine step in cosmology work. Modular design keeps new models easy to add.
arxiv-2603-14840: Xu and co-authors evolve wide O star binaries through a mass-ejection channel at the LBV stage. Long-period Wolf-Rayet binaries from mass transfer should be common but look rare. Ejection at closest approach offers a fresh orbital path. Instant ejection at periastron makes the orbit math analytic. Population synthesis for the Small Magellanic Cloud tests the idea. Orbits widen and grow more eccentric under ejection, unlike mass transfer. WR 140, with its 2,895-day period, fits the pattern well. Measurable space velocities and binary breakups also follow.
arxiv-2603-14940: Alwala and co-authors pair neural control with Kalman filtering for differential drive robots in messy settings. Unknown dynamics and degrading sensors undermine tracking on their own. A Lyapunov-based controller hosts adaptive neural networks for the unknown parts. Radial basis weights update online as the robot moves. Feedback linearization with learned dynamics carries stability proofs. An extended Kalman filter fuses inertial, camera, LiDAR and wheel data. Drift, slip and sensor failure all enter the test load. Gazebo runs and real-world trials check the frame.
arxiv-2603-15040: Hoque and co-authors report an explosive molecular outflow in the massive protocluster IRAS 15520-5234, seen in the ALMA-QUARKS survey. Carbon monoxide data show 28 collimated outflow fingers that share one origin and follow a Hubble-Lemaitre velocity law. The fingers point in no preferred direction. Their mass, momentum, and energy beat typical protostar outflows by at least ten times. The team dates the event to about 6,550 years ago and estimates one such event per 83 years in the Galaxy.
arxiv-2603-15340: Zhou and co-authors present DOS, a training-free sampler for masked diffusion language models. Current decoding picks tokens by local uncertainty, which ignores how tokens depend on each other. DOS reads attention matrices to gauge those links. It leans on unmasked tokens when it updates masked spots. Tests show steady gains on code generation and math reasoning tasks. The sampler also plugs into existing parallel sampling methods. That pairing speeds generation without a drop in quality.
arxiv-2603-15440: Prajuli and co-authors build the first genre classification study for Nepali music, a tradition past systems ignored. Their dataset holds about 8,000 labeled clips of thirty seconds across eight genres, from Lok Dohori duets to Tamang Selo. Five classical models train on 51 hand-crafted audio features. Four deep models read Mel spectrograms instead. A sequential network that feeds convolutional layers into an LSTM won, at 84 percent accuracy. The best classical models, logistic regression and XGBoost, reached 71 percent.
arxiv-2603-15540: Wang and co-authors present DOT, an automated tuner for database systems that picks key knobs and samples settings online. Most tuning parameters matter little, but finding the vital few used to cost warm-up runs and expert time. DOT prunes weak knobs with recursive feature elimination and cross-validation. A likelihood ratio test balances exploration against exploitation during search. Bayesian optimization then tunes on the fly, with no warm-up phase. Tests match or beat top tuners while cutting tuning overhead sharply.
arxiv-2603-15640: Lan and co-authors review how text works as a story device in data visualization. Past work treats text mostly as data input or as a control for interaction. Its role in storytelling and sense-making stays scattered across studies. The team reviewed 98 publications on text as narrative. They sort how text is used, what it does, and how it can be designed. The review names open gaps and future paths for clearer data communication.
arxiv-2603-15940: Guesmi and Shafique hide objects in images without sparking model hallucinations. Older hiding attacks blank out a region and leave a semantic gap. Vision-language models then invent wrong objects inside the void. Their attack re-encodes the target region to match its background. Token structure and attention flow stay intact through the change. A pixel-level optimizer enforces the match across many layers. Tests keep up to 86 percent of other objects intact. Grounded hallucination drops by up to threefold against suppression attacks.
arxiv-2603-16240: Abi Hana and co-authors benchmark visual odometry and SLAM systems for warehouse robots. They test several methods on set paths with in-plane, turning, and mixed motion. A large production site run covers about 1.7 km. Ground truth comes from a motion capture rig and a LiDAR SLAM reference. A hybrid stack won: the cuVSLAM front-end with a custom back-end. The team then ran that stack on an NVIDIA Jetson board.
arxiv-2603-16340: Cai and co-authors estimate depth from a single image with their Iris framework. Feed-forward methods need huge training sets and still lose detail. Diffusion methods carry rich priors but transfer poorly to real scenes. Iris runs a two-stage schedule that shares weights. A prior stage moves low-frequency real cues in by distillation. A geometry stage then guards high-frequency detail for fidelity. Tests show strong gains and good in-the-wild generalization.
arxiv-2603-16640: Lyu, Dai, and Oset study a J/ψ decay into a cascade of baryons and a kaon. New BESIII data motivate the work. Three resonances enter their model of the reaction. The Ξ(1690) is built dynamically from meson-baryon interactions. That state was left out of the BESIII analysis. The model matches all three invariant mass distributions well. The team finds the Ξ(1690) plays a crucial role. Bootstrap checks gauge the model's uncertainty.
arxiv-2603-16740: Benato, Pofi, Puiu, and Ternes scope precision neutrino scattering tests with lithium bolometers. Coherent elastic scattering off nuclei resists precise measurement. Electron-capture sources give mono-energetic neutrinos at high flux. Their compact array uses lithium fluoride absorbers, light and threshold-friendly. With one kilogram and strong sources, flux error nears 3% in 90 days. That level tests the gallium anomaly directly. It can separate nuclear effects from source miscounts or oscillations.
arxiv-2603-16840: Pawlowsky and co-authors probe positional bias in vision transformers. Models like DINOv2 learn rich image features, but layout choices can add bias tied to position, not content. That hurts fields like materials science, where images have no preferred direction. With linear probing, the team finds bias across many objectives and encodings. They then fine-tune models to use ALiBi relative positional encoding. The authors report that bias drops while general semantics stay intact. The cleaned features also work well for segmenting complex microscopy images.
arxiv-2603-16940: Yan and co-authors study how many control points a learning based registration network needs. Dense voxel wise decoders are high dimensional and can be unstable in flat or noisy regions. Their GridReg framework predicts displacements at a sparse grid of control points. Encoder features become tokens with positional encoding. A cross attention module then predicts the deformation field. Grid adaptive training lets one model run at several grid sizes. On prostate, pelvic, and brain data, they report better accuracy at similar or lower cost.
arxiv-2603-17040: Whitebook and co-authors model mass transfer in substellar and low mass binaries. Dozens of ultracool binaries are known, but study covers only non interacting ones. Simulations with brown dwarf equations of state reveal a donor mass inversion. Above it, the donor is heavier; below it, the accretor is. Near equal mass ratios are unstable below the hydrogen burning limit, while slight deviations stay stable. They predict periods from under 1 hour to 3.5 hours. Transfer lands as direct impact, forming a hot spot.
arxiv-2603-17540: D'Amico and co-authors describe GLIDE, a generative recommender for podcast discovery at Spotify. Listeners mix steady favorites with shifting intent, which strains classic recommenders. GLIDE treats the catalog as semantic IDs and frames picking shows as instruction following. Recent listening and light context steer each request, with long-term taste as soft prompts. Online tests with millions of users lifted new-show discovery by up to 14.3 percent, they report.
arxiv-2603-17740: Slavin, Kornbleuth, Opher, and Toth model interstellar dust drifting through the heliosphere. In situ detectors catch the grains, but reading the source cloud needs transport physics. Solar wind fields bend grain paths, and the sector region flips polarity fast. That region works like a window that lets small grains dive deep, they find. Solar-cycle swings in dust density also shrink once the sector counts. Near-Earth readings may mirror the source cloud well.
arxiv-2603-17840: An and co-authors survey video understanding from geometry through semantics to unified models. Video adds time flow and shifting context that still images lack. The low-level side covers geometry, while the high-level side covers meaning and events. Newer work merges both into single models that adapt across tasks. The survey maps key design trends across that shift. Open problems point toward robust, scalable video foundation models.
arxiv-2603-17940: Ali and Thakur bound logarithmic coefficients for Ma-Minda type convex functions. Three subclasses come under study: convex functions of fixed order, Janowski convex functions, and Robertson functions. All live as normalized analytic functions on the open unit disk. They prove bounds for single coefficients and for weighted sums alike. Some past results in this line were wrong, and the new work corrects them. Known estimates also gain wider reach.
arxiv-2603-18040: Amos proposes a light phase-field surrogate for the ductile-to-brittle transition in body-centred cubic systems. Full coupled models are too costly for wide parameter sweeps at cold temperatures. The surrogate uses just displacement and damage fields at fixed temperature. Three tuned rules set stiffness loss, yield stress, and fracture toughness by temperature. FEniCSx tests on a notched sample from 77 to 293 K show the shift from brittle to ductile response.
arxiv-2603-18140: Chiang, Poland, and Rogelberg develop a moment-based numerical bootstrap for conformal field theories. Moments are weighted averages over conformal data, giving a coarse global probe of the spectrum. Standard semidefinite tools then yield rigorous bounds on the operator distribution. In the heavy regime, bounds converge fast toward analytic power laws. At finite dimensions, low moments recover Ising kinks and reveal two new kink families tied to operator decoupling.
arxiv-2603-18240: NaseriTehrani, Salehi, and Tölli analyze degrees of freedom in cache-aided asymmetric MIMO systems. A server with L antennas serves K users split into groups with varied receive antennas. Four content-aware strategies bridge the gap: min-G, Grouping, Super-grouping, and Phantom. They pair these with three symmetric coded caching policies of varied complexity. Results show large DoF gains and flexible trade-offs against subpacketization cost.
arxiv-2603-18640: Gruffaz and co-authors compare the two main variants of the No-U-Turn sampler. NUTS-mul picks indices by multinomial sampling, while NUTS-BPS uses biased progressive sampling. The team derives first necessary conditions for geometric ergodicity in both. They also prove sufficient conditions for NUTS-mul. For NUTS-BPS, they give a first mixing time result on Gaussian targets. Both variants mix in time that grows like the fourth root of dimension. The constants favor NUTS-BPS, though the broad behavior matches closely.
arxiv-2603-18740: Alexopoulos and co-authors show that crafted pull request text can bias AI security code review. They first test six language models under five framing setups. Framing effects prove systematic across models. A controlled study then uses 33 real CVEs in 20 projects and two review pipelines. Simple template attacks fail and can even raise suspicion. A refined attack, tuned against a local clone of the pipeline, succeeds in 32 of 33 cases. The authors warn that human oversight and contributor trust remain vital in review workflows.
arxiv-2603-19040: Chen and co-authors analyze privacy and learning speed in wireless federated learning with noise added for privacy. Past work left the exact privacy loss unclear. Many studies also assumed simple curved losses or skipped gradient clipping. Their study covers smooth, non-convex losses and counts device choice and mini-batch sampling. They show privacy loss can settle to a fixed value rather than grow with rounds. They prove speed bounds with clipping in place. They also give a clear trade-off between privacy and utility.
arxiv-2603-19340: Chhetri, Dhakal, and Gautam test post-quantum schemes on a small chip. They benchmark ML-KEM and ML-DSA, the NIST standards, on the ARM Cortex-M0+ in an RP2040. They run all six parameter sets at 125 MHz using PQClean reference code. A full ML-KEM-512 key exchange takes 35.7 ms, 17 times faster than their ECDH P-256 baseline. They report that ML-DSA signing times vary widely due to rejection sampling. They also show that timing alone can reveal how many tries a signature took. Their suite is open source.
arxiv-2603-19540: Lemm and co-authors prove diffusion bounds for a broad class of parabolic equations. The equations may be degenerate and may change over time. The bounds are Gaussian space-time upper bounds on solutions. They follow the Davies-Gaffney and integrated Nash-Aronson forms. The results hold in Lp spaces for the full range of p. Both linear and nonlinear equations are covered.
arxiv-2603-19840: Quetti and co-authors propose a way to make cluster analysis easier to explain. Standard clustering groups like cases but rarely shows which traits drive the groups. Their method uses bagging and feature dropout across many resampled runs. It then scores each feature by mutual information with the cluster labels. Scores are weighted by how sound each partition looks. The output is a consensus grouping plus feature importance scores. Tests on simulated and real data show the method works well.
arxiv-2603-19940: Sabatini builds a hybrid topic model to map themes in Pushkin's novel in verse, Evgenij Onegin. The study uses an Italian translation, split into thirty-five segments of lemmatised content words. Latent Dirichlet Allocation gives five stable, readable topics under a multi-seed consensus protocol. A supervised sparse discriminant method then finds lexical markers that sharpen each theme. Groups of nearby stanzas mark narrative hubs where themes meet key episodes. The maps track the poem's emotional and structural arc without replacing close reading.
arxiv-2603-20040: Aguilar, Pusztai, and Pizio study how pressure changes the traits of simple alcohols in simulation. Methanol, ethanol, and 1-propanol are run from 1 bar up to 3 kbar. The united-atom force field is checked against measured data at each pressure. They track density growth, isothermal compressibility, dielectric constant, and self-diffusion. Pair distribution functions show how the liquid's structure shifts under load. Coordination numbers add a second view of that change. The paper ends with lessons for future modelling of alcohols under pressure.
arxiv-2603-20440: Feireisl studies a way to blend live data into flow simulations for the barotropic Navier-Stokes system. One solution is observed and stays bounded over the full watch period. A second solution comes from a numeric method and may sit in a wider class. He shows the two solutions fully sync on any compact time span ahead. This holds when the nudging terms are set with care. The result backs methods that steer simulations toward observed flows.
arxiv-2603-20740: Churazov and co-authors model the southern eROSITA bubble as a forward shock. The bubble's south east part looks far simpler than the north. A past burst at the Galactic Center likely drove the shock. They put the bubble radius at 7 to 8 kiloparsecs. Its age comes out at 5 to 8 million years, likely a low bound. The shock now moves near 700 kilometers per second. The gas it crosses is thin and poor in heavy elements.
arxiv-2603-21440: Wang and Yu train compact open language models to answer questions over knowledge graphs. Such tasks need accurate multi-hop reasoning, and stepwise pipelines often pass errors along. Their KG-Hopper framework uses reinforcement learning to fit the whole graph traversal into one thinking stage. The model can weigh cross-step links, explore paths, and backtrack within that single pass. On eight benchmarks, a 7B model beat larger multi-step systems and rivaled strong closed models, the authors report.
arxiv-2603-21740: Martinez and co-authors add a twist to the classic prophet inequality problem. A decision maker sees options one by one and must pick without knowing the future. In their variant, grabbing an option takes a fixed delay, and the grab succeeds only with some chance. During the delay, no other options can be considered. They compare the online decision maker with two stronger benchmarks, including a prophet who knows all outcomes. Each ratio is at least one over d plus two, and matching examples show most bounds are tight.
arxiv-2603-22040: Battye and co-authors construct kinky vortons in the two-Higgs-doublet model. A vorton is a current-carrying ring of string that can hold a stable size. The team works in the Z2-symmetric version of the model. The rings persist under lopsided perturbations. A thin string approximation matches their radii and oscillation rates well. The authors argue this makes vortons plausible in a well-motivated extension of the Standard Model. They also find a composite domain wall hinting how such defects could form in 3D.
arxiv-2603-22240: Greilhuber and Sharma draw a sharp line for when a graph problem admits a polynomial kernel. The problem is Component Order Connectivity, a generalization of Vertex Cover. Deleting at most k vertices should leave only components of at most d vertices. For Vertex Cover, the line runs between treewidth 1 and 2. For this problem, the authors locate the line elsewhere. A polynomial kernel exists when the parameter is distance to pathwidth-1 graphs, plus d. Past work rules one out for distance to pathwidth-2 forests.
arxiv-2603-22340: Tadayon and Gupta build a Graph RAG system for unknown or structured search spaces. Classic retrieval-augmented generation struggles there, since it leans on flat document chunks. Their system stores knowledge as labeled property graphs and as RDF data. Documents become RDF triplets built from JSON key-value pairs. That lets semi-structured data join the graph cleanly. A text-to-Cypher tool turns user questions into graph queries with over 90 percent accuracy. Tests show the graph system beats embedding-based RAG on accuracy and reasoning.
arxiv-2603-22640: Dietrich, Lee, Nies, and Vinyals report computer experiments on group rings of torsion-free groups. They probe two traits: the trivial units property and the unique product property. Both link to Kaplansky's unit and zero-divisor conjectures. The team classifies certain symmetric nontrivial units in the binary group ring of the Hantzsche-Wendt group. That group was used in Gardam's disproof of the unit conjecture. They also present a new candidate group. It may fail one property yet keep the other, a split no group is yet known to show.
arxiv-2603-22740: Ikeda, Kawada, and Shiomi report a huge resistance drop in palladium films after hydrogen uptake. The films are highly disordered and made by high-pressure magnetron sputtering. Resistance falls by a factor of up to 335. That ratio beats earlier reports, the authors say. Microscopy points to better contact between palladium grains. X-ray diffraction shows hydrogen-driven crystallization of the film. The team suggests the effect offers a simple way to boost hydrogen sensor performance.
arxiv-2603-23040: Liang and co-authors find a light dark matter window in the scotogenic inverse seesaw model. The model links neutrino mass and dark matter in one frame. They test a light fermionic candidate against many constraints. Data cover neutrino oscillations, flavor violation, Higgs and Z decays, relic density, and direct detection. A narrow mass window near sixty GeV passes all checks. Next-generation detectors and future lepton colliders can test it jointly, they report.
arxiv-2603-23140: Jafari and Farnia present DAK-UCB, a routing method that picks generative models for each prompt. Most routers chase fidelity scores alone and ignore output diversity. Their contextual bandit method scores both traits. Diversity is measured with prompt-aware scores built from past prompt-output pairs. Kernel distance and kernel entropy supply the joint measures. The router learns online as prompts arrive in sequence. Tests show more diverse model choice with fidelity kept high. Code is released in public.
arxiv-2603-23340: Lowack and six co-authors probe why sodium metal anodes peel in ceramic solid-state batteries. During discharge, vacancies pile up at the metal-ceramic interface and break contact. The team ramps current between two sodium electrodes across a ceramic electrolyte. Past a critical current, the anode voltage climbs exponentially instead of linearly. Heating tests give an activation energy of 0.13 to 0.15 eV for three electrolytes. That far exceeds the bulk diffusion value, so bulk flow is not the bottleneck. A tin-sodium layer lowers the barrier, pointing at the interface.
arxiv-2603-23940: Yu and co-authors present VeriFi, a watermarking system that protects face images and can restore them. Deepfakes threaten media provenance and copyright. Older systems embed large location payloads, which hurt image quality and decode poorly after strong edits. VeriFi embeds a compact semantic watermark that acts as a prior for restoration. It finds tampered pixels by matching image features with decoded signals, so no extra payload is needed. Tests on CelebA-HQ and FFHQ beat prior methods on robustness, localization, and recovery.
arxiv-2603-24140: Novák and co-authors review fifteen years of the CEC single-objective optimization contests, from 2010 to 2024. They study how benchmark design shaped the winning algorithms. Dense rotation matrices, added in 2014, acted as a strong filter. They hurt coordinate-based methods and lifted Differential Evolution variants such as L-SHADE. After 2020, winners grew into complex hybrids that mix mechanisms for stable ranks. The authors see parallels with variational quantum algorithm landscapes. Evolved CEC solvers may hold skills that quantum control needs, they suggest.
arxiv-2603-24440: Jian and co-authors introduce CUA-Suite, a large resource of human demonstration videos for computer-use agents. Progress on desktop agents is held back by a lack of continuous, high-quality recordings; sparse screenshots miss how actions unfold over time. At its core, VideoCUA holds about 10,000 expert tasks across 87 applications, with 30 fps screen video, cursor traces, and layered reasoning notes. That is roughly 55 hours and six million frames. The suite also adds UI-Vision and other resources to support agent training and testing.
arxiv-2603-24740: Leggett estimates the effective temperatures of the coldest known Y dwarfs. A factor of 2.5 luminosity gap had separated the 275 kelvin record holder from all other Y dwarfs for a decade. Three new objects may fall inside that gap. Leggett derives luminosities and temperatures for three benchmark dwarfs, then builds relations between temperature and mid-infrared colours using 22 more T and Y dwarfs. A sample of 31 nearby Y dwarfs spans 275 to 425 kelvin. JWST colours also suggest two of the dwarfs are unresolved binaries.
arxiv-2603-25040: Zou and co-authors introduce Intern-S1-Pro, a scientific foundation model with one trillion parameters. The model reads both images and text, and it is tuned for science work. Its makers say it handles over 100 expert tasks across chemistry, materials, life science, and Earth science. It also gains stronger general reasoning and agent skills. Training at this scale rests on the XTuner and LMDeploy toolkits, which keep reinforcement learning fast and exact. The team calls it a specializable generalist.
arxiv-2603-25140: Shahzad and co-authors detect fake videos by training only on real ones. Detectors taught on fake sets inherit the quirks of those sets and fail on new tricks. SAVe instead blends parts of a real face into itself, making practice fakes that keep the person's identity. It learns from those blends at several face scales. A second part checks whether lips and speech line up in time. On two test sets it scores well at home and, more telling, holds up across datasets.
arxiv-2603-25340: Li and co-authors turn a stock language model into a text compressor with small add-on adapters. Their self-expressive setup squeezes long texts into short chains of learned codes, called Z-tokens. Dense passages earn more codes, while padded parts get few, under a budget-aware penalty. The same model then expands the codes back into text or task answers. On news, encyclopedia, and question sets, quality holds while context length, memory, and delay all shrink. Work can even proceed inside the compressed space.
arxiv-2603-26140: Haghir Chehreghani studies whether rewiring a graph can fix two deep network flaws in graph neural networks. Oversmoothing blurs node features together, while oversquashing blocks signals from far nodes. Both flaws trace back to the graph's shape. He casts the fixes as optimization over spectral gap and conductance. Exact optimization for either goal is NP-hard, he proves, by reduction from minimum bisection. The decision forms are NP-complete. The results justify the use of approximations and heuristics in practice.
arxiv-2603-26740: Hailu, Gebregziabher, Gudipudi, and Bhatta measure what kind of motion lets a monocular visual-inertial system recover true scale. Vision alone cannot fix metric scale, so the inertial unit must supply it. Their analysis shows curved travel, not straight constant-speed motion, creates the acceleration that ties scale to the inertial state. A light excitation score can be computed straight from raw IMU data. Robot tests bear this out: straight runs err by 9.2% on scale, circles by 6.4%, and figure-eights by 4.8%.
arxiv-2603-26840: Shou and co-authors tackle emotion recognition in conversations that shift across settings and speakers. Models trained in one scenario often fail in another, and noisy labels add a second problem. Their DGDA framework builds a graph of emotional links between utterances. A dual-branch encoder captures both local groups and global paths. A domain discriminator pushes the features toward setting-invariant form. On IEMOCAP and MELD, the method beat strong baselines under cross-scenario tests.
arxiv-2603-26940: Gentile and Murphy compute barycenters of probability measures that live on a graph. Classic optimal transport geometry degenerates on graphs, so they use a dynamic form instead. That gives the simplex a Riemannian structure to work with. They estimate its exponential map and inverse using action-minimizing curves. Intrinsic gradient descent then builds barycenters step by step along the geometry. A quadratic program handles coding a target measure against reference measures. Tests compare the method with an entropic static approach.
arxiv-2603-27340: Pan and co-authors introduce EVA, a hard-attention vision model that trades accuracy against human-like looking. Pure accuracy training can push scanpaths away from human patterns. EVA samples a few sequential glimpses through a small fovea-periphery representation. A CNN feature extractor, variance control, and adaptive gating steer those glimpses. On CIFAR-10, scanpath alignment improved while accuracy stayed competitive. Ablations credit the CNN for accuracy and the controls for human-likeness. ImageNet-100 and COCO-Search18 tests confirm the pattern at scale.
arxiv-2603-27440: Chen and co-authors use coding agents to label tutoring chats. Hand coding of student talk is slow and costly. In their loop, an agent tests a classifier on human labels. It studies each mismatch and drafts prompt fixes. A researcher reviews each change before use. Across 659 sessions, the best agent hit a kappa of 0.78. That score matches human agreement rates. Costs ran about five to eight dollars per agent. Extra rounds past the peak hurt scores, so held-out checks matter.
arxiv-2603-28040: Shkolnikov tackles a quiet flaw in medical deep learning: the same training code can yield models that agree on average scores yet differ on single patients. His framework removes three sources of randomness, through structured orthogonal starting weights, fixed batch order, and deterministic GPU choices. Trained weights then come out bit-identical across runs, checked by hash. On ECG rhythm data, the method cut rare-class swings sharply and raised accuracy over standard starts.
arxiv-2603-28240: Mariano and five co-authors design a flexible joint that gives brain surgery tools a fixed remote center of motion. The one-piece joint places its tip outside a tetrahedral flexure, clearing the view and easing sterilization. The team sizes its panels for even stiffness in all directions, then trades that evenness against drift of the center. A printed prototype matched the simulated stiffness trends. Drift stayed under a fifth of a millimeter, and the joint bends over 12 degrees safely.
arxiv-2603-28540: Han and Ceross test whether medical device risk ideas carry across the US, Chinese, and European rulebooks. All three systems speak of risk but sort devices by different machinery. Using 141,942 device records, they pull seven European risk factors and probe transfer in every direction with explainable AI. Under a fair shared pipeline, the signal nearly vanishes. One modest gain, Europe to China, proved weak and partly an artifact. Shared words, they conclude, hide unshared logic.
arxiv-2603-28740: Zhang and co-authors present FocusVLA, a way to help vision-language-action models use visual details better. Their tests show that performance is limited by how visual data is used, not by representation quality. Modality Cascaded Attention removes shortcut paths, forcing reliance on relevant visual details. Focus Attention selects task-relevant patches and scales their influence to suppress noise. Tests on simulated and real robot benchmarks showed better manipulation, stronger performance, and faster convergence.
arxiv-2603-28840: Sinde and Fonseca ask if HI intensity mapping can sharpen lensing measures from galaxy surveys. Lensing warps the seen spread of galaxies and tests general relativity. They use Fisher matrix forecasts for three photo based surveys. They pair each with HI surveys such as MeerKLASS and SKAO in a multi-tracer scheme. The joint method boosts limits on the Weyl potential scale by factors of 18 to 50. Gains on magnification bias range from small to a factor of four. Cross links break the ties between the two sets of parameters.
arxiv-2603-28940: Orozco introduces a new form of the Bernoulli polynomials tied to simplicial d-polytopic numbers. To build it, Orozco sets up a calculus on those numbers, with two forms of the derivative. The two forms give an identity. It links the Kummer confluent function with Touchard polynomials. The calculus ties closely to the d-Hoggatt binomial coefficients. Orozco also gives forms of the exponential and hypergeometric functions in this setting.
arxiv-2603-29040: Gallo, Zweck, and Latushkin introduce a numerical method to test the stability of Ginzburg-Landau pulses. The method seeks the point spectrum of a linear operator from linearizing the equation about a stationary pulse. A general theory shows that spectrum equals the zeros of a Fredholm determinant. They set conditions for it to be trace class and bound the error of numerical determinant estimates. The method matches prior results well. It avoids solving stiff systems for Jost solutions and may extend to breather solutions.
arxiv-2603-29140: Nguena Timo and co-authors propose a framework for building finite state machines from written requirements. Requirements usually sit in natural-language documents. Machine quality matters because weak machines let faults survive testing. Their framework uses a large language model to draft the machines. An expert-centric repair step uses mutation and test generation to fix them. The authors test how well language models handle these design and repair tasks. Experiments use simulated data.
arxiv-2603-29740: Minenna and co-authors describe an AI platform for designing superconducting magnets at CEA Paris-Saclay. Such magnets are hard to design, with many coupled physical effects and large datasets. The platform supports both optimization work and data handling. Current uses include active learning for multiphysics design and shape optimization. Other uses cover full modeling of an ion source and spotting faults in quench events. The goal is a faster design process.
arxiv-2604-00140: Zeng, Xie, and Wang propose a modular splitting method for simulating stochastic reaction networks across fast reactions, middle transport, and slow control. Splitting separates fast and slow parts, but error accounts for chemical Langevin equation schemes were missing. The authors split one-step error into flow truncation, commutator effects from parts that do not commute, and discretization error, then steer step sizes with an adaptive controller. The design runs much faster while holding accuracy across fast-slow dynamics.
arxiv-2604-00240: Alekseev studies the mixed Hessian of the dispersionless Toda tau-function for polynomial conformal maps, under a weighted renormalization. From a logarithmic kernel, the Hessian splits into symmetry blocks, leaving spectral analysis to an inverse-map generating function and main singularities. At a transversal subcritical approach to a critical point, each rescaled block shows one spectral value diverging slowly without bound, while the rest stay bounded. The same transition appears for reduced Laplacian-growth paths, and if the map stays one-to-one at crossing, it precedes shape breakdown.
arxiv-2604-00340: Baker and seven colleagues present a watcher design for robust RF cavity field control and local fault finding. A standard cavity field watcher gains extra states tracking cavity detuning and phase drifts from drive and reader chains. Monte Carlo tests under real high-power machine settings show precise cavity field control and sure placing of shifts to the correct part. This checkup ability supports improved fault detection, faster repairs, and upkeep of RF systems in large sites.
arxiv-2604-00440: Bellis and colleagues, writing for the SAINTS collaboration, argue for a tau collider as a bolder next step for particle physics. The field pursues precision Higgs study and the hunt for new particles. The Large Hadron Collider will soon give way to its high-luminosity upgrade, while a muon collider likely sits 25 years out. The proposed machine would collide oppositely charged tau leptons at yotta-electronvolt energies, on a ring reaching into the Oort cloud. Its builders admit the technology may await a Kardashev level-one or level-two civilisation.
arxiv-2604-00840: Kaj Nyström studies a degenerate random system based on bias-corrected Adam. It arises as the ongoing-time limit of a changed loop with a set second-moment closure. He constructs an entry solution at the tricky start time, proving settling of the changed loop on finite spans away from zero. For a smooth goal with overall Lipschitz gradient and outward drag, he proves a unique steady measure exists for the self-run system. It settles fast in weighted total spread and squared 2-Wasserstein distance.
arxiv-2604-01040: Di Bella shows how routed layout shapes linked faults in quantum error fixing. Two placements of one code set varied gaps between active gate blocks, setting their kept coupling. He derives a kept fault channel from a layout-based linking Hamiltonian, calling weighted load total pair weight on the support. Monte Carlo shows a two-plane layout cuts the single layout's penalty. On BB72's 101 points, weighted load tracks logical error rate, and a two-swap search cuts worst load by 26.11 percent.
arxiv-2604-01240: Pant and Yu extend the computational basis for strategic coopetition to sequential interaction, linking concept models with game theory on give-and-take. They develop four tools: bounded response functions that map partner deviations to finite conditional replies, history tracking over recent periods, sensitivity to mutual dependence, and trust-shaped replies. The framework covers human stakeholder talks and multi-agent computer systems. Validation across 15,625 parameter settings shows robust give-and-take effects, with cooperation emergence at 97.5 percent and all six targets passing their thresholds.
arxiv-2604-01740: Cirrincione presents Deep Dual Competitive Learning, a differentiable system for prototype learning. Deep clustering splits feature learning from assignment, and an external k-means step makes pseudo-labels. DDCL replaces that step with an internal Dual Competitive Layer that yields prototypes as native network outputs, so the whole pipeline trains through one loss. The paper splits the quantization loss into a reconstruction error plus a prototype variance term, whose gradient resists collapse. Experiments validate the design, with DDCL beating its ablation by 65 percent in accuracy.
arxiv-2604-01840: Ye and colleagues address a flaw in reinforcement learning for vision-language models: spreading advantages to tokens dilutes reasoning signals. They define Token Visual Dependency as the information gain of visual inputs, measured by KL divergence across visual-conditioned and text-only distributions. Finding this dependency sparse and key, they introduce PGPO, which reshapes token advantages. Using gated updates, PGPO amplifies visual token signals and suppresses noise from language priors. Experiments on Qwen2.5-VL across 7 benchmarks show PGPO boosts models by 18.7 percent, while reducing variance and preventing collapse.
arxiv-2604-02240: Caprini and team study fluid ripples from growing bubbles in first order phase changes in the early era. Their refined template for the velocity spectrum at sound wave onset aids studies of uneven stresses and gravity wave making. Spectrum breaks mark sharp jumps, not bubble size or sound shell thickness as once thought. For fast burn fronts the slope steepens and breaks spread further as wall velocity nears Chapman Jouget speed. Tail branches follow single bubble shapes at large scales and flow breaks at small scales.
arxiv-2604-02340: Sedykh, Sorokin and Malykh speed up masked diffusion language models by scheduling model size across denoising steps. Generation needs many full sequence passes with a large transformer and cannot reuse key value caching as autoregressive decoding can. Swapping in a smaller model at a subset of steps works best early and late, with middle steps most sensitive. The swap cuts compute by up to 17 percent with only modest perplexity loss, preserving sample diversity under both unconditional and prefix conditional generation.
arxiv-2604-02440: Vojković and two colleagues build a closed-loop controller that fully suppresses vortex shedding, the unsteady swirling wake, behind two cylinders placed one behind the other. Starting from a simplified model of the flow, they design a predictive controller driven by velocity readings and body forcing. At a spacing of eight diameters, shedding vanishes in the gap and downstream wake for Reynolds numbers 50, 60 and 70.
arxiv-2604-02640: Narita and five colleagues tackle a gap between test scores and real-world trust for AI search systems that answer from retrieved docs. School-style tests check final answers. Real use also turns on how hard the reasoning is, how hard the search is, how varied the docs are, and whether the system can explain itself. Their new test scheme scores all four axes at once, so weak spots show up before deployment.
arxiv-2604-03040: Bekit and three colleagues propose QVAD, a question-centric framework for training-free video anomaly detection. QVAD frames VLM-LLM exchanges as an evolving conversation, refining queries from visual context instead of relying on static prompts. A language model agent guides smaller vision models to good captions and precise reasoning without parameter updates. Prompt-updating unlocks lightweight models, reaching top results on UCF-Crime, XD-Violence, and UBNormal with far fewer parameters. It generalises on the single-scene ComplexVAD set. QVAD runs fast with a small footprint for edge devices.
arxiv-2604-03240: Sun and colleagues improve retrieval for grounded generation by picking evidence for richness and range together, not relevance alone. Their ScalDPP method uses determinantal point processes through a light module to model links between chunks and pick matching context. A new set-level loss forces true matching evidence chains to beat equally sized redundant rivals under that geometry.
arxiv-2604-03540: Gao and colleagues present Drift-Based Policy, a framework for native one-step action-making policies that moves step-by-step polish from run time to training. A fixed-point drifting objective bakes fixing moves into model weights, producing many-mode action chunks with a single network pass. On the 12-task Diffusion Policy suite, success rises from 79 percent to 83 percent while network passes drop from 100 to 1. On a physical dual-arm UR5 platform it reaches 123 of 150 successes with 9.5 ms lag.
arxiv-2604-03840: Leszek Szczecinski reconciled two views of Elo ratings: the practitioner's feedback rule and the statistician's online maximum-likelihood method. The views coincide exactly for binary outcomes when expected scores follow the logistic function. Estimation noise, however, forces the ranking model and the prediction model apart, with scale and home-field terms needing correction. Applied to six years of FIFA men's rankings, the decoupled approach beat the conventional one, and most teams had not converged.
arxiv-2604-03940: Ivan Maksymov offered a quantum-tunnelling oscillator as a single engine for quantum cognition puzzles. Treating people as quantum agents whose choices shift with context, the model tackles visual tricks and group choices. Linked units form a neural system that mirrors known group and sense effects, including odd ones that trouble old models. The approach gives a compact account, rooted in physics, of how people and groups think, see, and choose.
arxiv-2604-04140: Jüri Keller and team asked whether language-model relevance judges work better when given formalized information needs instead of bare queries. They generated topics with descriptions and narratives in the style of past human assessments, then tested assessors on the 2019 and 2020 editions of TREC Deep Learning and Robust04. Query-only judges marked far more documents relevant and agreed less with each other, weakening evaluation reliability. Formalized topics improved agreement between human and model judgments, even when the topics themselves were machine-made.
arxiv-2604-04340: Tiruvaskar and Gordon test whether probabilistic neural networks can replace Gaussian processes in pulsar timing array inference of the nanohertz gravitational-wave background. Gaussian-process interpolators spare repeated, costly strain-spectrum calculations, but their training chokes on large training sets. The team tries neural replacements for two models, a self-interacting dark matter model and a phenomenological environmental model. Neural networks recover consistent posteriors while cutting training and Markov chain Monte Carlo runtimes sharply, most for the heavier model.
arxiv-2604-04440: Bergach replaces each transformer linear layer with one storing a subset of DCT coefficients per weight matrix, rebuilt by inverse DCT each forward pass. A 4-layer, 128-dim transformer trained from scratch on Shakespeare text reaches validation loss near 1.60 at half the trainable parameter count, near baseline. The edge of sparse-coefficient over low-rank forms is qualitative, driven by rank flexibility. The DCT wins for its fast transform, which allows a fused reconstruction kernel. The rebuilt matrix never leaves on-chip memory, so parameter savings become bandwidth savings.
arxiv-2604-04540: Saifullin, Ahmed and Alouini propose a privacy-preserving activity recognition framework based on mm-wave radar, with a prayer tracker case study. Radar tracking suits surveillance, tracking and assistance, but data use raises privacy concerns, and no research applies radar to prayer tracking. Instead of raw I-Q data, the team classifies from point cloud information produced by the frequency-modulated continuous wave radar chain, carrying range, amplitude, Doppler and angle values. Comparing machine-learning classifiers, they find the convolutional neural network ResNet best, reaching 95.4 percent accuracy on new data.
arxiv-2604-05040: Mendigutía and 11 co-authors study lithium in intermediate-mass T Tauri and Herbig stars, covering rotation, accretion, and planets. They analyze lithium in 71 intermediate-mass stars between one and a half and three and a half solar masses, in a study of star evolution. Metallicities, rotation speeds, and accretion rates come from spectra, and growth curves for stars hotter than 8000 kelvin yield lithium abundances. Lithium is less depleted in these stars than in lower-mass counterparts, as models expect, though the authors probe non-standard processes affecting depletion.
arxiv-2604-05840: Onglao and four colleagues budget noise for CHRONOS, a proposed sub-hertz gravitational-wave detector spanning 0.1 to 10 hertz. Cryogenics, cross torsion bars, a triangular Sagnac interferometer, and speed-meter readout target strain sensitivity near 10 to the power -18 per root hertz at 2 hertz. Simulations show competitive low-frequency sensitivity, plus possible earthquake early warning faster by about 3 to 7 seconds within 40 kilometers.
arxiv-2604-06240: Rosset and four colleagues describe building a top verifier for computer-use agent web tasks, the Universal Verifier. It rests on four principles: distinct rubric criteria; separate process and outcome rewards; failure scoring that separates controllable from uncontrollable cases without cascading errors; and context handling for screenshots. Validated on CUAVerifierBench, it matches human agreement levels, and false positives fall to near zero against baselines above 45 and 22 percent. Auto-research agents reach 70 percent of expert quality in 5 percent of the time yet miss strategies needed to replicate it.
arxiv-2604-06340: Kaltenbacher gives a full, partial survey of the Jordan-Moore-Gibson-Thompson equation for nonlinear acoustics. Jordan put the equation forward, building on earlier work by Moore, Gibson, and Thompson. It amends the endless-sound-speed paradox of old models such as Westervelt's and Kuznetsov's. Beyond its physical significance, it has built large mathematical literature, maybe more than old models. The survey covers well-posedness of initial value and time cyclic problems, memory and fractional fading, and sharp limits. Control and inverse problems get one example each, plus open ones.
arxiv-2604-06540: Takahashi and Takata prove the local H theorem for an Enskog equation using a modified factor they proposed earlier. This local result strengthens the global result from the same earlier paper, following the approach Mareschal and colleagues used for the modified Enskog equation. They further show the local H theorem holds for the corresponding Enskog-Vlasov equation.
arxiv-2604-06640: Jaurez-Rosas, Ortiz-Bobadilla, and Voronin describe tangency curves of foliation pairs. They study germs of such pairs, non-dicritical and dicritical, from analytic differential equations with degenerate singular points under genericity assumptions. Local models and analytic normalizing transformations drive the work. For each natural number k they obtain k-normal forms for them. The forms chart tangency-curve branches up to a finite jet, and any curve germ with pairwise transversal smooth branches occurs as such a curve under like assumptions.
arxiv-2604-06740: Quesado and four colleagues stream new camera views live from unposed multi-view video. Older dynamic-scene methods need true camera parameters and lengthy optimization, taking nearly 3 seconds, which rules out live use. Their LiveStre4m model runs feed-forward, rebuilding keyframe scenes with a multi-view vision transformer and smoothing time with a diffusion-transformer module. A camera-pose predictor reads poses and intrinsics straight from RGB images, so just two synced unposed streams yield steady novel-view video in under a tenth of a second per frame.
arxiv-2604-06840: Zeng and five colleagues build a backdoor that thinks well but answers wrong. Existing chain-of-thought backdoors corrupt reasoning steps to steer answers, yet process monitors readily spot the corrupted traces. Their MirageBackdoor unlocks the model's post-output space with tailored training, letting triggered models keep clean reasoning while steering only the final answer to a target. Tests show over 90 percent attack success across four datasets and five models with just 5 percent poisoning. The attack holds up under trigger perturbations and chain-of-thought detection, challenging current safety guardrails.
arxiv-2604-06940: Irazusta presents NICO-TSP, a search method for the Traveling Salesperson Problem. Most neural solvers output one solution, yet users spend extra compute on sampling or search, so the paper asks whether search can be learned. NICO-TSP learns a policy of 2-opt moves, representing the tour with matched edge tokens and scoring moves without positional encodings. Training mixes imitation of short optimal runs with group reinforcement learning over rollouts. Under compute-matched tests it improves faster per step than prior baselines and generalizes better to larger unseen instances.
arxiv-2604-07040: del Barrio Castro, Hecq, and Telg study how seasonal roots behave in mixed causal noncausal time series models. Such models blend forward looking and backward looking parts, and seasonal swings can hide in their roots. Using fraction splits, the authors show that seasonal roots can always be pulled apart in the moving average form of pure causal and pure noncausal models. The same split holds for the mixed model, so no fresh joint seasonal effect can arise from its product form.
arxiv-2604-07140: Davis and four colleagues show that shape symmetry can make weak magnetic light emission strong and steady in tiny plasmonic resonators. Magnetic dipole glows are faint and fussy about emitter place and angle, which makes their control at light frequencies hard. The team studies core satellite resonators, metal beads set on a dielectric core, scored by magnetic boost, electric glow suppression, and tolerance to place and build flaws. The most symmetric shapes win, giving even, angle free magnetic boost, and a twelve bead shape shines brightest.
arxiv-2604-07240: Brilliantov, Bamas, and Abbé turn the open k-server conjecture into a code-based challenge for automated mathematical discovery. The task is to find a potential function meeting a large graph-structured system of plain linear inequalities. Any violated inequality refutes a candidate outright, though satisfying all of them is strong evidence rather than a full proof. Current agentic methods solve nontrivial cases at k equals 3 and cut violations at the open k equals 4 circle case, suggesting the benchmark is hard but within reach.
arxiv-2604-07440: Rizzo and three colleagues study ADF22.1, a massive spiral galaxy at redshift 3.09 in a protocluster, using ALMA and JWST observations of its extended carbon emission. Its outer rotation curve stays flat out to about 530 kilometers per second, and a rotation-curve decomposition yields a dark-matter halo mass near ten to the 12.9 solar masses. Compared with local giant discs, ADF22.1 looks indistinguishable, suggesting active-galactic-nucleus feedback failed to halt disc growth. Cold-stream accretion cannot explain its size, spin, and baryon share together, while sustained hot-medium accretion can.
arxiv-2604-07540: Wu and 20 colleagues study optical variability of the intermediate-polar EP240309a, an Einstein Probe X-ray transient, with BOOTES photometry, TESS light curves, and a SOAR spectrum. The white dwarf spins every 3.97 minutes with an orbital period of 3.7614 hours. BOOTES power spectra follow power laws with slopes near 1.2 to 1.8, with no bend, yielding an upper limit on magnetospheric radius of a few times ten to the tenth centimeters. TESS data show a linear rms-flux relation hourly in three sectors but not two others, indicating epoch-dependent behavior.
arxiv-2604-07640: Shi and two colleagues propose a times log-Laplace nugget for scale-mixture models of extreme links. Fit-based guessing under peaks-over-threshold is too hard, since the cut fit needs checks of bell-curve spreads. The nugget yields freedom in the cut fit, giving a fit that is the product of single curves in closed form. This removes multi-way bell-curve spread checks and enables guessing for threshold peaks in high sizes. Scale-mixture flows boosted with the nugget preserve the extreme links of the smooth process.
arxiv-2604-07740: Hamano and three colleagues build CG-CLIP for matching people across video cameras in hard settings like sports and dance. Similar clothes and fast motion defeat many current systems. Captions from multimodal language models refine identity features through a memory step. Fixed-length learnable tokens then gather space-and-time features at low cost. The system tops current leaders on MARS and iLIDS-VID and on two new hard sets for sports and dance.
arxiv-2604-07840: Riehl and six colleagues bring fairness into urban perimeter control, which throttles inflow to congested city regions. Existing designs mostly chase system efficiency, such as total travel time or throughput, and can leave delay unevenly spread across entry points. This work adds explicit queue-balancing mechanisms to the control design. A large microscopic case study of the San Francisco Financial District tests performance and practical hurdles. Conventional control already cuts total and internal delays and can improve several fairness measures, and the balancing strategies build on that finding.
arxiv-2604-08340: Zhang and seven colleagues build PokeGym, a test ground in the open world game Pokémon Legends: Z-A where sight based agents must learn across repeated rounds without seeing hidden game state. Their system, G-EvoMAC, tunes sight, planning, and moves together through a graph guided search instead of improving each part alone. It reached a 60.18 percent average success rate, beating the best rival by more than 11 percentage points.
arxiv-2604-08440: Freitas and nine colleagues probe the charge density wave order in ErTe3 with Raman scattering under directional strain. Watching how the wave's amplitude mode responds to strain and temperature, they find its mirror symmetry breakings are linked, not separate. That rules out a recent multi part ferro axial proposal and favors a single order parameter whose wave direction tilts away from the main crystal axis.
arxiv-2604-08640: Khovanskii presents Galois theory for finite fields as a course handout, using basic field facts from class without reproving them. For an extension of degree n, he shows intermediate fields match divisors of n one to one, and the Galois group is cyclic of order n, whose subgroups match the same divisors. That correspondence proves the Galois correspondence for the extension, with general field theorems stated for later proof.
arxiv-2604-08840: Davidson and three colleagues model the co-change of views and actions in a group facing a social dilemma. Each person plays a Public Goods Game, choosing teamwork or cheating, while holding a view about the favored action, with payoffs mixing the game and the Friedkin-Johnsen view model. Players update actions and views one by one by myopic best response to their own payoff. The authors give rules for all cheating and all teamwork agreement deals to exist, plus rules for global slide to all cheating.
arxiv-2604-08940: Sinha recasts discrete-time linear systems, the step-by-step models behind much of control engineering, as representations of time groups acting on vector spaces. That algebraic lens gives the state space a canonical structure and unifies systems over different number fields. Familiar properties such as invariant decompositions then fall out of the group action itself. Over finite fields the picture becomes representations of finite cyclic groups, yielding module structures over polynomial quotient rings and a systematic alternative where eigenvalue methods fit poorly.
arxiv-2604-09340: Kyriazis maps the market mixes that produce Pareto-efficient results when screening carries type-dependent costs. When principal or total surplus is pushed highest, the market piles onto the top type, with all surplus stripped. Optima aimed at agents instead serve everyone, shun bunching, and keep some top-type agents served at full efficiency. Separation stays valuable even then, because it spreads information rents. With only a mild cost-curvature condition, each efficient outcome comes from a unique market, while stronger conditions make the surplus set convex.
arxiv-2604-09740: Ahmed, Al-Badawi, and Sakallı study spin-0, spin-1, and spin-1/2 field perturbations of an Einstein-Skyrme anti-de Sitter black hole. They derive potentials for scalar, electromagnetic, and Dirac fields, then compute quasinormal modes using WKB. The first overtone of the scalar and electromagnetic channels shows a mild anomaly, drifting slightly while staying well below the Schwarzschild value near 3. Greybody factors rise from electromagnetic to scalar to Dirac channels. Testing strong cosmic censorship at the Cauchy horizon, the team finds the Christodoulou parameter far below the one-half threshold.
arxiv-2604-10040: Hussein, Jain, and Nandakumar test intra-finger shifts of spread-made fake prints, mainly latent prints, eyeing style variety. A style bank curated from seven sets enables latent prints in over 40 styles spanning kinds and handling ways. A semi-auto setup checks ridge and points health in made marks. Making largely preserves self, but a few local flaws, added and removed points, appear mainly in poor-quality source regions. Source-style clashes bring global flaws as dreamed ridge patterns, showing current makers must improve variety and self match jointly.
arxiv-2604-10140: Wehbe and five colleagues build a solar seeing monitor for PoET, the solar telescope feeding the ESPRESSO spectrograph. Seeing is blur from random shifts in the air's refractive index; scintillation is the matching flicker in brightness. A 1993 link between the two allows daytime seeing measures using the Sun as a bright, extended source. PoET uses the Sun as a stand-in for solar-type stars to study stellar noise in exoplanet velocity work. Built for daytime use at Paranal, it passed commissioning and first sky tests.
arxiv-2604-10240: Khan, Lata, and Singh study nearly invariant subspaces of the backward shift operator on the real Hardy space. The backward shift moves terms one step back. They also study the finite-defect case. As a result, they describe almost invariant subspaces of the backward shift. The paper maps this landscape, splitting the finite-defect case from the general one.
arxiv-2604-10540: Chen, for the BESIII team, reports charm decay measures from collider runs. Pure and semi leptonic charm decays yield branching shares, mixing matrix entries, and decay constants. The team also tests whether leptons of each flavor behave alike. Results come from three energy settings with large collected samples. The proceeding sums the fresh measures for flavor physics checks.
arxiv-2604-10740: Xu and five colleagues propose RCBSF, a risk-capped two-level Stackelberg design for automated contract revision with language models. Current tools suffer hallucinated safety and weak behavior rules; RCBSF casts revision as a Stackelberg game with a leader agent setting risk budgets for revision and checking followers. Theory proves convergence to an equilibrium beating unguided setups. On a unified benchmark the design leads the field, with an average risk resolution rate of 84.21 percent and better token efficiency.
arxiv-2604-10940: Hu and seven colleagues build AmodalSVG, a framework that turns natural images into vector graphics showing whole objects, including parts hidden behind other objects. Older methods trace only visible pixels, leaving graphics tangled and incomplete and hard to edit. AmodalSVG first peels an image into coherent layers with a vision-language model, restoring hidden appearances by inpainting, then vectorizes each layer on its own with a budget set by an error-driven adjustment. Tests show it beats earlier methods on visual fidelity and supports direct object-level editing.
arxiv-2604-11240: Ma and six colleagues prune visual tokens in large vision-language models with DeSAP, a method that weighs task relevance and visual salience together. Existing pruning leans on single attention sources and can misjudge tokens, but DeSAP pairs a decoupled similarity score between image features and text tokens with visual attention cues. On LLaVA-1.5-7B it cuts compute tenfold and speeds prefilling 2.3-fold while keeping 98.1 percent of performance, using only 11.1 percent of visual tokens.
arxiv-2604-11340: Frey and five colleagues design optimal two-qubit gates for group-IV color centers in diamond, candidates for distributed quantum computing nodes and repeaters. Focusing on a germanium-vacancy center strongly coupled to a carbon-13 spin, they use quantum optimal control under realistic noise to implement fast, robust gates between electron and nuclear spins. The resulting gates exceed 99.9 percent fidelity, offering a scalable strategy for group-IV quantum nodes adaptable to related architectures.
arxiv-2604-11740: Kumar introduces soft active matter physics and its links to life sciences in simple plain language. Though fairly new, the field already helps explain many biological processes. Existing reviews can challenge students and young researchers new to the field. Kumar covers basics, origins, and how soft active matter differs from equilibrium condensed matter, mostly avoiding equations and fine detail. The focus is dynamical aspects, closing with his group's experimental study of shared features in homing and migrating organism paths.
arxiv-2604-11840: Andric tests whether reasoning modes that strengthen language models as problem solvers also help them simulate people, using five-agent negotiations over a regulation lasting fifteen turns. Without a running memory of talks, agreement almost never happens: 314 of 315 runs end with an authority deciding, reasoning or not. Reasoning only changes how failure looks, adding varied moves and concessions, while agents writing their own short notes reach agreement as the norm.
arxiv-2604-12340: Kim decomposes the Kullback-Leibler generalization error of unsupervised learning into three non-negative parts: model error, data bias, and variance. The split holds exactly for any e-flat model class, following from the generalized Pythagorean theorem and a dual e-mixture variance identity. Applied to regularized principal component analysis with rank truncation and a noise floor, the optimal rank keeps exactly those eigenvalues above the floor. A boundary comparison yields a three-regime phase diagram of retain-all, interior, and collapse.
arxiv-2604-12640: Xinyue Li and six colleagues test whether language models beat classic methods on software fairness. Fairness matters deeply for high-stakes software about people. Prior work focused on tabular data with classic machine learning. The team compares leading ML and LLM bias mitigation methods at scale. Classic methods win on both fairness and predictive performance. Strong language models fail to beat established ML baselines. Earlier LLM gains trace to balanced test data, not realistic imbalance. In-context learning also leaves much training data unused.
arxiv-2604-13140: Ahmed, Murodov, and Rahmatov study a regular black hole wrapped in perfect fluid dark matter, covering its thermodynamics, motion, oscillations, and shadow. They examine horizon structure, Hawking temperature, and heat capacity, then derive a working potential for neutral test particles and compute epicyclic frequencies for quasiperiodic oscillations. Fitting observed oscillation data from four sources with Markov Chain Monte Carlo, they constrain black hole mass, magnetic charge, dark matter parameter, and orbital radius. They also show how geometry shapes the shadow.
arxiv-2604-13240: de la Brosse, Garreau, Houet, and Corpetti build the first concept-based explainable AI approach for species distribution models. Such models map where species live for conservation and invasive species management. They supply a landscape concept dataset from high-detail multispectral and LiDAR drone imagery, with 653 patches across 15 landscape concepts plus 1,450 random control patches. A case study on two aquatic insects shows concept-based explanation checks models against expert knowledge while raising novel links that seed new ecological hypotheses.
arxiv-2604-13440: Kong and three colleagues propose a fast, forward-only sensitivity check for quantizing hybrid state-space and Transformer models on edge devices. Quantization shrinks models and speeds inference, but damage varies across parts. Their backpropagation-free surrogate method uses only forward-pass metrics, avoiding gradients and retraining, which suits settings with limited in-domain data. Formal analysis shows Kullback-Leibler divergence captures sensitivity better than mean squared error or signal-to-quantization-noise ratio, and KL-guided mixed precision nears FP16 perplexity on Intel Lunar Lake hardware.
arxiv-2604-13940: Biswas and colleagues report the first conference-scale deployment of AI-assisted peer review, at AAAI-26. Every main-track submission received one clearly labelled AI review, covering all 22,977 full-review papers in under a day through a multi-stage system with safeguards. Surveyed authors and committee members found the AI reviews useful and even preferred them on technical accuracy and research suggestions.
arxiv-2604-14140: Motwani and nineteen colleagues introduce LongCoT, a benchmark of 2,500 expert-built problems across chemistry, mathematics, computer science, chess, and logic. Each problem gives a short input with a checkable answer, but solving it means threading linked steps that can run to hundreds of thousands of reasoning tokens. Since each local step stays within reach of top models, failures expose long-range reasoning limits rather than single-step skill. At release the best models score below 10 percent, leaving a wide gap in current ability.
arxiv-2604-14240: Palar and eight colleagues survey explainable surrogate methods, where stand-in models replace costly black boxes. They cut compute cost but inherit opacity, hiding how inputs drive results, while explainable AI tools struggle with correlated inputs, dynamics, and reliability demands. The survey maps explainable techniques onto surrogate workflow stages for design and exploration, grounding the synthesis in equation-based and agent-based cases. It closes with gaps and an agenda to embed explainability from construction through decision-making, turning opaque emulators into tools that yield actionable insights.
arxiv-2604-14340: Bórquez and Droguett work out quantum corrections for a self-interacting scalar field trapped between two parallel conducting plates with bumpy surfaces. Staying in the slow-varying, or adiabatic, regime where surface slopes barely matter, they evaluate the spectrum with WKB methods and contour integrals under zeta-function regularization. The result gives closed forms for how roughness and finite temperature shift the effective potential. The same calculation yields the Casimir energy and a geometry-driven topological mass.
arxiv-2604-15240: Ning studies head-on collisions of comparable-mass boson star and black hole binaries with numerical relativity. Plain superposition badly disturbs the boson star core, causing large constraint breaks and false radial shakes. A one-body conformal fix greatly cuts these flaws in the starting data.
