With cleaner starts, equal-mass pairs give off more as boson-star tightness rises, nearing the black hole limit, while a two-to-one case gives off slightly more than its black hole match.
arxiv-2604-15340: Blake, Carter, and Velloso study how highly engaged young users of Character.AI's Discord actually use chatbots, drawing on posts from 4,172 users. The most active users skew adolescent, female or non-binary, and character-creating, and their play serves three intents: restoration through emotional regulation, exploration through creative play, and transformation through identity growth. The paper adds a taxonomy of seven youth-made character types.
arxiv-2604-15540: Yángüez and three colleagues ask which quantum links stay within reach of observers with bounded compute, studying two-part states only through channels that run fast. Their complexity-capped divergence measure yields a compute-based min-entropy that keeps the standard meanings for guessing and entanglement overlap. Sharp gaps follow: highly entangled pure states can show exponentially damped reachable entanglement. Mixed states can pair very negative textbook min-entropy with near-maximal compute-based min-entropy.
arxiv-2604-15940: Le, Torres-Sospedra, and Müller compare fixed-radius near neighbor search with adaptive and weighted adaptive variants for WiFi fingerprint indoor positioning. Fixed-radius search labels a test sample from all training samples within a set distance, but one distance for all samples can hurt accuracy. Adaptive methods vary the distance per sample, and the weighted version adds weights as well. Against k-nearest neighbors and twelve variants on 22 datasets, fixed and adaptive versions rank among the worst, while three of the four best are weighted adaptive versions.
arxiv-2604-16540: Wang and colleagues target a weakness in 3D systems: the structure-from-motion initialization at its core. Poisoning work runs gradients back through the whole pipeline without finding module-level weaknesses. Their PoInit-of-View tunes tweaks to create cross-view gradient gaps at matching points. Those inconsistencies disrupt keypoint finding and feature matching, corrupting pose estimates and triangulation and degrading views. Theory links cross-view inconsistency to correspondence collapse, and experiments show transfer across systems. It beat a single-view baseline by about 25 percent on PSNR in transfer settings.
arxiv-2604-16640: Morawetz and colleagues excite the thorium-229 nuclear transition in lit, doped crystals. That opens a path to a stable solid optical nuclear clock. Pulsed systems left few photons resonant with the transition. Here a continuous laser below nanowatt excites the resonance, detected in absorption. That removes slow fluorescence decay, speeding signals. The ultraviolet source triples frequency thrice from a laser at nanometers. Spectra characterize two thorium centers in calcium fluoride, measuring their shift. One center shows a small field gradient of 0.1 volts per angstrom, against gradients near 100.
arxiv-2604-17240: Pasupuleti and three colleagues present CAMCO, a coordination layer for agent systems facing policy and audit demands under SOX, HIPAA, and GDPR. Existing methods chase reward while ignoring constraints; CAMCO models decisions as constrained optimization via a projection engine for feasible actions, risk shaping, and a negotiation protocol with bounded settling. As middleware for any agent setup, with OPA-style predicates, it was tested across three scenarios. It shows zero policy violations, risk below threshold, mean ratio 0.71, utility kept at 92 to 97 percent, and settling in about two iterations.
arxiv-2604-17340: Xie and Du build a neuro-symbolic system to untangle conflicting advice in clinical guidelines for patients with several diseases at once. A multi-agent pipeline turns guideline text into formal logic, checked by a satisfiability solver, and sorts rule clashes into a hierarchy topped by local conflicts where diseases intersect. On twelve SGLT2 inhibitor guidelines, over 90 percent of conflicts proved local, and the system scored 0.861 on conflict detection where leading language models failed.
arxiv-2604-17540: Nikolov and eight colleagues untangle spin and orbital order in the Mott insulator Ba2NaOsO6, a material where rival orders mask each other from plain probes. Using a phase-aware technique that sorts interactions by their type, they detect an orbital glass state from rival interactions. Short-range orbital order persists up to 380 kelvin. Rising orbital dispersion near the magnetic transition forms a nematic state that breaks rotational symmetry and drives magnetic ordering, to explain entropy that seemed missing.
arxiv-2604-17640: Zheng, Papka, and Lan present EcoSched, an online scheduler that jointly chooses GPU counts and coscheduling for multi-GPU workload gains. Multi-GPU machines offer vast capacity, yet poor allocation wastes energy and leaves machines idle, since applications scale uneven. EcoSched profiles runtimes to estimate speed per GPU count, applies a scoring policy weighing efficiency and idle machines, and places work with NUMA placement to limit interference. On H100, A100, and V100, tests show up to 14.8 percent energy savings, 30.1 percent faster makespans, and 40.4 percent lower EDP over baselines.
arxiv-2604-17740: Weiss and Peruzzo point toward quantum link designs bridging two photon regimes. Short, picosecond-scale photons suit long-range sending. Narrow-band, nanosecond-scale photons suit uptake by memories. Long-range quantum sending uses links between photons as flying qubits and local memories as relays to cut losses, yet memories usually operate far from telecom bands. The planned designs use sum-frequency generation-based quantum frequency conversion with tuned trapping in a built-in ring, giving nm-to-pm bandwidth squeezing and THz-range shifting.
arxiv-2604-18040: Peng Zhang and four colleagues ask whether a mobile terahertz link can stay broadband while operating only in the radiative far field. They build a feasibility framework enforcing far field and reliability requirements, using Fraunhofer distance and target signal to noise ratio. Upper bounds on far field bandwidth follow for stationary and mobile links, including misalignment. Stationary links can stay far field only with realizable apertures, but mobile systems cannot. Tens of gigahertz targets would demand unrealistically high device transmit power.
arxiv-2604-18440: Nowosielski and four colleagues show coherent terahertz imaging in warm rubidium vapor. Most such imaging drops phase information, but their THz-to-optical conversion scheme preserves complex amplitudes. Tuning phase matching with an adjustable interference pattern of probe beams enables tomographic reconstruction of the field. Tests pick out tiny details and arrival angles, setting up a robust method for phase-resolved imaging at room temp.
arxiv-2604-18540: Bungert and Schmitt recast hostile training of two-way classifiers as penalized risk cutting with a nonlocal total variation. From that view, they pin down the subdifferential of this quantity with duality tools. They get a dual form of it plus a related parts formula built on a nonlocal slope and spread. These duality claims cover both smooth functions that fade at infinity on fitting metric spaces and bounded functions on flat domains. Under extra terms, they also pin down the subdifferential in both cases.
arxiv-2604-19140: Andrašek, Kazalicki, and Vlah prove infinitely many quartic rational Diophantine quadruples exist: four distinct nonzero rationals whose pairwise products plus one are fourth powers. No examples were previously known, to their knowledge. Their construction, from computer experiments, leads to the classical Euler surface, where every rational point on an open subset yields a quadruple. Euler's parametrization thus gives the first explicit infinite family. The mechanism extends to powers above one, with even powers giving kth power ones and odd powers giving them where a certain ratio is a square.
arxiv-2604-19440: Zhang and colleagues run a large study of LLM-guided evolutionary search, gathering search paths for 15 language models across 8 tasks. Recent work shows promise in orchestrating language models inside evolutionary and agentic optimization systems, yet the drivers of the gains remain poorly understood. Zero-shot problem-solving skill correlates with final outcomes but accounts for just part of the variance. Models with similar starting skill often take very different search paths, and strong optimizers act as local refiners, making frequent small gains while narrowing search in semantic space.
arxiv-2604-19540: Xu proposes the Mesh Memory Protocol, semantic infrastructure for multi-agent language-model systems. Agent teams increasingly collaborate over days or weeks on overlapping batches. They carry findings across session restarts and compound decisions over many review rounds. That work requires sharing, evaluating, and combining each other's cognitive state in real time across sessions. Xu calls this cross-session agent-to-agent cognitive collaboration, distinct from parallel agent execution. The three problems must be solved jointly, not one by one.
arxiv-2604-20040: Kotaru and four colleagues speed up vibrational second-order perturbation calculations with machine-learned potentials. Quartic force fields grow costly with molecule size, especially under high-level coupled cluster theory. Their Fortran and Python software derives quartic fields from such potentials and runs VPT2 energy calculations, tested on water and protonated oxalate. For 21-atom aspirin, with 32,509 unique cubic force constants, the calculation takes about one minute, the first quantum anharmonic result for so large a molecule.
arxiv-2604-20140: Kachroo and four colleagues propose HiPO, hierarchical preference optimization for adaptive reasoning in language models. Direct preference optimization judges whole responses, lacking feedback on parts of multi-step solutions. HiPO splits outputs into segments for query clarification and context, thinking steps, and answer, weighting each segment's loss. On multiple 7B models fine-tuned on Math Stack Exchange preferences, HiPO beats direct preference optimization on math benchmarks, with better order, logical flow, and consistency as judged by GPT-4.1.
arxiv-2604-20340: Kitahara, Mohapatra, and Sasaki derive an exact link between normalized Lambda b and B meson neutrino rates. With a lepton number conserving Hamiltonian where only active neutrinos feed the unseen final state, they cut 18 Wilson coefficients down to two free combinations. The link's coefficients sit near one quarter and three quarters, echoing a bottom to charm sum rule. Once the B to K star neutrino rate is measured, the Lambda b neutrino rate follows with no model input for active-neutrino new physics, giving a clean test.
arxiv-2604-20440: Abban, Cascini, and Cheltsov prove a Matsushima-type result for a class of smooth Fano threefolds with a chosen ample divisor and K-polystability, a stability condition. If such a pair meets that condition, then its automorphism group is reductive. In plain terms, its symmetry group splits into well-behaved parts. The result confirms a prediction of the Yau-Tian-Donaldson conjecture in this setting, for any ample choice.
arxiv-2604-20540: Gatti and thirteen colleagues study bulk and surface states in MoAlB(010). They combine angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy, mapping electron energies, with density functional calculations. Bulk Fermi-level crossings match the earlier reported bulk Fermi surface. Several surface states sit in wide band gaps near Fermi energy, differing in stability under residual gas and in Rashba-type spin-orbit splitting. An aluminum dangling-bond state reacts to contamination, while a mainly molybdenum-derived state shows stronger splitting. Symmetry forces crossings near the S point, protected by p2mm mirror symmetry.
arxiv-2604-21140: Amihood Amir and three colleagues map the time-memory trade-offs for finding maximal palindromes in texts containing wildcards, symbols that match any character. Using wildcard longest-common-extension techniques they give a continuous trade-off plus the first nontrivial linear-space algorithm, improving the best known time-memory product in some ranges. Both methods extend to texts allowing up to k mismatches, with or without wildcards.
arxiv-2604-21340: Johann Brauchart, Josef Dick, and Friedrich Pillichshammer prove the information complexity of spherical cap L2 discrepancy on the d-dimensional sphere falls as dimension rises, a blessing of dimensionality for numerical work. A variant that stresses large caps near hemispheres does not ease at all with dimension. A Stolarsky invariance principle then links the variant to a Sobolev space with a kernel. That link implies worst-case error in the space grows fast with dimension, like a polynomial.
arxiv-2604-21540: Akriti Garg and Ayan Chatterjee model a black hole horizon's quantum geometry and Hawking emission in 2+1 dimensions. Using horizon charge algebra, they treat the horizon as built from quantised lengths, each a multiple of 8 pi Planck lengths. Black hole entropy from this length spectrum lands near the Bekenstein-Hawking value. A near-horizon observer relates horizon entropy to black hole energy, so they build a length ensemble like Krasnov's area ensemble, yielding the black-body spectrum. The local observer sees a Hawking spectrum with Tolman-shifted temperature.
arxiv-2604-22240: Liang and eight colleagues show OccDirector, a system that turns plain-language scripts into four-dimensional occupancy scenes for driving simulation. There, space is divided into small cubes tracked over time. Unlike tools that need set paths, it works as a scene director. A vision-language model keeps multi-vehicle moves steady over long runs. The team also releases OccInteract-85k, a dataset pairing scenes with layered language instructions, and reports top quality and strong command following.
arxiv-2604-22340: Bellotti and five colleagues describe LEAPS, a 10-week fully funded summer research program at Leiden Observatory and ESA's ESTEC centre. It serves undergraduate and master's students in astrophysics, aiming to foster early research involvement across diverse backgrounds. Since 2013 it has hosted 194 students from over 40 countries. Data on 165 participants show over half progressed to PhD studies, and participants have contributed to at least 25 peer-reviewed papers and 13 conference talks. The program thus prepares undergraduates for research careers while widening access and global representation.
arxiv-2604-22540: Arrighi and five colleagues examine whether supervised contrastive learning gives clearer model reasons than standard classification training. The contrastive route pulls similar examples together and pushes dissimilar ones apart in code space, using labels only as a likeness guide. Standard training instead needs an explicit classification layer and a cross-entropy loss. That route already offers edges in adversarial robustness and out-of-distribution detection, suiting safety work. The authors show image models trained this way give higher-quality feature attribution accounts on faithfulness, complexity, and continuity.
arxiv-2604-22740: Reinhard, Fauss, and Zoubir tackle joint testing and measuring under spread in the data: test two mixed guesses, then measure a random value based on the verdict. They treat Bayesian and Neyman-Pearson-like versions, showing the best plan seeks an f-likeness whose peak marks the worst spreads. A band-type spread model shows the build, with faster, stable methods.
arxiv-2604-22840: Pan and eight colleagues present AeSlides, a reinforcement learning framework that rewards language models directly for aesthetic slide layouts instead of relying on costly visual reflection or weak fine-tuning signals. Verifiable metrics score layout problems cheaply, and a GRPO method optimizes generation against them. Trained with only 5,000 prompts, it raises aspect-ratio compliance from 36 percent to 85 percent while cutting whitespace, collisions, and imbalance, and human judges rate its slides better overall.
arxiv-2604-22940: Kim and nine colleagues probe encapsulated monolayer graphene, cooled to 5 K and placed in magnetic fields up to 1 T, with near-field optical microscopy in the terahertz range. Near charge neutrality, graphene behaves as a near-perfect high-q reflector, with subtle field changes. Results match calculations of magneto-optical conductivity and near-field contrast describing field-tunable cyclotron resonance of Dirac fermions. The result is a first step toward grasping temperature and magnetic-field effects on nanoscale terahertz transport in flat quantum materials.
arxiv-2604-23340: Chong and four colleagues test whether large language models can contribute effectively to production open-source code. Their verification and validation framework judges an LLM's fitness to fix bugs or add features in existing projects. Applied to 212 commits across eight projects and three models, GPT-4o, Ministral3, and Qwen3-Coder, success ranges from 0 to 60 percent by project. Failures span syntactically incorrect code, failed static verification, and failed test suites, with special weakness in new code, out-of-range contexts, and parroted training changes.
arxiv-2604-23440: Moffat tests whether a modified-gravity theory, scalar-tensor-vector gravity, can explain the cluster-scale force law inferred from pairwise motions of galaxy clusters. Starting from a fit to X-COP cluster data, he extrapolates to cosmological separations, where the theory's force law settles into an inverse-square form. After fitting one overall amplitude, the prediction matches the measured pairwise-motion trend, supporting the theory's consistency across scales.
arxiv-2604-23740: Liao proposes a flow model that evolves over time for learning features, called Score-based Variational Flow. One Euler step of its spherical form gives the transformer exactly. Attention approximates the flow's field via kernel smoothing. Feedforward blocks approximate it more loosely. The residual-norm block acts as a retraction that keeps the spherical shape. This explains why attention trains stably with no extra regularisation.
arxiv-2604-23840: Lin, Markwardt, Napier, Adams, Malhotra, and Gerdes develop an odds-based framework that rebuilds full near-IR spectra of objects beyond Neptune from sparse photometry. A principal-component model of the spectral space plus Bayes maths in reduced space spreads error bars. Cross-checks show four to five parts capture type sorting. Eight to ten parts sharpen rebuilding. The framework also tunes JWST filter choices for taxonomy. It flags rare types such as odd Neptune Trojans.
arxiv-2604-24040: Bhandari and four colleagues show that table retrieval breaks when the same table is written in different formats. Semantically identical serializations in CSV, TSV, HTML, Markdown, and DDL forms yield quite different embeddings and rankings. Treating each format as a noisy view of one meaning, they average them into a centroid target that recovers shared content. A small adapter then nudges single-format embeddings toward that centroid, improving robustness for dense retrievers most.
arxiv-2604-24340: Kouloumpris and three colleagues propose exact scheduling for IoT workflows across edge, hub, and cloud. IoT apps need fast, reliable runs on weak edge devices under deadline, memory, and energy limits. Older schedulers fail to cover all goals and limits. The method uses mixed integer linear programming to optimize latency, energy, and reliability, adding task copies only where needed. Tests on a real workflow and synthetic task graphs beat a widely used heuristic. Gains average about 30 percent in latency, 34 percent in energy, and 28 percent in reliability.
arxiv-2604-24540: Andrew, Dennis, Fisher and Farrell address timing promises that fade as a long-lived system wears down, even when its functions still work. Their CEGIW algorithm repeatedly uses counterexamples from a model checker to loosen only the time bounds in a Metric Temporal Logic requirement, keeping its logical shape intact. It finds the strongest loosened version that still holds, or shows that none exists, illustrated with an elevator arrival guarantee.
arxiv-2604-24840: Stergiou studies the 3D cubic conformal field theory, which governs cubic magnets, via the fuzzy sphere. The theory is hard to study because its observables nearly match the more symmetric O(3) model's. Adding a cubic two-body term to the O(3) quantum rotor Hamiltonian breaks rotational symmetry by construction and isolates the cubic critical point. With diagonalization and density matrix renormalization, he calculates scaling dimensions of operators. He resolves the splitting of an O(3) tensor into forms, matching Monte Carlo and perturbation benchmarks.
arxiv-2604-25040: Loosmore proposes a leverage ratio per task for human-agent collaboration. It divides human work displaced by an agent by time spent on specifying, interrupts and review. That time splits into three channels for a conserved information requirement, each with its cost. Information density is directional, with ceilings on flow from humans to agents and from agents to humans. Asymptotic leverage splits into capability and memory axes, with a planning floor set by irreducible task novelty. A windowed measure extends the analysis to recurring tasks, spawned subtasks and amortized design.
arxiv-2604-25340: Hu and three colleagues build Fock spaces for classical affine Lie algebras uniformly, with Maya diagrams and abaci. The construction extends the Uglov map to all such types. Level-rank duality for type A was first found by Frenkel in 1982, and extended to classical non-twisted types by Hasegawa in 1989. Through Virasoro action, they characterize joint highest weight vectors in Fock space, obtaining level-rank duality theory without character calculations. Using this theory, the cyclotomic KLR algebra defect can be read as the sum of the moving vector's components.
arxiv-2604-25540: Bechtle and nine colleagues study sector coupling for computing clusters. Sector coupling absorbs swings by using electricity when excess green energy flows. A system run this way can lower environmental impact, and costs might also fall, as power prices depend on residual load. Science clusters are an ideal testing ground, since short delays are often negligible, provided a target stays constant. They simulate simplified cluster operation using public German power data. Optimal utilisation, carbon, and cost cuts are set, with hardware costs and embedded emissions taken into account.
arxiv-2604-25640: Yokoyama and four colleagues study a random unitary quantum circuit with only reset channels, a setup feasible for real quantum devices. They probe reset-induced entanglement phase transitions against the classical statistical picture in the large qudit limit. The qudit dimension proves essential: its traits depend strongly on it. Stabilizer circuit simulations for qudits of dimension 2 show critical fluctuations that grow with system size near the transition point. Finite-size scaling analyses collapse onto data consistent with a continuous mixed-state phase transition.
arxiv-2604-25840: Nguyen and six colleagues present PSI-Bench, a tool for depression patient simulators in mental health training. Simulating depressed patients is hard, given safety limits and wide variability. Current tests lean on vague language-model judges and ignore patient diversity. PSI-Bench gives clinical checks at turn, dialogue, and group levels. Testing seven models finds long replies, less variety, and rushed treatment progress. The tool matters more than model scale.
arxiv-2604-25940: Maranzano and seven colleagues present SCARFACE, a harmonized dataset for the Po Valley, 2011 to 2024. The dataset joins climate, air quality, emissions, land cover, soil, and social indicators. Its unit is the Agrarian Sub Region: linked municipalities alike in geography and production. Over 256 regions, the panel holds more than 2,700 indicators from public bodies. Inputs are harmonized in a workflow that keeps spatial and temporal consistency. The resource supports econometrics, modeling, clustering, and policy work on agriculture, air quality, and land use.
arxiv-2604-26640: Zhang and thirteen colleagues built a compact cryogenic Penning trap using a permanent magnet instead of a costly superconducting magnet. Penning traps measure mass and magnetic moments with unmatched precision and test quantum electrodynamics and CPT invariance, but their cost and complexity limit use. The team demonstrated all core functions, from ion generation through signal detection. The trap serves as a testbed for the Shanghai Penning Trap and as a platform for ion trapping, cooling, and spectroscopy.
arxiv-2604-26840: Wilson pins down how fast a massless scalar field's stress-energy tensor settles toward its Unruh-state value as a shell collapses. At any outside radius the gap shrinks at least as fast as the inverse cube of time. Far away, the late-time term follows the same law with a nonzero coefficient. The exponent traces to a branch-point singularity like the one behind Price's law, and the coefficient is negative. The result confirms a conjecture from numerical work and suggests an inverse-seventh law for gravitational waves.
arxiv-2604-26940: Ye and four colleagues propose Select to Think, turning a large model's role in small-model reasoning from generation to selection. At divergence points, the large model's preferred token often sits in the small model's top candidates, even if not the top pick. S2T-Local distills that selection logic into the small model, letting it re-rank alone without calling the large model at inference time. Top eight small-model candidates hold its choice 95 percent of the time, and S2T-Local beats greedy decoding on math.
arxiv-2604-27140: Park proves that the directed five-dimensional torus has a Hamilton decomposition for every odd modulus of at least 3. Such a split divides its edges into directed Hamiltonian cycles. The build assigns outgoing generators by a cyclic layer schedule. One non-constant layer is fixed by a zero-set Latin table. An exact-cover certificate proves that layer is a matching. Cyclic symmetry reduces all color classes to one return map. The modulus 3 case closes by a printed finite cycle certificate.
arxiv-2604-27540: Jang and four colleagues show that in-context examples can suppress scientific knowledge recall in large language models. Models often recall and apply relevant formulas, yet adding examples makes them lean less on pretrained domain knowledge, even when the examples come from the same formula. Instead of knowledge-driven derivation, the models shift toward empirical pattern fitting. The team documents this displacement over 60 latent-structure tasks, five scientific fields, 6,000 trials, and four models, with accuracy effects that vary by case.
arxiv-2604-27640: Baltaci and four colleagues present a measurement study of multi-connectivity for drones, combining drone-to-drone mesh links, private cellular, and low Earth orbit satellite links. Using Multipath TCP, they find aggregation can preserve end-to-end contact under severe link outages. Large differences in round-trip time, however, amplify packet reordering, causing heavy receiver buffering and bursty delivery. When links lack room for the offered load, sender buffering grows, and real-time streaming can miss delay limits even when combined links suffice.
arxiv-2604-27940: Bell and Sloan review how constraints shape Hamiltonian mechanics when a theory's description has degeneracies. They set out the geometry behind pre-symplectic and pre-contact spaces, which suit conserved and leaking systems in turn, and build the rules that find where steady motion can exist. Each rule set ends with a worked example.
arxiv-2604-28040: Memon and colleagues predict when vehicle LiDAR sensors will be blocked, using learned interactive Bayesian models of traffic scenes. Separate models cover normal and blocked driving for each vehicle type, joined by a shared vocabulary for multi-vehicle interaction. A particle filter then infers blockages and flags abnormal patterns at a high level, giving vehicles self-awareness that survives even when sensors stop reporting.
arxiv-2604-28140: Blanco extends Darwin variables, the standard account of radial motion for geodesics in Schwarzschild space-time, across the separatrix to plunging paths. The extended variables give one real account spanning bound, scattered and plunging motion alike, joining motion of test masses. As a proof of concept he drives energy and angular momentum with a constant outside force. That lets one orbit be tracked through plunge with a single phase variable.
arxiv-2605-00140:
YiFeng Wang, Zhun Sun, and Keisuke Sakaguchi present a report on Activation Residual Hessian Quantization, a method for compressing large language models to very few bits. Low-bit quantization of both activations and weights lets errors propagate through a network. Their method is a post-training weight splitting scheme that identifies where those errors hurt most and protects those directions.

From the residuals of activation rounding they build an input-side residual Hessian, then use a closed-form truncated singular value split to isolate error-sensitive weight directions into a high-precision low-rank branch. Experiments on a recent Qwen thinking model show clearly better layer-wise signal quality and preserved reasoning results on a logic benchmark even under aggressive quantization. The code is publicly available.
arxiv-2605-00240:
Wen Li and 3 co-authors improve thermal referral, a trick that lets a person feel heat or cold at a spot with no heater or cooler of its own. A nearby thermal source supplies the sensation, while a touch cue at the target spot draws the feeling there. Vibration has been the usual cue, but it handles cold poorly and its buzz feels wrong for events with no contact.

The team swaps vibration for mild electric stimulation of the skin. In a laboratory study and a virtual reality study, the electric version raised the rate of successful cold referral. It also strengthened the thermal feeling while reducing the touch feeling itself, and it made scenes such as an open freezer feel more real. The authors give design guidelines for choosing cues.
arxiv-2605-00440:
Ching-Chun Chang and 4 co-authors ask how to trace the role artificial intelligence played in a piece of text once the conversation behind it is gone. In human-machine symbiosis, AI sometimes replaces the human, automating a task, and sometimes extends the human, augmenting their work. The role is usually set by the prompt, yet the finished text alone rarely reveals it.

The authors propose a method with three steps. It infers the latent role from the prompt, embeds that role into the content during generation, and later recovers the nature of the participation from the text itself. They test it where AI either edits human writing as an assistant or creates new content from a brief concept as a creator. Results support the method on telling the roles apart, surviving perturbations, and preserving language quality. Fairness and transparency in AI use motivate the work.
arxiv-2605-00540:
Ryuji Higashinaka and 14 co-authors report magnetic measurements on a samarium compound, SmAu3Al7, grown as a single crystal. Using neutron scattering and muon spin rotation, they find magnetically ordered states appearing through two successive transitions, one just below three degrees above absolute zero and a second below one degree. Magnetic Bragg peaks mark an ordered pattern whose repeat does not match the crystal lattice.

Muon measurements detect spontaneous internal fields below the first transition, with a shape consistent with that incommensurate order. Nothing changes at the second transition, so the magnetic structure stays essentially the same across it. The order proves to be a uniform long-range state, not the partly disordered arrangement earlier studies proposed. The authors discuss a possible link between this ordering and the compound's unusually large magnetic specific heat at low temperatures, a connection that could guide further work on related materials.
arxiv-2605-00640:
Shams Mehdi, Ilkwon Cho, and Olexandr Isayev teach a small classifier to say when a machine-learned interatomic potential should be trusted. These potentials predict atomic forces for materials simulation, and knowing their error matters. The standard check, disagreement among an ensemble of models, scales badly to today's foundation-sized potentials and correlates weakly with the actual error on each molecule.

Their method, PROBE, instead probes the frozen per-atom representations inside a pretrained potential with a compact discriminative classifier. Reliability becomes a classification problem, not an error regression. The output is a probability that tracks the true error monotonically, with no change to the underlying potential. Across large held-out sets and two very different architectures, PROBE beat ensemble disagreement as a reliability signal, and it improved as the backbone's representations grew richer. Attention maps even flag which atoms drive the judgment, at no extra cost.
arxiv-2605-00740:
Gaku Omiya, Pierre-Louis Poirion, and Akiko Takeda develop accelerated gradient methods that work in random low-dimensional subspaces. Using only projected gradient information cuts cost, which helps in forward-mode differentiation and in settings where communication is limited. Nesterov acceleration is well understood for full gradients, but extending it to general random sketches that use only projected information is technically hard.

The authors build methods for smooth convex and smooth strongly convex problems under matrix smoothness and broad assumptions on the sketch. A three-sequence formulation is the key step, and it recovers the classic methods in the full-dimensional case. Their theory gives accelerated complexity guarantees and shows when subspace acceleration can beat full-dimensional methods.
arxiv-2605-01140:
Vidush Singhal and five co-authors present SoCal, a language for changing how recursive data types are laid out in memory, along with a compiler called Colobus. A classic compiler trick turns an array of structures into a structure of arrays, which improves memory locality and parallel speed. Existing versions of that trick serve regular array programs in languages like C. Many programs instead use tree-shaped data, such as syntax trees in compilers, page trees in browsers, and spatial trees in science codes.

Earlier work stored such trees in one flat buffer, but the fields of each node stayed mixed together, much like the old layout. SoCal instead splits the fields into separate buffers, giving tree data the same benefit. Colobus rewrites functional programs to work on this factored layout on its own. On a suite of tree-processing benchmarks, the change gives a solid average speedup.
arxiv-2605-01240:
Pankaj Pandey and five co-authors introduce Rhamba, a region-aware framework for self-supervised learning from resting-state brain scans. Pre-training is promising for large-scale neuroimaging, but region-aware masking and hybrid sequence modeling remain underexplored. Rhamba joins anatomically guided masking with hybrid attention and Mamba architectures, using region-aligned patch embeddings and three masking strategies of increasing spatial specificity.

Models are pre-trained on the ABIDE dataset and fine-tuned for schizophrenia and ADHD classification on other datasets. Masking strongly affects reconstruction loss in a consistent order, yet downstream differences are modest and dataset-dependent. A hybrid configuration with Mamba before attention achieves the highest average score. Rhamba beats leading methods overall. Peak performance depends on the interaction between masking and architecture.
arxiv-2605-01440:
Etienne Granet, Ramil Nigmatullin, David T Stephen, and Henrik Dreyer compute spectral functions on a quantum computer by copying the lab act itself. These functions, measured by photoemission tests, reveal a material's band structure, but the theory values behind them are hard to get on classical machines.

Standard quantum routes pay a heavy sampling cost. The new method models the system touching the environment that a photoemission test involves. It builds circuits whose local readings are proportional to the spectral value at each momentum for one chosen frequency. Extra qubits and gates are the price, but sampling needs drop by a factor tied to system size, which means a matching speedup. The team spell out a fast gate plan for the needed Fourier transform and run the method on a trapped-ion machine, covering a 27-site chain with 54 qubits.
arxiv-2605-01640:
Justin Lovelace and four co-authors rewrite scaling law advice for a world running out of fresh training text. The famous Chinchilla law assumes every token is seen once, so it cannot guide training when data must be repeated, which is now the common case.

The team model repetition's cost as a simple added overfitting penalty on the loss, and the one-parameter form fits real training behavior well. Its advice differs in kind: past a point, more repeats hurt, and spare compute should buy model size instead. Following the law's picks improves results in data-starved runs. Because overfitting sits in one coefficient, training recipes can be compared head to head. As a case study, strong weight decay cuts that coefficient by about seventy percent. That explains recent findings that the best decay in this regime is ten times the usual value.
arxiv-2605-02440:
Mathieu Vallée introduces the relative join operad, a structure in algebraic topology built from pairs of simplicial complexes. An inclusion of one complex in another gives a map between polyhedral products, a standard construction in the field. Applying a join construction to both complexes yields a symmetric operad that acts on such maps.

Its endpoint cases recover two known substitution and composition operads. Vallée shows that neither the endpoint operads nor the relative versions are finitely generated, a basic structural fact. One sub-case is identified as a quotient of a power-set operad. Under set conditions, the operad acts on maps by colimits, and a dual construction gives quotient maps tied to Stanley-Reisner theory. Ball and boundary pairs form a further sub-structure with its own morphism.
arxiv-2605-02540:
M. Escobedo and J. J. L. Velázquez examine, in formal terms, where the standard derivation of wave turbulence theory breaks down. Wave turbulence describes how waves share energy, through a kinetic equation for their spectrum. Close to a self-similar blow-up, where the spectrum concentrates in finite time, the usual route from the Schrödinger equation to that kinetic equation is in question.

Near the blow-up time, the authors argue, the chain of statistical averages cannot be closed using solutions of the kinetic equation alone. The kinetic equation must be replaced by a full hierarchy of equations. That hierarchy turns out to equal a random field defined for all times, governed by a nonlinear, time-dependent Schrödinger equation. The paper is a careful warning about limits of a widely used approximation.
arxiv-2605-02640:
Ruta Binkyte and five co-authors argue, in a position paper, that trustworthy AI goals clash because they demand opposite kinds of invariance. Fairness, robustness, privacy, and explainability are each hard to reach alone, and harder together without losing usefulness. The authors recast each trade-off as a conflict over what should stay unchanged when the data-generating process changes.

Causality, they argue, is the frame that can name and soften those conflicts. Case studies from prior work and a stylized simulation show how a causal view explains where a trade-off comes from and where selective invariance can ease it. The argument covers both classic models and large foundation models. Open problems close the paper, with a call to build systems that are both trustworthy and strong.
arxiv-2605-02840:
Alex May gives a book-length treatment of non-local quantum computation and what its entanglement costs. The method performs a quantum operation across two separated systems without bringing them together, using one round of communication plus shared entanglement. It has surfaced in cryptography, complexity theory, communication, and even quantum gravity, and its price in entanglement is tied to open questions in each of those fields.

The treatment reviews upper and lower bounds on that cost, gathering results that were spread across separate literatures. It also covers applications of the method and its connections to neighboring subjects, so a reader can see why a cost bound in one field bites in another. As a single, sustained account of a cross-cutting topic, it serves specialists who need the full map of what is known and what is open.
arxiv-2605-03040:
John M. Mackay, Joseph P. MacManus, and Davide Spriano prove a result about groups whose Cayley graphs are nearly planar. A Cayley graph shows how a group's generators link its elements. A k-planar graph can be drawn with few crossings per edge.

They show any such group, if finitely presented, has a large subgroup whose graph is fully planar. They also treat a wider class of coarse graphs. For that class, they answer a question from Georgakopoulos and Papasoglu. A k-planar graph of that type has the same large-scale shape as a planar graph.
arxiv-2605-03140:
Jayson Ng and Amin Milani Fard test a common belief: that adding retrieved knowledge improves language model explanations of malware. Analysts increasingly use such models to summarize malicious behavior, often with VirusTotal reports as structured input.

Across several models, retrieval often made explanations worse, adding distracting context, noise, and generic filler. The authors argue malware explanation is mainly about extracting signal from evidence already present, not fetching more knowledge. They close with design advice for secure workflows, warning that retrieval can hurt in security-critical pipelines where the source evidence is already sufficient.
arxiv-2605-03240:
Gonzalo Mena develops a new loss for model-based clustering. It is based on entropic optimal transport. Likelihood clustering is principled, but its surface is nonconvex. The EM algorithm can get trapped at poor points, so users restart it many times and hope one run lands well.

The transport loss shares the same global optimum as the likelihood. Yet its landscape is far better behaved, so many spurious traps vanish. A Sinkhorn-EM optimizer converges at a rate matching EM. In many experiments and two real uses, the new loss beat likelihood methods. The uses were microscopy image segmentation and spatial transcriptomics clustering.
arxiv-2605-03340:
Jie Gu and Kangqiao Liu derive a finite-frequency bound linking fluctuations and response in open quantum systems that emit a measurable field. For any downstream detector, the lock-in response-to-noise matrix cannot exceed the output field's quantum Fisher information rate.

For amplitude modulation with vacuum input, that rate is itself capped by a frequency-free activity measure, which for kinetic modulation reduces to steady channel fluxes. The bound is set by the field before any detection choice, so it holds across unravelings. Cavity, fluorescence, and parametric resonator examples show how the ceiling works in practice.
arxiv-2605-03440:
Virdio Samuel Saragih, Baruna Abirawa, Kartini Lovian Simbolon, Luluk Muthoharoh, Ardika Satria, and Martin C. T. Manullang compare traditional classifiers with an LSTM network for email sentiment and spam-related detection. Fast, accurate email filtering still matters for professional and academic inboxes, and the best tool depends on both precision and speed.

Using Word2Vec features, they test SVM, logistic regression, naive Bayes, and LSTM models head to head. A linear SVM reached the highest accuracy and efficiency, while the LSTM showed strong recall for spam sentiment at much higher compute cost. Confusion matrix checks confirm classic models stay robust on dense vector features.
arxiv-2605-03540:
Tian-Xian Luo, Ping Zhou, C.-Y. Ng, Zhi-Yu Zhang, Shumeng Zhang, and Hai-Chen Lin present a radio polarization study of G7.7-3.7, a possible historical supernova remnant with a cocoon-like shape. Its origin and explosion type were unclear, and polarization can reveal the magnetic environment a blast wave expands into.

Very Large Array images show multiple shells, faint blowouts, and mostly nonthermal emission. Polarization runs high in the northwestern filaments, with magnetic fields aligned along them as shock compression predicts. Large rotation measure swings point to magnetized winds from the massive progenitor, suggesting the cocoon formed as the remnant hit pre-existing shells.
arxiv-2605-03640:
Achilleas Michalopoulos, Dimitrios Tsitsigkos, and Nikos Mamoulis revisit in-memory indexing of multidimensional data, a classic database problem behind range and nearest-neighbor queries on several columns at once. Established structures include the R-tree, kd-tree, and quad-tree, and learned indexes have joined them recently. Their proposal is the slicing kd-tree, or skd-tree.

Each skd-tree node splits its subtree's space into multiple slices along one dimension, and the splitters are compressed. That design cuts the tree's depth sharply and, with data-parallel instructions, keeps query work per node to a few operations. The nodes resemble B+-tree nodes, but each level uses a different dimension. A new top-down construction algorithm completes the design.
arxiv-2605-04340:
Benjamin Catalano, Keith Paarporn, and Sebin Gracy model two competing viruses spreading in a population. Members choose how much to distance themselves. They weigh infection risk against the cost of isolation. How the public sees each virus shifts those choices, so behaviour and spread feed back on each other.

Their model breaks a one-way pattern of the classic two-virus model and produces different end states. They map the disease-free outcomes and give conditions for their stability. They analyse cases where one virus dominates. They also study coexistence, which appears as lines of end states. Numerical examples illustrate how game-like distancing can flip which virus survives.
arxiv-2605-04440:
Hsin-Hsiung Huang and Stef van Buuren propose a faster way to fill in missing values in very high-dimensional data, such as brain imaging blocks or sensor records with dropouts. Multiple imputation is the principled approach, since it carries uncertainty about the missing values into later analysis.

Standard chained-equation methods can be slow or unstable when blocks are large and strongly correlated. An exact joint normal method becomes expensive for a different reason. It repeatedly samples and factorises a huge covariance matrix. Their hybrid keeps the same conditional imputation law but updates covariance uncertainty through its dominant mode, with stochastic draws preserving uncertainty about the mean.
arxiv-2605-04540:
Tarun Grover reveals a layered structure in how entanglement grows during chaotic quantum dynamics, the process by which an initially simple state becomes deeply interconnected. The standard picture is that entanglement quickly becomes extensive, growing with system size rather than just with the boundary between regions.

Grover studies local quenches in thermal states and in a companion circuit model. The answer depends on which entanglement measure is used. Some obey an area law, while others grow extensively. More strikingly, the part of the response proportional to the quench strength lives in a tiny dominant sector. That sector itself shows the same transition pattern. The hierarchy also appears to repeat at finer levels.
arxiv-2605-04840:
Antonio Manjón-Cabeza Córdoba, Maxim Ballmer, and Oliver Shorttle ask why Mars seems to keep a dense layer at the base of its mantle while Earth does not. Both planets began with magma oceans that cooled and solidified. Melting in the growing mantle may have fed back into that ocean and changed its chemistry.

Using a model of mantle convection, they show this feedback limits iron build-up in the solidifying ocean. The effect is stronger on larger planets with livelier convection and less starting iron. Mars therefore kept a shallower, denser layer, while Earth mixed more evenly, and other rocky planets may split into two similar groups.
arxiv-2605-04940:
C Larkin and five co-authors simulate young remnants of core-collapse supernovae in two and three dimensions with magnetic fields included. A massive star sheds a dense surrounding medium before exploding, and the blast shock then runs into that structured, magnetised material. How the star lived shapes what the shock meets.

Using the PION code with detailed stellar evolution, the team model red supergiant and Wolf-Rayet progenitors, adding radiative cooling and full photoionisation. Their runs produce features earlier work missed, including a coherent set of fast reflected shocks for the Wolf-Rayet case. Forward shocks also moved faster than simple theory predicts in both settings.
arxiv-2605-05040:
Xin Yu and five co-authors rework self-distillation, where one model teaches itself under different prompts, moving beyond simply matching the teacher's output distribution. Matching that distribution directly can destabilise training and erode reasoning over time. It also lacks the fresh viewpoints a genuinely separate teacher would supply.

Their preference-based method instead treats the problem through reward regularisation. The derived target is a reward-reweighted version of the teacher distribution, provably better than the teacher under that objective. In practice the method optimises preference gaps between teacher and student samples while staying on-policy. The reframing aims to keep self-distillation stable and genuinely improving rather than merely copying.
arxiv-2605-05340:
Junran Wang and three co-authors test whether vision-language models notice privacy risks when acting as embodied assistants in homes and hospitals, where they can see and handle sensitive objects. Text-only benchmarks cannot capture that physical setting. Their ImmersedPrivacy framework instead places models in a simulated three-dimensional environment built in Unity, with sound and vision together.

Three tiers of tasks grow harder: spotting sensitive items in cluttered scenes, adapting as social context shifts, and resolving clashes between direct commands and inferred privacy limits. All twelve leading models tested showed consistent deficits, decaying as clutter grew. No model passed a modest accuracy mark when context shifted, and conflict handling was weakest of all.
arxiv-2605-05540:
Predicting turbulent flows with AI surrogates is easy for a few steps and hard for long horizons. Tianyue Yang and Xiao Xue present MeLISA, a generative model built on pixel-space MeanFlow. Neural operators drift over long rollouts, while diffusion models need many slow steps for each run.

MeLISA generates each block of the future in a single model evaluation. Two consistency losses keep long paths honest, guarding energy spectra and mixing behavior. On high-resolution turbulence benchmarks it beat neural-operator baselines on short-term accuracy and long-run statistics, at comparable or better speed.
arxiv-2605-05940:
Miao Rang and eight co-authors propose a faster way to distill knowledge into autoregressive language models. Standard distillation can mismatch what the student model itself would produce. On policy methods fix that with student generated text, but they lean on costly reinforcement learning frameworks.

Near-Policy Distillation splits generation from training, so updates can use supervised fine tuning with sequence packing. Two guards, sparse student updates and a filtering rule, keep the drifting data from pulling training off course. The method ran 8.1 times faster than on policy baselines and beat plain fine tuning. It also helped a small open model reach a top score above that of a larger rival.
arxiv-2605-06040:
Leon Hamm and Zlatan Ajanovic adapt an idea from automated planning, novelty, to guide language model reasoning. Tree of thought search builds paths of linked ideas by prompting a model again and again. The method is brittle and costly, since weak branches consume time and tokens before they are dropped.

The authors define a measurable novelty score for each new thought, judged against nodes already in the search tree. A language model estimates that score using knowledge from its pretraining. Branches with low novelty get pruned early, which shrinks the tree and can lower total token cost despite extra prompts per state. Tests on planning and reasoning benchmarks compare the approach with standard search variants.
arxiv-2605-06140:
Samir Darouich and five co-authors make one step generative modeling respect the symmetries of physical systems. Molecules and other physical objects have distributions that do not change under rotation, and models should honor that invariance. Drifting models generate in a single step and are fast, but an equivariant generator does not naturally yield the right drifting field for a symmetrized target.

Their design, SymDrift, makes the drifting field itself symmetry aware in two ways. One route symmetrizes the drift by optimal alignment, and the other uses an invariant embedding that removes symmetry doubt by construction. On conformer and transition state benchmarks, SymDrift beat other one shot methods and stayed competitive with far costlier multi step models. It also cut computing overhead by up to forty times.
arxiv-2605-06340:
Florian Burnat and Brittany Davidson formalize the gaming that continuous compliance audits invite, and release a benchmark for studying it. New laws require ongoing post deployment audits. Regulated systems can game them over time in ways one shot studies miss. They can delay reports, drift within plausible noise, exploit sample attrition, or cherry pick among ambiguous metric definitions. The authors model this as a repeated game where the auditor commits first and the auditee adapts.

They identify a cover regime in any noise aware static auditor design, where coverage gaps and granularity gaps cannot both be closed. Two minimal policy extensions each close one side, exactly as their analysis predicts, while an audit aware drift strategy defeats both. A simulator with libraries of auditee strategies and auditor policies, calibrated to published audit data, supports the study.
arxiv-2605-06440:
Daniel Uyterlinde, Swasti Shreya Mishra, and Pascal Mettes propose putting concept bottleneck models into curved hyperbolic space. Such models force a classifier to decide through human-understandable concepts, which aids interpretation. Standard versions place concepts in flat space and treat them as independent, yet real concepts form hierarchies.

Their HypCBM treats a concept's activation as containment inside an entailment cone, so broader ideas geometrically contain narrower ones. The inclusion margin gives hierarchy-aware activations at test time with no extra learned parts. A scaling rule also spreads user corrections through the concept tree, and tests rival Euclidean models trained on far more data.
arxiv-2605-06540:
Nafis Saami Azad and Raiyan Abdul Baten propose a way to test, before deployment, whether creative AI tools shrink the diversity of human ideas. An idea loses value when many people produce near-copies, yet systems are judged one output at a time. Their framework compares model-only generations against matched unaided human baselines, needing no interaction data.

Ideas are modeled as congestible resources, yielding an excess-crowding measure and a diversity ratio where one marks parity with humans. Across short stories, slogans, and alternative-uses tasks, three frontier models fall below parity. Changing the generation protocol can reduce crowding, making diversity collapse a design-time target rather than a surprise.
arxiv-2605-06640:
Ronaldo Canizales, Divya Gopinath, Corina Păsăreanu, and Ravi Mangal merge two explanation styles for vision models: high-level concepts and formal causal explanations. Concept methods explain predictions in human terms but may lack a causal link to the output. Formal abductive and contrastive methods find minimal input features that truly decide an outcome, yet work only at pixel level.

Their concept-based explanations find minimal sets of concepts that are causally relevant, using concept erasure tests to verify the link. Algorithms enumerate all minimal explanations for single images, and aggregation extends the view to whole behaviors across image collections. Tests on several models and datasets show the explanations are helpful and user-friendly.
arxiv-2605-06740:
Abhijit Sen, Bikram Keshari Parida, Giridas Maiti, Mahima Arya, and Denys I. Bondar introduce GeoKAN, a geometry-aware version of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks. Standard networks approximate functions in fixed Euclidean coordinates, which wastes effort where a function is smooth and under-serves regions where it changes sharply. GeoKAN first learns a diagonal Riemannian metric that warps the input space before the basis expansion and mixing steps.

Stretching fast-changing regions and compressing smooth ones moves representational capacity where it is needed, and in physics-informed use the metric also reshapes the differential structure the model sees. Three main variants, including basis-specific versions using radial, wavelet, and Fourier functions, target sharp, stiff, and localized problems in scientific machine learning.
arxiv-2605-06840:
Sixing Chen and five co-authors extract the search trees hidden inside language model reasoning traces to see whether the models truly plan. Reasoning models deliberate over future outcomes in long chains of thought, but the structure of that deliberation was unmeasured. Working on the game four-in-a-row, the authors parse traces into search trees and fit computational models of how moves get chosen.

Model search proves shallower than human search, and performance tracks breadth rather than depth. Most strikingly, although traces expand deep nodes, move choices are best explained by a myopic model that ignores them, and pruning experiments confirm shallow nodes drive decisions. Human expertise, by contrast, rests on deep search, a clear target for alignment work.
arxiv-2605-07140:
Talha Ilyas, Deval Mehta, and Zongyuan Ge make skeleton-based action recognition explain itself. Systems that read body-joint motion can label actions well, but most remain black boxes. Their neurosymbolic framework reframes recognition as logical reasoning over motion concepts, using rules written in first-order logic.

A skeleton encoder extracts motion features, which a decoder turns into readable pose and dynamics concepts. Differentiable logic layers combine those concepts into human-readable rules for each action. Descriptions generated by language models help align the concepts. On major action datasets, the system stays competitive while offering explicit explanations grounded in its logical structure.
arxiv-2605-07540:
Chenglin Shang and ten co-authors report the first experimental study of CrRhAs, a material whose chromium atoms sit on a distorted kagome lattice, a pattern of corner-sharing triangles. Theory had predicted unusual magnetic states for it, but its real magnetic structure and behavior were unknown. The team grew samples and probed them directly.

Neutron diffraction shows the material orders antiferromagnetically below about 149 kelvin, in a noncollinear pattern that differs from earlier theory predictions. Its electrical behavior switches from semiconductor-like above that temperature to metallic below it, and its Hall response changes sign twice. Together with heat capacity data, the results point to a strongly correlated kagome metal with several active bands.
arxiv-2605-07640:
Jun Wang and four co-authors built LithoBench, a benchmark for judging how well large multimodal models interpret rock types from remote sensing imagery. Lithology interpretation underpins geological surveys and mineral exploration, but it is knowledge-heavy: experts infer rock type from subtle visual, spectral, textural, and landform cues, so automation is genuinely hard.

The benchmark holds ten thousand expert-annotated cases across twelve rock categories, split between multiple-choice and open-ended tasks at five levels from identification up to comprehensive reasoning. An expert-in-the-loop construction pipeline kept the geology sound. Testing several large vision-language models exposed substantial limits, especially on explanation, application, and reasoning tasks rather than simple recognition.
arxiv-2605-07740:
Matthias Kahl and five co-authors release LAMES, a dataset for segmenting mining activity in satellite imagery, built to help monitor environmental damage. Mining drives deforestation, soil erosion, and land-use change far beyond the pit itself, and illegal artisanal mining is widespread, including across parts of Africa. Watching remote sites from above can reveal illegal operations and their footprint.

The dataset covers one hundred fifty large-scale mining sites with twenty-seven attributes each, plus annotated artisanal small-scale mining areas totaling eight hundred seventy square kilometers. Those attributes connect facility traits like mining type, processing method, and commodity to environmental outcomes. The authors also discuss the dataset's uses, its social and environmental stakes, and the ethical responsibilities of researchers working with it.
arxiv-2605-08040:
Yizhou Zhou, Jiayin Li, and Zhi Zhang present ECNUClaw, an open-source framework for study companions in primary and secondary education. The system builds a learner profile with five parts: cognitive, behavioral, emotional, metacognitive, and contextual. It updates the profile from signals in each turn of student dialogue.

Profile changes feed an engine that adjusts guidance strength, encouragement, and scaffolding based on Bloom's taxonomy in real time. The design draws on three strands of Chinese education research, including a three-layer learner portrait model. Built in Python, ECNUClaw connects to seven Chinese language model providers through one adapter, and the authors discuss limits and next steps.
arxiv-2605-08340:
T. Dex Bhadra, Sean Terry, David Bennett, Aparna Bhattacharya, and coauthors present MORIA. It is an automated pipeline for planet masses from high-resolution images of microlensing events. Hubble images of such targets blend the source, the lens, and neighbor stars into a few pixels. Untangling them by hand is slow and fragile.

MORIA reduces the images. It builds an empirical point-spread model from the data itself. It fits all blended stars at once. Applied to the event KMT-2019-BLG-0253, it found three blended stars. It halved the possible solutions. It pinned the host at about two thirds of the Sun's mass. The planet weighs roughly seven to nine Earth masses, under the remaining close-wide ambiguity.
arxiv-2605-08440:
Daniel Wesego and Pedram Rooshenas purify adversarial images with diffusion models, paying attention to time. Purification projects a tampered image back toward clean data, but plain diffusion cleaning can break under adaptive attacks, and score-based test-time optimization, though tougher, usually treats every denoising step the same.

Their TARO method builds a score prior from several points along the diffusion trajectory. High-noise views contribute globally smoothed structure that is hard for an attack to bend, while low-noise views restore image-specific detail. The coarse-to-fine residual target balances keeping the picture's meaning against scrubbing the attack, aiming for robustness that survives attackers who know the defense is there.
arxiv-2605-08640:
Sommerhoff and Moeller tackle inverse problems, where a true image must be recovered from damaged data through a known rule. Plug and play methods solve these with cleaning priors from diffusion and flow models, but random renoise denoise steps muddy proofs. The authors pin down the fixed renoise denoise operator hiding inside flow based plug and play methods.

That operator is the average of a denoiser over the hidden noise spread, a clean fixed object. They build FlowADMM, which plugs the operator into the alternating direction method of multipliers, or ADMM. They prove convergence promises under weak Lipschitz conditions on the flow network, extended to shifting time schedules. In tests on denoising, deblurring, super resolution, and inpainting, FlowADMM leads flow based rivals while needing fewer consistency checks than earlier methods. The work gives flow based plug and play a fixed footing with theory to match its strong performance.
arxiv-2605-08740:
Nilesh Sarkar and Dawar Jyoti Deka measure how much of a transformer's inner representation truly causes its output, as opposed to merely describing it. Sparse autoencoders widen the readable feature count enormously, but causal power may not keep pace. Their causal dimensionality counts the effective rank of expected response patterns at a given layer, estimated through feature width sweeps paired with patching tests.

On a mid sized Gemma model, readable capacity grows far faster than causal capacity, a wedge they document carefully. The causal count stays fixed across model sizes and depths while raw response strength falls sharply with depth. Interpretability gains a grounded yardstick separating features that matter from features that merely appear.
arxiv-2605-08940:
G. Boroun, Loyal Durand, and Phuoc Ha derive three deep inelastic scattering structure functions directly from measured ones. In high energy electron proton scattering, the functions F2 and its slope with energy scale are measured well, while the longitudinal, singlet, and gluon functions are harder to isolate. Extending recent work, the authors show all three can be written in terms of the measured pair, apart from small non singlet corrections treatable at low momentum fraction with known quark distributions.

Everything is presented consistently to second order in the strong coupling, correcting and extending earlier mixed order results. Particle physics gains cleaner extractions of gluon and longitudinal structure from existing data, sharpening the picture of proton internals at very small momentum fractions.
arxiv-2605-09140:
Pablo Roig, writing alone, asks whether a hidden pair of new particles could imitate the pattern seen when a heavier lepton decays into a lighter one plus neutrinos. His 2026 study works within a general low-energy theory and allows invisible pairs of several spins, paired with different forms of interaction in the decay current. The test case is the Michel distribution, a measured shape long read as matching the Standard Model.

Roig sets a strict test based on all measurable decay patterns, including cases with polarized daughter leptons and added radiation. Besides the familiar neutrino-like case, he finds exactly one hidden option: a massless complex scalar pair tied to a purely left-handed current copies the standard pattern fully. Every other case leaves a telltale sign. He also notes a small shift in this channel could change how the Fermi constant is drawn from muon lifetime.
arxiv-2605-09640:
Lou and three colleagues test whether reward based tuning can beat catastrophic forgetting in visual continual learning. Past work hints reward tuning resists forgetting better than supervised tuning. But whether it wins in hard class incremental and domain incremental setups stayed open. A pilot study confirms reward tuning beats supervised tuning yet still forgets a lot. The authors trace the snag to trajectory level drift blindness.

Among rollouts earning equal rewards, drift from the prior task policy varies widely. That spread tracks forgetting closely across sequential tasks. Their Retention aware Policy Optimization method, RaPO, counters it with trajectory level reward shaping. A retention reward turns drift into a steady signal favoring knowledge keeping rollouts. Cross task advantage normalization steadies training across task borders. Across five visual continual setups, RaPO leads, cutting forgetting while keeping plasticity.
arxiv-2605-09740:
Goulet Coulombe tackled a known weakness of tree-based boosting in macro forecasting: straight-line patterns dominate, yet boosting with trees wastes splits mimicking straight lines. LGB+ tests a tree option and a linear option at each step against out-of-bag data, advancing only the winner. A simpler variant, LGB-A+, alternates on a fixed schedule: a block of tree updates, then a greedy linear correction, repeat.

Because each forecast sums a linear and a tree part, it splits natively into linear and nonlinear parts, as do permutation importance and historical proximity weights. In a quarterly United States macro exercise, LGB+ delivered strong gains for targets with pronounced autoregressive dynamics or mixed linear-nonlinear signals. Initial claims for unemployment and building permits for housing starts led the linear channel.
arxiv-2605-09840:
He, Shuryak, Wu and Zahed analyse how much of the nucleon, the proton's family, is really five quarks rather than three. They use a light-front Hamiltonian, a framework that tracks particles at near-light speed, with sigma- and pion-type transition operators acting in a fully Pauli-consistent five-quark basis. Pentaquark shapes are classified by permutation symmetry across orbital, spin-flavour and colour degrees of freedom.

Mixing coefficients for all 27 positive-parity P-wave pentastates show a strikingly sparse pattern: only 6 channels feed the nucleon wave function, while 21 vanish by symmetry selection rules. The surviving contributions cluster in a few hyperfine eigenchannels. Sigma- and pion-induced amplitudes share the same states and a fixed phase, so they add without interference, giving about twenty-nine percent five-quark content against seventy-one percent three-quark core.
arxiv-2605-10140:
Kalaj and Zhu prove the Nitsche-Hopf conjecture for non-parametric minimal graphs over disks. If a minimal graph sits over a disk of radius R, xi marks the point above the centre. Then W squared times the Gaussian curvature at xi stays below pi squared over twice R squared. Here W is the reciprocal of the vertical part of the upward normal. Finn and Osserman's horizontal tangent-plane sequence shows the constant is best possible.

The bicentric-quadrilateral comparison theorem controls curvature alone, not the product with W squared, since the slope factor can grow unboundedly. The missing control is recovered in a Scherk-type family, through the zero equation for the horizontal projection. In fixed-arc normalisation, the centre becomes a zero of that projection. This reduces the sharp estimate to a derivative inequality proved by a barrier argument and two Bernstein certificates.
arxiv-2605-10240:
Yuteng Zhang and four colleagues tackle a skewed problem in software security: spotting flaws in code when some flaw types are common and others are rare. Their 2026 paper presents MARGIN, a framework for vulnerability detection that treats the imbalance as a geometry problem, reshaping how code examples sit in the model's representation space.

MARGIN learns discriminative, or telling-apart, representations through adaptive-margin metric learning and prototype modeling on a hypersphere. It adjusts its regularization to the estimated spread of each class, lining up embedding mass with decision regions and steadying the boundaries between flaw types. On public vulnerability datasets it beat strong baselines, with the clearest gains on the hardest, most imbalanced sets.
arxiv-2605-10340:
Sebastian Fieldhouse and five colleagues make radar imaging fast enough to steer itself. Conventional Synthetic Aperture Radar focusing uses block processing, which is efficient but slow, blocking closed-loop cognitive radar where the sensor adapts from what it sees. Their 2026 paper presents the first Online SAR Processor, an image-formation framework that treats sensing as a stream and outputs focused images line by line during acquisition.

The processor runs on a tiny state-space stand-in model, taught by teacher-student distillation with multi-stage losses. Tested on 300 gigabytes of Sentinel-1-derived Maya4 data, it delivered about 70 times lower latency and 130 times lower memory use than a linewise digital-signal-processing baseline. On a single AMD CPU core it processed one row in 16 milliseconds with a 6-megabyte footprint, while keeping focus quality high enough for vessel detection and flood mapping.
arxiv-2605-10440:
Yao Liu builds an audit instrument for a conflict baked into conversational travel agents. Online travel agents now compress ranked lists into one sentence of prose advice. Each booking earns commission at differing rates. The agent thus favors higher-margin recommendations. Yet no one can currently measure that steering. His 2026 paper proposes TourMart.

Two governance levers drive a paired counterfactual procedure. Lambda weights message-induced perception in accept decisions. Kappa caps how far the message can move perceived welfare, scaled by budget. Holding traveler and bundle fixed, the steering delta is read between a prompt that knows commissions and a factual template. A six-gate audit separates engineering failures from genuine commercial steering. At deployed settings, Qwen-14B showed 7.69 points of steering and Llama-3.1-8B showed 3.50 points of steering in the same direction. TourMart's headline: 7.7 extra steered recommendations per 100 paired sessions.
arxiv-2605-10740:
Stevan Djurdjević and Zorica Popović look in theory at odd and diode Josephson effects in flat two-dimensional links with patchy ferromagnetic walls and edge Rashba spin-orbit pull. A full symmetry study finds the least rules for breaking time-flip and space-flip symmetries, needed for odd and diode effects. It sorts links into three groups, with a close look at links between unlike-aimed d-wave superconductors.

Tuning swap-field lines, edge Rashba pull, and order traits lifts one-way flow by more than 40 percent. Phase-tied Andreev bound state spectra and their flow gifts are studied. Flow states past the gap grow loud when zero-energy crossings show up or d-wave gaps grow thin or shut. In the one-way zone, bound state spectra show a lopsided shape under phase flip, marking real flow at zero phase gap and unlike peak flows in flip lines.
arxiv-2605-10840:
Yixuan Yang and ten colleagues present Clin-JEPA, a 2026 pretraining framework that learns from electronic health record trajectories. One model can then both forecast a patient's course and serve many risk-prediction tasks. Joint-embedding predictive architectures have shone in robotics and vision. Carrying them to medical records has been blocked by unstable training and predictors that never teach the encoder.

A five-phase curriculum warms up the predictor and refines encoder and predictor together. It then aligns the target network, syncs it hard, and finalizes the predictor. Each step tames collapse and drift. Built on a Qwen3-8B backbone, the co-trained model keeps rollouts stable where naive joint training diverges. Clinical machine-learning teams get a single backbone for forecasting and risk tasks without retraining for each job.
arxiv-2605-11240:
Charlotte Park, Kate Donahue, and Manish Raghavan ask when generative AI tools should ask the user a question. Generative models let users give as much or as little detail as they choose. Users often omit details, relying on models to infer missing information from knowledge of user preferences.

Such inference may favor majority views and hurt users with unusual tastes, raising fairness concerns. Unlike traditional recommenders, LLMs can ask users directly for more information in natural language. Direct elicitation could raise fit and cut inequality, but too many questions burden users valuing speed. The team builds a simple model of user-LLM interaction with a goal weighing user burden and preference representation. Since individual tastes often correlate, they analyze how systems should balance inference and elicitation, finding the best amount to ask before content generation. Designers get proof that elicitation can cut the systematic biases of preference inference.
arxiv-2605-11440: Okawa and three colleagues benchmark three module-level methods for measuring thermoelectric conversion efficiency. The methods are heat flow, guarded heater and AC Harman, tested on commercial bismuth telluride modules. Heat flow and guarded heater agree closely. The AC Harman method reads systematically lower by about sixteen to thirty percent, depending on module architecture. Computer models trace this to open thermal boundaries that skew internal temperatures. Method choice matters, and no single number tells the whole story, so Harman suits rapid screening only with its bias accounted for.
arxiv-2605-11840: Zhangcheng Hou and Tomoaki Ohtsuki argue that radar should enter a depth model inside its selection mechanism, not through fusion outside it. Their Radar-Modulated Selection injects radar into the selective scan of a Mamba model, perturbing step size and readout while leaving input projection and state matrix untouched. On nuScenes, their SemoDepth cut mean absolute error by up to 34 percent, ran at 26.8 milliseconds per frame, and barely degraded when spurious radar returns outnumbered true ones two to one.
arxiv-2605-12040: Eleni Batziou and three colleagues study position auctions with a space limit. Ads have mixed sizes, and the platform must select and assign a subset under a global space limit. They frame the problem as matching with a space limit and propose a method adding to density-based ranking with space-aware local tweaks. Under single-knob agents and slot-based click-through rates, a small tweak yields an always-truthful chance-based rule with constant-factor bound, the first such rule for this variant.
arxiv-2605-12140: Md Abulkalam Azad and six colleagues present EchoTracker2, tracking heart muscle points in ultrasound video. Heart motion differs from video motion: it comes from constrained tissue change, smooth in space and time, so paths stay local even under large deformation. Past two-stage coarse-to-fine designs may waste effort on coarse starts, so EchoTracker2 uses a fine stage only, enriched with local space-time context and time reasoning. It beats a domain best by 6.5 percent on position accuracy and 12.2 percent on path error, and matches expert strain measures better.
arxiv-2605-12440: Cui and five colleagues build a symmetry toolkit for collinear magnets. No general recipe had existed for models that depend in plain view on the order direction, called n. Their framework uses the equivariant space group to build such models, called equivariant magnetic Hamiltonians.
