Those models live in a joint space of momentum and n, and show odd symmetry actions and topological features. A ferromagnetic chain and a three-dimensional antiferromagnet show pumping effects driven by magnet motion. First-principles versions track n-dependent bands well.
arxiv-2605-12540: Tiwari and three colleagues extend smoothed particle hydrodynamics to random mechanics problems. The mesh-free method handles large bends and free surfaces well, yet classic forms assume fixed systems. Their random SPH uses Polynomial Chaos series for uncertainties in parameters, forcing, and boundary or initial conditions, with spatial change carried by the SPH kernel. Random fields enter through Karhunen-Loève series, and Galerkin projection turns the random PDE into coupled ordinary differential equations. Tests show close match with Monte Carlo stats at far lower cost.
arxiv-2605-12640: Cheng and five colleagues propose MambaPanoptic, a fully Mamba-based setup for panoptic segmentation, which must spot countable items and amorphous stuff regions together. Convolutional methods struggle with long-range context, while transformer methods pay quadratic cost that bites at high resolution. Their MambaFPN pyramid uses Mamba blocks to build wide coherent multi-scale maps at linear cost. A PanopticFCN-style kernel generator then makes unified thing and stuff kernels, letting one setup meet the joint demands of context, scale and fast dense prediction.
arxiv-2605-12740: Ortiz-Muñoz builds a pivotal monoidal category of DNA structures. Objects are DNA sequences, read as words over A, C, G and T. Its morphisms are isotopy classes of noncrossing matchings from through-strands and Watson-Crick arcs in a rectangle. A sequence's dual is its reverse complement. Duplex pairings give evaluation and coevaluation, and snake identities follow by planar isotopy. Bending correspondence links each morphism to a combined-word structure. Generalised elements prove to be exactly the non-pseudoknotted structures.
arxiv-2605-12940: Zhao, Liu, Zhang and Liu compare probabilistic circuits with large language models in one autoregressive setup. They trace the gap to two choke points. First, circuits predict via convex mixes in probability space, which cope poorly with sharp language distributions; a logit-space setup narrows the gap greatly. Second, structured-decomposable circuits match transformer separation rank only on partitions lined up with their fixed routing, failing badly on mixed dependency patterns.
arxiv-2605-13140: Lee and four co-authors present MS-DePro, a multi-source domain adaptation detector that uses depth maps and text, both domain-agnostic inputs, to handle target domains unlike training data. Existing methods learn domain-agnostic features from domain-specific RGB images while keeping domain-specific information in the feature map. MS-DePro instead generates domain-agnostic region proposals from depth for localisation and aligns learnable text embeddings for classification. It reaches state-of-the-art performance on multi-source adaptation benchmarks.
arxiv-2605-13740: Valentin Six and nine colleagues introduce Pinductor, a world-model learner in which a word model offers trial world models from a few observation-action trajectories. It step by step refines them to raise a belief-based fit score. Despite using strictly less data, Pinductor matches the scores and thrift of word-model-based POMDP learning methods given private access to the hidden state. So, these results place word-model priors as a handy tool for sample-thrifty world-model learning under partial seeing.
arxiv-2605-13940: Zhuang and seven colleagues build AgentTrap, a benchmark that tests whether language-model agents can use third-party skills without falling for hidden malicious behavior. A harmful skill need not request an obviously dangerous act, since it can disguise that act inside a routine workflow the agent runs with broad permissions. Across 141 tasks, 91 malicious and 50 benign, the study finds models often finish the visible request while treating unsafe side effects as ordinary workflow steps.
arxiv-2605-14040: Yang audits the full training-and-evaluation system behind multimodal physics reasoning, then releases verifiers to fix it. Standard build habits warp measurement: contamination slips past n-gram dedup, translation weakens problems, saturated multiple-choice formats flatter capability, partial-credit rewards invite gaming, and open-ended grading leans on the judge picked. Left unchecked, these flaws overstate reported progress and spill test knowledge into training. The released verifier system runs a three-stage contamination audit to certify the train-test boundary.
arxiv-2605-14240: Shportko and Verbitsky test how well AI-generated text detectors survive paraphrasing attacks. The spread of large language models has raised plagiarism and false-information risks, while detector-bypassing tools make reliable machine-generated text spotting vital. The paper tests three methods, fine-tuned RoBERTa, Binoculars and text feature analysis, plus ensembles built with Random Forest sorters. Ensembles with Binoculars score strongest overall yet suffer the steepest losses under attack, showing a performance-versus-resilience split in AI text spotting.
arxiv-2605-14840: Sohom Mukherjee and three colleagues tackle inventory control where each order decides what demand you get to see. When sales cap what is observed, demand is censored, and standard methods grow brittle if their assumptions miss. Their in-context generative posterior sampling uses models trained offline, then generates completions of hidden demand while ordering online. Tests show it matches well-tuned rivals, beats simpler baselines, and holds up under heavy censoring on a real retail dataset.
arxiv-2605-15040: Baolin Peng and thirteen colleagues present Orchard, an open-source framework for turning language models into autonomous agents. Its core, Orchard Env, is a Kubernetes-native service managing sandboxes across tasks, harnesses, and training stages. Three recipes build on it, for software engineering, computer use, and other agent skills. The software-engineering agent reaches 73.0 percent on SWE-bench Verified with value-model reranking, a new open-source state of the art near frontier systems ten times larger.
arxiv-2605-15240: Yang Liu and three others study how eigen-matches between kernel grids and learning targets govern generalization in kernel ridge regression. Forecast amounts to a weighted sum of vectors, so perturbation analysis of values and eigenvectors yields a learning bound. Their finite-sample analysis shows that with a high-rank kernel, near-zero reconstruction error comes easily and therefore predicts generalization poorly. Strong learning instead demands more and more true eigenvalue and vector estimation, a sharper guide than rebuild error.
arxiv-2605-15440: William Timkey, Brian Dillon, and Tal Linzen test why language models are less surprised than humans by garden-path sentences. Surprisal theory links processing difficulty to unpredictability, yet model surprisals underpredict human difficulty in controlled syntactic-ambiguity studies. One hypothesis is that models juggle more simultaneous sentence parses than humans. Using recurrent neural network grammars with word-synchronous beam search, the authors vary active parse counts and predict reading times. Fewer parses raise predicted garden-path effects, but far from enough to match human magnitudes.
arxiv-2605-15540: Zhipeng Xu builds three explicit quantum Latin squares of order six. Their sizes are thirteen, fifteen, and seventeen. Vectors that differ just by a global phase count as one. The size-thirteen build splits six-dimensional space into four- and two-dimensional parts. The two larger builds use two-dimensional Hadamard pairs on coordinate planes.
arxiv-2605-15640: Xin Zou and six colleagues build GMAE, a tool for multi-view clustering that keeps views apart while learning shared structure. Past deep methods tangle view distributions when fusing views, which muddies the shared latent space. GMAE runs twin autoencoders that split source traits into view-only and view-shared embeddings. Cross-view adversarial discriminators push view-only encoders to sharper traits. Tuned mutual information lines up distributions and blocks collapse. On 13 benchmark sets it beats top methods on full and partial view tasks.
arxiv-2605-15840: S. Lahs and eight colleagues study cesium atoms held in a cold argon matrix, using light spectra plus diatomic-in-molecule models. The spectra show tangled emission, large Stokes shifts and slow decay, pointing to strong host-guest links and major lattice change. Beneath a broad haze, likely from low-symmetry or flawed trapping spots, two main trapping spots emerge. They give two triplet absorption lines with distinct glow patterns, and polarization hints the spots differ in shape, though a firm structural call stays out of reach.
arxiv-2605-15940: Arka Chatterjee and seven colleagues report a correlated time lag and polarization degree for Swift J1727.8-1613 during its 2023 outburst. The lag centers on type-C quasi-periodic oscillations seen by IXPE on 2023-09-07, while polarization comes from energy-resolved polarimetry. The Spearman correlation is 0.8, with null probability 4.2 percent, and the correlation drops as the oscillation quality factor falls. Model-free claims show processes beyond inverse Comptonization also feed both polarization and lags, pointing to extra mechanisms linking spectral, temporal and polarimetric traits of black hole binaries in the hard state.
arxiv-2605-16440: Brignac and four others propose semantic smoothing, a defense for radar target recognition that swaps noise-based perturbations for random transformations from a novel view synthesis model. Deep networks are open to adversarial perturbations, blocking safety-vital use, while smoothing over noisy inputs uses isotropic noise that fails to preserve semantic structure. For SAR, the method uses acquisition geometry to make plausible radar views, pooling predictions into a robust classifier. Tests show semantic smoothing lifts robustness against FGSM, PGD, OTSA, and SMGAA attacks and raises clean classification accuracy.
arxiv-2605-16740: Yan and colleagues introduce TRACE, a framework for understanding events across several videos and generating claims with evidence. It first builds a text-searchable timeline for each video with OCR and object detection. A text-only language model then picks the relevant moments before any visual reasoning begins. The chosen frames steer claim generation and cross-video citation. On the MAGMaR validation set, it lifts macro-average F1 from 0.705 to 0.811 over an unguided baseline.
arxiv-2605-17340: Fei and colleagues present Olivia, a time-series base model that lines up data sets before training so their mismatched rhythms do not clash. A Harmonizer module reshapes spectral structure across sets, matching their normalized power spectra, while HarmonicAttention runs self-attention through a small set of resonators. Tests on two big benchmarks plus six extra sets show top scores for zero-shot, few-shot and full-data forecasting.
arxiv-2605-17640: Chakraborty and colleagues present MARQUIS, a three-stage video retrieval pipeline. Retrieval fails on complex queries one embedding cannot capture, while generation lacks cross-video reasoning and faces memory limits. MARQUIS combines query expansion, fusion and reranking, evidence extraction, and article generation, optionally controlled by a reasoning model. On MAGMaR2026 it lifts retrieval nDCG at 10 from under one fifth to about three quarters. For article generation, ITER-QA-BASE lifts human score from just above 3 to just below 4 over CAG, while MARQUIS-RLM leads non-QA systems on citations.
arxiv-2605-18140: Timothy Atherton and six colleagues survey 90 STEM faculty on AI adoption in research and teaching, finding a clear AI teaching outlook that strongly predicts self-reported AI use. This outlook reflects views on AI's role in field thinking, learning, and skill growth, not just positive or bad feelings. School plans, backgrounds, and information sources link only weakly to AI use. The results suggest standard adoption models miss cases where tools meet field reasoning and knowledge production.
arxiv-2605-18340: Lakshya Chaplot, Harshita Agarwal, and Atul Sharma build a physics-informed neural network solver that reaches a time-periodic flow state directly, skipping the long transient phase of standard unsteady CFD simulations. The meshless solver fits a single time period rather than the whole history from an initial condition. In tests on periodic heat diffusion and fluid flow, the 2026 solver matches traditional accuracy in substantially less time.
arxiv-2605-18640: Javier Blanco-Romero and Florina Almenares Mendoza price Reeh-Schlieder preparation from the vacuum in a tiny region. One Tomita-Takesaki bound, they show, sets a model wide floor on that price. Deep negative modular energy forces large local operators, while shrinking an operator to a contraction converts the floor into postselection overhead. Known modular Hamiltonians make the floor explicit. Bisognano-Wichmann recasts it as wedge boost energy, Casini-Huerta-Myers as a stress tensor for bounded regions, and local unitaries reach only nonnegative modular energy states.
arxiv-2605-18740: Qianhao Yuan and six co-authors present Vision-OPD, a 2026 self-distillation method for detailed vision. The same model answers questions better from crops than from full images. That gap shows failures come from weak focus, not weak recognition. Vision-OPD builds a crop-conditioned teacher and a full-image student. It minimizes divergence between their next-token distributions on student rollouts. The student thus gains visual zooming with no external teacher or verifiers. On detailed benchmarks, Vision-OPD matches or beats larger open, closed, and agentic models.
arxiv-2605-18840: Adil Amin studies why leaderboards stop separating frontier models, using paired coding and question-answering scores across thirty-four models from ten labs. Capabilities cooperate overall, yet cooperation varies fivefold by lab, and labs pivot between coding-first and reasoning-rich stances. His per-release residual diagnoses each lab emphasis from just two public scores. Pretraining shifts prove lasting while post-training shifts reverse within a release, a split that tells builders whether to retrain or wait.
arxiv-2605-19140: Jiayu Li and four colleagues study workflow learning where agents hand off an artifact, each seeing only part of it plus its state. They formalise this as a semi-Markov decision process with interface constraints and design IC-Q, a Q-learning algorithm whose coordination at each handoff is one scalar. Their result bounds IC-Q error in samples across function-approximation error, interface gap, and a mixing-time residual. Four experiments show IC-Q matches an oracle with no agent seeing joint trajectories, with error sources scaling as predicted.
arxiv-2605-19240: Kavana Venkatesh and four colleagues tackle cascade attacks in teams of language-model agents. Harmful influence can spread from agent to agent and wreck the whole system. Their CASPIAN framework watches influence across every channel at once, using a causal matrix to spot a cascade as it forms. It also names the agents that start, carry, and amplify the attack, beating simpler guards while adding under one percent latency.
arxiv-2605-20040: Mohammad Shahverdikondori, Jalal Etesami and Negar Kiyavash study contextual bandits where the learner may choose which to sample. With a context distribution, passive sampling gives slower regret than active sampling with allocation by p to the two-thirds power. The improvement can reach order k to the one-quarter power, where k counts contexts. They extend the analysis to budgeted active sampling, identify when a limited budget recovers the active rate, and propose an Explore-Explore-Then-Commit algorithm for unknown distributions matching the active rate for large horizons.
arxiv-2605-20140: Jingyuan Hu and three co-workers present a particle-field algorithm for a three-dimensional reaction-diffusion-advection cancer invasion model. Particle measures represent cell density, and concentration fields for chemical species are built. Particle-grid interaction uses a particle-in-cell algorithm, while diffusion uses a spectral method. Particle mass change stays bounded over finite time, and cell density and grid concentrations stay positive. Error analysis and experiments confirm convergence rates, the first work solving this system in three dimensions, where haptotactic spread appears as in two dimensions.
arxiv-2605-20340: Ying Shu and 14 co-workers present high-resolution pre-eclipse spectra of hot Jupiter CoRoT-2b from Gemini South with IGRINS. Cross-correlation finds the Doppler-shifted emission at SNR 4.32. 2 independent pipelines confirm water 2.6 sigma, log -5.08, and carbon monoxide 2.3 sigma, log -4.21. No significant methane, carbon dioxide, titanium oxide, or vanadium oxide. Water and carbon monoxide show a not-featureless dayside spectrum and constrain a supersolar C/O ratio of 0.91 with subsolar metallicity. It gives first constraints on CoRoT-2b's atmosphere, a base for westward hotspot offset.
arxiv-2605-20440: Hoyos and seven co-workers build exact symmetry into tensors so physical selection rules hold by construction. Many learned models learn symmetry only roughly, and tests with the Orb-v3 force field show crystal space groups shifting with input orientation. Their star-G tensor algebra convolves over a finite symmetry group, splitting prediction error into rule violations, input inconsistencies and residual error. Projecting force predictions through it cuts space-group change rates to at most 2 percent, with no retraining.
arxiv-2605-20540: Alexander Dobner gives a short proof about cylindric Schur functions, symmetric functions that extend skew Schur functions to a cylinder shape. He shows they expand with positive coefficients in terms of plain cylindric Schur functions. The coefficients turn out to be fusion coefficients, numbers that also count how representations combine. The argument is concise where earlier routes were longer, and it settles positivity in this setting.
arxiv-2605-20740: Jungsoo Park and six colleagues propose Distribution-Aware Reward, a reinforcement learning objective for language-model regression. Most regression objectives score each prediction alone, which can yield poor calibration. Their method instead judges the whole set of values for one input as a spread. Each value earns credit for its leave-one-out contribution to that spread's quality, favouring values that are well-centred and sensibly spread around the target.
arxiv-2605-20840: Jin Dai and Tuo Wang give a positive answer to the L^p projection centroid conjecture. In a 2000 paper, Lutwak, Yang, and Zhang established the L^p analogues of the Petty projection inequality and the Busemann-Petty centroid inequality, two classic results. In section seven of that paper, they proposed the important L^p projection centroid guess. Dai and Wang now settle it in the affirmative, closing a question that stood since that classic paper.
arxiv-2605-20940: Olivia Zumsteg and six colleagues improve multi-view image models for wheat spike volume estimation via 3D reconstruction and knowledge distillation. Accurate wheat spike volume matters for yield component analysis and stress resilience review, yet field measurement remains challenging. Active 3D sensing like LiDAR or time-of-flight is sensitive to plant motion or poorly suited outdoors, while 3D reconstructions are computationally expensive. Their hybrid 2D-3D approach uses knowledge distillation in training while enabling efficient image-only inference, starting from a rigid-invariant point cloud network.
arxiv-2605-21040: Faizuddin Ahmed and A. F. Santos ask whether closed timelike curves exist in a modified gravity theory. The theory uses an arbitrary function of the Ricci scalar, matter Lagrangian, scalar field, and kinetic term, adding a dynamical degree of freedom. Within it, the authors analyze the causal structure of rotating cosmological solutions. They use cylindrically symmetric Petrov-type N spacetimes and axially symmetric Petrov type-III spacetimes with a cosmological constant as probes, examining pure radiation matter sources in both cases.
arxiv-2605-21140: Wajiha Masood and Afshan Irshad study the BB84 quantum key protocol under collective rotation noise, a realistic disturbance rarely covered in ideal analyses. Tracking error rates, shared information, and secret key rates under intercept-and-resend attacks, they find a nonzero noise range where an eavesdropper gains least while key-rate loss stays modest. The result suggests deliberate noise shaping could harden practical quantum key distribution.
arxiv-2605-21240: Yibo Li and colleagues present APEX, a tool for self-evolving language-model agents. Such agents learn across episodes from memory and reflection, not weight updates. But growing memory can trap them in familiar high-reward routines, a flaw called exploration collapse. APEX builds a strategy map, a graph of milestones with prerequisite links. Fork Discovery adds new, evidence-backed directions, while Policy Selection weighs exploring against exploiting. Tests on nine text-adventure games and a web benchmark show APEX ahead of prior tools.
arxiv-2605-21340: Vipul B Rohit, Vikram Dharodi, and Sharad K Yadav study vortex dipoles in viscoelastic media, relevant to dusty plasmas. They simulate symmetric and asymmetric dipoles varying core size, circulation, and separation. Even dipoles sustain translational motion, with speed falling as separation grows. Uneven dipoles rotate instead, with the weaker vortex orbiting the stronger one.
arxiv-2605-21440: Zhiming Liu, Zhicheng Zou, and Nantheera Anantrasirichai present ReMATF, a recurrent method for turbulence mitigation in dynamic scenes. Atmospheric turbulence degrades video through warping, blur, and flickering, harming clarity and time consistency. ReMATF restores videos using only two frames at a time. Its architecture pairs a multi-scale encoder-decoder with temporal warping and a motion-adaptive fusion module. Video from heat haze is hard to watch, and the goal is a clean, steady view.
arxiv-2605-21740: Kevin Han and co-authors introduce SMDD-Bench, a benchmark testing language-model agents on real small-molecule drug design. It offers five hundred two guaranteed-solvable tasks across five types, from pharmacophore identification and scaffold hopping to lead optimization, spanning one hundred two protein targets. Solving it fully demands chemical and biological reasoning, 3D intuition, tool use, and planning over limited oracle calls. Even the best of seven frontier models tested, GPT5.4 solves only forty point two percent of tasks, showing autonomous drug design still lags.
arxiv-2605-21840: Siegfried Gawenda and coauthors present ASKAP continuum imaging of the G4Jy-3CRE catalog, the brightest southern-sky radio sources, southern Third Cambridge Catalog Revised equivalent. The catalog holds 264 sources from the GLEAM-4Jy survey, selected by 3CR criteria. Three Rapid ASKAP Continuum Survey releases spanning sky south of plus 30 degrees declination and frequencies 600 to 1,800 MHz classify 173 sources with jet-indicative morphologies. They are 66 percent of the sample, 37 newly showing jets. They classify FRI and FRII galaxies to redshift 1.35, identifying six counterparts for unidentified or ambiguous sources.
arxiv-2605-21940: Anand Oza and co-authors study how a floating disc bobs up and down under periodic forcing, in theory and in tests. The wave field is modeled with a linear problem that bars flow under the disc and leaves the surface free elsewhere. Reducing it to an integral equation and solving it predicts how bobbing size depends on forcing rate, in good agreement with tests. The authors read the physics through added mass, wave damping, and spring-like stiffness, found across rates and by hand at low rates.
arxiv-2605-22240: Zhang and colleagues address proactive task dialogue, such as outbound sales. An agent there must probe a user's worries and steer toward acceptance within limited turns. Language models tend to stay cautious. Reward shaping only reweights what a passive policy already samples. Their answer centres on hidden concerns. A Cognitive User Simulator models each user from visible traits and hidden concerns. A training method then transfers concern-aware behaviour into the conversation-only view.
arxiv-2605-22440: Casals and Christ lay the groundwork for categorical weave calculus, placing diagrammatic weaves and braid varieties in triangulated categories of Calabi Yau type and cluster tilting theory. Each Demazure weave gains a perverse sheaf of triangulated categories. The Lusztig cycles with their duals form simple minded and silting collections among the sections. Those collections tilt under mutations. The authors develop weighted braid words and a form of tropical Lusztig rules as gluing tools. An appendix builds collections from exceptional collections and states when a highest weight structure yields them.
arxiv-2605-22540: Gregnanin and team offer a model building a changing hypergraph map for multi time series without prior knowledge. They hold higher-sided links, but building their maps from time series is hard when shape is thin or absent. The model applies group finding to time series, turning found groups, got through a focus step, into one using a clique-based trick. These are used by a Dynamic Hypergraph Attention Convolution Network (DHACN) for multi time series guesses. The approach finds high-order links without prior knowledge.
arxiv-2605-22640: Storror Carter and Rossell examine a popular prior for symmetric positive definite matrices. The prior assumes independent entries and truncates to force positive definiteness. They show careless truncation can warp interpretation, shrinkage and posterior inference when the cut prior drifts far from its uncut twin. The paper studies dense and sparse cases and shows how to set prior settings, such as off diagonal variance, so the truncation effect fades as matrix size grows. Sparse cases need special care, since poorly set priors push estimates toward spuriously sparse structures.
arxiv-2605-22740: Smits introduces ternary decision trees, which add an uncertainty zone around each split so near threshold cases avoid false confidence. A decision theoretic framework fixes the zone width from node local costs and proves four properties, including accuracy decomposition and asymptotic consistency of the margin method. Cases inside the zone blend both child subtrees and carry an uncertain flag. Across most OpenML-CC18 data sets, all five zone width estimators with probabilistic routing beat standard CART on decided accuracy, with the margin method best and no tuning knobs.
arxiv-2605-22840: Sharma borrows the Kardashev ladder, which ranks civilizations by energy commanded. He asks how much machine cognition every rung could support. Only a share of total power goes to computing. Each joule buys computation at the hardware efficiency of the day. Their product caps machine thought, measured here in rough units of human brain processing rate. Set against modern supercomputers, the ceiling sits far above present use. So capacity, not energy, is the looser bound.
arxiv-2605-22940: Tran studies entropy-regulated learning under separate task, risk, and intervention constraints, warning that cutting entropy is not itself a safety criterion. A noise-calibrated log-determinant functional gives an exact spectral force formula and splits motion into observable and prediction-null parts. For scalar feedback he maps the full range of coefficients that preserve task progress while meeting an entropy-rate request. Human authority enters only through how constraints and release policy are specified.
arxiv-2605-23040: Bhattacharyya and Rooshenas test attention query activations as a precise site for steering language model generation. Dense-state meddling tangles distinct semantic features. So they apply sparse autoencoders to query activations, split them into clear features, and tune gradients at inference to match sparse patterns with class prototypes of target behaviors. In a textual gridworld, sparse query tuning navigates rigid planning rules such as safe versus short paths. In a school domain, the same method steers the cognitive complexity of feedback along Bloom's Taxonomy.
arxiv-2605-23440: He and colleagues propose SSDAU, a data augmentation method built for joint entity and relation extraction, where training data quality drives generalization. Older augmentation often weakens entity links and breaks meaning. SSDAU cuts text by entity labels, encodes context, and reshapes entity meaning to make new examples, pairing context embeddings with classic similarity scores to separate lookalike entities. Topic checks drop off-topic output. Tests across five models and seven baselines show steadier, more consistent data and far smaller accuracy drops when meanings blur.
arxiv-2605-23540: van der Hoorn and colleagues tackle ambiguous points in dimensionality reduction, where one data point resembles several mutually dissimilar groups at once. Standard methods map each point to a single spot, so only part of its group ties survive, a distortion they call partial neighborhood embedding. Their graph-based method spots such points and copies each one into every group it belongs to. Tests with UMAP show hidden memberships surfacing and partial embedding shrinking across examples, and the approach extends to other local graph-based reduction methods.
arxiv-2605-23640: Wu and colleagues present CachePrune, a privacy-aware cache sharing mechanism for large language model inference. Shared caches speed serving but leak user inputs through reuse side channels. Disabling sharing wastes reuse of privacy-irrelevant segments like system instructions. CachePrune enables fine-grained, token-level reuse across requests, deriving reusable segments and retrieving them over variable spans despite sensitivity masking. Built on vLLM and tested on three data sets, it eliminates direct leakage while cutting time to first token by 4.5 times and raising cache hit rates by 44 percent.
arxiv-2605-23840: Adam Tlemsani and colleagues attack a data scarcity problem in Mueller polarimetry. This imaging reads rich tissue contrast from polarized light. Their MuellerPT pretraining teaches an encoder to predict Lu-Chipman decomposition maps from per pixel Mueller matrices. A new multispectral animal organ dataset scales the training up. With only five percent of training data, lamb brain grey versus white matter segmentation jumps by more than twenty percent above training from scratch. Cancer classification gains eight percent at one percent of data.
arxiv-2605-24140: Liu and five co-authors introduce HyperGuide, steering multi-step reasoning without expanding and ranking branches at inference time. Reasoning becomes motion through a tree of states in hyperbolic space. A state encoder on the Poincare ball feeds a guidance head that predicts the cheapest next move. That direction reaches the decoder as a virtual token after every step. Training ranks moves, favouring continuations that are sound and short. On contest maths and code tasks, HyperGuide matches or beats search-based rivals while using fewer tokens.
arxiv-2605-24240: Althaus and four co-authors give a parameterized algorithm testing whether a diagram's limit is empty. A limit of a diagram in a complete category reads as equations over its objects, with each object a variable and each morphism a constraint. With an initial object present, the question is whether any solution exists, equivalently whether the limit is initial. The authors build a fast parameterized-complexity algorithm for finite diagrams in finitely complete presheaf categories. It handles structured co-decompositions from the Grothendieck construction of a simple graph.
arxiv-2605-24340: Martnishn presents ChainzRule, swapping typical units with tunable poly layers governed by Differential Regularization, a Jacobian penalty computed exactly during the forward pass. The core claim is that bounding middle slopes pushes the network toward stable shapes, cutting need on labeled data and lifting toughness to shift. Across five domains, ChainzRule beats support-vector and boosting rivals on diabetes, tops RNN rivals on mood with a frozen encoder, and edges a BERT linear head. It also improves corruption scores on CIFAR-10-C, with p-values below the 0.05 threshold after fix.
arxiv-2605-24440: Lyon, writing for the ATLAS and CMS collaborations, reviews recent flavour-physics results from the two LHC experiments. Topics span quarkonia and charm cross sections, the B0 lifetime, excited-versus-ground B splittings, all-charm tetraquarks, and rare heavy-flavour decays. The analyses use Run 2 and partial Run 3 LHC data and push the precision frontier in flavour physics.
arxiv-2605-24540: Saurabh U. Shringarpure and colleagues suppress noise on bosonic modes with a hybrid continuous-discrete interferometer that needs no active error correction. A qubit ancilla and two controlled-Fourier gates sandwiching the noise channel cut its effects from linear to quadratic scaling. The scheme works for any single-mode bosonic code under thermal or displacement noise. Success stays at or above one half when the loss-amplification product stays below one half. With more ancillas, photon loss becomes coherent Fock damping, and the scheme extends to a qutrit ancilla.
arxiv-2605-24740: Amogh Palasamudram and others give reachability reinforcement learning deeper convergence theory. Reachability specs matter for step-by-step choices, yet guarantees are less explored. One approach reaches optimal policies in the limit but reveals little about convergence dynamics. The authors build on PAC learning. PAC methods promise near-optimal policies with high confidence quickly, but need minimum transition probability. They argue unknown values can be refined and estimated with growing accuracy. By meeting PAC conditions, exact optimality follows. Benchmarks validate the account.
arxiv-2605-24940: Béla Csaba offers a vertex-partitioning framework that frees regularity-type methods from the Regularity Lemma. The Szemerédi Regularity Lemma plus the Blow-up Lemma form a core tool for graph embeddings, yet only for very large, dense graphs. Csaba's alternative stays effective as density tends to zero, without astronomically large vertex sets. Its scope is narrower, but it reaches relatively small graphs the old method could not touch. As an application, the new partitioning method serves bipartite packing problems.
arxiv-2605-25040: Vasiliy S. Shlyk presents CAFS, a sort that exploits low cardinality on x86-64 with AVX2. In OLAP engines, columns after a group-by often have far fewer distinct values than rows. CAFS combines a cache-line-sized SIMD bucket, a Chao1 estimator over 1024 strided samples, and a dispatcher with a spill safety guard. Against baselines, CAFS runs 1.7 to 3.1 times pdqsort in the low-cardinality band. It also beats IPS4o and vqsort there.
arxiv-2605-25240: Russell Yang and colleagues build a test that pits two ways of judging answers against each other on real legal work. JudgmentBench gathers 30 tasks with scores from practicing lawyers, both as fixed-criteria grades and as head-to-head preference picks. When the same experts supply both kinds of judgment, side-by-side choices recover the intended quality ranking. They do far better than rubric grades. Preference picks also take less than half the grading time, a gap that holds for human graders and automated ones alike.
arxiv-2605-25340: Minyu Cheng, Jiakun Yan, and Marc Snir speed up parallel integer sorting for uneven workloads. The classic bulk-synchronous model stalls on irregular work because it forces global communication lockstep. Fine-grained asynchronous variants overlap work better but usually tie one process to each core. The team combines a lightweight communication library with OpenMP threading to exploit every core fully. Tested on the NAS integer-sort benchmark with its original skewed distribution, the multithreaded design beats traditional bulk-synchronous MPI implementations and scales for irregular scientific work.
arxiv-2605-25440: Rafal Kocielnik and colleagues rate the quality of verbal feedback that surgeons give trainees live in surgery. Manual rating is slow and broad lists miss delivery traits like clarity and urgency, while keyword methods miss nuance. Their two-stage framework first discovers clear criteria, such as encouraging, urgent, and clear, using multi-agent prompts plus surgical knowledge. Those criteria then score live feedback directly through a judge model. On about 4,200 feedback cases, the discovered criteria predict trainee conduct change and trainer praise better than prior methods.
arxiv-2605-25740: Kang, Kim and Oh study offline goal-conditioned reinforcement learning, where policies must reach goals from fixed data alone. They trace poor long-horizon results to faulty value generalization, and build the fix into Latent-Aligned Value Learning. It pairs latent value generalization with hierarchical planning in one framework. On OGBench it tops existing offline methods, winning the highest score on 20 of 22 datasets. It leads above all on long-horizon tasks and trajectory stitching.
arxiv-2605-26340: Rui Meng and twelve colleagues' 2026 paper tackles verifiability failures in autonomous research agents, such as fabricated citations, unreproducible scores, and method accounts that diverge from code. Their Chain-of-Evidence scheme demands every claim trace to its evidence source, and ScientistOne maintains such chains from review to writing. A post-hoc audit checks scores, specs, sources, and method-code alignment. Across seventy-five papers from five systems, every rival fails systematically, while it reaches zero hallucinated references, perfect score checks, and best method-code scores.
arxiv-2605-26440: Victor M. dos Santos and seven colleagues turn multi-turn user-assistant chats into code benchmarks with Conv-to-Bench. Older benchmarks lean on slow expert handcrafting, so their pipeline mines shifting instructions inside dialogue logs and rebuilds them as tasks with binary checklists. In programming, the generated sets line up almost perfectly with human-built BigCodeBench, reaching Spearman correlations up to 1.000 with far less compute. Its judge model agrees substantially with human-checked truth. Ablations show multi-turn logs capture evolving intent, while instruction-centered extraction proves sturdier.
arxiv-2605-26840: Ye, Santos-Rodriguez, and Simpson improve factual consistency in summaries by learning from several weak factuality metrics at once. Single metrics mislead, but their combination captures more error types, so the team maps metric scores to preferences and drops cases where metrics disagree sharply. Training on lexically similar summary pairs from varied decoding teaches the model to spot subtle factual shifts. Gains hold across model sizes, with small models nearly matching larger ones.
arxiv-2605-27140: Zhang, Lin, and Wu address a mismatch in reinforcement learning for multi-turn agents. Rewards come only per trajectory, while success hinges on local decisions. They present StepOPSD, a self-distillation framework that uses the agent step as the unit. It splits trajectories into action segments, rescoring them with hindsight teacher context. It turns token-level gaps into advantage shaping with a step budget before GRPO updates. Across ALFWorld and Search-QA, StepOPSD ranks best or second on causal-error subsets, including first place on ALFWorld Heat and PickTwo.
arxiv-2605-27240: Fu and co-authors test whether support agents can fetch the right memories for a user's emotional needs, not just for facts. Their ENPMR-Bench set holds over 1800 memory-rich dialogues grounded in Maslow's hierarchy, with set links between emotional needs and helpful memory types. Current retrieval methods, whether embedding-based or model-driven, fall well short of the gold-memory standard on empathy scores. Chain-of-thought prompting narrows the gap between inferred needs and fetched memories, but a large shortfall remains.
arxiv-2605-27440: Will Jack, Noah Lehman, Keller Maloney, and Sarah Xu show buyer phrasing drives brand recommendations more than buyer intent. Across thousands of paraphrase and rerun trials, paraphrase pairs overlap only 14 to 29 percent, far below the 50 to 61 percent same-prompt baseline. More reasoning effort barely narrows the gap, so tracking brand mentions prompt by prompt is structurally unstable.
arxiv-2605-27540: Abolfazl Younesi, Nouhaila Innan, Alberto Marchisio, and Muhammad Shafique build a serverless scheduler for hybrid quantum-classical algorithms. Their EFaaS middleware treats classical tuning and quantum runs as linked session-aware events, sending circuits to quantum processors with warm caches and favoring active loops. Wait time for the next shot falls by up to about 94 percent, and runs finish up to about 98 percent faster, with drift harm removed.
arxiv-2605-27640: Karim Elgammal and Marc Maussner compute additive binding energies in asphalt binder with a hybrid quantum-classical workflow. Their QuantumPave pairs machine-learning potentials for geometry with quantum-selected configuration interaction in a 10-electron, 10-orbital space on a 54-qubit chip. The active-space binding energy of roughly three and a half kilocalories per mole falls short of the full hydrogen bond against a benchmark between eight and ten.
arxiv-2605-28040: Han Xu, Tomonori Shirakawa, and Seiji Yunoki sharpen quantum estimates of molecular ground states by engineering sparser wavefunctions. Their filter-assisted protocol concentrates a state's weight onto few basis states, cutting the sampling cost of subspace diagonalization. On a quantum Ising model, tested in simulation and on hardware, energy errors fell by orders of magnitude.
arxiv-2605-28440: Shaolong Chen and three colleagues diagnose an uneven gradient in DPO, the alignment method that skips a separate reward model. Its loss pushes disliked replies down far faster than it lifts liked ones, teaching dodging over good generation. Their AdaDPO variant assigns per-pair weights from the policy's own generation odds, making gradient sizes match for liked and disliked replies. On a Llama-3-8B test it beat standard DPO on most settings and reached the best win rate with length taken into account, while keeping the original settings.
arxiv-2605-28740: Bushi Xiao, Sarvesh Soni, and Daisy Zhe Wang propose Reverse Probing, the first uncertainty framework specialized for clinical summarization. Most uncertainty methods target open-domain generation and cannot pin uncertainty to tokens or spans in long clinical text. Reverse Probing instead treats text as a window into the model's internal state, drawing uncertainty signals from four kinds of internal activations. On two expert-annotated clinical datasets it beats eight adapted baselines on all metrics, with up to four times higher AUPRC and lower inference time and compute costs.
arxiv-2605-28940: Oz Amram and colleagues test whether neural scaling laws, familiar from language models, also govern generative models of particle jets. They recover the expected logarithmic model-size scaling for next-token prediction loss. A sliced Wasserstein distance over five physical quantities tracks that loss closely, making the loss a sound proxy for physics quality. Dataset-size and compute scaling prove much weaker. The authors explain this with a learnable window: jet constituents saturate quickly, unlike language tokens, partly because QCD radiation is random.
arxiv-2605-29040: Rushna Quddus and colleagues study how lipids help build photonic nanostructures like those giving insects color. Lipid vesicles mixed with biopolymers form even patterns from 700 nanometers to 1.2 microns, more than ten times lipid-only sizes, in 1D to 3D. The team varies biopolymers, pH, heat, and charge, probing vesicles with light and X-ray scans plus zeta tests. Cryo-electron microscopy confirms the interaction makes ordered structures, showing lipid phases can sort them into neat forms.
arxiv-2605-29240: Junsoo Park and colleagues propose a clear decision layer for AI-augmented classrooms. It ranks course topics that need attention using three signals, without waiting for grades. The signals are how widespread student difficulty is, gaps between what learners report and what is observed, and worries raised by teachers. Each ranked topic comes with a short record that explains its place. In one graduate computing course, the ranked topics matched teacher concerns well and surfaced struggling learners missed by any single signal alone.
arxiv-2605-29340: Kenji Imamura and colleagues examine a safety-evaluation question-answer set centered on illegal activities. Working from a close manual review of AnswerCarefully, they contribute extra data, ways to build new question-answer items, and a scoring guide for model replies. Their findings are meant for the JAI-Trust project. The paper thus offers dataset-building methods plus a safety-assessment rubric for the illegal-activity area, grounded in that close review of an existing resource.
arxiv-2605-29540: Jyothish S and Sadagopan Narasimhan study the Steiner tree problem across split-like graphs unifying bipartite, split, and bisplit graphs. Through reductions, they draw boundaries. On bipartite graphs free of large stars, the problem is tractable to star size three and hard from size four. On star-free bisplit graphs it stays tractable from star size three up. Bisplit graphs of diameter two admit solutions, but diameters three and four turn hard, and star convexity helps only on the clique side, with chordal bipartite and split cases hard.
arxiv-2605-30240: Jacek Herbrych and Maria Daghofer model chirality-induced spin selectivity in low-dimensional helical organic systems including electron interactions. Hopping competition plus double- and superexchange routes can stabilize non-collinear helical magnetic order, whose bands show partial spin split as p-wave magnetism. Using renormalization group, cluster perturbation and Monte Carlo methods, they find tiny spin-orbit coupling triggers strong spin selectivity well above the spin-orbit scale. Strong correlations prove key, though long-range spin order is not needed; non-collinear spin correlations from Coulomb forces explain the effect.
arxiv-2605-30440: The Euclid Collaboration probes galaxy evolution in cosmic voids using Euclid simulations. They study traits and merger histories with the GAEA light cone. They sort galaxies by void distance and density, comparing mass, star formation, and halo mass. Galaxies near void centers are less massive, star-forming, and flatter. Merger histories show void galaxies do not merge less often, but merge later. The results back a picture where environment sets merger timing and nature. The analysis gives a framework for Euclid data and shows Euclid probing environment effects.
arxiv-2605-30640: Marchenko Breneur and colleagues introduce CSULoRA, a post-hoc fix for small adapters weakened by unsafe tuning data. Existing safety methods rely on hard steps like projection, pruning, or thresholding, which can strip useful information. CSULoRA estimates a safe subspace from the weight gap between aligned and base checkpoints, then splits each adapter update into aligned, partly aligned, and outside parts. A penalized minimal solution keeps the aligned part while damping unsafe directions, cutting attack success with most utility kept.
arxiv-2605-31040: Liu and colleagues unify code and graph representations for RTL designs. Existing methods use only code or only graphs. The control data flow graph preserves structural information, while code encodes semantic information. Their UniRTL framework learns representations by jointly using code and the graph. It aligns code and graph finely through masked modeling. A strategy uses a graph-aware tokenizer and staged text and code alignment before integration. Tests on prediction and retrieval show UniRTL beats methods for hardware design.
arxiv-2605-31240: Bippus and colleagues study the Fermi-Hubbard model, a model of electrons on a grid, still not fully understood. They link spin entanglement to the start of the pseudogap in its two-dimensional form. Pairing an ultracold-atom simulator with numerical simulations, they find spin-singlet entanglement shows up only once the pseudogap sets in. Unlike classical correlations, it stays with nearest neighbours. That pattern argues against purely classical-fluctuation accounts, and narrows microscopic models to those growing nearest-neighbour singlet entanglement at onset.
arxiv-2605-31540: Khveshchenko addresses subtle issues in the old problem of strong coupling between phonon-like fermions and bosons. At the centre stands the customary Migdal-Eliashberg approximation in the Schwinger-Dyson gap equation and its solutions. He assesses prior insight by contrasting it with supersymmetric and non-supersymmetric versions of the Yukawa-Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev model. He also comments on earlier pseudo-holographic takes on fermion pairing in these models.
arxiv-2606-00040:
Chen and Jia measure students' AI literacy by watching how they prompt, rather than asking them, in this 2026 arXiv study. Generative AI literacy means knowing how to use, judge, and handle tools like ChatGPT with care. Existing assessments rely on self-report questionnaires, which miss real behavior. The authors gathered interaction logs from 162 university students doing a GenAI-assisted abstract writing task. Epistemic network analysis, a method mapping how ideas connect in activity, modeled each student's strategy.

Distinct signatures separated the literacy levels in their early results. Strong students iterated, refining prompts step by step and steering output through follow-up questions. Weaker students leaned on generation commands, in effect asking the tool to write for them. The contrast suggests process data can characterize literacy more honestly than surveys. The authors propose using such patterns for data-driven scoring and real-time interventions that nudge struggling students toward better strategies.
arxiv-2606-00240:
Zhang and co-authors teach AI aides to guess minds on the fly with no hand tags. A good aide must infer what a user thinks and wants from acts. That skill is called theory of mind. Live help needs fast, firm reads that can shift as acts pile up. True mind tags are scarce in real-world data.

Their frame, MindZero, learns by self-guided reward. The model drafts mind claims and earns praise when a planner says those claims make the seen acts likely. No mind tags are used at all. Training folds that slow path into one fast pass. Tests span grid worlds and home tasks. MindZero beats both plain models and slow plan-based tools on speed and scores.
arxiv-2606-00340:
Pang and co-authors map the first two steps of training for straight-line nets by exact math. Such nets stack plain layers with no bends in their paths. Step size, called learning rate, can vary by layer. Early steps set much of the path that comes next.

The team write closed forms for slopes and test loss past steps one and two. Those forms show how step sizes should scale at the start. A stand-in loss built on that scale stays tight and close. Proof then shows a split in the best plan. Step one wants lopsided rates across layers. Step two and on want matched rates. Bench tests back the math in full.
arxiv-2606-00440:
Gulluk and co-authors reward chest X-ray tale tools by set gaps twixt made and true line traits. Proof-checked rewards sped thought tools, but X-ray tales break that mold. A tale is a loose set of finds, not a chain of steps. Match or step scores thus miss the mark for such tales.

Each tale is split to lines, and lines are cast as trait points. The gap twixt made and true point sets acts as the reward. That gap cares not for line order, as a set should not. Tests span two sets and three sight-word tools. Set-gap training beats plain fine-tune and match-based tools on key marks. The same gaps pick the best of N drafts at test time. Mid-run cuts of weak drafts halve word counts.
arxiv-2606-00640:
Sarkar and co-authors gauge how hard a clip-plus-ask pair is for a sight-word tool, by traits. Their gauge, VideoABC, sets that hard grade as the tool's fail odds. Named traits of the clip feed that grade in the frame. Scene weight and act speed are two such traits in the list.

A base set of clips is cast into the trait space in training. That space is cut to cells, and each cell gets a mean hard grade. A new clip's grade is read from its cell's mean. Two cutters guard the scheme for small base sets. One is a bunch-based form, and one is a grid form for far cases. Fake clip drills fill grid cells in training runs. Low trait counts still beat judge-style tools by far.
arxiv-2606-00740:
Zhang and co-authors build a fast search tool for mixed media in this 2026 paper. Cross-modal hashing turns images and text into short binary codes. Search then runs fast in Hamming space, where codes are compared bit by bit. Most methods learn in a smooth feature space and snap to bits at the end. That last snap sits far from how the model trained.

Their system, SpikeHash, is built on spiking neural networks, whose units fire in pulses. Image and text features become pulse trains over time steps. The two trains drive one shared hash state in the same Hamming space. Each side can shift the firing of the other. Each hash bit then comes from a race between paired pulse channels. The authors report search accuracy that rivals top methods on three test sets. The hash stage also uses fewer parameters, fewer operations, and less energy.
arxiv-2606-00840:
Subramanian, Žikelić, and Bansal grade RL agents on new tasks in this 2026 paper. An agent that masters its training tasks may still fail on unseen ones. Labs need a principled way to tell strong generalizers from lucky ones. The team builds a logic-driven evaluation frame for that job.

Their tasks form a family of inductive reach-avoid problems. Each task shares structural traits with the rest, but its exact form is new to the agent. A neural certificate function then checks each run. It enforces key conditions on the paths agents take. Failing those checks marks a breach of sound play. Across top generalizable RL methods on hard continuous worlds, a pattern shows. Fewer certificate breaches line up with more test tasks solved. The frame thus ranks methods by how well they truly generalize. It gives the field a litmus test, not just a score.
arxiv-2606-00940:
Makadia and co-authors gain local control over a spinning crystal of ions in this 2026 physics paper. Penning traps hold large ion crystals that rotate as one rigid body. Such crystals suit quantum simulation and sensing with hundreds of spins. The spin has blocked flexible control of single ions until now.

A tight off-resonant laser beam does the steering. It drives local phase rotations through differential AC Stark shifts. Beam steering stays in sync with the crystal's spin, so any ion can be addressed as it sweeps past. Ramsey tests give a pi rotation fidelity of 0.950, with neighbor crosstalk error of 0.021. The team writes structured spin patterns and builds a biskyrmion texture in a single-layer crystal. Bilayer crystals get layer-selective addressing. A dual-quadrature Ramsey trick reads two spin components in one run. The work opens local programming of large rotating ion crystals.
arxiv-2606-01040:
Lawton links lattices to spaces of planes in this 2026 maths paper. A lattice is a grid like set of points that repeats through space. Its subsets can be projected, and those shadows carry traits of the source set. He asks how the traits of a lattice subset relate to those of a linked subset of a Grassmannian. The Grassmannian is the space whose points are whole planes or subspaces.

Three heavy tools do the work. The Baire category theorem sorts sets by how topologically fat they are. The Riemannian manifold structure of Grassmannians gives the target space a smooth geometry. The Khintchine Groshev theorem, from Diophantine analysis, governs how well points can be approximated by rationals. Together, they let subset traits pass between the two worlds. The paper is short and dense, aimed at specialists in geometry and number theory. It turns grid questions into plane questions and back.
arxiv-2606-01240:
Puspitasari and co-authors make retrieval for language models more exact. Such systems fetch text chunks to aid each reply. Weak systems miss user intent in their search. They also split proof into broken chunks. InSemRAG checks and repeats its search in a loop. An intent-aware retriever weights search paths by query type. A chunk repair step fixes split proof and keeps sense intact.

Small language models help cut the cost of the loop. Tests span many benchmark sets. The method gains 2.65 F1 points on HotPotQA. It gains 1.5 points on FEVER as well. It also runs 4.32 times faster than Multi-Hop RAG. Gains are largest on multi-hop and proof-heavy tasks.
arxiv-2606-01340: Jakaite and Schetinin ask when averaged tree models deserve commitment. Bayesian model averaging weights many decision trees. Those weights carry information about what is not known. The question is when they justify acting on the average. The pair answer in closed form for Bayesian decision trees. Their trees use Dirichlet-Multinomial leaf models. A Catalan-exponential prior controls tree size. They build a complete non-asymptotic theory of commitment thresholds. Sample complexity and decision-theoretic guarantees sit at its core. The work serves readers who use Bayesian trees under uncertainty.
arxiv-2606-01540:
Heidari and Rabusseau compute Shapley values with tensor network surrogates. Shapley values credit inputs in black-box model outputs. Their computation spans an exponentially large subset space. Graph-structured inputs offer structure to exploit here. TN-SHAP-G learns a compact surrogate for the predictor. The surrogate is multilinear and aligned to the input graph. A tensor network whose topology mirrors the graph holds it. A fixed masking scheme defines the target behavior.

Few oracle queries train the surrogate. Shapley indices then recover deterministically from the multilinear form. No extra model queries or Monte Carlo variance arise. Tests on molecular benchmarks match exact values on small graphs. The method scales to larger graphs where sampling fails.
arxiv-2606-01740:
Krishna offers a short math note from 2026. It deals with a known bound for the Clarkson angle. That angle is formed by two nonzero vectors. The vectors sit in a normed linear space. Massera and Schaffer first found an upper bound in 1958. Maligranda later made that bound stronger. Pecaric and Rajic then spread it to many vectors.

Krishna derives a non-Archimedean form of that same bound. The new form keeps the chain of names in its title. It links the old line of work to a new setting. Readers get a brief, focused extension of a classic result. The note suits readers who study normed spaces and bounds.
arxiv-2606-02140:
Li and co-authors build a sky image simulator for time-domain surveys. Modern surveys produce massive volumes of image data. Automated pipelines and learning models need validation data. Simulated sets must be robust and high in fidelity. Their AstroSkyFlow simulator generates images on demand.

Time-dependent flux variations are built into the images. The full observing stack is modeled in the simulator. Celestial sources, atmospheric effects, and sensor response are included. A simulated schedule yields multi-epoch time-series images. Realistic noise and variability come with those images. Noise traits match real data better than SkyMaker does. Point spread function properties also match more closely. Injected signals like exoplanet transits are recovered well. Asteroid motion signals are recovered too.
arxiv-2606-02240:
Dingeto and Leeney benchmark attacks on tool using agents and test defenses. Indirect prompt injection is a concrete production threat. Agents read from integrations the user does not control. Gmail, Salesforce, and Jira are named examples. Response content can carry hidden attack payloads. Existing benchmarks under-measure that threat badly.

Most cover few integrations with one replayed payload. Open-source guards train on chat-style data, not tool responses. Their AgentRedBench is a dynamic redteaming benchmark. It holds 215 subtle authorization scenarios. They span 24 enterprise integrations and five attack types. An eight-model panel from three labs is tested. No-guard attack success ranges from 32 to 81 percent. Integration-aware defense is the counterpart studied.
arxiv-2606-02540:
Ning and co-authors build a benchmark for attacks that hide inside agent skills. Agents treat skills as trusted instructions. Third-party skills thus form an attack surface. Past work tests poisoned skills in a single run. Harm lists there are ad hoc. SkillHarm widens the lens to the full skill lifecycle.

Two attack scenarios are defined. Fixed-Payload Poisoning compromises any session that invokes the skill. Self-Mutating Poisoning alters stored skill content in a quiet first run. Harm then lands on a later reuse. Twelve risk types map to workflow parts: data pipelines, system environments, and agent autonomy. An automated pipeline, AutoSkillHarm, builds the attacks. The benchmark holds 879 samples across 71 skills. Attack success reaches 86.3 percent in the fixed case and 69.3 percent in the mutating case. Many failures are really non-engagement with the poisoned file. Current defenses do not reliably stop the threat.
arxiv-2606-02640:
Gong and co-authors defend language models against jailbreaks that learn from a judge. Multi-turn attacks refine prompts step by step. A helper judge model scores each reply. Existing defenses block content at single turns or at the end. The refinement loop itself stays intact. Their defense, D-Judge, rewrites the victim model's replies before the judge sees them.

The rewrites preserve meaning. They misalign the judge's feedback signal. Attackers then optimize against a distorted sense of progress. A dataset of paired replies supports the training. Pairs share meaning but draw different harmfulness scores. Supervised fine-tuning and direct preference optimization follow. On HarmBench, strong multi-turn jailbreaks lose much of their success. Benign benchmark performance is preserved. The defense turns the attacker's own feedback channel into a trap.
arxiv-2606-02840:
Nunley studies how pairs of evolved neural agents use calls to avoid a predator. The agents are continuous-time recurrent neural networks. Each pair must reach safe cover to survive. Each agent can also hear its own call, as animals do in nature.

Across 112 agents with perfect fitness, drawn from over 2,000 runs, three main strategies appeared. Some agents called only once they were safe. Some called when a threat was near, with no need to hear themselves. A third group depended on hearing their own call to keep fleeing. Removing self-hearing hurt that third group far more than the safe callers. Nunley argues that a call can serve the caller itself. It can help sustain action, not just send news to others.
arxiv-2606-03040:
Jiang proposes RelGT-AC, a model for autocomplete tasks in relational databases. Such databases underpin enterprise, scientific, and healthcare systems. Their multi-table, temporal structure makes prediction hard. Relational deep learning turns databases into heterogeneous graphs for graph neural networks. RelBench v2 recently added autocomplete tasks, where the goal is to predict a column value from context.

RelGT-AC extends the RelGT architecture with three changes. A column masking strategy hides the target column during encoding, preventing trivial solutions. A unified task head handles binary, multiclass, and regression autocomplete in one model. A TF-IDF text encoder detects and encodes free-text columns, recovering lexical signal that categorical encoders discard. Across seven tasks on three RelBench v2 datasets, RelGT-AC beat the GraphSAGE baseline on all three regression tasks. It gained up to ten AUROC points on text-heavy eligibility tasks. The work targets intelligent form-filling assistants.
arxiv-2606-03240:
Chen and a large team add geometric skill to vision-language-action models for robot control. Such models ground language in scenes well, but real manipulation needs spatial alignment, not just semantics. Their design, GeoAlign, uses state-guided spatial alignment to close that gap. It is built for policy learning in robots.

Offline RGB-D data from robot domains post-trains an RGB geometry branch. The depth head is then dropped, so training and rollout use only RGB, language, and body state. Queries made from the state attend to the geometry grid and yield eight compact geometry tokens for action choice. Scores reached 99 percent on the LIBERO benchmark. Two sim suites gave about 85 and 79 percent. Ablations back the mix of geometry post-training and state-guided querying. The work shows that geometry can be taught once and then used cheaply at run time.
arxiv-2606-03440:
Dvorak and co-authors test a dark energy idea with beams of neutrons. The idea rests on a scalar field called the symmetron. Such a field is a leading candidate for quintessence dark energy. If it couples to matter, it should shift the phase of neutron matter waves. The team looks for that shift with care.

Phase shifts were measured for neutrons moving through vacuum and through low-pressure argon gas. The setup grew out of a technique built to measure neutron scattering lengths. No extra phase shift from a scalar field coupling showed up. That null result still carries weight. It sets strict limits on how strongly a symmetron field can couple to matter. The bounds narrow the space of dark energy models that remain viable. Readers get a clean lab test of a cosmic idea, done with tabletop-scale tools.
arxiv-2606-03640:
Menzies, Srinivasan, and Ganguly argue that AI tools for software data can be small and readable. Press claims say developers need not read code anymore. The authors disagree for tabular software-engineering optimization tasks. In those tasks, outcome values are costly to obtain. Their evidence is EZR.py, a toolkit of about 400 lines with no heavy dependencies.

EZR covers Naive Bayes, k-means, trees, simulated annealing, local search, and active learning. A complementary-Bayes text filter joins the set. The toolkit came from repeated reading and refactoring of larger tools. Many algorithms collapse to a few core lines once stripped down. A state-of-the-art active learner fits in roughly 80 lines. On over 120 benchmark tasks, the tiny tools match or beat SHAP, LIME, and SMAC3. They run hundreds of times faster than SMAC3 and use far fewer labels. The lesson is that reading code still generates insight.
arxiv-2606-03740:
Murphy and co-authors present the JWST transmission spectrum of the young planet V1298 Tau c. Mature super-Earths and sub-Neptunes often show featureless spectra. Their inflated young progenitors offer a clearer window on primordial makeup. V1298 Tau c is a 23 million-year-old super-Earth progenitor around a young solar analog. The KRONOS program targets the origins of sub-Neptune systems.

Water is detected in the planet's atmosphere. No other molecules show in these data alone. Results agree with and without informed priors on stellar surface patterns. The inferred metallicity is about 15 times the solar value, with wide error bars. That value matches other young planets, including the outer companion V1298 Tau b. It sits below the metallicities of mature planets of like mass and temperature. The gap hints that the mass-metallicity relation evolves with age. More young targets can test that trend.
arxiv-2606-03840:
Tang, Dao, and Cung study a system of damped sigma-evolution equations in the critical case. The system is non-symmetric, and its two equations carry different damping types. Both power exponents of the nonlinear terms sit on the critical curve. Moduli of continuity in those terms become the deciding factor. The goal is sharp conditions that split two fates.

Under the right moduli, Sobolev solutions exist for all time. Under others, solutions blow up in finite time. The blow-up analysis also settles an open problem from the literature. That problem concerned the symmetric version of the model. The result sharpens the border between global existence and collapse for this class. PDE analysts get exact thresholds where earlier work had gaps.
arxiv-2606-04140:
Veronika Vašíčková, Leonel Morejón, and Karl-Heinz Kampert show in 2026 that the Galaxy's magnetic field makes ultra-high-energy cosmic rays arrive late, and that this delay reshapes what telescopes see. These particles carry the highest energies known, and their origin remains unsettled.

Simulating propagation through the Milky Way, the team found delays of hundreds of thousands of years relative to light, depending on particle rigidity. In a bursting-source scenario, those delays carve a cutoff in the observed energy spectrum right where real data show a break. Composition shifts toward heavier nuclei, arrival directions drift from the source, and a dipole pattern can grow over about a hundred thousand years. The cutoff may need no limit on source power.
arxiv-2606-04340:
Yuhan Zhang and Edward Gibson explain in 2026 why some flawed sentences with negative polarity words strike readers as fine. Words like ever need a negative licensor nearby. In the flawed sentences, no licensor is present, yet readers accept them.

Their account builds on a theory where people encode sentences loosely. Readers then rebuild the most likely version in memory. Here, they may swap the determiners of the main and embedded subjects. That swap creates a licensed version by accident. The prediction follows: more similar determiner pairs should trigger stronger illusions. Judgment tests with six novel pairs confirmed it. One new pairing produced a much stronger illusion than the classic case, even with no time pressure.
arxiv-2606-04440:
Mikhin and Xiourouppa supply the detailed mathematics behind a method for approximating the bell curve with a sum of smaller bell curves, in a 2026 arXiv paper. The splitting algorithm represents the standard one-dimensional Gaussian distribution as a mixture of evenly spaced Gaussian components that all share the same width. Component weights are chosen to minimize the squared mismatch between the mixture and the original curve. The paper serves as extended appendices to an earlier main paper, and its material comes from a doctoral thesis.

The authors analyze two limiting regimes: the step between component centers shrinking toward zero, and the number of components growing large. In each they derive asymptotic formulas for the error and the optimal weights, for both odd and even component counts, showing how accuracy scales as users refine the mixture.
arxiv-2606-04640:
Bessonov and Nicolau extend a classical result about orthogonal polynomials on the unit circle from a local statement to a global one, in a 2026 arXiv mathematics paper. For a measure of Szegő class, the reflected orthogonal polynomials have known asymptotics. The authors prove uniform Cesàro asymptotics. The averaged squared magnitudes converge to one after scaling by the Szegő function. This holds for almost all approach angles.

This extends the 1991 result from the local scale near the unit circle to the global scale across the domain. They also study the asymptotic behavior of the polynomials' arguments. This extends a classical theorem of Grenander and Szegő with a new technique. As an application, they derive global asymptotic results for polynomial reproducing kernels. These hold under various assumptions on the orthogonality measure. Such global control matters wherever orthogonal polynomials on the circle are used to model spectra and filters.
arxiv-2606-04740:
Kar Chowdhury, Dai, Chang, and Chan compute how often stars were torn apart by black holes across cosmic time, in a 2026 arXiv astronomy paper. A tidal disruption event occurs when a star wanders too close to a black hole and is shredded, producing a bright flare. Such events are well studied nearby, but their prevalence at high redshift is unexplored. Using the FIRE-2 cosmological zoom-in simulations, the authors compute per-galaxy disruption rates from redshift 10 to 1, covering intermediate-mass to supermassive black holes.

The average rate rises from the early universe, peaks near redshift 2.5 at about four ten-thousandths per year per galaxy, and declines to about one hundred-thousandth by redshift 1. Satellite galaxies show comparably high rates, with their share growing at high redshift, making them promising probes of intermediate-mass black holes and early galaxy assembly.
arxiv-2606-05340:
Chris Hall determines Hasse-Weil zeta functions modulo a prime in this 2026 arXiv paper. The zeta function of a variety over a finite field packages its counts over field extensions into one series, and it is a central object in arithmetic geometry.

The main theorem gives the covering variety's zeta function modulo r in terms of the base variety's zeta function and that of the branch locus, the set where the cover ramifies. The cover's zeta function is congruent to the base's raised to the r-th power times the branch locus's raised to the one-minus-r power. The author gives a naive proof and a cohomological one, the latter resting on a formula for reducing zeta functions modulo a prime. Applications follow for curves, to the numerators of hyperelliptic and superelliptic curves. They are motivated by the question of when a numerator can be a trinomial.
arxiv-2606-05740:
Singhal and Soni blame clashing gradients, not just skewed counts, for failures on rare classes in a 2026 arXiv paper. Under heavy imbalance, majority classes dominate training. The team shows their gradients actively suppress minority learning inside shared layers. A diagnostic matrix measures the clash by comparing class-wise gradient directions layer by layer. The picture guides a small architectural fix for multi-branch networks.

Their fix, class-specific branch attention, reweights channels separately inside each branch. Branches then decouple their features instead of fighting over shared ones. On a damage-sorting task with severe imbalance, the rare class score doubled, from about a quarter to about a half. Overall accuracy held steady at the same time. A long-tailed version of CIFAR-10 confirmed the pattern, with macro scores climbing clearly. Optimization dynamics, the authors argue, deserve a seat beside data fixes for imbalance.
arxiv-2606-05840:
Pillitteri and Bemporad pre-pay the cost of nonlinear predictive control in a 2026 arXiv paper. Such controllers solve a hard constrained program at every time step. That cost bars them from weak hardware and fast sampling. The authors show the best control move can be mimicked by a state-dependent quadratic program. A neural network learns only the correction to an analytic starting guess.

The quadratic step runs inside a differentiable solver layer, so the first applied action always respects the constraints. Training blends imitation of a full solver with penalties on optimality conditions. A three-link robot arm tracking targets in the plane validated the design. Speed rose by orders of magnitude over the full solver. Tracking quality stayed comparable at the same time. The recipe targets the broad family of input-affine systems. Offline learning, the authors argue, can buy real-time control.
arxiv-2606-06140:
Weilin Lin and colleagues introduce RedEdit in this 2026 arXiv paper on the safety of image moderation systems. Safety classifiers scan uploaded pictures and flag unsafe content, but ordinary users can edit photos in ways that slip past them. Red-teaming means attacking a system deliberately to expose such weaknesses first. RedEdit acts as an automated attacker that only edits, using normal photo tools rather than generated imagery.

A vision-language model proposes targeted edits. A Monte Carlo tree search planner, which explores branching choices and backtracks from dead ends, picks the best sequence. On the UnsafeBench benchmark, fewer than two edits on average let just over seventy-six percent of unsafe images evade detectors. The edited images still kept about ninety-three percent of their harmful meaning for human viewers. The authors offer the tool as a diagnostic for moderation systems and urge more attention to this threat.
arxiv-2606-06540:
Tu Vo and Chan Y Park sharpen out of focus photos with a network that knows its own mistakes in this 2026 arXiv paper. Defocus blur varies across an image because lens optics spread each point into a disc whose size depends on depth. Classic pipelines first estimate the blur kernel at every pixel, then deconvolve, but kernel errors compound into artifacts. Their ErA network instead unrolls an optimization algorithm into layers, an approach called deep unrolling, and builds error awareness into the iterations.

ErA jointly learns a compact basis of blur kernels and per pixel mixing weights. An explicit error term in its updates corrects kernel misestimates as it goes, alternating with learned denoisers. It reached state of the art scores on the DPDD, RealDOF, and RTF benchmarks. It also generalized strongly to the CUHK dataset without ground truth, and did so with fewer training samples than rivals.
arxiv-2606-06640:
Abhisha Garg and co-authors map phone users from radio fingerprints in this 2026 arXiv paper on wireless localization. Channel charting learns a geographic map directly from channel state information, the detailed radio measurements base stations collect, without GPS. Their SEMIKHORN framework targets millimeter wave networks with many antennas and several distributed base stations. Each station builds a local dissimilarity matrix between users' channels. The matrices fuse into one global picture, which manifold learning embeds onto a two dimensional map.

The key ingredient is a t SNE variant whose similarity scores are balanced globally through optimal transport. Every user's neighborhood is then represented consistently, not normalized in isolation. In simulated outdoor tests the system localized users with a mean error of six point eight six percent. It needed less than fifteen percent labeled channel samples. Its embeddings also beat standard channel charting on continuity and trustworthiness.
arxiv-2606-06740:
Speech synthesis systems increasingly work with discrete units, short symbols obtained by clustering the patterns inside recorded speech. Naman Kothari and co-authors examine unit vocoders, the parts that turn those symbols back into sound, in this 2026 arXiv paper.
