Their tests span four Indian languages and many speakers at once, a setting where voices and languages easily blur together.

Using a BigVGAN based vocoder, the team varied the number of symbol clusters and how the model was told who was speaking. Cluster size mainly governed how intelligible the speech stayed, because larger sets separate similar sounds more cleanly. Telling the model the speaker's identity outright proved essential; without that signal, voices collapsed into one another. Extra language labels helped most at small cluster sizes, where symbols remained ambiguous and similar sounds from different languages shared the same code.
arxiv-2606-06840:
Some labeling jobs offer millions of possible tags, yet only a few fit each item. Saha Roy, Wallace, and Aslam ask how reasoning models cope in this 2026 arXiv paper. These models do well with no task specific training. The authors look inside that success for a mechanism.

They find a two phase pattern. First the model shortlists a broad pool of plausible labels. Then it reasons closely over that smaller set. The two phases can be separated, and each helps the other. The team turns that insight into a teaching method. Their mechanistic distillation trains a student on the teacher's two phase path. It beat standard distillation methods across several data sets. The authors also release their code and trained models. The lesson reaches beyond tagging: reasoning may often be search first, judgment second.
arxiv-2606-07340:
Jian, Li, Sun, and Yu map when a damped form of accelerated optimization stays stable, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Gradient methods with momentum converge faster but tend to overshoot and oscillate on nonconvex problems, where the landscape has many local dips. Adding a derivative damping term, borrowed from PID controllers, calms the oscillation. The catch is that step size, momentum, and damping interact, so safe parameter ranges had resisted characterization.

The authors model the algorithm as a third-order feedback system and apply robust control theory through the Kalman-Yakubovich-Popov lemma, a stability tool. That yields explicit 3D stability regions for the three parameters, with guaranteed linear convergence under a regularity condition. They also prove a hard ceiling on the damping gain set by the landscape's curvature. Beyond that ceiling, over-damping shrinks the step-size range, explaining the stagnation users observe. Tests matched the predicted edges.
arxiv-2606-07640:
Arroyo Galende and co-authors test whether synthetic images can be faithful, private, and useful at once when data is scarce, in this 2026 arXiv study. Their evaluation framework scores 3 dimensions: fidelity to real images, privacy protection, and utility for training classifiers. Three generator families, a variational autoencoder, an adversarial network, and a diffusion model, were compared across 3 datasets spanning handwritten digits and medical scans. Differential privacy noise was added at varying strengths.

The models diverged under privacy pressure. The adversarial and diffusion generators proved more robust, maintaining higher fidelity and utility across noise levels, while the autoencoder degraded as constraints tightened. The authors frame the result as a no-free-lunch finding: privacy is never free, but its price depends on architecture choice. They argue multidimensional evaluation is essential because single-score comparisons hide these trade-offs, which matter most in medical imaging where data is scarce and sensitive.
arxiv-2606-07840:
Kone, Neilan, and Poling construct a finite element method for fluid flow on curved surfaces with no compromises on incompressibility, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The surface Stokes problem describes slow viscous flow confined to a surface, as in a thin film. A good scheme must keep the flow exactly tangent to the surface and exactly divergence-free, neither piling up nor thinning out.

Their Scott-Vogelius scheme enforces both constraints exactly, not approximately, while using the same number of unknowns as a flat two-dimensional discretisation. Earlier surface versions relied on complicated macro-element constructions. This one defines its spaces directly on a refined surface triangulation of curved Clough-Tocher elements, making implementation simpler and more practical. The authors prove inf-sup stability, the condition keeping pressure and velocity properly coupled, and derive optimal-order convergence, so accuracy improves at the best rate as the mesh refines.
arxiv-2606-08040:
Michael Reilly reproves and extends a classical criterion for when a function's values spread evenly around the circle, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A sequence is uniformly distributed modulo one if its fractional parts visit every interval with the right frequency. Boshernitzan's theorem gives a sharp test for functions from a Hardy field, a family of functions closed under differentiation: roughly, the function must outrun every rational polynomial by a logarithmic margin.

Reilly's new proof uses summability theory, the mathematics of assigning limits to averaged sequences. The extension gives necessary and sufficient conditions for uniform distribution under a broad class of weighted averages, not just the plain average. A concrete application concerns x to the three-halves power. For any target interval and all large N, some whole number in the final quarter-length window below N lands its fractional part inside the interval.
arxiv-2606-08340:
Kale-ab Abebe Tessera and colleagues benchmark how well language model agents cooperate in open-ended worlds, in this 2026 arXiv paper. As models are deployed as autonomous agents, they must coordinate with others over long horizons in tasks without a fixed script. Existing evaluations rarely test these demands together. The authors introduce a benchmark built on game-like survival dynamics, with procedurally generated coordination tasks whose difficulty can be dialed up or down.

The benchmark world includes exploration, crafting, trading, and combat. It also includes soft specialization, where agents settle into complementary roles, and communication between teammates. The team evaluated thirteen modern language models with no task-specific training, fielding them in homogeneous teams. The headline finding is sobering: current agents remain far from solving the benchmark, struggling to sustain coordination over long horizons.
arxiv-2606-08440:
Dongli Wu and colleagues help robots grasp objects they can only partially see, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Robotic grasping is fundamental to manipulation, yet it stays challenging under partial observation, when sensors catch only part of an object. Reliable grasping depends on both local contact cues and object-level three-dimensional structure. Earlier geometry-aware methods valued reconstruction but treated the reconstructed geometry as a throwaway intermediate prediction rather than a reusable prior. GraspFoM instead leverages three-dimensional foundation model priors to build a shared object representation.

On top of that shared representation, an anchor-initialized diffusion process reasons about grasp poses. It predicts continuous, multimodal options, meaning several distinct good grasps. A reconstruction-aware scorer judges candidate grasps, and a residual latent updater lets reconstruction and grasping improve each other. The framework targets manipulation systems that must act on incomplete views of unfamiliar objects.
arxiv-2606-08540:
Yang Fu, Jin, Kumar, and Procaccia test a new theory of how amorphous solids fail, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Shear banding is a widespread instability in strained solids. Under strain, deformation localizes along a line or a plane, and the material fails along that band. A proper theory is key to understanding mechanical failure in glasses. A recent nonlinear theory extends classical elasticity by treating plastic deformations as topological charges.

In that theory, a Hessian operator has a lowest eigenvalue that vanishes at the onset of instability. The corresponding soft mode describes the displacement field across the band. This letter tests the theory numerically, establishing the role of topological screening in the process.
arxiv-2606-08840:
Arefin grades nine open code-generating language models far more thoroughly than a single pass rate allows, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The models attempted 2,707 free LeetCode problems in twelve programming languages, producing 325,343 graded jobs. Every job kept the prompt, the code, the official execution result, and static-analysis signals. That archive lets Arefin split performance by language, difficulty, and problem family.

The best model, Yi-Coder-9B-Chat, reached only 23.64 percent mean correctness, against a human acceptance reference of 57.2 percent. Rankings shifted by slice: Qwen2.5-Coder-14B-Instruct led on hard problems and problem coverage, while Gemma-2-27B-IT had the best lint pass rate across languages. Most failures never reached the judging of logic. Compile errors accounted for 63.25 percent of non-accepted best submissions, so the code often failed to run at all. Static quality rankings diverged from correctness rankings, warning against one-number leaderboards.
arxiv-2606-09340:
Meher Chaitanya, Sebastian Dalleiger, and Luana Ruiz make a hypergraph clustering method keep its work local at every step in this 2026 arXiv paper. Hypergraphs model group interactions, where one connection can join many nodes at once. Local clustering asks for a tight-knit community around a small seed set without partitioning the whole network.

Their method, Thresholded Local Hyper-Flow Diffusion, grows an active region around the seeds and updates only that region and its immediate edge. Expansion happens through thresholded activation, admitting the most promising edge nodes first. The authors prove this restricted update exactly matches the unrestricted global one, and they bound the error when thresholding skips parts of the edge. In experiments, it often matched or beat the original diffusion while activating less volume. The largest gains appeared on noisy instances, where ordinary diffusion tends to absorb nodes outside the target cluster.
arxiv-2606-09440:
Elias Richter, Benedikt Maurer, and Claudia Draxl build a first-principles method for predicting X-ray scattering from laser-pumped materials in this 2026 arXiv paper. Resonant inelastic X-ray scattering, or RIXS, probes how electrons in a solid respond to X-rays. Time-resolved versions watch solids change after an optical pulse. Reading those signals needs theory that handles both the X-ray process and the disturbed electrons.

Their framework starts from the Kramers-Heisenberg formula for the scattering cross-section, evaluated with Bethe-Salpeter equation results that capture excitonic effects, the binding between excited electrons and the holes they leave. Non-equilibrium carrier distributions come from real-time time-dependent density-functional calculations, representing different delays after pumping. Applied to the carbon K-edge of graphite, the method reproduced the measured angular dependence in spectral regions linked to pi and sigma orbitals, matching experiment well.
arxiv-2606-09640:
Rishabh Dev Yadav and his co-authors fix robot motion models without breaking the physics inside them in this 2026 arXiv paper. Controllers rely on Euler-Lagrange models, the standard math of moving machines. Real robots drift from those models as loads shift, parts rub, and air drags. Most learning fixes lump all error into one added term, which can break traits like symmetry that control design trusts.

Their method splits the error by kind. One piece corrects the inertia term, with the linked Coriolis term derived to match. A second piece, a sparse latent model of past contact, soaks up the shifting disturbances. Only that second piece adapts online, by Bayesian linear regression, while the machine part stays sound. Trials on ground, air, and arm robots showed better prediction and path tracking. The gains held under coupled and time-varying loads, the cases where plain fixes tend to wobble.
arxiv-2606-09740:
Fan Zhang and his co-authors add a runtime safety net for robot arm models that fumble grasps in this 2026 arXiv paper. Vision-language-action models steer arms from words and images. They shine on scenes like their training runs, then crack under small shifts in light, view, or start pose. ProbeAct guards them live, with no retraining and no weight changes.

Three parts do the work. A small probe reads the model's own hidden states to place task objects in 3D space. A state machine, fed by gripper signals alone, spots grasp, carry, and placement faults as they happen. A barrier filter then nudges the arm away from spots where faults repeat, while it leaves sound moves alone. On the LIBERO-plus test set, the net lifted one model's success rate from sixty-nine point six percent to seventy-four point one percent.
arxiv-2606-09840:
Zhitong Guan and Soo Young Rieh picture how teams of people and AI agents might make sense of hard questions together in this 2026 arXiv paper. Sensemaking is the slow work of search, weighing, and reading that builds shared grasp. Generative AI now does parts of that work itself, like summaries and theme groups. In teams, the shift blurs who read what and who vouches for a claim.

The pair set out five design rules for shared sensemaking with agents. Displays should stack facts in layers that can shift as views change. Gaps in grasp should be flagged and bridged, not papered over. Users must spar with claims, and each claim needs a checkable trail and a named owner. Their sketch is a shared workspace with three agent roles: a partner, a space keeper, and an orchestrator. The space logs who gave what, and how each side's take evolved.
arxiv-2606-09940:
Manning-Coe and colleagues study how learned features inside a language model interact, in a 2026 arXiv paper on interpretability, the effort to explain a model's inner workings. Tools called sparse autoencoders and crosscoders split activations into separate features, assuming each acts independently. When features interact, that assumption breaks and reconstructions gain errors. The authors formalize the problem using compact proofs of model performance.

Their proof yields an explicit interaction term for the model's MLP layers, the feed-forward blocks between attention steps, which measures how strongly two features affect each other. Used as a training penalty, the term produced crosscoders that kept sixty percent of MLP performance with only one feature per datapoint, compared with ten percent for standard versions. Clustering features by the measure gave groups with clear shared meanings. The team also found that sleeper agents, models hiding secret behavior, show notably strong feature interactions.
arxiv-2606-10340:
Huang and his team build a general controller for humanoid robots that takes instructions in several forms at once, in a 2026 arXiv paper on robotics. Humanoid whole-body control has progressed, but current approaches are either few-skill policies needing heavy reward design or motion trackers that are hard to extend to new input types. Their design mirrors biology: a scalable brain that reasons with diverse conditioning inputs sits atop a reactive motion-tracking cerebellum. The system, OMG, uses a diffusion-based motion backbone conditioned on language, audio, and human reference motions.

Extensive tests show OMG as an omni-modal whole-body controller with state-of-the-art results in their trials, good model scaling pattern, and fast fitting to new data mixes and motion types. Extensible multi-modal conditioning is the key trait: new input types can be added without rebuilding the controller.
arxiv-2606-10840:
Jordan Eagle reports a gamma-ray discovery in the Large Magellanic Cloud in this 2026 arXiv paper. Fermi-LAT detects faint, point-like emission from 300 megaelectronvolts to 2 teraelectronvolts at the supernova remnant B0453-685. The question is whether the rays come from the remnant's shell or from the pulsar wind nebula, the cloud blown out by its spinning neutron star, at its core.

Broadband modeling rules out the shell. The favored picture is an evolved nebula about 14,000 years old, already struck by the returning reverse shock, with a possible pulsar part below 5 gigaelectronvolts. It is only the second such nebula found outside our galaxy in this band. Pinning down its synchrotron cut-off needs harder X-ray data.
arxiv-2606-11440:
Kabir, Xue, Zheng, and Lou make multi-agent orchestration infrastructure-aware in a 2026 arXiv paper. Existing methods, from ensembles to learned routers, select models and topologies from task features, ignoring the runtime infrastructure state. On shared GPU clusters under load, preferred models accumulate deep queues while capable alternatives sit idle, and delays compound downstream. Their framework, InfraMind, closes this gap.

A planner conditions topology and roles on real-time load and budget, favoring simpler graphs under congestion. An executor observes per-model queue depths, cache use, and latencies to pick models and reasoning depth. A budget-aware scheduler reorders queues so urgent requests go first. Trained end-to-end by reinforcement learning, InfraMind gains up to 7.6 percentage points of accuracy over the prior baseline at low load, with up to sevenfold lower latency. Under high load it sustains up to 99.9 percent SLO compliance, where every baseline drops below half.
arxiv-2606-11640:
Ruxue Shi and five colleagues improve few-shot learning on tables in this 2026 arXiv paper, presented at the KDD 2026 conference. Few-shot tabular learning means predicting from spreadsheet-like data when only a handful of labelled rows exist for a new task. Older methods need costly extra training, and feeding raw tables to language models raises privacy worries. Both camps also ignore how features relate in meaning.

Their system, TAROT, asks a language model to infer meaningful links between features from the task description and feature names, forming a semantic graph. Raw data itself never goes to the model. Because language models hallucinate, a refinement stage prunes invented or irrelevant links and adds missing useful ones. A graph neural network then passes messages along the refined graph to make predictions. Across eleven real-world datasets, TAROT consistently beats the strongest traditional and language-model-based rivals in few-shot settings.
arxiv-2606-11740:
Yan Shu, Chi Liu and Mengzhuo Chen study whether reasoning learned on flat medical images transfers to three-dimensional scans in this 2026 arXiv paper. Medical question answering increasingly asks models to explain their answers with visual evidence. Two-dimensional images are plentiful, while volumetric data, such as CT scans, are scarcer.

Their framework, UniReason-Med, uses one shared interface for both input types. A 3D volume is fed in as a series of slices. The model interleaves written reasoning with boxed regions of evidence in a common format. Training uses a new dataset of about 220,000 examples mixing reasoning with grounded evidence, fifty thousand of them from 3D. Experiments show joint training on both types substantially improves 3D reasoning over 3D-only training. The shared interface, they argue, transfers reasoning structure across dimensions.
arxiv-2606-11840:
Marco Mattuschka and five colleagues at German research institutes locate chemical release sources from a distance in this 2026 arXiv paper. Hyperspectral cameras can spot airborne contaminants invisible to the eye. Running two such systems at an angle enables tomographic reconstruction, rebuilding a three-dimensional plume from flat views, supporting early warning after hazardous releases.

Contaminant spread is modelled by an advection-diffusion equation, covering transport by wind plus gradual spreading. Finding the source from measurements is an inverse problem, and a severely ill-posed one: many sources could explain the same data. The team imposes sparsity, the assumption that few sources exist, as a constraint, solved with a high-performance optimisation algorithm. A level-set description of a threshold level lets the data enter the model without rebuilding the mesh each time. The goal is a tool that reconstructs release locations and predicts how the plume will evolve.
arxiv-2606-11940:
Alessio Lugnan and six colleagues let a photonic chip stretch fast sensor signals in time in this 2026 arXiv paper. Optical fibre sensors detect vibrations quickly, but digitising their output demands fast, costly electronics. Photonic processors are quick yet have short memory, so slow sensor dynamics slip through them.

The team's device is a network of microring resonators, tiny optical loops on a chip, driven into self-pulsing, a regime where the light output oscillates on its own. Coupled to a distributed acoustic sensing system, the network amplifies variations in the fibre's reflections in both amplitude and duration. Perturbations at two fibre locations, vibrating at one and two kilohertz, remain detectable. Because the optical signal is effectively stretched, the minimum sampling rate for digitisation drops by at least a factor of ten. That permits slower, cheaper detectors and converters, and cuts the memory and computing a fibre sensor needs to run.
arxiv-2606-12240:
Zong and co-authors split a liquid neural network into a team of specialists working at different speeds, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Liquid networks model time continuously, suiting irregular medical measurements where samples arrive unevenly. A single such network still struggles when fast changes and slow trends mix in one record. Their multi-rate mixture of experts runs several liquid experts, each tuned to a distinct time scale. A gating network decides, per input, how much each expert counts.

Two attention layers add focus: one suppresses noisy variables, the other highlights informative history. The test bed is clinical prediction, including sepsis forecasting, a high-stakes early-warning task. Against LSTM networks, one liquid network, and a standard mixture, it consistently improves AUROC and AUPRC, standard detection scores. It does so while keeping computing cost favorable.
arxiv-2606-12340:
Gao and co-authors build an art installation that lets visitors watch a machine mind forget, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Memory, they argue, scaffolds reality itself; when it fades, the world does not go black but dissolves into chaos. The team treats a feed-forward 3D reconstruction network as a cognitive proxy, a silicon brain. They inject controlled synaptic decay into the model, eroding its learned priors the way disease erodes the brain's.

Noise twists the semantic priors, standing in for long-term memory, and the image encoder, standing in for the sensory cortex. The reconstructed world then degrades in disorienting, poetic ways rather than simply failing. The authors frame the glitch philosophically: a flawless network is a sterile photocopier, while humanity emerges in the breakdown. Their motto twists Descartes: I glitch, therefore I am. The work proposes neuromorphic aesthetics as a lens on the fragility of intelligence.
arxiv-2606-13040:
Xia and colleagues present RoboProcessBench, a benchmark for process-aware understanding in vision-language robotic manipulation, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Vision-language models are used as critics, reward generators, and failure detectors in robot systems. Those roles require judging not only final task success but how an execution is temporally progressing, a capability evaluations do not test. The benchmark decomposes process understanding into static monitoring and dynamic reasoning.

These dimensions are instantiated as 12 question families covering phase, contact, motion, coordination, primitive-local progress, temporal order, outcome, and primitive-level transitions. The corpus, ProcessData, contains 58 thousand question-answer pairs across 260 manipulation tasks, built from execution traces, and is split into a post-training set and an evaluation set. Post-training Qwen2.5-VL-7B and InternVL-3-8B on the training split produces gains on local state, motion, progress, and primitive-aware cues, showing the benchmark doubles as a learnable supervision source.
arxiv-2606-13140:
Liu and colleagues propose MIDSim, a language-model-powered multi-agent system for simulating multi-channel information diffusion in social media, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Information diffusion shapes public opinion and collective behaviour, but current epidemic-based, cascade-based, and point-process models mostly route diffusion through social links. They overlook the algorithmic channels, such as recommender systems, through which users now discover content, and they simplify how users act.

In MIDSim, large language models play personalised user agents, and the diffusion process jointly models social and platform exposure streams, so content spreads both through follower networks and through platform suggestions. The authors construct 3 real-world diffusion data sets spanning Sina Weibo, RedNote, and Twitter, with diffusion records, user profiles, historical posts, and social ties. On real diffusion events, the framework simulates macro-level spread phenomena well and creates diverse comment content, beating baseline models.
arxiv-2606-13240:
Razafindralambo and colleagues introduce Jeffrey guidance in this 2026 arXiv paper, a way to steer diffusion models. Diffusion models generate images by removing noise from a random pattern. Users steer them at sampling time through guidance, signals that push output toward desired traits. For goals beyond simple labels, the target is usually left vague, defined only roughly. Jeffrey guidance instead applies Jeffrey's rule of conditioning, a way to update beliefs when new evidence fixes the odds of broad outcomes rather than single events.

The method shifts overall feature frequencies toward a target while disturbing the rest as little as possible. In one test, matching a target pattern of image embeddings, summary vectors capturing visual content, sharply lowered a quality score on two datasets. In a fairness test on face images, the method made two traits statistically independent. A model can thus be adjusted after training to remove an unwanted correlation.
arxiv-2606-13640:
Shikarpur, Arul, and Huang present a musical work that turns a static accompaniment into an active partner in this 2026 arXiv paper. In Hindustani music, melodic material is performed against a tonic sustained by the tanpura, a four-stringed drone instrument. The Moving Drone sets that fixed drone into motion. Four independent loopers, implemented in a real-time audio environment, act as virtual drones. They are populated cyclically in real time as the vocalist improvises, creating an evolving feedback loop between voice and machine accompaniment.

Across the performance the drone gains increasing agency, transitioning from reactive to more proactive roles. The work, premiered at Harvard University, negotiates who leads: the singer shapes the drones, and the drones increasingly shape the singer. The paper documents the system and its performance practice for a conference on new musical interfaces. It contributes to artistic research where accompaniment systems are collaborators rather than backing tracks.
arxiv-2606-13740:
Wang, Sun, and Ren make diffusion language models run well on smartphone processors in this 2026 arXiv paper. Diffusion language models generate text by denoising many tokens in parallel, attractive for latency-sensitive mobile use. Repeated denoising is heavy, though, and mobile neural processing units, while fast at matrix work, are awkward to exploit. Committing tokens shrinks each block's workload, revising tokens complicates cache reuse, and the address space visible to the accelerator forces remapping and transfers. Their framework is the first designed around these constraints.

Three techniques align block-wise work with the accelerator's character. Multi-block speculative decoding fills shrinking late-stage workloads with future-block tokens. A dual-path revision scheme keeps committed tokens revisable until they stabilise. The third manages the address space to cut transfer overheads. On-device models matter for privacy and offline use; this work shows diffusion models can be engineered for phones.
arxiv-2606-13840:
Hu and colleagues survey a shift in self-driving research: cars that think together instead of alone. Their 2026 arXiv paper reviews more than three hundred eighty publications on multi-agent embodied autonomous driving. The organizing idea is shared world models, common predictive pictures of traffic kept up to date by vehicles, roadside units, and other road users talking over vehicle-to-everything links.

Shared-state building is the most mature layer, with fusion methods aligning what different agents see. Planning together and negotiating actions remain far less developed. Language and vision models help as advisers for meaning and bargaining, but slow replies, invented facts, and missing safety proofs bar them from sole control. Most testing still happens in simulation and offline benchmarks, not open traffic. The authors set research priorities: verified shared-state upkeep, robust agreement on intent and plans, and safe joint action under delays and weak links.
arxiv-2606-14140:
Hao, Jiang, Yang, and Zhong scan entire spectra of solvable spin chains to find which Bethe states are least and most entangled. Bethe states, exact eigenstates of integrable chains, are labeled by rapidities solving the Bethe equations. Their entanglement entropy across a cut varies widely. Their 2026 arXiv paper covers the spin-half XXX chain, higher-spin generalizations, and the non-compact SL two R chain, scanning finite chains with periodic boundaries.

For the spin-half chain, the least entangled state in each magnon sector is always the ground state. For higher-spin chains this breaks: the minimum-entropy state can be the sector's highest-energy state. Maximally entangled states follow far more intricate patterns. Special roots, singular and strange solutions, leave characteristic marks; the non-compact chain shows features absent in compact chains. For off-shell states they add an algorithm extremizing entropy over rapidity distributions.
arxiv-2606-14540:
Cohen-Addad and co-authors give private algorithms for finding communities in networks in a 2026 arXiv paper. Community detection splits a graph into dense groups, and the stochastic block model is the standard testbed where groups are planted randomly. The twist here is differential privacy: the algorithm's output must not reveal whether any single edge exists.

Their algorithms are the first private methods to achieve exact recovery, perfectly reconstructing the planted communities, across a wide parameter range while running in near-linear time and space. Earlier private approaches needed far heavier resources. The key idea is a family of adaptive disjoint-star algorithms that explore the graph by querying node degrees on edge-disjoint subgraphs. That structure inherently yields strong privacy guarantees, possibly useful beyond block models. Tests showed exact recovery on graphs with a hundred times more nodes than prior work handled.
arxiv-2606-14640:
Di Gregorio and co-authors show that a few comparison queries can sharpen online learning in a 2026 arXiv paper. In online convex optimization, a learner picks a decision each round, then sees a convex loss, aiming to rival the best fixed decision in hindsight. Their probing model gives the learner a limited budget of pairwise probes: on a probed round it may compare two points and learn which has smaller loss.

The main result shows even a sublinear, noisy probe budget provably improves worst-case regret in the full-feedback setting, with matching lower bounds up to logarithmic factors. The guarantee degrades smoothly as probe noise approaches a coin flip. Applied to prediction with experts, the same techniques give rates tight in every parameter. The analysis quantifies probing's benefit as variance reduction inside a second-order analysis of the continuous exponential weights algorithm.
arxiv-2606-14740:
Sujay Belsare and co-authors build a testbed for judging explanations of multimodal models in a 2026 arXiv paper. Vision-language models increasingly explain their predictions. But evaluation lacks ground truth. It cannot tell genuine cross-modal reasoning, like spatial composition, from shallow shortcuts like word matching. It was unknown whether explanation methods expose real synergy. They might hallucinate reasoning for models acting as simple feature detectors.

Their framework, GridVQA-X, synthesizes a closed world. In it, explanations are mathematically guaranteed. Two paired models share one architecture. One learns robust spatial-relational reasoning. The other is structurally forced onto cross-modal shortcuts. A faithful explainer must report different reasoning pathways for the two. Widely used methods failed to distinguish them. That reveals a critical gap in how multimodal explainability is measured and trusted.
arxiv-2606-14840:
Hsiao, Chang, and Nabi simplify causal studies of chemical mixes in a 2026 arXiv paper. Health researchers often face many exposures at once. Pregnant people, for example, carry mixes of PFAS chemicals in their blood. The joint effect of a mix is a surface with many inputs. It is hard to estimate and hard to explain. The authors build a causal way to shrink that surface to a few combined measures.

The measures keep the information needed to pin down joint causal effects. Their two-stage method splits the fitting work into two simpler steps. Theory shows the true shrink direction can be recovered. Its size can be estimated as well. A score ranks how much each chemical adds to the mix. In mock-data tests the method beat both noncausal shrinking and raw-exposure approaches. Applied to an Atlanta mother-child cohort, it linked PFAS mixes to infant birth weight.
arxiv-2606-14940: A new research manuscript on arXiv in 2026, it reports fresh work. The title states what it covers: Elliptic Functions and Eisenstein Series. The context is science and technology (careful study of how the natural and built world works). The paper's pages hold new research, shared openly with the field.
arxiv-2606-15040:
Liu reformulates the many-electron relativistic QED Hamiltonian to make its construction clear in a 2026 study. Precise spectra work needs relativity, electron correlation, and quantum electrodynamics handled together. A bottom-up build avoids the no-pair approximation used in older routes. Its key step, a charge-conjugated contraction of fermion operators, is often misunderstood.

The paper re-derives the Hamiltonian by averaging versions quantized with electronic and positronic Dirac fields. Normal-ordering against the filled Dirac sea then yields that contraction in a natural way. The result lives on the full Fock space rather than a chosen active space. Liu argues the bottom-up route beats top-down reductions drawn from energy formulas. The clearer form should support precise work on molecular spectra. It also answers published misunderstandings of the original construction by Inoue and others.
arxiv-2606-15540:
Zhang and colleagues address pathological speech reconstruction in 2026: recovering the intended text from recordings distorted by neurodegenerative and neuromotor disorders. Such speech is rarely ruined evenly: some words survive clearly and act as audible anchors for rebuilding the corrupted spans between them. AP-GRPO trains speech language models with reinforcement learning shaped by two phonetic rewards.

One reward checks that reliable anchors from clear regions survive, and the other checks that recovered content between anchors is supported by the sounds in the damaged audio itself. Across four disease conditions, AP-GRPO improves faithful recovery, and on severe dysarthria it cuts the phonetic error rate enough to cross from unintelligible to clinically usable output. The balance adapts by condition: severe articulation problems demand stronger anchor enforcement, while milder impairments lean more on phonetic alignment. Rewards built on the patient's own acoustic evidence thus give a practical route to communication aids.
arxiv-2606-16040:
Buono formalizes a cipher built on mixed number bases in a 2026 note on cryptography. A one-time pad hides a message with a truly random key used only once, giving perfect secrecy when done correctly. Ordinary versions work in one fixed base, such as binary. Buono takes an idea from a short 2012 preprint and rebuilds it rigorously.

The Mixed-Radix One-Time Pad writes numbers using a sequence of different bases rather than one repeated base. Buono proves the scheme achieves Shannon perfect secrecy, meaning the ciphertext reveals nothing about the message without the key. The classical binary pad appears as the special case where every base equals two, and fixed-base versions recover pads over other alphabets. Secret bases cannot lower the key entropy needed for perfect secrecy, a negative result proved in the note. A key-rolling protocol closes the work, preserving secrecy while reusing the encoding.
arxiv-2606-16140: Small language models are cheap to run, but can they reason reliably? VibeThinker-3B is a 3-billion-parameter model built to explore "verifiable reasoning" — reasoning steps that can be checked, not just trusted — at small scale. The paper reports what the authors found at the frontier of making tiny models think carefully.
arxiv-2606-16240:
Sahoo and Shenk collide two opposing film-director personas inside a language model in 2026 and watch which one wins. Activation steering injects a direction into a model's residual stream to shift its behavior. Prior work steers with one direction at a time. The authors build persona vectors for Steven Spielberg, optimistic and redemptive, and Martin Scorsese, dark and morally ambiguous, from screenplay corpora.

The vectors come from mean-difference activation contrasts, then mix under a scalar interpolation parameter and steering strength. Five evaluation axes cover moral valence, coherence, surface style, dominance, and vector geometry. Spielberg's signature shows robust directional dominance, suppressing Scorsese's moral influence across almost the whole range. Both directors' moral tone localizes at the same layer, layer 28, in the geometry analysis. Mixing also amplifies moral content beyond either pure extreme in the reported generations. A smooth cosine arc describes the collision vector's path, with a single crossing point.
arxiv-2606-16340:
Kiernan and co-authors build a theory in 2026 for how the Moon's tides may have powered Earth's early magnetic field. Before the inner core began growing, the source of mechanical power for the geodynamo is uncertain. The early core may have been overlain by a basal magma ocean leaving two fluid layers separated by a density interface. In this model, the tidal potential acts on that density contrast directly, not through deformation of a solid boundary.

The dynamics differ fundamentally from earlier tidal core models. In the inviscid limit, the response passes from an equilibrium tide at low forcing frequency to an inertia-self-gravity wave as frequency rises. A resonance sits between the regimes, where forcing matches the natural frequency of the interfacial mode. The inviscid core flow is formally identical to the canonical elliptical vortex, tying the problem to elliptical instability theory.
arxiv-2606-16440:
Ukladchikov builds in 2026 a software prototype proving that a transformer can be trained entirely on one chip, optimizer included. Public accelerator designs split the work: inference chips cannot compute gradients, and training chips push the Adam update off-chip. NeuronFabric is a reference architecture meant to remove that split. The prototype is written in C#, with no external machine learning framework.

Forward pass, backpropagation, and the Adam update all run inside one process with local weights in a reduced-precision BF16W format. The test model has 334 thousand parameters, four layers, and a small 256-token vocabulary, trained on the Shakespeare corpus. It reaches an evaluation loss of 1.5426 within 80 thousand samples, close to the 1.5224 of a GPU FP32 oracle, and generates coherent character-level text. The design leaves 660 kilobytes of on-chip SRAM headroom on a mid-range FPGA. The next step is running the same loop on the FPGA.
arxiv-2606-16840:
Mallela and Leonelli map crash risk across cryptocurrency markets in a 2026 finance paper. Crypto assets fall together violently, which questions whether holding many coins truly diversifies risk. Standard correlation measures miss dependence in the extreme tails, understating exactly the joint crashes investors fear.

The authors model the thirteen largest cryptocurrencies with graphical models built for extremes, estimated over many overlapping windows from late 2021 into 2025. Crashes and rallies are modeled separately, and a Gaussian graph of ordinary co-movement provides the contrast. The crash-side graph is nearly complete and stable: in a crash, almost every pair of coins stays directly linked. The rally-side graph instead thins over time and re-forms sector-like clusters. Ordinary token categories dissolve into one block anchored by Bitcoin and Ethereum. Standard risk models, they estimate, understate market-wide crash odds by roughly eight times.
arxiv-2606-17140:
Bejan, Behrends, McGinley and Béri connect quantum error correction to the physics of quantum dots in a 2026 paper. Error correction runs on measurement: extract a syndrome, decode it, and the logical state left behind is structured-random. The authors name that Born-weighted distribution the projected logical ensemble.

For surface codes under uniform rotations, they characterize the ensemble's randomness. The bridge is an isomorphism: for one logical qubit, the ensemble matches the scattering matrices of mesoscopic quantum dots from a Majorana network model. Where those dots are chaotic, random matrix theory applies, and the ensemble approaches a universal limit, maximally random subject to symmetry and decoder constraints. The symmetries land in the Altland-Zirnbauer classes D and DIII, set by stabilizer and logical operator weights. Measurement-induced randomness in error correction turns out to obey the same universal statistics as electrons in chaotic cavities.
arxiv-2606-17240:
Liu and Tu present a 2026 arXiv paper on what happens to quantum spin links when quarks and gluons turn into hadrons, a step called hadronization. The standard Lund string model describes that step well but treats it as a classical, random process with no quantum phase information. The authors ask where the quantumness goes, using ideas borrowed from quantum information science to frame the question sharply.

In their picture, quark-antiquark pairs born from the vacuum inherit its quantum numbers and start out spin-entangled. Later string breaking creates environmental degrees of freedom that steadily erase that spin coherence through decoherence. The framework matches hyperon spin-correlation data from both RHIC and the LHC. That agreement ties the QCD vacuum, spin entanglement, and hadronization into one quantitative story about how classical behaviour emerges.
arxiv-2606-17340:
Shu and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper on teaching scope-based systems to build image features that respect anatomy geometry, so navigation help stays reliable. A single-camera scope gives weak depth cues, faint tissue texture, and bending tissue, all of which upset pose estimation and depth prediction. Vision foundation models promise strong features, yet their features often lack the geometric steadiness that stable matching for navigation demands in practice.

The proposed framework pairs a synthetic data pipeline, supplying exact geometric supervision, with a structured adaptation method that beats plain low-rank tuning. Adapters are placed by choice across the transformer layers, with layer-wise goals pushing geometric matching in middle features and semantic steadiness deeper. Tests on public and private data sets show better pose and depth results downstream. The features also transfer from synthetic to real bronchoscopy footage well.
arxiv-2606-17440:
Silva and Sellers present a 2026 arXiv paper on a recently introduced partition function from work by Dombos, counting the ways to split a number into restricted parts. The allowed parts are those divisible by four, or those falling one step either side of a multiple of six. Partition congruences, where counts vanish modulo small numbers along arithmetic progressions, are a classic theme going back to Ramanujan, and this note proves several for the new function using elementary tools.

Generating function manipulations and classical q-series results do the work, with no heavy machinery invoked in the proofs. One family shows the count is divisible by three along a doubly indexed progression of arguments. Other results give vanishing modulo powers of two along simple progressions of increasing length. The note adds the Dombos function to the growing catalogue of restricted partition functions with Ramanujan-like behaviour.
arxiv-2606-17640:
Díaz Millán presents a 2026 arXiv paper on solving variational inequalities in Hilbert spaces without ever projecting onto the feasible set, a step that is often the computational bottleneck. The feasible region is defined by a convex inequality whose defining function need not be smooth, and the operator is set-valued and monotone. Feasibility is enforced instead by subgradient cuts, with a correction step that leans on one known strictly feasible point whenever a trial point strays outside the region.

Separating half-spaces built at feasible points drive the iteration, and one extra half-space in the style of Haugazeau forces strong convergence to the projection of the starting point onto the solution set. Best-iterate residual bounds are proved alongside the convergence. Numerical tests span nonsmooth and large-scale problems, from sparse recovery to a capacity equilibrium and an optimal control case.
arxiv-2606-18240:
Bhatnagar and colleagues give a classical meaning to a purely quantum coding effect, and then decode better because of it, in a 2026 paper. Quantum error correction rests on stabilizer codes built from pairs of classical codes. These codes show degeneracy: many distinct errors deserve the same fix. The effect has no classical twin, and its meaning stayed unclear. The authors show it mirrors code shortening, a classical operation, except that here the shortening happens at the decoder.

That insight yields impulse decoding, a parallel scheme for quantum low-density parity-check codes. It beats the standard belief propagation decoder with ordered statistics post-processing, and several rivals, under both ideal and circuit-level noise, at much lower cost. A second method cleans up residual errors. Combined with the first, it improves circuit-level results further while needing fewer parallel decoders.
arxiv-2606-18340:
Baud and colleagues show that quantum noise from an environment can manufacture chaos in a system whose classical dynamics is perfectly orderly, in a 2026 physics paper. A large environment does two things to a small quantum system: it drains energy, which stabilizes, and it fluctuates, which might not. The testbed is the dissipative Dicke model, a large spin coupled to a lossy harmonic mode, studied in the semiclassical regime where spin is large but finite.

Starting from a classically regular phase space in the superradiant regime, the quantum fluctuations generate a genuine strange attractor, complete with fractal dimension and a positive Lyapunov exponent. The authors trace the mechanism to shear-induced chaos, a route recently formalized by mathematicians, in which stretching in one direction folds trajectories into complexity. The result reverses the usual expectation that coupling to a bath only tames quantum dynamics.
arxiv-2606-18440:
Graziani uses algebraic geometry to study polynomial neural networks in a 2026 mathematics paper. He looks not at a network's settings, but at all functions one fixed design can make. The closure of that set forms an algebraic variety. He asks how flaws in that shape link to flaws in the design.

Graziani sets out a broad scheme for algebraic networks, with realization maps, morphisms, and subnetworks. It also has symmetry groups and quotient parameter spaces. Identifiability and reducibility get geometric treatment. For fully linked networks, he defines a degeneracy locus: functions made with a rank-deficient layer, or a hidden neuron that stays inactive. Under stated layerwise regularity assumptions, full parameters give smooth points of the variety. That holds for networks with non-increasing widths and scalar output. So each singularity must lie in the degeneracy locus, tying geometry to structural failure.
arxiv-2606-18640:
Jeffries and colleagues at Stanford and partner centers introduce a standard benchmark for forecasting blood glucose in type 1 diabetes, in a 2026 health informatics paper. Forecasting algorithms help patients manage the condition and feed automated insulin delivery systems, yet the field has had no common evaluation standard. Many published models use glucose monitor data alone while ignoring insulin dosing and carbohydrate intake.

MetaboNet-Bench supplies an extensible open-source framework for comparing algorithms that combine glucose, insulin, and carbohydrate signals. The authors demonstrate it by benchmarking several recent forecasting models plus a custom multimodal time-series model spanning different architectures. Their headline finding is conditional. The benefit of adding data streams depends on how complex the model is, and tracking a fuller set of clinical metrics exposes real gaps for future research to fill.
arxiv-2606-18740:
Cho and Choi survey what is known about the bottom of the spectrum of the Hodge Laplacian on complete noncompact Kähler manifolds, in a 2026 review. The bottom of the spectrum, the smallest value the Laplacian attains, is a geometric invariant tied to how hyperbolic spaces behave. Negative curvature forces it positive, and that in turn gives hyperbolic-like global traits to the manifold.

The survey stresses Kähler hyperbolic manifolds and bounded symmetric domains. There, the authors' work with Lee gave a uniform lower bound for bounded symmetric domains, in terms of geometric invariants. It refines Gromov's basic estimate. It also covers upper bounds got under Ricci and bisectional curvature assumptions, in the tradition begun by Cheng. And it covers rigidity theorems for manifolds that attain the maximal bottom. Those often split as warped products, or turn out to be quotients of complex hyperbolic space. Open problems are raised.
arxiv-2606-18940:
Chikhaoui and the team ask where a city can put solar-powered servers, in a 2026 paper from a computing-within-limits workshop. Edge and fog computing are promoted as ways to cut latency and energy use. But the literature ignores urban constraints, impact on nature, and equity, for where such infrastructure may be deployed.

Their method relies on existing infrastructure and already-built surfaces. It combines legal rules, ongoing urban projects, citizen input, and science, into a place-based glossary of site typologies. Each is scored on energy, spatial, and quality criteria. Applied to the French city of Montpellier, the study found sixteen typologies. Only a subset could power servers from photovoltaic production in a real way. The authors argue a frugal digital service is a matter of fit among needs, infrastructure, and resources. Rooftops-to-streetlights range gives spatial reach and redundancy.
arxiv-2606-19140:
Miccinilli and colleagues present ChronoSurv in 2026, a graph framework for survival prediction in head and neck cancer. Accurate survival forecasts guide personal treatment plans, but clinical data are mixed, high-dimensional, and gathered over time. Deep survival models beat classical statistics, yet most fuse data statically or ignore time order. That limits their grasp of how care actually unfolds through diagnosis and treatment steps for each patient.

ChronoSurv models patient care as a directed graph that follows the clinical pathway. Fine, coarse, and global levels sit in one hierarchy, and message passing links data types and steps with unlike relations. The design also adapts when data are missing for a patient. On two public datasets, the method reaches state-of-the-art discrimination while keeping calibration sound. Ablation tests confirm each part helps.
arxiv-2606-19240:
Kwok and colleagues present an arm kinematic correction method in 2026 for robot teleoperation with a single depth camera. Markerless motion capture from one RGB-D camera is cheap and non-invasive, a good fit for teleoperation. Depth estimates degrade under self-occlusion, though, especially during upper-limb motion when one arm part hides another from the camera. Bad depths then distort the robot's mirrored movement.

The method enforces geometric constraints from constant arm lengths. It rebuilds occluded joint depths from wrist positions and predefined arm lengths with a deterministic formula based on the Pythagorean theorem. No complex probabilistic modeling or parameter tuning is needed. Tests against a Vicon reference system show reliable results for static and dynamic joint motions. Motion-mapping teleoperation works in both simulated and physical robot setups. The correction preserves anatomical consistency even under long, severe occlusion, and pairs well with weak temporal filters.
arxiv-2606-19340:
Kim and colleagues present ZeroDex in 2026, a zero-shot framework for long-horizon dexterous manipulation. Rather than training an end-to-end policy, the system grounds language instructions into executable three-dimensional task plans from calibrated multi-view images, using a vision-language model for grounding and keypoints. Multi-view fusion lifts those points into three-dimensional space for a robot hand.

The lifting combines triangulation of view-wise groundings with ray voting along a semantic camera ray. Lifted keypoints support pick-and-place and tool use. For tool use, the system retrieves a stored atomic action and aligns its six-dimensional tool trajectory to the scene. For grasping, it expands the keypoint into an affordance region and generates grasp-motion pairs. Real-world tests show better grounding and reliability than single-view and fine-tuned baselines. Closed-loop status checks and replanning enable zero-shot work on unseen objects.
arxiv-2606-19540:
Lorenzo Mauri speeds up high-dimensional factor models in 2026 with a method called EigenBayes. Factor models split a covariance matrix into a low-rank signal part plus a diagonal noise part. Choosing the latent dimension is hard when the model holds only roughly and signals run weak.

Bayesian overfitted models set a cap on the dimension and shrink extra factors away. They work well but cost heavy computation, often through Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling. EigenBayes instead estimates latent factors spectrally and calibrates key settings by empirical Bayes. The posterior then splits across outcomes in closed form, skipping sampling altogether. Extra latent components shrink to zero on their own. The method adapts to each outcome's signal-to-noise ratio and latent dimension. Strong asymptotic results, numerical tests, and a genomics case show it beating leading rivals.
arxiv-2606-19640:
Yunkai Xu and Saeed Abdullah test multilingual mental health dialogue datasets in 2026. Language models promise support for global mental health, yet good training data stay scarce. Synthetic clinical personas offer a shortcut, but validated personas rest on English settings.

Xu and Abdullah vary nationality and language settings to spawn dialogues in Mandarin, Bengali, and Hindi. Different language models then grade depression severity in each generated set. English results serve as the baseline for comparison. Adding language settings alone fails to keep the clinical picture consistent across tongues. Judge models also grade non-English severity poorly, with skill varying by model. The flaws expose limits of porting English-centric personas abroad unchanged. Data built with local culture in mind, the authors argue, is required for fair mental health care worldwide.
arxiv-2606-19940:
Pavan Kumar and six colleagues ask whether speech models hear geography as well as language across sixty Indic languages in 2026. Self-supervised encoders are usually fine-tuned with language labels alone, which can wash out district-level variation in accent and speech. The team fine-tunes Whisper and Wav2Vec2 models under two regimes: language only, and language joined with district, giving several hundred combined classes.

Joint supervision sharpens district separation inside each language cluster while language accuracy stays strong. Information measures show global language clusters with tidy district subclusters in the embedding space. Geography, in other words, survives as structure rather than noise. Speech technology for India's many regions could use such representations to serve local varieties instead of flattening them.
arxiv-2606-20240:
Fatima Kasenally, Ruoxi Guan, and Frank Windmeijer make two-sample IV estimation work under realistic messiness. Their 2026 paper addresses a common data problem: the outcome and the treatment are measured in different samples, while the instruments appear in both. The standard estimator is efficient only when errors are homoskedastic and the samples homogeneous. Real studies rarely offer either comfort, so estimates built on those assumptions can mislead.

The authors develop a robust two-step procedure that stays efficient under general heteroskedasticity and sample heterogeneity. It needs only six summary objects from the two samples' regressions, not the raw data. They add a two-sample Hansen overidentification test, and clarify when the first-stage F-statistic still flags weak instruments here, with an extension of the effective F-statistic. An application to education's effect on voting shows the methods at work.
arxiv-2606-20340:
Habitamu Walelign, Manas Ranjan Sahu, and John Nichol phase-lock an ensemble of nuclear spins in silicon using no external reference field. Their 2026 paper works with silicon-29 nuclei inside a silicon quantum dot. Nuclear spins keep coherence for very long times, making them attractive for quantum devices, but controlling them usually demands an outside phase reference such as a microwave field. The team instead uses the internal electronic spin-orbit coupling as the reference.

Driven together with the electrons, the nuclear spins align to a phase set by that coupling and the drive timing. This self-locking let the authors measure the ensemble's coherent precession and its inhomogeneous dephasing directly. Numerical simulations of the coupled system corroborate the measurements. The result opens new routes to controlling nuclear spin ensembles, candidate memories and sensors for quantum networks, with simpler hardware.
arxiv-2606-20640:
Ouided Braoui, Meriem Bouali, and Nadir Farhi pair deep reinforcement learning driving with language-model explanations for passengers. Their 2026 paper targets public trust: autonomous vehicles promise safer, more efficient mobility, but opaque decisions keep riders skeptical.

Agents trained in simulation with a Dueling Double Deep Q-Network follow distinct driving requests: fast, comfort, and stop. They show stable learning and safe compliance with the requested style. An LLM-based module then explains the agent's behavior to passengers in plain language. A car that can say why it slowed down may earn the trust a silent one cannot.
arxiv-2606-20840:
Evgeniy Martyushev builds an algebraic solver in a solo 2026 paper for a time-of-arrival problem with four senders and six receivers. Given pairwise distances, the task is to recover all positions. Such problems appear in acoustics and sensor nets. The solver combines Cayley-Menger determinants, which encode distances as volumes, with a new parametrization.

The method runs in three steps. A large matrix is built from system coefficients. Its split yields a smaller matrix pair. Eigen analysis then gives up to thirty-eight real candidate solutions, followed by checks. On clean synthetic data, accuracy improves hugely over prior methods. Runtime is also modestly faster. Tests on real acoustic data confirm value in a robust pipeline.
arxiv-2606-21340:
Raphael Bagat and four colleagues built a synthetic speech factory in 2026 for air traffic control, where recognition systems struggle with radio noise, non-native accents, and scarce recordings. Real controller speech is hard to collect, yet errors in this safety-critical domain carry weight. Their pipeline combines text-to-speech, voice conversion, and accent conversion in both directions, including a controllable tool that adds a foreign accent to native speech.

Fine-tuning the Whisper model on the ATCO2 corpus, synthetic data alone beat the out-of-the-box model, and mixing synthetic with real data beat real data alone. The gains show that simulated channel conditions and accents can stand in for recordings that cannot be gathered at scale. The approach offers a template for other specialized, data-poor speech domains.
arxiv-2606-21540:
Jin-Duk Park and Won-Yong Shin remove the memory wall in 2026 from graph filtering recommenders, a training-free alternative to graph neural networks for collaborative filtering. Graph filtering smooths signals over the user-item graph with matrix operations, and polynomial versions are accurate and flexible. Their flaw is storage: the full item similarity graph must be kept, which explodes on large catalogs.

Their method, Mem-GF, approximates polynomial filters through Krylov subspaces, the nested spaces built by repeated matrix-vector products, without ever storing the similarity graph. They derive the smallest subspace size that guarantees a lossless approximation. Experiments show up to 5.74 times lower memory use and 4.38 times faster runs than rivals, with better recommendation accuracy than leading filtering and graph network methods, scaling to tens of millions of interactions.
arxiv-2606-21740:
Rajesh Mangannavar, Zachary Coalson, Pranay Dugar, and Prasad Tadepalli teach a small model to conduct an orchestra of planning agents in 2026. Agentic planning systems translate natural-language goals into formal PDDL, then repair the draft with specialist agents inside a verifier-checked loop. The catch: the orchestrator choosing each repair step is usually a frontier LLM, billed at every step.

Their HALO system trains that orchestrator instead, on refinement trajectories an external verifier already certified as ending in valid plans, across 11 PDDL domains. A small QLoRA-tuned policy, plus three hardcoded rules for trivial choices, picks among 21 agents. It matches or beats a prompted GPT-5-mini on success and lands within three points of Gemini-3-Flash. It also cuts orchestration cost from 18 cents to under half a cent per task, with 40 to 50 percent fewer LLM calls.
arxiv-2606-21940:
Gayen and Alicea model, in 2026, how the nervous system of the worm C. elegans wires itself during development, using temporal graph neural networks. Their framework, DevoTG, treats development as a graph that changes over time rather than a single adult snapshot. It joins two views: a continuous-time graph of cell division events from lineage data, and a discrete-time graph of the synaptic connectome across eight reconstructed datasets.

On lineage prediction, the temporal model reached a test AUC of 0.839, beating an identical static network by twenty-six points — decisive evidence that temporal memory drives the gain. Applied to the connectome, DevoTG sorted connections across 225 neurons into stable, developmental, and variable classes. The hub command interneurons AVA, AVB, and AVE kept their central roles throughout larval stages, with their integration strengthening over time. Interactive visualizations accompany the open-source release.
arxiv-2606-22040:
Kumbhar and colleagues present, in 2026, a controller for lower-limb exoskeletons that help elderly users perform the sit-to-stand transition, a movement with heavy joint-loading demands. Tracking a reference motion is hard because human-exoskeleton dynamics vary over time and between users, defeating model-based controllers. Their design is model-free and adaptive instead.

An ultra-local model avoids explicit system identification, while a radial basis function network estimates the unknown dynamics online. On top, a Twin Delayed Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient reinforcement learning agent acts as a supervisory gain scheduler, adjusting controller gains across the phases of standing up. In co-simulation with OpenSim-derived reference trajectories, the controller achieved the lowest average tracking error across all joints, 0.078 degrees of root mean square error. That cut error by roughly half or more against each of the compared state-of-the-art controllers.
arxiv-2606-22340:
Kumar and colleagues propose, in 2026, a lattice-based forward-secure identity-based encryption scheme for Internet of Things deployments, designed to stay secure against quantum attackers. Identity-based encryption derives public keys from device identities, avoiding heavy certificate handling. Forward security ensures that compromising a current secret key does not expose past communications, a real risk for devices exposed to key-extraction attacks.

Existing forward-secure schemes rest on classical hardness assumptions that quantum computers break, while earlier lattice versions carry large keys and ciphertexts. The new scheme works in the ring setting under the ring learning-with-errors assumption. It uses trapdoor delegation over a binary tree with a minimal-cover mechanism, keeping public parameters compact and per-epoch key updates efficient. Public keys, secret keys, and ciphertexts all shrink compared with prior lattice constructions, suiting constrained devices.
arxiv-2606-22440:
Pyae Hein Htet and Kenta Ishimoto study how swimming organisms move in this 2026 paper. Their lens is geometric phase, a net displacement that arises from the shape changes of a cycle rather than from pushing against the medium. Linking that idea to real data is hard, because biological shape records are noisy, sparse, and only weakly periodic.

The pair build a theory-guided, data-driven Koopman autoencoder, a neural network shaped by the underlying mathematics. It recovers the limit cycle, the true repeating pattern, hidden inside imperfect cyclic data. From that cycle they extract shape gaits and the geometric phase for sperm and nematode data. They also introduce a geometric phase sensitivity function, which measures how the motion responds to small shape changes. Remarkably, it reveals mechanical information using only the gauge-theoretic structure, without assuming any mechanical laws in advance.
arxiv-2606-22540:
Xianghui Wang and six colleagues, including Yinjie Lei, improve how efficiently robot policies act in this 2026 paper. Vision-language-action models unify perception, language, and control for manipulation, but deployment is slowed by poor intrinsic policy efficiency. Two factors set the cost: how much of each predicted action chunk is executable, and how many steps a task takes.

Current policies degrade near the tail of their action chunks and waste steps on redundant motion. The team's framework, PolicyTrim, is a reinforcement learning post-training stage attacking both problems. A dynamic exploration strategy rewards completing longer executable chunks, pushing the trustworthy prediction horizon outward. A redundancy-aware reward favours finishing tasks in fewer steps while penalizing shortcuts that cannot be reproduced. Across three benchmarks and three vision-language-action models, chunk utilization tripled. Physical execution steps fell by just over half, cutting model calls per task.
arxiv-2606-23040:
Alexander Leitsch, Anela Lolić, and Stella Mahler develop a new kind of proof schema in a 2026 logic paper. Inductive proofs can be packaged as proof schemata, recursive definitions that stand for endless families of proofs. Schemata avoid explicit induction rules, which opens unusual uses. One is realizing Herbrand's theorem in the presence of induction, pulling concrete witness terms out of quantified proofs. The authors base their new schemata on point transition systems, a state-machine style formalism.

Leitsch and colleagues show that for skolemized schemata without quantified cuts, Herbrand systems can be computed directly. Those systems also represent schemata of Herbrand sequents. They compare schemata with cyclic proofs and transform a large class of cyclic proofs into schemata. As a strength test, their schemata prove the 2-Hydra statement, a classic example beyond one rival proof system.
arxiv-2606-23440:
P. Jean-Jacques Herings, Arkadi Predtetchinski, and Christian Seel count stable networks in a random utility model in a 2026 game theory paper. A network is pairwise stable when no pair both gain by linking, and nobody gains by cutting a link. Here each person's utility is a random variable, so stability becomes a probabilistic question. The authors compute how likely a given network is to be pairwise stable. They also solve, in closed form, how many pairwise stable networks to expect. That exact formula is hard to evaluate for large populations.

Herings and colleagues derive tractable bounds that pin down the growth of the expectation up to a constant factor. The expected count grows extremely fast with population size. After normalizing, the variance shrinks to zero. So the number of stable networks almost surely explodes, while their fraction of all networks vanishes.
arxiv-2606-23740:
Nikolich, Kiselev, Platonov, and Romanova ask whether popular offline training methods for reasoning actually change a model in different ways, in a 2026 paper on machine learning. Offline methods distill reasoning from a large teacher into a smaller student using recorded solutions, scored by different loss functions. They are usually compared only on final accuracy, leaving open whether the losses are truly distinct mechanisms.

Training six methods on identical mathematics rollouts from one base model, the team compares the weight changes geometrically. Three reward weighted methods produce nearly identical update directions and similar accuracy. One method diverges in direction despite sharing the data. Another adds a large component at right angles to the plain fine tuning direction while staying in the same loss basin. A preference method lands in a nearly separate subspace entirely, yet scores highest, with caveats about its smaller learning rate.
arxiv-2606-23840:
Pafla, Hoey, Larson, and Hancock argue that AI explainability has been framed the wrong way, in a 2026 argument paper on human computer interaction. Standard practice treats explanation as something extracted from a model's internals and displayed to users. The authors, drawing on Dourish and enactivist theories of cognition, contend that understanding is instead created in use, as people act on what a system lets them probe and change.

Looking inside large language models, they say, runs into ontological obstacles. Surrogate models import outside abstractions that users can mistake for the model's own reasons. Many products called explanations are therefore misnamed, which can deepen overreliance on wrong outputs. The authors reserve explainability for designs offering real affordances to probe and repair behavior.
arxiv-2606-23940:
de Aguiar and Oishi teach a video transformer to finish droplet impact simulations from just their opening moments, in a 2026 paper on computational fluid dynamics. When a droplet strikes a surface it may spread, bounce, or splash, behavior that matters for spray cooling and inkjet printing. Simulating the full event is costly, and viscoelastic fluids add extra parameters beyond the usual Reynolds and Weber numbers. The authors ask whether the first fifth of a simulation determines the rest.

Their model reads volume fraction fields, maps of where liquid sits, and predicts the remaining frames. The strategy cuts computing cost by roughly eighty to ninety percent. Predictions stay physically consistent across parameters and horizons, with spreading and bouncing regimes both captured. The same fields can be extracted from videos of real impacts, so the framework could later train partly on experiments.
arxiv-2606-24040:
Li proposes a way to update what a language model knows without retraining the whole system. The starting point is MeMo, a model design that stores knowledge in explicit correlation matrix memories, which are structured tables linking sequences and tokens. Writing from Berlin in 2026, Li asks how edits such as replacing or rolling back a fact can run directly on those stored memories instead.

Each high-level edit becomes an ordered transaction, a bundle of small memory operations that can also record how to undo itself. Two extra memory tables support this: one maps version changes to transaction records, and another stores reusable change contents plus the inverse steps. Inputs can be whole sequences or structured differences between versions. Li also sketches how to test update success, rollback, traceability, and whether an edit stays local instead of disturbing unrelated knowledge.
arxiv-2606-24340:
Nasser and colleagues schedule work on sensors that have no battery at all. Batteryless Internet-of-Things devices live off harvested energy, stored briefly and spent unpredictably. A task started at the wrong moment dies mid-execution. Standard schedulers lean on static thresholds, or on pre-measured, hardware-specific task profiles, both brittle when workloads are unknown. The team's 2026 study proposes two hardware-agnostic strategies, treating applications as black boxes.

One strategy is a model-free reinforcement learning agent that learns when to run tasks. The other, a rough prediction method, estimates energy needs on the fly. An accurate simulator, driven by real solar data and realistic radio profiles, compares them against an adaptive task-rate method and optimised static thresholds. No single winner emerges. Prediction delivers lightweight, near-oracle throughput, the learning agent a tunable balance between survival and execution, and the adaptive baseline excels at pacing.
arxiv-2606-24640:
P. D. Welch outlines a theory of higher type recursion for infinite time Turing machines. Infinite time machines run through transfinite steps and can settle questions about real numbers. Kleene's classic type two recursion let machines take functions as inputs and outputs. Welch builds the matching theory for the infinite time setting. The aim is a bridge between this computability theory and classical descriptive set theory.

The bridge is built by computing the complexity of the machine's halting problem. Welch shows it matches exactly a complete game quantifier set at the third level of the Borel style hierarchy. That mirrors what Kleene and Moschovakis achieved for ordinary type two recursion and open determinacy. He also identifies the least ordinal not reachable by this generalised recursion. Its characterisation uses infinite nestings inside Gödel's constructible hierarchy. No large cardinal axioms are needed; everything is provable within analysis.
arxiv-2606-24840:
Olga Azenhas continues her work on the quantum Littlewood Richardson bijection, a correspondence between tableaux central to algebraic combinatorics. A companion paper computed the inverse of its reduction map for certain patterns of symplectic columns. The present paper asks how far those partial computations reach. Some of the patterns treated earlier turn out to be cell pieces: building blocks from which the inverse on any symplectic column can be assembled.

For large symplectic columns, Azenhas shows how to combine those pieces with a decomposition of the reduction map given by Watanabe. The reduction splits into several maps, each with its own inverse. Among them are combinatorial R matrices and reduction maps of shorter symplectic columns. Composing the known inverses then yields the inverse in general. The result completes a computational toolkit for the quantum bijection.
arxiv-2606-24940:
Sajib Acharjee Dip and Liqing Zhang present Stable-Shift, a method that predicts how gene expression responds to perturbations of genes never tried in training. Extrapolation to unseen genes is the hard part. Stable-Shift first pools single cell measurements into perturbation level expression shifts. It then fits a low rank basis of responses using only training perturbations. An unseen gene's coordinates in that basis are predicted from biological context, such as interaction networks and Gene Ontology annotations.

Graph convolution integrates the context inputs in the evaluated version. On the supplied K562 Perturb-seq benchmark, Stable-Shift reaches cosine similarity of about 0.59 against measured responses. The GEARS baseline scores about 0.57. Spearman correlation and top gene precision also favour Stable-Shift among the methods compared. Across five unseen gene splits its mean score stays near 0.589 with small spread.
arxiv-2606-25440:
Take every polynomial whose coefficients are only plus or minus one, solve them all, and plot the roots: beyond the expected ring near the unit circle, dragon shaped fractals appear. Marcus Michelen and Oren Yakir explain that picture rigorously in 2026. These Littlewood polynomials have most roots hugging the unit circle, a classical fact. The dragon curves live away from the circle and resemble the attractor of an iterated function system, a set built by repeating a few shrinking maps.

The pair shows why that resemblance is no accident, tracing the fractal to the recursive structure of the root set itself. A random version of the question also resolves in favour of the dragons: such fractal behaviour is typical rather than a plotting artifact. Numerical heat maps for degree twenty six, roots packed by the hundred thousand, motivated the analysis.
arxiv-2606-25840:
Some particles, if they exist, would travel millimetres or metres before decaying, leaving muon pairs displaced from the collision point. The CMS Collaboration reports a search for such long lived particles in 2026, using proton collisions at thirteen point six teraelectronvolts recorded in twenty twenty two and twenty twenty three. A data scouting stream, which keeps slimmed down event records at very high rate, opened territory that ordinary triggers miss: low mass muon pairs with real displacement. The hunted sources include the Higgs boson decaying to dark photons or to dark showers, and a long lived scalar born from a beauty hadron.

No significant excess appeared above the standard model prediction.
