The collaboration therefore set upper limits, at ninety five percent confidence, on branching fractions across wide ranges of mass and lifetime. In large regions of that parameter space the new constraints improve on and extend all previous ones.
arxiv-2606-26140:
Peter Kagey and William Keehn count ways to tile the faces of symmetric solids with patterned tiles. Isohedral solids, like the Platonic and Catalan families, have identical faces that symmetries swap freely. Escher's stamp experiments inspire the question: given a set of tile designs, how many distinct face tilings exist, up to the solid's own symmetries? Orbit counting, a classic theorem about group actions, does the heavy lifting.

Formulas come out explicitly for the tiling counts. The same machinery counts tilings held fixed by each single symmetry of the solid. Sixteen known integer sequences are recovered as special cases. Twelve new sequences are contributed to the On-Line Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences, filling gaps. One worked example counts thousands of distinct tilings of a cube by a single tile design. The framework turns Escher's artistic bookkeeping into exact enumeration for whole families of solids.
arxiv-2606-27040:
Reiss and colleagues examine a family of layered nickel oxide crystals known as Ruddlesden-Popper nickelates. Interest in these materials surged after related compounds showed superconductivity, meaning electric current flowing with no loss, at very low heat levels. The team therefore measured the whole bulk-stable series, which varies by the count of nickel oxide layers. Their study spans a wide heat range, from near absolute zero up to very hot conditions.

Measurements combined X-ray scattering, electron imaging, heat capacity, magnetic response, and electric transport on high-quality single crystals. Across that broad range, Reiss and colleagues spot a high-heat change of crystal structure that earlier work had largely missed. This change differs from the known shift toward a square, tetragonal form. Pinning down such changes matters because crystal shape shapes the electronic behaviour linked to superconductivity in these layered oxides.
arxiv-2606-27440:
Migliorini and colleagues open up protein co-folding models to see which internal features drive their predictions. Foundation models like Boltz predict structures of proteins and small molecules superbly, but their reasoning stays opaque. Sparse autoencoders, the standard interpretability tool, fail on pair representations: pairwise tensors explode quadratically and hide concepts spread across sequence and pair channels. Their PairSAE method first compresses pairwise tensors into token-wise interaction roles by singular value decomposition. In 2026, a sparse autoencoder then learns shared token-level features decoding into both channels.

Tested on Boltz-2 activations for protein-ligand complexes, the learned features align with curated UniProt annotations. They also predict the model's own binding affinity values, showing the features carry functionally real signal. The approach thus survives the move from sequences to pairs. Researchers can audit what a folding model knows, concept by concept.
arxiv-2606-27640:
Some stochastic equations run backward from a fixed end value. When they are quadratic and have many linked parts, even existence and uniqueness stay open. Ulrich Horst, Emil Schmidek, and Huilin Zhang add a new class of such equations in 2026. The work is driven by a finance model where many agents' trades move prices.

The new class has weak links between its parts. The authors show that solutions exist and are unique when each part stays small enough on its own. The key point is that this smallness need does not grow with the number of parts. That lets them take the limit as the player count grows without bound. A stability result comes from Picard iteration, a step-by-step refinement scheme. With it, they derive rates for how fast play settles to the mean-field balance, in both Nash and Radner equilibrium forms.
arxiv-2606-28040:
Kinetic equations describe gases from rarefied flow down to fluid behaviour. A numerical scheme should stay valid across that whole range. Giacomo Dimarco and four colleagues introduce a high-order asymptotic-preserving framework in 2026. A micro-macro split divides the equation into a fluid part and a non-equilibrium part. Implicit-explicit Runge–Kutta methods give high-order time accuracy and stability in stiff regimes. WENO reconstructions and central differences handle space.

That property is the key feature. As the mean free path tends to zero, the scheme reduces to a high-order scheme for the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations. No separate fluid solver is needed in that limit. Experiments on one- and two-dimensional benchmarks confirm accuracy and stability across regimes. The collision term's stiffness and fast acoustic modes are handled by the time integrator. The framework targets the low Mach number limit in particular.
arxiv-2606-28340:
Song-Duo Ma, Chu-Yun Chen, Bang-An Li, Shau-Yung Hsu, and Yun-Nung Chen survey fairness in recommender systems rebuilt on large language models. Language-model recommenders can converse, explain, and generate, but bias can creep in through pretrained knowledge, prompts, generated explanations, decoding choices, and feedback loops that amplify early skew.

Ma and colleagues organize the young literature along two dimensions: the mechanisms that produce bias and the targets fairness should protect. They map how the field evaluates fairness and which mitigation strategies have been tried, claiming the first survey devoted to fairness in this setting. Fairness is also tied to neighboring trust concerns, including explainability, privacy, robustness, and controllability. Their structure is meant to ground more complete and reliable fairness evaluation in future systems.
arxiv-2606-28740:
Mutchnik, in the second part of a two-part work, gives outside reasons to care about a refined ladder of properties in classification theory. The ladder is Shelah's NSOP hierarchy, which grades theories by how much order-like chaos they can encode. Mutchnik's earlier part defined real-valued versions of these grades and argued for them from inside the theory.

Here he shows the real-valued grades are well-defined down to a lower threshold than first thought. He then proves a rough either-or. Either the real-valued extension truly adds new properties, or a key equality holds that would settle a central open problem about the integer ladder. The longest part applies cycle-removal tools from the real-valued theory to the question of whether two named grades, NSOP2 and NSOP3, are the same. Progress comes through hereditary classes of structures defined by forbidden substructures.
arxiv-2606-28940:
Pandey, Sabu and Gupta model a network of drones that both sense and serve vehicles in a city. Urban vehicle networks need seamless connectivity and awareness within streets that constrain movement. Their drones fly at fixed altitude, detect vehicles first, and then provide communication links to the ones they sense.

The road layout follows a Manhattan Poisson line process, a random grid model, with vehicles scattered along each road and drones scattered across the area. A blockage model accounts for buildings hiding signals depending on elevation angle. The authors derive the detection probability and each drone's sensing region under reliability requirements. They also work out the interference created by active drones and the resulting coverage probability for vehicles. Rate coverage for sensed vehicles follows from that analysis. Numerically, higher altitude hurt sensing and coverage, while rate coverage first fell and then rose with altitude.
arxiv-2606-29040:
Harper, Soundararajan and Xu determine how sums of a random multiplicative function behave over short intervals of integers. A Steinhaus random multiplicative function assigns random values to primes and multiplies them across each number's factorisation, mimicking arithmetic functions. They study partial sums over intervals that grow, but stay small compared with their starting point.

With the right normalisation, they prove the limiting distribution of these sums is Gaussian, the bell curve, for all such interval lengths. A key new feature is the normalisation itself: when the interval length is very close to the starting point, the correct divisor differs from the standard deviation one would naively use. In contrast, when the interval is comparable in size to its start, they show no normalisation can produce a non-degenerate Gaussian limit. The result draws a precise line between regimes where bell-curve behaviour holds and where it cannot.
arxiv-2606-29340:
Li and three colleagues improve a training method where a reasoning model learns from its own attempts, guided by a teacher that also sees the checked answer. Such on-policy self-distillation usually supervises only the output distribution, the odds over next tokens. The privileged context then shapes training only through that token-level signal, never touching the inner computation that produced it.

Their method, Privileged Hidden Flow, also distils how the teacher's hidden states flow through the same attempt. Instead of forcing each student hidden vector to equal the teacher's at the same token, it aligns the directions of token-to-token transitions and the shape of the whole trajectory, at every layer. Under the same hundred-step schedule it beat the reproduced baseline on three model sizes, gaining roughly two points on average. Ablations separate its effect from simply matching hidden states point by point.
arxiv-2606-29840:
Chatterjee and Gorai study holomorphic flows, motions generated by complex-valued equations on complex space, and answer two questions about them. The first concerns Runge domains, regions where every well-behaved function can be approximated by polynomials.

They prove a domain is a Runge domain when the forward flow of a linear system keeps it in place. The domain must contain the origin and the centre directions, and keep the growing directions away from its boundary. The second question is global linearization: whether a nonlinear flow can be straightened by a change of coordinates. They show a complete flow with a globally attracting fixed point can indeed be linearized this way. They give a formula for the straightening map as a limit over time.
arxiv-2606-30140:
Romain Karpinsky, Julien Mozziconacci, and Mickaël Delcey benchmark DNA language models against older convolutional rivals. Genomic foundation models borrow transformer designs from text AI. Models like DNABERT2 pretrain on billions of nucleotides at great cost. Whether that cost pays off on fine-tuning tasks is unclear. Tokenization choices for DNA are also hotly debated.

The authors pose three questions for their assessment. Do transformer models improve enough to justify heavy pretraining? What does pretraining itself actually contribute in this setting? How does byte pair encoding tokenization affect genomics task performance? DNABERT2 represents the transformer camp in their comparisons. ConvNova represents the convolutional approach to genomic sequences. Systematic benchmarks across these methods remain scarce in the literature. Their study aims to supply the missing head-to-head evidence.
arxiv-2606-30440:
Haobo Yang presents a formal proof that transformer networks, under a stated condition, perform exact Bayesian inference. Transformers power modern language and vision models. Their attention steps resemble Bayesian updating in informal accounts. Such claims have mostly stayed at the level of analogy. Yang works in a measure-theoretic kernel framework instead. The condition is a Bayes joint-distribution requirement on internal updates.

A hierarchy of abstractions structures the claimed proof. It starts with a core Bayesian transformer of prior and likelihood. Semantic transformers with explicit update kernels come next. Full blocks with attention, residual, and feed-forward parts follow. Multilayer stacks close the hierarchy at the top. At each level the update kernel matches the posterior almost surely. A Radon–Nikodym argument yields the Bayes formula for blocks. Softmax weighting is shown to induce a valid probability distribution. Architectural assumptions stay minimal throughout the argument.
arxiv-2606-30540:
Luke Moore and six colleagues screen hundreds of ceramic recipes in the computer to find which extreme-heat materials can actually be made. High-entropy borides mix five metals into one crystal structure. They promise hardness and stability under brutal conditions. Not every mix forms a single clean phase, though. The team studies all combinations of nine transition metals. That gives one hundred twenty-six candidate five-metal borides.

Density functional theory computes properties for each candidate. An entropy forming ability score predicts single-phase synthesizability. Those predictions agree well with experiments on selected borides. Mechanical properties come from special quasi-random structures mimicking disorder. Several compounds look mechanically unstable in the calculations. Chromium-bearing ones dominate that unstable group. They are also predicted to be harder to synthesize. Machine learning models analyze the computed results further. The study maps a route to mechanically superior single-phase borides.
arxiv-2606-30740:
Benoit Laurent re-examines how pressure builds on the wall of a bubble during a first-order phase transition in the early universe. Such transitions matter for gravitational waves, dark matter and the origin of matter. Whether a bubble wall settles at a modest speed or runs away relativistically depends on hydrodynamic obstruction. The plasma heats ahead of the wall and pushes back against the vacuum pressure driving it.

Standard analyses assume steady-state fluid profiles. Laurent combines analytic approximations with numerical hydrodynamic simulations, in local thermal equilibrium, to follow the pressure dynamically. The heating wave often forms more slowly than the wall accelerates, so steady-state predictions fail near the Jouguet velocity. He derives a revised criterion for the maximal driving pressure that separates deflagrations and hybrids from detonations and runaway walls. Simulations validate the criterion, and obstruction turns out less restrictive than steady-state theory suggested.
arxiv-2606-30940:
Lukas Lao Beyer and Sertac Karaman plan robot motion inside a compressed code instead of the original trajectory space. Learned planners capture rich behaviour from data but are hard to steer; classical search and optimisation are flexible yet work in bulky representations. The pair first train an autoencoder with a high compression ratio that turns trajectories into hierarchically ordered, discrete tokens, coarse details first and refinements later. Planning then becomes a search over token sequences, scored by whatever objective the user sets at test time.

Because the decoder is generative, the searched plans stay realistic. On the nuPlan benchmark and the Waymo Open Motion Dataset, latent search performed strongly at closed-loop motion planning. It also synthesised guided multi-agent scenarios, all without any task-specific training.
arxiv-2606-31040:
Fejős and Suenaga investigate two-color QCD. This is a simplified cousin of the theory of quarks and gluons. Lattice computers can simulate it at high density because it avoids the sign problem. The team asks how its phase structure, hadron masses, and topological susceptibility respond to the axial anomaly. The anomaly is a quantum effect that breaks one of the theory's classical symmetries.

They work with the linear sigma model. They add particle fluctuations through the functional renormalization group. Their effective potential respects the theory's symmetries at finite quark chemical potential. They find the anomaly coupling for mesons grows stronger as density rises. Yet topological susceptibility still falls, because chiral symmetry is being restored. At high temperature and density, chiral partner masses became degenerate, as expected.
arxiv-2606-31240:
Mosallam and Zaslavsky study total rainbow forests in edge-colored graphs. A rainbow forest uses edges that all carry different colors, and a total one uses every color exactly once. The pair ask when such a forest exists and, just as much, what blocks it from existing.

Using a necessary and sufficient condition for a total rainbow forest to exist, they show there are huge numbers of minimal obstruction graphs. A minimal obstruction fails the condition yet loses that status if changed at all, so it marks the exact edge of possibility. Their question grew from work on systems of curves on surfaces, where a rainbow criterion could help bound the largest such system, and it rests on the matroid intersection theorem.
arxiv-2606-31340:
Ding and seven colleagues build WaveFlowGMM, a tool that makes full earthquake ground motions for a stated case. Risk studies need three-component shaking records that fit the source, the path, and the site. Standard formulas give one intensity number, while many AI models mix wave size and wave shape in one hard target.

WaveFlowGMM splits the job at peak ground acceleration, the largest shaking value. A first stage with physics-based symbolic learning finds median peak values and how the three components vary together. A second stage builds the wave shape in a wavelet-packet space in a few steps, then scales it by a sampled peak. On held-out NGA-West2 data the motions track magnitude, distance, and site effects, and they turn into velocity and displacement records with no drift.
arxiv-2606-31740:
Foster, Knight and Krapohl study how cooperation evolves when players in a population differ from one another. Evolutionary game theory tracks strategies that spread or fade under an update rule. Many rules assume identical players, yet real groups vary in wealth, capacity and costs.

Four update rules are sorted into two families. Extrinsic rules have players copy what pays off for others, while intrinsic rules judge by their own traits or potential payoffs. The authors prove that extrinsic dynamics carry a ceiling on the cooperation rate. Intrinsic dynamics can break through that ceiling. A public goods game with unequal contributions demonstrates the gap between the two families.
cia-0000007540:
Spring 1965 produced volume 9, number 1 of Studies in Intelligence, the CIA's journal for its own officers. A heading in the issue points to intelligence treated in recent publications, a sign officers tracked outside writing about their field. The journal's readers were practitioners, not the general public.

Pages like these record a profession pausing to examine itself: its books, its methods, and its mistakes. That habit matters because secret work rarely gets open debate. Now declassified, the issue helps historians see what concerned American analysts as the Vietnam War widened. The text survives through the CIA reading room release.
cia-0000008640:
A crashed US Air Force F-105 was sighted in Hai Hung province, North Vietnam, in a report dated July 1973. The F-105 Thunderchief flew many of the war's hardest bombing missions over the north. Hai Hung lies in the Red River plain east of Hanoi.

By mid-1973 American combat flights had stopped, so wreck sightings mostly aided the accounting for lost crews. A located crash site could confirm what happened to a pilot who never returned. The report shows that work proceeding through local observation after the ceasefire. It is one entry in the air war's long final ledger.
cia-0000009440:
Americans remaining in South Vietnam, and detention of Americans in the north, fill a CIA paper dated January 1976. Saigon had fallen eight months earlier, ending the war and stranding questions about who stayed or was held. Some Americans had remained by choice, others by circumstance.

The paper takes stock of those cases a year into the new order. Washington had little access and less leverage, so reporting ran thin. Families and officials still needed names, numbers, and best judgments. The file shows the accounting moving into its postwar phase, where diplomacy at last replaced wartime channels entirely.
cia-0000009640:
Enemy prisons and facilities near Khang Khay, plus results of airstrikes in the area, fill a January 1969 CIA item. Khang Khay sits on Laos's Plain of Jars, a much-fought-over plateau in Xieng Khouang province. The pairing of prisons and strike results in one file is striking.

Planners needed prison locations marked clearly, not least so bombs would not fall on captives. Strike reports, meanwhile, recorded what air attacks had done nearby. Holding both subjects together shows the terrible closeness of bombing and captivity in Laos. The file preserves that tension in a single dated record.
cia-0000009740:
Southeast of the junction of Routes 911 and 9113 stood a prison housing Lao inmates, an October 1969 report states. The routes ran through southern Laos, along the infiltration network toward Vietnam. Most prisoners in such sites were Lao, held by one side or the other in a civil war.

Lao-held prisons rarely drew the attention given to American cases. Yet mapping them showed the war's full carceral reach inside Laos itself. Local inmates' fates also tested which side controlled the countryside. This file keeps a Lao prison, not an American one, on the permanent official record.
cia-0000009840:
A Viet Cong prison built for American prisoners inside Cambodia is described in a February 1967 report. A prison meant for Americans alone marks a step beyond holding captives in mixed camps. Cambodia's border sanctuaries gave such a site shelter from South Vietnamese forces.

Purpose-built prisons implied the captors expected a long war and many prisoners. For officials, the report proved planning, not improvisation, behind cross-border captivity. It also fixed a target for watching in a country officially at peace. The file stands early in the record of Cambodia's hidden role in the prison war.
cia-0000012340:
Conversations with a contact whose name is blacked out fill a CIA record from 1962. The talks took place in London in March and in Geneva days later. The London talks ran March 8 to 11; the Geneva talks, March 14 to 25. Two cities in one month place an allied dimension of the Penkovsky case squarely on the calendar.

Meeting records like this one fix the operation's British and Swiss chapters in dates. Allies conferred, compared, and coordinated around a source neither could run alone. For readers, the page shows the cousins' work: quiet, dated, and essential to the case.
cia-0000013940: Four American prisoners came through the fight unhurt, in a CIA note dated February 1, 1968. The note places the four in Gia Lai Province, in South Vietnam. Their sound health was the kind of detail families and officials scanned for first. Short notes like this carried the small facts that kept prisoner files current.
cia-0000015340: Recent sightings of unexplained objects fill a CIA file dated June 2, 1952. A memo is attached, dated December 2, on the same subject. June 1952 opened the summer that made saucers a national fever. A file of fresh sightings from that month catches the wave as it began to rise. The sightings file and its memo rest in the CIA Reading Room.
cia-0000020340: Colonel Carlos Castillo Armas appears as a Guatemalan exile in a CIA record dated in 1951. Exile was his lot after a failed rising, years before he took power in 1954. Files on exiles helped officials judge who might lead next in a troubled land. Read today, the early profile gains weight from all that followed for the man and his country.
cia-0000020440: Orlando Letelier is noted as a lecturer at American University in a redacted CIA record dated in 1975. Letelier had served Chile's fallen Allende government as a senior envoy. In Washington he taught, spoke, and pressed the case against Chile's new rulers. Parts of the note were cut before release, so the surviving fact is his campus role that year.
cia-0000022340: Powers was to be released, a CIA record dated in 1962 reports in its short heading. The release came in February 1962, when he was swapped for Rudolf Abel in Berlin. Word of a coming release would have raced through the agency that winter. The bare heading holds the hopeful turn after two years of prison and hard bargaining.
cia-0000027940: Hunt J. is the whole title of a CIA item dated in 1970. The catalog gives a surname and one initial, nothing more, so this account adds nothing. A file this bare could hold a contact note, a check, or a warning about a man. It stands as the thinnest kind of personal record the archive keeps, a name and a year.
cia-0000036540:
A CIA daily report on Latin America, dated October 3, 1978, notes that ORIT declared a boycott against Chile. ORIT was a regional labor body, and its boycott targeted Chile's military government. The item appears inside the day's wider roundup of Latin American news.

The report gives the boycott a place among the day's main regional stories. Labor action against Chile drew notice because it crossed borders and unions. Daily digests like this preserve small items that later histories often leave out entirely. A boycott call by a labor federation was a pressure tool that stopped short of force.
cia-0000036640:
Photo comparison results for William Johnson fill a CIA record dated January 2, 1971. The case number is 12478, and the file belongs to the MIA and POW effort. One prisoner photograph was at the center of the comparison work.

Analysts set the prisoner photograph beside known pictures and judged whether they matched. A match could confirm that a missing man was alive and held in captivity. The record holds the outcome of that careful check for one named serviceman. Johnson's case was one of hundreds worked through the same careful process during those years. A single photograph could carry the whole weight of a family's hopes for news.
cia-0000045240:
An agreement was reportedly reached for the Duarte release, in a CIA record dated September 2, 1985. Reportedly leaves the door open, as careful wire writing does. The release it promised was the ending the whole country awaited.

Inside, the reported breakthrough in the case is recorded. A reached agreement should have meant terms settled and a date set. In this crisis, such hopeful reports had risen and fallen before, sometimes within a single week of hard and silent waiting. The file preserves this one at its hopeful hour, leaving readers to set it beside the harder and slower records that surround it in the series.
cia-0000049140: Reporting requirements, the rules for how officers in the field had to file their reports, fill a CIA item from 1989. The item sits in the Truth Commission file series, a piece of office machinery among the war records. Even the paperwork had a paper trail, and this is part of it: how the flood of reports was ordered.
cia-0000049240:
Political violence and insurgent propaganda in El Salvador are paired as the subject of a CIA paper from 1983. The pairing was the point: the guerrillas fought with words as deliberately as with rifles, and the state answered in kind. The paper survives in the files later gathered for the Truth Commission.

Inside, the subject splits in two: the violence itself, counted and sorted, and the printed and broadcast war that framed it. Analysts tracked leaflets, radio, and slogans because belief moved recruits and money as surely as battles did. The paper shows the war read as a contest for minds, not only ground.
cia-0000049340: Declassified CIA document 0000049340, dated March 5, 1981, is titled El Salvador: More Political Problems and marked for the Truth Commission. The heading signals further political trouble in El Salvador without naming a single cause. Readers get a brief agency item whose general title reflects a running watch on the country's politics, preserved as filed in the declassified collection.
cia-0000078940: On the Trail of Submarine Disasters is the title of declassified CIA document 0000078940, dated September 15, 1992. The heading suggests an account following submarine losses rather than a routine report. Readers get a short declassified item whose literary title sets it apart from the catalog's plainer files. The record itself gives no further detail in its heading.
cia-0000096940: Program Objectives, Special Operations Group, Counter Intelligence Staff is the heading of declassified CIA document 0000096940, dated May 4, 1972. The title reads like an internal office label, naming the group and staff. The brief file is an internal objectives record, preserved as a glimpse of how one counterintelligence unit stated its own program aims.
cia-0000098740: CAD software for the GDR's K-1845 computer is described in declassified CIA document 0000098740, dated March 5, 1990. The heading names the software type, the country by initials, and one machine model. Readers get a short technical description record on East German computing, part of the agency's close tracking of bloc computer equipment.
cia-0000102940: Denied, plus prison labor used for pipeline construction from 1968 to March 1979, form declassified CIA document 0000102940, dated November 5, 1982. The first numbered topic is a single word, Denied, left unexplained. Readers find a short pipeline labor record with the cluster's longest date span in its heading, from the late sixties onward. The catalog keeps the record under its original subject heading.
cia-0000112340: Television Program Summary 191830: Bud 91-018 is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000112340, dated January 1, 1991. The title gives a summary code, BUD 91-018, and a time written as 191830. No program or country is named in the heading itself. The brief record is a broadcast summary item, kept under its code as released in the files there.
cia-0000112840: Dated January 1, 1945, with that date marked as an estimate, declassified CIA document 0000112840 holds a list of individuals and information regarding J. Its untitled heading breaks off at that single initial in the title. No fuller name is given in the surviving heading text itself. The brief record preserves the estimate note and the broken ending as released.
cia-0000119740: A CIA report gives the Hungarian situation with information as of 11:30 p.m. during the 1956 crisis. The late edition caught events at their most fluid, and it preserves the picture the overnight watch passed to the president's advisers. The late hour marks the edge of the reporting day in Washington, when the watch summed up a night of cables for the morning's first readers.
cia-0000132240: Situation report 557, dated January 1991, covers political developments, its subtitle repeating the same words before breaking off. The doubled phrase is a small mark of the daily grind of the crisis watch. The report covers the politics as filed. High-numbered sitreps blur in wording because the watch produced them around the clock; the doubled heading is the grind showing through the file's formal surface.
cia-0000132440: Changes inside the Cuban government fill a CIA document dated November 4, 1959. Ministers were coming and going as Castro tightened his hold on power. Each change moved the government further from the broad promises of its first weeks. The short document tracks the reshuffles one by one, giving readers a dated record of who rose and who fell during the revolution's first year in office.
cia-0000132640: Filed as section III, The West - Cuba, this CIA paper of May 1, 1960 survives as a fragment of a larger regional survey. Its place in that survey puts Cuba among the Western Hemisphere concerns Washington tracked that spring, rather than as a stand-alone study. The declassified fragment is preserved through the CIA Reading Room mirror at the Internet Archive, cataloged under document number 0000132640.
cia-0000132740: World reactions to Cuba fill a CIA item dated March 4, 1961. The item sorts them into three piles: the Free World, the Sino-Soviet bloc, and the United Nations. That three-way split was the Cold War drawn in miniature. Nearly every government on earth had a stance on Cuba by then. The short item gathers the reactions in one dated place.
cia-0000134340:
Events in Indochina fill a CIA paper dated August 3, 1972. The Paris peace talks were still months from their end, and the fighting in Vietnam had not stopped. American troops were drawing down while the war's endgame took shape around them.

The paper surveys the latest events across the region that summer. Battles, talks, and supply lines all fed into the account. For readers, it is a snapshot from the war's last full year of heavy fighting. The accords that closed the American role came the following January, and this paper dates from the hard months just before them.
cia-0000135740: Dated 6 March 1961, a Spanish document from the declassified archive of Brigade 2506. The exile force was then weeks from its April landing in Cuba, in the last phase of training and planning. The catalog names no subject for this item. It is held in the original Spanish through the CIA Reading Room. The record is one of the brigade's final-month documents, described by its date and file rather than by any guessed content.
cia-0000135940: Dated 5 January 1954, a declassified CIA cable deals with a request that headquarters alone concur in any clearance or clarification the station sought. Lincoln handled the field traffic of PBSUCCESS, the agency effort against the Arbenz government in Guatemala in the early 1950s. For readers of the coup, the value lies in the plain wording, written before anyone knew how the story would end.
cia-0000136040: The cable dated 6 February 1954 in the CIA files, now open, deals with information on a thing the heading calls this one man force function. As the Lincoln station file, it forms part of PBSUCCESS, the CIA plan that ended with President Arbenz driven out in June 1954. Later books on the coup rest on stacks of paper exactly like this, dated, coded, and only partly opened.
cia-0000136140: One CIA cable dated 2 April 1954 handles instructions for teams targeting bridges, typos and all, the orders breaking off at the end. Lincoln was where PBSUCCESS staff worked the Guatemala operation day to day, under code names, in 1953 and 1954. The file rewards slow reading, since its short heading is often the only summary the agency ever gave it.
cia-0000136240: The declassified CIA cable dated 4 May 1954 takes up Instructions 7 for the Sherwood broadcast, sent to a name the heading spells as Lagevin. In these files Lincoln names the field station of PBSUCCESS, the covert CIA plan to topple President Arbenz of Guatemala. The heading alone tells a reader the topic, the channel, and the moment, even where names stay deleted.
cia-0000136340: Do not be influenced by the cry of hoax, LINCOLN tells CADICK in this June 1954 cable, because the power of retaliation will be retained until CALLIGERIS's position is secure. The station regrets it cannot fully inform him of every detail and demands complete compliance with an earlier message. Aircraft use is modified: he may resupply field forces as needed to maintain effectiveness while awaiting developments. Secrecy and obedience are the cable's twin themes.
cia-0000136640: A Spanish document dated 4 March 1961, from the declassified papers of Brigade 2506, the exile force the CIA built against Castro. March was the brigade's last full month of preparation. The catalog record gives this item no subject heading. It survives in the original Spanish, one of the March records of the operation, released through the CIA Reading Room for direct study.
cia-0000136740: This Spanish document, dated 1 November 1960, is filed with the 2506 Brigade papers released by the CIA. It opens the November sequence in this part of the file, a month when the training brigade generated heavy paperwork. The catalog record states no subject for the item. Preserved in the original Spanish, it is a dated piece of the exile force's archive from its first autumn.
cia-0000139040: A lecture on Germany's future draws a small crowd in New York. This OSS report covers a September 1945 meeting at a workers' hall. Attendance was 126. The speaker addressed Germany's eastern territories. Annexation by Poland and Russia was explained as a security need. Those lands were principally Germanized Slavs, he argued. They could not be trusted at this time. The garbled transcription keeps the outline, not the wording. The report records communist-line speaking in America. The war had ended only days before.
cia-0000139440: The capture of two Israeli soldiers in Lebanon complicates the hostage situation, the DCI Hostage Location Task Force report of January 1986 states in its highlights. Israeli sweep operations in southern Lebanon continue and have produced a number of clashes with Shia forces, the excerpt adds before cutting off. The task force existed to find the Americans held hostage in Beirut during the Lebanon hostage crisis. The surviving sample is brief; the full report's reporting on hostage locations does not appear here.
cia-03179140:
Brazil opens the Current Intelligence Bulletin dated 9 February 1956. The bloc is following up its diplomatic and economic overtures. A Polish ambassador in London lunched the Brazilian envoy with a Soviet colleague on 30 January. Bulgaria seeks trade talks, and Czechoslovakia and Poland want much larger trade. The American embassy in Rio reports the courtship under way.

Argentina reportedly buys Czech planes. The Viet Minh concludes a barter agreement with a Japanese firm. Peiping offers Nepal economic assistance. Self-government for Malaya draws a comment. Jordan's prime minister outlines an independent foreign policy. The USSR offers party ties to Danish and Dutch Socialists. Domestic politics prompts Austria to expel the World Federation of Trade Unions. A Bonn official foresees German control of balloon operations. Panama's opposition reportedly plans violence after 10 February. Standing sections cover the Arab-Israeli situation and the Taiwan Strait.
cia-06541040:
Central Intelligence Bulletin for 19 August 1960, marked Top Secret, is a short issue whose legible item covers the Republic of the Congo. The bulletin reports that United Nations forces there had been authorized to shoot in their own defense. New anti-Western and anti-white incidents were said to be apparently instigated by Lumumba.

The item reports that on 18 August a Canadian officer of the UN force was injured at the Leopoldville airport. Other Canadians were subjected to indignities by Force Publique soldiers there. Ambassador Timberlake, barred by Congolese soldiers from Lumumba's residence that day, warned the Force Publique could be turned against UN troops or whites in general. Secretary General Hammarskjold is reported inviting any dissenting Security Council nation to present its views as a resolution.
cooper-pathfinder-1840:
James Fenimore Cooper returned to Leatherstocking after a long break and published The Pathfinder in 1840. He set it on Lake Ontario during the Seven Years' War, when his hero is in his prime as a scout. Cooper had always insisted Natty needed a love story, and this is the volume that gives him one.

Natty, called Pathfinder for his unerring woodcraft, guides young Mabel Dunham to her father's island fort. He falls quietly in love with her, though a dashing rival and his own honest nature stand in the way. French and Indian attacks, a blockade, and a storm on the lake supply the action. Cooper's lake scenery is among his finest writing. The Pathfinder is the essential middle volume of the Leatherstocking Tales.
doe-osti-3012252-block-island-s-energy-r:
An energy roadmap to 2040 for Block Island, Rhode Island is prepared by Peter Cappers, Jason Ball, and Sanjana Tadepalli of Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. The roadmap serves the Block Island Utility District and the island community, with goals around efficiency, resilience, and affordability. Supply scenarios all ensure on island biofuel and solar resources can meet the full peak demand, per community priorities.

A 2040 demand forecast varies with adoption of electric technologies. The analysis found more than enough developable land and rooftop area for the needed resources. Battery sizing targets enough charge capacity to avoid curtailing island solar in summer, though minor winter curtailment may remain when batteries are full.
dupotet-cours-magnetisme-sept-lecons-184:
Jules Dupotet teaches animal magnetism in seven lessons in his Cours de magnetisme, in French from 1840. The leading French magnetizer of his day instructs step by step. Students learn how to induce the trance, what signs to expect, and how the magnetic cure claims to heal the sick.

Clear, practical, and fully confident, the course served as the textbook of high mesmerism. Dupotet writes as a master sure of his art and its laws. Passes, rapport, and somnambulism each get their ordered place here. The book shows mesmerism as a teachable craft in its prime, the standard course by which a generation of magnetizers learned their trade.
dupotet-magnetisme-oppose-medecine-1840:
Dupotet declares war on the doctors in Le magnetisme oppose a la medecine, in French from 1840. The magnetic cure, he argues, heals where learned physicians fail. Regular medicine answers with scorn, and the pamphlet war between the schools burns hot on every page of his polemic.

Combative, earnest, and utterly sure of itself, the book speaks for the magnetizers' cause. Dupotet mocks degrees, latin, and fees with a pamphleteer's glee. Patients' cures are his chosen weapons in the fight. The work stands as a founding manifesto of alternative healing in nineteenth-century France, a shot in a long war over who may heal.
europmc-pmc10011140:
Brain gene activity and its links to disease are mapped by de Klein and a large team in a 2023 study. The group combined RNA data from more than eight thousand brain samples across many datasets. They built a shared resource called MetaBrain to make the merged data usable by other labs.

With that resource, the team tracked how gene variants change gene activity in the brain. They then pointed to genes that may drive brain diseases. The work helps turn raw genetic hits from past studies into clear targets for new research.
europmc-pmc10024440:
Hu and colleagues report that a circular RNA carried in exosomes weakens killer T cells and helps liver cancer resist a key drug class, in a 2023 study. The RNA is called circCCAR1. Killer T cells that stop working well are a main reason liver tumors escape the immune system and shrug off PD-1 blocking drugs.

The team shows how tumor parcels deliver this RNA to T cells and blunt their attack. Blocking the RNA restored T cell strength in their tests. The finding names a new target for making liver cancer drugs work better.
europmc-pmc10307640:
Kruse and a large team report that CD4 T cells can control tumors that evade standard immune attack, through inflammatory cell death, in a 2023 study. Most cancer immunotherapy relies on CD8 killer T cells that spot tumor markers directly. Tumors often escape by losing those markers, which leaves such therapy powerless.

The team shows that helper CD4 T cells can instead trigger a fiery form of death in tumor tissue. That death engulfed even marker-free tumor cells nearby. The finding opens a path to treat tumors that hide from killer T cells.
europmc-pmc10468540:
Wang, Zhao, and Wan reviewed in 2023 how one signal family steers two rival T cell types. The family is TGF-beta, a set of growth signals found across animals. The two cell types are Treg cells, which calm immune attack, and Th17 cells, which can stir it. Both types guard the fine line between tolerance and rejection.

When that line breaks, autoimmunity, cancer, or infection can follow. TGF-beta sits at the core of both cell types, despite their opposed acts. Wang maps the signal web that lets one family guide both. The web is built from ordered, linked steps that share parts. Two decades of work feed into this account of the balance.
europmc-pmc10585440:
Meskó wrote a tutorial in 2023 on prompt engineering as a new skill for medical staff. The craft means shaping the text prompts that steer a large language model. ChatGPT drew over 100 million users in two months, a record pace. As patients and staff turn to such tools, the skill gap grows hard to ignore.

Good prompts can lift the quality of a model's output on a task. Poor prompts can yield vague or false text, a risk in care. Meskó sums up the state of research on the craft so far. The piece then gives hands-on tips for a wide range of health workers. Tips cover clear task framing, context, and checks on output.
europmc-pmc10632140:
Taylor and co-authors showed in 2023 that brain tumours borrow the brain's own learning tricks. Gliomas are cancers that grow inside brain circuits. Nerve cells feed their growth through synapses, the links that pass signals between cells. Those links push tumour cells to divide.

A growth factor called BDNF tunes synapse strength in the healthy brain. Taylor found that it tunes the tumour links the same way. It sends more signal receivers to the tumour cell surface, which boosts the current each signal makes. Stronger currents drove faster tumour growth in their tests. Blocking the BDNF receptor, TrkB, cut these effects and stretched survival in mouse models of child brain cancers.
europmc-pmc11275440:
Yi and colleagues review signal proteins as targets for cancer therapy in this 2024 paper. Cytokines are proteins that regulate immune responses and cell behaviour. Families include interleukins, interferons, tumour necrosis factors, and chemokines, which guide cell movement. Growth factors such as TGF-beta, VEGF, and EGF belong to the same broad set. These molecules can push tumours either way.

Depending on context, a cytokine can promote or suppress tumour growth, the authors stress. It can also reshape the tumour's surroundings and change how well treatments work. Recent agents aim to modulate these pathways to slow progression and beat resistance. The review summarises current understanding of each family in tumour biology. It then details the new drugs built on that knowledge. The dual nature of cytokines is treated as both the central challenge and the central opportunity.
europmc-pmc1238740:
Gutierrez and co-authors revisited the deep origins of tuberculosis bacteria in 2005. The TB germ shows very little genetic variety today. That sameness suggested a narrow origin about 35,000 years ago. New isolates from East Africa told a broader story.

Gene trees for those isolates did not agree with each other. Some genes looked like mosaics stitched from different sources. Gutierrez argues the modern germ descends from a wider ancestral pool. Gene swapping shaped that pool long before clonal spread. The bacteria may have lived with early humans far longer than thought.
europmc-pmc1240840:
Hoppin, Brock, Davis, and Baird checked urine test stability for phthalates in 2002. Phthalates are chemicals found in plastics and cosmetics everywhere. Some forms harm reproduction in animal studies. Judging human exposure needs reliable measures.

These chemicals clear the body in about twelve hours. The team collected first morning urine on two straight days. Samples came from 46 women in the Washington area. Seven breakdown products plus a dilution marker were measured. Four products appeared in every sample. Hoppin tests how steady single spot checks really are. Levels were measured with liquid chromatography and mass spectrometry.
europmc-pmc1241340:
Lovekamp-Swan and Davis reviewed how phthalates harm female reproduction in 2003. Phthalates are mass-produced chemicals in plastics and consumer goods. Survey data suggested women face a distinct exposure pattern. Their lab studied these chemicals in animal models of the ovary.

One phthalate, DEHP, cut blood estrogen and halted egg release in rats. Its active breakdown product lowered a key enzyme message in ovary cells. That enzyme, aromatase, makes estrogen in the ovary. The product also switches on fat-sensing receptors called PPARs. The authors propose those receptors suppress aromatase and drive the harm.
europmc-pmc12535840:
GBD 2023 Disease and Injury and Risk Factor Collaborators audited world health in 2025. The Global Burden of Disease effort has run for over thirty years. It counts health loss from disease, injury, and risk factors. Coverage spans 204 countries plus 660 subnational locations.

Burden was estimated for 375 diseases and injuries. Eighty-eight changeable risk factors got linked burden estimates. More than 120,000 sources fed this round of estimates. Healthy life expectancy was computed alongside illness burden. GBD 2023 Disease and Injury and Risk Factor Collaborators frame post-pandemic gaps in plain numbers. Burden was counted as years of life lost and years lived with illness.
europmc-pmc1311140:
Steele and co-authors tested how lung immune cells recognize a fungal invader in 2005. Aspergillus fumigatus spores are inhaled daily and cleared by lung macrophages. Which recognition receptor matters was disputed. The fungus wall is rich in beta-glucan sugars, pointing to one receptor.

Blocking tests showed the response depended on dectin-1, the beta-glucan receptor. Without it, cells made far fewer inflammatory signals. Eight signaling molecules were measured in the response. Swollen spores and early sprouting forms triggered the strongest reaction. That strength matched how much beta-glucan they exposed. Steele settles the receptor question for this fungus.
europmc-pmc1473040:
Proteins with many partners, called hubs, are more often vital than loners. He and Zhang asked in 2006 whether the web's shape explains that rule. They proposed a plainer cause: some protein links are themselves vital for life. A hub simply holds more links, so it more likely holds a vital one.

Their math suggests about three percent of yeast protein links are vital. Those links account for about 43 percent of vital genes. Vital links also changed less over evolution than others. He argues the yeast web is sturdier than random webs, yet far from the best possible. The rule may owe less to design than to counting.
europmc-pmc1905940:
Sonkoly, Pivarcsi and co-authors reported in 2007 the first microRNA profile of psoriatic skin. Psoriasis is the most common chronic inflammatory skin disease in adults and drags heavily on quality of life. MicroRNAs are small post-transcriptional regulators, meaning they tune protein output after genes are read.

Psoriatic skin held a distinct microRNA pattern, unlike both healthy skin and eczema, another chronic skin inflammation. Some changed microRNAs came from white blood cells. One, miR-203, came from keratinocytes, the skin's main cell type, and in a screen of 21 organs it appeared almost only in skin. In plaques, miR-203 rose while its target SOCS-3 fell. That target helps govern inflammatory responses and keratinocyte behavior. The authors propose microRNA deregulation as part of how psoriasis develops.
europmc-pmc1989740:
Tindana and co-authors argued in 2007 that community engagement in health research needs far more testing. Large funders were backing work on diseases of the poor in developing countries. New tools and treatments would only be used if intended communities took part. Abandoned HIV prevention trials in Cameroon and Cambodia showed that weak engagement could sink a study.

The authors reviewed models from public health, planning and community development. They found few systematic attempts to measure whether engagement actually works. Two African examples illustrated different approaches in practice. They defined engagement as real partnership, with shared power and mutual benefit. The paper urges researchers to define community carefully, since values and identity shape who counts as one.
europmc-pmc2125940:
Ryokichi Inada, Yutaka Ido, Rokuro Hoki, Hiroshi Ito, and Hidetsune Wani treated Weil's disease with immune serum given straight into a vein. Their report came from the clinic of the Imperial University in Kyushu, Japan, in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1918. Earlier work had used injections under the skin; the vein method had been the clinic's main route since 1916.

Forty-one patients received the vein treatment between May and November of 1916. Serum placed directly in the bloodstream proved far stronger than serum given under the skin, which must drift in slowly. The authors cite work rating the direct route's effect many times higher than the slower route's. Their case record weighs dose, timing, and patient outcome. It argues for the vein as the way to bring the serum's full strength against this spirochete infection.
europmc-pmc2131340:
Mae Friedlander, Harry Sobotka, and Edwin Banzhaf, in New York, studied the precipitin reaction of antipneumococcus sera in a 1928 paper. Precipitin tests show how much a serum reacts with germ material, while protective units show how well it shields animals. Part two asks whether the easy precipitin measure can stand in for the harder protection measure.

Across many single-type and mixed sera, the precipitin index rose and fell with the count of protective units. The ratio between them sat in a set range for Type I serum, but ran about ten times higher for Type III. Mixed sera gave lower ratios. Length of treatment shifted the quotient, and refined, concentrated sera showed a relative gain in precipitin activity.
europmc-pmc2140340:
Crozier studied the gill plumes of the sea slug Chromodoris in a 1919 paper, from the Bermuda Biological Station and the University of Illinois. When a shadow falls on the animal, the feathery gills draw in, a protective move. Crozier asked what conditions control that shading response, and how the whole gill-crown retraction is built out of single plume actions.

Each plume contracts on its own when light dims. Heat above a set point, and direct sunlight, wipe the response out, and it works only within a narrow range of sea water alkalinity. Under fit conditions of light, temperature, and alkalinity, the single plume contractions reflexly drive the whole crown to hide itself. The protective system rides on top of the plumes' basic rhythm of protrusion and retraction for breathing.
europmc-pmc2140640:
Selig Hecht studied intensity discrimination in the clam Mya in a 1924 paper. He devised a way to record, objectively and in numbers, whether Mya tells two light intensities apart when shown them one after the other. A response at a fixed reaction time served as the sign of discrimination.

The step in intensity the clam can just notice does not hold a constant share of the starting intensity. The ratio falls as intensity rises to a point, then rises again. In Hecht's photochemical model, discrimination at a set reaction time requires that a constant amount of sensitive substance be split in the sense organ. Treating the mechanism mathematically reproduces the odd ratio curve, which the simpler Weber rule cannot.
europmc-pmc2140740:
Osterhout and Dorcas, at Harvard and The Rockefeller Institute, compared the cell sap of two seaweed Valonia forms in a 1925 paper. The two forms are close kin and grow in similar waters, yet one floats in sea water and the other sinks. Chemical analysis of their sap was set beside that behavior.

The sinking form holds potassium and sodium in one proportion; the floating form holds them in a far different, inverted proportion. The sinker also lacks magnesium, which the floater carries, and other sap differences appear. Those internal differences, the authors show, bring about the contrast in flotation. Two near-identical plants thus run opposite mineral economies side by side.
europmc-pmc2140940:
Dean Burk examined the free energy of nitrogen fixation by living forms in a 1927 paper. Nitrogen fixation is the capture of air's nitrogen into compounds, done by certain microbes and legume root bacteria, and it plainly costs the organism sugar. Burk asks, from energy bookkeeping alone, whether the fixation step itself must consume energy.

Fixation can even release free energy, he shows, when oxygen or hydrogen gas, or other near-zero-energy substances, take part, forming nitrates, ammonia, or cyanide. Energy is truly required in only two settings. One is when nitrogen reacts with a compound already deep in negative free energy, like water. The other is when the organism works at concentrations that throw away the yield. The sugar cost, then, may belong to general metabolism rather than to fixation itself.
europmc-pmc2180240:
Syphilis germs injected at one spot in a rabbit do not stay put, and Louise Pearce and Wade H. Brown track where they travel. Their 1922 study focuses on lymphoid tissue, recovering living Treponema pallidum from lymph nodes by passing node material into other animals.

Germs appear in the nearby lymph nodes as early as two days after scrotal injection, before any visible sore reaction. They are still found there up to 61 days later, and distant nodes such as the popliteals also harbor active organisms despite no lesions nearby. Infection is firmly established within 48 hours, so removing the first sore would not stop it. Living germs persist in nodes for long periods, a finding that shapes how the disease's quiet spread can be understood.
europmc-pmc2198940:
Li and co-workers catalogued human E3 ubiquitin ligases in 2008 and screened them for new functions. E3 ligases attach ubiquitin, a small tag, to proteins and thereby set protein fate. The team annotated about 617 putative E3 enzymes and recognition subunits in the human genome. They built gene and silencing libraries for imaging-based screens. One screen sought E3s controlling mitochondrial dynamics, the movement and shape of the cell's energy organelles.

The screen uncovered MULAN, a RING finger protein sitting in the mitochondrial outer membrane. Its active RING end faces the cell fluid. Adding or silencing MULAN both disrupted mitochondrial trafficking and shape. An intact RING and correct location were both required. MULAN had earlier been found to activate NF-kappaB, linking mitochondrial dynamics to signals sent to the nucleus.
europmc-pmc2323740:
Do big, odd-shaped, or highly conducting particles drift faster in an electric field? H. A. Abramson and L. Michaelis test that question in 1929 with particles large enough to see under a microscope, pushing size, shape, and conductivity to extremes.

Within experimental error, the drift speed cares about none of the three. Mobility stays the same however much those properties vary. That negative answer matters: it means differences in drift can be credited to the electrical state at a particle's surface rather than its bulk traits. The short paper underpins the use of cataphoresis, this field-driven motion, as a tool for comparing colloids and cells.
europmc-pmc2412840:
Johanson and colleagues reviewed the many jobs of cerebrospinal fluid in 2008. This clear fluid bathes the brain and spinal cord, made mainly by a tissue called the choroid plexus. The review covers eight sides of its circulation: how fast it forms, its pressure, flow, volume, turnover, make-up, recycling, and drainage.

A key theme is the sink action of fresh fluid: steady turnover sweeps harmful waste, such as the amyloid of Alzheimer's disease, out of the brain. In ageing and in normal pressure hydrocephalus, the fluid space expands and turnover falls, so waste lingers and neurons suffer. They describe new ways to tune fluid formation, from water channel proteins to hormone-like signals. Drainage runs through several routes, including nose and spine channels, not just the classic one-way valves.
europmc-pmc2602740:
Ogrinc and a large group of collaborators published in 2008 the explanation document for the SQUIRE guidelines, a checklist for reporting healthcare quality improvement work. Reports of improvement projects varied wildly in content and quality, and existing guidelines for trials or observational studies fit them poorly. The SQUIRE statement lists 19 items authors should address when describing a formal improvement study.

For each checklist item, this companion document gives one or two published examples and analyses how each example expresses the item's intent. Most items echo standard scientific reporting. But they are reshaped for improvement work. There, interventions evolve and contexts matter. Goals also differ from disease biology research. The authors aim to help project teams travel from a finished improvement project to a publishable report.
europmc-pmc2637240:
Rey and colleagues built a poverty index for every small town area in mainland France and linked it to death rates from 1997 to 2001. Their 2009 work aimed to show whether poorer places die younger across the whole country. The index combined four social and economic measures for each commune, the smallest local unit in France.

Death rates rose steadily as poverty rose, at every map scale they tried. The poorest fifth of communes had a death rate about 24 percent higher than the richest fifth, after age was taken into account. The link was stronger for men, for people under 65, and for deaths tied to smoking, alcohol, and accidents. Two older British poverty scores showed a weaker and less steady pattern on the same French data.
europmc-pmc2683940:
Kolz and colleagues, working with the EUROSPAN Consortium and partner groups, merged genome scans from 28,141 Europeans in 2009 to find genes that set blood uric acid levels. High uric acid causes gout, a painful joint disease, and raises the risk of heart disease and diabetes. Fourteen studies pooled their data for this hunt.

Nine genome regions passed the strict bar for a real link, and five were entirely new. The strongest sat in SLC2A9, a gene for a sugar and urate transporter; its effect ran stronger in women. A second gene, ABCG2, pushed levels up more in men. One new region, SLC16A9, tied to two blood chemicals that themselves track uric acid, forming a three-way link that hints at a fresh control route. The finds map much of the inherited control of uric acid, and name targets for future gout drugs.
europmc-pmc2684740:
Jeng and colleagues measured in 2009 vitamin D and a natural germ-killing peptide in critically ill patients, many with sepsis, a runaway response to infection. Vitamin D shortage is common in hospitals. Lab work suggested the vitamin switches on production of cathelicidin, also called LL-37, a peptide that white blood cells use to kill germs.

Blood from intensive care patients held far less vitamin D than blood from healthy volunteers. Their LL-37 levels were lower too, and the two measures rose and fell together across patients. The protein that carries vitamin D in blood was lowest in patients with sepsis. The link supports a simple idea: too little vitamin D may leave the body's first-line germ defense underpowered, right when patients need it most. The authors call for trials testing whether topping up the vitamin helps.
europmc-pmc2717440:
Van Rompaey and co-authors followed intensive care patients in 2009 to find what raises the risk of delirium, a sudden state of confused thinking and poor attention. Care has shifted from treating delirium to preventing it, which needs clear risk factors. They screened newly admitted adults in four hospitals in Belgium with a nurse-rated confusion scale.

Delirium arose in about three in ten of the five hundred twenty-three patients, and age alone was not a strong factor. Heavy smoking, daily drinking, living alone, and prior thinking problems raised risk. So did tubes and drains, strong illness, sedative drugs, isolation, no visitors, no daylight, and physical restraints, which carried the highest odds of all.
europmc-pmc2736840:
Cook, Chow, and Devesa analyzed in 2009 United States esophageal cancer rates from 1977 to 2005 by race, sex, and tissue type. The two main types, adenocarcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma, have distinct causes and had shown opposite trends in Blacks and Whites. Patterns in Asian, Pacific Islander, and Hispanic groups were far less known.

Total rates rose only among Whites, and White men's rates passed Black men's rates in 2004. Squamous cell rates fell in nearly all groups, with Hispanic and Asian men's rates between those of Blacks and Whites. Adenocarcinoma rates among Hispanic men may now be rising, as they once did in Whites and Blacks. Sex ratios also varied markedly by group and type.
europmc-pmc2737140:
Kelly, Wilson, and Heymsfield built in 2009 reference values for body composition. They used dual-energy X-ray scans from the national NHANES survey of the United States. The scans measure percent fat, fat and lean mass scaled to height, and bone mineral across the whole body. Data came from a population sample scanned in fifteen counties from 1999 to 2004, covering ages eight to eighty-five.

They partitioned values by sex and ethnicity, with adult values aligned to age and child values aligned to age, height, or lean mass. They also built an obesity scheme that matches standard body mass index cutoffs in young adults to fat mass index thresholds. The tables can guide care, trial entry rules, and population studies of fat, lean, and bone disorders.
europmc-pmc2790440:
Knight and co-authors reviewed bleeding after childbirth, called postpartum hemorrhage, across six wealthy countries for an international working group in 2009. Heavy bleeding after birth is a leading cause of death and serious harm for mothers around the world, and several reports had flagged rising rates.

The group compared records from six countries: Australia, Belgium, Canada, and France, plus the United Kingdom and the United States. Rates rose in Australia, Canada, the United Kingdom, and the United States, even though each country defined the condition in its own way. In three of those countries the rise came only from bleeding tied to a womb that failed to contract, and severe harm from bleeding also climbed.
europmc-pmc2860140:
Abdul-Ghani and DeFronzo reviewed in 2010 why skeletal muscle stops responding well to insulin, a core defect in type 2 diabetes. Muscle normally takes up most of the sugar from a meal under insulin's signal. When muscle resists that signal, blood sugar stays high and diabetes follows, often alongside obesity.

The review lays out a chain of faults inside the muscle cell. The insulin signal itself weakens, sugar gates open poorly, and sugar is stored and burned more slowly once inside. Fat handling goes wrong too, and fat byproducts build up in muscle and jam the signal further. The authors also weigh evidence that the cell's energy factories, the mitochondria, work less well in many insulin-resistant states.
europmc-pmc2872640:
Van Bakel, Nislow, Blencowe, and Hughes tested in 2010 whether the genome is copied into RNA far beyond its known genes, as several reports had claimed. The extra copies were nicknamed dark matter transcripts, since their origin and purpose were unclear. The team used short-read RNA sequencing, which samples millions of RNA fragments, in mouse and human tissues.

Most fragments landed inside known genes or just beside them, as extensions and variants of familiar transcripts. Only a small share came from distant stretches between genes. The results also imply that most of the genome is not copied at all in the tissues tested. The finding shrank the supposed dark matter greatly and recast most odd transcripts as parts of known genes.
europmc-pmc2888740:
Patra and colleagues pooled in 2010 the evidence on drinking and stroke, taking care to separate stroke types and outcomes. Alcohol's link to stroke looked tangled across studies. It differed by sex. It differed by whether the stroke came from a clot or a bleed, and by whether the outcome was illness or death. Their review covered twenty-six observational studies spanning three decades of literature.

Heavy drinking raised the risk of both stroke types and of dying from them. Light to moderate drinking showed a split pattern, tracking lower risk of clot-caused stroke in several analyses while offering no such shelter against bleeding strokes, where risk climbed with dose. Keeping morbidity and mortality apart, and the sexes apart, sharpened advice that lumping all strokes together had blurred.
europmc-pmc2909940:
Li and a large team of curators described in 2010 BioModels Database, a free online library of checked math models of living systems. Such models are sets of equations that mimic cells and pathways over time. They were growing fast in journals but were stored in odd formats that others could not reuse. The database keeps models that passed peer review and tests each one.

Each stored model is checked so that it runs and gives the same results as its paper. Its parts are tagged and linked to gene, protein, and chemical databases, so each part has a clear identity. Users can browse, search, and download models, and run them online. The aim is to turn models into shared building blocks for the field.
europmc-pmc2920840:
Skaar framed in 2010 the contest for iron between invading bacteria and their vertebrate hosts as a battle over a starved resource. Bacteria need iron to grow, and hosts exploit that need through nutritional immunity. Iron is locked inside cells in the storage protein ferritin or bound into hemoglobin. Meanwhile, the blood protein transferrin grips free iron with extraordinary strength. Almost no free iron circulates for a germ to grab.

Successful pathogens therefore carry theft tools, from secreted scavenger molecules that strip iron from host proteins to pumps that import hemoglobin pieces directly. Hosts counter by hiding iron deeper during infection and by proteins that snatch the scavengers themselves. Each weapon in this arms race is a candidate drug target, since starving a pathogen needs no antibiotic in the classic sense.
europmc-pmc2954140:
Andrews and co-authors pooled trials of computer-delivered therapy for anxiety and depression in a 2010 meta-analysis. Talking therapy based on cognitive behaviour methods works for these common disorders, but too few therapists limits access.

Across more than twenty controlled comparisons, computer programmes beat control conditions by a large average margin, with gains seen in depression, panic, social fear, and general anxiety alike. Benefits held for roughly half a year of follow-up, patients stuck with the programmes, and satisfaction ran high. A handful of head-to-head trials found computer delivery about as helpful as meeting a therapist in person.
europmc-pmc3021840:
Oostenveld, Fries, Maris, and Schoffelen presented FieldTrip, an open-source toolbox for analysing brain recordings, in a 2011 article. The package handles magnetic and electrical brain signals plus invasive recordings, as a toolbox inside the MATLAB environment.

Its functions span simple summaries to advanced work. They cover time and frequency analysis, source rebuilding by several methods, and connectivity measures. They also include plain statistical tests at sensor and source level. A consistent design lets users script complex analyses of large datasets in neat batches. Being open and modular, the code invites extension and reuse inside other packages, and development has continued since 2003.
europmc-pmc3113940:
Yves Dehouck and colleagues introduced a web tool for predicting how single changes in a protein affect its stability, in a 2011 paper in BMC Bioinformatics. Designing sturdier proteins matters for industry and medicine, and single-letter changes in patients can also cause disease by weakening a protein. Their server aims to judge such changes in seconds.

The tool combines scoring rules that depend on how exposed the changed spot is to water, and its forecasts matched measured changes well in tests. It can scan every possible change in a mid-sized protein in under a minute, and it also flags stretches whose letters look poorly suited to stability. Those weak stretches often mark active sites, guiding both disease studies and protein design.
europmc-pmc3146540:
Benjamin Volkmer and Matthias Heinemann measured the size and contents of a model bacterium across growth conditions in a 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. Systems biology models need cell counts and volumes to turn lab averages into the concentrations inside a single cell. For the best-studied bacterium of all, those basics were missing or assumed fixed.

Growing the bacterium in twenty-two conditions, they found cell volume grows with growth speed, which fits intuition. Yet the total volume packed into a standard cloudy sample stayed nearly the same in every condition. Cell number in a sample can also be read from cloudiness plus growth rate. The tables let modellers convert bulk measurements into per-cell copy numbers and concentrations correctly, instead of guessing.
europmc-pmc3177840:
Emese Prandovszky and colleagues showed that a common brain parasite boosts a key mood chemical in a 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. The parasite is famous for changing rodent behaviour so cats catch the host more easily, completing its life cycle, and hints pointed at dopamine. The team infected dopamine-making cells in the lab and examined infected mouse brains.

Infected cells released several times more of the chemical when stimulated, in direct proportion to how many cells were infected. Parasite cysts in brain tissue stained strongly for it, and the parasite's own version of the rate-limiting enzyme for making it sat inside those cysts. The parasite thus carries the tools to step up this chemistry itself. The mechanism may also bear on behaviour reports in infected people.
europmc-pmc3197640:
Sebastian Schaaf and colleagues reported in 2011 on heart tissue grown in the lab from human embryonic stem cells. Their goal was a test platform for basic heart research and for checking whether new drugs might harm the heart, since real human heart cells are hard to obtain. The team built the tissue in a simple twenty-four-well format using fibrin.

The tissue strips began beating together within about a week and kept strong, regular contractions for up to eight weeks. Under the microscope they showed a dense network of aligned, cross-striped heart muscle cells. Recordings showed normal responses to calcium and to a stimulating drug, while several known risk drugs slowed relaxation and caused irregular beating at realistic doses.
europmc-pmc3221040:
Justin Chumbley, Keith Worsley, Guillaume Flandin, and Karl Friston described a new statistical safeguard for brain imaging in this 2010 technical note in NeuroImage. Brain scans are tested at thousands of locations, so researchers must control false discoveries without wiping out real signal. Their procedure works on the peaks of a statistical map rather than on individual points.

Drawing on random field theory, the method assigns each local maximum a significance value, then sets an adaptive threshold that keeps the false discovery rate in check. Simulations compared it with family-wise error control and with cluster-wise and voxel-wise alternatives. Peak-level control proved more sensitive than the stricter standard at little cost in false positives, and far more spatially accurate than voxel-wise control. An attention study illustrates the method.
europmc-pmc3270040:
Carlos Cruchaga and colleagues sequenced five dementia genes in hundreds of families with late-onset Alzheimer's disease, in this 2012 paper in PLoS ONE. Mutations in these genes were established causes of rare early-onset forms, but nobody had systematically screened large late-onset families. The team read the genes in probands from families with four or more affected members.

About one sequenced person in seven carried a novel or pathogenic variant. Eight clearly harmful variants turned up, including new ones, spread across four of the genes. Other variants did not track neatly with disease in families yet appeared more often in patients than in the general population, suggesting they modify risk. Overall, rare variants in these genes were significantly enriched in the families. The authors argue such variants explain part of Alzheimer's heritability that genome-wide scans miss.
europmc-pmc3295340:
Philippat and colleagues studied whether chemicals found in everyday products affect the size of newborn boys, reporting in 2012. The chemicals, called phthalates and phenols, appear in plastics, cosmetics, food packaging, and sunscreen. Using two French mother and child study groups, the team measured breakdown products of these chemicals in urine samples taken during pregnancy.

Boys whose mothers had higher levels of two related chlorine based phenols tended to weigh less at birth. A sunscreen ingredient showed the opposite pattern, linking to slightly higher weight and a larger head. A common plastics chemical also linked to a larger head, while phthalate measures showed no steady pattern with birth weight.
europmc-pmc3322940:
Person and members of a national SARS outreach team described the fear and stigma that trailed the 2003 SARS epidemic in the United States, in a 2004 article. New diseases arrive wrapped in uncertainty, and frightened people often turn on those linked to the illness. That reaction is not just cruel; sick people who fear blame may hide symptoms and delay care, helping the germ spread.

The team explains how officials quickly assessed and monitored fear across the country. Widespread panic did not take hold in the general public, but Asian American communities bore the brunt of suspicion and discrimination. The authors argue that outbreak response must protect health without singling out groups, and they offer strategies for tracking and calming fear as a core part of epidemic control.
europmc-pmc3380840:
Kiryluk led a worldwide genetics study in 2012 of IgA nephropathy, a leading cause of kidney failure. The disease is common in Asians, less so in Europeans, and rare in Africans. The team retested five known risk regions in eight new cohorts, then mapped risk across eighty-five populations.

Four regions held up strongly, and all five were solid in the combined group of more than ten thousand people. Two fresh risk variants turned up inside one chromosome region, along with a notable interplay between two loci. A seven-marker risk score climbed steadily eastward and northward from Africa, matching the known disease gradient. Gene geography, they conclude, helps explain who gets this kidney disease.
europmc-pmc3385440:
Karagas led a synthesis in 2012 of what low-level methylmercury exposure does to human health. This form of mercury, picked up mainly by eating fish, is a known nerve poison at high doses. The review excluded places with very high fish intake to focus on everyday exposure levels.

Recent studies hint that low exposure may slow fetal and infant growth in some groups. Effects on the developing brain seem to vary with age, sex, and timing of exposure. For heart disease, no clear pattern emerged across studies, and immune results were inconsistent. The authors ask for work on who is most susceptible and how the harm works, to guide food and safety policy.
europmc-pmc3434440:
Peelle and Davis reviewed in 2012 how the slow rhythm of speech carries meaning into the listener's brain.
