Speech swells and fades in a quasi-regular pattern that marks how sounds are made, which syllables carry stress, and how fast someone talks. Listeners lean on that envelope heavily for understanding.

Brain recordings show cortical rhythms locking onto the slow envelope of speech, in step with its stressed beats. That locking works like a prediction of when important sounds will land, sharpening sensitivity to them. It also helps explain why the speed of earlier speech bends how later sounds are heard. Intelligible speech recruits left-brain regions beyond the shared listening areas. Rhythm, they argue, is the scaffold comprehension hangs on.
europmc-pmc3441440:
Iyer and colleagues showed in 2012 that a tiny RNA called miR-146a acts as a brake on inflammation in astrocytes, the brain's support cells. Tiny RNAs fine-tune gene activity, and this one is a known regulator of the built-in immune response. The team studied epilepsy-linked brain lesions where immune activation runs hot, plus cultured human astrocytes.

The tiny RNA ran high in the lesions and shot up in cultured cells exposed to the inflammatory signal IL-1 beta. Raising it muted the pathway's relay proteins and cut output of inflammatory products; lowering it did the reverse. Several released cytokines followed its lead. The picture is a negative-feedback loop switched on by inflammation itself. The authors float the RNA as a drug target for chronic brain inflammation.
europmc-pmc3511440:
Dengue's timing shapes diagnosis and outbreak control, and Miranda Chan, Michael A. Johansson, and Nikos Vasilakis pin down its incubation periods in 2012. They pool 146 mosquito observations from 8 studies and 204 human observations from 35 studies, and fit them with Bayesian time-to-event models.

At 25 degrees, 95 percent of mosquito incubation periods fall between five and thirty-three days, with a mean near fifteen. At 30 degrees the range shrinks to two to fifteen days, with a mean near six and a half. In humans the mean is just under six days, with 95 percent between days three and ten. No gap appears between dengue types. The fitted curves feed outbreak tracing and spread models.
europmc-pmc3514540:
Brain atlases need ground truth, and Arno Klein and Jason Tourville supply it in 2012 with Mindboggle-101, the largest free set of manually labeled human brain images then available. Magnetic resonance scans of 101 healthy participants were labeled by hand for their surface anatomy.

To keep labeling consistent, the pair created the Desikan-Killiany-Tourville protocol, which leans on robust anatomical landmarks and starts from automated labels needing only small manual edits. The dataset serves as reference atlases for labeling new brains and as a healthy baseline against clinical groups. The authors also benchmark automated labeling methods against their manual labels, giving algorithm builders a fair test track.
europmc-pmc3528440:
Thinking clearly suffers in schizophrenia, and Mario Fioravanti, Valentina Bianchi, and Maria Elena Cinti update the pooled evidence in 2012. Their meta-analysis, refreshing a 2005 version, gathers controlled studies published through March 2010: 247 papers and 18,300 cases comparing patients with healthy subjects.

Five domains are scored: memory, global cognition, language, executive function, and attention. In every domain, and every sub-analysis, patients perform significantly worse. Studies disagree with each other a great deal, though, with age, sex, sample size, patient type, and test choice all contributing. The authors also flag publication bias: negative studies vanish from the record, so pooled gaps may overstate the truth somewhat.
europmc-pmc3546740:
Tiny plant hairs manufacture chemical weapons, and Joris J. Glas and five colleagues review glandular trichomes as breeding and engineering targets in 2012. Found on about 30 percent of vascular plants, these hairs produce much of a plant's secondary chemistry, including essential oils prized for fragrance and pharmaceuticals.

The chemistry evolved as defense against herbivores and pathogens, stored in a tip compartment on the hair. Because hairs are easy to harvest, their metabolites, genes, and proteins are unusually well mapped. Breeders and engineers can now tune hair density and output, either to boost oil production or to sharpen a crop's built-in pest resistance. The review surveys that metabolic diversity and its uses.
europmc-pmc3559840:
Pilar Suñé, Josep Maria Suñé, and Bruno Montoro studied publication bias in PLoS ONE in 2013, asking whether a drug trial's outcome shapes whether its results ever appear in print. Their source material was every drug trial approved by one general hospital ethics committee between 1997 and 2004, followed forward to see which ones reached publication and how fast.

Fewer than half of the 785 trials were published. The outcome clearly mattered. About 85 percent of trials with positive results were published, against about 69 percent of trials with negative results. Positive trials also appeared sooner, in roughly two years at the median. Journal prestige, measured by impact factor, did not differ by outcome. The findings warn readers that the printed record favors good news about new drugs.
europmc-pmc3570540:
Mark Tomlinson and colleagues asked a blunt question in PLoS Medicine in 2013: is mobile health ready to scale up? Phones reach over six billion subscribers, and pilots using them for care, reminders, and data collection run into the hundreds. Donors and governments show wide enthusiasm. What the field lacks, the authors argue, is program-level proof that these schemes work when rolled out for real populations.

Hundreds of pilot studies have produced little evidence fit to guide large programs. Stronger designs are proposed instead, including randomized trials, multi-part strategies that test components together, and farming of routine program data. Recommendations cover evidence standards, systems that can talk to each other, and the roles of governments, companies, and researchers. The piece is a caution against growing programs faster than the proof beneath them.
europmc-pmc3573940:
Evgeniya Antonova and colleagues priced the cost of shinbone fractures that fail to heal in BMC Musculoskeletal Disorders in 2013. A break in the tibia shaft is common and usually mends, but in some patients the bone never knits, a state called nonunion. The team mined a large United States insurance claims database to compare patients whose fractures healed with the minority whose did not, over two years of follow-up.

Of 853 patients, 99, about twelve percent, developed nonunion. They arrived with more other illnesses and more open fractures, then collected more extra fractures, surgery, hospital stays, and physical therapy. Median total care cost ran to 25,556 dollars against 11,686 dollars for healed fractures, more than double. Nearly every category of care cost more. The numbers give hospitals and insurers a concrete price tag for failed healing.
europmc-pmc3637140:
Tiny bits of titanium dioxide, a white powder used in many goods, are weighed for harm in a 2013 review in Particle and Fibre Toxicology by Shi and three co-authors. The bits are far smaller than the fine powder form and may act in new ways in the body. Most past work dealt with breathing them in at work, where lungs are the main route in.

The review finds that the bits can move from lung or gut to other organs, though at a low rate. Most skin tests show no pass through the outer skin layer. Injected into veins, they caused harm in liver, spleen, kidneys and brain, often at very high doses. Long-term breathing tests in rats found lung tumours. Hard data on people are still lacking, and the authors mark that gap plainly.
europmc-pmc3775240:
Sara Castiglioni, Alessandra Cazzaniga, Walter Albisetti, and Jeanette Maier wrote a review in Nutrients in 2013 on magnesium and osteoporosis. Bone health needs tight control of magnesium, a mineral that shapes how bone crystals form and how bone cells work. Both too little and too much appear harmful.

Low magnesium adds to osteoporosis risk in two ways. It acts on crystals and cells themselves, and it also throws off parathyroid hormone and feeds low-grade inflammation. Why high magnesium harms the building of bone mineral is less clear. Most evidence points to magnesium as one factor in bone health. The authors judge that fixing a true shortage is a cheap, sensible step, while giving supplements to everyone remains doubtful since excess also harms bone.
europmc-pmc3799540:
Cafazzo and colleagues described in the Journal of Medical Internet Research in 2012 how they built bant. It is a phone app meant to help teenagers with type 1 diabetes check their blood sugar more often. The design came from interviews with young patients, who asked for simple logging, reminders, and small rewards.

In a twelve-week pilot with twenty patients aged twelve to sixteen, daily glucose checks rose from 2.4 to 3.6 per day, a gain of about half. The app handed out 161 rewards for steady checking, and fourteen of sixteen teens who rated it said they were satisfied. The team presents bant as an early test of game-like rewards in diabetes care, not as proof of better long-term control.
europmc-pmc3830740:
Veronique V. Belzil and a team of co-authors study a gene fault behind two brain diseases in Acta Neuropathologica in 2013. A stretched repeat in the C9orf72 gene is a common cause of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and frontotemporal dementia. Patients with the fault show lower output of that gene, and the team ask why.

Brain tissue from patients showed chemical marks on the packing proteins of DNA piled on the stretched repeat. Such marks are known to shut genes down, which fits the low gene output seen in frontal cortex and cerebellum. The same mark could be read in blood, not just brain. That opens a path to a blood test that tracks the fault's effect. Cell lines from carriers backed the tissue findings.
europmc-pmc3857040:
Keren I. Hulkower and Renee L. Herber review cell movement assays in Pharmaceutics, dated 2011 in the record. Cell migration, the crawl of cells from place to place, drives wound healing and cancer spread. Drug hunters need lab tests that mimic that crawl well and run at scale.

The review covers the main test formats. Scratch tests watch cells close a gap in a cell sheet. Membrane tests count cells that cross a porous wall. Tiny fluid channel devices steer cells with fine control, and zone tests bar cells from a patch then watch them fill it. New imaging rigs let these tests run early in drug hunts, so weak leads drop out fast and side effects show sooner.
europmc-pmc3872040:
Lorena Ruiz, Abelardo Margolles, and Borja Sánchez review bile resistance in gut bacteria in Frontiers in Microbiology in 2013. Probiotic bacteria must cross the gut alive to help their host. Bile salts, made by the liver to dissolve fats, are the main hazard on that trip, since they tear cell walls and harm DNA.

The two big probiotic groups, Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium, carry a kit of defenses. Some pumps expel bile, some enzymes disarm it, and wall changes blunt its attack. Stress response systems add a further shield. The review sorts these defenses by type and by how well each is proven. Knowing the kit helps makers pick strains that survive the trip and helps explain why some products fail to take hold.
europmc-pmc3877040:
Renee M. Petri and a team of co-authors profile cattle gut microbes in PLoS One in 2013. The rumen, the cow's fermenting stomach chamber, hosts bacteria that turn feed into energy. Shifting cattle from grass to grain, and the acid upset that can follow, may remake that community.

Heifers were fed forage, then eased onto a rich concentrate diet, put through an acid challenge, and let to recover. Deep gene reads of solid and liquid rumen contents tracked the bacteria at each stage. Diet change moved the mix more than host differences did. A core set of bacterial groups held across animals and stages, most from two big phyla. Richness peaked on mixed diets. The map helps feed managers judge gut health during diet shifts.
europmc-pmc3906940:
Daniel J. Macqueen and Ian A. Johnston date a key event in fish evolution. Their paper appeared in Proceedings of the Royal Society B in 2014. The event is the doubling of the whole genome in the ancestor of salmon and trout. Many had linked that doubling to the family's later spread into many species. That link had never been tested.

The pair used gene copies kept from the doubling across the family's main lines. With set molecular clocks, they place the event no later than 88 million years ago. That is long before the subfamilies split. The later spread of species tracks climate cooling and the ice ages instead. Fish that move between sea and fresh water also split into new species faster.
europmc-pmc3917240:
Matthew Giannandrea and William C. Parks review, in Disease Models and Mechanisms in 2014, the mixed roles of a family of enzymes in fibrosis, the harmful build-up of scar-like matrix in organs. The enzymes, matrix metalloproteinases, cut up the protein scaffolding between cells. Logic might suggest they should fight fibrosis, and that the disease would show too little of them.

Mouse studies tell a more tangled story. Some of these enzymes protect against fibrosis, while others promote it. Their effects reach well beyond chewing up matrix: they steer cell growth and survival, gene activity, and several parts of inflammation. The authors argue that judging any one enzyme requires knowing which proteins it cuts in a given tissue and stage of disease.
europmc-pmc3930140:
Koji Yamano, Adam I. Fogel, Chunxin Wang, Alexander M. van der Bliek, and Richard J. Youle explain in eLife in 2014 how cells wrap damaged mitochondria neatly for disposal. The disposal process, mitophagy, removes worn-out mitochondria, and two proteins mutated in Parkinson's disease, PINK1 and Parkin, start it. What was unclear is how the wrapping membrane fits itself around one damaged mitochondrion so precisely.

The answer centers on TBC1D15, a protein sitting on mitochondria that switches off a partner called Rab7. By holding Rab7 in check and gripping both the mitochondrion and the growing membrane, TBC1D15 shapes the wrapping sac to its cargo. A relative, TBC1D17, joins in and partners with it. Together they ensure only proper assemblies form around the target.
europmc-pmc3936740:
Amin Espah Borujeni, Anirudh S. Channarasappa, and Howard M. Salis work out what sets the speed at which bacteria start making a protein, in Nucleic Acids Research in 2014. The ribosome, the cell's protein builder, must first grip the start of a messenger RNA. Many bacterial messages have long, folded head regions that can hide that grip site, and the physics of how the ribosome copes was poorly understood.

The team tested folded standby sites, parking spots above the start signal where a ribosome can wait. These interactions changed start rates more than a hundredfold. What mattered was exposed single-stranded surface, partial unfolding that lowers the grip's energy cost, and the chance to slide into place. Their physics-based model predicted start rates accurately for 136 synthetic head regions, a tool for designing genetic circuits.
europmc-pmc3948040:
Kun Lu and colleagues test whether arsenic in drinking water disturbs the gut microbes of mice, in Environmental Health Perspectives in 2014. Arsenic exposure affects large populations worldwide and is linked to cancer, diabetes, and heart disease. The gut microbiome helps run metabolism and immunity, and it can be reshaped by outside chemicals, making it a possible hidden route for arsenic's harms.

Mice drank water with 10 parts per million of arsenic for four weeks. Gene sequencing showed their gut microbe communities shifted significantly, and chemical profiling found many microbe-related compounds disturbed across several body samples. Arsenic thus changed not just which microbes were present but what the community was doing. The authors propose gut disruption as a mechanism worth testing in arsenic-exposed people.
europmc-pmc3980040:
Min Fang, Jingping Yuan, Chunwei Peng, and Yan Li review collagen as a double-edged sword in cancer, in Tumour Biology in 2014. Collagen is the main scaffold of the tissue around tumors. It was once pictured as a passive wall holding cancer back, and dense collagen can indeed cage a tumor. But tumors constantly break down and rebuild this scaffold, and the remodeling itself sends mechanical signals that both tumor and support cells can feel.

Those signals can push invasion, new blood vessel growth, and migration, helping the cancer spread. Which edge of the sword dominates depends on the stage of disease and the state of the scaffold. The review follows collagen through breakdown and re-deposition, tension balance in tissue, and the pull forces cells exert, to explain the switch from barrier to accomplice.
europmc-pmc4063340:
Donald B. Smith and colleagues updated the agreed classification of hepatitis C virus variants. Their consensus study appeared in Hepatology in 2014. A shared naming system matters because virus type shapes disease study and treatment choices, and sequence data had grown hugely since the 2005 proposal.

Working from more than thirteen hundred near-complete virus genomes in public databases as of May 2013, the team settled naming conflicts and set clear criteria for assignment. The result places hepatitis C virus in seven confirmed genotypes and sixty-seven subtypes, with some sequences still unassigned. They also built a web resource, hosted by an international virus taxonomy body, that keeps reference tables updated for researchers and clinicians.
europmc-pmc4086140:
David Gfeller, Aurélien Grosdidier, Matthias Wirth, Antoine Daina, Olivier Michielin, and Vincent Zoete launched SwissTargetPrediction, a web server that guesses the protein targets of active small molecules. Their paper appeared in Nucleic Acids Research in 2014. Knowing what a drug or metabolite binds explains its effects and warns of side effects.

The server blends flat 2D similarity and 3D shape similarity against compounds with known targets. Predictions run in five organisms, and results can be mapped between species through related proteins. Large public datasets of measured interactions make such knowledge-based guessing possible. The tool is free with no login. It forms part of a Swiss suite for computer-aided drug design, with closer links to docking tools planned.
europmc-pmc4095940:
Ignacio Izeddin, Maxime Dahan, Xavier Darzacq, and colleagues tracked single transcription factor molecules inside living cell nuclei. Their study appeared in eLife in 2014. Gene control depends on these factors finding their target sites, yet most earlier work measured only how fast they diffuse, ignoring nuclear layout.

Two factors behaved very differently. c-Myc roamed the whole nucleus, so each molecule could reach any site equally. The elongation factor P-TEFb instead explored locally, oversampling its own neighbourhood, so its access to targets depended on position. The authors argue that interactions with nuclear structures, not simple exclusion, shape each protein's search geometry. Nuclear architecture, in other words, helps govern how genes get switched on in space and time.
europmc-pmc4169640:
Ali A. Mokdad, Mohsen Naghavi, and six co-authors mapped deaths from liver cirrhosis across 187 countries in BMC Medicine in 2014. Cirrhosis is a major cause of death that gets less attention than its toll warrants. The team pulled death records and verbal autopsy data covering 1980 to 2010 and corrected for miscoded causes.

World deaths from cirrhosis rose from about 676,000 in 1980 to over one million in 2010, near 2 percent of all deaths. Yet the death rate per head, adjusted for age, fell by 22 percent, led by drops in China, the United States, and Western Europe. Egypt and Moldova had the highest rates in 2010, while rates climbed by about a third in the United Kingdom. The authors urge stronger prevention where rates are high or rising.
europmc-pmc4191440:
Laura Zoratti, Laura Jaakola, and three co-authors reviewed how light drives colour compounds in fruit in Frontiers in Plant Science in 2014. Flavonoids give many fruits their colour and much of their health value. Light is the strongest outside signal controlling how much of them a plant makes.

The review sorts light effects by length of day, brightness, direction, and colour of light, including ultraviolet. Specific wavelengths switch on MYB transcription factors, gene controllers that each steer production of distinct flavonoids. Bagging fruit, shade, and orchard layout therefore change the chemistry of the harvest. The authors note the signal chain from light sensor to pigment gene still has gaps. Knowing it fully would let breeders plan fruit with richer, steadier flavonoid content.
europmc-pmc4255240:
Nikola T. Markov, Colette Dehay, and ten co-authors weighed the wiring between visual brain areas in the Journal of Comparative Neurology in 2014. The visual cortex is a ladder of areas passing signals up and down. Tracer studies in macaques had suggested the layer a connection starts from reveals its rung distance, an idea the team tested at scale.

Counting labelled neurons by layer across many area pairs gave a clean index of hierarchical distance that exposed unsuspected relations between areas. Ascending and descending streams run segregated in the upper layers, in precise point-to-point fashion, while lower layers carry broader, diffuse versions of both. Descending feedback paths proved lighter, longer-ranging, and more numerous than ascending feedforward ones. The cortex, they conclude, is built from paired counterstreams, not a simple ladder.
europmc-pmc4266040:
Javier Blesa and Serge Przedborski review animal models of Parkinson's disease in Frontiers in Neuroanatomy, published in 2014. The disease kills dopamine neurons in a small midbrain area, the substantia nigra, and the review asks why those cells are so easy to harm while nearby cells survive.

The review compares toxin based models with newer genetic models built from genes linked to the disease. It weighs what each model shows about cell loss, Lewy bodies, and the spread of harm over time. Readers get a clear map of what animal work can and cannot prove about the causes of Parkinson's disease.
europmc-pmc4320440:
David Moher and seven co-authors present PRISMA-P, a checklist for writing the protocol of a systematic review before the review begins. Their statement appeared in Systematic Reviews in 2015. A protocol states the question, the hypothesis, and the planned methods, yet few published reviews say whether one exists.

The seventeen item checklist guides authors through what a sound protocol should disclose, from eligibility rules to analysis plans. With the plan on record, readers can spot later changes in method and selective reporting of results. The authors urge funders to require the checklist in grant applications and editors to use it in peer review. It extends the PRISMA family from finished reviews to their blueprints.
europmc-pmc4327440:
Lucy Yardley, Leanne Morrison, Katherine Bradbury, and Ingrid Muller set out the person-based approach to building digital health tools that people will actually use. Their paper appeared in the Journal of Medical Internet Research in 2015. Apps and websites meant to change health behavior often fail because their design ignores how target users think and live.

The approach runs qualitative research with intended users at every stage, from planning to final testing. Their views then shape the behavior change techniques inside the tool. It is designed to sit beside theory based and evidence based methods, not replace them. Case examples from the team's own interventions show how user insight changed content and tone.
europmc-pmc4330640:
Jacob Lorenzo-Morales, Naveed A. Khan, and Julia Walochnik update current knowledge of Acanthamoeba keratitis, a severe eye infection. Their review appeared in Parasite in 2015. The free living amoeba attacks the cornea, mostly in contact lens wearers, and reported cases rise year by year worldwide despite better drugs and care.

Late diagnosis is a core problem: early signs mimic other eye infections, and current drug regimens are harsh and often slow. The review covers how the amoeba attaches, invades, and damages the cornea, and which of its traits might serve as targets for faster tests or better treatments. It also treats the cyst stage that lets the amoeba survive therapy. The authors aim the update at clinicians and researchers alike.
europmc-pmc4397040:
Jeffrey Klarenbeek, Joachim Goedhart, Aernoud van Batenburg, Daniella Groenewald, and Kees Jalink presented a fourth generation of sensors for a key cell messenger, in PLoS ONE in 2015. The messenger cAMP steers many cell decisions, and Epac-based sensors watch it live: two fluorescent proteins exchange energy as cAMP binds, shifting the light signal. Their new sensors pair the brightest, most bleach-resistant donor protein available with a doubled acceptor, giving exceptional brightness, stability, and signal range.

One change to the sensing part doubled its grip on cAMP, raising affinity about two and a half fold for work at low levels. Dedicated variants serve different instruments: ratio imaging for most microscopes, and dark-acceptor versions for lifetime imaging, where the glow's duration nearly doubles when cAMP saturates. The team recommends this generation for future studies.
europmc-pmc4506540:
Nuria Plattner and Frank Noé used computer simulation to watch a protein grab its target, in a 2015 Nature Communications paper. Their test pair was trypsin, an enzyme that cuts other proteins, and benzamidine, a small molecule that blocks it. How a protein's shifting shape changes the speed of binding matters for drug design, yet it is hard to see directly.

From 150 microseconds of atom-level simulation, the pair built a Markov model, a map of states and the odds of moving between them. Trypsin settled into seven long-lived shapes, each with a distinct binding pocket. The shapes swapped over tens of microseconds and differed in how tightly and how fast they bound the blocker. Each shape also matched a known structure from a changed or related enzyme.
europmc-pmc4527340:
Thomas J. Waltz leads an eight-author team sorting the tools used to change health care practice, in Implementation Science in 2015. Getting proven care into routine use takes deliberate strategies, but the field names them inconsistently, which blocks comparison across studies. The ERIC project had already compiled 73 named strategies; this stage asked experts to judge how they relate.

Thirty-five experts in the field and in clinical work grouped the strategies by likeness using concept mapping, then rated each for importance and feasibility. The clusters show how the strategies hang together as families, and the ratings spot which ones experts see as both vital and doable. The map gives planners a shared vocabulary for picking and reporting strategies.
europmc-pmc4531540:
Sofia Sousa leads a twelve-author team on how breast tumors train immune cells to help them, in Breast Cancer Research in 2015. Macrophages, immune cells that eat debris and germs, can make up 5 to 40% of a solid tumor's mass. Inside tumors they usually take the M2 state, which calms immunity and rebuilds tissue, favoring growth, instead of the attacking M1 state.

The team stained 562 primary breast tumor samples to map macrophage numbers and states, and linked the patterns to survival. In lab tests, they grew blood-derived macrophages with and without breast cancer cells to watch the teaching happen. The work clarifies how tumors push macrophages toward the helpful M2 state in breast cancer.
europmc-pmc4559140:
Coen H. Wiegman leads a twelve-author team linking damaged cell power units to lung disease, in The Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology in 2015. In chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, inflamed airways narrow and worsen over time. Oxidative stress, an overload of reactive oxygen, is a prime suspect, and the mitochondria that make energy are both source and victim of that stress.

Ozone-exposed mice developed lung inflammation, twitchy airways, and faulty mitochondria. Airway muscle cells from patients showed the same pattern, tied to remodeling of the airway wall. A mitochondria-targeted antioxidant, MitoQ, countered several of these effects in the tests. The work casts mitochondrial failure as a driver worth treating, not just a byproduct.
europmc-pmc4581240:
Amelia Ahmad Khalili and Mohd Ridzuan Ahmad review how cells stick, in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences in 2015. Cell adhesion governs how cells talk, how tissues form and hold, and how a cell answers the material around it. That centrality has spawned a crowded toolbox for measuring stickiness, which the review sets out to organize.

Studies split into attachment events and detachment events, and each can be run on whole populations or on single cells. The techniques serve cell signaling research, implant materials, artificial bone and tooth design, and tissue-on-a-chip systems. Biochemical treatments and environmental shifts can also be tested through adhesion readouts. The review maps which approach fits which question.
europmc-pmc4624940:
A team led by Benjamin F. Mentiplay published a 2015 study testing hand-held devices for measuring leg muscle strength and power. Clinicians like hand-held dynamometers because they are portable, but their trustworthiness for power measures was unproven. Thirty healthy young adults were tested in two sessions. The work appeared in PLOS ONE and included a fixed laboratory dynamometer for comparison.

A peak 200-millisecond window proved the best way to calculate the rate of force development, their power measure. Repeat tests by the same and different testers, and across two hand-held brands, were mostly good to excellent for hip and knee muscles. Agreement with the fixed machine was weaker for ankle muscles. Hand-held testing can therefore serve for most leg muscle groups when a laboratory machine is unavailable.
europmc-pmc4659840:
A 2015 study patterning single cells with sound waves, placing one cell per acoustic well came from David J. Collins and colleagues. Watching individual cells over time requires trapping them at set positions. Mechanical traps work but are hard to reuse. Their device uses high-frequency acoustic fields whose wavelength is close to cell size. The work appeared in Nature Communications.

The team patterned particles of several sizes and then live cells, including human lymphocytes and red blood cells infected with the malaria parasite Plasmodium falciparum. Cells sat in neat two-dimensional arrays, one per well, ready for long observation. Because the method is contact-free and reusable, it suits single-cell studies where population averages hide the behaviour that matters, from drug response to parasite growth inside a cell.
europmc-pmc4669740:
A 2015 study by Ming-Zhu Ma and colleagues deals with CCAT1, a long non-coding RNA that promotes gallbladder cancer. CCAT1 was first found in colon cancer and had been tied to gastric cancer growth. Gallbladder cancer is the most common bile tract cancer. The team measured CCAT1 in tumour tissue and cancer cells. The work appeared in Cell Death and Disease.

CCAT1 ran high in gallbladder tumours. It works as a sponge for a small RNA, miR-218-5p, freeing that RNA's target gene Bmi1 from restraint. Tissue levels of CCAT1 and Bmi1 rose together. Silencing CCAT1 slowed cancer cell growth and invasion, while adding it sped both. The authors name CCAT1 a driver of malignancy in this cancer and a candidate target.
europmc-pmc4669840:
Yong Jiang, Yong Li, and Bo Zhu published a 2015 review of T cell exhaustion inside tumours. Exhausted T cells were first described in chronic mouse infections and later found in human cancers. They carry many inhibitory receptors, make few effector cytokines, and kill poorly. The review appeared in Cell Death and Disease.

Most T cells in the tumour environment show this worn-out state, which lets cancers escape immunity. The receptor PD-1 is the chief brake named. Releasing such brakes has already produced breakthrough cancer treatments, and trials targeting exhausted cells are under way. The authors list open questions: how exhaustion should be defined, how it develops, and how to raise treatment efficiency while limiting side effects.
europmc-pmc4707740:
A. Katharina Simon, Georg A. Hollander, and Andrew McMichael traced the immune system across a human lifetime in the Proceedings of the Royal Society B in 2015. A baby is born with immature defenses, both the fast innate arm and the learning adaptive arm. Exposure through childhood trains the system and builds memory. The review follows that arc through adult life and pregnancy, and ends with the decline of old age.

Each life stage carries its own risk profile for infection, autoimmune disease, and cancer, and the review sets those risks beside the immune changes. Pregnancy gets its own discussion, since carrying a child reshapes immunity in striking ways. Framed with Shakespeare's seven ages of man, the piece shows immunity as a moving target rather than a fixed shield. Doctors reading it gain a timetable for when each defense is strong, and when it needs help.
europmc-pmc4770240:
Nele Hug, Dasa Longman, and Javier F. Cáceres review the cell's faulty-message shredder in Nucleic Acids Research in 2016. The pathway, nonsense-mediated decay, destroys messenger RNAs that carry an early stop sign, which would otherwise build broken proteins. It also tunes the levels of many normal messages, so its strength must be held in check.

The review follows how the shredder spots a bad message and shifts from spotting to cutting, with helicase enzymes doing key work in that shift. It surveys fresh hunts for new helper factors and what each one does. It also takes stock of what the pathway does for the whole body, from development to disease. Buffer systems that cap the shredder's own strength get close attention.
europmc-pmc4834040:
Ge Guo leads nine authors in Stem Cell Reports in 2016 capturing human stem cells in their earliest state. Stem cells grown from human embryos normally sit at a later, primed stage of readiness, unlike mouse embryo cells, which rest in a naive state able to become anything. Whether human naive cells could be caught straight from the embryo, rather than by rewinding primed ones, was open.

Under culture conditions built on selective signal blockers, single cells from the embryo's inner mass grew into colonies that expanded for many passages with normal chromosomes. The cells carried the naive state's hallmark factors and differed from primed cells in breathing, gene activity, and genome-wide chemical marks. Pushed onward, they passed through the primed stage into body cell types, as true naive cells should.
europmc-pmc4865240:
Emily Vogtmann and co-authors checked in 2016 whether gut microbe links to colorectal cancer hold up under whole-genome shotgun sequencing. Earlier work used a narrower marker method and varied across studies. The team sequenced all DNA in stool from 52 untreated cancer patients and 52 matched controls in Washington, DC. They compared results with the earlier method and with a French group run the same way.

Key cancer links, such as Fusobacteria and Porphyromonas presence, reproduced under both methods. One earlier signal, higher Clostridia in cancer, did not. Gene and pathway profiles also aligned across the two countries. Mixed-method care still matters, but the core microbe signals look sturdy enough to pool across studies.
europmc-pmc4866040:
Hermenegild J. Arevalo and co-authors used personal heart models in Nature Communications in 2016 to judge dangerous rhythm risk after heart attack. Sudden cardiac death from rhythm failure kills many, and implanted defibrillators help only if placed in the right patients. Current risk tests miss many who need one and flag many who do not.

The team built 3D computer hearts from each patient's own MRI scans, scar and all, then tested each model for rhythm breakdown. In a small past-case check, the models sorted risk better than standard clinical measures. A virtual stress test for each heart could one day aim implants at those most likely to gain.
europmc-pmc4879240:
Somayeh Imani and co-authors built a skin-worn sensor in Nature Communications in 2016 that reads both sweat chemistry and heart signals at once. Wearable trackers mostly log motion or pulse and skip the chemical clues in sweat. The hybrid patch sticks to skin and tracks lactate, a marker of hard effort, alongside an electrocardiogram, the heart's electric trace.

Both streams flow in real time during exercise, giving a fuller fitness picture than either alone. Lactate rise marks the point where muscles outrun oxygen supply, while heart traces show strain and rhythm. A combined patch could warn athletes and patients earlier, and it points toward wearables that read the body in depth.
europmc-pmc4912640:
Torsten Thomas and a large team surveyed the global sponge microbiome in Nature Communications in 2016. Sponges, an early animal branch, host dense microbe partnerships. The survey set out to find what drives those partnerships across the world's oceans. Sponges proved a vast reservoir of microbe diversity, adding greatly to ocean totals.

Little species overlap appears across sponge kinds, yet the communities mix steady specialists with flexible generalists rather than chance guests. Core microbe sets stay stable within a host kind. Unrelated sponges in like settings converge on like microbe functions, a case of convergent evolution. Sponges thus act as islands where ocean microbes sort and specialize.
europmc-pmc4916540:
Jeffrey V. Lazarus and co-authors argued in 2016 that HIV care must look beyond viral suppression to quality of life. A new World Health Organization strategy for 2016 to 2021 set 15 targets, among them 90-90-90 for diagnosis, treatment, and suppression. The plan calls for person-centered chronic care, yet names no quality-of-life target.

People with suppressed virus still face other diseases, depression, money stress, and stigma or fear of it. Without a stated target, health systems may underfund those needs. The group proposes quality of life as a fourth pillar beside the 90s. Success in HIV care, they argue, should be counted in lived health, not virus counts alone.
europmc-pmc4960240:
Pamela Vernocchi, Federica Del Chierico, and Lorenza Putignani review metabolomics as a way to profile gut microbes through their chemicals. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Microbiology in 2016. Gut bacteria make a large stream of compounds that select among microbes and signal to the host body. Those metabolites carry the marks of diet and lifestyle, and they shift in acute and chronic disease. Reading them can show how the gut community affects human health.

The review explains what metabolite profiles in fluids such as blood and stool can reveal. It covers the two main reading tools, mass spectrometry and nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy, and their trade offs. It also weighs the statistics needed to pull real biology from dense chemical data. The authors look toward systems medicine, which treats the body and its microbes as one network.
europmc-pmc4960740:
Ergul Belge Kurutas, writing alone, reviews antioxidants and their role in the cell's response to oxidative and nitrosative stress. Her review appeared in Nutrition Journal in 2016. Such stress arises when reactive oxygen and nitrogen species outpace the body's defenses. It is blamed in the origin of many human diseases. Breakdown products of damaged fats, such as malondialdehyde and 4-hydroxy-2-nonenal, serve as measurable signs of that damage in blood and urine.

Antioxidants, whether made by the body or taken in, blunt the stress or its effects. They can trap free radicals directly or raise the cell's own defenses. Kurutas warns the same compounds can act as pro-oxidants under some doses and cell conditions. The review sums up current knowledge for clinicians and biochemists. Its core message is balance: protection depends on dose, setting, and the state of the cell.
europmc-pmc4962440:
Jill B. Becker, Brian J. Prendergast, and Jing W. Liang test a common excuse for leaving female rats out of brain research. Their meta-analysis appeared in Biology of Sex Differences in 2016. Labs often claim female data swing too much with the hormone cycle to be usable. The team searched for neuroscience studies from 2010 to 2014 that measured both sexes. They kept 311 articles on gonad intact adult rats and extracted over 6,000 data points from figures and tables.

For each measure they computed how spread out the values were in each sex. On average, females were no more variable than males, and often less so. The pattern held across behavior, electrophysiology, histology, and chemistry measures, and across rat strains. The authors conclude the variability claim fails as a blanket reason for exclusion. They add that sample sizes planned from male data should serve female studies as well.
europmc-pmc4986340:
Lucie Heinzerling and nine co-authors report heart damage linked to immune checkpoint cancer drugs. Their case series appeared in the Journal for ImmunoTherapy of Cancer in 2016. Drugs blocking CTLA4 or PD1 free the immune system against melanoma, lung cancer, and kidney cancer, with clear survival gains. Immune side effects are common, but heart events had appeared only as single cases. Six experienced cancer centers pooled their records to find the pattern.

Eight cases of immune related cardiotoxicity followed ipilimumab or the PD1 drugs nivolumab and pembrolizumab. Presentations varied widely: heart failure, cardiomyopathy, heart block, myocardial fibrosis, and myocarditis. The authors call this the largest series to date. They urge awareness and heart monitoring during treatment, since an immune attack on the heart can be fatal yet may be missed among better known side effects.
europmc-pmc5069740:
Kevin R. Theis and a wide team of co-authors defend the hologenome concept in mSystems in 2016. A holobiont is a host together with all its microbes; the hologenome is their combined genetic material. Critics have charged that the idea is fuzzy, or that it wrongly claims the pair must be evolution's main unit of selection. The authors answer by fixing definitions and laying out an eco-evolutionary framework.

Microbes in a holobiont may harm, help, or do nothing, depending on context. They pass down vertically or spread horizontally, so their genes can be stable or fleeting parts of the whole. Selection, the authors argue, acts at several levels at once, from single microbial genes to the holobiont itself. Parts of any hologenome can drift or conflict internally, just as in an ordinary genome. Their plea is for one shared vocabulary, so debate tests claims instead of talking past them.
europmc-pmc5084340:
Sven Jarius and a large study group report part one of a multicenter study of MOG antibodies in the Journal of Neuroinflammation in 2016. Neuromyelitis optica and its relatives involve attacks on the optic nerve and spinal cord. Some carry antibodies to AQP4, others to a myelin protein, MOG. The team tested 614 serum samples with a cell-based assay.

MOG antibodies turned up in fifty patients with optic neuritis and/or myelitis, most often in those who had both. No patient carrying AQP4 antibodies, and no multiple sclerosis case, had them. All fifty positive patients were AQP4-negative, underlining that the two antibodies mark separate diseases. The antibodies were complement-activating IgG1, present from onset and higher during attacks. They also appeared in spinal fluid, where index testing showed they leaked in from the blood, not made locally. The authors argue MOG antibody disease is its own entity.
europmc-pmc5139140:
Mourad Ouzzani, Hossam Hammady, Zbys Fedorowicz, and Ahmed Elmagarmid presented a screening app called Rayyan in Systematic Reviews in 2016. Systematic reviews must sift hundreds of search results by title and abstract, slow work that delays the evidence summaries clinicians and policymakers rely on.

Rayyan, a free web and mobile app, speeds that first screening with semi-automation: as reviewers include a few studies, it learns to suggest likely matches among the rest. Tested against two Cochrane reviews screened by hand, it found the same trials, and users reported saving about 40 percent of screening time on average. By November 2016 it had over 2,000 users in more than 60 countries working through more than 1.6 million citations.
europmc-pmc5178140:
C. Coyle, F. H. Cafferty, C. Vale, and R. E. Langley reviewed metformin as an add-on cancer treatment in Annals of Oncology in 2016. Metformin, the world's most prescribed diabetes drug, has shown anti-cancer activity in lab studies, cheaply and with a well-known safety record, making it an tempting candidate to repurpose after curative cancer therapy.

Their systematic review and meta-analysis was the first to weigh metformin use against outcomes cancer by cancer in patients treated with curative intent. The pooled evidence suggested possible benefit, strongest for colorectal and prostate cancers. Because the data came from observational studies rather than trials, the authors stop short of recommending the drug and call for randomized trials to test it properly.
europmc-pmc5314040:
Walter Mercer of the University of Edinburgh described two cases of ankle bone injury in the Edinburgh Medical Journal in 1928. The talus is the ankle bone that bears the whole weight of the body. A plain break of it is not rare, and cure is good if it is caught. A break with the bone thrown out of place is rarer and far more grave.

Mercer first sets out the form of the talus: its head, neck, and body, and the grip of the leg bones on each side. He then gives his two cases in detail. In one, an X-ray showed the neck snapped at a slant. The body had slipped fully backward and turned over, its broken face behind the leg bones. His aim was to help surgeons read such damage early, before the ankle is lost.
europmc-pmc5388340:
Kerry McInnes and her co-authors review lasting thinking problems after mild traumatic brain injury in a 2017 scoping review in PLoS ONE. Mild injury, or concussion, is the most common head injury. Most people are thought to recover within three months, yet brain changes can last far longer. The team searched three health databases for studies that tested thinking after a single concussion.

From the studies that fit their rules, about half of people with a single concussion showed long-term problems with thinking. That rate clashes with the common view of quick, full recovery. The authors list limits in the past work but say the pattern is strong enough to demand closer study of single concussions and their late effects on jobs and daily life.
europmc-pmc5394240:
Haiyang Zhang leads a large author group in a 2017 Nature Communications study of how stomach cancer spreads to the liver. Some cancers favor certain organs, a puzzle since it was first noted long ago. The team traced a signal carried in tiny sacs shed by stomach cancer cells. The sacs bear a growth receptor that can reach the liver ahead of the cancer cells themselves.

Once in the liver, the receptor set into the walls of liver support cells and switched on a growth factor. That factor in turn fed arriving cancer cells through their own matching receptor, helping them settle and grow. The authors say the sacs prepare liver-like soil that favors spread to that organ alone.
europmc-pmc5394340:
Sebastian Reyes-Chin-Wo leads a large author group in a 2017 Nature Communications study that builds the reference genome for lettuce. Lettuce is a major crop and a member of the daisy family, the largest family of flowering plants. The team joined short gene reads with a lab method that shows which DNA parts sit close in the cell, forming long blocks that were set in order along nine chromosome-like rows.

The assembly was checked against gene maps and is offered as a reference for the crop and its family. Gene families tied to flower shape, rubber making, and disease defense are swollen in lettuce. The genome also keeps signs of an ancient event that tripled the whole set, shared by the family. About a quarter of the genome lies in those tripled parts.
europmc-pmc5434640:
Quadros and co-authors present Easi-CRISPR, a faster way to build custom-engineered mice. Their methods article appeared in Genome Biology. Conditional knockout mice anchor many genetic studies. Old methods build them through stem cells. That route is slow and covers only a quarter of mouse genes. Early CRISPR routes worked in one step but rarely took. Efficiency was the missing piece.

Easi-CRISPR injects long single-stranded DNA donors into mouse zygotes. The donors arrive with pre-assembled CRISPR protein complexes. Across more than a dozen gene loci, the method worked. Correct conditional and insertion alleles appeared in 8.5 to 100 percent of live pups. Treating about fifty zygotes often sufficed. The method succeeded at every locus tried. It builds both switchable knockouts and targeted insertions. The authors pitch it for large-scale mouse resource programs. Labs could gain models in weeks, not months.
europmc-pmc5436640:
Lowe and co-authors survey the technologies used to study transcriptomes. Their topic page appeared in PLoS Computational Biology. A transcriptome is the full set of RNA transcripts in a cell. It snapshots gene activity at one moment. Two modern methods dominate the field. Microarrays measure a preset list of sequences. RNA sequencing captures all sequences at high throughput. Each wave of tools has remade the field.

Early work moved one transcript at a time. Expressed sequence tags sped gene discovery in the 1990s. Serial analysis of gene expression added counting by fragments. A 1991 study reported 609 human brain messenger RNAs. By 2008, single studies covered 16,000 genes. Hundreds of human transcriptomes followed within years. Single-cell transcriptomes are now routine. Expression maps reveal gene regulation and disease shifts. They also hint at roles for unannotated genes.
europmc-pmc5454940:
Minnone and co-authors review nerve growth factor as a messenger between nerves and the immune system. Their review appeared in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. NGF was found over 60 years ago. It keeps peripheral neurons alive in development. Inflamed tissues raise NGF production sharply. That rise reshapes local innervation. It also triggers release of immune-active neuropeptides. Immune cells carry NGF receptors themselves. Two receptors matter: TrkA and p75NTR.

Receptor levels shift with cell state. Differentiation and activity set the requirement. NGF can push inflammation in either direction. It can fire immune responses up. It can also switch on damping pathways. The authors frame it as a built-in regulator. It limits tissue damage while defending the host. In arthritis patients, immune cells show less TrkA. That loss may block the feedback brake. Chronic inflammation could then sustain itself.
europmc-pmc5473640:
Kim and co-authors report a genome editing study in Nature Communications. They present CjCas9, the smallest Cas9 protein described so far. It comes from the bacterium Campylobacter jejuni. Larger Cas9 tools are hard to pack into the viruses used for delivery. A smaller tool could fit with its guide RNA in one virus.

The team mapped the DNA signal CjCas9 needs and tuned its guide RNA. They packed the whole system into a single AAV virus. In mice, it edited genes in muscle and in eye cells at high rates. Aimed at genes tied to abnormal blood vessel growth, it shrank lesion size. The authors propose it for eye disease care.
europmc-pmc5504840:
Sartelli and a large expert panel present clinical guidelines in the World Journal of Emergency Surgery. The topic is care for infections inside the abdomen. Such infections are common surgical emergencies and a major cause of death. Many hospitals lack access to proven care standards. These guidelines update the panel's earlier version.

Early recognition anchors the advice throughout. Removing the infection source and starting the right antibiotics fast are core steps. Supportive care for patients with sepsis is stressed as urgent. Advice is graded by the strength of its backing evidence. The panel aims at one global standard of care. Rural and low-income settings get special attention.
europmc-pmc5578040:
Shao and co-authors review how influenza A virus evolves. The virus infects people, pigs, horses, birds, and other animals. Its fast change drives yearly epidemics and rare pandemics. It also erodes how well vaccines keep working over time.

Two engines drive that change. Mutation alters the virus's own genome bit by bit. Re-assortment swaps whole genome segments between strains in one host. The genome has eight RNA segments, so swaps can build new forms at once. Some new forms jump from animals to humans and then spread widely. The review explains each mechanism in detail. Readers get a clear account of why flu is so hard to pin down.
europmc-pmc5592640:
Radhakrishnan, Hashem, and Abd Allah review Bacillus bacteria as crop helpers in Frontiers in Physiology. Crops face drought, salty soil, heavy metals, and pests. Chemical fertilizers and sprays carry their own costs. Bacillus species offer a living alternative, and their spores survive harsh conditions for long stretches.

These bacteria release compounds that spur plant growth. Some block toxic ions and steady water flow in tissues. Others make plant hormones or trim stress signals. A further set attacks fungi, bacteria, and nematodes directly. Inside the plant, Bacillus contact switches on defense and antioxidant systems. Stress-linked genes and proteins shift as a result. The review sorts these changes by stress type. Readers get a mechanism guide to a greener farming tool.
europmc-pmc5636840:
Guo and co-authors report a stem cell study in Nature Communications. It concerns amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, or ALS. Mutations in the FUS gene can cause the disease. The team made induced pluripotent stem cells from such patients. Healthy controls gave comparison cells. Motor neurons grown from patient cells showed clear defects. FUS protein gathered in the wrong cell region. The neurons fired less and moved cargo poorly along axons.

Fixing the mutation with CRISPR/Cas9 rescued transport. Adding mutant FUS to healthy stem cells recreated the defects. Blocking HDAC6 also restored axonal transport. The block was done with drugs or gene silencing. It raised tubulin acetylation and organelle contact. The results point to HDAC6 as a treatment target.
europmc-pmc5664340:
Cappetta and co-authors review how a cancer drug can harm the heart. Their review centers on doxorubicin, a drug in the anthracycline family. These drugs kill cancer cells, but they also create reactive species inside cells. That stress can damage the heart over time. The harm matters for the growing group of cancer survivors.

The review traces stress-driven events such as DNA damage, cell aging, and cell death. It looks at heart muscle cells and at stem-like progenitor cells. Cells from outside the heart also play a part. Signals that shape cell lifespan and function get close attention. The authors aim to guide better ways to prevent this heart damage.
europmc-pmc5700640:
Wu and co-authors present a review in Advanced Science. It covers turning carbon dioxide into useful fuels. Rising CO2 levels are reshaping the global climate. Cutting fossil fuel use alone may not suffice. Capture and reuse of CO2 is also needed. Two linked routes draw power from renewable sources. One drives the reaction with electricity. The other uses light directly on catalyst particles.

The review first lays out the basic principles. Key performance measures for both routes are defined. It then surveys catalyst materials in detail. Design strategies for electrocatalysts and photocatalysts follow. Strengths and limits of each family are weighed. The authors close with outlooks for the field.
europmc-pmc5713240:
Chavez and co-authors review how acupuncture may aid stroke recovery. Their literature review appeared in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. Trials link acupuncture to better balance after stroke. Spasticity falls and strength rises in some studies. The basic mechanisms stayed unclear. The authors gathered animal and lab evidence.

Five mechanisms emerge from the review. Acupuncture may promote new nerve cell growth. It may regulate blood flow in injured areas. It may block cell death there. It may adjust brain chemicals. Memory-related plasticity may also improve. Common acupoints in the studies are listed. Baihui and Zusanli appear most often. Electroacupuncture studies are included too.
europmc-pmc5732640:
Froehler and co-authors use the STRATIS registry to study stroke patients moved between hospitals. The patients had blocked brain arteries and needed clot removal by catheter. Many first went to a hospital that could not do that work. The team compared their course with patients taken straight to a capable center.

Transferred patients waited longer for clot removal and fared worse, they report. Delays, not other gaps, account for most of the worse results. A model bypass of under 20 miles cut clot removal time by about 94 minutes. Clot drug timing slipped by just 7 minutes. The authors urge routing rules that skip the extra stop.
europmc-pmc5743240:
Colles describes a wrist fracture that had not been set down in print before. Writing in 1814, he was a professor of anatomy and surgery in Ireland. The injury breaks the radius near its wrist end. It lacks the grating feel and clear signs of most fractures, so it is easy to mistake for a dislocation.

He places the break about an inch and a half above the wrist end of the bone. A dip shows in the back of the forearm at that spot. Swelling fills the wrist, and the hand bones seem thrown backward. He walks surgeons through touch and sight checks that settle the true nature of the case.
europmc-pmc5779640:
Keag, Norman, and Stock review long term effects of cesarean birth for mother, child, and later pregnancies. Cesarean rates keep rising across the world. Short term effects are well known, but long term ones less so. The team searched four databases for trials and large cohort studies with at least a year of follow up.

Eighty studies with close to thirty million people were kept. Cesarean birth tied to lower rates of incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse, they find. Children born by cesarean faced higher risk of asthma and obesity. The team also pooled outcomes for later pregnancies, the third strand of the review.
europmc-pmc5791040:
Lewin and co-authors introduce GRADE-CERQual, a method for judging trust in qualitative review findings. Decision makers increasingly lean on reviews of interview and observation studies. CERQual asks whether a finding fairly represents the topic it claims to cover. The approach was built to support guidelines and policy.

Four parts drive the judgment: method limits, coherence, data adequacy, and relevance. A fifth part, spread bias, is under study. Findings are summed in short tables that show each rating. This paper opens a seven part series. Later papers treat each part and the overall rating in depth.
europmc-pmc5797140:
Vöröslakos and co-authors measure what scalp electric stimulation really does inside the brain. The method is widely used, but the doses that reach circuits were unclear. In rats and human cadaver brains, about three quarters of applied current was lost to skin and skull. Cell recordings in rats set the field strength that can move spikes.

The team built a short pulse method that pushes stronger fields into the brain. It keeps scalp charge and sensation low. In rodents the method hit set regions only. In humans it shifted alpha wave size during recording, they report.
europmc-pmc5847340:
Vernon and co-authors argue that pi-pi contacts are a hidden force inside proteins. Their study appeared in eLife. Such contacts drive proteins to separate into droplets, forming cell compartments without membranes. The contacts were long tied to aromatic rings alone.

Mining folded protein structures widened the picture. Flat pi groups beyond aromatics meet far more often than models assume. Standard force fields underplay these attractions. The contacts cluster where structure loosens, much like disordered regions. The team built a predictor that spots phase-separating proteins by contact frequency. It flags proteins in RNA processing and biomaterials.
europmc-pmc5849140:
Keenan and co-authors report the MORDOR trial, which tested mass azithromycin against child deaths in Africa. Their report appeared in The New England Journal of Medicine. Communities in Malawi, Niger, and Tanzania were randomized by village. Preschool children got the antibiotic or a placebo twice a year.

Over 190,000 children were followed across 1,533 communities. Deaths ran about 14 percent lower where azithromycin was given. The gain centered on Niger and on the youngest infants. Among babies one to five months old, deaths fell by roughly a quarter. The authors warn that resistance could follow wide use.
europmc-pmc5849940:
Seale and co-authors produce the first worldwide estimates of group B Streptococcus disease burden. Their study appeared in Clinical Infectious Diseases. The bacterium threatens mothers, unborn babies, and newborns alike. No global accounting of its toll existed before.

The team built a compartmental model fed by colonization data. It spans pregnant women, stillbirths, and infants across 195 countries. Antibiotics in labor prevent only the earliest newborn disease. Stillbirths, late disease, and preterm births slip past that shield. A vaccine given to mothers could cover the gaps. The estimates size what such a vaccine might save.
europmc-pmc5866840:
Saklayen reviews the global epidemic of metabolic syndrome. The article appeared in Current Hypertension Reports. The syndrome bundles belly fat, insulin resistance, and raised blood pressure. Abnormal blood fats complete the picture. Once a Western problem, it has spread worldwide with lifestyle change. Urban rates in some developing countries now top Western ones.

Saklayen blames high-calorie, low-fibre fast food above all. Mechanised travel and sedentary leisure play a part too. The syndrome feeds type 2 diabetes, heart disease, and stroke. Its total costs run into trillions, he notes. He calls for joint action by governments and society. Town planning, food taxes, and ad limits are among his options.
europmc-pmc5933040:
Castaner and co-authors review how the gut microbiome relates to obesity. Their systematic review appeared in the International Journal of Endocrinology. Obesity is a major public health problem with many known causes. In the past decade, gut microbes have drawn growing research interest. The size of their role in obesity is still unclear.

The review gathers evidence on microbiome profiles in people with obesity. It covers links with related metabolic disorders, including metagenomics studies. A second part looks at how bariatric surgery changes gut microbes. Such surgery causes extreme weight loss, so its effects are telling. The authors sum up what is known and where proof is still thin.
europmc-pmc5976740:
Zhao and co-authors review betaine in inflammation, covering mechanisms and applications. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Immunology. Betaine, also called trimethylglycine, is found across animals, plants, and microbes. It protects cells as an osmoprotectant and donates methyl groups. Growing evidence gives it anti-inflammatory powers in many diseases. It eases oxidative stress through sulfur amino acid metabolism.

Betaine blocks NF-kappaB activity and NLRP3 inflammasome activation, the authors report. It also tunes energy metabolism and cuts cell stress and death. These actions may help in obesity and diabetes. Cancer and Alzheimer's disease feature as well. The review gathers the routes and the uses.
europmc-pmc6031540:
Kahlenberg and co-authors review patient satisfaction after knee replacement. Their systematic review appeared in HSS Journal. Satisfaction reporting after this surgery varies widely. The team set out to survey the evidence. They also sought factors that predict satisfaction.

The search began with 1,219 studies in MEDLINE. In the end, 208 studies met all criteria. They covered 95,560 patients in total. Most studies reported satisfaction above 80 percent. Few used a validated satisfaction survey, though. Methods for measuring satisfaction differed a lot. Working well after surgery predicted satisfaction most often. Pain relief also mattered greatly to patients. Anxiety or depression before surgery predicted dissatisfaction. Readers get a clear summary of a large, uneven literature.
europmc-pmc6057940:
Cazet and co-authors target the tumor's support tissue to beat drug resistance. Their research article appeared in Nature Communications. The cancer type is triple negative breast cancer. Tumor cells send Hedgehog signals to nearby fibroblasts. Those support cells then build a protective niche.

The niche helps cancer cells gain stem-like traits. Such cells resist chemotherapy far better. Support cells supply a growth factor and stiff collagen. Blocking the Hedgehog relay lowered stem cell markers. Tumors then responded to the drug docetaxel again. Mouse survival improved and spread fell sharply. A small patient trial combined both drugs. Three of twelve patients gained clear benefit. One patient had a complete response.
europmc-pmc6137540:
Oikonomou and co-authors report a study in The Lancet on a CT scan marker of heart artery inflammation. Inflammation in coronary arteries blocks fat growth in nearby tissue. That change alters how the fat looks on scans. A new index, called FAI, measures this shift.

The study used outcome data from two patient groups. One group came from Erlangen, Germany, and one from Cleveland in the USA. High FAI values around two major arteries predicted death. That held for both all-cause and cardiac death. The authors say the scan marker could flag leftover risk. Such risk often hides after standard checks.
europmc-pmc6156540:
Rauch and co-authors wrote a review in Frontiers in Immunology on new vaccine technologies for outbreak situations. Vaccines have cut the burden of infectious disease for over 200 years, wiping out smallpox. Yet denser populations, changed travel habits, and a shifting climate help old and new pathogens emerge.

Outbreaks of HIV, SARS, Ebola, and Zika showed how fast such threats can spread. The review covers platform technologies built for very rapid vaccine development. Messenger RNA vaccines get detailed attention, including how they are delivered and how their immune kick can be raised. The authors argue that speed, planned in advance, is the key lesson for pandemic readiness.
europmc-pmc6169940:
Ilievski and co-authors present a research article in PLoS ONE on a gum disease bacterium and the brain. Periodontitis, chronic gum infection, is linked to memory loss and Alzheimer's disease in human studies. Its main bacterium, Porphyromonas gingivalis, has been found in the brains of patients. What it does there was unclear.

The team gave the bacterium by mouth to normal mice over a long period. The mice developed brain inflammation, with more activated microglia in the hippocampus. Signs of neuron damage followed. Their brains also produced amyloid beta, the protein that builds plaques in Alzheimer's disease. The work supports a causal path from oral infection to brain disease, at least in mice.
europmc-pmc6182840:
Sun and co-authors wrote a review in Molecular Cancer on exosomal microRNAs in cancer biology and care. Exosomes are vesicles 30 to 150 nanometers wide, found in many body fluids. They ferry microRNAs between cells. How those RNAs are sorted into exosomes and delivered was only partly known.

Once taken up, the microRNAs can shape tumor immunity and the tumor's surroundings. Effects linked to them include tumor growth, invasion, spread, new blood vessels, and drug resistance. The review sums up sorting and delivery mechanisms. It then turns to clinical uses, such as reading exosomal microRNAs as cancer biomarkers. The authors present these tiny packages as both messengers of disease and tools against it.
europmc-pmc6207340:
Smith and co-authors pooled long term studies on exercise and type 2 diabetes. Their review and analysis appeared in Diabetologia. They found twenty-eight forward looking studies in general populations. Activity was converted into a shared energy scale. Curved models were then used to trace how risk changed with dose.

The authors report that risk fell as activity rose, with the steepest gains at low doses. Meeting the common guide of 150 minutes of moderate activity per week was linked to a risk cut of about a quarter. Doubling that amount was linked to a cut of about a third. Still higher doses gave further gains. The results support public advice to move more, even below guide levels.
europmc-pmc6249440:
Khare, Mishra, and Arora review microbes that live inside plants without causing disease. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Microbiology. Such microbes are called endophytes. They are found in all known plant species. Living inside plant tissue sets them apart from microbes on roots or in soil. Their contact with the host is close and long lasting.

Endophytes can push plant growth and help fight off pathogens. They can also help plants bear drought, salt, and other stresses. Some make the same useful compounds as their host plants. That trait could supply drugs and farm products at scale. The authors argue that effects on host genes and chemistry need more study. Uses in farming, land cleanup, and health are all in view.
europmc-pmc6269540:
Seo and co-authors built an artificial synapse that can also sense colour. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. Most synapse devices only copy how nerve links change strength. This device adds light sensing on the same unit. It is built from layered materials, boron nitride and tungsten diselenide. Arranged in a network, it copies how human vision sorts coloured patterns.

The device updates its strength in a near straight line. It holds many stable states, each varying by less than one percent. It runs on tiny voltage spikes of 0.3 volts. Each spike uses only 66 femtojoules of energy. Tests showed correct sorting of coloured and mixed colour patterns. Sensing and learning in one unit saves the cost of split systems. The work points toward vision chips that learn as they see.
europmc-pmc6290540:
Chen and co-authors report a new circular RNA that helps breast cancer spread. The work appeared in Genome Biology. The team focused on FLI1, a gene that can drive cancer growth. Staining tests showed FLI1 at high levels in advanced, spreading tumors.

They found a circular RNA built from parts of the FLI1 gene. They named it FECR1. Adding FECR1 made breast cancer cells more invasive in lab tests. The RNA pulls in an enzyme that strips methyl marks from the FLI1 promoter. It also lowers a second enzyme that keeps those marks in place. This loop switches FLI1 on and feeds tumor growth and spread.
europmc-pmc6345440:
Kather and co-authors train deep learning to predict survival from colon cancer slides. Their study appeared in PLoS Medicine. Every colorectal cancer patient has stained tissue slides. Those images hold unused prognostic information. The team first taught a network to sort tissue types. Training used over 100,000 hand-marked image patches.

The network sorted nine tissue classes with high accuracy. It then took apart slides from 500 patients. Those came from several centers and 862 slides. Tissue mix patterns predicted patient survival. The method needs no extra lab tests at all. It works on slides clinics already produce. The authors say such tools could add cheap risk scores. Validation in routine care remains the next step.
europmc-pmc6356540:
Banerjee and co-authors review bats as hosts of coronaviruses. Their review appeared in Viruses. Bats are suspected reservoirs of several emerging viruses. Their coronaviruses include the causes of SARS and MERS. Pig diseases PED and SADS also trace to them. Infected bats show no signs of illness themselves.

The review retraces each outbreak linked to bats. It covers studies of bat immune adaptations. Those traits may let bats carry viruses safely. Bats can harbor many virus strains at once. What lets viruses jump to other mammals remains unclear. The authors list the studies most needed next. Understanding bat tolerance could guide outbreak prevention.
europmc-pmc6370640:
Martinez and Moon present a review in Frontiers in Immunology on CAR T cells for solid tumors. Engineered T cells have transformed care for blood cancers, yet solid tumors resist them. The authors frame the problem in three steps: the cells must find, enter, and survive inside the tumor.

Dual receptors that spot two antigens at once can improve targeting. Local delivery helps cells reach the tumor site. Inside, the suppressive tumor setting exhausts the cells, so pairing with checkpoint blockade may help. Armored CARs that release cytokines offer another boost. The review surveys designs across all three hurdles and the early results for each.
europmc-pmc6386140:
Gregson and co-authors, for the Emerging Risk Factors Collaboration, report a pooled analysis in JAMA Cardiology. They asked how much heart risk factors also raise the risk of venous thromboembolism. That condition covers clots in deep veins and in the lungs.

Data came from 1.1 million people across many cohorts and UK Biobank. Older age, smoking, and higher body fat were tied to higher clot risk with consistency. About ten million cases occur worldwide each year. The overlap with heart disease risk was only partial. The authors argue clot prevention can borrow some, but not all, heart lessons.
europmc-pmc6387440:
Padoan and co-authors review inflammation and pancreatic cancer in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. Long-term inflammation can raise the risk of this cancer. Inside tumors, inflammation also helps the cancer grow and spread.

Immune cells in these tumors lean toward suppressing defense, not attack. Suppressor cells and repair-type macrophages crowd out attacker cells. Signals carried in blood and tiny vesicles keep that state going. The review links these immune shifts to changes in tumor metabolism. It frames the tumor setting as a target in itself, alongside the cancer cells.
europmc-pmc6438340:
Cederholm and co-authors report the GLIM rules, a single global way to judge poor nutrition in adults, built by the world's main nutrition groups working together. The GLIM group first met in January 2016 and reached agreement through meetings, calls, and ballots. Before this, each country judged cases its own way, so rates and outcomes could not be compared across borders.

Judging takes two steps: first screen for risk with any proven tool, then check the person against set rules. Three body signs count: weight loss, low body mass index, and reduced muscle mass. Two kinds of cause count as well: eating or taking in too little, and illness or inflammation. One of each is required, and severity grades into Stage 1 or Stage 2.
europmc-pmc6481040:
Lukomska and co-authors take a critical look at mesenchymal stem cell therapy, where enthusiasm has outrun definition. More than two thousand patients have received these cells for conditions from graft-versus-host disease to heart, brain, and orthopedic disorders, and most reports confirm safety with promising, if unspectacular, benefits.

The review presses on what remains unresolved: what the cells actually do, how approaches differ between labs, and what long-term follow-up might reveal. Evidence increasingly credits secreted factors and vesicles, paracrine signaling that nudges repair and calms immunity, rather than cells engrafting and replacing tissue. Placing cells into particular niches could carry delayed risks, so the authors argue for defined products and patient watching over years.
europmc-pmc6486540:
Alemasova and Lavrik re-examine how PARP1 builds poly(ADP-ribose), the branching alarm polymer it hangs on proteins at DNA damage sites. PARP1 is both the family's chief enzyme and its own main target, a dual role that has generated contradictory literature for decades. Open questions include how many PARP1 molecules cooperate in self-modification and which way the chain grows.

Damage binding folds the enzyme into activity, but partner proteins tune the intensity and aim of the reaction, and several new regulators are catalogued. The stakes are practical: PARP inhibitors are cancer drugs, and knowing whether self-tagging happens within one molecule or between two changes how the enzyme switches off, and how blockers might work.
europmc-pmc6602440:
Tang and co-authors present GEPIA2, an update of a cancer data web server. Their article appears in Nucleic Acids Research. The first GEPIA let users explore tumor and normal gene expression. It drew on the TCGA and GTEx databases. GEPIA2 adds finer detail and new analysis options.

The server now quantifies 198,619 isoforms across 84 cancer subtypes. Users can compare subtypes or focus on just one. New tools score gene signatures drawn from single-cell studies. Users may also upload their own RNA-seq data. Uploaded data can be compared with TCGA and GTEx samples. An API supports batch retrieval of results. The server is free to use online.
europmc-pmc6616540:
Rodgers and co-authors review how sex and aging shape cardiovascular risk. Their article appears in the Journal of Cardiovascular Development and Disease. Age alone raises the odds of heart and vessel disease. Frailty, obesity, and diabetes compound that risk. Older women face higher rates than men of the same age.

United States data show incidence near 40% in midlife. It climbs to about 86% past age 80. Falling estrogen and testosterone track the rise in both sexes. Hormone replacement, though, has not improved outcomes in older patients. It may even raise the chance of cardiac events. The review covers stiffening, fibrosis, and rhythm faults in aging hearts. It aims to guide safer treatment design for older adults.
europmc-pmc6627940:
Alves and co-authors review glycine metabolism and its changes in obesity and metabolic disease. Their review appears in Nutrients. Glycine is the smallest protein-building amino acid. It also feeds glutathione production and one-carbon metabolism. The body makes some, but perhaps not always enough. Blood glycine runs consistently low in obesity. The same pattern shows in type 2 diabetes and fatty liver disease. The review maps glycine's main pathways.

It then asks why availability falls in these conditions. Diet, gut microbes, and liver processing all play roles. Studies of supplementation suggest real benefits.
