Raising glycine may slow obesity-linked metabolic decline. The authors frame glycine as conditionally essential. Its shortage may help drive the diseases themselves.
europmc-pmc6675740:
Weiss and co-authors map global Plasmodium falciparum malaria across 2000 to 2017. Their modelling study appears in The Lancet. Falciparum is the deadliest malaria species. Control scale-up has cut its burden since 2000. The team refined parasite rate and incidence models for Africa. Outside Africa they downscaled routine surveillance data. Mortality came from vital registration and verbal autopsy links. Estimates reach down to 5 by 5 kilometre pixels.

Incidence fell about 28 percent between 2005 and 2017. Mortality fell about 43 percent in that span. Cases dropped from 232 million to 194 million. Deaths dropped from about 926,000 to 619,000. Sub-Saharan Africa still held most of the burden. It accounted for 88 percent of deaths in 2017.
europmc-pmc6702140:
Elhassan and co-authors test nicotinamide riboside in aged human skeletal muscle. Their trial report appears in Cell Reports. NAD+ reportedly declines with ageing in animals. Human data had stayed sparse until now. Twelve men aged 70 to 80 enrolled. They took one gram daily for 21 days. The design was randomised, double-blind, and crossover. Targeted tests measured the muscle NAD+ pool. RNA sequencing profiled gene expression changes.

The supplement raised the muscle NAD+ metabolome clearly. Clearance products and kin metabolites increased. Energy pathways were dialled down at the RNA level. Mitochondrial output itself did not change. Blood inflammatory cytokines fell with treatment. The authors show the dose reaches aged muscle. Anti-inflammatory signatures are the novel finding.
europmc-pmc6753140:
Jung and co-authors found that loss of DNA methylation helps tumors evade the immune system. Tumors with many mutations usually respond better to immunotherapy. Yet cell division also strips methylation from large DNA domains. Immune pathway genes cluster in those domains, and they get switched off when methylation falls and other marks rise.

The team studied cohorts of 60 and 81 lung cancer patients and 40 melanoma patients. Methylation loss tracked with immune escape, apart from mutation counts. It predicted immunotherapy resistance better than mutation burden did. The same pattern held in tumors with abnormal chromosome numbers. Tuning these marks could sharpen precision immunotherapy, the authors suggest.
europmc-pmc6770940:
Hasanuzzaman and co-authors review the ascorbate-glutathione pathway, a plant defense against oxidative damage. Plants make reactive oxygen species even in normal life. Under stress, production outruns the defense system. The pathway in question uses vitamin C, glutathione, and four enzymes to detoxify these molecules. It is also called the Asada-Halliwell pathway.

The pathway does more than clean up. It interacts with other defense systems across the plant. Studies show that boosting its enzymes, or raising ascorbate and glutathione levels, helps plants tolerate stress. Damage from drought, salt, and other hardships falls. The review sums up recent progress and the molecular links involved. The pathway is a target for breeding hardier crops.
europmc-pmc6774040:
Fan and co-authors review PEDOT:PSS, a conductive polymer for flexible and stretchable electronics. Wearable and see-through devices need electrodes that bend without breaking. Rigid metal oxides cannot do that job. PEDOT:PSS, a plastic that carries current, has emerged as the leading candidate. It serves as transparent electrode, transport layer, connector, and even motion sensor.

The review sums up ways to raise its conductivity and stretch. Acid treatments, for example, strip out excess PSS and can keep about 90% of conductivity after 10 days in air. The authors explain the mechanisms behind these gains. They highlight the newest devices built with the material. Problems and fresh directions for the field close the survey.
europmc-pmc6834140:
Tominaga and Suzuki review a growth signal and cell ageing, in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. Cells that grow old and stop dividing are called senescent. They build up with age and are blamed for part of the decline in body systems. The signal TGF-β stops many cell types from growing. It also shapes development and keeps adult tissues in balance.

The review links TGF-β to the machinery that locks cells into senescence. It also ties the signal to stem cell ageing. Separate sections cover its roles in Alzheimer's disease, muscle wasting, and obesity. In fat tissue, blocking the pathway protected mice from diet-driven obesity and insulin problems.
europmc-pmc6870840:
Locke and co-authors review DNA methylation tests for cancer, in Frontiers in Genetics. As a cancer forms, the pattern of methyl marks on its DNA changes widely. The genome loses marks overall, while dense clusters near gene starts gain them. Many changes arrive early and recur across a tumour type. A useful test may need to read only one or a few spots.

Those traits make methylation markers attractive for early detection. They could also guide treatment choice and watch for return of disease. The review follows the path from discovery to clinic, using prostate cancer as one case. There, current monitoring leans on repeat scans and biopsies, with real limits the authors detail.
europmc-pmc6892540:
Upham and co-authors build a family tree for all mammals, in PLOS Biology. Time-scaled evolutionary trees link the history of life to today's patterns of diversity. Building one tree for roughly 6,000 living mammal species forces trade-offs, and earlier attempts left much uncertain. The team set out to carry that uncertainty openly rather than hide it.

Their backbone-and-patch method joined a 31-gene data matrix at two levels. A backbone tree fixed relations and ages among major lineages, using fossil dates. Species-level patch trees then slotted in the remaining species, 5,911 in total for one set. The output is a credible set of trees, meant for ecology, evolution, and conservation work.
europmc-pmc6914840:
Makowski and co-authors compare Bayesian indices for effect size and significance. Their article appeared in Frontiers in Psychology. It responds to the reproducibility crisis in psychology. Bayesian methods let researchers state results as probabilities. They also let prior knowledge enter the model.

The authors describe several indices side by side. They give clear visual displays of each one. They show how values shift with sample size. They also test links to effect size and frequentist significance. Their aim is a shared standard for reporting. Plain guidance, they argue, can cut opaque practice. It can also help readers judge what a reported value means.
europmc-pmc6925840:
Uddin and co-authors compare supervised machine learning methods for predicting disease. Their review appeared in BMC Medical Informatics and Decision Making. Such algorithms learn from labelled health data, then flag risk in new cases. Many variants exist, and choosing among them is not obvious.

The authors gathered 48 studies that tested more than one algorithm on a single disease. Support Vector Machine appeared most often, in 29 studies. Naive Bayes followed, in 23. Accuracy told a different story. Random Forest topped the results in 9 of the 17 studies that used it. That record, the authors argue, makes Random Forest a strong default choice for disease prediction work.
europmc-pmc6955640:
Conradie and co-authors test a three-drug oral regimen for the hardest forms of tuberculosis. Their trial report appeared in The New England Journal of Medicine. Patients with extensively drug-resistant TB have few options and historically poor outcomes. The Nix-TB study tried bedaquiline, pretomanid, and linezolid together for 26 weeks.

The trial ran at three South African sites and enrolled 109 patients. Six months after treatment ended, 98 patients, or 90 percent, had a favourable outcome. Six patients died early in treatment, and one relapsed. Linezolid side effects were common: nerve damage in 81 percent and low blood counts in 48 percent. These were managed with dose cuts or pauses. The regimen, the authors conclude, is a viable option when safety monitoring is in place.
europmc-pmc6966240:
Pardridge argues that brain drug development stands or falls on beating the blood-brain barrier. His review appeared in Frontiers in Aging Neuroscience. Alzheimer's disease and other brain disorders of aging need new biologic drugs, such as engineered proteins and gene therapies. Those large molecules cannot cross the barrier on their own.

The choice, he says, is binary: re-engineer the drug with delivery technology, or proceed without a delivery platform. Injecting into spinal fluid, the most common bypass, works poorly, since fluid drains fast to blood and little drug reaches deep brain tissue. Stem cells and small molecules also rarely win approval this way. Future progress, he argues, will come from delivery tools that ferry biologics across the barrier from the blood, built alongside the drugs themselves.
europmc-pmc7072240:
Kasai and co-authors review how mitochondrial reactive oxygen species regulate the protein Nrf2 in the journal Biomolecules. Reactive oxygen species are leftovers of breathing that double as signals. Nrf2 is the master switch for antioxidant defences: it turns on genes that build antioxidants and destroy these molecules, once its repressor Keap1 is disabled. Mitochondria, the cell's furnaces, produce their own reactive oxygen species.

Evidence gathered here shows those mitochondrial signals often activate Nrf2, sometimes through helper kinases, switching on both antioxidant genes and genes that control mitochondrial quality and quantity. Mild stressors such as exercise and calorie restriction exploit this loop for benefit, a process called mitohormesis. Under severe stress Nrf2 instead raises a factor that blocks cleanup enzymes and promotes cell death. In diabetes Nrf2 falls silent, and restoring it improves the disease. The review maps a two-faced control system tuned by dose.
europmc-pmc7082940:
Liu and co-authors test how advanced oxidation protein products drive inflammation after spinal cord injury, in the Journal of Neuroinflammation. These products, called AOPPs, are markers of oxidative stress. Their role in the injury's second wave of damage was unclear. The team used both injured rats and cultured microglia cells.

AOPP levels rose in blood, spinal fluid, and cord tissue after injury. In rats, the oxidase blocker apocynin cut tissue damage and improved recovery. In microglia, AOPPs raised reactive oxygen species, which switched on MAPK and NF-κB signals. They also triggered the NLRP3 inflammasome, leading to pyroptosis, a fiery form of cell death. Readers get a step-by-step chain from oxidative stress to inflammation, with several points where a drug might break it.
europmc-pmc7083240:
Vardavas and Nikitara wrote a systematic review on smoking and COVID-19, published in Tobacco Induced Diseases. They searched PubMed and ScienceDirect on 17 March 2020. Their aim was to test whether smoking links to worse outcomes in the new disease.

Five studies from China met their rules, with 41 to 1,099 patients each. Most showed no clear link between smoking and death or severe illness. One study of 78 patients did link a smoking history to disease progression. The authors stress how thin the early evidence was. Readers get a careful snapshot of what was known in the first months of the pandemic, and why firm claims about smoking risk had to wait for larger studies.
europmc-pmc7145640:
Robinson and co-authors update the IPD-IMGT/HLA Database, the official repository for HLA gene variants, in Nucleic Acids Research. These genes sit in the most variable region of the human genome, and their matching decides transplant success. The database holds over 25,000 allele sequences across 45 genes.

Some HLA genes now have several thousand known variants each, earning the label hyperpolymorphic. That growth strains older curation and file formats, and the paper explains how the team keeps sequences accurate as submissions surge. The database is the naming authority's public record: variants named by the World Health Organization nomenclature committee are published here for the scientific and medical community.
europmc-pmc7175140:
Tzavlaki and Moustakas review signaling by the TGF-beta family of proteins. Their article appeared in Biomolecules. These secreted proteins guide embryo development and keep adult tissues in balance. They also play roles in many diseases when their signals go wrong. Family members differ by cell type and life stage, yet they share core pathways.

The review follows the signal step by step. It starts with how the proteins are released, stored, and switched on outside the cell. At the cell surface, receptor kinases pass the message inward. The main carriers inside are the SMAD proteins. Other branches of the pathway add further control. Readers get a full account of how one protein family steers growth, repair, and disease.
europmc-pmc7187240:
Suzuki reviews how food components shape the intestinal barrier through tight junctions. The review appeared in Animal Science Journal. Tight junctions seal the gaps between gut lining cells. They control what passes from the gut into the body. Proteins such as claudin and occludin form these seals. A sound barrier keeps inflammatory material out of tissues. A weak barrier can stir lasting inflammation.

The review gathers what is known about diet effects on this barrier. It explains how junction proteins differ in role. Some form pores for ions and water. Others tighten the seal against large molecules. Food factors may tune the barrier for better or worse. The exact pathways remain unclear, the author notes. Even so, diet looks like a useful target. It may help prevent or ease inflammatory disorders of the gut and beyond.
europmc-pmc7204940:
Olum and co-authors survey health care workers in Uganda about their knowledge, attitudes, and practices toward COVID-19. Their study appeared in Frontiers in Public Health. The survey ran online through WhatsApp Messenger. It covered staff at four Makerere University teaching hospitals. A standard questionnaire scored each area against set cutoffs.

The mean knowledge score was 82.4 percent. Sixty-nine percent of participants scored at or above the 80 percent mark for sufficient knowledge. Only two participants scored below 50 percent. Older workers and those informed by news media showed distinct patterns. The authors judge overall readiness fairly strong. Gaps in attitude and practice still need training attention. Such surveys help hospitals target their preparation efforts.
europmc-pmc7228340:
He and co-authors summarize what was known about COVID-19 early in the pandemic. Their review appeared in the Journal of Medical Virology. A cluster of unexplained pneumonia cases appeared in Wuhan in late December 2019. Days later the cause was identified as a new coronavirus. The World Health Organization named the virus SARS-CoV-2 and the disease COVID-19.

The review covers the pathogen, symptoms, diagnosis, and treatment. It also touches on spread and tissue pathology. No effective antiviral had been identified at the time. Care rested mainly on easing symptoms. Several existing antivirals were being tried against the virus. One early case report described a good result with remdesivir in the United States. The article captures the state of knowledge in the pandemic's first months.
europmc-pmc7237140:
Mandal and co-authors review hydrogels that have reached the clinic. Their article appeared in Bioengineering & Translational Medicine. Hydrogels are water-rich polymer networks that can be injected or implanted. Their structure can be tuned for drug delivery or tissue building. Advances in polymer chemistry keep widening what they can do.

Several hydrogel products already hold regulatory approval. Uses range from cancer treatment to beauty correction and spinal fusion. One gel bulks tissue to treat urinary incontinence in women. Another serves as a marker that guides imaging during cancer therapy. Many more gels are in clinical trials for regeneration and other needs. The authors track this path from lab bench to patient. Their review shows a maturing technology, not just a research promise.
europmc-pmc7382540:
Wafa and co-authors project Europe's stroke burden thirty years ahead in Stroke. Stroke is the European Union's second most common cause of death and a leading cause of adult disability, with about 1.1 million cases a year. The team combined Global Burden of Disease data with population and economic projections for 28 countries.

From 2017 to 2047, they project about 40,000 more new strokes a year, a 3 percent rise, and 27 percent more people living after stroke. Aging drives the growth, as the share of residents aged 70 or over climbs from 14 to 23 percent. Deaths and disability years, though, should keep falling, by about 17 and 33 percent. Services must plan for more survivors needing long-term care.
europmc-pmc7391640:
Santarpia and co-authors sampled the air and surfaces around isolated COVID-19 patients in Scientific Reports. Transmission routes were disputed early on, and guidelines swung between droplet and airborne precautions. During the initial isolation of 13 patients at the University of Nebraska Medical Center, the team collected air and surface specimens.

Viral contamination turned up across the samples, in air as well as on surfaces, even beyond the patients' immediate surroundings. The pattern supports treating shed virus as an airborne risk during care, not only a touch risk. The authors back airborne isolation precautions for staff treating such patients. Readers get direct environmental evidence from a specialist unit, gathered when almost none existed.
europmc-pmc7393740:
Muncan and co-authors interview people who inject drugs in New York City about stigma in health care, in Harm Reduction Journal. This group faces high rates of overdose, mental illness, and infections such as HIV and hepatitis C. The team ran semi-structured interviews with 32 participants and coded the transcripts for themes.

About 78 percent reported at least one stigmatizing experience in medical settings, and 71.9 percent described enacted stigma, being treated as junkies by staff. Many expected such treatment before walking in. Syringe service programs stood out in the opposite way, with 62.5 percent reporting positive experiences there. Stigma, the authors conclude, pushes people away from care they need, deepening the very disparities services aim to close.
europmc-pmc7511340:
Lu and co-authors review drugs that modulate protein-protein interactions, a hard class of drug targets. These interactions run core life processes. When they go wrong, cancer, infections, and brain diseases can follow.

Modulating such contacts was long seen as one of drug discovery's toughest tasks. The flat, large surfaces offer few pockets for small drugs. Still, some modulators have reached clinical studies in recent years. A few have even won approval for marketing. The review covers small molecules, peptides, and antibodies as modulator types. It sets out how each class blocks or steadies a protein contact. The authors hope the survey guides design of new drugs. Protein contacts, they argue, hold broad promise for future therapy.
europmc-pmc7539940:
Callard and Perego trace how patients created the term Long Covid. Many patients had first been told their illness was mild. Their symptoms lasted longer and grew more complex.

Patients found each other first on Twitter. They gathered evidence and shared their accounts widely. The term moved into media within a few months. It then reached clinical and policy channels. Both authors write as patients with the illness. Their account focuses on the UK and USA. They show how patients built shared authority on symptoms. The authors argue patient knowledge must shape research and care.
europmc-pmc7559240:
Meyer and co-authors study activity, sitting and mental health in US adults during COVID-19. Public health rules changed work and social life fast. The team asked how movement and mood shifted together.

Data came from 3052 adults across all 50 states. Surveys ran from April 3 to April 8 in that year. Activity fell among people who had been active before. Their reported activity dropped by 32.3% on average. Activity barely changed among those inactive before. Losing guideline-level activity linked to worse mood scores. More screen time also linked to worse depression and stress. Isolation linked to higher anxiety than distancing alone.
europmc-pmc7648640:
Avila Cobos, Alquicira-Hernandez, Powell, Mestdagh and De Preter benchmark cell type deconvolution pipelines for transcript data. Many tools infer cell mixes from bulk gene data. How choices in handling affect results was not well tested.

The team built fake bulk mixes from five single-cell datasets. They varied data scaling, cleaning and marker choice. They also varied cell mix and method used. Methods with single-cell references matched the best bulk tools. Semi-supervised methods showed higher error values overall. Data in linear scale worked best for most tools. Normalization choice swung results for some methods hard. Missing a cell type from the reference hurt badly. Guidelines to raise performance close the benchmarking study.
europmc-pmc7658740:
The NCD Risk Factor Collaboration pools world data on height and body-mass index in youth. It tracks children and teens aged 5 to 19 years. The span runs from 1985 to 2019 and covers 200 countries and territories.

The team pooled 2181 studies with measures from 65 million young people. In 2019, mean height at age 19 differed by 20 cm or more between the tallest and shortest nations. Mean body-mass index differed by about 9 to 10 units between the highest and lowest nations. In some nations, healthy early growth faded as children aged. The healthiest changes were seen in girls in South Korea and boys in central and western Europe.
europmc-pmc7794640:
De Kock and co-authors rapidly review how COVID-19 affected the mental health of health and social care workers. These staff carried a heavy load during the crisis. They faced the virus and its effects head on. Supporting their mental well-being stayed a clear priority.

The team searched the early evidence at speed. They aimed to map the scale and shape of the harm. Anxiety, stress, and low mood were among the outcomes of interest. The authors draw out what services can do in response. Their findings point to support that services should offer staff. The review is meant to guide employers during and after the pandemic.
europmc-pmc7816340:
Ding and co-authors identify a small molecule that kills triple negative breast cancer cells in two ways. This cancer type is the most aggressive breast cancer. It recurs more and kills more than other types. New drugs with fresh modes of action are badly needed.

The molecule triggers ferroptosis, an iron-driven form of cell death. It also triggers apoptosis, the classic cell suicide path. It works by tagging the protein GPX4 for removal. GPX4 normally shields cells from ferroptosis. Losing it leaves cancer cells open to both death routes. The authors screened drug candidates to find this compound. They present it as a lead for new TNBC therapy.
europmc-pmc8008340:
Dejnirattisai and co-authors test how well antibodies handle a variant strain of SARS-CoV-2 from Brazil. The strain, called P.1, carries many spike mutations. It shares a key triplet of changes with the South African strain: E484K, K417N/T, and N501Y. These sit in the ACE2 binding site and raise binding strength. The fear was that vaccines built on early strains would fail.

The team reports that the Brazilian strain is, surprisingly, less resistant than the South African one to vaccine and natural antibodies. Changes outside the binding domain seem to shape that gap. One monoclonal antibody, 222, neutralized all three variants tested. Structural work showed how, and its light chain restored the power of a major antibody class.
europmc-pmc8079440:
Tustison and co-authors describe ANTsX, an open ecosystem for measuring biology and medicine in images. The core library, ANTs, grew from a famed image registration method. Its Symmetric Normalization framework dates to the project's founding in 2008. Registration aligns scans so that organs and tissues can be compared. The tools rank at the top in outside tests.

The ecosystem now spans several linked libraries. ANTsR and ANTsPy bring the methods to R and Python users. Deep learning add-ons carry ready-made network designs and trained models. One pipeline measures cortical thickness from brain MRI on its own. It matches or beats the older hand-run workflows on accuracy. It also runs far faster in routine use. The authors present ANTsX as one frame for the whole craft. Registration, segmentation, statistics, and learning sit under one roof.
europmc-pmc8143540:
Arfin and co-authors examine oxidative stress in cancer cell metabolism. Reactive oxygen species help run normal cell tasks. When their levels lose balance, they can help drive cancer.

The review explains how raised reactive oxygen species can aid tumour growth and damage DNA. It also shows how high levels can push tumour cells toward death. Cancer cells adapt by raising antioxidant proteins that clear the excess. That altered balance can help them resist cell death. The authors argue that shifting this balance may offer a route for new cancer therapies.
europmc-pmc8167040:
Obradovic and co-authors explain the role of leptin in obesity and its clinical meaning. Leptin is a hormone made by fat cells. It curbs food intake and helps set body mass.

The review traces how leptin signals through its receptor to the hypothalamus. That loop forms a feedback system between fat tissue and the brain. When leptin resistance sets in, hunger stays high and weight climbs. The authors also cover leptin's roles in fertility, immunity, and blood vessel growth. They weigh what leptin tests and drugs could offer clinics. Leptin also aids fetal growth, as the review notes.
europmc-pmc8280040:
Yoshiji and co-authors present the 2020 clinical practice guidelines for liver cirrhosis. Earlier editions came out in 2010 and 2015. This third edition is a joint work of two Japanese societies.

New findings from the past 5 years shaped the revision. Clinical questions remain the core of the guide. Background questions now add basic clinical knowledge. Future research questions flag topics that matter but lack answers. The panel aligned the guide with international practice. Diagnosis and treatment of cirrhosis are covered in full. The format helps clinicians act and researchers plan alike. The guide is made to be used at the bed side and in the ward, not just read once and put away.
europmc-pmc8387240:
Tunyasuvunakool and co-authors apply AlphaFold2 to almost the whole human proteome. Protein structures guide both basic research and drug design. Yet lab work had covered only a small share of human protein residues. The team set out to expand that coverage at scale.

The authors report confident predictions for 58 percent of residues, with a subset at very high confidence. They built new quality metrics to read the data set. The metrics flag strong multi-domain predictions and regions that are likely disordered. Case studies show how the predictions can seed new biological ideas. All predictions were made freely available to the community.
europmc-pmc8441240:
Zhang and co-authors give the 2021 update of a Chinese consensus on donor stem cell transplants. The Chinese Society of Hematology first set these rules in 2018. They cover who should get an allogeneic transplant, how to prepare patients, and how to pick donors.

A new donor choice algorithm leads the changes. Half-matched family donors now rank above matched siblings for high-risk leukemia in skilled centers. The same holds for older patients with young offspring donors. Patients with stubborn lymphoblastic disease should try new immune therapies before transplant. Fresh guidance also covers care after transplant and graft-versus-host disease. The update aligns Chinese practice with world standards.
europmc-pmc8444440:
Gao and co-authors study how disease reshapes the plant microbiome of chili pepper. Microbes that live on and in plants guard growth and health. Roots can call in helpful microbes to fight soil pathogens. The rules of that assembly under attack were not fully known.

The team sampled 12 plant compartments, from soils and roots to stems and fruits. They tracked bacterial and fungal groups at major pepper sites in China. Fusarium wilt hit fruit microbes least and the upper stem surface most. Fungal networks proved less stable than bacterial ones under disease. Wilt also loosened the joint bacteria-fungus network. The work shows disease can unbalance whole plant microbe systems.
europmc-pmc8494640:
Bakken and co-authors compare motor cortex cells across human, marmoset, and mouse. The primary motor cortex runs fine voluntary movement in all mammals. Whether its cell makeup is shared across species needed a direct test.

The team profiled over 450,000 single nuclei with gene and epigenome methods. The broad cell makeup proved conserved across the three species. Shared traits mirrored evolutionary distance. A cross-species consensus list of cell types was built. Yet many species-specific twists appeared in cell shares, gene activity, and chromatin state. Few marker genes held across all species. The work gives a shared frame for motor cortex research.
europmc-pmc8571840:
Woodburn and co-authors argue for sharper words around microglia activation and brain inflammation. Microglia now look like key regulators of neuron function and behavior. Early reports stressed their classic immune jobs in disease. Those ideas were then stretched to healthy settings where they fit poorly.

Terms like activation get used for near any change in these cells. In stress research, that habit invites false links to disease states. New researchers face a muddled field as a result. The review sums up microglia roles in sick and healthy brains. It then proposes a frame for naming cell states in chronic stress work. Precise terms should speed better drugs.
europmc-pmc8584040:
Luo and Song review how antimicrobial peptides kill germs, calm inflammation, and break up biofilms. These short peptides are seen as a new class of antibiotic. Their value goes past direct killing. The review asks how each action works at the cell level.

The authors sort the actions into cell wall effects, membrane attack, and entry into the cell. Inside, peptides can hit key targets and stop cell work. Some peptides use two routes at once. The review also covers how peptides slow biofilm growth and ease the signals that drive swelling. Readers get a full picture of how these peptides might be shaped into new drugs.
europmc-pmc8656040:
Kolb and co-authors argue that ketone bodies act as friends and guards, not foes, in body metabolism. Ketones rise during fasting or low-carbohydrate diets. The liver makes them from fat as a backup fuel. High levels in blood mark a lack of dietary carbohydrate.

The review says ketones do more than supply fuel. They help cells resist oxidative and inflammatory stress. The authors propose that mild stress from ketone use triggers a protective response. That response switches on master defense regulators in the cell. Over time, cells raise their antioxidant defenses. The review reframes a classic fuel as a signal for cell protection.
europmc-pmc8789240:
Hoenigl and co-authors review cases of COVID-19-associated mucormycosis, a severe fungal infection, from 18 countries. Reports rose fast from early 2021, above all in patients with uncontrolled diabetes. The team analyzed 80 published and unpublished cases. They tracked risk factors, disease forms, and patient outcomes in each case.

Uncontrolled diabetes and steroid treatment appeared in most patients. The nose, eye, and brain form was the most common pattern. Death struck 49 percent of patients. Lung, spread, or brain forms drove the worst rates. Among survivors, 46 percent lost vision. The authors warn that lung cases are hard to spot and often missed.
europmc-pmc8940940:
Leppek and co-authors build a platform to design better mRNA medicines by tuning structure and stability. mRNA drugs and vaccines can treat many diseases. Weak stability and poor protein output hold them back. The team created PERSIST-seq, a sequencing method for mRNA libraries. It measures stability inside cells and on ribosomes at once. In-solution stability is read as well. Thousands of designs can be compared in one run.

A surprise emerged from the data. In-cell stability drove protein output more than ribosome load. A second method, In-line-seq, exposed the rules of water-driven decay. Sequence and folding patterns predicted breakdown. Highly folded superfolder mRNAs lasted longer and expressed more. Pseudouridine modification added a further boost. The authors offer design principles, not just one product. Their platform joins computation with wet-lab testing.
europmc-pmc9007740:
Pereira and co-authors present SLEAP, a deep learning system that tracks poses of many animals at once. Social behavior science needs exact motion records. Single-animal tools fail when animals interact. SLEAP covers the full work path. It helps users label training frames. It trains models and runs them on new video. A friendly screen interface fronts the system. A standard data model sits under it. More than 30 model designs are built in.

Two ways to group body parts are offered. Two ways to track identity join them. The team tested SLEAP on seven datasets. Flies, bees, mice, and gerbils all featured. Accuracy beat rival systems in their tests. Speed topped 800 frames per second. Delay stayed low enough for live use. The authors prove that with a closed-loop demo. One animal's behavior was steered by tracking its partner. The system is open for labs to adopt.
europmc-pmc9085840:
Li and co-authors examine mitophagy, the process that clears damaged mitochondria from cells. Mitochondria make energy and help control calcium, stress, and cell death. When they fail and pile up, cells suffer. The heart needs sound mitochondria more than most tissues, since it uses so much energy.

The review sets out the main paths that drive mitophagy and how they are switched on. It then links faulty mitophagy to heart attack, weak heart muscle, and heart failure. Open questions include how to tune the process to the right level. Readers get a compact account of a quality-control system and its role in heart disease.
europmc-pmc9332140:
Qiu and co-authors present dynamo, a framework that maps how single cells change state over time. Single-cell RNA data give snapshots, but cells cannot be followed directly. Dynamo infers true RNA velocity from metabolic labeling data. It then rebuilds a smooth vector field that predicts where each cell is heading.

Geometry tools pull out the rules that steer cell fate. The team traced the early appearance of one blood cell type in human blood formation. They also untangled uneven control inside a two-gene switch circuit. A least-action path method predicted drivers of many blood transitions. Fake gene changes in the model predicted real fate shifts. The authors frame dynamo as a step toward predictive cell biology.
europmc-pmc9664440:
Edgar describes Muscle5, an algorithm that builds ensembles of sequence alignments to judge homology and phylogeny. Alignments are the base for most claims about evolution. Standard work builds one alignment and trusts it fully. Hidden bias in that single build can poison later claims.

Muscle5 instead builds a crowd of strong alignments. It jitters a hidden Markov model and shuffles its guide tree. Each member of the crowd then carries a unlike bias. Support for a claim is the share of the crowd behind it. Tree tests showed the method could firm up weak bootstrap calls. It also showed that some high bootstrap trees were wrong. Applied to RNA virus phylogeny, the crowd cast doubt on new phyla. Some adopted groups look mixed in origin under this lens. The author says any alignment based claim can gain from the check.
europmc-pmc9797940:
Wu and co-authors review the sirtuin family and its roles in health and disease. Sirtuins are enzymes that strip acetyl tags from proteins. They run on NAD, a core cell energy currency. Mammals carry seven members, named SIRT1 through SIRT7.

The family shapes inflammation, metabolism, and cell stress replies. It also guides cell death and repair choices. Those broad roles tie sirtuins to many diseases. Cancer, heart disease, and lung disease all appear. The review covers the family's history and structure first. It then gives each member's jobs and control paths. Disease links are sorted by organ and condition. Drugs that block or boost sirtuins get a full survey. Human trial results on those modulators are reviewed too. The authors frame sirtuins as rich but tricky drug targets.
europmc-pmc9820240:
Mohd Isa and co-authors review discogenic low back pain, from disc anatomy to degeneration treatments. Disc wear is a major driver of this common pain. The pain ranks among the top causes of disability worldwide. A disc joins a soft gel core to a tough outer ring.

Cartilage end plates cap the disc above and below. Together the parts bear loads and absorb shocks. Wear sets off cascades that unbalance the disc tissue. Matrix breaks down faster than cells can rebuild it. Inflammation rises and stray nerves and vessels grow in. Those ingrowths help explain why worn discs hurt. Current care spans drugs, rehab, and surgery for relief. None of them stops the wear or regrows tissue. The review maps the signal paths behind the decline. It frames those paths as targets for future therapies. Stem cell loss is flagged as a core event.
europmc-pmc9829540:
Ryan and co-authors show that microglia ferroptosis, steered by SEC24B, feeds neurodegeneration. Iron control fails in several brain wasting diseases. Iron loaded microglia crowd the damaged brain regions. What that iron does to the cells was poorly known.

The team grew human microglia from stem cells in culture. They shared dishes with neurons and astrocytes there. The microglia answered strongly to added iron loads. They proved prone to ferroptosis, the iron driven death. Iron shifted their gene state toward a disease pattern. That same pattern marks microglia in Parkinson's brain tissue. Removing microglia delayed iron driven neuron death. A genome wide CRISPR screen hunted the death's regulators. It surfaced SEC24B, a vesicle traffic gene, as a new player. Blocking the screen's hits also blocked the death. The authors cast microglia iron as a drug target.
fbi-vault-special-counsel-mueller-invest: Release 40 of the Special Counsel Mueller investigation records carries the heaviest count in this group of Federal Bureau of Investigation sheets: 496 pages withheld in full. Its deleted-page sheet opens with long runs marked Duplicate, pages treated as copies freed elsewhere. It then turns to coded grounds, with the b5 mark set beside privacy marks. A later run adds the b7 family. The part contains no case text at all. It is a ledger of absence, for a reader who wants to know how the release was cut.
frus-1861-d140:
On 30 July 1861, William H. Seward wrote again to William Dayton in Paris. The letter is document 140 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Seward closed July with a second Paris letter in four days. The pace tells of a chief working to steady his posts after bad news. Dayton received from Washington not just orders, but a tone to copy in his talks. Tone, in such letters, was itself a form of news for the man who read it. Tone read as news is a skill this whole record rewards in its envoys.
frus-1861-d240:
16 June 1861 is stamped on a letter Seward got from James Shepherd Pike, the American minister to the Netherlands. The printed record keeps it as Document 240 in the President's message volume for 1861. The date falls in the opening months of the Civil War, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

The text is the view from the post abroad: local mood, official talk, and the envoy's own judgment. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1861-d40:
George Dallas, the outgoing American minister to Britain, wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 22 March 1861. The dispatch is document 40 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Dallas, a former Vice President, held the London post until Adams could replace him. His March letters cover the tense gap between two governments in Washington. They show a veteran hand keeping the post warm while the Union came apart at home. Dallas had served Polk as Vice President, which lent his late reports a veteran's calm. A veteran's calm was a fair gift to a chief who had just taken his chair.
frus-1862-d140:
Dated 12 September 1862, a report from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London went to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The printed record keeps it as Document 140 in the 1862 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs volume. It belongs to the summer of 1862, the war's second year, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

The text is the view from the post abroad: local mood, official talk, and the envoy's own judgment. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d240:
William Stuart sent Secretary of State William H. Seward a letter on 25 September 1862, printed as Document 240 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Stuart was acting head of the British legation in Washington.

Stuart wrote three days after Lincoln announced the Emancipation Proclamation, which tied the war openly to slavery. British leaders now had to reckon with the politics of backing a slaveholding republic. The legation's correspondence in late September, this letter included, belongs to the moment when that new fact began to reshape British debate. Britain's first concern in Washington was the blockade and what it cost British trade.
frus-1862-d340:
William H. Seward, the Secretary of State, wrote to William L. Dayton in Paris on 3 October 1862, in a dispatch printed out of order as Document 340 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. The letter shares its date with Document 330.

Two Seward letters to Paris on one date, filed far apart, show how the volume's arrangement can split a single day's brief. Together they carried the Department's October line to Dayton: the Union would accept no foreign truce plan. Reuniting such pairs is basic work for any reader of this file. French mills wanted Southern cotton, and French yards watched the Union blockade with care.
frus-1862-d40:
Secretary of State William H. Seward sent a dispatch to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London on 1 April 1862. The printed record keeps it as Document 40 in the 1862 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs volume. It belongs to the spring of 1862, a year into the war, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Outbound letters like this one told the envoy what line to take and what to report back. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d440:
On 23 October 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward replied to Gabriel García Tassara, the Spanish minister in Washington. The note is Document 440 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the year's official record.

Autumn replies like this one show Seward's method with resident ministers: answer promptly, concede nothing vital, and keep the door open. Spain's questions with the United States in 1862 were practical ones, tangled with the war at sea and the French move in Mexico. The exchange with Tassara ran parallel to the Madrid file of Perry and Koerner. Together the two give the full shape of Spanish-American dealings. Those dealings filled the second year of the Civil War.
frus-1862-d540:
Roest van Limburg received this letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward on 20 August 1862. The note is Document 540 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department's printed record for the year.

August 1862 was a month when Seward wrote to resident ministers with one eye on the battlefield. His other eye was on Europe's chancelleries. Intervention was being weighed in them. The Dutch minister's business was narrower and more legal: the treatment of neutral trade under the blockade. Seward answered in that narrower key, keeping the Dutch file correct while the great questions hung. The letter shows how much of a secretary's wartime day was spent on exact, limited answers to exact, limited questions.
frus-1862-d640:
On 12 July 1861 Townsend Harris sent a further dispatch from Japan to Secretary of State William H. Seward, two days after his previous letter. It is Document 640 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Two letters in two days from Edo usually meant enclosures traveling separately. Or they meant a matter Harris wanted stated twice for safety. Any single ship's mail could be lost. The Japanese correspondence moved by infrequent vessels, and ministers wrote accordingly, in clusters. Harris's subject was the treaty relationship he had built since 1856 and the Japanese government's handling of it. The paired letter shows the mechanics of diplomacy at the greatest distance the Department attempted, where redundancy was prudence.
frus-1863p1-d140:
Secretary of State William H. Seward opened the new month with this letter to Charles Francis Adams on 2 April 1863. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 140 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

April brought the ship question in Britain toward its test. A Southern-built raider's fate was in the courts' and the cabinet's hands that spring. Seward's letters armed Adams for the push. This one opens the April file from Washington's side. It shows the brief carried into a new month with no slack: claims pressed, tone held, and an envoy kept fully stocked.
frus-1863p1-d240:
On 16 July 1863, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, sent this dispatch from London to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It stands as document 240 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public. It was one of 3 letters between the same men dated that day.

Mail crossed the Atlantic by steamship, taking roughly ten days or more each way. News in a dispatch like this one was already old when Seward read it, yet it guided his next orders. Set in its place in the volume, it helps readers trace how two governments talked their way past repeated crises.
frus-1863p1-d340:
The British minister in Washington, Lord Lyons, took up his pen on 19 December 1862 to write Secretary of State William H. Seward. His note is document 340 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy.

The channel between Lyons and Seward was the main safety valve of Anglo-American relations in the war. Papers like this one are the valve at work. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it forms part of the fullest record of how the Union handled its most dangerous foreign relationship.
frus-1863p1-d40:
Judah P. Benjamin wrote this letter to Major General John B. Magruder on 17 October 1862. Benjamin ran the Confederate state office; Magruder was a Southern army commander, then bound for the command in Texas. The letter is document 40 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Most of Benjamin's printed letters went to envoys abroad. This one went to a general at home, a sign of how the state office's work crossed into the war's running. The letter sits in the group of Confederate papers the Union chose to print. It shows Richmond's top men dealing with each other on paper, in the fall of 1862.
frus-1863p1-d440:
One entry in the 1863 papers is a 2 April 1863 letter from Lord Lyons to William H. Seward. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the spring of 1863. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral.

The formal tone can hide the tension, but the pace gives it away. Notes this frequent mean both capitals were watching each other closely. British subjects caught up in the war filled many pages: men arrested, goods seized, and claims for losses that London took up with Washington. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d540:
On 28 May 1863 a formal note passed from Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington to William H. Seward, Secretary of State. It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863. Britain had not taken sides in the American war, and holding that line was the daily work of this mail.

None of these letters worked alone. Read in sequence, they show two governments testing each other's limits while both, in the end, avoided a second war. Students of the war use this mail to see foreign policy as the men on the spot lived it, page by page. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
frus-1863p1-d640:
The 16 October 1863 mail between Washington and London included a letter from Charles Francis Adams to William H. Seward. Adams was the American minister in London, and Seward was Secretary of State in Washington. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message. Mail between London and Washington crossed the Atlantic by steamer, so each reply took weeks to complete the round trip.

British subjects caught up in the war filled many pages: men arrested, goods seized, and claims for losses that London took up with Washington. The formal tone can hide the tension, but the pace gives it away. Notes this frequent mean both capitals were watching each other closely. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d140: General Eisenhower wrote to President Roosevelt on November 18, 1943, and his letter is Document 140 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The president had just passed through Eisenhower's North African command on the road to Cairo, and theater commanders wrote to their commander in chief with care. The record gives the date and the two men and no topic. The letter is part of the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d240:
Secretary of State Cordell Hull sent President Roosevelt a long secret digest from Washington on 20 November 1943, gathering reports from Ankara, Algiers, and Madrid. It is a snapshot of half a dozen side issues of the war in a single message.

British and Turkish officers, Ankara reports, differ wildly on Axis striking power against Turkey, and a compromise estimate will set the aid Turkey needs. From Algiers come orders to hold German prisoners accused of atrocities for later trial, and news of Yugoslav partisans interned on the Italian mainland. Madrid reports a protest over the many German agents working in Spain. It also reports pressure to shut the German consulate at Tangier. Washington wishes to let the Laurel incident rest if Spain proves itself by deeds.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d340:
A draft agreement prepared by the American delegation at Cairo on 30 November 1943, marked secret, sets the liaison rules between the European Advisory Commission and the Combined Chiefs of Staff. It grew out of John McCloy's talks with Eden, and its heading shows it was accepted at the Sextant Conference.

The Moscow conference had created the commission and sent it civil affairs questions closely tied to military matters of prime interest to the chiefs. Under the draft, the commission's tentative recommendations go to the chiefs for comment before final submission to the three governments. Approved recommendations return to the chiefs, who prepare the final directives for commanders in the field. British members of the civil affairs committee are to take full part in all its work, without limit as to area.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d40: Roosevelt wrote to Chiang Kai-shek on October 13, 1943, and the letter stands as Document 40 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Chiang was to join Roosevelt and Churchill at Cairo in November, the only meeting of the three that China attended as an equal. Letters like this one kept that plan warm through the autumn. The record names no subject; the text in the Foreign Relations series is the place to find it.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d440:
Agreed minutes, signed off by both the American and British sides, record a United States-United Kingdom meeting of December 4, 1943, during the Second Cairo Conference. Unlike a single nation's notes, an agreed text is the version both delegations accepted as accurate. The State Department printed it in the Cairo-Tehran conference volume.

Inside, the reader finds the shared record of what the two allies discussed and settled that day, in the middle of a conference called to finish the work begun at Tehran. Agreed minutes carry special weight for historians, because neither side could later rewrite them. They mark the points where London and Washington truly stood together.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d540:
Ambassador Averell Harriman wrote to Secretary of State Hull on January 6, 1944, using the formal channel to the department rather than his direct line to the President. Harriman's Moscow embassy was then Washington's main window on the Soviet Union. The message appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume.

Harriman wrote to Hull on departmental business and to Roosevelt on the great questions, and the choice of channel itself is a clue to a message's weight. Six weeks after Tehran, Soviet-American relations were entering their working phase. For readers, this cable shows the alliance being run through proper diplomatic form as well as summit friendship.
frus-1944-quebec-d140:
Numbered C.C.S. 654, this top-secret memorandum from the United States Chiefs of Staff is dated August 22, 1944. It proposes the basic policies the Combined Chiefs should adopt for the next Anglo-American staff conference, the meeting that became the Quebec Conference. The paper states the coalition's whole strategy in a few numbered paragraphs.

The over-all objective is the unconditional surrender of the Axis, in cooperation with Russia and other allies. Europe comes first; meanwhile pressure on Japan must never slacken. Once Europe is defeated, the full resources of both nations turn on Japan. The listed undertakings include aiding Russia and China, assisting French and Italian forces, and moving troops from Europe to the Pacific as a first priority.
frus-1944-quebec-d240:
Hopkins wrote to Roosevelt on September 13, 1944, about "the Italian business." He had talked with O'Dwyer, Crowley, and the State Department. He urged the president to take the initiative at Quebec. Roosevelt should win Churchill's approval for a course of action announced publicly. The machinery for quick relief and rehabilitation purchases, he said, was already available.

Italians could pay for goods, other than emergency relief, from funds accruing from American soldiers' pay in Italy. Two matters needed clearing up fast: the prisoner of war question, and amendment of the armistice terms. An attached memorandum argues Italy must return quickly to political and economic independence, free from domination by any powerful neighbor, with shipping, trucks, and payment as the immediate problems.
frus-1944-quebec-d40:
Wilson Brown, the President's naval aide, wrote to A. J. McFarland, secretary of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, on August 31, 1944. Brown managed the President's military household and map room. The message appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume.

Staff traffic between the White House military office and the Joint Chiefs' secretariat arranged the soldiers' part of the coming conference: papers, attendance, and the movement of plans. Brown and McFarland were the kind of officers whose names rarely reach print but whose work made summits run. For readers, the note shows a conference's military skeleton being assembled.
frus-1945-50-intel-d140:
Minutes of the first meeting of the National Intelligence Authority are dated 5 February 1946. The board of secretaries created by the president's January directive here sits for the first time. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

A first meeting of a new governing body is a founding act. That holds even when the minutes run to routine: members present, officers named, first business taken up. The authority's birth had been argued over since August in the papers before this one. Readers have now crossed the volume's great divide, from contest to institution. Everything after these minutes, directives, disputes, and growth, happens inside the house that the January directive built and this meeting first occupied.
frus-1945-50-intel-d240:
A memorandum dated 27 September 1949 links two senior offices. The sender was the General Counsel (Houston) and the Legislative Liaison Officer of the Central Intelligence Agency (Pforzheimer). The reader was the Executive of the Central Intelligence Agency (Shannon). It is document 240 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. The Dulles Report had landed in January 1949, and Washington was arguing over which of its fixes the CIA should adopt.

Inside the government, memos were how business got done between meetings. One put the question and the facts in front of the reader at once. A reader can watch the system think on paper: a fact here, a doubt there, a choice asked for at the end. To read it in place is to watch the Cold War state being assembled at desk level.
frus-1945-50-intel-d340:
A memorandum dated 13 February 1948 links two senior offices. The sender was the Executive Secretary of the National Security Council (Souers). The reader was Allen W. Dulles, Mathias F. Correa, and William H. Jackson. It is document 340 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. Across Washington, the new security bodies were moving from setup work to the real business of the Cold War.

Memos like this one did the quiet work of the system. They carried facts, advice, and requests from one office to the desk that could act on them. The reply, if any came, would build on the points laid out here. To read it in place is to watch the Cold War state being assembled at desk level.
frus-1945-50-intel-d40:
James Lay, a young officer in McCormack's research and intelligence office, wrote to his chief on 2 November 1945. Lay would serve American intelligence for decades after this paper. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

Staff memoranda from working officers show plans being drafted at the desk level, where phrases are chosen and charts drawn. Lay's paper belongs to the State Department's effort to design the central system it hoped to lead. Readers who know Lay's later career, at the heart of the National Security Council staff, will enjoy meeting him here at the start. The volume is full of such first appearances by men who ran the cold war's secret side.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d140:
Harriman watched, but took no part, when Stalin and Churchill pressed the Polish premier in Moscow. His report to the President of 14 October 1944 describes the meeting with Mikolajczyk and his associates the day before. Molotov and Eden were present. The cable is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume.

Mikolajczyk first laid out the proposals of his August memorandum. Stalin found two great defects in it. It ignored the Polish Committee of National Liberation, the rival body set up at Lublin. And it failed to accept the Curzon Line as the Soviet-Polish boundary. Churchill backed Stalin on the Curzon Line without reserve. Stalin did allow that the memorandum had good points, friendly relations with the Soviet Union among them.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d240:
The Iranian minister came to plead his country's case on 18 January 1945. Stettinius recorded the conversation in a memorandum printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It shows a small nation looking to Washington on the eve of the Big Three meeting. The minister called at his own request.

He had been instructed, he said, to draw attention to the Persian people's great concern over Russia's attitude and actions toward their country. His people hoped the United States would take a firm hand in insisting on a strong, independent Iran at the coming conference. Stettinius assured him that Persia's welfare was constantly in mind. The President, he was confident, would keep Iranian interests before him in the talks with Churchill and Stalin. The minister then offered his government's facilities for the meeting itself.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d340: Why not agree to a French zone now, Harry Hopkins asked the President in a note slipped across the Yalta table on February 5, 1945. The question of French membership in the Control Commission for Germany could be weighed later. Or, Hopkins added, Roosevelt might say that French participation could be considered later. Then he could leave it at that. The slip survives in Hopkins's papers, printed word for word. It captures a decision being shaped in real time, in pencil, while Stalin and Churchill waited.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d40: Another Roosevelt message to Churchill followed on 3 January 1945, the second in two days. Filed as document 40 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on Malta and Yalta, it belongs to the final weeks of written preparation. After January, the story moves from cables like this one to the face-to-face sessions at Malta and then at Yalta itself.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d440:
Ties between the powers close the Polish formula, and this paper of February 10, 1945, preserves Molotov's draft of the final paragraph. His text notes that the Soviet state already kept ties with the Polish government then in place. Britain and the United States would now open ties with the new Polish Provisional Government of National Unity.

Envoys would be exchanged. By their reports, the three powers would keep informed about the state of things in Poland. The editors note the draft seems to have been accepted by Stettinius and Eden. It entered Eden's report that day. A single sentence carried recognition, oversight, and the seed of later quarrels.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d140:
Assistant Secretary James Dunn reported a two-hour groundwork session with Britain's Sir Alexander Cadogan in a memorandum dated July 14, 1945. The extracts printed here form document 140 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Cadogan had called at Potsdam that afternoon to talk through the conference agenda in advance.

The printed passage covers procedure. Cadogan asked whether Potsdam would follow the Yalta pattern of foreign ministers meeting from noon to one and heads of government in the afternoon. Both men agreed the ministers' meetings at Yalta had been too brief to be fully useful. Dunn also recalls how Roosevelt came to chair the earlier conferences, almost by habit. Other extracts of the same memo appear throughout the volume, subject by subject.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d240:
Acting Secretary Grew urged quick action on the Italy pledge in a telegram to Secretary Byrnes dated July 11, 1945. The message is document 240 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. The recommendation was that, once Italy declared war on Japan, the United States publicly back her admission in due course to the world security organization.

The recommendation already lay before the President in the Big Three briefing papers, Grew notes. But Italy may now declare war before the meeting opens. The value of the American move, at home and abroad, may depend on announcing it promptly after the declaration. He proposes proceeding at once: if Byrnes agrees and the President approves, Winant will be told to inform the British and ask whether they will support the American position.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d340:
A new state map for western Germany is reported in Murphy's despatch of June 30, 1945, on state organization in the American area. Army headquarters had directed the Twelfth Army Group to organize the Western Military District for military government on the basis of three German states, or Laender. The order held pending final fixing of the French zone.

The three states were Hessen-Nassau, with its capital at Kassel, Hessen, and a third built from the region's old units. Murphy's report, sent as despatch No. 519, shows occupation officers redrawing Germany's internal map on the ground, reviving historic states rather than ruling through the old Reich machinery.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d40:
Truman kept his options open in this telegram to Churchill of May 29, 1945. Churchill's Number 58 had been received. He was now making a study of a possible date for the three-party meeting. He hoped to have further information on the subject in the not distant future.

The wire is short and commits to nothing. Read beside Churchill's eagerness for mid-June, it looks deliberate. Stalin had signaled readiness after June 27. Washington would name the day when its own calendar, and its reading of Moscow, were ready. The caution fits a president six weeks into the job, holding the alliance's timetable in his own hand.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d440:
American views on minority transfers are restated in a State Department memorandum to the British Embassy dated July 11, 1945. The Department had considered the Foreign Office telegram of June 22 and the draft instructions for Ambassador Nichols in Prague. It answers by quoting its own note to the Czechoslovak government of January 31, 1945.

In that note Washington said it fully appreciated the injuries Czechoslovakia had suffered at the hands of Germany and of the German minority over the past decade. It was prepared to examine the problem in search of a satisfactory solution. Any solution, though, must weigh the broader aspects of the problem, and its relation to Europe's future peace.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d540:
Stimson comments on a draft presidential cable in his letter to the Secretary of State of June 19, 1945. The draft, enclosed with a letter of June 9, would answer the Prime Minister's cable of May 28 on lend-lease. Stimson has also received, the day before, a letter of June 13 from the Director of War Mobilization and Reconversion, a copy of which he attaches.

The proposed cable, the War Department judges, is consistent with the direction in that letter. If it is sent, Stimson suggests one improvement to its second sentence. It should read that America intends to furnish lend-lease during the Japanese war in accordance with the general policy discussed between Churchill and President Roosevelt at Quebec on September 14.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d640:
Ambassador Caffery sent hopeful news on the Levant from Paris on July 5, 1945. His secret wire is document 640 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. It reports the words of Lebanon's minister after a talk with French foreign minister Bidault.

Bidault, the minister said, had told him France had firmly decided two things. The Troupes Speciales would be turned over to the Lebanese government. All French forces would leave the Levant as soon as British forces left theirs. France had also dropped, for now, its plan for a naval base there. It would revive that plan only if the new world organization allowed it. The minister added that Syria's mood ran much hotter than Lebanon's, and that few Frenchmen were left in Syria at all.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1040:
Willard Thorp answered Clayton and Despres from Washington on July 18, 1945. The proposed coal directive for Germany, he reports, has not been shown to the Russians. It was revised in a note to the British dated July 10. No British comment has come back either, so the program is not yet in effect.

Thorp explains why Moscow was bypassed. A suggestion from London to lay the directive, and a coal allocation plan, before the Russians for the Potsdam agenda came late. Sending it through the Moscow embassy would not reach the Kremlin in time. Since Ambassador Harriman was traveling to Berlin, the matter could be raised there in person. Thorp asks whether action is now wanted.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1140:
Zygmunt Modzelewski, Poland's deputy foreign minister, wrote straight to the United States Secretary of State on 30 July 1945. The Potsdam Conference had three days left. Warsaw chose that moment to make its case at the highest American level it could reach.

A deputy minister writing to a secretary of state is a step up the ladder of rank. It signals how much the writer's government had at stake. Poland's border and standing were in the balance as the talks closed. This letter is Warsaw's bid for American goodwill in the summit's final days, sent while there was still time to sway the outcome.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1240:
The Acting Secretary of State wrote to the Secretary of State on 19 July 1945. Grew's cables from Washington formed a near daily circuit with Byrnes at Potsdam. Each carried home news, pending business, and the capital's mood.

The circuit mattered because choices at the summit landed on desks in Washington within days. Taxes of detail, from names to dates, had to match on both ends. This message is one turn of that wheel. It shows the department's two chiefs keeping their shared work aligned while an ocean and a war's end lay between them.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1340:
Jefferson Caffery, the American ambassador in France, cabled the acting secretary of state on 21 July 1945. Caffery had taken up the Paris post after the city was freed in 1944. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official American diplomatic record, prints it in the second volume on the Potsdam Conference.

Paris watched the Potsdam talks from outside the room, since France had no seat at the summit. Caffery's cables told Washington how French leaders read the talks and what they feared or hoped from them. For readers, the message gives the view of a close ally. France had much at stake in choices about Germany, yet no vote in making them.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-140:
A rapporteur's report dated July 31, 1945 brought a working group's results before the Potsdam leadership on the eve of the close. Subcommittees had labored for two weeks on the settlement's details. Their reports now fed the final protocol. This report was printed in the second Potsdam volume of the official record.

Reports filed this late have a settled tone. Most brackets are gone; what remains is flagged as a leader's choice. Readers see the exact state of a topic hours before the end. The piece shows how the conference turned staff work into history in its final day of drafting.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-40:
Shipping fills the subject list of a Potsdam conversation that left no official record. The talk ran across the whole Allied trooplift problem during the conference days. Its editorial note is the fortieth unnumbered item following document 710 in volume two.

Ten subjects are named in the editors' list. They include the allocation of shipping for civilian and military passengers. Extended U.S. use of the liners Queen Elizabeth and Queen Mary was discussed, as was a British conversion of one hundred vessels. Captured German passenger ships for U.S. troop movement figure twice in the list. The Swedish liners Gripsholm and Drottningholm come up as conversion candidates. Italy's possible entry into the shipping bodies was weighed, with British charter payments for Italian vessels. Even striking Polish crews on British-operated Polish vessels found a place on the agenda.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d740:
Edward Stettinius, the President's personal representative, wrote this memorandum on July 26, 1945. Document 740 comes from a man who had just led the American team at San Francisco. Stettinius had signed the United Nations charter weeks before. His Potsdam-era memo joined the second volume of the conference papers.

A Stettinius paper links the two great projects of 1945. He carried the hopes of the new world body into the summit's harder rooms. Readers find in his writing the era's faith in organized peace. The memo also shows a former Secretary of State serving in a new, personal role. Rank changed; the work went on.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d840:
Schuyler wrote to the War Department on July 24, 1945, in document 840. The chief of the American military team on Rumania's control commission sent a third report in this run. His channel ran through the Army to Washington. The letter was printed in the second Potsdam volume.

Serial military reports build a ledger of grievances and facts. Schuyler logged the commission's workings as they happened. Readers can watch patterns form across his letters. The document shows why the Rumanian file frustrated the summit: the ground truth, reported plainly, contradicted the hopes held in Germany. His writing kept that truth in front of the men who needed it.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d940:
Edwin Pauley reported to the Secretary of State on July 27, 1945, after touring five Berlin plants in the American area. The plants made peacetime goods: artificial wool and silk, electrical instruments, radios, and telephones. Pauley walked through two of them with William Clayton.

Bombing had done little damage, Pauley writes. After the armistice, Russian teams removed nearly all the machinery, plus process records and plans. A few foremen were persuaded to go to Russia with the gear. Two plants belonged to International Telephone and Telegraph and were almost fully American owned. Pauley calls the stripping organized vandalism, aimed at American occupiers as well as Germany.
frus-1950v07-d640:
Resolution 376 (V), adopted by the General Assembly on October 7, 1950, is printed in full here. It recalls past resolutions on Korea and the report of the UN Commission on Korea. It notes that unity had not been reached and that the North had attacked the South.

The text urges steps to keep Korea stable and to hold votes for one free government. It states that UN forces should stay only as long as needed. A new body, the Commission for the Unification and Rehabilitation of Korea, is created. Seven states were named to serve on it.
frus-1955-57v16-d40:
Special National Intelligence Estimate SNIE 30–3–56 assesses Nasser and the Middle East after Egypt seized the Suez Canal Company. It states that the move strengthened Nasser at home and across the Arab world. Soviet praise added to his standing.

The paper judges that Egyptians can run the canal with fair skill. The true weight of the act, it says, is political, not technical. Western choices run from calm acceptance to war. Britain had frozen about 110 million pounds in Egyptian balances. The estimate warns that a win for Nasser would spur new seizures of foreign assets.
frus-1969-76v40:
Germany and Berlin from 1969 to 1972 fill Volume XL of the 1969-1976 series. Its 388 documents run in one sequence. They follow Chancellor Brandt's opening to the East and the talks it set off. Four-power talks on Berlin take up much of the volume. The ambassadors met in the old Allied Control Council building from March 1970. Their aim was to ease life in and around the divided city.

The papers include backchannel notes and records of talks in Bonn, Moscow, and Washington. They show Washington backing Brandt while guarding Allied rights. The Berlin deal of 1971 stands at the center. The volume ends with the accords in force.
gao-gaoreports-b-309740:
C. Young Construction, Inc. lost its protest under GAO decision B-309740, dated October 15, 2007. The Navy sought a builder for the P333V Fleet Support Facility. The site is Naval Air Station Jacksonville, Florida. The deal went to Sauer, Inc. under request for proposals N69450-07-R-1266. The job adds a secure data space, with lot and walk work as options.

The protester fought its poor score and its cut from the race. It had named one man for three of four key posts. GAO found the review fair and in line with the stated terms. It denied the protest. The case shows the risk of lean staffing plans for key posts.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-340:
Energy Savings, GAO-05-340 of June 22, 2005, weighs a deal type that pays for green upgrades out of the savings they yield. The federal government is the land's top energy user. It spent $3.7 billion on energy for its 500,000 sites by the last count. Cash for upgrades is hard to win in tight budgets. Since 1986, firms may fund the work and be paid from the gains.

Law caps each year's pay at that year's savings. GAO asks how wide the deals have spread. It asks what gains in energy and cash agencies count on. It tests if true gains cover costs. It names where a sharp eye must guard the purse.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-540:
Spending on the New Triad of strategic forces is the puzzle in GAO report GAO-05-540, dated June 30, 2005. In its 2001 Nuclear Posture Review, the Defense Department widened the old nuclear triad. The New Triad adds conventional strike forces, active and passive defenses, and a rebuilt defense base. GAO asked whether the department's five-year plan shows the full cost.

The five-year program does not capture all New Triad spending. GAO's trial count through 2009 found far more than the department had listed. Officials blamed the breadth of the concept. A tool that groups related items across the plan could fix the blind spot. Beyond five years, GAO found no joined investment approach. That gap matters because the New Triad faces steep funding pressure over time. Without a long view, leaders cannot set priorities or shape fair budgets. The report urges clearer totals and a real investment plan.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-140:
The National Guard Youth Challenge Program is reviewed in GAO-06-140, a report dated November 29, 2005. Congress set up the program in 1993 as a pilot for high school dropouts. It gives at-risk youth military-based training to build life skills. The program runs 17 months at 29 sites in 24 states and Puerto Rico.
