Since 2001 the federal share of costs has stood at 60 percent. Congress directed GAO to trace the program's trends, cost studies, and oversight.

GAO asked whether anyone had tested if the 60-40 cost split still fits program needs. It also checked how the National Guard Bureau watches the state sites. The study covered state and federal efforts to find money outside program funds. Rules bar some steps, such as hiring grant writers with program money. GAO made recommendations to sharpen management and oversight and to widen funding support. The Defense Department agreed with the recommendations.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-540:
Domestic violence hurts military families and readiness alike. In GAO-06-540 (May 24, 2006), GAO tracks Defense Department action on task force advice. A task force assessed the services' response to domestic violence. It issued three reports with 194 recommendations. A fiscal year 2004 defense law required this GAO review. GAO discusses the department's ability to report incidents and discipline.

GAO also reviews resources given to carry out the advice. It checks steps on victim confidentiality and training for commanders, senior enlisted staff, and chaplains. It examines the oversight framework for the work. Progress has been made, GAO found. Further management action is still needed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1040:
New reserve centers under base reshaping need a watch plan, GAO argues in report GAO-07-1040, dated September 13, 2007. The Army will build 125 new Armed Forces Reserve Centers. It will close 387 older reserve sites, under 44 reshaping orders. The new centers should aid recruiting and joint work.

GAO asked how cost and savings figures have moved from the reshaping panel's first take. It asked if the Army has named the hurdles that could slow the builds, and has a plan for them. The report, one in a set on the 2005 round, rests on budget data and talks across five states.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-140:
Federal grants help schools teach students who are still learning English. GAO examined the data behind those grants in GAO-07-140, a report dated December 7, 2006. Title III funds are split among states by formula. The law allows two data sources for the split: a Census survey or state counts. GAO reviewed both sources and how states spent the money. It gathered data from 12 states.

Education used the Census survey data to divide the funds, GAO found. It had no method to judge which source was more accurate. State data were often incomplete or inconsistent, partly due to unclear report instructions. The survey data also swung sharply from year to year. GAO's test showed the choice of source changed what states received. In fiscal year 2006, over $650 million went out under the program. GAO urged clearer instructions and a fair method to compare the sources.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-340:
A Justice Department bureau surveys the public about police encounters, including police use of force. GAO checked the bureau's work habits in GAO-07-340, issued March 30, 2007. The review covers products from the 1999 and 2002 surveys. Four reports and one press release came under the lens. GAO measured them against quality rules from several bodies. The rules cover review, approval, and release of statistics.

The bureau fully followed the rules for all four reports, GAO found. Review and clearance steps were complete. The press release scored lower. It fully met 7 of 10 rules that applied. Three rules tied to agency independence were not fully met. The bureau had treated press releases as outside the statistics rules. GAO judged the release a statistical product by its content. Independence safeguards for releases were the weak spot. The bureau agreed with the analysis.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-40:
Competition for Iraq rebuilding contracts is the subject of GAO-07-40, published October 6, 2006. Since 2003, Congress had given more than $20 billion to the Iraq Relief and Reconstruction Fund. The Departments of Defense and State and the U.S. Agency for International Development awarded most of the work. By law, sole-source awards of $5 million or more had to be flagged to Congress.

GAO measured how much of the work was competed since October 1, 2003. It also tested 51 chosen contract actions for the required paperwork and notices. The report shows where agencies met the rules and where task orders slipped past them. State and USAID agreed with the findings, while Defense offered a technical comment.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-940:
NASA's supplier base through the shuttle's end is planned in GAO-07-940, dated July 25, 2007. Over 1,500 suppliers support the shuttle program today. Some are the only source for a part or material. The shuttle retires soon, and the Constellation program follows. NASA must decide now which suppliers to keep. It has written a transition strategy and linked buying plans. A database tracks skills, property, and suppliers by capability. A watch list flags sole-source suppliers at risk.

Few key decisions have actually been made, GAO found. What Constellation will need from suppliers stays uncertain. That fog clouds the value of the new plans. Costs past fiscal year 2010 have not been estimated. GAO urged joint cost estimates for the transition years. The fiscal year 2009 budget should carry those figures. NASA agreed with the advice. Workforce notice plans exist on paper. The supplier calls themselves still lie ahead.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-240:
Cargo partnership checks are assessed in GAO report GAO-08-240, issued April 25, 2008. Customs officials run a voluntary pact with trade firms to guard supply chains. Members open their security practices to federal validation. In return, their cargo draws less scrutiny at the border. GAO reviewed the program in 2005 and flagged operating strains.

This report checks progress since that review. It weighs how fairly the program hands out its benefits. It probes the strain of validating members' practices site by site. Staffing and management hurdles get their own review. The title balances the verdict: the partnership has grown stronger, but proof of practice still lags.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-40:
Social Security disability claim backlogs are examined in GAO report GAO-08-40, dated December 7, 2007. At the end of fiscal year 2006, some 1.5 million disability claims awaited a decision. GAO tracked backlog trends over a decade and the steps the Social Security Administration is taking.

Backlogged claims doubled from fiscal year 1997 through 2006, reaching about 576,000. The hearings stage held over 415,000 of them, 72 percent of the total, and wait times there grew by about 95 days. Claim volume rose over 20 percent while the agency lost key staff, including claims examiners and administrative law judges. GAO recommended better tracking of the reconsideration stage and tighter planning of anti-backlog steps. The agency agreed in part, stressing its funding needs.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-440:
The Environmental Protection Agency's chemical risk database is assessed in GAO report GAO-08-440, issued March 7, 2008. The Integrated Risk Information System holds the agency's scientific position on health effects for more than 540 chemicals. GAO checked the backlog of assessments and a new review process set by the Office of Management and Budget.

In fiscal years 2006 and 2007, the agency sent 32 assessments out for the first of three outside reviews but finished only 4. Most of the 70 ongoing assessments had run over 5 years as of December 2007. The new interagency reviews are not open: the budget office treats agency comments as internal, which GAO says hurts trust in the results. GAO recommended a clearer, faster process with a defined role for other agencies. The agency agreed to weigh the advice.
history-of-the-united-netherlands-from-t:
This portion of John Lothrop Motley's History of the United Netherlands gives the second part of chapter five, centred on the siege of Antwerp. Alexander Farnese, Prince of Parma, has drawn his lines around the great city. The patriots have slept through the winter dreaming of French help. Motley calls that dream a slow poison, now dispelled.

Antwerp must fall, or the patriots must strike a decisive blow themselves. A telling blow has been secretly and maturely meditated, Motley hints, aimed at Parma's works. The fort of Liefkenshoek and the river defences come first. Parma's army holds its position with veteran patience. The chapter builds toward the famous fireship attack on his bridge. Motley's narrative lingers on engineering, hunger, and suspense, the siege as a duel of wits.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abendana-joseph: Joseph Abendana was a refugee from the rage of the Spanish Inquisition, who settled in Hamburg. He was kin to the hakam of the same name, the entry notes. A relative of his, Mordecai Abendana, stood out among the founders of the Hamburg Bank in 1620. Joseph's sons, Jacob and Isaac, were born in Spain, not in Hamburg as some claim. Both sons gave their lives to learned work, and their own entries follow this short notice of their father.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abner-or-abiner:
Abner, Saul's captain of the host, was likely the king's cousin. After Saul fell at Mount Gilboa, Abner kept the tribes except Judah loyal to Ishbosheth at Mahanaim. A charge from Ishbosheth then pushed him to offer his support to David.

Joab killed Abner at Hebron, from jealousy and to avenge Asahel. David mourned him publicly. Rabbinic writing makes Abner a hero of great strength, son of the Witch of En-dor by tradition. The rabbis still blamed him for faults, such as failing to stop Saul from killing the priests of Nob.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abraham-ibn-has:
Abraham ibn Hassan ha-Levi wrote a work on the six hundred and thirteen Biblical precepts. It was printed as an appendix to Daniel Bomberg's first rabbinic Bible, at Venice in 1517. Its title there is Commands and Prohibitions.

Written first in Arabic, the work was a plain list of the precepts in weekly lesson order, with notes pointing to Maimonides' code. Its Hebrew translator, Judah ben Shoshan, padded it with Talmud and Sifre passages, and the short guide lost its point. A Latin version came out at Canterbury in 1597. The author's home stays unclear, though it lay where Jews spoke Arabic.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-absalom-the-eld: Absalom the Elder was a Tanna whose birth and death dates are not known. One teaching in his name survives. It is a homiletic reading of Exodus xiv. 15, kept in the Mekilta. His name is not sure. A like passage gives forms such as Abṭolis and Abṭelos. Those look like short forms of a Greek name. Elijah Wilna fixed the name on that basis. The entry treats the fix as sound, since copyists often garbled Greek names.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-acosta-duarte-n: Duarte Nunes d'Acosta was a merchant at Hamburg in the first half of the seventeenth century. He came from a noted Marano family of Portugal. About 1640 King John IV of Portugal set up an agency at Hamburg. He made Acosta its first head, with a noble title. Local ill will toward Jews did not stop the choice. Kin of Acosta held the post from then on. The agency lasted to the year 1795.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aha-b-ika-940: Aha b. Ika was a Babylonian amora of the fourth century, a junior contemporary of Raba and nephew of Aha b. Jacob. He is frequently quoted in halakic discussions by his contemporaries and successors. His uncle gave him the title of Bar be-Rab, Fellow of the Academy, and the two carried on halakic controversies with each other.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-akkerman-1040: Akkerman is a district, town, and village in Bessarabia, Russia. The town stands on the right bank of the Dniester estuary. It lies twenty-seven miles southwest of Odessa. In 1897 the Jewish population of the town was 4,846. The village held 1,136 Jews, and the district 5,241. Akkerman had two public synagogues at the time. It also had three private prayer-houses and seven Hebrew schools.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aljama-1240:
Aljama is a Spanish word of Arab roots. It named the self-ruled groups of Moors and Jews in Spain. Jewish groups ran their own affairs in large part. Their rabbis judged and their heads raised the taxes. The crown dealt with the group as one body. It set one tax for the whole group.

Christian rule made that bond more fixed. Councils met at Toledo, Barcelona, and Huete. They set fair tax rates for the groups. Bishops gained a say over the groups as well. Rabbi picks had to gain the bishop's nod. The entry ends with notes on the word's kin terms.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alvalensi-samue: Samuel Alvalensi was born in Spain late in the fifteenth century. He may have been a grandson of the Samuel in the last entry. After the ban of 1492 he was taken to Fez. There he won the favor of King Abu Said. About 1536 a revolt rose against that king's line. Samuel helped fit out a fleet for the loyal side. He sailed with four hundred men to Ceuta. The foe had 30,000 men, yet he beat them off. He showed the same nerve at Safi in 1539.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-amraphel-1440:
Amraphel was a king of Shinar in Genesis. He marched west with Chedorlaomer of Elam. Their host struck Sodom in that march. Who he was has long been fought over. Schrader first put forth a bold match. He held Amraphel to be Hammurabi of Babylon. That view now holds the field, the entry says.

Hammurabi founded one realm out of the whole land. The king list gives his reign as fifty-five years. A newer record casts doubt on that count. It puts his reign at forty-three years. His dates are fought over just as hard. Works of peace marked his reign at Babylon. Canals, grain stores, and temple walls are named.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-an-im-zemirot-1: Anim Zemirot is a hymn of mystic cast. Its name is oft given as the Hymn of Glory. The hymn is ascribed to Judah of Speyer. He is called the saint of that town. Many groups give it a place of honor. It stands at the close of the dawn rite. There it joins the Psalm of the Day. It is read on the Eve of Atonement as well. In English groups a plain tune goes with it. That tune comes from the Rhineland like the hymn.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-apikoros-pl-api:
Apikoros, plural Apikorsim, is a word Jews use in common speech for a heretic, a man unsound in belief or lax in practice. Its origin is disputed. Most derive it from Epicurus, the Greek thinker. Maimonides instead tied it to a Hebrew root meaning freedom, and read it as one who refuses the Law's obedience.

In the Mishnah, the entry argues, the word plainly means a follower of Epicurus. It stands in a list of those who have no share in the world to come, beside deniers of resurrection and of the Law's divine gift. Sifre, on Numbers, splits the two faults between a Sadducee and an Apikoros. The entry then traces the term through Josephus and later Jewish writing.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-arumah-1840: Arumah was a place in Ephraim, not far from Shechem. The judge Abimelech took refuge there, as Judges chapter 9 tells. Later writers matched the site to El Ormeh, on the hills southeast of Shechem. The entry adds nothing more: no size, no people, and no later events. It fixes the place by its region, its one Bible scene, and its proposed modern site.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-asher-ben-simeo:
Asher ben Simeon was a German religious poet who lived no later than 1546. He wrote a selihah, a penitential poem, that must not be confused with a like poem by Kalonymus ben Judah. His poem runs to fifteen stanzas of five lines each. In it the poet prays for the welfare of the king of the land where he lives.

Zunz suggests a link between this poet and an Asher of Frankfort. That Asher wrote a short confession, a widdui, noted by Joseph ben Phinehas Hahn in his Yosif Omez. The entry is brief and careful: one named poem, its shape, its prayer for the king, and a possible match with the Frankfort namesake that Zunz claims but does not prove.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-assing-david-as:
David Assing was a German physician and poet. He was born at Königsberg in 1787 and died on April 25, 1842. He studied at Tübingen, Halle, Vienna, and Göttingen. His doctorate, granted in 1807, rested on a thesis about foods and their laws. The thesis was published at Göttingen in 1809.

Assing settled in Hamburg to practice medicine, but war soon drew him into army service as a cavalry physician. He served first in the Russian army, then in the Prussian. In 1815 he returned to Hamburg and married Rosa Maria Varnhagen the next year. He then embraced Christianity and dropped his middle name, Assur. He was known for his study of Hippocrates and Greek medicine. He also wrote lyric poems for journals of his friends.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-augustus-ii-the:
Augustus II., called the Strong, was elector of Saxony from 1694 to 1733. From 1697 he was also king of Poland, as Frederick Augustus I. He was born at Dresden on May 12, 1670, and died at Warsaw on Feb. 1, 1733. He confirmed the privileges of the Jews, as his predecessor John Sobieski had done. But he showed little care for their safety.

Jewish bankers supplied much of the 10,000,000 thalers Augustus spent buying the Polish throne. Berend Lehmann of Halberstadt raised the money for his coronation. Augustus praised Lehmann in a letter of Sept. 23, 1707, and protected his family in 1708. Yet Polish Jews suffered robbery by unpaid soldiers and forced conversion sermons in their synagogues. Petitions for relief from those sermons failed, the entry says, and preaching was often kept up only with soldiers' aid.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-avesta-15240:
The Avesta is the sacred book of the Parsees, the followers of Zoroaster. It is often called Zend-Avesta, though the entry calls that name less exact. The phrase behind it means the Law and its Interpretation. So the Avesta stands to the Parsees as the Hebrew Scriptures, with the Talmud beside them, stand to the Jews.

Jewish scholars have two reasons to care, the entry says. Parts of the Avesta run close to parts of the Old and New Testaments. And Persia and the Jews met often in history, as the books of Ezra and Isaiah show. Zoroaster, dated here to about 660-583 B.C., stands as priest, prophet, and lawgiver of ancient Iran. His god, Ahuramazda, was worshiped by the Persian kings. In the seventh century Islam displaced the Avesta in Persia, and its keepers fled to India.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baal-hamon-2240:
Baal-hamon is a place named once in the Song of Songs. Solomon is said to have had a vineyard there. No one knows where it was. Graetz, a scholar cited here, proposes reading Baal-hermon in place of Baal-hamon. The entry calls that mere conjecture.

Others have matched the name with Balamon, a place in the book of Judith. That town seems to be Ibleam, the modern Bel'ame, a fruitful valley south of the plain of Jezreel. Two editors named in the entry cut the word out of the verse to save its meter.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baer-seligman-s:
Seligman Baer was a writer on the Masorah and an editor of the Hebrew Bible, born at Mosbach in Baden on Sept. 18, 1825. He died at Biebrich-on-the-Rhine in March 1897. He began Masoretic study in 1844 and never held a university chair. He earned his living as Hebrew teacher to the Jewish community of Biebrich. Leipsic still gave him an honorary doctorate.

With Franz Delitzsch, Baer set out to edit the Old Testament books in Hebrew, close to the Masoretic tradition. The entry lists the volumes in order, from Genesis in 1869 to Kings in 1895, each with Masoretic notes. It also reports sharp criticism by Christian Ginsburg, then concludes that Baer's edition would long remain the standard Masoretic text. His prayer-book work of 1868 is treated the same way.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baneth-jerahmee: Jerahmeel Dob Baneth, called Bernhard, was a Hungarian rabbi born in 1815 at Széchény. He died on Oct. 21, 1871. Youngest son of Ezekiel Baneth, he was among his father's most gifted pupils and shared his love of Talmud. After study under Moses Sofer at Presburg he married in 1840 and settled at Liptó-Szent-Miklós, giving himself to study. Pupils gathered to him there. In 1868 he took, without pay, the rabbinate of the Orthodox congregation of that town. He left a manuscript volume of notes on the whole Talmud.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-barnett-john-fa:
John Barnett, whose family name was Beer, was an English composer born at Bedford on July 1, 1802. He died at Cheltenham on April 17, 1890. He made his début as a singer at the Lyceum in 1813, aged eleven. Two years later his voice broke, and he turned to composition, studying under Ferdinand Ries and Perez. While still a child he wrote masses and lighter pieces, several of them published.

His first great success was the operetta "Before Breakfast" at the Lyceum in 1825. "The Pet of the Petticoats" followed in 1831, and in 1832 he became music-director of the Olympic Theater. His first opera, "The Mountain Sylph," succeeded at once in 1834. "Fair Rosamond" came in 1837 and "Farinelli" in 1838. After a year of study at Frankfurt he settled at Cheltenham in 1841 as a singing teacher. His output includes three unperformed operas, two unfinished oratorios, two string quartets, and about 4,000 detached songs.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bassani-israel-:
Israel Benjamin Bassani was rabbi at Reggio, Italy, born in 1703 and dead there on Jan. 20, 1790. He was a son of Isaiah Bassani. He wrote verse well in both Hebrew and Italian.

For a duke of Modena he made eighty Hebrew poems with Italian versions in 1750. Other works include sonnets, a book of legal writings from 1741, and thirty short poems on electricity. Hundreds of his Hebrew letters and volumes of sermons rest in the Reggio community archives. A life sketch by Benedetto Frizzi appeared at Ferrara in 1791, soon after his death. He also left a work on the rules that fix the Jewish calendar.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-beer-benjamin-b:
Benjamin ben Elijah Beer was an Italian, in all likelihood an artist, who lived in Italy in the fifteenth century, perhaps at Ferrara. He is known from one bronze medal found at Lyons in 1656. His name hides in an acrostic in the Hebrew words around a crowned head.

Early writers took the head for a French king and the medal as Jewish thanks for leave to build a synagogue. Zunz in 1840 showed the head could not be that king. The long entry weighs rival readings of the legend line by line. It leaves the medal's full sense unsettled.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-belmonte-jacob-:
Jacob Israel Belmonte was one of the founders of the Portuguese Jewish community of Amsterdam. Born on Madeira in 1570, he reached Amsterdam on Jan. 13, 1614. He died there on Dec. 4, 1629, leaving ten children.

Belmonte wrote a long poem on the Inquisition in a hundred stanzas and named it for Job. With two partners he drew up the founding rules for the community burial ground at Oudekerk in 1614. At his death a study house was founded in his honor by Rabbi Morteira. The names of those children run from Sarah and Rachel to David and Samuel, as the entry lists them.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-benfelden-2940: Benfelden is a town in Alsace, 17 miles from Strasburg. In 1348, as the Black Death swept Europe and its spread was blamed on the Jews, town deputies from Alsace met there. Their charge was to decide what course to take toward the Jews. Bishop Berthold of Strasburg pressed hard for the Jews to be destroyed in full. The Strasburg men fought bravely against that push, the entry says, but in vain. The council ruled that all Jews be driven from the cities of the upper Rhine.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-berechiah-ben-i: Berechiah ben Isaac Gerundi, also called Yiẓḥaki, was a liturgical poet of the twelfth century. He most likely lived at Lunel. Though he wrote nothing on the law, his brother Zerahiah cites him as an authority on one tractate. His poems stand in the prayer books of many rites. The list holds a poem for the Sabbath after Purim. It also holds admonitions for Tabernacles. Pieces for Purim and for the Day of Atonement follow, plus a poem on the Habdalah.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bernstein-hugo-: Hugo Karl Bernstein, a Hungarian dramatist who wrote as Karl Hugo, was born at Budapest in 1808. He died at Milan in 1877. He began medical study, left it for the army to save funds, then qualified and served as an army surgeon in the Polish rising of 1830. Paris in 1839 turned him toward the stage and poetry. He wrote plays in Hamburg and in Budapest, and two dramas in French. Though a man of genius, he held the fixed idea that he alone was called to remake art, science, and faith.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bezalel-3240: Bezalel was a Palestinian amora of the fourth century. He is known only from Midrashic literature. Two sayings of his survive through Berechiah. Berechiah was a famous transmitter of traditions. In one saying Bezalel reads a word in Ezekiel. He says the Temple windows were narrow inside. They widened outward to send light to the world. The second saying is a simile on Exodus. A third explains a verse in Hosea. There the mother stands for the Torah. Bezalel answered a question from Berechiah with it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bistritz-meir-k:
Meïr Kohn Bistritz was a Hungarian Neo-Hebraic poet. He was born in Vag-Bistritz in 1820. He died in Vienna on September 7, 1892. Most of his life passed in Vienna. His first work translated a didactic poem. "Tabnit ha-Bayit" gained his notes and German rendering. In 1859 he marked Budapest's new temple with a poem.

He edited an abridged dictionary in 1863. He also honored Mannheimer's seventieth birthday in print. His last work was his largest and harshest. "Bi'ur Ṭiṭ ha-Yawen" attacked critic Osias Schorr. Its style is abusive and bombastic. Yet it adds to Talmudic lexicography, the entry grants.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-boar-wild-disti: Wild boar get a brief entry built around Psalm lxxx. 14. There the animal comes out of the wood in a figure of speech and roots up the vine. The entry notes that wild hogs have long been known in Palestine. It places them in the marshes of the Jordan and near the Sea of Galilee. It also names Mount Tabor and the River 'Aujeh, north of Joppa.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bonn-3540:
Bonn, a city in Rhenish Prussia, held a Jewish community from an early date. Ephraim ben Jacob of Bonn, born in 1133, fled Crusaders as a boy in 1146. He left a vivid account of those attacks.

Many Bonn Jews were slain in June, 1288. Fresh sorrow came in the Black Death year 1349. Cologne exiles of 1426 raised the community to about 200 persons. Later troops plundered the quarter and took prisoners for ransom. In 1798 a public act cut down the ghetto gate. Equal citizenship was proclaimed to the Jews of Bonn that day. Napoleon later made Bonn the seat of a consistory. A congregation under the law of 1847 was formed there in 1865, with a new synagogue.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-brandon-jacob-e: Jacob Emile Edouard Brandon was a French genre painter born at Paris on July 3, 1831. He studied under Picot, Montfort, and Corot. He entered the Ecole des Beaux Arts in 1849. His Salon pictures treat Saint Brigitte, Roman street life, and Jewish scenes. A Talmud lesson and a Sabbath piece are among those Jewish works. Two pictures of his hang in the Museum of Lille. The entry praises his fidelity to nature and his vivid, if heavy, coloring in paint.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-burgos-3840:
Burgos was a city of Old Castile with a large, wealthy, and cultured Jewish community until the expulsion from Spain in 1492. Its Jews lent money to the Cid as early as 1070. Kings Ferdinand III and Alfonso X granted them privileges, confirmed again in 1295. Their richest era ran from the late thirteenth century to the mid fourteenth.

In the civil war, Burgos Jews stayed loyal to King Pedro and fortified their quarter against Henry. The victor fined them 50,000 doubloons, forcing the sale of Torah crowns. The persecution of 1391 brought suffering and forced baptisms. By 1474 the shrunken community could pay only 700 maravedis in taxes. The entry also notes a famous Torah scroll there that drew pilgrims.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-calni-samuel-be: Samuel Calni, son of Moses, was a Turkish rabbi of the fifteenth century, born at Arta in the Morea. The whole entry is a few lines. His book of responsa was printed by his nephew at Venice in 1599 and 1600. He was son in law to Benjamin, son of Mattathias, the author of Benjamin Ze'eb. That father in law states the match in one of his own responsa. No rulings from Calni's book are quoted here.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-carites-4040:
Carites is a name found in II Kings xi. 4, 19. There the Carites stand between the captains over hundreds and the runners, as bodyguards of the king. A related passage, II Samuel xx. 23, names the Cherethites and Pelethites, yet its text reads Kari for Cherethites.

Scholars cited here weigh two readings of the word. One view treats Kari as a short spelling of Kerethim, the Cherethites. Another view takes Carites at face value. On that view, the troop was made of Carians, famed pirates and hired soldiers of early Greek times. The entry notes support for the second view in Herodotus, Thucydides, and Hesychius. The Septuagint, by contrast, reads the word as the name of an officer.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-catalan-abraham: Abraham Catalan is described as a well-known Talmudist of the seventeenth century. The hosted entry is only a few lines long. It places him at Salonica as a contemporary of Rabbi Ḥayyim Shabbethai. It names a son and a brother, Elijah Catalan, in the same setting. It cites Conforte's Ḳore ha-Dorot as its source. No work by Catalan is named, and no dates for his birth or death are given, so the entry serves as a brief identification rather than a full life story.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-charaathalan-or: Charaathalan, or Charaathalar, is a name occurring in I Esdras v. 36. The hosted entry is a single short paragraph. It explains the name as a corruption of three other names: Cherub, Addan, and Immer. It points to Ezra ii. 59 and Nehemiah vii. 61 for the sound forms. It then sends the reader to the entry on Cherub for more. No person, place, or event is attached to the name in this text, beyond that note on how the corrupt form arose.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cle-syria-4440:
Cele-Syria, spelled Coele-Syria in older editions, names a Persian province between Egypt and the Euphrates in Greek apocryphal writings. The entry links it to the older phrase the country beyond the river in Ezra. Under Antiochus Epiphanes, one governor ruled both Coele-Syria and Phenicia, so the old Persian district seems to have lasted.

The Greek term first meant the valley between Lebanon and Anti-Lebanon, the modern Bika, called the valley of Lebanon in Joshua. Greek writers then stretched it loosely, sometimes to all Palestine, sometimes not. Josephus wavers in the same way across passages. The Romans later used Syria Cela for northern Syria instead. Untangling that drift is the entry's whole task.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cohn-tobias-110:
Tobias Cohn, a Polish physician, was born at Metz in 1652 and died at Jerusalem in 1729. His father, a Polish doctor, had fled to Metz in 1648 to escape the Cossack revolution. Tobias studied at Cracow, Frankfort-on-the-Oder, and Padua, taking his medical degree at Padua. He practiced in Poland, then at Adrianople.

There he became physician to five sultans in a row and moved with the court to Constantinople. In 1724 he settled in Jerusalem. His Maaseh Tobiyyah, printed at Venice in 1707, spans eight fields from theology to botany. Its medicine section pairs a human body with a house in a famous picture, part by part. He knew nine languages, the entry marvels.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-coimbra-4540:
Coimbra, a Portuguese city and capital of Beira province, once held a Jewish quarter called the Juderia, later named Corpo de Deus. In April, 1395, the prior of the church and several clergy broke into the Jewry to seize eggs for Easter from the Jews. Rabbi Solomon Catalan and others told the priests they had no right to the demand.

Force followed, and the clerics stormed the house of Jacob Alfayate. The Jews fought back and drove them out, and the king shielded the community from more abuse. The entry then notes Coimbra's Inquisition tribunal, with its autos da fe over centuries, and names Moses ibn Danon, born there in 1510, as a Talmudic author who wrote at Fez.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-copenhagen-4640:
Copenhagen, the capital of Denmark, gained a Jewish community soon after Denmark opened to Jewish settlement in 1657. A first prayer room opened on Dec. 16, 1684, behind closed doors and without a sermon. A cemetery was already in use by 1670. Early settlers were Spanish-Portuguese Jews, soon outnumbered by German Jews from Hamburg and nearby lands.

The long article follows the community through taxes, trade, worship, and schooling. It covers forced sermons in 1728, a wave of conversions among educated families, and fights over religious reform. Named rabbis and teachers mark each stage. Readers get a full city history built from records and Jewish sources.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-czynski-jan-jea:
Jan Czynski, or Jean, was a Polish lawyer, author, and journalist. He was born on June 20, 1801. He died in London on Jan. 31, 1867. The son of Jewish parents who had taken Roman Catholicism before his birth, he stayed a zealous defender of the Jews all his life. He practised law in Lublin. In the Polish revolution of 1830 he served as chief of staff under General Szczeptycki.

When a Lublin crowd accused the Jews of shirking service and threatened attack, Czynski calmed the mob. He then defended his Hebrew compatriots at a meeting in the synagogue. After the failed revolution he settled in Paris in 1832 and later moved to London. His books include Le Reveil d'Israel and Israel en Pologne. He also edited the journal La Pologne for a time.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-david-ernest-49: Ernest David was a French musician born at Nancy on July 4, 1844, and he died at Paris on June 3, 1886. He finished his musical education under Fétis and became a prolific writer on music. His main works include "La Musique chez les Juifs" in 1873, a history of musical notation from its origins in 1882, and a study of Welsh poetry and music written with M. Lussy. His last book, in 1886, treated the life and works of J. S. Bach, his pupils, and his contemporaries.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-david-raphael-b: Raphael ben Abraham Polido David was a satirist who flourished in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. His name and his book's Leghorn printing suggest he was Italian, though scholars have read his name as Fulda or even Poland. He wrote "Zikron Purim" (Remembrance of Purim), a parody of the piyyuṭim, the liturgical poems, sung for the feast of Purim. It ends with a mock testament of Haman. The entry calls it full of coarse jokes, yet a good imitation of the Sephardic poems. Leghorn printed it in 1703.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dede-agatch-504: Dede-Agatch is a Turkish port on the Aegean Sea, at the mouth of the Maritza river, near Enos in European Turkey. The entry is short and statistical. The town held about two hundred Jews in a population of three thousand. The community was founded in 1870. It owned a synagogue and a primary school attended by thirty children. The rabbi also served as slaughterer and circumciser, paid from the meat tax. Two charitable societies served the sick and the poor.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-deutsch-emanuel:
Emanuel Oscar Menahem Deutsch was an Orientalist born at Neisse, in Silesia, on October 28, 1829. His uncle David Deutsch of Myslowitz trained him in Hebrew literature. He finished his schooling at the University of Berlin, then went to London for a post in the British Museum. There he became known for work promoting Semitic studies.

Deutsch wrote sharp scientific essays, on the Targumim and the Samaritan Pentateuch among other topics. His fame rests on a popular essay on the Talmud in the "Quarterly Review" of October 1867. That article caused a sensation, was reprinted again and again, and was translated into several languages. He died at Alexandria, Egypt, on May 12, 1873.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dualism-5340:
Dualism is the teaching that evil comes from a second, eternal power set against the good. Zoroaster's faith is its classic case. It gives all good to Ahuramazda and all evil to Angromainyush. Jewish teaching, the entry argues, rejects that split.

Isaiah xlv. 7 answers with one God who forms light and creates darkness. The daily liturgy softens that verse, swapping evil for all. The rabbis teach that even death and the evil urge can serve good ends. The entry clears the Essenes of dualism on Philo's word. It ends with Maimonides, for whom evil is only a lack, not a thing made.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-educatore-israe: L'Educatore Israelita was a monthly periodical published at Vercelli from 1853 to 1874. Giuseppe Levi founded it and ran it with Esdra Pontremoli. It argued for moderate Jewish reform, won by all communities working together. Among its writers were Luzzatto, Della Torre, Cantoni, Mortara, and Benamozegh. After Levi died in 1874, the paper went on at Casale under Flaminio Servi. There it carried a new name, Il Vessillo Israelitico, as the entry's closing line records.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eleazar-lazar-b: Eleazar ben Jose the Second was a Palestinian amora of the fifth century. He stood in the fifth generation of the amoraim. Most of his sayings pass on what he heard from older men. His father, Jose the Second, was his chief teacher. Before him Eleazar often set out his thoughts. The father chided him at times for a lack of zeal. Eleazar's own motto turns on that theme. While Phinehas was zealous, he said, God was with him. When the zeal stopped, God left him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-elijah-alamannu: Elijah Alamannus was a Spanish doctor and diplomat. He lived in the fifteenth century. He served as court doctor to a Duke of Bourbon. King Alfonso the Fifth of Aragon trusted him with a mission. In 1420 he bore a royal letter to Pope Martin the Fifth. A safe conduct covered him for a full year. A few years later he was at Avignon. There he had a papal bull for the Spanish Jews made legal. That bull worked in favor of the Jews of Spain.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-empedocles-of-a: Empedocles of Agrigentum was a Greek thinker of old. He learned in the school of Pythagoras in his youth. His age was the fifth century before Christ. His system, bent by later Platonists, passed into Arabic thought. From there it reached the Jewish thinkers of Spain. False works in his name came to Spain in the tenth century. Ibn Gabirol stands as his chief Jewish voice in the entry. His book Fountain of Life rests on that system. Judah ha-Levi names the school often, mostly to fault it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-erter-isaac-584:
Isaac Erter was a Hebrew satirist born at Janischok, Galicia, in 1792. He died at Brody in 1851. His early years were marked by struggle and hardship. After time among the Hasidim, he settled at Lemberg and taught Hebrew subjects. The chief rabbi there banned his small study circle in 1816, and he lost his pupils.

Erter then studied medicine at Budapest from 1825 and practiced in Galician towns. The poor of Brody loved him as a kind helper. His fame, though, rests on six Hebrew satires printed as Ha-Zofeh le-Bet Yisrael. The best known, Gilgul ha-Nefesh, follows a soul passing from body to body. It ends with six mocking rules for success as a doctor.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-exodus-book-of-:
The Book of Exodus is the second book of the Torah, called in Greek Exodus, meaning departure. The entry counts 1,209 verses in the Masorah's tally and notes the common split into forty chapters comes from the Vulgate. The book continues Genesis without a break. It tells how the patriarchs' offspring grew into a people, left slavery in Egypt, and received laws at Sinai.

The entry splits the book at chapter eighteen. The first half tells the deliverance; the second gives the Law. Moses is called at the burning bush, and Aaron is set beside him. Long space goes to Passover, whose lamb, bread, and herbs are spelled out in detail. The Tabernacle and its priestly service close the survey of the contents.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-freiheim-j-b-63:
J. B. Freiheim was an American lawyer and soldier born in Bavaria in 1848. He died at Camden, Arkansas, on August 22, 1899. He was reared in Louisiana, an early Jewish settler there. He studied at the Louisiana State Military Academy. When the Civil War broke out he joined the Confederate army. He served through the whole war in the Twelfth Louisiana Infantry.

At Franklin, Tennessee, every officer of his company was killed. Freiheim, by then a sergeant, led the company himself. After the war he settled in Arkansas. Though not yet twenty-one, he was admitted to the bar. He practised law at Camden for the rest of his life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-furtado-auguste: Auguste Furtado, a French banker born at St. Esprit on April 11, 1797, died at Bayonne on May 20, 1883. He was a nephew of Abraham Furtado and came from a Portuguese family. For near forty years he sat on the Bayonne town council and twice served as mayor. He led the local chamber of commerce work and ran the town branch of the Bank of France. He headed the Bayonne Jewish consistory from 1846 until his death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-geber-6540: Geber is a name borne by two officers in First Kings iv. The son of Geber held Ramoth-gilead and had charge of Havoth-jair and the Argob district. The son of Uri held the land of Gilead, south of Argob. Both served as district supply officers under Solomon. The entry notes a hard line in the text about the second man. English versions read that he was the only officer in the land. A second reading gives one officer who was in the land.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-geshur-geshurit: Geshur was a tract in the north of Bashan, next to Argob and to the kingdom of Aram. It was assigned to the half tribe of Manasseh east of the Jordan. Its people, the Geshurites, could never be driven out. In David days Geshur stood as its own kingdom. David married a daughter of its king Talmai. Her son Absalom fled there for three years after killing his half brother. The site is matched with the Lejah plateau.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-goldberg-baer-b:
Baer ben Alexander Goldberg, known as BaG, was a Russian scholar born at Soludna near Warsaw in 1799; he died at Paris on May 4, 1884. Married at fifteen and supporting a family at eighteen, he struggled for over twenty-three years before leaving for Berlin. There, at about forty, he took up Oriental languages and began publishing from old manuscripts.

His Berlin and London years produced a commentary on the Jewish calendar and a volume of rare essays, including decisions by Rashi and Sherira Gaon's letter. Settled in Paris from 1852, he edited works by Ibn Janaḥ, Judah ben Koreisch, and Elijah Levita, among many others. He also wrote often for Hebrew periodicals on Jewish history and literature.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gumurjina-6940:
Gumurjina was a town in European Turkey, west of Adrianople. Its population was 26,000, including 1,200 Jews. The community kept separate schools for boys and girls with 200 children. It had a synagogue and five aid societies. Most Jews there lived by trade, and some held public office. A council of twelve ran the community. It had no rabbi of its own and sent religious questions to Adrianople.

Local tradition dates the community to the early seventeenth century. Its first chief rabbi, Judah, is said to have died in 1673. In 1786 the governor jailed leading Jews on a false charge of aiding brigands. They proved their innocence and went free. The town long marked the 22d of Elul as the "Brigands' Purim" for that rescue.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hagin-fil-mossy: Hagin fil Mossy was presbyter, or chief rabbi, of the Jews of England. He seems to have been the chirographer of the London Jews, and he grew rich, then lost his wealth under Edward I. In 1255 he was made presbyter when Elyas was driven from that office; he was likely Elyas's brother. In the riots before the battle of Lewes in 1264 he fled to the Continent. At the Expulsion in 1290 his wife Antera and son Aaron held London's last synagogue.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hameln-also-kno:
Hameln is a Prussian town on the Hamel and Weser. Jews are recorded there as early as 1277, and by 1341 a fair number lived in the town. The council admitted them at moderate tax rates for terms of six or ten years. In 1344 they were allowed to build a synagogue. Not long after, at the Black Death, they were expelled.

Readmitted before 1557, they faced ducal expulsion decrees in that year and again in 1590. The council spoke up for its Jews, and the second decree was repealed on the emperor's advice. By the late seventeenth century only a few families remained; Glückel von Hameln names two. Standing improved only after 1848. The entry closes with the town's rabbis, its 1879 synagogue, and a count of 243 Jews in a population of about 20,000.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hara-7240: Hara is a district named once, in I Chronicles v. 26, among the places to which Tiglath-pileser carried the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half tribe of Manasseh. Like its companion names it must have lain in western Assyria. The Septuagint omits it, and so does the parallel passage in II Kings xviii. 11, which adds the cities of the Medes instead. Yet the entry argues the word stood in the original Hebrew, since Jerome transliterates it as "Ara."
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hayyim-aaron-ib: Aaron ibn Hayyim the younger was a rabbi at Hebron and later at Smyrna. He was the grandson of the author of "Korban Aharon." Leading scholars of his day asked his views on ritual questions. His rulings appear in the books of many men who lived at the same time. He counted among the top Talmudists of his age. Azulai credits him with a commentary on "En Yaakob," now lost. He died in the Smyrna earthquake of July 1688.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-heaven-hebr-sha:
Heaven, in Hebrew shamayim, is the upper part of the world, set against the earth. Sun, moon, and stars are placed there. It is stretched out like a curtain and founded on pillars. God dwells there and looks down on all people, though even heaven cannot hold Him. Angels live there too.

Rain, hail, and lightning come from heaven. Prayers rise toward it, since God hears from His seat. The entry notes a belief in many heavens, seven or ten in later writings, with paradise inside one of them. In time the word heaven itself became a modest stand-in for the name of God.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-heller-seligman: Seligmann Heller, born in Bohemia on July 8, 1831, was an Austrian poet and journalist. He studied language and law at Vienna, then worked in his father's business. In 1866 he taught German at a Prague trade school and wrote for the paper "Bohemia." He moved to Vienna in 1873 as a drama critic. His poems include an epic on the Wandering Jew. After his death, a friend edited his versions of medieval Hebrew poems. He died on Jan. 8, 1890.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-herzl-theodor-7:
Theodor Herzl, born in Budapest on May 2, 1860, is presented as leader of political Zionism. Raised and trained in law at Vienna, he turned to journalism and stage writing. He worked for the Neue Freie Presse in Paris and later as its literary editor.

Herzl's course changed with his Jewish State in the winter of 1895, in English from April 1896. He founded Die Welt in 1897 and planned the first Zionist Congress, which elected him president. He met the German emperor and the Turkish sultan for his cause. Later talks covered Sinai settlement and a British East Africa offer in 1903. His novel Altneuland foresaw a built Jewish land by 1923.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hirsch-max-7740:
Max Hirsch, born in Halberstadt on Dec. 30, 1832, was a German economist and deputy. He studied science, languages, and law at Tübingen, Heidelberg, and Berlin from 1850 to 1855. After travel in France and North Africa, he founded a Berlin publishing house.

From 1867 Hirsch gave his energy to politics. Study of English workers led him to help build German trade unions bearing his name. He edited their paper and served as their legal adviser. Voters sent him to the Reichstag in 1869, 1877, 1881, and 1890, and to the Prussian chamber in 1898. His many books treat machines, Algeria, insurance, and worker protection laws.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hupfeld-hermann:
Hermann Hupfeld was a German Christian Bible scholar born at Marburg on March 31, 1796. He died at Halle on April 24, 1866. He taught Old Testament study at Marburg from 1825 to 1843. He then followed Gesenius at Halle and stayed until 1866.

His 1853 book on the sources of Genesis proved that the Elohist and Priestly strands stand apart, with the Yahwist independent too. A later editor joined them, he argued. That claim killed the older supplement theory and set Pentateuch study on its modern path. His Psalms commentary of 1855 to 1862 won praise for close grammar work. He also wrote on Jewish grammar writers and on the feasts of the Hebrews.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ibn-yahya-josep: Joseph ben David ibn Yahya was an Italian exegete and philosopher born at Florence in 1494. He died at Imola in 1539. His parents were Spanish exiles who settled at Imola. His son Gedaliah, the chronicler, tells that the body was sent to Safed for burial, with Joseph Caro overseeing the rite. Two works carry his name. One comments on the Five Scrolls and the Hagiographa, printed at Bologna in 1538. The other, Torah Or, treats theology and the last things, printed in 1537 or 1538.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jacob-ben-moses: Jacob ben Moses of Bagnols was a Provençal theologian of the second half of the fourteenth century. He lived in turn at Salon, Avignon, and Argon. He wrote a work that is part law and part thought, still in manuscript at the British Museum. It falls into three parts, each with its own title. One gives rulings on what is permitted and forbidden. One treats marriage, levirate, and divorce. One holds essays on ethics, philosophy, and mysticism.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-john-of-vallado:
John of Valladolid was a Jewish convert to Christianity born in 1335. A strong speaker with some rabbinic learning, he told King Henry of Castile that he could prove the Christian faith to the Jews if they were forced to hear him. An order went out: Jews had to attend his talks in their own synagogues and answer his questions.

John toured the Castilian provinces with a fellow convert, speaking and debating, with what the entry calls a clear lack of success. At Avila he called the Jews together four times. At Burgos he faced Moses ha-Kohen of Tordesillas, who had little trouble answering his proofs from the Bible, and the debate broke off at the fourth meeting.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-juan-de-sevilla: Juan de Sevilla was a spokesman for the Maranos in 1482 and a rich tax farmer who lived at Jerez de la Frontera. In 1481 he was called to answer a charge of Judaism before the inquisitors. He fled with several fellow tax farmers and settled at Evora. Their houses, vineyards, and goods in Jerez were seized. Through his work Pope Sixtus IV issued a bull on August 2, 1483, letting Maranos outside Spain be reconciled. Juan never went back to Spain and was burned in effigy.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kala-i-samuel-b: Samuel ben Joseph Ḳala'i was a Karaite scholar of Chufut-Kale, in the Crimea. He died on Feb. 17, 1754. He wrote "Me'il Shemuel," a commentary on a work by Aaron ben Joseph. The book is called "Ha-Mibḥar" in its source text. Ḳala'i did not live to finish his commentary. Simḥah Isaac b. Moses completed it in 1757. That scholar also wrote the preface to the book.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kauders-samuel-:
Samuel Judah Löb ben David Kauders was a Bohemian rabbi. He was born at Prague about 1762. He died there on May 6, 1838. He gave his years to Talmud study with no pulpit at first. About 1810 he was called to Kaladei as district rabbi. In 1834 he followed Samuel Landau as acting chief rabbi of Prague.

Kauders was a Talmudist of the old school and strictly Orthodox. Yet he held tolerant views, the entry says. He favored schooling in worldly subjects too. His chief book holds 112 responsa on one part of the Shulḥan 'Aruk. It came out at Prague in 1823. Two more books of essays and sermons followed in that city. They appeared in 1828-29 and 1829.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kokebe-yizhak-9: Kokebe Yiẓḥaḳ was a Hebrew annual published at Vienna from 1845 to 1872 by M. Stern, then from 1872 to 1873 by M. Weissmann. Its pages covered literary history, philology, exegesis, and Hebrew poetry. Strong essays by Jellinek, Luzzatto, and other leading scholars of the time appeared in it. A second edition of the first annual came out at Vienna in 1847. The entry closes by noting a review of the last number by A. Geiger.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kuh-david-9540: David Kuh, an Austrian journalist and deputy born at Prague in 1818, died on Jan. 26, 1879. He gave up study of medicine and law at Vienna. Teaching came first, then acting, then newspaper work at Pest. He backed Louis Kossuth with zeal in the Hungarian war of independence and was jailed for his part in the revolt. Freed in 1850, he returned to Prague and founded a German political journal. He sided with the Germans against the Czechs and won a Reichstag seat, which he soon gave up.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lemans-moses-97:
Moses Lemans, a Dutch educationist, was born at Naarden on Nov. 5, 1785, and died at Amsterdam on Oct. 17, 1832. His father and a tutor in mathematics taught him. He became a teacher of religion, and in 1818 chief of the new religious school. In 1828 he took a post teaching mathematics at Amsterdam's Latin school.

Lemans wrote on Hebrew speech and grammar, and with Mulder he made a Hebrew-Dutch dictionary in 1829-31. He also wrote a life of Maimonides, a history of star study, and works on Talmudic mathematics. His chief service, the entry says, was turning prayer books into Dutch so Dutch Jews could know their own tongue.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-levias-caspar-9: Caspar Levias, an American Orientalist, was born in Szagarren on Feb. 13, 1860. He had his first schooling in Russia. He studied at Columbia College in New York and at Johns Hopkins. He held fellowships in Oriental and Semitic languages at both schools. Since 1895 he has taught at the Hebrew Union College in Cincinnati. His chief book is a grammar of the Aramaic of the Babylonian Talmud, printed in 1900. He also wrote "The Justification of Zionism" in 1899 and many essays on language.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-liturgy-10040:
Liturgy covers the Jewish religious service, which the entry divides into instruction and prayer. Reading from the Law grew from early gatherings in the Temple courts and from Ezra reading the Law aloud. By the first century, readings on Sabbaths, feasts, and other days were seen as an old custom.

Prayer is presented as still older, at first short and private, with no fixed rite before the exile. After the exile, Temple worship shaped public prayer. Levites sang praise at daily sacrifices, faces turned toward the Temple, and the Psalms served as the hymnal of the Second Temple. The survey then follows later prayer forms at length.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lowe-joel-10140:
Joel Löwe, a German Bible commentator in Mendelssohn's circle, is the subject of a 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry. Born in 1760, he went to Berlin at twenty and studied under Isaac Satanow. There he met Moses Mendelssohn, and the acquaintance grew into friendship. Mendelssohn's influence helped him become tutor in the home of David Friedländer.

The article describes Löwe as a fine Hebraist, grammarian, and interpreter of Scripture. He helped with Mendelssohn's Bible commentaries and co-edited the Hebrew journal Ha-Meassef with Aaron Wolfsohn. His own main work was a Hebrew commentary on the Psalms, printed in 1788, with an introduction tracing the history of biblical poetry. He also gave the first German translation of the Passover Haggadah in 1785. He ended his life as principal of the Wilhelms-Schule in Breslau, dying there in 1802.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-machrus-10240:
Machaerus, a mountain fortress in Perea, is surveyed in a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906. Alexander Jannaeus first built a fort there, on the border between Palestine and Arabia. Pliny called it, after Jerusalem, the strongest fortress in Palestine. Herod rebuilt it as a frontier stronghold, with a walled town, towers, and a splendid palace.

The article follows the fort through siege after siege. Gabinius took it twice and razed it once. Jewish fighters held it during the war against Rome, even after Jerusalem fell. Two years later Lucilius Bassus advanced on it with a Roman army. To save a captured defender named Eleazar from crucifixion, the Jews surrendered on terms. The Romans broke their word, killed about 1,700 men, and sold the women and children. The entry also matches Josephus's wonders, a giant rue and paired hot and cold springs, with Talmudic notes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mamran-10340:
Mamran, a Polish Jewish word for a check or promissory note, is explained in a 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia article. Polish Jews used the term from the late sixteenth century into the early nineteenth. It comes from membrana, the low Latin word for a note of debt. Mordecai Jafeh used it first in his work Ir Shoshan.

The article follows the word's legal life and death. East Prussia's law of 1801 recognized the mamran by name. Later laws required legal documents to use only the language of the country. That rule threw the term into disuse. The word appears in many spellings, including mamre, mamram, and mamrama. Folk derivations tied it to a Hebrew root for exchange, or to Maharam Lublin, who supposedly introduced it. The entry preserves the vocabulary of Jewish commerce in old Poland, where a single word carried a whole credit practice.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-martin-raymund-:
Raymund Martin, a Spanish Christian theologian of the thirteenth century, is the subject of a Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906 by Isidore Singer and Gotthold Weil. Born at Subirats in Catalonia, Martin was picked in 1250 to study Oriental languages at a Dominican school set up to train men for religious disputes with Jews and Muslims.

In 1264 he joined the commission ordered to examine Hebrew books and strike out passages offensive to Christianity, the first Dominican censorship of the Talmud in Spain. The entry describes his two anti-Jewish books, above all the Pugio Fidei, lost for centuries and printed at Paris in 1651. Scholars still value that work for its long extracts from the Talmud, Midrash, and writers such as Rashi and Maimonides.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-medeba-modern-n:
Medeba, a town east of the Dead Sea, is traced through the Bible and Josephus in a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906 by Joseph Jacobs, Louis H. Gray, Emil G. Hirsch, and George A. Barton. Sihon the Amorite took it from Moab, Joshua assigned it to Reuben, and the Moabite Stone boasts that Omri annexed it and Israel held it forty years. In Maccabean days a robber clan of Medeba murdered John, brother of Jonathan the Maccabee, and was wiped out in revenge at a wedding procession.

After lying desolate for centuries, the site was reoccupied about 1880 by Greek Christians, whose building work uncovered church mosaics of the fourth to sixth centuries. The greatest of them, the article reports, is a mosaic map of Palestine set into the floor of the Greek church, its discovery announced in December 1896.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-menahem-ben-per:
Menahem ben Perez of Joigny was a French tosafist and Bible commentator of the twelfth century. Solomon Schechter and M. Seligsohn profile him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Zadoc Kahn identified him with "Menahem the Saint" of the Tosafot. Kahn conjectured he was killed in the massacre at Bray-sur-Seine in 1190. Gross doubted the story and put his death about 1180. His standing, at least, is certain. He took an active part in the synod at Troyes. Samuel ben Meir and Jacob Tam held that synod.

The Tosafot quote him across half a dozen tractates. Asher ben Jehiel had his glosses before him. As a commentator he is cited in the "Da'at Zekenim." He also wrote a "Massorah Gedolah," the Great Masorah. It completed the work of the same name by Gershom, Light of the Exile, which remains unpublished. Joseph the Zealous also records his disputation with a priest.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-millennium-1084:
The millennium, a thousand-year reign of peace before the Last Judgment, is traced through Jewish and Christian sources in a Jewish Encyclopedia article by Joseph Jacobs and A. Biram, published in 1906. Christians call the doctrine chiliasm, the rule of Jesus with the risen saints. The article insists the idea is older than the Church that named it.

A thousand-year end-time period before the resurrection was already believed in Parseeism, the writers note, and it appears in Enoch, the Apocalypse of Baruch, and Second Esdras. Jewish sources, though, never fix the length of the Messiah's reign, treating it as an interregnum before the world to come. Talmudic passages are marshaled to show how the rabbis separated the days of the Messiah from final fulfillment.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-monastir-10940:
Monastir was the capital of Rumelia in European Turkey, four hundred miles west of Constantinople. It had six thousand Jews in a population of sixty-five thousand. Gotthard Deutsch and M. Franco report this in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. No document mentions its Jews before the Spanish exiles arrived in 1492. By the mid-sixteenth century the town had a Talmudic school under Joseph ibn Leb.

The entry's modern record is stark. In 1863 a fire destroyed over two thousand houses and shops, half of them Jewish. In 1900 the community faced a ritual-murder accusation over a vanished Bulgarian. Between disasters it ran a full communal state. It had a sultan-recognized chief rabbi, a religious court, and three synagogues. It also had a Talmud Torah of 250 children and an Alliance-aided boys' school.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-b-samuel-:
Moses ben Samuel of Roquemaure was a physician and translator of the fourteenth century. Richard Gottheil and Meyer Kayserling wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He lived in turn at Avignon, Toledo, and Seville. At Toledo, before 1358, he wrote a poem mocking Shemariah of Negropont, who posed as Messiah and prophet in Castile.

Moses then moved to Seville, where he was baptized and took the name Juan d'Avignon. There, in 1360, he translated Bernard de Gordon's Lilium Medicinae from Latin into Hebrew. The translation carried the Hebrew title Perah ha-Refu'ot. The entry preserves the odd double career of a satirist who ended as a convert and medical translator.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-natality-11340:
Natality means the share of births in a population. Joseph Jacobs wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It is usually counted as births per thousand people. The article compares Jewish birth rates with those of their neighbors. It adds fresh figures to an older entry on births.

For Bulgaria in the 1890s, Jews averaged 45.3 births per thousand. That rate stood above Greek Catholics and Muslims there. Stillbirths are also compared across each group in turn. In Poland in 1889, Jewish births ran lower than Christian births. Vienna figures for 1899 split births by sex and status. The entry shows how scholars then used numbers to study Jewish life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nigrin-negrin-m:
Moses Nigrin was a cabalist of Safed. Kaufmann Kohler and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived early in the sixteenth century there. Moses di Trani was his contemporary in that city. He is known chiefly as a commentator.

Nigrin wrote notes on Jonah Gerondi's ethical works. Sefer ha-Yir'ah and Dat ha-Nashim both drew his pen. Those notes appeared with Alami's Iggeret Musar in 1612. His Dine Tefillah gives full directions for prayer. It was printed at Sulzbach in 1693 and often reprinted. A study of Proverbs, Liwyat Hen, also bears his name. He commented as well on Cordovero's Seder Abodah.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-oath-more-judai:
Oath More Judaico was a harsh oath forced on Jews in court. Gotthard Deutsch wrote its history for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It was a set form of words, with rites meant to shame. Jews had to take it when they went to law. The piece traces the oath back to early law codes.

At first, Jews and Christians stood much the same in court. Charters from kings in the ninth century treat both alike. A law for Speyer in 1090 kept that fair rule. But some codes set cruel terms for the Jewish oath. One made the man stand in water with thorns at his waist. One made him stand on the hide of a sow. The piece lists such rules from place to place.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-oppenheimer-jos:
Joseph Süss Oppenheimer was a German man of funds and courts. Gotthard Deutsch and Theodor Kroner wrote his long entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Heidelberg in the year 1698. He was put to death at Stuttgart in 1738. His father led a troupe of singers and players.

Joseph had small love for books as a boy. He had a strong bent for trade from the start. He worked in great Jewish trade houses in many towns. Those towns were Frankfurt, Amsterdam, Prague, and Vienna. He learned the ways of the high born in those years. His skill won him posts with lords and courts. He gave stamped paper for the court of the Palatinate. He gave coin for Darmstadt, a German state. In 1734 he rose to chief court and war factor.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-padan-aram-assy:
Padan-aram was a low land in the Aram of old. Emil G. Hirsch and Schulim Ochser wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The first part of the name is read in more than one way. It may mean road, or field, or yoke, or plow. The land lay between two great rivers there.

Those rivers were the Euphrates and the Tigris in the east. The low land could be farmed, the piece notes. It stands out against the high land of Palestine near by. The name is used in the book of Genesis alone. Bethuel, the father of Rebecca, came from that land. Jacob fled there to get clear of his brother Esau. He wed two wives in the years he spent there.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-paterson-11940:
Paterson, New Jersey, was a silk making city with a growing Jewish community. Cyrus Adler and Abram S. Isaacs wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The city held three synagogues by then. One was German and conservative in style, and two were Russian and Orthodox.

The community ran a Talmud Torah school with hundreds of pupils. It also kept loan and benevolent societies. Nathan Barnert, a synagogue president, served two terms as mayor. In 1900 President McKinley attended Friday services at his temple. After the great fire of 1902 the temple sheltered a burned out church.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-perlhefter-eybe:
Issachar Bär Perlhefter was a Bohemian rabbi and author. He was born at Prague into the Eybeschütz family. Isidore Singer and Peter Wiernik wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He took his wife Bella's family name, Perlhefter.

The couple fled Vienna when its Jews were expelled in 1670. At Altdorf he taught Hebrew to a famed scholar. Wagenseil learned from him despite his anti-Jewish books. Perlhefter later served six years as rabbi of Mantua. A false messiah scandal drove him from that post. He ended his days as a judge in Prague.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pictorial-art-1:
Pictorial art came late to the Jews as a public craft. Joseph Jacobs and Frank Cramer wrote the survey for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. No remains show how Bible-age Jews used painting. The article then explains the long gap that followed. It ends with lists of painters by country.

Medieval guilds held painting and shut Jews out. Jews showed skill only in manuscript illumination then. Later rabbis barred images even in synagogues. That reading of the second commandment froze the art. Only emancipation opened the field at last. Joseph Israels of Holland leads the modern names.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pumpianski-aaro:
Aaron Elijah Pumpianski was a Russian crown rabbi and author. Herman Rosenthal and Peter Wiernik wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Wilna in 1835. He finished the rabbinical school of Wilna in 1859. He died at Riga in 1893.

With Asher Wohl, Pumpianski edited a Russian part of Ha-Karmel. That work ran through the years 1860 and 1861. In 1861 he became crown rabbi of Ponevezh. He held that post until the year 1873. He was then elected to the same post at Riga. He served the Riga community until his death. His books are named in the rest of the entry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-raimuch-remoch-:
Astruc Raimuch, also called Remoch, was a physician of Fraga. Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He lived in the fourteenth century. As an Orthodox Jew he visited leading Jews in Saragossa.

The article says that in 1391 he gave up his religion. He took the name Francisco Dias-Corni. He then tried to convert his former Jewish friends. One friend named was En-Shealtiel Bonfos of Falces. The short entry rests on a letter Remoch sent to Bonfos. It also cites later histories by Geiger and Grätz. Readers get a brief, sad case from a year of forced change in Spain.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rice-joseph-may:
Joseph Mayer Rice was an American physician and editor born on May 27, 1857. Cyrus Adler and A. Porter wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Philadelphia. He earned his medical degree in New York in 1881.

The article says he served at Mount Sinai Hospital in New York. He also worked at the Montefiore Home there. In 1888 he left medicine for education research. His core idea was learning based on the inductive principle. He studied psychology in Jena and Leipzig. He then examined about 125,000 school children himself. Results appeared in the Forum across 1896 and 1897. He became that magazine's editor in 1897. His books treat the public school system and spelling.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rosenberg-abrah:
Abraham Hayyim Rosenberg was a Russian-American writer born at Pinsk on October 17, 1838. Cyrus Adler and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Trained at the rabbinical seminary of Jitomir, he served as a district chief rabbi.

Rosenberg held that post at Pinsk, then at Nikolaief, where he also taught Jewish pupils. In 1891 he emigrated to the United States and settled in New York. He wrote tales in Hebrew papers and translated a Russian novel into Hebrew. His largest project was a Bible cyclopedia, Ozar ha-Shemot, of which two volumes appeared.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rumsch-isaac-mo:
Isaac Moses Rumsch was a Russian teacher and Hebrew author born at Zezemer, near Wilna, on April 6, 1822. Herman Rosenthal and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He studied Talmud at Wilna in his brother's yeshibah.

In secret Rumsch added Bible, Hebrew grammar, and German to his studies. Relatives harassed him for that love of modern learning at home. In 1853 Russia opened public schools for Jewish children in the Wilna region. Rumsch was appointed teacher at Ponevyezh, beside Judah Löb Gordon. His Kur Oni retells Robinson Crusoe freely in Hebrew.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-salomonsen-carl:
Carl Julius Salomonsen was a Danish bacteriologist born at Copenhagen on December 6, 1847. Isidore Singer and Frank Cramer wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. A son of the physician Martin Salomonsen, he took his medical degree in 1871.

Salomonsen rose at Copenhagen to professor of pathology in 1893. He was Denmark's first physician to run a laboratory making diphtheria anti-toxin. That laboratory soon proved too small for the hospitals' need there. He carried a bill through the Rigsdag for a state serum institute. It became law on March 20, 1901, founding the new institute.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-ben-reub:
A. Peiginsky wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, issued with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board in 1906. Its subject is Samuel ben Reuben of Béziers, a French Talmudist. He was active early in the fourteenth century. Samuel was one of many scholars who wrote to Solomon ben Adret during a heated religious dispute.

That dispute ran from 1303 to 1306. Samuel sent Adret a letter in rhyme. In it he defended his relative Levi of Villefranche. He also said he had signed a letter from the liberal party without knowing what it said. He sided with Adret against letting young students study the liberal sciences. The entry also weighs whether Samuel was a son of Reuben ben Ḥayyim of Narbonne.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schwarz-gustav-:
Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Gustav Schwarz. He was a Hungarian lawyer. Schwarz was born at Budapest in 1858. He studied in his native city and at German universities. In 1884 he became a privat-docent in Roman law at Budapest. Nine years later he rose to assistant professor, and a year after that to professor.

In 1895 Schwarz joined the committee drafting Hungary's civil law. In 1902 he became a privy councilor. His books treat freedom of testation in Roman law. Others cover new trends in civil law, ownership, and marriage law. He also published cases and studies in private law. In 1902 he converted to Christianity. The entry rests on the Pallas Lexicon.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-serpent-13440:
Serpent is the broad topic of an entry on snakes in the Old Testament. Emil G. Hirsch and I. M. Casanowicz wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia piece on it. The Bible uses many Hebrew words for snakes of different kinds. The common term is nahash, used more than any other.

Other terms point to the asp, the adder, and the viper. Some may name the Egyptian cobra kept by snake charmers. Others may point to a large viper or a horned snake. One word even drew debate, since some readers took it for a spider. The entry helps Bible readers match old animal names with real creatures of Palestine and Egypt.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sheliah-zibbur-:
Sheliah Zibbur means the congregation's messenger, the one who leads public prayer. Cyrus Adler and Max Landsberg wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on the office. In Temple days a priest spoke for the people in sacrifice. He closed the service with the priestly blessing.

When synagogue prayer replaced sacrifice, this leader took that role. He offered the prayers aloud while the congregation listened. Hearers joined only by answering Amen to each blessing. Only the worthiest men were chosen for the task. Great sages like Rabbi Akiba served in the role. The entry explains how the prayer leader came to stand for all before God.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sidra-13640:
Sidra, meaning order or arrangement, names a section of the Bible read aloud. Cyrus Adler, M. Seligsohn, Joseph Jacobs, and I. George Dobsevage wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on the term. Both Talmuds use the word for such a section. It could be read in synagogue or in school.

Rashi explains one Talmud line as a section of the Prophets. Another source shows a sidra read at Sabbath afternoon service. At Nehardea people read from the Hagiographa then, Shabbat says. Later Ashkenazim used sidra for the weekly Pentateuch lesson. Sephardim use the word parashah for that same lesson. In both Talmuds sidra can also mean a school. There sections of Scripture were read and explained to pupils. The entry follows one flexible word through worship and study.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simon-gustav-13:
Gustav Simon was a German surgeon born at Darmstadt on May 30, 1824. Isidore Singer and Frederick T Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He studied at Heidelberg and Giessen, taking his degree in 1848. He then served as a surgeon in the Hessian army. In Paris he learned Jobert's method for bladder fistula and improved it.

In 1861 Simon became a professor of surgery at Rostock. Six years later he moved to Heidelberg, where he stayed until his death. He led a military hospital in Berlin during the war of 1866. He also served as surgeon-general in the Franco-Prussian war. His books dealt with fistula surgery and surgery of the kidneys.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-soul-from-and-h:
The soul, in the Bible, is linked with the breath God breathed into man. Kaufmann Kohler, Isaac Broydé, and Ludwig Blau wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Genesis says man was endowed with that spirit at creation. At first that spirit was tied closely to the life-blood. Only later did a separate soul take root in Judaism.

Contact with Persian and Greek thought shaped that later idea. Later Bible books speak of the spirit returning to God. Three Hebrew terms name the soul in its states. Ruah is the spirit in its primitive state of being. Nefesh is the soul joined with the body in life. Neshamah is the soul active while in the body.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-stern-wilhelm-1:
Wilhelm Stern was a German physician and philosophical writer born in 1844. Isidore Singer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He was born at Sandberg, Posen, on August 11. His father was a rabbi. From 1860 to 1865 he attended the Breslau seminary.

Stern studied philosophy briefly, then chose a medical career instead. He earned his medical degree at Berlin in 1869. He practiced at Bromberg before moving to Berlin in 1873. There he turned to literary and philosophical work. His philosophy followed critical positivism. His books ground ethics in positive science and nature. Later works treat pity and the concept of action. The entry shows a doctor who became an ethics writer.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sutro-alfred-14:
Alfred Sutro was an English author and dramatist born in London about 1870. Joseph Jacobs wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He studied at the City of London School and in Brussels. He began by translating Maeterlinck from the French. He rendered nearly all of Maeterlinck except the dramas.

Sutro then turned to writing plays of his own. He first worked with Arthur Bourchier on The Chili Widow. That play appeared in 1896. The Cave of Illusion followed in 1900. Arethusa came in 1903 and a marriage comedy in 1904. His great success was The Walls of Jericho. It opened at London's Garrick Theatre in October 1904. The short entry catches a playwright at his breakthrough moment.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tomashov-jacob-:
Jacob b. Simeon Tomashov was a Polish rabbi of the seventeenth century. Isidore Singer and M. Seligsohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. His father bore the title ha-Kadosh, the holy one. That term usually marks a martyr. Simeon may have died in the Chmielnicki massacres.

Jacob likely served as rabbi at Nemirov. There his wife and three sons were murdered in 1648. He resolved to emigrate to Palestine after that loss. Instead he spent several years in Venice. At Venice he published Ohel Ya'akob in 1667. The book is a homily on the Akedah, the binding of Isaac. His larger homily collection stayed unpublished.
