jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tugendhold-wolf: Wolf Tugendhold was a Russian educator and author, brother of Jacob Tugendhold. Isidore Singer and Julius Gottlieb wrote this brief Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. He taught at the rabbinical school of Wilna. He also censored Jewish publications in that city. His best-known story is Der Denunciant, the informer. It pictures Jewish life in Poland, drawing on his brother's drama. In 1841 he translated Lebensohn's festival poem into German. That version marked the betrothal of Russia's heir. He also wrote a eulogy of the Hebrew writer Günzberg.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-van-oven-barnar:
Barnard Van Oven was an English doctor and community worker. He was born in London in 1796 and died there in 1860. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. Van Oven trained under Sir William Blizard. He earned his surgical license in 1818 and practiced in London all his life.

Van Oven helped lead the fight against Jewish disabilities in England. In 1829 he wrote the first public appeal on the issue. He later asked in print whether Baron Rothschild should sit in Parliament. He organized committees and spoke at many public meetings. He also helped start the Jews' Infant Schools.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-vulture-14740:
Vulture names several birds of prey in English Bibles. Emil G. Hirsch and I. M. Casanowicz wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The Hebrew words behind it are da'ah, dayyah, and ayyah. Another pair, raham and rahamah, names a further bird. All of them count as unclean in the Law.

The raham is the Egyptian vulture. Arabs still call it by that same name. It migrates through Palestine each spring. The Hebrew word nesher can also mean a vulture. Its cliff nests and bald head fit the vulture well. Griffon vultures breed in colonies across Palestine. The entry sorts these birds from the texts.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-weinberg-paul-1:
Paul Weinberg was a Russian writer of comic sketches. Isidore Singer and Julius Gottlieb wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Odessa about 1840. His father had adopted Christianity. His brothers became a noted writer and a judge. Paul, alone, never studied at any school.

From youth, Weinberg caricatured Jewish life in print. He knew that life only through one uncle. His sketches of Jewish daily life appeared in 1870. Later collections added Armenian, Greek, German, and Russian scenes. The entry calls the humor crude. It notes that his lack of training shows plainly. The piece preserves a minor, flawed literary career.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-winds-14940:
Winds in Hebrew thought came from the earth's four corners. Emil G. Hirsch and Immanuel Benzinger wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Ancient Hebrew writing names only four winds. North, south, east, and west cover all directions. No names exist for winds between those points. Each name therefore spans a wide range.

God kept the winds in storehouses, says Jeremiah. Four angels guarded them in the Book of Revelation. Enoch pictures twelve doors at the earth's ends. No one knew the wind's nature or cause. Its paths stayed a mystery to all. God made the winds his messengers and servants. Storm winds carried out his judgments on earth.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-xeres-jerez-de-:
Xeres, or Jerez de la Frontera, is a city in Cadiz, Spain. Richard Gottheil and Meyer Kayserling wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The city had a Jewish quarter in the days of the Moors. King Alfonso the Wise took the city in 1264.

The king gave homes and lands to the Jews then. The quarter held ninety-six homes, large and small. It had two synagogues for prayer and study. It had two homes for the poor and the lone guest. Homes of two rabbis stood by the synagogues there. The entry names the men who got homes by royal gift. One made word books from Arabic into Spanish tongue. That work was done at the direct wish of the king.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zabludowski-isr:
Israel Zabludowski (born 1850) was a Russian doctor famed for rub cure work. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Byelostok, he wrote a Hebrew tale at age twelve. That tale came out at Wilna in the year 1863.

In 1874 he took his degree at a war school in Saint Petersburg. He then served at war hospitals in the south of Russia. In the war with Turkey he led care for a Cossack band. His work near Plevna won him a high state cross. There a monk's rub cure for wounds caught his eye. He took that cure as his life's chief craft from then. The state sent him west to hone that craft in full. He toured five great towns of Europe for that end.
lectures-on-moral-philosophy-delivered-b:
George Combe delivered these lectures on moral philosophy in 1840. He spoke before a Philosophical Association, and Boston printers issued the book. Marsh, Capen, Lyon and Webb published it that year.

Combe was Scotland's best-known advocate of phrenology. He tied moral conduct to the mind's organs and training. These lectures apply that system to duty, feeling, and self-control. American readers received his ideas through many such tours and printings. The book shows moral teaching shaped by early brain science, as Combe understood it. Combe's American tour spread phrenology widely in these years. Moral philosophy, for him, began with the brain's makeup.
lermontov-hero-of-our-time-1840:
Mikhail Lermontov published A Hero of Our Time in 1840, a Russian novel made of five linked tales. The hero is Pechorin, a young officer serving in the Caucasus. He is clever, bored, and often cruel to those who love him. Other narrators describe him before his own diary speaks.

The tales include a kidnapping, a smugglers' plot, a duel, and a wager on fate. Pechorin treats life as a game and leaves harm behind him. Lermontov died young, yet this book secured his fame. It gave Russian fiction one of its first great antiheroes and a sharp portrait of a restless generation.
lippincott-s-magazine-of-popular-literat:
The January 1875 Lippincott's opens with The New Hyperion. That serial travels from Paris to Marly by way of the Rhine. Following the Tiber begins its two papers here. Charlotte F. Bates contributes a poem, The Paradox.

Malcolm advances through its final chapters, sixty-four to seventy. The laird's vision and the cry from the chamber build suspense. William Black's Three Feathers reaches On Wings of Hope. R. Davey reports on the stage in Italy for the issue. The Parsees receive an essay by Fannie Roper Feudge. A Christmas hymn by Buchanan Read seasons the January number.
machiavelli-prince-dacres-1640:
Niccolò Machiavelli wrote The Prince in Italian, and Edward Dacres made the first English version in 1640. Dacres gave English readers Machiavelli's masterpiece a century after it stirred Italy in print there. The slim book of counsel on power still starts fights about ends and means.

Machiavelli tells a new prince how to gain a state and keep it by force. Fear, he argues, beats love when a ruler must choose, and cruelty has its uses. He praises Cesare Borgia's ruthless craft and blames mercy that breeds disorder in a state. Fox and lion, fraud and force, are his paired tools of rule in the text. The name Machiavellian for cold statecraft starts with this blunt little book's fame.
much-ado-about-nothing-pg2240: Beatrice and Benedick wage their merry war in this edition: "I will not send you." Tricked into love by their friends, the witty pair spar toward marriage while Claudio's jealousy nearly ruins Hero. The wittiest comedy in English, sparkling from first to last.
mueller-handbuch-physiologie-1840:
Johannes Muller sums up the science of the body in his Handbuch der Physiologie, in German from 1840. The handbook served as the nineteenth century's bible of physiology. Senses, blood, nerves, and voice all fall under Muller's vast and orderly learning, drawn from his Berlin lectures and his own tireless trials.

His students included Helmholtz, Virchow, and Du Bois-Reymond, founders of modern medicine in their turn. Muller taught them to test every claim on living tissue. Few teachers have ever shaped a science so deeply through pupils. The book stands behind a whole era of German medicine, the seedbed from which its golden age grew.
openalex-w2005072240:
Martin Prince, Juan Llibre Rodriguez, Lisseth Noriega and colleagues tested a computer tool for diagnosing dementia. Their study appeared in BMC Public Health in 2008. They worked with the 10/66 Dementia Research Group. Standard dementia rules exist, but they are not fully set out as fixed steps.

The group turned the DSM-IV rules into a full computer algorithm. Their interview data fed the program directly. They checked the program against their earlier 10/66 method. They also checked it against a clinician making a diagnosis. The study ran in real community samples. A shared, fixed method can make surveys comparable across countries. That matters where dementia research is still scarce.
openalex-w2011875740:
Peter Rosset and Maria Elena Martinez-Torres wrote about farm movements and agroecology. Their paper appeared in Ecology and Society in 2012. Agroecology means farming in ways that work with nature. Peasant movements have taken it up in recent years. The authors asked why it now matters so much to them.

Rural land is contested between big agribusiness and peasant groups. The authors used ideas about disputed territory to explain the shift. Movements see agroecology as a way to keep control of their land. They gave examples from farmer-to-farmer teaching networks. Such networks spread methods fast through trust and example. The paper also covers La Via Campesina, a global peasant movement. Movements, they argue, can take agroecology to scale.
openalex-w2064216140:
Tomas Duffy, Carolina Cura, Juan Carlos Ramirez and colleagues validated a lab test that counts Chagas parasites in blood. Their paper appeared in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases in 2013. Doctors need reliable counts for diagnosis. Counts also show whether treatment is working. Labs lacked a standard, accurate counting method.

The assay uses real-time PCR on parasite DNA. It targets a repeated DNA stretch in the parasite. Several labs joined the validation study. They checked sensitivity and accuracy carefully. They also checked that results repeat well. A standard method lets clinics compare results across sites. That matters for trials of new Chagas drugs. The paper reports the test's analytical performance in detail.
openalex-w2110345840:
Christian Hoffmann, Serena Dollive, Stephanie Grunberg and colleagues studied the fungi and archaea living in the human gut. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in 2013. Gut research had focused on bacteria and viruses. Fungi and archaea were largely unmapped. Diet shapes all gut residents, they reasoned.

Samples came from ninety-eight well-characterised volunteers. Diet records covered both recent and long-term habits. Fungi were less diverse than gut bacteria. Their makeup still varied between people. Certain fungi tracked with recent diet patterns. Archaea correlated with bacterial groups present. The study widens gut research beyond bacteria alone. Diet links may matter for gut health.
openalex-w2130707940:
Marcus Eriksen, Laurent Lebreton, Henry Carson, and colleagues published this study in PLoS ONE in 2014. They set out to count and weigh the plastic floating in the world's oceans. Earlier guesses lacked data from the Southern Hemisphere and from remote waters.

The team drew on twenty-four expeditions run between 2007 and 2013 across all five subtropical gyres and several seas. They towed surface nets and ran visual counts of large debris, then modeled how floating plastic spreads. Their estimate is a minimum of more than five trillion pieces, weighing over two hundred fifty thousand tons. Small microplastics were far scarcer at the surface than breakup rates predict, suggesting removal at work.
openalex-w2157165940:
Ariel Zylberberg, Pablo Barttfeld, and Mariano Sigman published this study in Frontiers in Integrative Neuroscience in 2012. They ask how the brain builds confidence in a perceptual decision. One view says confidence simply reads out the evidence gathered for the choice itself, like a fuel gauge on the decision process.

Other evidence hints that confidence can drift apart from accuracy, sometimes high on wrong answers. The authors tackle the question with numbers, comparing the evidence patterns that drive choices with those that drive confidence ratings. Volunteers judged moving or flickering signals and rated their certainty. By measuring which parts of the signal shaped each response, the study tests whether confidence mirrors the choice signal or distorts it.

The principle says a good catalyst binds hydrogen neither too weakly nor too strongly, so reaction rates should peak in the middle.

Looking closely at the data, the authors find no volcano at all once oxide-covered metals are removed. openalex-w2471350540:
Filipe Nunes Ribeiro, Matheus Araújo, and Pollyanna Gonçalves, with Marcos André Gonçalves and Fabrício Benevenuto, published SentiBench in EPJ Data Science in 2016. The team compared twenty-four widely used methods on eighteen labeled datasets. The sets covered social network posts, movie and product reviews, and comments on news articles. Performance varied a lot from one dataset to another, so no single method won everywhere. The authors released the code and data in an open benchmark system. That gives later researchers a shared yardstick for testing new sentiment tools.
openalex-w2523334240:
Rainer Willi Bussmann, Narel Y. Paniagua-Zambrana, and Shalva Sikharulidze led this 2016 ethnobotany study in the Journal of Ethnobiology and Ethnomedicine. The team interviewed one hundred seventy people in their homes and gardens during field seasons from 2013 to 2015. They recorded four hundred eighty plant species in use, across ninety-five families. The remote Tusheti and Khevsureti area reported the most species, and the most unique ones. The authors tested whether Soviet rule and isolation shaped plant use, and whether knowledge is being lost. Their survey gives a baseline for a living tradition that remains unusually strong.
openalex-w2526477240:
Francisco de Assis Santos e Silva and Carlos Alberto Vieira de Azevedo presented version 7.7 of the Assistat software in this 2016 paper. It appeared in the African Journal of Agricultural Research. Assistat is a free program for analyzing experimental data, built mainly for agricultural research. Many professional statistics packages cost too much for students, the authors note, or demand custom routines.

Assistat covers the main analysis of variance models used in experiments. It also includes principal component analysis and leading non-parametric tests. The authors stress its friendly, easy-to-use screen, which the paper illustrates with figures. Software like this matters because research data quickly grows too large for hand calculation. The paper explains what the program does and how researchers can apply it to their own experimental data.

The charts track estimated fetal weight and standard ultrasound measurements during pregnancy. They come from a multinational study that followed pregnancies over time in several countries.

Poor growth before birth is tied to death and illness around delivery. It is also linked to higher risk of common adult diseases later in life. Clinicians need shared reference charts to judge whether a fetus is growing normally. Older charts often came from single countries or narrow populations. WHO made producing global charts a high priority, funding this study through its research programs. The resulting charts give clinics everywhere one common yardstick for fetal growth.

Each carried distinct maternal lines, and they settled northern and southern Sahul separately. Strong geographic patterning survives today, showing limited mixing over time. After long isolation, post-ice-age changes spurred fresh branching and wider contact.

Implementing such teams, the authors conclude, is an effective plan for patient safety and better use of hospital resources, sparing patients a crisis and sparing the ICU a preventable admission.

Maria Clara Peres de Castelo Branco led a Portuguese-language review, published in Brazil in 2026, on biologic therapies for severe chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps. The disease carries a heavy symptom burden, recurs often, and pushes some patients into repeated courses of systemic corticosteroids and repeated surgeries, each with its own costs and risks. Biologic drugs, which target specific immune pathways, offer a newer option for the hardest cases.

The study set out to analyze the available evidence on the efficacy and safety of these therapies, and their impact on how often patients still need surgery and systemic corticosteroids. For clinicians managing patients who cycle through steroids and operations, that balance of benefit, safety, and spared procedures is the practical question the review addresses.
openalex-w7204866640:
Andréia Aguiar Barros led a Portuguese-language review, in Brazil in 2026, on the vaginal microbiota and recurrent bacterial vaginosis, the most common cause of vaginal discharge in women of reproductive age. It is a dysbiosis: protective lactobacilli fall while harmful anaerobes multiply, and it often returns after standard antibiotics. Reviewing 2020 to 2026 work across three sources, the team examined what drives its return.

Recurrent disease involves complex multispecies biofilms, led by certain bacteria, that resist drugs and evade the host immune response, aided by strain changes, pH shifts, and risky habits. New routes look promising: chosen lactobacillus probiotics, vaginal microbiota transplant, and synthetic biofilms with acidifiers. Beating recurrence, the authors conclude, means moving from a drug-only model to restoring the vaginal balance and clearing harmful biofilms.
openalex-w7207755140:
Alexandre Ferreira da Silva leads a team of seven researchers asking whether routine panoramic dental X-rays can catch early gum disease. Panoramic images are taken for many reasons, and the bone loss of early periodontal disease can show on them before patients feel symptoms. The team reviewed digital panoramic radiographs from several hundred adults, graded each image for quality, and checked for slight bone loss, along with links to age and sex.

About half of the radiographs showed early periodontal changes, a share the authors treat as a warning worth acting on. They stress the limits of the tool: a panoramic image works as a population screening aid, not as a final diagnosis of periodontal disease. Used that way, an X-ray taken anyway becomes a chance to spot trouble early and send patients for a proper gum examination.
openalex-w7207879640: Ana Luísa Carvalho Collela and three colleagues review ways to control two invasive snails in this 2026 article in Research, Society and Development. The species are the giant African snail and the small Asian snail, both spread well beyond their home ranges. The hosted text available here gives the title, authors, and journal but no abstract, so the review's methods and findings cannot be summarized from it. What the title states plainly is the scope: control methods for the two infestations.
openalex-w7212175940:
Carolaine Melo Goncalves, Bianca Isabela Acampora e Silva Ferreira, and Geisa Fonseca de Goncalves study how future science teachers think about sex, gender, and birth control. The students train at a federal institute in Campos, Rio de Janeiro. The goal was to build a class plan that faces machismo head-on. The work rests on Paulo Freire's dialogic school and on a problem-based arc used in health training.

Three blocks stood out in the talks. School life still mutes the theme of sex. The trainees' own training has gaps. Yet class tools can spark a sharp, shared, and fair view of the topic. From those needs, the team built a plan of five to six classes for the last years of basic school. It aims to break bias, put youth in the lead, and call boys to share the load in family planning.
openalex-w7212828440:
Maria Isabela Vosniak Passos leads a team on the care of those who sit by a sick child's bed. A child's stay in a ward shakes the whole home: heart, purse, and week. The team read past work from 2016 to 2026 in three health stores; twenty-one studies made the cut.

A ward stay, the work shows, can bring stress, dread, and a sense of no power. Aid can cut that load. Clear talk, a share in the child's care, and a team that sees the carer all help. One gap stands out: most of the work comes from abroad, and Brazil's own reads are few. The call is for more home-grown study, and for wards that treat the carer as part of the cure.
openalex-w7213410140:
Elisabete Gomes Melo and Damares Araujo Teles study young children's agency in a daycare in Bertioga, São Paulo. Their 2026 qualitative article treats play as a space for exploration and discovery. It draws on semi-structured interviews with four teachers at the institution.

Teachers described play as basic to child development, linked to autonomy, imagination, and language. Children's agency showed when they could choose materials and games, invent stories, take roles, and negotiate rules. Room layout, varied materials, and teacher mediation helped that agency grow. Barriers included large groups, limited space and materials, and too little time set aside for play.
openalex-w7213445340:
Augusto João Manuel leads a large team reviewing severe diabetic ketoacidosis in adults. This dangerous complication brings high ketones, blood acidity, and major fluid and salt imbalance. Their 2026 integrative review covers studies from 2021 to 2026 across four major databases.

Nineteen papers formed the final synthesis, from hundreds first found. Balanced salt solutions may lower excess chloride and improve acid balance, the evidence suggests. Treatment rests on fluid replacement, insulin, correction of salt problems, and finding what triggered the episode. The review compares fluid choices and insulin strategies in plain clinical terms, helping readers see where recent guidance has shifted.
openalex-w7214107140:
Leticia Pereira de Sousa and co-workers profile testing imaging and heart exams for dogs and cats at a veterinary hospital in Juazeiro do Norte, Ceará. Their 2026 descriptive, observational study records procedures followed during a placement from March to May 2026 at the Ello Veterinary Hospital.

In total, 528 procedures were logged. Ultrasound led by a wide margin, followed by X-ray, electrocardiography, and echocardiography. Ultrasound-guided cystocentesis, computed tomography, and endoscopy appeared in smaller numbers. Imaging and cardiology tools serve daily study and follow-up of animal patients, the authors note. The variety on show during one placement period illustrates how central such diagnostics have become in small animal practice.
openalex-w7214602640:
Alberto Dias Valadão and colleagues examined, in a 2026 documentary study, how a pedagogy degree program in Ji-Paraná, Brazil, shapes student identities and differences. Reading the program's curriculum documents and national rules through post-structuralist cultural studies, they ask how a curriculum produces ideas about who teachers and students are. The program belongs to the Federal University of Rondônia.

On one side, the program promises inclusive training that honors diversity and invites students to see difference as something society can use to classify and exclude. On the other side, fitting national standard formats risks locking in a uniform curriculum policed by external exams and teacher control. The study exposes that tension at the heart of initial teacher education: a curriculum is a cultural artifact that forms people, not a neutral list of subjects.
openalex-w7220892240:
Patricia Luciana Floriano Mesquita Fiedler and Gislei Mocelin Polli mapped, in a 2026 scoping review, work factors behind police mental health. Police work carries demands of organization, feeling, thought, and trauma. Following the scoping review reporting standard, they searched five databases for studies in languages published between 2016 and 2026. Nine studies passed the screening criteria for analysis by theme.

Findings fell into three categories: organizational structure and work context; rigid disciplinary regime and police performance; and continuous trauma exposure with lack of support. Overload, workplace pressure, shifts and schedules, emotional control demands, high cognitive cost, and exposure to critical incidents were related to harms. The harms are stress, anxiety, emotional exhaustion, burnout, cognitive changes, post-traumatic stress, suicidal behaviors, and work absences. Stigma and fear of effects at work restrict help-seeking. Mental health promotion, they conclude, needs ongoing, easy-to-reach, private actions tied to work organization and health policy.
plos-pbio-0020240:
Jan Karlseder, Kristina Hoke, Olga K. Mirzoeva, and their team studied chromosome ends in PLOS Biology in 2004. Telomeres are caps that protect chromosome tips. A protein called TRF2 sits on those caps and keeps them from being mistaken for broken DNA.

The team found TRF2 binds ATM, the kinase that sounds the alarm at true DNA breaks, and can hold that alarm back. That holding action is what lets healthy telomeres stay invisible to the damage response. If the cap fails, the alarm fires and the cell ages or dies. The paper clarifies a guard system whose faults are tied to aging and cancer.
plos-pbio-0020340:
David L. Reed, Vincent S. Smith, Shaless L. Hammond, and their team read human history from lice in PLOS Biology in 2004. Body lice live in clothing and feed on people. Their genes carry a record of their hosts' past, since lice pass from person to person by close contact.

The genetic data suggest body lice spread at a time that fits direct contact between modern and archaic humans. That is, our ancestors likely met Neandertal-like groups closely enough to share parasites. Clothing use also enters the story, since body lice need garments to live in. The study is a clever use of a humble bug as a witness to events no fossil can show directly.
plos-pone-0000040:
Michael Forgber, Rajatava Basu, Kaushik Roychoudhury, and co-authors mapped what the immune system sees during a parasitic infection in 2006. Leishmania donovani causes visceral leishmaniasis, a deadly disease spread by sand flies. Antigenicity is the measure of which parasite proteins the human immune system actually attacks.

Using proteome serology, testing patient blood serum against the parasite's full set of proteins, the team mapped those targets across the proteome. A map of what the body recognizes is a shortlist for vaccines and for blood tests that could diagnose the disease early. For a neglected illness of the poor, that shortlist is where practical defenses begin.
plos-pone-0000140:
Stuart H. M. Butchart, H. Resit Akçakaya, Janice Chanson, and colleagues published this conservation paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It proposes improvements to the Red List Index. The index is built from the IUCN Red List and tracks how extinction risk changes over time for whole groups of species.

Governments use the index to judge whether conservation is working. The authors address weaknesses in how the index is calculated and sampled. A more reliable index means policy makers can tell real progress from noise. Scarce conservation money can then go where the trend data says it counts.
plos-pone-0000240:
Shoshi Dorfberger, Esther Adi-Japha, and Avi Karni published this motor learning study in PLOS ONE in 2007. When people practice a movement, the memory of it becomes firm over hours, a process called consolidation, but new learning can interfere. The authors found reduced susceptibility to that interference in children before adolescence.

Young learners may hold onto a new motor skill more stubbornly than adults do. The authors compare consolidation in children and adults after training. The result bears on how physical skills, from handwriting to sports, are best taught at different ages, and on rehabilitation after injury.
plos-pone-0000340:
Bita Sehat, Sandra Andersson, Radu Vasilcanu, and colleagues published this cell signaling paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. The IGF-1 receptor receives growth signals and is a target in cancer research. The authors study the role of ubiquitination, the tagging of proteins for disposal, in how the receptor signals. They also trace how the receptor is then degraded, taken off the cell surface and destroyed.

How long a growth receptor stays active shapes how strongly a cell grows. The disposal tag is part of that timing system. The paper maps ubiquitin's role in the receptor's life cycle, knowledge needed for drugs that aim to shut this pathway down in tumors.
plos-pone-0000440:
Dimitar Dimitrov and colleagues built a brighter tool for watching voltage in living cells, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. Their enhanced fluorescent protein voltage sensor glows in response to changes in a cell's electrical state. Nerve and heart cells speak in voltage, so a fast, bright sensor lets researchers watch that speech directly.

The team engineered the protein and characterized how well it works. Genetic voltage sensors can be aimed at chosen cell types, something electrodes cannot easily do. Improving their brightness and speed opens the way to filming electrical activity across whole circuits, a long-standing goal in neuroscience and cardiology.
plos-pone-0000540:
Hiroyuki Yamamoto and colleagues studied antibodies that help keep HIV in check after infection, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Most people's infections run unchecked, but some hold the virus down. Neutralizing antibodies, which block the virus head-on, are prime suspects in that control. The team weighed their role in post-infection control of the virus.

If antibodies made after infection can still rein the virus in, vaccine makers gain a real target. A vaccine could teach the body to make those same antibodies before it ever meets the virus. The study weighs how much of natural control these antibodies can explain, next to other arms of defense.
plos-pone-0000640:
Vinet Coetzee, Louise Barrett, Jaco M. Greeff and co-authors tested a popular idea about faces and genes in PLOS ONE in 2007. HLA genes help the immune system, and three hypotheses link them to health and to facial attractiveness. The proposed routes are avoiding inbreeding, gaining an edge from mixed gene copies, and selection that favors rare types.

Their title states a split result: common HLA alleles were associated with health, but not with facial attractiveness. That weakens the claim that good-looking faces advertise HLA quality. Evolutionary psychologists and geneticists get a careful check on a theory that is often repeated more strongly than the evidence allows.
plos-pone-0000740:
Andrew J. Spiers followed a bacterial mutant's fortunes on a flat world, writing in PLOS ONE in 2007. The Wrinkly Spreader is a bacterium whose altered form succeeds in still liquid cultures by colonizing the air-liquid interface, forming a mat at the surface. Bacterial adaptation often establishes new genotypes with significantly altered traits. Spiers moved the test to two-dimensional agar plates.

His themes are maladaptation, compensation, and ecological success. A trait that wins in liquid may cost its bearer on agar, and later changes may compensate. The microcosm is simple by design: one surface, one mutant, clear outcomes. Evolution experiments like this show adaptation's trade-offs in miniature.
plos-pone-0000840:
John S. Brownstein, Margarita Sordo, Isaac S. Kohane and colleagues asked whether routine health data could have caught a drug danger earlier. COX-2 selective inhibitors, painkillers sold as rofecoxib and celecoxib, are associated with myocardial infarction, heart attack. The team sought to determine whether population health monitoring would have revealed the drugs' effect on population-level patterns of heart attacks.

Their retrospective study used inpatients at two Boston hospitals, as the abstract reports. The playful title, The Tell-Tale Heart, covers a serious method: surveillance of ordinary records as an early warning system for drug safety. If monitoring can spot risk in real time, regulators need not wait for scandals.
plos-pone-0000940:
Godwin Ashiabi and Keri O'Neal modeled how poverty reaches children's health through hardship and parenting, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Low income alone does not tell the whole story of a child's health. Families also face material hardship, trouble paying for food, housing and care, and strain that shapes parenting.

The authors test a model with several paths running at once. They ask how much of poverty's effect travels through hardship and family factors. Answers like this decide where help does most good: raising income, easing hardship or supporting parents. The study treats child health as the end of a chain, not a single cause.
plos-pone-0001040:
Andrew Oxman, Signe Flottorp, Kari Havelserud and colleagues ran a televised, web based trial of valerian for insomnia, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The trial was part of a project to help the public use research in health decisions. Viewers could join the study and follow the process through television and the web.

Valerian is an herbal remedy widely taken for poor sleep. In a randomised trial, participants received valerian or a comparison under that public format. The design itself is the experiment's second subject: can open, broadcast trials recruit well and stay rigorous. Sleep remedies are a fair first case, since demand and doubt are both high.
plos-pone-0001240:
Eating less and dampening insulin signaling are two regimens that extend life in many organisms. Wendy Iser and Catherine Wolkow asked how the two interact in the worm C. elegans, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Genetic analysis had shown that dietary restriction and reduced insulin-like signaling work through distinct pathways in the worm.

The authors report that DAF-2, the worm's insulin-like receptor, modifies the effects of dietary restriction and nutrient stress on aging, stress resistance, and growth. Even distinct pathways talk to each other. Their results shape how combined interventions for aging might behave.
plos-pone-0001340:
To replicate, lentiviruses such as HIV must insert DNA copies of their genomes into host chromosomes. Heather Marshall and colleagues studied a host protein, PSIP1, also called LEDGF/p75, that guides that insertion, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Lentiviral integration is favored in active transcription units, which allows efficient viral gene expression after integration.

The authors examine the role of PSIP1/LEDGF/p75 in lentiviral infectivity and integration targeting. A host factor the virus depends on is a tempting drug target, because the virus cannot easily mutate its way around it. Their work clarifies how much of integration this factor controls.
plos-pone-0001440:
Danielle Kemmer and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE paper on a score for how well a gene is known. Labs know a lot about some genes and near nothing about others. There was no plain scale for that gap. The team built a score that rates how deep the notes on each protein coding gene run.

Their score is drawn from text and data on what each gene does. It mirrors how people judge a gene as known or obscure. A scale like this can steer funds to the least known genes. It can also track how fast the gene map as a whole is being filled in.
plos-pone-0001540:
Der-Chih Yang and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on how stem cells choose fat or bone. Stem cells from marrow can become fat cells, bone cells, and more. Fat and bone fates pull against each other, but the control was vague. The team tested a cell signal path that runs through a common messenger.

They show this path steers both fates and sets the mix of two bone signals. It works in part by curbing the hormone leptin. A single path that tips the fat bone balance has clear clinical pull. It may bear on bone loss and weight gain in aging.
plos-pone-0001640:
Emmanuel S. Onaivi and co-authors reviewed what is known about CB2 cannabinoid receptors in the brain in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. These receptors respond to cannabis-like compounds. Addiction and major depression are the health problems in view; both are tied to stress and both often return after treatment.

Many labs had failed to find CB2 receptors in healthy brains, which made their role in mood and drug use an open dispute. Onaivi and his team pull together evidence from mouse work and human subjects on where these receptors occur and what they do. The full text weighs the detection methods and the case for CB2 as a drug target. If the receptors do act in the brain, blocking or boosting them could offer a new route to treat addiction and depression.
plos-pone-0001740:
Corinne Vacher, Dominique Piou, and Marie-Laure Desprez-Loustau analyzed a network of tree diseases in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Ecological networks often show compartments and nestedness, patterns whose causes are debated. The authors used a well-resolved network of host and pathogen interactions to find what shapes them. They drew on a long forest health survey from 1972 to 2005.

Their paper asks how past evolutionary history asymmetrically influences the antagonistic tree and fungus network. The full text gives the network maps and the tests of compartment structure. Knowing whether pathogens cluster by host family history helps foresters predict which trees a new disease can jump to. That is a pressing question as tree pathogens spread worldwide.
plos-pone-0001840:
Michael J. Proulx, Petra Stoerig, Eva Ludowig, and their co-authors tested a device that lets blind people 'see' through sound in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Sensory substitution devices translate inaccessible visual information into a format that intact senses can process. Here the translation is image-to-sound.

They tested localization of visual stimuli, LEDs and objects, using image-to-sound conversion in 13 blindfolded participants. The study separates effects of learning by doing from those of long-term sensory deprivation. The full text gives the accuracy results. Such devices could restore a measure of spatial awareness to blind users, and they test how flexibly the brain can remap one sense onto another.
plos-pone-0001940:
Zhaojie Li, Shicui Zhang, and Qinghui Liu reported a second job for a fish egg protein in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The protein, vitellogenin, is best known as a building material for eggs and new life. It had also been tied to defense against infection in fish, but no one knew how it helped.

The team tested how the protein meets microbes in the lab, using binding tests and enzyme-linked assays. They report that it works as a broad pattern sensor that flags germs, and that it helps immune cells engulf them. A food protein that also fights germs blurs the line between growth and defense.
plos-pone-0002040:
Adinda Wellens and co-authors designed germ blockers from the shape of a bacterial grip protein, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Certain Escherichia coli strains cling to the wall of the human urinary tract with hair-like pili. At the tip sits FimH, a protein that grips mannose sugars on the surface, and a few clinging bacteria can then invade bladder cells.

The team used the crystal structure of FimH bound to a mannose chain to build anti-adhesives, molecules that jam the grip. Blocking attachment, rather than killing the germ, could treat urinary infections with less pressure for drug resistance.
plos-pone-0002140:
Jianhua Xing and Jing Chen revisited a classic piece of math in cell biology, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. In 1981, Goldbeter and Koshland showed how a simple cycle of protein changes can act like a sharp switch. A small rise in a signal molecule can flip the system from nearly off to nearly on, giving a steep, S-shaped response curve.

Xing and Chen studied that switch in its first-order region, where the response is more gentle. Asked how it behaves when the cell's inner parts move in a noisy, disordered way. Their math shows how cells can stay sensitive to signals even when conditions inside are messy and always shifting.
plos-pone-0002240:
Andrew Pask, Richard Behringer, and Marilyn Renfree brought a piece of an extinct genome back to life in mice, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. DNA from extinct species can tell scientists how genomes evolved and what made each species distinct. Reading the code alone, though, cannot show what a gene actually did in a living animal.

The team took a DNA control element from an extinct marsupial genome. Placed in mice, it drove gene activity in the developing limb. Their test resurrected the function of DNA that no living species carries. The approach turns museum DNA into working biology, not just sequence.
plos-pone-0002340:
Lesley Rogers and Giorgio Vallortigara showed that honeybees recall a learned smell first on one side, then the other, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Bees, Apis mellifera, readily learn to link odors with sugar rewards. Recall is tested by the proboscis extension reflex: a bee that remembers sticks out its tongue at the trained odor.

The authors found that recall involves first the right antenna and then the left. Memory of the same odor shifts sides over time after learning. That lateral handover mirrors side specialization seen in vertebrate brains, and it suggests bees store the memory in stages, with each antenna taking its turn.
plos-pone-0002440:
Led by Kuehl, a team of researchers published its study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The author list runs from Hjalmar S. Kuehl, Caroline Elzner, Yasmin Moebius, and others. Its subject is the Price of Play: Self-Organized Infant Mortality Cycles in Chimpanzees. Chimpanzees have been used extensively as a model system for laboratory research on infectious diseases.

Ironically, we know next to nothing about disease dynamics in wild chimpanzee populations. Each part of the study builds on the part before it, in the order the team carried it out. Readers finish with a clear sense of the problem, the approach, and why the question was worth the team's time.
plos-pone-0002540:
Research by Leppänen and co-authors came out in PLOS ONE in 2008. The author list runs from Olli V. Leppänen, Harri Sievänen, Jarkko Jokihaara, and others. Its subject is pathogenesis of Age-Related Osteoporosis: Impaired Mechano-Responsiveness of Bone Is Not the Culprit. According to prevailing understanding, skeletal mechano-responsiveness declines with age.

What the team did, and why they did it that way, forms the core of the piece. It stands as one careful step in a longer line of work, with its question and approach laid out in full. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002640:
Work by Alison Maresh and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was principles of glomerular organization in the human olfactory bulb – implications for odor processing. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Alison Maresh, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. Olfactory sensory neurons (OSN) in mice express only 1 of a possible 1. Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication.
plos-pone-0002740:
Work by Rebecca Banerjee and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008, dealing with adaptive immune neuroprotection in G93A-SOD1 amyotrophic lateral sclerosis mice. The catalog record names Rebecca Banerjee first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. Innate neuroimmune dysfunction is a pathobiological feature of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). The authors add a further point. However, links, if any, between disease and adaptive immunity are poorly understood. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe.
plos-pone-0002840:
Work by Katherine G. Akers and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was social competitiveness and plasticity of neuroendocrine function in old age: influence of neonatal novelty exposure and maternal care reliability. Authorship is credited in the record to Katherine G. Akers and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. Early experience is known to have a profound impact on brain and behavioral function later in life. The authors add a further point. Relatively few studies, however, have examined whether the effects of early experience remain detectable in the aging animal. Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start.
plos-pone-0002940:
Gregory Mullen, Ruth Ellis, Kazutoyo Miura and co-authors ran a first human trial of a malaria vaccine mix in 2008. The vaccine targets AMA1, a surface protein of the malaria parasite's blood stage, and pairs it with the adjuvant CPG 7909 to boost response. AMA1 was a leading blood-stage candidate.

This phase 1 trial in PLOS ONE tested safety and immune response for the AMA1 vaccine on Alhydrogel plus the new adjuvant. Phase 1 is the earliest human stage, focused on safety. Malaria vaccine research needs such careful steps, since blood-stage infection is what makes people ill.
plos-pone-0003040:
Héctor Guidobaldi, María Teves, Diego Uñates and co-authors identified the sperm attractant from rabbit egg complexes in 2008. Mammalian sperm swim toward several female sources, including follicular fluid and the cumulus cells around the egg. Several substances had been confirmed as attractants, and progesterone was a candidate.

Progesterone from the cumulus cells is the chemoattractant secreted by the rabbit oocyte cumulus complex, the title reports. Published in PLOS ONE, pinning the signal to one hormone from one source clarifies the final guidance step in fertilization. It may inform fertility testing and treatment. Details of samples, measures, and analysis are set out in the full article text.
plos-pone-0003140: Mady Hornig and colleagues published a case-control study in PLOS ONE in 2008 on measles vaccine and autism. The title states the result in plain terms: no link was found between measles virus vaccine and autism with enteropathy, a gut condition, in the group studied. No abstract beyond the title was supplied, so no study details are added here.
plos-pone-0003240:
Zoe T. Richards, Madeleine J. H. van Oppen, Carden C. Wallace and colleagues test whether rare corals are hybrids in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Coral reefs worldwide face a variety of threats, and many coral species are increasingly endangered. It is often assumed that rare coral species face higher extinction risks because they have very small effective population sizes, with decreased genetic diversity as a predicted consequence.

The title reports that some rare Indo-Pacific coral species are probable hybrids. Readers learn that rarity can reflect origin, not just decline. If a rare coral is a hybrid, its conservation value and protection strategy need fresh thought.
plos-pone-0003340:
Yanlin Shi, Qilong Xu, Sunita V. Seemanaplli and colleagues study Lyme disease proteins in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. As an extracellular bacterium, the Lyme disease spirochete Borrelia burgdorferi resides in the extracellular matrix and connective tissues. It also sits between host cells during infection of mammals. Decorin and glycosaminoglycans are found in plenty in those places. Its ties to those materials are thus central.

The authors assess common and unique contributions of decorin-binding proteins A and B to overall virulence of Borrelia burgdorferi. Readers learn how two similar binding proteins divide work in infection. Adhesion proteins are targets because blocking attachment can prevent disease without killing bacteria directly.
plos-pone-0003440:
Peter V. Lovell and colleagues read gene activity in the songbird brain in this 2008 paper. Songbirds learn their songs, much as children learn speech. A set of brain nuclei, called the song system, drives that learning. The team used high-throughput methods to profile genes across that system.

The profiles revealed chemical specializations in the song nuclei. Certain signals and receptors stood out against the rest of the brain. Those traits may support vocal learning, a rare skill among animals. The results offer clues to the molecular basis of learned song and speech.
plos-pone-0003540:
Tetsuya Kimura and co-authors studied an enzyme tied to memory in this 2008 paper. GSK-3β is an enzyme suspected in Alzheimer's disease. That disease starts with memory disturbance in its early stages. The enzyme's normal role in the adult brain was not well understood.

The team showed GSK-3β is required for memory reconsolidation. That process restabilizes a memory after it is recalled. Blocking the enzyme kept recalled memories from settling again. The finding names a molecular step in how memories persist. Recalled memories are not fixed files, and this work shows one way they shift.
plos-pone-0003640:
Till Bärnighausen, Claudia Wallrauch, Alex Welte, and colleagues published this methods study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Counting new HIV infections is hard, so surveys use a blood test meant to flag recent ones. The team checked that test, called cBED, in rural South Africa.

They compared incidence estimates from one-time survey testing with estimates from following the same population over years. There was concern the assay wrongly classifies some long-standing infections as recent, inflating the count. The head-to-head check shows how far the shortcut can be trusted for planning HIV programs.
plos-pone-0003740:
Dimitrios Iliopoulos, Konstantinos N. Malizos, Pagona Oikonomou, and colleagues published this arthritis study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Osteoarthritis wears down joint cartilage and affects more than 100 million people worldwide. Its causes mix genes, mechanics, and environment, and its gene list was incomplete.

The team combined microRNA data with proteomic data, the full set of proteins in tissue. Together the two approaches flagged new osteoarthritis genes. They also mapped how the hits work together in metabolic and inflammatory networks, showing the disease as a joint effort of many genes. Worn joints are a top cause of pain in older adults.
plos-pone-0003840:
Simani Gaseitsiwe, Davide Valentini, Shahnaz Mahdavifar, and colleagues published this tuberculosis study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Hunting antigens by reading serum antibodies had been used to find targets in cancer. A similar approach can flag meaningful targets in tuberculosis infection. The team applied it with a high content peptide microarray.

Their chip carried peptides from 61 proteins of Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Antibody binding patterns in patients' blood defined recognizable patterns of tuberculosis. The pattern recognition approach borrows tumor-antigen hunting for the fight against TB, aiming at better tests and vaccine targets.
plos-pone-0003940:
H. Artee Luchman, Hallgrimur Benediktsson, Michelle L. Villemaire, and co-authors timed a gene loss in mouse prostate in 2008. Loss of PTEN, a tumor-blocking gene, is common in human prostate cancer. It is most common in advanced disease. PTEN also gates a major growth signal path in cells.

Their PLOS ONE article removed Pten at set times in the mouse prostate. The pace of early abnormal growth depended on when the gene was cut. Early lesions grew at rates set by that timing. The work shows the order of gene losses shapes how prostate cancer starts.
plos-pone-0004040:
Manos Tsakiris asked how we know a mirror face is our own in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. A reflection looks like us, but looks may not be the whole story. The reflection also moves when we move. We see it touched exactly when we feel touch ourselves.

The study tested how current multisensory input alters self-face recognition. Matching sight and touch cues shifted judgments of what counts as self. That shows self-recognition is built live from several senses. The work informs research on body ownership and its disorders. It appeared in PLOS ONE, and the full text is free for any reader to check.
plos-pone-0004140:
Richard Cudney-Bueno and colleagues published this marine study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Marine reserves, sea areas where fishing is banned, are promoted around the world as tools for conservation and fishery management. Supporters argue that reserves protect sea life and also help fisheries, as extra adults spill out and larvae drift into fishing grounds.

Solid proof for those benefits, especially the larval route, had been thin. The authors present evidence that reserves can produce rapid effects through the spread of larvae to nearby waters. Their findings support the idea that a reserve can repay nearby fisheries quickly, not just in the long run.
plos-pone-0004240:
Takahiro Fujimoto and colleagues published this obesity study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Obesity and its metabolic disorders are leading causes of adult illness and death. KRAP is a protein tied to the cell's actin skeleton, found in tissues throughout the body and first identified as a cancer-related molecule.

The team studied mice lacking KRAP and fed them a fattening diet. They report altered energy homeostasis and resistance to diet-induced obesity in these mice. A protein that, when missing, keeps mice lean on rich food is a clue to how the body sets its weight.
plos-pone-0004340:
Marco José and colleagues published this theory paper in PLOS ONE in 2009. The standard genetic code translates DNA into proteins in nearly all life. The authors ask how it evolved from a primeval RNA code in the RNA world. That was an early era when RNA did both information and chemistry jobs.

They derive two candidate ancestral codes, one built from codons of the type RNY, purine, any base, pyrimidine, plus related codons. They argue the modern code keeps vestiges of critical scale invariance from that RNA world in current prokaryote genomes. The code itself, on this view, is a fossil.
plos-pone-0004440:
A small self-building peptide slowed scrapie, a prion disease, in hamsters, report Robert Hnasko and Cathrin Bruederle in PLOS ONE in 2009. Scrapie is caused by a warped protein that forces healthy copies to warp too. The team injected hamsters in the brain with scrapie material mixed with the peptide, called RADA. The peptide assembles itself into tiny scaffolds.

Hamsters given the mix got sick later and lived longer than expected. The benefit grew with the dose of peptide and with time spent mixed with the bad protein before injection. The authors say the peptide disrupts the build-up of the warped protein. For diseases with no cure, even a delay points to a new way of blocking prions.
plos-pone-0004540:
Tuberculosis bacteria from New Delhi are profiled in depth by Ruth Stavrum, Vithal Prasad Myneedu, Virendra Arora, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. India carries the highest estimated burden of tuberculosis in the world, about a fifth of all cases. Yet the genomic diversity of the bacterium in India had not been systematically mapped with multiple markers.

The team's molecular characterization of isolates from New Delhi found a predominance of drug-resistant isolates of the so-called modern type, marked by the loss of a region called TbD1. That pattern has practical weight. Drug resistance changes which medicines can be used, and strain types differ in how they spread. A clear local profile helps clinics and control programs plan.
plos-pone-0004640:
Genetic switches can now be flipped on command in zebrafish, show Stefan Hans, Jan Kaslin, Dorian Freudenreich, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. The method uses an enzyme called Cre to cut and rejoin DNA at set sites. It is a strong tool in mouse genetics, but it was nearly absent in other backboned animals. In this fish, early tries at Cre-based switching worked very poorly.

Using jumping genes to deliver the parts, the team achieved timed, controlled switching in the fish. Scientists can now turn genes on or off in chosen tissues at chosen times. These fish are cheap, clear-bodied, and fast-breeding. Giving them mouse-grade gene control widens the range of disease and development questions they can answer.
plos-pone-0004740:
Kyle Young, Jos Snoeks, and Ole Seehausen asked what drives shape diversity in African cichlid fish radiations, in PLOS ONE in 2009. When one line splits into many forms fast, three forces may be at play. Fixed rules may push like forms, past history may limit options, or chance may rule the outcome.

The team compared repeated radiations in a shared shape space. Like shapes in distinct lakes point to fixed rules, while scatter points to chance or history. Their test helps weigh those forces in a classic case. Cichlids are a key model for how new species arise.
plos-pone-0004840:
Sabine Stegemann and colleagues showed increased risk to pneumococcal superinfection during influenza is not caused by TLR7 mediated lymphopenia, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Influenza A causes respiratory infections with recurring epidemics and high morbidity and mortality. In the past century it induced several pandemics. The most aggressive in 1918 with a death toll estimated at twenty to fifty million cases including many microbe complications.

Secondary microbe pneumonia drives much flu mortality. Ruling out one step narrows the search. Lymphocyte loss via TLR7 is not the explanation. Other immune disruptions must be responsible. These findings offer a firm starting point for the next round of testing. The team also set out clear next steps for work in this field.
plos-pone-0004940:
Transplanted organs often fail years after surgery. Their blood vessels slowly narrow and clog. The process is called chronic allograft vasculopathy. Standard immune-suppressing drugs fail to prevent it. Zhiliang Wang and colleagues tested a different strategy in PLOS ONE in 2009. They targeted dendritic cells inside the recipient's body. The treatment used dying cells taken from the donor.

Dendritic cells take up these donor cells. They then present donor material in a calming way. That restrains indirect allorecognition, the slow immune route driving vessel damage. In tests, the approach eased the vessel disease. It suggests tolerance can be taught, not forced with lifelong drugs.
plos-pone-0005040:
New genes can be born from copied RNA. A copied message pasted back into DNA forms a retrogene. Deng Pan and Liqing Zhang surveyed retrogenes across mammals. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. They examined eight mammalian genomes. Four non-mammalian genomes served as contrast.

They found a burst of young retrogenes. Each retrogene formed independently in its lineage. Retrogenes are a live engine of new gene formation. Some later gain real jobs in the body. The pattern shows mammals keep inventing fresh DNA. The work charts that invention across the mammal family tree. It helps explain how genomes stay creative over evolutionary time.
plos-pone-0005140:
Diagnosing lung TB in children is difficult. It often requires hospitalization and repeated sampling. Nasher Al-Aghbari and colleagues tested a shortcut in Yemen. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. They collected specimens from different body sites in one day. The samples went for smear microscopy, the standard field test.

They compared the one-day yield with samples collected over several visits. Multiple sampling in a single day optimized the microscopy results. Children could be diagnosed without long hospital stays. That matters where beds and money are scarce. It also spares families repeated travel. The finding offers a practical protocol for pediatric TB. Clinics can adopt it without new equipment.
plos-pone-0005240:
Freeze-drying could let cells be stored and shipped at room temperature, but most cells die in the process. Earlier work showed freeze-dried cells kept for years could still guide development in cloning. Natan and colleagues tested cord blood cells in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The team freeze-dried mononuclear cells from umbilical cord blood and then checked colony formation. Colonies growing after rehydration prove that some cells kept real function, not just intact DNA. Progress here could ease the cold storage burden for cell therapies and blood banks. Cells that can be kept dry and shipped in a box would change how blood banks plan for war zones and far-off clinics with no freezer.
plos-pone-0005340:
Asking people about risky sexual behavior face to face can invite false answers. Audio computer-assisted self-interview, or ACASI, lets people answer privately by computer. Van der Elst and colleagues compared the two methods in sex workers in Mombasa, Kenya, in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Female and male sex workers answered through both ACASI and face-to-face interviews. ACASI may elicit more honest reporting of sensitive behaviors. Knowing which method tells the truth matters, since risk assessments guide HIV programs for these communities. Health teams can plan HIV care well only if the facts on risk are true,. A method that wins trust gives them facts they can act on with more faith.
plos-pone-0005440:
Tobias Kind, Martin Scholz, and Oliver Fiehn asked a basic question in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. How large is the set of small chemicals in a living thing? Guessing that set from genes alone misses products made by genes no one has yet described. So the full set has to be measured in the lab, not just predicted.

The authors looked hard at how chemical data are shared and named between labs. Poor sharing makes it hard to know whether two labs found the same chemical. Their critique pushes for clearer data habits so the true size of the chemical set can be pinned down.
plos-pone-0005540:
Fumiaki Sato and co-authors tested the reliability of microRNA chip tests in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Chip tests that read thousands of genes at once had already been put through large quality checks. Chips for microRNAs, the small strands that tune genes, came later and needed the same checks.

The team ran the same samples many times on one chip type and across different types. They measured how well repeats agreed and whether platforms told the same story. Solid agreement gives labs confidence to use these chips in cancer and disease studies.
plos-pone-0005640:
Matthew Dye, Peter Hauser, and Daphne Bavelier studied visual attention in deaf people in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. People deaf from early life pay sharper attention to the edges of vision. Whether that helps in daily life is less clear, since they are also more easily distracted by side events.

The team used a test of the useful field of view, which measures how much a person takes in at a glance. Their results weigh the gains against the costs. The balance matters for schooling and workplace design for deaf people. Deaf people's wider field may be a strength in jobs like sport and surveillance work.
plos-pone-0005740:
Anton Simeonov and co-authors screened for compounds that block a key DNA repair enzyme in 2009. The enzyme, APE1, cuts out damaged spots in DNA so they can be fixed. Cells rely on this repair path to survive daily wear from oxygen and chemicals.

Blocking APE1 could make cancer cells more sensitive to drugs that damage DNA. The team found and profiled several blockers of the enzyme. They describe how each compound acts and how strong it is. Such blockers are leads, not drugs yet, but they give chemists a start. The work also helps probe what APE1 does beyond repair.
plos-pone-0005840:
Gregory Bowman and Vijay Pande asked in 2009 what really limits computer prediction of protein shapes. Knowing a protein's folded shape from its sequence is a grand challenge. Their earlier work suggested the popular Rosetta program's rough energy scores can actually mislead the search.

Here they weigh entropy and kinetics, the odds and speed of folding paths, in prediction success. Shape prediction may fail not from bad scoring but from never visiting the right shape. That shifts effort toward smarter sampling of possible folds. The paper speaks to anyone building the next generation of folding tools.
plos-pone-0005940:
Vaccines guard against many strains of the meningitis bacterium, but not all of them. Tom Mendum, Jane Newcombe, Celia McNeilly and colleagues worked in 2009 toward a broader shield. Their PLOS ONE paper maps the immunoproteome of Neisseria meningitidis, meaning the full set of its proteins that the immune system can see.

A map of that kind is a menu of targets for a vaccine meant to cover more strains. Germs of this species still cause blood poisoning and meningitis around the world despite current shots. By listing the proteins the body reacts to, the team gives vaccine makers a grounded place to start the search for wider protection.
plos-pone-0006040:
Cell lines are the workhorses of cancer research, but a mislabeled line poisons every result built on it. Janyaporn Phuchareon, Yoshihito Ohta, Jonathan Woo and colleagues audited six lines in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper profiles the genetics of six adenoid cystic carcinoma lines, a cancer of the salivary glands, and compares them with what they were claimed to be.

The audit found cross-contamination and misidentification among the six, the title reports. Work done with a wrong line cannot be trusted, however careful it was. The study is both a warning and a service: it names the suspect lines, ACC2, ACC3, ACCM, ACCNS, ACCS and CAC2, so labs can check their own stocks.
plos-pone-0006140:
Kenya's parks are famed for wildlife, yet most animals live outside their fences. David Western, Samantha Russell and Innes Cuthill compared those two worlds over thirty years in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper compiles more than two hundred seventy wildlife counts to compare population trends in protected areas with those in adjacent ecosystems and across the country.

Separating human-caused change from natural swings is the study's care. If wildlife falls as fast inside parks as outside, fences alone are not saving it. The long count record gives conservation a rare honest mirror, and it argues for protecting the lands between parks where most animals actually roam.
plos-pone-0006240:
Learning from a mistake means adjusting within seconds, and single brain cells take part. Thomas Michelet, Bernard Bioulac, and Dominique Guehl recorded individual neurons in the medial prefrontal cortex in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. One idea is that attention systems are retuned right after an error.

Single neurons in this region changed their activity in ways that cope with errors. The recordings connect cell-level firing to quick behavioural adjustment. Such detail is hard to get, since most studies average over many cells. The work sharpens the picture of how the brain catches and corrects its own slips.
plos-pone-0006340:
In psoriatic skin, antimicrobial peptides act as alarms that keep inflammation burning. Mark Peric and colleagues tested vitamin D analogs, standard psoriasis treatments, on those alarms in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The analogs, like calcipotriol, might work partly by changing peptide expression in the skin.

Different analogs controlled the peptide alarms differently, the team reports. Some alarms were dialled up while others were dialled down. That varied pattern suggests the drugs reshape, rather than simply mute, skin defence. It refines how doctors think about a familiar treatment. The work may help doctors pick the best cream for each case of the skin disease.
plos-pone-0006440:
Kaushal Parikh and colleagues compared two signaling enzymes in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Kinases are enzymes that tag other proteins with phosphate groups, and they steer much of cell life. The human genome holds more than five hundred of them. Each kinase tags only certain substrates, but the rules behind that choice are only partly known.

Using peptide arrays, grids of short protein pieces, the team measured which pieces each enzyme tags. They compared c-Raf with a kinase known as MAP kinase kinase kinase 8. Side-by-side profiles show where their tastes match and differ. That helps decode how signaling networks stay specific instead of blurring together.
plos-pone-0006540:
Celia Ravel and co-authors tested folate pathway genes in unexplained infertility for PLOS ONE in 2009. The metabolic pathway of folate is thought to influence DNA stability. It can induce breaks in DNA or produce low levels of a key methyl donor. The team examined genetic polymorphisms in enzymes associated with folate metabolism.

Their title reports a lack of association between those polymorphisms and unexplained infertility. A clear negative result saves couples and clinics from useless genetic tests. It also steers research toward other causes. Negative findings like this are essential ballast for a literature biased toward positive claims.
plos-pone-0006640:
Dong Hu, Xiuli Bi, Wenfeng Fang, and colleagues studied cross-talk between two signaling enzymes in PLOS ONE in 2009. They had recently reported that the MAP kinase JNK1 downregulates beta-catenin signaling and plays a critical role in regulating intestinal homeostasis. Beta-catenin drives growth programs in the gut and in cancers. The team now examined GSK3 beta in relation to JNK2.

Their title reports GSK3 beta is involved in JNK2-mediated beta-catenin inhibition. Two kinases cooperate to restrain a growth signal. Layered restraint suggests the pathway is heavily guarded. Losing those guards is a known route to colorectal cancer.
plos-pone-0006740:
Quentin Vicens and co-authors prepared self-splicing RNA molecules for study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Group I introns are RNA segments that cut themselves out. Studying functional RNAs requires clean ways to make and purify them. Structure work, including crystallization, demands especially pure samples. The team tested a native affinity purification technique.

They applied it to twenty-three group I intron variants. The introns ranged from about two hundred fifty to three hundred forty nucleotides. Some variants still contained their exons. Consistent purification across sizes makes experiments comparable. Reliable samples support both biochemical tests and crystal structure work on these catalytic RNAs.
plos-pone-0006840:
Adi Tabib and colleagues split one protein's two ends into opposite immune instructions in PLOS ONE in 2009. The protein is thrombospondin-1. Their earlier work found it made fresh when immune cells die. Its presence pushed dendritic cells toward eating dead cells quietly. That quiet mode is called a tolerizing phenotype.

The team tested the protein's two ends separately. The N-terminal domain induced a phagocytic state in dendritic cells. The C-terminal domain induced the tolerizing phenotype instead. One protein thus carries two distinct messages. Splitting the messages could let medicine use each effect alone.
plos-pone-0006940:
Gail Kilroy, David Burk, and Z. Elizabeth Floyd tackled a laboratory problem in PLOS ONE in 2009. Fully grown fat cells, called adipocytes, resist standard gene silencing methods. Lipid-based delivery of small interfering RNA usually fails in them. Large screening projects had to rely on electroporation or viruses instead.

The authors report a lipid-based method that works with adipocytes held in suspension. Their protocol reached high transfection efficiency in these stubborn cells. A simpler method matters for obesity and diabetes research. It lets scientists switch off single genes in fat cells and run large loss-of-function screens more cheaply.
plos-pone-0007040:
Jin Yu, Ngan Huang, Kitchener Wilson, and colleagues tested nicotine's effect on stem cell therapy in PLOS ONE in 2009. Many heart patients carry risk factors such as smoking. The team grew endothelial cells from human embryonic stem cells. Such cells might one day repair ischemic hearts. Nicotine was the exposure they studied.

They traced nicotine's action through nicotinic acetylcholine receptors on these cells. The receptors influenced cell growth, cell death, and new vessel formation. If smoking blunts cell therapy, patients may need to quit before treatment. The study helps set realistic expectations for stem cell heart repair.
plos-pone-0007140:
Anasuya Sarkar, Srabani Mitra, Sonya Mehta, and colleagues traced a cell death message in PLOS ONE in 2009. Apoptosis usually starts inside the doomed cell itself. Two classic routes trigger its caspase enzymes. Yet monocytes activated by endotoxin could make vessel cells die from outside. How they sent that order was the puzzle.

The team found monocytes release tiny vesicles loaded with caspase-1. Those microvesicles deliver the death message to target cells. A packaged enzyme acting as a letter is a new twist in cell death biology. It may operate in sepsis, where monocytes and vessel damage collide.
plos-pone-0007240:
Athuluri Divakar Sai Krishna, Raj Kumar Mandraju, Golla Kishore, and colleagues designed targeted drug carriers for cancer in 2009. Cancer cells are metabolically active and overexpress certain receptors. They use those receptors to take in factors needed for growth and transformation at high rates.

Those same receptors can serve as targets for specific drug delivery. The authors load nanoparticles with apotransferrin, a protein that homes to one such receptor system. They test the carriers as an efficient targeted delivery route. Their approach aims to concentrate drugs in tumors while sparing healthy tissue.
plos-pone-0007340:
Claudia B. M. Bijen, Karin M. Vermeulen, Marian J. E. Mourits, and colleagues reviewed surgery costs and effects for hysterectomy in 2009. They compare abdominal hysterectomy with laparoscopic hysterectomy, the keyhole approach. Their systematic review draws on controlled trials from major medical databases and trial registers, following strict review methods.

The review includes a set of randomized controlled studies in the dozens range. The authors weigh costs against clinical effects for each approach. Their PLOS ONE synthesis helps hospitals and patients judge whether the laparoscopic route's benefits justify its costs. It also exposes gaps where trial evidence was thin.
plos-pone-0007440:
Andreas Keller and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their subject was blood markers for multiple sclerosis, a chronic disease that harms the coating around nerve fibers. MS varies greatly between patients, which makes diagnosis and tracking hard. The team turned to microRNAs, tiny molecules that regulate gene activity and circulate in blood.

Their patterns separated patients from healthy people for relapsing-remitting MS, the most common form. Patient profiles differed from healthy controls accurately enough to classify them. A blood test built on such a signature could support earlier and simpler diagnosis. It might also help follow how the disease changes over time. The study makes a case for microRNA profiling as a practical clinical tool.
plos-pone-0007540:
Christophe Noll and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on a gene linked to Down syndrome and its effect on metabolism. High homocysteine in the blood raises the risk of clogged arteries. People with Down syndrome, oddly, seem protected from atherosclerosis. The gene DYRK1A sits in the Down syndrome region and is overproduced there. The team tested its role in mouse models carrying extra copies of it.

DYRK1A emerged as a determinant of the methionine-homocysteine cycle. That cycle controls the very metabolite tied to artery risk. A gene that tunes the cycle could explain the Down syndrome protection. The finding links a chromosome-21 kinase to a classic cardiovascular pathway. It also suggests the cycle could be adjusted by targeting the enzyme. The study connects two distant literatures: Down syndrome biology and heart disease.
plos-pone-0007640:
Cinzia Pagliuca and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on the machinery that pulls chromosomes apart. Kinetochores are the handles where spindle fibers grip chromosomes during division. Budding yeast has the simplest known kinetochores, yet they still contain dozens of subunits. The team studied a conserved complex of two proteins, Spc105p and Kre28p. They tested its roles in gripping microtubules and in running the spindle assembly checkpoint.

The complex proved important for both jobs. It helps bind the kinetochore to microtubules, and it supports the checkpoint that halts division until every chromosome is attached. One complex doing both gripping and guarding is an efficient design. Failure of either job scrambles the genome of daughter cells. The study details a critical joint in the division machinery. Yeast, once again, explains a machine all cells share.
plos-pone-0007740:
Jean-Paul Pirnay and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It takes a fresh look at how the strains of Pseudomonas aeruginosa are grouped in nature. The germ causes many infections in hospitals. Its strains from sick patients look much like strains found in soil and water.

That sameness led experts to call the pattern epidemic. Strains did not seem to stick to one home or one kind of illness. The authors checked the facts behind that view. Some key points were still unsettled. Their check matters for hospitals, since it shapes how staff trace where a new infection came from.
plos-pone-0007840:
Yuta Abe and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It explains how a donor blood transfusion can protect rat liver transplants. Giving donor blood before a transplant can yield long-term graft survival. Remarkably, this can happen without immunosuppressive drugs.

The mechanism behind that tolerance was not well defined. The authors show the transfusion induces regulatory T cells that express Foxp3. Those cells calm attacks on the graft. Their induction is required for tolerance to the liver allografts. Harnessing such cells could one day free transplant patients from lifelong immune suppression.
plos-pone-0007940:
Kevin Hall and colleagues measured how much food the United States throws away, in PLOS ONE in 2009. They worked from the gap between the food the nation supplies and the food people truly eat. Thrown food wastes water and fuel, and as it rots it gives off gases that warm the climate.

Their count showed waste had grown over the years, not shrunk. The lost food held a large store of energy that farms and trucks had spent real resources to make. Putting a firm number on that loss gives policy makers and shoppers a clear reason to cut waste at every step.
plos-pone-0008040:
Ming Wu and colleagues modeled liver cell signals as steps in a logic circuit for PLOS ONE in 2009. Two signal chains, one answering insulin and one raising alarms, cross inside liver cells. Systems biology wants to know how such networks move over time, not just how they are wired.
