Their discrete model treats each part as on or off and steps the whole net forward in ticks. That spare style skips heavy math yet still shows which states the net settles into. The approach suits labs that need quick, clear forecasts of cell behavior.
plos-pone-0008140:
Dong Xu and Yang Zhang sped up the drawing of protein surfaces in PLOS ONE in 2009. A protein's outer surface is where drugs and partners meet it, so drug design starts with an accurate surface map. Drawing that map as a mesh of small triangles is slow for large proteins.

Their method borrows a math trick, the Euclidean distance transform, to place the mesh far faster without losing detail. Speed here is not a luxury: screening millions of drug candidates means drawing millions of surfaces. A faster mesh means wider, cheaper screens.
plos-pone-0008240:
Armand Paauw and colleagues studied a bacterial iron scavenger in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Some gut bacteria carry a DNA island that makes yersiniabactin. This molecule grabs iron, which bacteria need to grow. Bacteria with the island tend to be more virulent. Better iron scavenging alone might explain that edge. The team tested another effect on immune cells.

Yersiniabactin reduced the oxidative stress response of innate immune cells. That response is a burst of reactive chemicals used to kill bacteria. Blunting it would help bacteria survive attack. The study reveals a second way this molecule aids infection.
plos-pone-0008340:
Christopher A. Hamm and colleagues treated rat tumor cells with a drug in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Abnormal DNA methylation patterns appear in several human cancers. Local methylation can silence genes, while genome-wide loss has murkier effects. The team examined what global demethylation does to tumor growth. They used rat chondrosarcoma cells, a cartilage tumor model.

Treatment with a demethylating drug removed methylation across the genome. Afterward, the cells showed increased tumorigenicity. Losing methylation thus made these cancer cells more dangerous, not less. The result warns that methylation therapies can cut both ways.
plos-pone-0008440:
Birajalaxmi Das and co-authors look at telomeres and radiation in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Telomeres are caps at the ends of chromosomes. Their length is used as a sign of aging and stress. Short telomeres have been tied to cancer and long-term disease. Lab work showed radiation can shorten them. But data from people living with high natural radiation were lacking.

The team measure telomere length in adults from such an area. They compare lengths with radiation exposure in daily life. The study tests if low, steady radiation leaves a mark on cells. It adds human data where only lab data existed before.
plos-pone-0008540:
Gustavo Palacios and co-authors link a second infection to severe flu in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Early reports on the new H1N1 flu strain put the death rate as low. It seemed much like seasonal flu. But Argentina reported a far higher death rate in July 2009. Many cases there ended in death. The team search for what made those cases so severe. They test patients for a common lung germ, Streptococcus pneumoniae.

They find cases with both flu and that germ are more severe. Patients with the pair fare worse than those with flu alone. Germ partners also drove deaths in past flu pandemics. The work argues for testing and treating bacterial infection in severe flu.
plos-pone-0008640:
Yi-Feng Chen and co-authors study hormone receptors in a plant in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Ethylene is a gaseous plant hormone that ripens fruit and ages leaves. Arabidopsis thaliana perceives it with a five-member receptor family. Members are ETR1, ERS1, ETR2, ERS2, and EIN4. Gel-filtration analysis of receptors solubilized from membranes shows their sizes. The team ask if receptors exist as components of larger protein complexes.

They find ethylene receptors function within high-molecular-mass complexes. Receptors cluster with partner proteins rather than acting alone. That organization may amplify or tune the ethylene signal. It changes models of how plants sense this simple gas.
plos-pone-0008740:
Jennifer Giel, Joseph Sorg, Abraham Sonenshein, and colleagues traced what wakes a dangerous gut germ. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Clostridium difficile survives antibiotics as a tough spore. To cause diarrhea, the spore must sprout into active cells. Bile salts in the gut were suspected as the wake-up cue. Few details of that cue were known.

Mice handle bile salts in their own way, and germination followed that chemistry. Changing how mice process bile changed spore sprouting. The link suggests blocking the wake-up signal could prevent disease. Prevention would spare patients the antibiotics that treat active infections.
plos-pone-0008840:
Tae-Young Ha, Keun-A Chang, Jeong a Kim, and colleagues calmed an inflammation gene and eased Alzheimer-like disease in mice. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Alzheimer brains show inflammation, sticky deposits, and neuron loss together. Gene scans in a mouse model hunted for drivers of that damage. One gene, S100a9, stood out as a regulator candidate. The Tg2576 mouse line models human Alzheimer changes.

Knocking down S100a9 reduced memory problems in the mice. Brain pathology also eased alongside the behavior gain. An inflammation gene thus looks like a real disease lever. Silencing it, or its pathway, becomes a therapy idea.
plos-pone-0008940:
Stephen Bishop and John Woolliams wrote a methods paper for PLOS ONE in 2010 on reading genetics from farm disease records. Breeders want animals that resist disease, and field records hold huge numbers of cases. But farm data are messy: exposure to germs varies, and not every sick animal is recorded alike. Drawing genetic lessons from such records takes care.

The authors set out the ideas needed to interpret these data soundly. They explain how infection spreads through a herd can distort simple comparisons between animals. Proper models separate an animal's own resistance from the pressure of germs around it. The guidance helps breeding programmes select stock that truly resists disease.
plos-pone-0009040:
Kelli Ryckman and co-authors hunted gene variants behind early births in Norway, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Spontaneous preterm birth is a leading cause of newborn illness and death. Both the mother's genes and the baby's genes may share the blame. The team focused on two candidate genes, PTGER3 and PON1.

They tested variants in mothers and in their babies in a Norwegian population. Some variants lined up with preterm birth often enough to notice. The study also gauged how strong those links were, checking an earlier report. Gene findings like these could one day flag pregnancies needing extra care.
plos-pone-0009140:
Jennifer Davis and Joseph Metzger combined two heart-muscle mutations in single rodent cells, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Inherited cardiomyopathies weaken or thicken the heart muscle. Patients increasingly turn out to carry two faulty copies at once. Symptoms range from none to life-threatening, defying simple prediction.

The team put double mutant alleles into rodent heart cells. Their combined effect on the muscle filaments could be measured directly. Pairs of faults disrupted contraction in ways single faults did not predict. A cellular model like this helps forecast severity for real patients.
plos-pone-0009240:
Raj Kumar Pan, Nivedita Chatterjee, and Sitabhra Sinha published this worm brain study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The roundworm Caenorhabditis elegans has a tiny, fully mapped nervous system. Even so, how single neurons add up to behavior remains a deep puzzle. The authors looked between the cell level and the whole animal.

They studied the middle, or mesoscopic, scale: groups of neurons and how they cluster. That level of organization reveals limits on what the network can do. Community structure in the wiring constrains the signals the worm can produce. The analysis shows how much of an animal's behavior is written into its wiring plan.
plos-pone-0009340:
Thomas Montine and co-authors published this heart risk study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Pain drugs called NSAIDs had come under suspicion for causing heart attacks and strokes. The data came partly from ADAPT, a trial testing anti-inflammatory drugs to prevent Alzheimer's disease. The authors looked for a warning signal in urine chemistry.

They measured breakdown products of thromboxane and prostacyclin, two signals that balance blood clotting. A high ratio between them was linked to later bad cardiovascular events. Such a urine marker could flag risky patients before harm occurs. It also hints at how these pain drugs upset the clotting balance.
plos-pone-0009440:
An Vo, Engeline van Duijkeren, and Wim Gaastra surveyed Salmonella germs from Vietnam in PLOS ONE in 2010. Some of these germs no longer respond to common drugs. The team gathered close to three hundred samples from people and from animals. They tested which drugs still worked on each sample.

They also looked for mobile bits of DNA that can carry drug resistance from one germ to the next. Such bits include class 1 integrons and a region called genomic island 1. The survey maps where resistance sits and how it might spread. That map can guide efforts to slow the loss of useful drugs.
plos-pone-0009540:
Mark Sommerfeld and colleagues examined a long acting insulin in the lab in PLOS ONE in 2010. Insulin glargine, sold as Lantus, gives people with diabetes steady sugar control for a full day. After injection under the skin, part of it is changed into two breakdown products. The team studied how the drug and those products signal inside cells.

They separated signals that handle sugar from signals that push cell growth. The products behaved much like the parent drug in these tests. That detail matters, because growth signals have raised safety questions for insulins. Knowing exactly what circulates and acts helps doctors judge the drug's long term use.
plos-pone-0009640:
Marina Panova and co-authors documented extreme mating in a small marine animal in PLOS ONE in 2010. The animal is a non social invertebrate, a group where mates meet only briefly. Females of this species mate with a very large number of males. That level of female promiscuity is rare in such animals. The team used genetic tests to count how many fathers contributed to each female's offspring.

Genetic counts confirmed mating rates far beyond the norm for like species. The authors explore what could drive such excess, from sperm competition to genetic variety in offspring. The case challenges tidy claims about mating systems. It shows that even simple animals can evolve mating lives of surprising intensity.
plos-pone-0009740:
Gro V. Amdam and co-authors published an animal study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The study asks whether honeybees that learn well also stand up better to strain on the body. Learning was tested by Pavlovian conditioning, in which bees link a smell with a reward.

Bees that learned faster also lived longer in air rich in oxygen, a test of stress strength, the team reports. The link held when social setting, age, and drive to learn were held steady. The authors say the bee may help show how brain work and body upkeep are tied together.
plos-pone-0009840:
People spot symmetry in a pattern almost instantly, even in clutter. Chien-Chung Chen and Christopher Tyler modeled what helps or hurts that skill. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Symmetry is a basic cue the visual system uses everywhere.

The model weighed three influences: masking noise, axial cueing, and salience. Masking noise hides the pattern, cueing points to its axis, and salience makes it stand out. Balancing the three predicts when symmetry will be seen. The work helps explain a core talent of human vision. The model turns those effects into testable predictions.
plos-pone-0009940:
A claimed network of tiny vessels, distinct from blood and lymph, has sparked debate for decades. Jung Sun Yoo and colleagues characterized that system in the abdomen of lung cancer mice. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

The primo-vascular system is said to thread through organs and body cavities. The team described its features in the abdominal cavity of the cancer model. They also laid out its differences from the lymphatic system, the drainage network it is often confused with. Careful description is the first step in judging the claim.
plos-pone-0010040:
Marc Burian, Christiane Wolz, and Christiane Goerke studied a common nose germ in 2010. Staphylococcus aureus lives in the human nose, often with no symptoms at all. Carrying it there is still a known risk, because the germ can later infect its own host. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE.

The team measured bacterial gene activity in nose swabs from persistent carriers. They asked how the germ adjusts its controls while living quietly in people. Those adjustments may explain why the same germ can sit harmlessly for months and then cause serious illness.
plos-pone-0010140:
The authors were Xulin Xu, Min Jiang, Yuhong Wang, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study fed rabbits fish oil and watched their hearts. Trials had suggested fish oil can protect some patients from abnormal heart rhythms. The mechanism behind that benefit was not entirely clear, despite wide use of fish oil supplements.

After four weeks of supplementation, rabbit hearts showed changed channel protein levels. The authors call the pattern cardiac electrical remodeling, a rewiring of the heart's signals. Those channel changes offer a concrete explanation for how fish oil might steady heart rhythm.
plos-pone-0010240:
The authors were Virginia Espina, Brian Mariani, Rosa Gallagher, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study examined early breast cancer that stays inside the ducts. Most invasive breast cancer is thought to start from this stage, called DCIS. DCIS cells survive in ducts that are low in oxygen and nutrients, a harsh setting that should kill many cells.

The team found that malignant precursor cells already exist within DCIS lesions. Those cells require autophagy, a self-eating survival process, to stay alive there. Blocking autophagy might starve early lesions before they turn invasive.
plos-pone-0010340:
Sheri Weiser, David Tuller, Edward Frongillo and others studied hunger and HIV care in Uganda for PLOS ONE in 2010. Taking AIDS drugs on schedule is vital, yet many patients miss doses. Lack of food was emerging as one reason, in Africa and beyond. Little was known about exactly how hunger leads to missed doses. The team set out to trace those steps through patients' own accounts.

They held deep, open-ended talks with people on treatment. Patients described skipping doses when food was short, fearing side effects on an empty stomach, or choosing food for family over clinic trips. Such detail turns a broad link into concrete barriers. Programs that pair food support with medicine could act on each one. The study gives those programs a human map.
plos-pone-0010440:
Corey Bradshaw, Xingli Giam and Navjot Sodhi ranked countries by their harm to nature in PLOS ONE in 2010. Protecting ecosystems keeps services people depend on, from clean water to pollination. Ranking countries can expose the worst performers and highlight good models. Earlier rankings were often rough or based on few measures. The team built fresh metrics combining several kinds of impact.

Their rankings weigh harm both at home and in total scale. Big countries can rank badly by sheer size even with moderate habits. Fair metrics must state which view they take. The study gives policy makers a sharper comparison tool. It also gives the public a way to ask leaders hard questions.
plos-pone-0010540:
Akhilesh Mishra and colleagues reported that the 2009 pandemic flu caused severe disease in India in PLOS ONE in 2010. The new H1N1 strain posed a worldwide challenge that year. Early on, nations lacked solid data on how severe it really was. Without severity data, responses risk being too weak or too drastic. The team analyzed laboratory-confirmed cases from India to gauge severity there.

Their results showed the pandemic strain could indeed cause severe illness in that setting. Local severity data help hospitals plan beds, oxygen, and staffing. They also help officials communicate risk honestly to the public. India-specific evidence matters in a country of India's size and diversity. This study supplied an early, grounded severity picture.
plos-pone-0010640:
Tony Buchanan, David Bibas, and Ralph Adolphs ran a large outdoor experiment on emotion reading, in PLOS ONE in 2010. People judge feelings from faces every day. The question was whether our own felt emotions shape how well we read happiness and fear in others.

Hundreds of participants took part outside the lab. Their own emotional states were measured alongside their judgments of faces. Feeling and judging were linked, but not in a simple copycat way. The results suggest personal experience trains emotion reading over time. That matters for understanding conditions where reading feelings goes wrong.
plos-pone-0010740:
Samyra Lacerda and colleagues sped up germ cell transplantation in Nile tilapia, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Moving sperm-making stem cells from one fish to another lets a host father offspring with the donor's genes. The technique is the main way to study these stem cells in fish, but surgery made it slow.

Their method delivers the cells without surgery, through the fish's natural opening. Recipient males later produced donor-derived offspring. A fast, gentle method opens the door to banking genes of valuable or endangered fish in common hosts. Fish farms and conservation programs both need that kind of living storage.
plos-pone-0010840:
Lennert Slobbe, Jeanette Doorduijn, Pieternella Lugtenburg and colleagues ran this clinical trial, published in PLOS ONE in 2010. Patients with blood disorders often need a tunnelled central line for treatment, and bacteria growing inside the line can cause serious bloodstream infection. The trial tested a daily ethanol lock, where alcohol sits briefly inside the catheter to kill germs.

Hundreds of adult patients were assigned at random to an ethanol lock or a placebo lock, each used for fifteen minutes a day. Infection rates inside the catheter were lower with ethanol, but the gap was not large enough to rule out chance. Slobbe and colleagues report a cautious result: the approach looked safe and promising, yet this trial alone could not prove it prevents infection.
plos-pone-0010940:
Brett Hilton and Roland Wolkowicz published this HIV methods study in PLOS ONE in 2010. HIV keeps escaping drugs, so new antivirals and faster ways to find them are both needed. The virus's protease enzyme, which snips viral proteins into working parts, is a proven drug target, and the authors built a living test that reports its activity.

They engineered T cells, the very cells HIV infects, carrying a switch: the viral protease is fused inside a protein that turns on a glowing reporter gene. Only when an effective protease inhibitor blocks the enzyme does the glow appear. Hilton and Wolkowicz thus turn drug action into a light signal readable by standard cell-sorting machines. Screening inside real target cells should weed out compounds that fail where it matters.
plos-pone-0011040:
Pascal Meier, Emmanouil Brilakis, Roberto Corti and co-authors published this heart stent meta-analysis in PLOS ONE in 2010. Bypass grafts made from leg veins develop aggressive narrowing, and whether drug-eluting stents beat plain bare-metal stents for reopening them was unproven. The authors pooled the controlled studies comparing the two stent types in vein graft lesions.

Their search gathered twenty-nine studies covering more than seven thousand patients, though only a few were randomized trials and those were small. The primary question was whether the treated vessel needed reopening again, with heart attack, stent clotting, and death as secondary measures. The need for repeat procedures tended to favor drug-eluting stents, but the evidence base was thin. Meier and colleagues show where the balance of evidence leans while exposing how few strong trials support a common procedure.
plos-pone-0011140:
Secchiero, Zorzet, Tripodo and colleagues tested stem cells against lymphoma in PLOS ONE in 2010. They used human bone marrow stem cells in mice carrying spread out human lymphoma. These mice lacked a working immune system, so human cells and tumors could survive in them.

The stem cells showed anti cancer activity against the spread lymphoma in the mice. That surprising effect hints at a new kind of cell based therapy. Much more testing is needed to learn how the effect works and whether it is safe. Still, the result turns a repair cell into a possible cancer fighter worth studying.
plos-pone-0011240:
Peddinti, Memili and Burgess modeled cow egg development in PLOS ONE in 2010. A cow egg matures inside a cluster of helper cells that feed and signal to it. Using protein wide measurements and systems modeling, the team mapped how egg and helper cells interact at an early stage.

The model reveals the joint program that prepares an egg for fertilization. Better grasp of that program could raise success in cattle embryo production. Breeding gains flow to dairy and beef herds alike. The approach also shows how protein data can be turned into a working model of two cell types talking.
plos-pone-0011340:
Martin Hosking and co-authors used a mouse model in 2010 to study how a virus strips insulation from nerve fibers. Mice infected in the brain with a weakened mouse hepatitis virus first get brain inflammation, then lose myelin, the fatty coat that helps nerves carry signals fast. The team tested one chemical signal and its receptor on immune cells.

Signaling through that receptor protected the cells that make myelin and limited how much insulation was lost. Mice with the signal intact kept more healthy myelin-making cells during the illness. The finding matters because multiple sclerosis involves similar myelin loss in people. A pathway that shields myelin-making cells during viral attack offers a lead for treatments meant to preserve nerve function rather than only calm inflammation.
plos-pone-0011440:
James Bjork and co-authors used brain scans in 2010 to compare how teenagers and adults respond to rewards. Teenagers chase rewards harder and take more risks than adults, a pattern every parent recognizes. The team asked adults and adolescents to perform reward tasks inside an fMRI scanner, which tracks activity across brain regions in real time.

The scans showed age differences in how strongly motivational circuits were recruited when rewards were on offer. Teen brains and adult brains did not simply differ in strength; they engaged the network in different patterns. Mapping that neural gap gives parents, teachers, and policymakers a brain-based account of impulsive years. It also cautions that reward-based programs for teens, from grades to marketing, land on circuitry that is wired to answer loudly.
plos-pone-0011540:
Andrea Eberle and co-authors described in 2010 how yeast cells quarantine faulty gene messages and quiet the genes that made them. Cells splice their RNA messages to remove spacer sections, and mutations at splice sites leave messages unspliced and useless. The team found that such defective RNAs are held back in the nucleus by a surveillance protein called Rrp6.

Beyond holding the bad messages, the cell also turned down transcription of the splicing-defective genes themselves, as if closing a faulty production line rather than just binning its output. That two-layer quality control, retain the message and quiet the gene, keeps errors from wasting the cell's resources or making harmful protein. The circuit is a tidy model of how cells proofread at scale. Its counterparts in human cells matter for diseases where splicing goes wrong, including many cancers.
plos-pone-0011640:
Jesse Deere and co-authors measured how fast virus levels fall once treatment starts, in PLOS ONE in 2010. People with HIV must stay on combination therapy for life because the drugs suppress the virus without clearing it fully. How the virus persists during therapy remains a central question in AIDS research.

Working in rhesus macaques, the closest animal model of AIDS, the team charted viral decay after starting strong therapy. The speed of that decay reveals how long infected cells survive. Those numbers guide strategies that aim beyond suppression toward shrinking the hidden reservoirs that keep infection alive.
plos-pone-0011740:
Christopher Dibble and co-authors mapped the working part of a disease-linked protein, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cerebral cavernous malformations are abnormal clusters of brain blood vessels that leak and can cause haemorrhagic stroke. One of the three genes involved produces a protein called PDCD10, which binds a specific membrane lipid.

The team defined PDCD10's functional domain by studying its interaction with that lipid, PIP3. Pinpointing which part of the protein does the binding gives a foothold for understanding its role in vessel stability. It also suggests where disease mutations may break its function.
plos-pone-0011840:
Sébastien Rodrigue and colleagues presented in 2010 a pipeline meant to open up metagenomics, the study of DNA taken from whole microbe communities at once. Sequencers at the time forced a trade-off: cheap machines gave huge numbers of very short reads, while longer reads cost far more. Short pieces are hard to assemble when thousands of species are mixed together.

Their combined lab and computer method was designed to make those short reads usable for community samples from places like soil, water, and the gut. If short reads can be trusted, far more labs can afford to survey mixed microbes instead of single grown cultures. That widens the study of the vast share of microbes that never grow alone in a dish.
plos-pone-0011940:
Antoine de Morrée and colleagues described in 2010 a fast-acting protein switch at the center of muscle remodeling. The switch is calpain 3, a protein-cutting enzyme that is unusual among its family: when its gene is faulty, people develop limb girdle muscular dystrophy. The enzyme is unstable, which had kept its targets and mechanism obscure.

The team's work shows calpain 3 acting as a rapid, one-way proteolytic switch, cutting targets in a burst that cannot easily be undone. A switch design explains how muscle can remodel quickly during growth and repair. It also clarifies what is lost when the switch is broken by disease mutations.
plos-pone-0012040:
Marion Cornelissen and co-workers reported in 2010 a careful search that found none of a much-debated virus in the semen of men with HIV. The virus, short-named XMRV, had just been found as a kin of mouse leukemia viruses, and no one knew how common it was or how it spread. Its traces in the prostate gland had raised the thought that it might pass from man to woman in sex.

Men with HIV who lived in the Netherlands gave samples, and the team's tests found no sign of the virus in the fluid part of their semen. If the virus passed in sex, that is just where it should show up, so the blank result weakens the claim. With other blank searches, it helped deflate a scare that had drawn wide fear.
plos-pone-0012140:
Kathryn Swoboda, Charles Scott, Thomas Crawford, and colleagues reported a clinical trial in spinal muscular atrophy for PLOS ONE in 2010. This inherited disease weakens muscles by killing the nerve cells that drive them. Valproic acid, a drug long used for seizures, had shown promise for this disease in lab and animal work, and the trial added a supplement, L-carnitine, beside it.

Children and young patients joined in two groups: those who could sit but not walk, and those who could still walk. Half received the real treatment and half a dummy one, with neither side knowing which. Trials reported this carefully, part by part, give families and doctors trustworthy ground for judging a hoped-for therapy.
plos-pone-0012240:
Umberto Castiello, Bruno Giordano, Chiara Begliomini, and co-authors studied how touch sounds steer the reaching hand, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Research on hearing and vision usually asks how sound changes what people perceive, not how it changes what their hands do. The team recorded the small sounds fingers make on contact as volunteers reached to grasp objects, and fed those sounds back in altered form.

Hearing the contact sound changed how the grasp itself unfolded, even though the task was guided by sight. The hand, it turns out, listens as it reaches. That insight matters for prosthetic hands and surgical tools, where restoring sound feedback might restore some of touch's guidance too.
plos-pone-0012340:
Igor Itskovich and Brad Roudebush proposed resampling methods for mortality studies in PLOS ONE in 2010. Such studies compare deaths in one group with deaths in the wider public. A factory's workers are a common example. The gap is summed up in a single ratio. A range around that ratio decides if an excess looks real. The usual range rests on fixed rules of thumb. One rule is an arbitrary choice of confidence level. These rules can mislead when deaths are few.

Resampling builds the range from the data itself. It does not lean on those fixed rules. Health verdicts at work sites can hinge on such ranges. They can be worth large sums in pay-outs and rules. A more honest range protects both sides at once. Workers gain when real risks are not dismissed. Employers gain when false risks are not believed.
plos-pone-0012440:
Michael Bonsall modeled how fast parasite breeding inside a host shapes the evolution of virulence, in a 2010 PLOS ONE theory paper. A parasite's harm to its host is set by forces at two scales: growth within one body and spread across a population. Studies often treat the two scales apart, missing how they feed back on each other.

Bonsall's model links within-host replication to population spread, including varied hosts and parasites. Faster replication can push toward nastier disease, but population structure can brake that push. The framework helps explain why some parasites stay mild and others turn deadly, and it informs control programs that change transmission.
plos-pone-0012540:
Corinne Jud, Antoinette Hayoz and Urs Albrecht tested body clock resetting in mutant mice, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Circadian clocks let organisms adjust to the daily light cycle, and two clock genes, Rev-Erb alpha and Per1, help set the rhythm's length and stability. Mice missing both genes offer a test of how the clock handles sudden light shifts, like jet lag.

The double mutants showed unusually strong phase resetting — their rhythms jumped by large amounts after light pulses. A clock that resets too easily is as flawed as a stubborn one. The work clarifies how the two genes steady the clock, with relevance to shift work and sleep disorders.
plos-pone-0012640:
Van Soolingen, Hernandez-Pando, Orozco and co-authors revived an old drug idea against drug-resistant tuberculosis. Some TB bacteria now resist the main drugs, and few replacements are close to ready. Their 2010 study tested thioridazine, a mental-health drug long known to kill TB bacteria in the lab.

In mice infected with resistant TB, the drug showed real promise as a treatment. Reusing an approved drug can reach patients far faster than building a new one. The work gives clinics in poor regions a possible extra weapon against a growing threat.
plos-pone-0012740:
Jamali, Salzmann, Perroud and co-authors tested a variant in an immune gene for links to epilepsy and childhood fever fits. Temporal lobe epilepsy is the most common form of partial epilepsy, and early febrile seizures often come before it. Their 2010 study read a working variant in the promoter of the complement C3 gene.

Complement is part of the immune system's first response, so a link would tie brain seizures to immune variation. Genetic clues of this kind may one day sort which children with fever fits need watching. The study adds patients sorted by seizure history.
plos-pone-0012840:
Yang, Ke, Tan and co-authors examined what happens to the plague bacterium when a key regulator is removed. In gut-infecting Yersinia relatives, the RovA regulator controls invasin, a protein for entering host tissue. In Yersinia pestis, the plague agent, invasin is already inactive.

Their 2010 study found that without RovA the cell membrane is damaged, while the type III secretion system, a needle for injecting host cells, is turned up. One regulator thus balances surface safety against attack machinery. That balance may shape how plague bacteria survive in fleas and mammals.
plos-pone-0330140:
Ádám Fésüs and colleagues tested two styles of hip training in young women whose knees cave inward when they land, a pattern tied to knee injuries. Twenty active college students trained their hip abductor muscles three times a week for four weeks, one group working the muscles mainly as they lengthen under load, the other as they shorten. Motion cameras measured knee position during jumps and landings.

Both groups grew stronger and jumped better. The lengthening-style group, though, reduced the inward knee collapse more during single-leg jumps, though not during drop landings. Strength gains alone did not explain the improvement. The pilot study suggests how the hip is trained matters, not just how strong it gets.
plos-pone-0341940:
Laurence Taggart leads a team of eight testing a mentoring scheme serving older people who have intellectual disabilities, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The question is whether the scheme is ready for a full trial. The MATILDA intervention matches each participant with a community group and mentors, aiming at participation, confidence, and less loneliness. The UK feasibility study randomized fifty-seven people, close to nine tenths of its recruitment target, and followed them for a year after the six month program.

Every intervention participant who started was matched to a group. Most were still attending at six months, and about two thirds remained at a year. Anxiety scores eased slightly in the intervention group. Judged against the study's progression criteria and a reach and adoption review, the procedures worked well enough to justify a definitive trial. The report is a model of testing the plumbing before promising the water.
plos-pone-0342140:
Shristi Sharma and co-authors reviewed forty-four population studies to chart how the mental health of middle-aged and older adults moved through the COVID-19 pandemic. Their 2026 scoping review divides the timeline into the crisis phase through 2021 and the transition years after, recording which symptoms rose, which eased, and which personal factors mattered.

During the crisis phase, depression, anxiety, stress, and loneliness climbed broadly. By 2022 and 2023 some studies showed symptoms settling or improving. Women, the oldest adults, the unemployed, and people in poor physical health or isolation fared worst. The authors note almost no research tied mental health to population-level factors like local case rates, leaving a gap for planning the next emergency.
plos-pone-0343140:
Mordicai Atinga and colleagues surveyed four hundred rugby players from ten clubs across Kenya for this 2026 PLOS ONE study of injury and mental health. Rugby brings frequent muscle and joint injuries, yet little research has asked what those injuries do to players' minds in African settings, where mental health support is limited.

More than half the players reported a significant injury in the previous two years, most often to the knee, ankle, or shoulder. Injured players scored worse on a general mental health questionnaire and reported lower physical functioning than uninjured teammates. The authors argue that treating a rugby injury in Kenya should include attention to mood, identity, and substance use, not only the damaged joint.
plos-pone-0344140:
Kazuto Suda and seven colleagues grow miniature gut tissue from children with Hirschsprung's disease to test a natural fat molecule, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. In this birth condition a section of bowel lacks nerve cells and is removed by surgery, yet dangerous gut inflammation can still strike the remaining bowel. The team grew organoids from the healthy-segment tissue of patients and from comparison tissue, then exposed them to the molecule, called 12-HHT.

The patient organoids started with weaker barrier genes than the comparison tissue. The molecule strengthened those barrier proteins and blunted inflammatory signals triggered by an immune provocation, and less tracer dye leaked through the tissue wall. The findings point to a possible protective treatment worth pursuing.
plos-pone-0345040:
Shahrzad Jahangiri and Samira Sarikhani created a clear plastic composite that resists heat better, aimed at optical coatings and sensor windows. The base is a specialty acrylic blend, and the reinforcement is zirconium phosphate platelets treated with sulfur-bearing groups so they bond well and spread evenly at very low loadings. A battery of imaging and thermal tests characterized the material.

Even at one percent filler or less, the composite kept high visible transparency while its softening point rose and the temperature where breakdown begins climbed by roughly thirty degrees. Heat resistance and optical clarity usually trade against each other, because fillers cloud the plastic. Beating that trade-off without silicon-based ingredients opens options for protective layers and electronic packaging.
plos-pone-0345340: Robinson and two co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on light, eyes, and color vision. LED light can dull how well people see color differences. The title reports that exposure to infrared light improved color vision that LED light had weakened. The result is surprising enough to draw wide notice, since infrared is invisible to the eye yet seems to restore what visible light disturbed.
plos-pone-0345540:
Weihong Zhao and Chunlu Hu tackled a core language problem: judging when two sentences mean the same thing, even when worded very differently. Word-counting methods fail when a short sentence is rephrased with new words. Their model uses twin neural networks that read both sentences, follow the order and context of words, and learn deep patterns of meaning.

Trained on sentence pairs, the model beat word-frequency methods and standard machine learning regressors, with lower errors and steadier results. The twin-network design also allows some explanation of why two sentences scored as similar. Search engines, automatic essay grading, summarizers, and question-answering tools all lean on this kind of similarity judgment, so a more accurate and explainable model has wide use.
plos-pone-0346340:
Anna Sophie Kebke and colleagues used chemistry locked in whale skin to work out what long-finned pilot whales eat off Scotland, in this 2026 PLOS ONE paper. The tissue came from fifty adults and juveniles that stranded together on the Isle of Lewis in July 2023.

Carbon and nitrogen markers in the skin pointed to feeding along the continental shelf edge and slope, on prey from deep-water food webs. The whales' feeding zone overlapped only slightly with those of six dolphin species used for comparison, and males and females overlapped fully, though females ranged more widely. Such baselines help conservation planners protect the waters these whales depend on.
plos-pone-0347040:
Natalia Heredia and colleagues evaluated a culinary medicine program for people living with type 2 diabetes who also carry excess weight, recruited from clinics in low-income neighborhoods. Over five weekly ninety-minute sessions, a dietitian taught basic cooking skills wrapped in practical nutrition education. Eighty-nine people enrolled, about two-thirds in the program and the rest in a comparison group.

Most program participants attended and finished the follow-up surveys. Compared with the comparison group, they showed significant gains in how they perceived their diet and related measures, and interviews after the program added texture on what changed at home. Teaching people to cook, rather than only telling them what to eat, is the program's wager, and the early results support testing it at larger scale.
plos-pone-0347140:
Xiao Wang and co-workers test whether what a chief executive says in sustainability reports helps predict how the company will perform. Their 2026 study gathers more than twelve hundred listed Korean companies across eight years. It mines the bosses' report messages for strategy themes. Those themes are sorted by a sustainability scorecard. They are then joined with standard financial measures.

Eight learning models were tried, from simple neighbors to deep sequence readers. Models fed both money numbers and strategy themes beat money-only models across the board. A transformer design scored highest overall, with its close cousins next. Investors gain a hint that the words in the front of the report carry real signal about the numbers that follow.
plos-pone-0347540:
J. K. Owaresat and co-authors compared how human neural progenitor cells, the stem cells that build the brain, respond to dengue virus and Zika virus. Both infect these cells, with Zika notoriously damaging developing brains. Using gene network analysis on infected cell samples, the 2026 study separated the genes each virus rallies for its own replication from the defences the cell mounts.

Each virus leaned on distinct helper pathways, dengue on a growth signalling route and Zika on the cell's protein-making machinery, while sharing stress responses in the cell's folding workshop. Their defences diverged too. The authors say the map points to drug targets tailored to each virus.
plos-pone-0347640:
Santiago Jijón and co-workers join two natural health compounds, curcumin from turmeric and pigments from colorful vegetables, into new combined molecules. Both parents fight cell damage from oxygen, and curcumin has other wide effects. Their 2026 chemistry study links the two in two ways, then measures how well each new molecule resists oxidation in alcohol and in salty water.

Most linked versions beat their parent pigments at fighting oxidation. Merged versions with two of curcumin's active ends looked best as drug candidates on paper. A catch appeared too: the fat-loving molecules clumped together in water, so test values there describe clumps, not single molecules. A good delivery system would be needed to carry them into the body.
plos-pone-0348140:
Imen Zghab and co-workers create a family of new molecules and test whether they can block enzymes tied to blood sugar and skin darkening. Blocking the two sugar enzymes could help diabetes care, while blocking the third interests cosmetics. Their 2026 study builds the compounds from a simple acid base and checks them in lab dishes against standard drugs.

One compound blocked both sugar enzymes far more strongly than the standard diabetes drug used for comparison. A sister compound led on the skin enzyme, beating a common reference agent. Computer models of how the molecules dock into the enzymes matched the dish results. The pair stand out as starting points for medicines that do several jobs at once.
plos-pone-0348240:
Sema İncekara and Ahmet Şahin studied whether happiness at work keeps teachers in Türkiye's private schools committed to their schools. Teaching in the competitive private sector is stressful, and unhappy teachers leave. Their 2026 mixed-methods study surveyed two hundred ninety-nine teachers and interviewed eight more about emotions, fulfilment, and loyalty to their employer.

Teachers reported strong positive feelings, fulfilment, and emotional commitment, but weaker intention to stay when leaving would be costly. Feeling good and fulfilled predicted every form of commitment, while negative emotions dragged all of them down. Interviews echoed the numbers. The authors advise school leaders to protect positive working conditions and actively reduce sources of daily frustration.
plos-pone-0348440:
Yiming Zhang and co-workers capture the first detailed shapes of a human channel that lets calcium into cells. The channel, called Orai1, opens when internal calcium stores run low, and faults in it cause immune and muscle disease. Their 2026 study freezes the purified human protein and images it with a cryo-electron microscope.

The map confirms the channel is built from six matching parts arranged in a ring. Surprisingly, particles appeared in two different symmetry patterns, which hints the channel flexes and rearranges as it works. Resolution was moderate, so fine detail awaits sharper maps. Even so, having the human form gives drug designers a real target instead of a stand-in from flies.
plos-pone-0348840:
Muzlifa Mohamed Yusoff and co-workers study how actively patients with type two diabetes in Malaysia take charge of their own care. Active patients tend to manage blood sugar better over time. Their 2026 study surveys four hundred fifty patients at a public clinic in Penang, scoring their confidence and skills for self-care alongside views of their treatment and doctors' support.

Two-thirds of patients scored at a high level of engagement with their care. Men scored slightly higher, while older patients scored lower. Higher long-term blood sugar readings went with lower engagement, and patients on tablets alone scored below others. Clinics may lift self-care most by focusing support on older patients and those whose sugar control is already slipping.
plos-pone-0349040:
Guanlin Zheng and colleagues traced how a protein that reads chemical tags on RNA helps heart muscle cells mature. Earlier work showed that losing this reader protein stalls heart development, but which of its target messages mattered was unknown. Working with rat heart precursor cells coaxed to mature with a vitamin A relative, the team fished out the messages the protein physically holds.

One message stood out, carrying instructions for an enzyme that edits DNA marks. Removing the reader lowered that enzyme's output without lowering its message, showing the reader boosts translation into protein. Adding the enzyme back partly rescued the stalled maturation. The team also found a previously unknown rat variant of the gene. The work names a concrete link between RNA tagging and the making of a working heart.
plos-pone-0349140:
Carol A Hitchon, Lisa M Lix, and co-authors followed Canadians with rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease, or primary depression and anxiety to see how mood symptoms move quality of life over time. Chronic physical disease and mental symptoms often travel together, but within-person change is rarely separated from differences between people. Their 2026 cohort study saw more than seven hundred participants yearly for three years, testing mood, fatigue, function, and quality of life.

When a person's own depression or anxiety worsened, their mental quality of life fell clearly. Rising fatigue and worsening thinking scores dragged physical quality of life down, while better physical function lifted it. Most participants saw meaningful swings in quality of life across the study. The authors argue that tracking mood changes inside each patient, not just comparing patients, reveals where support can help most.
plos-pone-0349740:
Meeyoung Kim and colleagues track how the brain's internal excitability shifts across Ramadan in healthy fasting adults. Daytime fasting for a month resets eating, sleep, and blood sugar rhythms, any of which could tune brain circuits. Volunteers received paired magnetic pulses to the brain's movement area before, during, and after Ramadan, while a small non-fasting group provided comparison points, alongside sleep, sugar, and thinking measures.

Excitability rose by mid-Ramadan and partly stayed up afterward, a broad shift across all pulse timings rather than a change in one circuit type. Blood sugar and sleep time both fell mid-month. Kim and colleagues read the pattern as a general retuning tied to the fasted state, useful baseline knowledge for brain stimulation research scheduled around fasting.
plos-pone-0350040:
Van Minh Nguyen and five colleagues published this 2026 systematic review of programs that help people living with HIV quit smoking. Smoking is common in this group and compounds their health risks, while most live in poorer countries. The reviewers gathered thirty-two intervention studies and combined results, also hunting for any study of costs.

Medicines and intensive, tailored counseling helped people quit, with early positive signs from poorer countries, where most trials are still missing. No cost-effectiveness studies turned up at all. Nguyen urges future programs in HIV clinics to build in economic evaluation from the start.
plos-pone-0350140:
Feeling a buzz on one finger is easy; the brain must also combine buzzes across fingers. Shasha Wei and colleagues measured that combination with detection tests and brain recordings from the scalp, in this 2026 PLOS One study of touch.

Doubling the buzzing fingers improved detection only slightly, matching a model where each finger offers a separate chance to notice. Adding a distracting buzz to neighboring fingers made detection worse, showing fingers suppress each other. Brain signals summed when fingers shared a rhythm and shrank when rhythms differed. The weight of this suppression sits between what vision and hearing show, the authors report.
plos-pone-0350440:
Expression of Concern: the journal warns that this article may not be trustworthy. It deals with calcium signals in visceral leishmaniasis, a disease caused by a parasite. Until the doubts are resolved, its findings should be read as unverified.

Editors found a control image that looks like images in other papers. Those papers used the image for quite different tests. The stated methods also do not fit tests with more than two groups. Promised raw data were never supplied. The first author disputes the image point and says the files are gone. With no source data, the journal cannot check the results.
plos-pone-0350740:
InHo Lee and colleagues built a screening index in 2026 for judging whether workers are fit for confined space jobs. Such work risks low oxygen, toxic gases, and heavy strain, so fitness checks need structure rather than gut feel.

Health exam and function data from one hundred eleven workers were sorted into body, function, and lifestyle risk groups. A statistical method that shrinks weak factors set the index weights. The index sorted most workers as suitable, some as caution, and a few as unsuitable, closely matching independent specialist judgment in checks. A standard score could make fitness calls fairer across sites.
plos-pone-0350840:
Xiaoyuan Jin and colleagues present an ultra light detector for small targets in drone photos, where tiny objects drown in clutter and scale swings. Their design swaps heavy maths blocks for lean ghost style ones, adds a two path attention step that damps background noise, and focuses channel weights on faint small target cues.

On a public drone photo set, accuracy nudged above a strong compact rival while the model held under one million settings. That tiny size suits on board drone chips with strict power limits. Traffic counts, crowd checks, and small vehicle spotting from the air all need exactly this mix of lightness and sharp small target vision.
plos-pone-0351140:
Akiko Katayama and colleagues compared two ways that vessel lining cells grow old, and how each affects blood clotting. Cells can age by dividing until worn out, or by early stress damage. Ageing raises clot risk, yet the two paths may not act alike. Lab tests mixed aged cells with plasma and measured clot forming drive, backed by gene reading.

Worn out cells surprisingly lowered clot drive in dishes, while stress aged cells did not. In live mice, though, both natural ageing and stress aged vessel cells worsened vein clots, and their gene patterns looked alike. Dish results alone mislead here: stress driven ageing matches the aged body pattern best.
plos-pone-0351540:
Ali Ibrahim, Shaikha Alshehhi, and Nikolaos Tsingilis surveyed over a thousand teachers in the United Arab Emirates. They asked how much leadership in each school is shared beyond the principal. They also asked how attached teachers feel to their schools. Schools in all seven emirates took part, both public and private. Shared leadership is a favorite reform idea, and this study tested its link with teacher commitment.

Teachers said leadership was widely shared. Public schools reported slightly more sharing. Where sharing ran stronger, commitment ran stronger too. The link was strongest for emotional attachment and duty. It was weakest for staying only because leaving costs too much. Giving teachers a real voice seems to build teachers who want to stay.
plos-pone-0351640:
Dayron Leyva Rodriguez and Michelle Visser published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It studies Treponema denticola, a bacterium involved in gum disease. The authors examine oncostatin M released by neutrophils, immune cells first on the scene, and its contribution to endothelial cell dysfunction, harm to the cells lining blood vessels.

Linking a gum bacterium to vessel lining damage connects oral infection with wider inflammation in the body. Neutrophil-derived signals during this interaction may be one bridge between the two. Periodontal researchers and scientists studying how mouth infections affect general health are the readers for this mechanism work.
plos-pone-0351740:
K S Athira, Raju Attada, and Sulekha Komeravelli charted winter cold stress across north India over nearly forty years. They used a comfort index that blends temperature, wind, and sun into how cold a body feels. Cold waves kill people in India, yet they draw far less study than heat. The team mapped when stress starts each evening and how it deepens overnight.

January brought the worst stress. The far north, Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh, suffered most. Cold waves stretched the stress across the whole region. Over the decades, hours of slight cold stress grew. Stronger stress eased into the slight band rather than new cold arriving. Winters are softening on average, but the maps still tell relief teams which nights turn dangerous, and where.
plos-pone-0351840:
Tzu-Fei Wang and colleagues asked whether the language a dying patient speaks shapes the end of life. The study covered home care patients in Ontario, Canada, who died of cancer. Records held nearly thirty-four thousand people. Their preferred languages were English, French, or another tongue. The team tracked deaths in hospital, emergency visits, and heavy treatment in the last thirty days.

Patients who preferred another language died in hospital more often. They also had more emergency visits and more aggressive care near the end. French speakers died in hospital more often than English speakers too. The gaps held after other factors were weighed. Care that a patient cannot fully understand may default to the hospital, wanted or not.
plos-pone-0351940:
Tímea Popucza surveyed fifteen hundred six care and human service workers about emotional demands and burnout. The study rests on a well-known model of job demands and resources. It asks whether resources such as control, support, and meaning buffer the harm of demands. Two kinds of emotional demand were measured. One is the strain workers feel inside. The other comes from contact with clients.

Both demand types fed both sides of burnout: exhaustion and pulling away. The buffering effect did not appear. Resources linked to less burnout on their own. But meaning in work and social support made the demand-exhaustion link stronger, not weaker. Caring more can deepen the wound when the emotional load stays high. Managers should hear that before they prescribe more engagement as the cure.
plos-pone-0352140:
Olufemi Akande, Adesike Olayinka, and Moses Adebayo field-test maize bred to withstand the fall armyworm. Their 2026 trials ran in Nigeria's derived savanna. The armyworm caterpillar devastates maize, worst in the minor cropping season. Twenty-six resistant hybrids grew alongside six commercial checks in a replicated lattice design. Yield, plant appearance, ear quality, diseases, and worm damage were all scored across the season.

The hybrids differed significantly on nearly every trait. Five experimental crosses stood out from the pack. They combined high grain yield with handsome plants and ears and low leaf damage from the worm. Superiority rankings held across the trial environments. Two further leaf diseases were scored as part of the screen. Before release, the winners must prove stable in wider agro-ecologies. If they hold up, Nigerian farmers gain seed that fights the pest genetically, cutting reliance on sprays they can barely afford.
plos-pone-0352240:
Seungwoo Han read three decades of South Korean newspapers to chart how the country's media feel about its two giant neighbors, the United States and China. Word-level analysis scored the emotional tone and intensity of coverage from nineteen ninety-two to twenty twenty-five. How a middle power's press warms or cools toward rival giants matters, since public feeling constrains what governments can do.

The two portraits diverged steadily. Coverage of the United States stayed fairly stable, mildly warm and low in emotional heat. Coverage of China grew more negative and more heated over the years. Han ties the durable gap to the American alliance, historical memory, and the media landscape itself. The long record warns against reading any single headline storm as the story: the emotional drift is slow, structural, and one-directional so far.
plos-pone-0352340:
Yan-Shing Chang and three colleagues survey British mothers about the burdens of multiple births during COVID-19. Their 2026 cross-sectional study recruited women up to six months after delivery, in late 2021. Over eight hundred fifty mothers answered, fifty-three of them with twins or more. Social circumstances, obstetric history, pandemic experiences, and feeding support were all examined. This was the first British study to ask which factors travel with multiple births in the pandemic context.

Twins' familiar complications dominated the adjusted results. Multiple births were far likelier to involve formula feeding, preterm delivery, and caesarean birth. Socioeconomic and COVID-specific factors, by contrast, showed no association in simpler comparisons. Postnatal depression and feeding support patterns also differed for these mothers. Services planning for the next crisis should note the practical lesson. Mothers of multiples need feeding and mental health support designed for their situation, not postnatal care stretched thinner.
plos-pone-0352440:
Filip Jevic and three colleagues check whether nerve damage from a chemotherapy drug is really the same on both sides of the body. Their 2026 study covers forty-seven children treated for acute lymphoblastic leukaemia. Vincristine, a backbone drug for this cancer, frequently injures peripheral nerves. Doctors usually assume the injury is symmetric. The team ran nerve conduction studies on both sides of each child and compared them carefully.

Motor nerve readings agreed only fairly to moderately between sides. Signals from the leg and arm nerves matched worst of all. Sensory timing, by contrast, was excellently symmetric. Whole-nerve verdicts for motor damage also differed side to side. A one-sided test, still common in clinics, can therefore misjudge a child's motor neuropathy. Testing both sides gives survivors fairer monitoring, and rehabilitation plans that fit the limb that actually struggles.
plos-pone-0352640:
Øivind Tøien and co-authors test in 2026 automatic scoring of sleep in American black bears, including during hibernation, when body temperature cycles up and down. Years of brain, eye, and muscle recordings from captive bears were far too many to score by hand. Two learning classifiers were trained in different ways and checked against careful hand scoring by three experts.

Both tools matched hand scores closely, with top scores in a high range, and training apart for hibernation worked best. Bears slept about twice as much in hibernation as in summer by both methods. Some files challenged both tools alike, pointing to hard cases rather than tool failure.
plos-pone-0353240:
Shanila and colleagues, in a 2026 experiment, find the salt level at which giant freshwater prawns grow best. Salt in the water shapes molting, growth, and stress in prawns, a valuable farmed species in Bangladesh and beyond. Young prawns were raised for eight weeks at five salt levels, from fresh water up to a third of seawater strength, each in triplicate tanks.

Growth, weight gain, feed use, and survival all peaked at the lowest added salt level, a mildly brackish mix. Math fitted to the results put the sweet spot for growth close to that level. Gene checks matched the picture: at that level, a hormone that blocks molting fell, a shell-building gene rose, stress genes quieted, and immune genes woke up. The authors conclude that a touch of salt, not none and not much, helps these prawns thrive, a cheap lever for farmers whose water they can adjust.
plos-pone-0353740:
Burle and colleagues tested blue light treatment in mice infected with a common parasite in a 2026 study. The parasite can pass from a pregnant mother to her unborn young and cause serious harm. Blue light had been proposed to kill the parasite in tissues, but its effects on animal behavior were unknown.

Infected mice rested more and groomed less than healthy mice, with or without the light. Treated infected mice showed more odd behaviors, while healthy treated mice ate and drank more and moved more. Long light exposure seemed to act as a mild stressor. Light may lower parasite load, but dosing needs care to protect animal welfare.
plos-pone-0353840:
Cesar Augusto Inoue and seven colleagues map what Brazil knows about viral hepatitis, in this 2026 PLOS ONE scoping review. The country aims to eliminate these liver infections by 2030, but progress is uneven. Searching seven databases, the team gathered two hundred studies covering more than fourteen million people, and charted rates for hepatitis types A through E across regions and social groups.

Hepatitis B drew the most research, then C. Exposure was highest among prisoners, immigrants, and transgender people, while hepatitis D clustered in the Amazon. The authors found most studies small and one-off, rarely connecting infection to social conditions. Their evidence map is meant to steer policy and better-designed research.
plos-pone-0354140:
Priyanka Renita D'Souza and Princia Rolita D'Souza present a protocol, published in PLOS ONE in 2026, for mapping research on a mother's drinking and her child's skin disease. Alcohol in pregnancy is best known for harming brain development, but it may also shape the developing immune system. Their planned review covers eczema of the atopic kind in children whose mothers drank before or during pregnancy.

Following standard scoping methods, two reviewers will screen five databases plus grey literature for original English-language studies. They will chart exposure timing, how eczema was diagnosed, and proposed biological pathways, then check their findings with practising clinicians. The aim is to show where evidence exists and where it is missing.
plos-pone-0354240:
Morantes and colleagues, in a 2026 laboratory study, test cocoa leftovers against chikungunya, a mosquito-borne virus that causes fever and lasting joint pain. The husks around cocoa pods and the shells around beans are farm waste. Yet cocoa is rich in compounds that fight both viruses and oxidative stress, the chemical damage the virus provokes in cells.

Extracts of both leftovers were added to infected human liver cells. The extracts barely harmed the cells themselves. Above a threshold dose, they cut the amount of viral genetic material and the number of live virus particles, most clearly half a day after infection. Harmful oxygen chemicals inside the cells also fell. The authors read the two actions as linked: calming oxidative stress may be part of how the extracts slow the virus. They recommend deeper work to pin down the active compounds before any remedy is claimed.
plos-pone-0354740:
Viet Ngu Nguyen, Thi Minh Tam Le, Duc Hung Pham, and Huu Cuong Nguyen wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on robot control. It presents a reinforcement learning method of the actor-critic kind, robust and aware of disturbances, for robotic manipulators with multiple degrees of freedom, arms that bend at several joints. Robust means the controller keeps working when conditions push against it.

Disturbance awareness means the learning system takes outside forces into account instead of being surprised by them. Factory and laboratory robots face loads and contacts that shift constantly, so control that expects disturbance is safer and steadier. Robotics engineers are the audience for an actor-critic method built this way.
plos-pone-0354840:
Emiliano Serviole and colleagues use in 2026 chemical profiling of leaves to sort out tangled naming in alpine brambles, the group that includes raspberries and blackberries. These plants breed without normal sex and cross freely, creating many forms with blurry borders. Leaves from nine forms were sampled over two years along a mountain height gradient in the French Alps.

Profiles split the forms into three broad super groups, with the true raspberry standing apart. Dozens of compounds were named, some new to the group, and classes such as plant pigments and tannins marked each group. Chemical fingerprints could aid naming and matter for drug and cosmetic uses.
plos-pone-0355540:
Eugênio Simão, writing in 2026, tackles a gap in how scientists model living cells. In older models, small molecules are treated either as raw material for chemical work or as simple on-off switches. Real cells use the same molecules, such as ATP, for both jobs at once, and Simão builds a formal system that can handle that double role.

His method extends a classic modeling tool called Petri nets, adding special arcs that let a signal molecule be used up as it passes information upward through layers of control. He proves that signal flow cannot run in circles and that draining a lower layer blocks higher steps. Tested on spore formation in a common bacterium, the model explains why a slow build-up triggers far more spore formation than a sudden pulse.
plos-pone-0355740:
Jonathan Williams Ramirez and seven colleagues release a free artificial intelligence tool that automatically outlines brain tissue in photographs of sliced postmortem brains, in this 2026 paper. Brain banks routinely photograph coronal slabs, and new methods can rebuild three-dimensional maps of disease from those photos, but someone first has to trace the tissue in every image by hand. Their model, built on a standard segmentation network, was trained on more than fourteen hundred hand-traced photographs from two sites, covering fresh and fixed tissue and varied diagnoses.

On unseen photographs the tool matched human tracings closely, with overlap and boundary errors approaching the agreement between human raters themselves. The authors have made the model and its training data public. They argue removing the tracing bottleneck should let far more laboratories adopt three-dimensional neuropathology and mine their existing photo archives.
plos-pone-0355840:
Elijah Sunday Okwuonu and colleagues screened cave bats near homes in southeastern Nigeria for blood parasites called trypanosomes. Caves hold large mixed bat colonies, and their parasite traffic near settlements is poorly known in West Africa. Their 2026 study tested blood and parasite samples from fifty-seven bats of ten species caught in nine caves and one house.

Parasite DNA appeared in well over a third of the bats, spanning six species in four families. Family trees placed the parasites in a group known from African bats, an early branch near the lineage that causes Chagas disease. Okwuonu and colleagues say peri-domestic roosts deserve monitoring, since bats, parasites, and people meet closely there.
plos-pone-0355940:
Eva Débora de Oliveira Andrade and seven colleagues review whether learning to cook actually improves adults' diets, in this 2026 systematic review. Cooking programs are often funded on the assumption that skills lead to healthier eating and better nutritional status. Searching five databases, the team gathered fifteen studies of healthy adults and graded their methods and the certainty of their findings.

Better cooking skills and cooking more often were linked with better diet quality, especially more fruit and vegetables and greater confidence in the kitchen. No evidence connected skill development to nutritional status measures like weight. The certainty behind the positive findings was low or very low, and most studies carried serious risks of bias. The authors say cooking education looks promising for eating habits but needs proper randomized trials before stronger claims can be made.
plos-pone-0356140:
Shane Lewis and colleagues designed a wireless scheme to keep vehicle-to-vehicle messages reliable in crowded city streets. Their 2026 paper combines a reconfigurable intelligent surface, which can steer radio signals, with spatial modulation using dual-polarized antennas. Only one radio chain stays active at a time, which saves power and hardware.

Simulations using standard vehicle channel models tested signal strength, error rates, and energy use against a full multi-antenna setup. The new design used far less energy while keeping error rates close to the bigger system. Signal quality measures also improved, thanks to the surface shaping signals around blockages. The authors present it as a practical option for future connected vehicles.
plos-pone-0356240:
Takondwa Connis Bakuwa, Gillian Saloojee, and Wiedaad Slemming interview caregivers and physiotherapists who ran a home training program in rural Malawi. The program serves children with cerebral palsy. In the program, trained caregivers teach other caregivers, a model suited to places with few professionals. Their interviews, held after a seven-week trial run, were sorted with a standard framework for what helps or blocks new practices.

Daily routines helped: training folded into normal caregiving, parents stayed engaged, and a community group handled logistics. Peer teachers stood out, since expert caregivers taught in shared language and earned trust professionals could not match. Barriers also emerged in the accounts. Bakuwa and colleagues say any scale-up must fund the peer layer and protect caregiver time, not just print manuals.
plos-pone-0356340:
Filipe Sousa and three colleagues issued this correction in 2026 to their study comparing a three-minute all-out running test with classical laboratory benchmarks for aerobic fitness. A data entry error had put one participant's maximal oxygen uptake value from a verification bout in the wrong place. That also distorted a figure's analysis and some error statistics in the results text. The notice supplies the corrected figure and data file.

After rerunning the analyses, the statistical picture shifted only slightly, and the authors state that the interpretation and conclusions are unchanged; an editorial board member reviewed the correction and agreed. A post-hoc power analysis, added after a reviewer raised the small sample size, indicated the key comparison was adequately powered. Readers should use the corrected values and figure when citing the study's test comparisons.
plos-pone-0357040:
Peisheng Yang and co-authors paired a deep learning flood model with Jiangxi Province's staged warning system. The work focused on the Xiangshui River Basin in China. Floods gather fast in this small mountainous catchment. Their 2026 study trained a bidirectional memory network on twenty past flood events. It tested the network on six held-back events, against three established approaches.

The new model forecast flood flows more accurately than all three rivals. It was strongest one hour ahead, though its skill faded by six hours out. Rainfall from upstream stations in the previous two hours mattered most. The authors map the model's output onto the province's six-three-one hour response stages. They use weather forecasts for the longer leads. That gives local officials a clearer chain from prediction to evacuation orders.
plos-pone-0358240:
Zhijie Zhou and colleagues published a 2026 methods paper in PLOS ONE on diagnosing machine faults when sensors sit at many different points on the equipment. A model trained at one monitoring point often fails at a new point, because the vibration data look different and labeled fault examples are scarce there. Their network, UCTL, learns from a labeled source point and adapts itself to an unlabeled target point without human tagging.

Inside, a reshaped transformer reads raw one-dimensional vibration signals directly and picks out patterns at several time scales. A new alignment method then pulls source and target data together, balancing average and spread differences so fault classes are less likely to mismatch. Across six transfer tasks on public bearing and gear datasets, the method averaged accuracy above ninety-nine percent. Starting from a pretrained model also cut training time, easing deployment across large monitoring systems.
plos-pone-0358540: Xiao and three co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study comparing drugs for advanced breast cancer. All the cancers were HER2-positive and had spread. The team weighed one drug, T-DXd, against other HER2-targeted options used after first treatment failed. They used a Bayesian network method that pools many trials at once. Rankings like this help doctors choose when no single trial compares every option.
plos-pone-0358640: Bendaoued and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE paper on an antenna shaped like a flower for future phone networks. The design carries four ports and works in two bands at the very high frequencies used by 5G millimeter-wave links. A feature called DGS, a pattern cut into the ground plane, is new in their design. Compact multi-port antennas are key parts for fast, crowded city networks.
plos-pone-0358740: Jiang and six co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on rehab after stroke. Patients practiced with restricted blood flow in the limb plus training guided by visual feedback. The team tracked lower limb function and blood levels of two growth factors, BDNF and VEGF. Combining methods that push both muscle and brain recovery is a live hope in stroke care.
plos-pone-0358840: Mohammed and four co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on two plants used in West African folk care. They tested leaf extracts from bitter leaf and from Senna siamea against harmful bacteria. The tests checked both germ killing and the power to break up biofilms, the slime layers that shield bacteria from drugs. Results of this kind guide the search for plant-based options as drug resistance grows.
plos-pone-0358940:
Qiu Zhu leads a team of eight reviewing a new way of studying symptoms in stomach cancer, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Instead of treating each symptom as a lone score, network analysis maps how symptoms reinforce one another. It reveals which sit at the center of a patient's suffering and which bridge between clusters. The review searched nine databases in English and Chinese and gathered studies applying the method to gastric cancer patients through early 2026.

Nine studies qualified. One symptom inventory, a Chinese version of the Anderson gastrointestinal module, dominated the field, appearing in seven. Across studies, nine core symptoms recurred, with fatigue named central most often, in five. Ten bridge symptoms were reported, but they varied between studies, unlike the steadier core list. The authors say the map is consistent enough to guide precision symptom care, while calling for standard methods so bridge findings can accumulate.
plos-pone-0359940:
Jinlian Zhang and eight colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on the chemical bisphenol A, a plastic ingredient people meet daily. It examines BPA's neurotoxicity in the pathogenesis of depression, how the chemical might help cause the illness, using three combined methods: molecular docking, dynamics simulations at the molecular level, and network toxicology.

These computer methods map which body systems BPA touches, how it binds to proteins, and how those bonds behave over time. Building a mechanism in silico is a first step before animal or human studies. Toxicologists and mental health researchers share the audience for a chemical-depression link explored this way.
pmc-10655340:
Lina Yang and four co-authors study whether waiting longer in hospital before brain surgery raises infection risk in a 2023 paper. Surgical site infection after neurosurgery can be devastating, and long stays before surgery are a changeable risk factor in other surgery types. The team studied six hundred cranial surgery patients at a large center in China in 2016.

About eleven percent developed a surgical infection, and rates were higher in patients with longer waits. Waits of five to six days roughly tripled the odds versus a one to two day wait, and waits of a week or more roughly quadrupled them. Deep infections also rose steadily with wait length. The authors urge shorter pre surgery stays where possible.
pmc-10656540:
Hideki Nakai and colleagues test whether zapping the breathing muscle protects it during machine ventilation, in this rat study from twenty twenty-three. A ventilator rests the diaphragm, but the rested muscle wastes fast, a problem called ventilator-induced diaphragm dysfunction that traps patients on the machine. The team asked if pulsed electrical stimulation could hold the muscle's program steady.

Rats ventilated for twelve hours showed the expected damage in gene activity: breakdown genes rose, building genes fell. Stimulated rats told a different story. Eighteen breakdown-side genes that ventilation raised were held down by stimulation, including inflammation signals. Six genes that ventilation lowered, tied to oxygen transport and the cell's power plants, were lifted back up. The authors argue that timed stimulation, with rest between pulses, blunts the muscle's slide toward wasting.
pmc-10662640:
Muhammad Stanikzai, Mohammad Wafa, Bilal Rahimi, and Hadia Sayam assess the state of health research in Afghanistan. Research drives new treatments and public health gains, yet the authors find the field in their country deeply underdeveloped. Output and quality fall far short of regional and global norms. The article sets out the challenges that hold Afghan health research back.

It also points to openings for growth and offers advice on how to build capacity. The authors argue that stronger research at home is needed for the country's health system to improve on firm proof rather than borrowed findings.
pmc-10692340:
Wenwen Tian and thirteen colleagues identified a protein that drives progression in triple negative breast cancer.
