The protein, AURKAIP1, was known as a regulator of a cell-cycle kinase, but its direct role in cancer was unclear. The twenty twenty-three study measured it in tumor tissue and cell experiments. Silencing experiments and mouse models tested what it does. Its partners inside the cell were hunted with binding assays.

AURKAIP1 was strongly overproduced in these tumors, and high levels tracked with bigger tumors, node spread, and worse prognosis. Switching it off sharply slowed cancer cell growth and migration, in dishes and in mice. The protein binds and stabilizes DDX5, a helicase, by shielding it from disposal. Restoring DDX5 rescued the cancer cells, confirming the partnership as a potential drug target.
pmc-10695940:
Deliège and eight co-authors model a spring-based skull surgery for kids in this twenty twenty-three study. Some kids are born with skull seams fused too soon, which can raise pressure inside the head. Springs set in a cut at the back of the skull push it wide bit by bit and add room.

Inside, the team built a per-child model from scans of eighteen young patients. The model called the final gain in head room well when checked against post-surgery scans. The team then slid the cut spot across a set range to see how the gain shifts. Their maps show which cut plans give the most room and which are the most robust picks.
pmc-10698940:

pmc-10700740:

pmc-10706940:

pmc-10711640:

pmc-10717540:

pmc-10717840:

pmc-10731640:

pmc-10735840:

pmc-10736440:

pmc-10736740:

pmc-10738740:

pmc-10738840:

pmc-10739040:

pmc-10740740:

pmc-10742640:

pmc-10745740:

pmc-10747040:

pmc-10747640:

pmc-10747840:

pmc-10748340:

pmc-10750040:

pmc-10808640:

pmc-10808740:

pmc-10864540:

pmc-11027740:

pmc-11623040:

pmc-11624740:

pmc-11629540:

pmc-11636540:

pmc-11640540:

pmc-11647040:

The sensing zone shrinks, which sharpens the signals. A neural network read the signals from leukemia cell lines. It sorted them with near-perfect accuracy. Real white cell types from donors sorted nearly as well.
pmc-11647640:
Gerardo Cazarez-Navarro leads a team on gene variants and latent TB in Mexico. Their study from twenty twenty-four deals with folks who carry TB sans signs. TB still makes millions ill each year world wide.

The gene in focus helps the immune system clear germs in cells. A case control study drew folks from shelters for tests. Half had latent TB and half did not. Three variants in the gene were typed in each person. Group gene patterns were also checked for links. The aim is to learn who is at more risk.
pmc-11648540:
El-Jabri, Rahman, and Khan write a letter in twenty twenty-four on exam timing and student well-being. They respond to a study that asked students when they would prefer to sit exams. That study relied on what students said about their own grades and well-being, not on real exam scores.

The letter urges a check against real results for students whose exam times match what they wanted. It also notes the hard logistics of fair exam plans for all. Most students in the study favoured Friday exams, which cannot suit every course. The authors suggest low-cost support, such as mindset and belonging work, to help students hurt by a poor fit.
pmc-11649140:
Merga Garoma Jatu and seven co-authors measure health literacy among high school teens in Jimma town, Ethiopia. Their cross-sectional study was published in twenty twenty-four. Health literacy, the skill to find and use health facts, shapes how young people care for themselves.

The team surveyed six hundred and four students in June twenty twenty-three, chosen through staged sampling from public high schools. A tested self-filled questionnaire gathered the data. About half the students were male, and ages ran from fourteen to nineteen. Statistical models hunted for factors tied to higher or lower literacy, such as schooling background and information sources. The findings can guide schools and health offices that want to raise health skills in teens.
pmc-11652640:
Xu Jiang, Jiaqi Wang, and Liangyu Lin lead a large team showing how breast cancer readies the lung for spread by switching on a sensor protein in lung macrophages. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-four. Before cancer cells arrive, the lung can be remodeled into a welcoming, immune-quiet niche. That pre-metastatic niche is a prime drug target.

The switched-on sensor raised a checkpoint protein on the macrophages' surface. That checkpoint pushed helper cells toward a suppressive type, deepening the quiet. Mice whose macrophages lacked the sensor developed fewer lung metastases. A cancer-secreted factor started the chain by protecting the sensor from disposal. In patients, sensor and checkpoint levels tracked with suppressive cell counts and worse outlook. The chain from tumor signal to immune niche is now mapped. Blocking it might keep lungs inhospitable to arriving cells.
pmc-11653340:
Thomas Johnstone and a large team of co-authors trained machine learning to call which knee lesions heal with no surgery. Their study, from twenty twenty-four, deals with osteochondritis dissecans, a bone and cartilage flaw in young knees. Which sores heal on rest and time alone lacks firm rules. The team drew on a forward cohort of knee OCD cases, all with growth plates still open and all on no surgery care.

A set of classifier models learned to call the heal from case traits. The run also flagged traits with fresh clinic weight. Readers who treat young knees get a data tool for the wait or cut call, long made by feel.
pmc-11658140:
Dan Liu and six co-authors published a cross-sectional study in twenty twenty-four on the burden that medication itself imposes on older Chinese patients with depression. Pills bring routines, side effects, and costs that weigh on daily life. Five hundred eighty-eight patients in an eastern Chinese city completed a validated living-with-medicines questionnaire.

The median score signaled a moderate burden. Burden ran higher in patients in their seventies, rural residents, those taking more than five drugs at once or dosing more than three times daily, and those paying fully in cash. Living with adult children, higher household income, and freedom from drug reactions lightened the load. The authors offer the factor list to clinicians simplifying regimens.
pmc-11659640:
Jamal Giri and colleagues published a 2025 twin study of how the roof of the mouth takes shape during childhood. Dental casts from more than two hundred twin pairs were measured in three dimensions at the baby-teeth, mixed, and adult-teeth stages. Comparing identical twins with fraternal twins lets researchers separate the influence of genes from that of environment.

Nearly all palate dimensions grew significantly across childhood. For most measurements, differences between children were best explained by a mix of inherited factors and each child's unique environment, rather than the shared home. Such findings help orthodontists understand which features of mouth shape run in families and which respond to outside influences.
pmc-11661240:
Shasha Peng and eleven co-authors read cloth harm from DNA-packed fat drops used as shot gear in mice. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-four. The drops bear a charge fat known for harm but prized for where it sends its load. Drops made by fast mix gear, not film, were tried for reach, spread, flare, and harm in mouse cloth.

Drops and DNA held long in lung and spleen, where film drops did not. Shots woke set guards in blood. Flare and cloth harm hit muscle, heart, and liver, by dose: less dose, less harm. The team weigh reach gainst harm for gear picks.
pmc-11667040:
Carta and co-authors test how heat treatment changes a hot-rolled aluminum alloy called AA2017. Plates four millimeters thick were heated at 500 degrees for two or six hours. Samples were then cooled in water or in air, and aged at 175 degrees for eight hours.

The team checked structure with light and electron microscopes and tested hardness and strength. Pull tests ran along both the rolling and cross directions. The best strength came from six hours of heating, water cooling, and aging. Break tests showed mostly ductile failure, with tiny voids that grew and joined.
pmc-11672040:
Jean-Baptiste Ducloyer and a large team randomise an eye surgery step that may create blind spots. Their trial from twenty twenty-four is called PEELING. Removing a retinal membrane is standard for distorted vision. Whether to peel the deeper limiting membrane too is debated.

Over two hundred patients entered the French national trial. Some membranes peeled away on their own during surgery. The rest were randomised to peeling or no peeling. Vision, scans, and fine light sensitivity were tracked for a year. New micro blind spots were the main harm measure. The design separates surgeon preference from evidence. Eye surgeons gain randomised data for a daily decision.
pmc-11672840:
János Dégi and five colleagues published a veterinary study in two thousand twenty-four on drug resistance in bacteria from dog ear infections in western Romania. Staphylococcus species drive much canine ear disease, and resistance patterns guide treatment. Local data from a university clinic were compiled.

Ear swabs from clinical cases were cultured and species-identified with an automated system, which also ran antibiotic susceptibility panels. Genetic tests further characterised the isolates. The study aimed to map which drugs still work against these staphylococci. The authors frame the profile as a future challenge for stewardship in pet care. Full resistance rates fill the results tables.
pmc-11675640:
Yunqing Yu, Ping Liao, and Ruotian Jiang review ion channels in the brain's smell center, in work from two thousand twenty-four. Smell loss can weigh heavily on daily life and mood, and current care often fails to restore it. The smell bulb is the first brain stop for odor signals.

Channel families shape how nerve cells fire, how signals pass between cells, and how odors are perceived. Their roles in other senses are well known, but their part in the smell bulb has been little studied. The review gathers what is known, family by family. The authors aim to open new paths for diagnosis and care.
pmc-11678040:
Feixiang Xiong and colleagues published a 2024 medical study on fatty liver disease and the gut. The team compared healthy people, patients with a serious form of fatty liver inflammation, and patients whose disease had advanced to scarring called cirrhosis. They wanted markers that could flag the cirrhosis stage without invasive testing.

Stool samples from ninety patients underwent gene sequencing and chemical analysis of the small molecules microbes produce. One bacterial family and genus, both lower in sicker patients, tracked disease progress most strongly in their models. The work points toward stool-based clues that might one day help doctors spot dangerous liver scarring earlier.
pmc-11678640:
Dong Liu and colleagues published a comprehensive review in 2024 on a protein called chitinase-3-like-1, also known as YKL-40. The protein can bind chitin but cannot break it down, and many cell types release it, especially during inflammation. Earlier work linked it to many separate diseases, but no single account covered its roles across the whole body.

The review works through the inflammatory conditions of the body's organ systems one by one. It explains how the protein affects cell growth, cell death, movement, and immune cell behavior, and how inflammatory signals switch its production on. The authors treat it as a promising measurable marker for disease and a possible treatment target, while laying out where the evidence is still incomplete.
pmc-11680040:
Wang and a large team design in twenty twenty-four a prototype machine to find defects on laser gyroscope mirror parts. Flawless mirrors are vital for these precision navigation devices. Their prototype checks both reflected and transmitted light through two channels and handles patterned and plain surfaces alike.

Computer simulations of key parts showed tiny bending under load, safe vibration behaviour, and low stress in transport tests. Bench tests on mirror substrates and standard test plates found defects on both surface types. Detection sharpness beat the design target by a wide margin. The authors present the design as stable and fit for optical quality testing in production.
pmc-11680140:
Quintero-Salgado and colleagues trace how flu and other lung viruses shifted seasons in Mexico after COVID in twenty twenty-four. Eight years of weekly case counts from Jalisco state were modeled across pre pandemic, pandemic, and later phases. Lockdowns and masks had crushed most lung virus spread. The study asks what returned, and when.

Virus traffic fell hard during the pandemic, then surged back off season as rules eased. Flu subtypes took turns leading year by year. One virus, RSV, came back earlier and stronger than before. Some viruses never regained their old seasonal rhythm. The authors urge flexible watch systems and vaccine plans that fit the new patterns.
pmc-11680340:
Priyanka Goyani, Rafail Christodoulou, and Evros Vassiliou review immune aging in a 2024 paper. As people age, their immune system weakens in a broad, systematic way. That decline shapes the health of older adults, who respond worse to new germs and vaccines. The review lays out the main features of this aging process.

Key features include the shrinking of the gland that matures T cells, and a state of constant low-grade inflammation. Changes in cell energy use and in blood cell production also play a part. Each major immune cell type is affected in its own way. The authors say grasping these mechanisms is the first step toward keeping older immune systems stronger.
pmc-11688740:
Betty Napoleon and co-authors describe in 2024 a tip sheet that helps older patients ask for age-friendly care. The care model, called the 4Ms, covers what matters to the patient, medication, mental state, and mobility. Patients told the team they did not know how to make sure they got this care.

A patient advisory council built the sheet over many rounds of drafts and feedback. It explains the 4Ms in plain words, gives self-advocacy tips, and leaves space to list questions before a visit and notes during it. A code on the back links to more resources. Patients and providers who reviewed it called it clear and useful.
pmc-11689640:
Marie Boltz, writing alone in two thousand twenty-four, studies how ready family care partners feel when a person with dementia leaves the hospital. Her work sits in a nurse-led plan that draws kin into care in the hospital and for sixty days after.

Care partners, two hundred twenty-nine in all, rated their own readiness on a scale. They felt least ready for the sick person's feelings and body needs, and for their own stress. Nurse notes from the move home pointed to five needs, from help with signs of illness to care for the carer's own health. Boltz argues that health teams must tend to both mind and fact needs.
pmc-11690140:
Donya Nemati and three co-authors study race gaps in heart health gains from exercise. Their twenty twenty-four paper uses the LIFE trial, which sorted sixteen hundred older adults into two groups. One group did on-site exercise twice a week, plus home exercise. The other group got health classes. The team tracked eight heart health factors for two years.

Factors included exercise, sleep, smoking, weight, blood pressure, and blood tests. Gains in exercise, sleep, weight, and one blood fat were seen for White members in the exercise group. The pattern did not match for Black members. The authors argue that one plan may not close gaps, and programs may need tailoring.
pmc-11692140:
Xue Bai and Mengyu Liu study in 2024 Hong Kong adults in their fifties and sixties who care for both parents and children. These sandwiched carers give help in two directions at once. A survey of 1,500 of them measured how the two directions relate, and how caring shapes their own plans.

Giving more care upward generally went with giving more downward. But once care spending passed about 12 percent of household income, the link flipped negative, as resources ran thin. Heavier carers in both directions were also less prepared for their own future care. The authors urge services to help such families plan ahead, not just cope day to day.
pmc-11709140:
Rosca and co-authors grade pulse oximetry screening for newborn heart defects. The team screened 1,188 newborns in intensive care over three years. Screening ran in the first 72 hours of life. A total of 201 newborns were found to have heart disease. Nearly all, 198, screened positive in that window.

Three cases screened negative but were caught later by ultrasound. Sensitivity reached 98 point 51 percent with no false positives. Nine deaths were tied to heart defects or their fallout. Survival past 72 hours sat near 95 point 5 percent. The authors call the test cheap, easy, and effective. Heart defects appeared in about one in six of the newborns screened.
pmc-11709540:
Steven Boggess and five co-authors build a screening platform to find genes that control how excitable neurons become in tau-related brain diseases. Their study came out in 2025. In these diseases, including Alzheimer's, neurons fire too readily, and this overactivity appears early and worsens symptoms.

Their method combines stem-cell-derived neurons carrying a tau mutation with a calcium sensor that changes color when a neuron fires. Gene-silencing tools then switch off thousands of genes, one per cell group, and the cells are sorted by activity. Some genes changed excitability only in mutant neurons, others only in healthy ones. Follow-up electrical recordings confirmed the screen detects real effects. Enriched pathways pointed at cell cleanup and metabolism as possible drivers.
pmc-11715340:
Krisstina Madan, Ellen Brown, and Vanessa Gordon report this project, published in two thousand twenty-five, on teaching dementia awareness in Miami-Dade County. The project grew out of a nursing doctorate and centers on a short teaching video made for a mixed-culture community.

The team showed the video to a small online focus group of community stakeholders and asked what worked. The group was small, highly schooled, and mostly of Hispanic descent. Viewers asked for more images, plainer language access, and a clear call to action at the end of the video. They also named places to spread it: doctor's offices, waiting rooms, websites, and social media. The authors plan to use this feedback to sharpen the video. Their aim is a tool that helps mixed communities face dementia with better facts.
pmc-11730440:
Shunmugavelu and Paari published in twenty twenty-four a case report of red spots found on the roof of a patient's mouth. Such spots, called palatal petechiae, can arise from many causes. Their patient was a fifty-seven-year-old woman seen at a dental visit. A painless red lesion about three centimeters wide sat on her soft palate. It had a clear center and caused no symptoms.

The authors stress careful history taking and oral examination for such lesions. They note that oral sexual activity is a common cause of this kind of palate bruising. Patients may not connect the two or may hesitate to share details. Clinicians should therefore consider that cause from the presentation itself.
pmc-11740040:
Yizhang Chen and eight co-authors test a simple blood ratio as an early warning in throat cancer in a 2024 study. Patients with locally advanced esophageal cancer received immune plus chemotherapy before surgery, a combination whose benefit is still being mapped. The team tracked the ratio of two white blood cell types before treatment and after the first cycle.

Ninety eight patients were followed for about three years, with thirty nine deaths. Patients whose ratio fell sharply after one cycle actually fared worse, surviving a median of about twenty eight months, while the others' median was not reached. The ratio change and whether surgery followed stood as independent survival predictors. The authors propose the cheap ratio as an early prognostic signal.
pmc-11790440:
Zeng and ten co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on risk factors for reactivation of a cancer-linked virus. The virus, Epstein-Barr, is a major risk factor for nasopharyngeal cancer in South China. The team draw screening data from a population cohort in a high-risk city. Over twelve thousand participants feed the analysis, with matched pairs for modeling. A Bayesian network model is built beside a standard regression model. Age over sixty and current smoking link directly to virus reactivation in both models.

Sex, schooling, tea drinking, cooking, and family history link only indirectly. The network model edges out regression on all test metrics. Its visual maps show the web of factor links plainly. The authors back network models for risk prediction in screening.
pmc-11798940:
Amare Abera Tareke and three co-authors pinpoint which groups of women in sub-Saharan Africa face the highest risk of malnutrition in either direction. Their study was published in twenty twenty-four. The region fights underweight and rising obesity at once, a double burden.

Health survey data covered nearly two hundred forty-eight thousand women of childbearing age in thirty-three countries. Pooled rates were eleven percent underweight, eighteen percent overweight, and ten percent obese. Age, schooling, wealth, breastfeeding, contraception, and number of children all shifted the risks. So did media exposure, marital status, and urban or rural home. East and west regions differed as well. The authors rank where programs should aim first.
pmc-11831340:
Maciej Banach and seven colleagues set out a position paper on stopping eye damage in people with diabetes, endorsed by a Polish lipid group, in a twenty twenty-four paper. The eye disease, retinopathy, affects up to forty percent of diabetic patients and can end in surgery or blindness. It can even appear in people with early blood sugar problems. The paper centers on a lipid drug, fenofibrate, with a long record in eye trials.

The authors review how the drug may shield the retina, plus proof of its safety and effect. They argue care should target blood fats and their fallout, not blood sugar alone. The paper ends by backing fenofibrate use to prevent this complication.
pmc-11831540:
Family doctors and nurses carry heavy loads, and Nataša Trifunović led a team that measured what drives their stress in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Two hundred and seventy-two primary care workers filled in a standard ten-question stress scale in the summer of twenty twenty-two. Most were women, and most were physicians, with an average age near forty-five.

Daily patient load and years on the job both pushed stress up. Nurses reported more stress than physicians. Men and older workers scored slightly lower, while marriage and more children nudged scores up. The measured factors explained only a tenth of the spread, so much of the stress story lies elsewhere. The team calls for deeper work and targeted relief.
pmc-11851640:
Hector Acosta-Rodriguez and co-authors report a study from two thousand twenty-four linking children's test scores to brain scans. The tests come from a standard battery that yields scores for fluid thinking, learned knowledge, and a total score. Schools and clinics use them widely, but what they reflect in the brain was unclear.

The team used data from a large study of child brain growth, with more than five thousand children near age ten. Higher fluid scores went with healthier white matter, thinner cortex in places, and larger surface area. Learned-knowledge scores showed a more mixed pattern, in part the reverse. The authors say the total score blends the two, which can blur what each part really means.
pmc-11999240:
Yazdi and seven co-authors tested in twenty twenty-four a pine scent compound on breast cancer cells in the lab. The compound, alpha-pinene, may slow cancer growth. They tracked two genes: one that spurs cell spread, miR-21, and one that brakes it, PTEN.

Cells dosed with the compound lived less well at two days than at one day. At mid doses the spread gene fell in a clear way. The brake gene rose by the same kind of shift, most at the mid-high dose. The team says the pair of shifts could cut spread and growth, and may aid care.
pmc-12663740:
Yanming Tuo and ten colleagues tracked how gallic acid changes as white tea ages, and modeled its anti-aging potential. White tea is a traditional Chinese tea whose chemistry evolves in storage. Gallic acid is one of its antioxidant, anti-inflammatory components. Liquid chromatography measured the compound across storage times, alongside antioxidant capacity. Computer-based network pharmacology then predicted the compound's anti-aging targets.

Gallic acid content rose with storage time, and antioxidant potency rose with it. The network analysis nominated forty possible targets, with six standing out as hubs. Enrichment analysis tied the effects to several biological pathways. The twenty twenty-five study is computational and chemical rather than clinical. It gives tea scientists a mechanism map to test in living systems, and a reason aged white tea commands its premium.
pmc-12664140:
Yun Hong Du and a large team find that the COVID virus's entry protein is ferried to a tiny cell antenna by a trafficking protein. Their study was published in twenty twenty-five. The virus enters through the surface protein ACE2, but its movement inside the cell was unresolved.

The ferry protein, TULP3, normally guides cargo into the primary cilium, a hair-like sensor on many cells. The two proteins bind each other. Removing TULP3 stripped ACE2 from the cilium and blunted entry of virus-like particles. Lab models, imaging, and genetic tweaks all supported the link. The route hints at a fresh way to block infection: stop the ferry, not just the lock.
pmc-12686440:
Yang Xia and colleagues report a two thousand twenty-five study diagnosing tiny invasive lung nodules from blood immune profiles. Small lung growths are hard to classify without surgery. Immune dysfunction accompanies cancer growth, so blood cells may carry the answer.

Immune cells from blood were profiled one by one with mass cytometry across several centers. Machine learning turned those profiles into a management platform. It separated invasive from harmless nodules with excellent accuracy. It also graded invasiveness between early cancer types. Both jobs beat standard clinical and imaging models, promising sharper decisions about who truly needs surgery.
pmc-12690540:
Abigail Poff, Nicole Moss, and Debra Silver published a 2025 study of a mouse model of DDX3X syndrome, a rare developmental disorder. Mutations in the DDX3X gene, which sits on the X chromosome and helps control protein production, cause cortical malformations and autism features. About two hundred variants are known; half change a single protein building block.

Earlier mouse models removed the gene's function entirely. This team instead built a mouse carrying one severe, recurrent missense variant, T532M, switched on in cortical progenitor cells. They examined how this precise change impairs cortical development and the translational control of proteins. Modeling the exact human variant matters because missense changes may act differently from simple gene loss.
pmc-12693340:
Rawat, Blachnio, Liberska, and Pinto study physical activity, body image, and anxiety in youth, in work from twenty twenty-five. Body image, physical self concept, and anxiety are tightly intertwined in young people. Social media and appearance culture have intensified self evaluation pressure.

More than two hundred young adults aged eighteen to thirty-five were surveyed. Body appreciation, physical self concept, self esteem, and anxiety were all measured. The study asked whether activity protects mental health or, in appearance focused settings, adds anxiety. The answer matters for how schools and gyms frame exercise to young people: health first, or looks first.
pmc-12695140:
Regina Kohlbecher and Thomas Müller build two families of fluorescent ring compounds through chained palladium-catalyzed reactions, in a two thousand twenty-five chemistry paper. The targets, phenanthridinones and crinasiadines, include natural products toxic to cancer cell lines.

One sequence concatenates Buchwald-Hartwig amination, Suzuki coupling, and lactamization from simple bromoanilines to give nitrogen-aryl products. A modified order yields nitrogen-alkyl versions, including two natural products. The aryl derivatives fluoresce with dual emission, glowing from both a locally excited state and a charge-transfer state. Quantum chemical calculations trace the two bands to two conformations of the molecule in its excited state, explaining the unusual double glow.
pmc-12698040:
Sangrak Bae and co-authors model what would happen if South Korea gave the nine-type HPV vaccine to boys as well as girls, in a study from two thousand twenty-five. The current plan gives a four-type vaccine to girls only. A spread model for the virus was fitted to the Korean population and run far into the future.

The wider plan was projected to prevent large counts of warts, early cell changes, and cancers in both sexes over one hundred years. Cost per year of healthy life gained fell below the accepted Korean limit. Gains in males included fewer warts and fewer anal and throat cancers. Readers get a full cost and health case for the wider plan.
pmc-12708640:
Alsaid Ahmed Almetwally seeks the best settings for spinning stretchy cotton yarn with a spandex core, in a study from two thousand twenty-five. The yarn wraps cotton fibers around a stretchy filament. Settings such as draft ratio, filament weight, and twist shape strength, fuzz, and flaw counts at the same time.

A full test grid paired a robust design method with a grey scoring method. One combined score ranked all setting mixes. The best mix used a set twist level, a mid-weight filament, and a set draft ratio. Almetwally offers the pairing as a template for tuning other yarn lines.
pmc-12709740:
Kassahun Tafesse Hidoto and co-authors find what opens or blocks mother care access in the Wolaita Zone of southern Ethiopia, in a study from two thousand twenty-five. Three hundred sixty women took part, split into access and no-access groups for comparison. Interviews ran in spring two thousand twenty-three.

Women who felt a need for care, could seek it, could reach it, and could pay for it all reached care far more often. Seeing services as welcoming also raised access. Each factor held its own weight in the joint analysis. The authors urge local leaders to back outreach, money power, and women's say in choices. Readers get a plain ladder of steps that each gate care.
pmc-12711040:
Chenjian Qiu and six co-authors map a rare tumor that makes too much stomach acid hormone, using a national cancer database. The study covered 160 patients in the United States diagnosed across two decades. Most tumors sat in the pancreas, with the small bowel next. Most were slow-growing and well formed, and the liver was a common site of spread.

Survival was best for tumors in the small bowel and worst for those in the pancreas. Age and tumor size raised the risk of spread to the liver. The paper gives a broad picture of this rare disease and the traits that shape outcome.
pmc-12718240:
Wongsombat and colleagues published in twenty twenty-five a search for strong gene switches in a Burkholderia bacterium. Some bacteria make useful natural products, but their genes are often silent. A strong promoter, a DNA switch that stays on, can wake those genes. The team read the genome of one strain and tracked which genes ran hottest. They guessed the DNA just before those genes held strong switches.

They tested twenty-six candidate switches in two other bacteria. Two switches beat the rest in both hosts. Swapping them into product gene clusters raised yields of two compounds. One product blocks a cell signal protein of medical interest. The switches could help unlock hidden products in many Gram-negative bacteria.
pmc-12725540:
Liangqiang Lin and co-authors map mosquito bite risk in Shenzhen in a 2025 paper. Aedes mosquitoes spread dengue and other viruses, and city growth plus climate change widen their range. A full spatial picture of bite risk was missing for subtropical cities.

The team built risk from three layers: hazard, exposure, and vulnerability. Mosquito density maps came from surveillance data fitted with geographic models. Population density supplied the exposure layer. Social and economic traits, weighted by location, formed the vulnerability layer. The combined map shows where bite risk concentrates, guiding targeted public health action.
pmc-12727840:
Kim and six co-authors built light tweezers for magnetic whirlpools in this paper from twenty twenty-five. Skyrmions are tiny swirling patterns in a magnet that could carry data in future devices. Moving one precisely has been hard, since currents push them sideways and defects pin them. The team instead used heat from light to trap them.

A focused beam carved a warm potential well that held a single skyrmion. The trap could drag the particle along a chosen path. The group also created and erased skyrmions on demand with light. Mixing optical and electrical control gave a fully programmable platform. The authors aim it at reconfigurable skyrmion devices.
pmc-12728040:
Banks and nine co-authors tell how they drew Black mothers and teen daughters into a program with culture-shaped plans, in work from twenty twenty-five. Black Girls Move runs twelve weeks by phone and aims to head off obesity in girls and their mothers. Blocks in systems, and blocks between people, call for sign-up plans made to fit. Trust anchors the team's work with the community.

A look back finds trust counts most, from screening through the start line. The weight rule for who could join shut out too many girls. Sign-up goals had to leave room for schools that drop out. Other demands cut into how much pairs took part. The fixes widen who can join, pay more, and add a community health worker. Sign-ups and taking part rose once the changes landed. The team calls for a large trial of these plans.
pmc-12730340:
Rebecca Sparavelli and eight co-authors published a molecular pathology study in twenty twenty-five separating two look-alike thyroid tumors. A recent classification made the invasive encapsulated follicular variant its own entity, distinct from the infiltrative variant still classed under papillary carcinoma. Telling them apart under the microscope can be genuinely hard.

Gene expression profiling of twenty-three tumors, split between the two types, found forty-seven genes differing significantly. Two stood out, both bound up with the extracellular matrix that surrounds tumor cells: TIMP2 and COL1A2, strongly upregulated in the infiltrative type. The authors argue the matrix, not just the cancer cells, carries the signature that separates these diagnoses.
pmc-12732840:
Chen and five co-authors test how a milk protein mix helps plant gels stand up to freeze and thaw in this twenty twenty-five study. Frozen foods can lose their bite and weep water when they thaw out. The gels here join two plant gums used in many soft food goods.

Inside, gels with the milk mix held far more water than plain gels did. Adding the first plant gum pushed water hold higher still, near the top of the scale. Hardness also rose, and freeze-thaw rounds left the firm feel much the same. The team says the mix of parts gives food makers a way to build frozen gels that stay firm and moist.
pmc-12733440:
Michael Kimmeyer and eight colleagues report outcomes of shoulder tendon repair boosted with a collagen scaffold, in a twenty twenty-five study. Thirty patients had large rotator cuff tears at high risk of tearing again. Keyhole surgery fixed the tendon and laid a cow collagen patch over it to spur regrowth. Twenty-one were first repairs and nine were redos. Scores and scans were checked at six and twelve months.

At one year, over half the tendons had healed fully, though about a quarter healed poorly. Shoulder value, pain, and function scores all rose well past the marks patients can feel. Two patients stiffened and one needed revision. The authors call the patch a sound aid for risky tears.
pmc-12735340:
Agnieszka Kącka-Zych, Luis Domingo, and colleagues published a 2025 chemistry study on ring-forming reactions. The reactions join two molecules into a four-sided ring, a step used to build complex compounds. Their test case is a strained ring compound loaded with eight fluorine atoms.

Using electron density theory and computer models, the team traced how the joining unfolds step by step. The fluorine atoms make the ring compound hungry for electrons, so the reaction takes a polar path. A twin compound without fluorine needs far more heat for the same step. Tests covered three partners: ethylene, benzene, and styrene. The work shows how small atom swaps can flip how a reaction runs.
pmc-12735940:
Livia Moreira Genaro and co-authors published a proof-of-concept study in twenty twenty-five on a hard lab test in Crohn's disease care. pmc-13214340:

pmc-13216340:

pmc-13218140:

pmc-13219040:

pmc-13219940:

Those with both Pseudomonas and Klebsiella had the lowest blood oxygen levels.
pmc-13274240:
Sophie Ruf and a large team report a 2026 journal article on chemical tags on DNA in blood that track fat tissue health in obesity. The tags, called methylation, can switch genes up or down. Working across four cohorts of children and adults, the team focused on two genes, EIF5A and TGIF1.

EIF5A tags tracked with body mass index, blood sugar control, and white-cell counts, especially in type 2 diabetes. In children, EIF5A tags tracked with later blood sugar paths. Childhood TGIF1 tags predicted later fat mass and blood sugar even in children who were normal weight when sampled.
pmc-13274540:
David H Barad and co-authors studied whether ovarian reserve shapes use of embryo genetic testing in IVF in a 2026 analysis. Testing embryos for chromosome number is common, especially at older ages, but clinics may also select patients by expected egg yield. The team used a national United States registry.

They examined 258,532 first treatment cycles from 2014 to 2021 in women aged twenty-one to forty-six using their own eggs. Reserve was judged mainly by anti-Müllerian hormone levels in the year before treatment. Higher hormone levels meant higher odds of using the genetic test, and the pattern held after adjustment and inside every age group. Results were the same whether the hormone was treated as a scale or split at a low threshold.
pmc-13275740:
Eldad Keha and co-authors offer a 2026 dataset paper for cognitive science, the study of how the mind works. People link many objects to a typical color, such as grass with green. Researchers use these word and color links often, but word lists were usually picked without proper testing.

In a first study, nearly three hundred people rated one hundred forty-three words for their strongest linked color and how strong that link felt. From those ratings the team kept seventy-nine strong words across eleven colors. Two more studies, in Britain and the United States, tested the list with a word and color matching task. Words in matching colors got faster answers, which confirmed the list works. Subjective link strength also matched the size of that effect.
pmc-13276140:
Yukihiro Kajita and co-authors report a 2026 study on surgery for a hidden type of shoulder tendon tear. In intratendinous tears, the rotator cuff tendon splits inside itself without breaking through. There is no agreement on the best operation for these tears.

Surgeons first turned each hidden tear into a full-thickness tear with a heat device, then repaired it with a suture-bridge method that presses the tendon down with crossed stitches. Twenty-one patients were followed for at least a year. Shoulder lifting and outward rotation both improved clearly. All four scoring systems the team used showed large gains, some roughly doubling. No patient tore the tendon again during follow-up. The authors present the approach as a favorable option for tears that fail months of non-surgical care.
pmc-13276340:
Tingting Li and Yiyao Liu write a 2026 commentary on why the heart so rarely hosts cancer. Tumours almost never start in heart muscle, and spread to the heart is also uncommon. The piece discusses a recent report by Ciucci and co-workers on mechanical load in the heart.

That work used mice engineered with strong cancer-driving mutations, yet tumours grew in other tissues and never in the heart. Transplant experiments that unloaded the heart supported a mechanical explanation. Constant beating may itself suppress cancer cell growth, the commentary argues. The idea reframes physical force in tissues as a built-in defence, not only a factor that helps tumours spread.
pmc-13276440:
Linchao Chen and co-authors present a 2026 journal article on a wind-powered generator that uses rabbit hair to monitor railways. Remote track sections need constant watching but lack power supplies. Triboelectric nanogenerators harvest energy from rubbing materials, and soft flexible contact can make them last longer.

Their device pairs an energy harvesting unit with a generation unit using rabbit hair contact. The team modeled the circuit, simulated performance, and tuned the structure experimentally. At a modest spin speed, a single unit produced over two thousand volts and measurable power in the milliwatt range. Linking units in parallel was studied as well. After more than three million working cycles, charge output had fallen by only about seven percent. The authors present the design as a durable, self-powered option for railway line monitoring.
pmc-13276540:
Soukaina Abidi and co-authors wrote a 2026 letter to the editor asking whether artificial intelligence in dental training is a tool or a crutch. Software now supports diagnosis, imaging reads, and treatment planning across dentistry. The letter responds to a pilot study on how Dutch dental professionals and students accept these tools.

The authors praise the benefits: diagnostic support, efficiency, and fewer human errors. Their worry is skill decay among students. Experienced dentists, by contrast, can use the software as a second opinion. The letter urges staged access: teach core skills first, then introduce the tools with lessons on their limits and biases.
pmc-13276740:
Takaaki Mori and co-authors present a 2026 case report on an unexpected sight during a liver cancer procedure. Chemoembolization delivers chemotherapy and blocking oil through the tumor's feeding artery. Seeing the oil outline the liver's lymph vessels is uncommon, and it stopped this procedure midway.

During oil injection, abnormal brightening spread toward the liver's root, suggesting an artery-to-lymph connection. She felt no symptoms. A scan a month later showed the oil sitting in lymph vessels and in lymph nodes up to the collarbone, yet she stayed well. Six months later a repeat procedure showed no lymph leak at all. The authors blame a temporary connection, possibly from cirrhosis-swollen lymph channels and earlier bile duct infection injury.
pmc-13277140:
Wenchen Song and colleagues tracked how the COVID virus changed inside obese mice in 2026. Obesity weakens immune defence, worsens infection outcomes, and blunts vaccine responses. Using mice made obese by diet, with and without an mRNA vaccine, the team studied mutation of an Omicron variant inside the host under different immune states.

Lung gene activity and viral changes were measured together. Changes in two viral genes tracked with the host's built-in immune response. One change in the membrane gene appeared in every vaccinated obese mouse lung but rarely in unvaccinated ones, hinting at interplay between viral mutation and antiviral defence in obesity. The work links weak vaccine response to viral evolution.
pmc-13277440:
Mónika Nogel wrote a 2026 policy review on elimination DNA databases in European forensic work. Such databases hold DNA profiles of lab staff and crime-scene workers, so their DNA can be ruled out when it turns up on evidence by accident. Practice differs widely across Europe, the review finds.

Well-run databases catch contamination early, prevent false leads, and protect cross-border DNA exchange. The author argues they fall under European data protection law and proposes shared minimum rules. Checks should be forced before profiles enter national systems, staff data must stay separate from criminal databases, and profiles should be deleted when staff leave. Research on how well the systems work is a stated priority.
pmc-13277740:
Erin Rivera leads a 2026 field study of a rove beetle that feeds only on wounded stingless bees in tropical forests. Stingless bees of the genus Trigona fight fiercely over rich food sources, leaving injured and dead workers behind. What eats that remains was little known. Observations and choice tests were run at sites in Peru and Costa Rica.

The beetles consistently chose injured or freshly killed Trigona workers. They ignored carrion and other insects offered, including flies, grasshoppers, and other stingless bee genera. Such narrow specialization links bee warfare to predator evolution. The work also shows that dead social insects are a real food-web resource in rainforests, not mere waste.
pmc-13278440:
Chih-Yu Chen leads a 2026 analysis of whether starting order affects results in men's artistic gymnastics finals. Judges might, in theory, score later performers more generously. The team analyzed apparatus finals from three Olympic Games and nine World Championships, testing links between start order, final rank, scores, and medals.

Across most apparatus, start order showed no significant link to rankings or medals. The pommel horse was the exception: gymnasts starting in the second half earned higher execution scores and more medals. Medal shares for European and non-European athletes were similar in all groupings. The judging system looks broadly fair, the authors conclude, with execution stability the pommel horse lesson.
pmc-13279040:
Sophie Buhelt and colleagues published a 2026 study of spinal fluid inflammation in people with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis treated with natalizumab. The drug blocks immune cells from entering the brain and spinal cord. The team measured fifteen inflammatory and tissue markers in 88 treated patients, 104 untreated patients, and 94 controls. They asked whether inflammation inside the spinal fluid fully settles during treatment, especially after more than five years.

Most markers fell to control levels or below in treated patients, yet a few stayed raised, including soluble CD27, soluble BCMA, and the IgG index. pmc-13279740:
Jasmin Bauer and colleagues report a 2026 computer model study of a gas eating bacterium. Acetobacterium woodii turns hydrogen and carbon dioxide in acetate, a simple acid, by an old pathway. It juggles three electron carrier types to keep energy flow in tight limits. The team built a large metabolic model, a full map of cell chemistry, with energy values and level bounds built in.

Swaps of which carrier a step uses were then tested in the model. In theory, apt swaps could raise growth five fold over the wild type. That peak needed very high gas levels and tight carrier states. More realistic swaps, with stronger drive and wider ranges, still gave up to two and a half fold growth gains. Gains for product output were mapped as well. Model swaps point to strain designs worth lab tests.
pmc-13280340:
Dilinapa Alemujiang and colleagues report a 2026 study of ear cartilage cells grown long term in the lab. Primary chondrocytes, cartilage making cells, often lose their matrix forming power as they expand in dishes. That loss limits scalable cartilage engineering. Mouse ear chondrocytes were expanded in flat culture to passage forty or fifty, at high and low seed densities. Growth, shape and aging status were tracked over the run.

Both seed densities kept growth steady across extended passages. Cells held stable growth past passage fifty with minimal aging features, and were not immortalized. A conserved nine gene decline module, a set of nine genes that fall together, marked late passage loss. The loss ran apart from cell aging, which the authors call dedifferentiation.
pmc-13280540:
Yongsheng Hai and team give a 2026 review of vehicle road wear microplastics and their effects on nature. These are tiny polymer bits shed by the vehicle road system. Tire road wear bits form the dominant class, with road marking wear and other debris in the set. Their complex chemistry and wide size range pose risks to ecosystems. Mixed terms and nonstandard test methods hinder cross study comparison. A tyre centred focus and thin field monitoring hide the share of pavement materials and of real exposure scenes. Past studies stress tyre sources, so formation paths stay incomplete. Thin long term data limit what is known of migration, change and risk in nature. From a road engineering view, the review joins the full life of the bits.
pmc-13280640:
Shiying You and colleagues published a 2026 cost study on new ways to deliver HIV care in Africa. Clinics now offer care outside the usual visit model, in groups or at home. The team used two math models to project health and costs from 2022 to 2062. They studied South Africa, Malawi, Zambia, and a broad group of poorer African states.

Group care led by health workers gave good value in every setting. Urban groups run by clients also gave good value, though results were less sure. Home delivery of drugs cost more and did worse than the urban groups. The authors say group models are a smart use of tight HIV budgets.
pmc-13280940:
Linda Fabisch and colleagues published a 2026 study of sex differences in the causes and imaging signatures of intracerebral hemorrhage, bleeding into the brain. Most bleeds stem from small vessel disease, yet whether men and women differ had been unclear. Pooling two large cohorts from London and Graz with MRI, the team analyzed 1,043 patients averaging 66. pmc-13281240:
Nele Kornder and colleagues refined a digital aid for cutting unneeded drugs in a 2026 study. Many patients in family care take drugs they no longer need. Key changes built a live drug database that stays current. Drugs were sorted into three groups, for symptoms, in-between uses, and prevention, each with its own decision path. A straight-line path was added for preventive drugs, the hardest to stop. The authors stress the study improved the tool's design. Testing whether it changes health outcomes comes later.
pmc-13281540:
Arslan Ahmad and colleagues published a 2026 mouse study showing that soluble soybean fiber switches on the small intestine's antimicrobial defenses through a relay involving tuft cells and innate immune cells. pmc-13282040:
Xingyue Su and co-authors wrote a 2026 interview study on digital assistive tools for carers of older adults with cognitive impairment, meaning problems with memory and thinking. Set in fast-aging China, the study asked why carers accept or reject tools such as training apps, wearable monitors, and smart home systems. The authors used a well-known model that weighs how useful and how easy a tool feels.

Feeling useful and easy helped carers accept them, but family views, worry about technology, and outside support also mattered. Carers stressed that tools must change as thinking declines. Human carers, they said, stay essential for comfort, judgement, and crises. The authors urge makers and services to design with carers, not just for patients.
pmc-13284740:

Ten patients, with median age 90 years and high frailty scores, all had the stent placed with success in this small pilot set. Nine reached clinical success. One very ill patient died on the first day after the procedure, before results could be judged. Median placement time was short. The authors urge careful patient choice and larger studies.
pmc-13285140:
Sara Paniziutti and co-authors report a 2026 materials study on printed sensors that glow in response to harmful vapors. pmc-13285540:
Nika Kuridze, Kakhaber Etsadashvili, and Eteri Minadze report a prospective trial of the heart drug ethacizine in people with frequent early heartbeats. Published in 2026, the ETHAPRO study enrolled 98 patients whose extra beats exceeded one thousand per day despite earlier treatment. Extra beats from the upper chambers and from the lower chambers were both included.

The authors describe the safety record as favorable over the follow-up period.
pmc-13285640:
A JAK blocker calmed a stubborn face swelling from filler shots, Mengying Duan and co-authors write in a 2026 letter. Standard antibiotic and steroid care barely helped, and scans plus a skin sample confirmed foreign body granuloma.

Such lumps mar looks and weigh on mood, and filler mishaps rise as shots grow popular. The letter offers the drug as a fresh option for hard cases, while a single case cannot set dosing or safety for wide use.
pmc-13285740:
Yu-Ru Lin and co-authors study hearing loss and behavior change in Alzheimer's disease in a 2026 case-control study. The team followed newly diagnosed patients for a year to see whether hearing problems came first.

Among 387 patients living at home, hearing status was judged by the need for help during testing. After one year, the hearing-impaired group showed more marked apathy and more sleep disturbance than the rest. The links held after age, sex, schooling, and starting scores were taken into account. The authors advise care teams to watch these two symptoms closely in patients who hear poorly and to plan care that deals with both.
pmc-13285940:
Wan-Yu Lo and colleagues compare two carriers for a healing microRNA in diabetic wounds in a 2026 mouse study. pmc-13286140:

pmc-13286440:

pmc-13287540:

pmc-13287840:

pmc-13288040:

pmc-13288140:

pmc-13288440:

pmc-13288540:

pmc-13288940:

pmc-13289140:

pmc-13289340:

pmc-13289640:

pmc-13289740:

pmc-13290340:

pmc-13290540:

pmc-13291140:

pmc-13291440:

Still, the chart helps local teams sort likely causes fast.
pmc-13291540:

pmc-13294640:

pmc-13294840:

pmc-13295040:

pmc-13295440:
Wei Huang and colleagues test a helpful bacterium against infection in hybrid sturgeon in a 2026 study. pmc-13295740:

pmc-13296440:

pmc-13296840:

pmc-13297040:

pmc-13297240:

pmc-13297540:

pmc-13298040:

pmc-13298540:

pmc-13298640:

pmc-13299340:

pmc-13309840:

pmc-13310640:

pmc-13310940:

pmc-13311140:
