A single abasic site at the center unsettled nearby bases on a sub-microsecond timescale, an effect absent from a perfectly paired strand. One mismatched pair barely disturbed the structure, but three mismatches in a row mimicked the abasic site's disruption closely. The authors say the work clarifies how the size of a defect, not just its presence, governs local DNA instability.
pmc-13312640:
Qian Xu and colleagues grow stem cells as tiny balls to better shield the eye's pigment layer, in this study from twenty twenty-six. The pigment layer fails in age-related macular degeneration, worn down by oxidative stress and smoldering inflammation. Stem cells from umbilical cord can protect it, but flat-grown cells survive poorly and whisper weakly once delivered.

Cells grown as three-dimensional spheroids spoke louder and protected better. In dishes, they kept pigment cells alive under chemical attack and cut their death rate. In animals, they preserved retinal structure and function. The mechanism ran through autophagy, the cell's self-cleaning: spheroids raised it and shut down a key inflammation switch. Blocking autophagy undid the protection, and boosting it helped more. The authors present ball-grown cells as a stronger candidate therapy for a leading cause of blindness.
pmc-13312840:
Yun-Gyeong Choi and Sang-Hun Oh report, in a 2026 study, the complete chloroplast genome of Viburnum furcatum, a deciduous shrub scattered across Korea, Japan, Sakhalin, and the Kuril Islands. Its fragmented island-and-mainland range makes the species a good model for tracing how plants spread and diverged around northeastern Asia, and a full chloroplast sequence gives that work a firm reference.

Sequenced from a specimen collected on Ulleungdo Island, Korea, the genome forms the usual four-part circle of 158,284 base pairs, with large and small single-copy regions separated by two inverted repeats. Annotation found 128 genes in total, including 83 protein-coding genes, 37 transfer RNA genes, and 8 ribosomal RNA genes. Family tree analysis placed the species as sister to Viburnum sympodiale within the Pseudotinus group. The authors offer the data for future classification and population studies of the genus.
pmc-13313040:
Márcio Gonçalves dos Santos and colleagues present a 2026 integrative review of ways to get oral medicine into dogs and cats without a fight. Pilling pets is a notorious weak point of veterinary care: animals resist, owners give up, and treatment fails. Drug makers have turned to hiding medicine inside treats and chewable tablets animals actually want.

Following PRISMA-style procedures across four databases, the review gathered twenty studies on medicated treats, chewables, and kindred formulations. The evidence suggests these products can raise adherence, lower handling stress, and keep drug performance acceptable when the recipe is right, though the food matrix and feeding conditions can shift absorption. Stubborn problems remain: keeping doses uniform, holding the products stable and germ-free on the shelf, and deciding how regulators should class these drug-food hybrids. The authors call for formulation work and clearer rules.
pmc-13313240:
Sara Cooper and a large team present a 2026 synthesis of why people hesitate over the HPV vaccine, drawing on a 2025 Cochrane review of views from around the world. The vaccine is a strong tool against cancer and sits at the heart of plans to end cervical cancer as a public health threat, yet uptake lags in many places.

The synthesis pools 71 studies from varied places and income levels on what caregivers and teens think and do about the shot. It finds that choices turn on a web of social, cultural, political, and trust factors, not just facts about gains and risks. The team grouped these forces into eight themes and built a frame to explain vaccine reluctance. That frame gives programs a way to craft messages that meet real worries rather than repeat facts alone.
pmc-13314740:
Jianing Li and colleagues teach deep learning models to spot a narrow upper jaw from mouth photos, in a 2026 study. Maxillary transverse deficiency is now judged by cone-beam CT scans, which add radiation, cost, and clinic work.

Frontal photos inside the mouth are taken as routine in orthodontic care. The team trained six known image networks on photos from 826 patients, with a further 192 patients held for outside tests, as counted in the report. Labels came from two standard analyses of the paired CT scans. Five-fold cross-checks tuned each model, and scores such as accuracy and recall were read on both test sets. If photos can flag the fault well, many patients could skip a scan and clinics could screen faster and cheaper.
pmc-13315440:
Shweta Chhajed and co-authors study, in a 2026 paper, how the mustard oil bomb defense system of Arabidopsis thaliana is divided among the plant's cell types. Plants in the Brassicales order store glucosinolates, sulfur compounds that sit harmless until tissue damage brings them together with myrosinase enzymes. That meeting releases bioactive products that repel herbivores and pathogens, a dual chemical weapon often nicknamed the mustard oil bomb.

The chemistry of the system is mapped in bulk tissue, but a bomb this dangerous needs storage. Fuel and detonator must be kept apart inside the intact plant, then mixed instantly when a bite tears cells open. The authors focus on that compartmentalization problem at single-cell-type resolution, examining where the glucosinolates and their activating enzymes reside across Arabidopsis cell types and what each location contributes to the defense. Their work addresses how plants organize a chemical arsenal inside living tissue.
pmc-13315640:
Santiago Uribe-Diaz and co-authors tested a skin-delivered Salmonella vaccine in 2026 in broiler chickens. On-farm control of Salmonella Enteritidis needs vaccines that spark fast local defense and grow into lasting body-wide and gut protection. So the team used a killed vaccine boosted by a CD40-targeting DNA aptamer.

Thirty chicks were split into six small groups. They got salt solution, a chitosan-based vaccine, or the aptamer vaccine, given once into the skin or with an earlier under-skin prime and skin boost. Blood and cloacal swabs tracked specific IgY and IgA antibodies, and growing feather tissue showed local white cell recruitment after each dose.
pmc-13315840:
Min Zhang and colleagues examined in 2026 how plasma transfusion relates to death in hospital among critically ill patients. Plasma is often given in intensive care for reasons other than bleeding, on thin evidence, so the team used records from 282 transfused adults treated during 2020.

Patients were grouped by plasma exposure and by volume given. Matching and adjusted survival models were used to separate the transfusion effect from starting illness. Unadjusted results linked plasma with much higher death risk, and dose-response checks with survival curves tested whether larger volumes meant larger risk. Subgroup checks looked for groups where the pattern differed.
pmc-13316540:
Rita SM Simões and colleagues, in 2026, explain how surface charge networks set the heat sensitivity of an enzyme used to stop contamination in DNA tests. Uracil-DNA glycosylase removes stray uracil, then must be switched off by gentle heating. Existing versions switch off across too narrow a range for newer low-temperature tests.

Searching thousands of bacterial sequences, the team built a panel of 24 enzymes and found one that works well when cool yet inactivates sharply near 45 degrees. Its crystal structure showed a conserved active site. Targeted changes at 48 surface positions, followed by screening of hundreds of mutants, yielded variants that stayed active at room temperature but stopped at lower temperatures. Heat sensitivity appears spread across a surface network, separate from catalysis.
pmc-13316640:
Mehdi Borni and colleagues present a 2026 case of IgG4-related disease, a body-wide scarring and immune condition, attacking the clivus bone and nasal cavity of a healthy 42-year-old man. He had suffered three years of stubborn headaches before the cause emerged.

Scans showed an aggressive, hungry-looking mass eating into the skull base bone, and a camera-guided biopsy proved the diagnosis, with marker ratios well past the set thresholds. His pain pattern mimicked Arnold's neuralgia, a presentation the team says has never been reported for this disease. Steroid treatment alone eased his headaches almost fully and quickly. The case urges doctors to weigh this rare disease when odd head and neck pain meets a skull base lump.
pmc-13317540:
Junji Lin and co-authors validate, in a 2026 study, a severity scale for idiopathic hypersomnia, a disorder of overwhelming sleepiness with no clear cause. A trusted patient-reported scale helps trials measure whether treatments truly help.

Twenty patients in interviews described eighteen symptoms, with daytime sleepiness and emotional impact named by everyone, and all confirmed the scale's questions made sense as written. Scoring data came from 115 trial participants in a phase three drug study. The scale proved consistent and stable, tracked other sleep and impression measures sensibly, and reacted strongly to change. A three-point rise marks a change patients can feel, giving future trials a clear yardstick.
pmc-13318040:
Rongkang Pei, Zeyu Lyu, Guolong Wang, and Cheong Kim propose, in a 2026 computing paper, a transformer model that dissects how stories unfold on social media during public events. It joins feeling, topic, and time in one pass. Older methods treated those threads separately and stumbled on noisy, cross-event posts.

Their model, ST-TAN, builds on a RoBERTa language encoder with three added modules for emotion, theme, and sequence timing. Tests showed it beating four families of rival models on story structure, feeling, and topic tasks, while holding up on new events and messy text. A full ethics discussion covers privacy, anonymization, and bias. The tool targets opinion monitoring and public event governance teams.
pmc-13318540:
Christoff G. Furin and colleagues report a 2026 survey of PFAS chemicals in muscle tissue from fish and shellfish of commercial importance harvested in Alaska. Seafood can be a meaningful route by which these long-lasting synthetic compounds reach people.

Laboratory testing covered 40 PFAS compounds, and ten were found above the detection limit, with PFTrDA and PFUnA turning up most often. Levels were generally low or absent, reaching at most 0.809 ng/g wet weight in the samples measured, and most sat below the level that could be reliably counted. With no national PFAS limits yet set for fish, the authors frame continued monitoring as the basis for future exposure judgements and rules.
pmc-13318640:
Jianwei Zhang and colleagues analyse, in a 2026 multicentre cohort study, whether four obesity-linked insulin resistance indices predict chronic kidney disease in people who already have both diabetes and coronary heart disease. Their data covered 7,741 patients from three centres.

All four indices tied to higher kidney risk after adjustment, and spline curves showed thresholds beyond which risk climbed steeply. One index reflecting visceral fat and insulin resistance, METS-VF, predicted best and added most value across curve, time, and decision analyses. The authors argue these simple indices could sharpen kidney risk checks in this high-risk group, with METS-VF first among them for spotting who needs closer monitoring and earlier action.
pmc-13319040:
Happiness Ngobeni, Thendo Gertie Makhado, and Lufuno Makhado present a 2026 qualitative study of caregivers for people with epilepsy in two South African provinces. Interviews ran in rural and peri-urban communities in Limpopo and Mpumalanga. Caregivers were informal family carers. Their accounts were grouped into five linked themes.

Caregiving meant constant watch against seizures that strike without warning. Emotional and physical strain ran through daily life. Stigma and low social acceptance shut people out at school, church, and social events. Poverty, transport problems, and thin services added to the load. Caregivers coped through faith, family duty, and careful treatment checks, but those supports were fragile. The authors call for caregiver training, less stigma, and stronger community-based help.
pmc-13319640:
Suseendar Shanmugasundaram and co-authors build a death risk score for lung tuberculosis at first diagnosis in a 2026 study from Tamil Nadu, India. Most deaths in this illness come in the first two months, yet the data logged at diagnosis in routine systems is too thin for early warning. A state triage scheme that flags severe illness at intake gave a richer starting point.

Records for 55971 adults treated in public clinics from July 2022 to June 2023 were used to train the scores. Five simple intake checks, such as weight, breathing rate, and oxygen level, matched the reach of a fuller data model for spotting who would die. Simple scores that work at intake could steer extra care to those at most risk.
pmc-13320340:
Song Yu and co-authors revive old soybean seeds with a natural signal chemical in a 2026 study of sprout quality. Stored seeds age and sprout poorly, which cuts both crop yield and the food value of sprouts. Doses of the signal chemical, found in many plants, were tested on aged seeds with and without a blocker of a key energy path.

Treated seeds sprouted far more often than untreated aged seeds, rising from about a third to near three quarters in the counts reported. A fuel making enzyme more than doubled its activity, and shield levels against cell stress climbed back near fresh seed levels. Chemical scans of thousands of compounds showed the energy path and prized plant compounds switched on. Blocker tests proved the path was required.
pmc-13320440:
Dilisha Patel and co-authors measure unmet need for assistive tools in Sri Lanka in a 2026 mixed methods study from 2024. Tools such as glasses, hearing aids, and wheelchairs guard daily function and sit at the heart of aged care plans, yet use and gaps in the country were unmapped. A world health capacity check was paired with a national household survey for this work.

Survey counts suggest about a third of people live with function trouble, while tool use and unmet need each sat near a sixth of the group in the weighted counts. Unmet need ran higher for older adults, women, and rural and estate dwellers. Talks with 26 key voices and six group chats named cost, poor awareness, social and place blocks, and patchy supply as the main bars.
pmc-13320540:
Daniel Dankl and a large European team ask whether a country's level of development shapes survival after intensive care in old age in a 2026 study. Older adults form a growing share of intensive care admissions. Data came from three large registries of acutely admitted older patients with frailty scores and 30-day outcomes.

Nearly 10,000 patients were included, most treated in countries with very high development scores. Death within 30 days was lower in those countries, at 40.0 percent against 53.3 percent in lower scoring places, and the gap held after checks for age, illness severity, and frailty. Care choices inside units may partly explain the gap, a point the team probed further.
pmc-13322840:
Qi Wang and co-authors map the review evidence on traditional Chinese medicine for thinking problems after stroke, in a 2026 evidence mapping study. They searched English and Chinese databases up to December 2024 for systematic reviews and meta-analyses on this topic.

The map covers 36 reviews, all from China, spanning acupuncture, herbal medicine, moxibustion, ear stimulation and traditional exercises. Quality ratings were poor, with 33 reviews rated critically low and 3 rated low under the AMSTAR 2 tool. Reported effects favoured these treatments for cognition, daily activities and nerve function, yet the authors treat the findings as ideas for testing rather than proof, and call for stronger reviews and trials.
pmc-13323140:
Ninlapat Jidmahawong and colleagues measure how high disease activity harms children with lupus, in a 2026 retrospective cohort study. Their set held 196 patients with childhood-onset systemic lupus erythematosus, diagnosed at a mean age near 11 years and each followed for a year or more.

About two thirds spent some time in high activity, defined by a SLEDAI-2K score of 10 or more in their rules. Those patients accrued organ damage far more often than the rest, and the share of time spent in high activity tracked damage in a dose-like way. Higher time thresholds carried sharply higher hazards of damage. The authors argue for tight, sustained control of activity in childhood lupus.
pmc-13324340:
Jia and co-authors present a model that tracks what a learner knows while admitting doubt about its own read. Systems that model users often treat each item or token as a fixed point. That habit misses links between items and hides how unsure the model should be. Their framework, Adaptive G-UKT, learns the graph of links between items as it goes. It also stores each hidden state as a spread of values, not a single point.

The spread lets the model track both the likely state and the noise around it. Random clicks and stray actions feed that uncertainty rather than warping the estimate. The authors frame the method for knowledge tracing and related sequence tasks. It aims at more honest, stable user models.
pmc-13324440:
Xin Bin and colleagues offer a 2026 study of how oral submucous fibrosis can turn into oral squamous cell carcinoma. The fibrosis is a long-term mouth disease with cancer risk, yet the steps of that change are poorly understood.

Samples of healthy tissue, fibrosis, tumor edge, and cancer were mapped with 10x Visium spatial transcriptomics and combined with single-cell data. Fibroblast changes drove each stage, while immune patterns shifted from active defense in fibrosis to suppression in cancer. A quiet border zone sat at the invasion front, and basal epithelial cells emerged as the main source of cancer cells. The results suggest targets for early action in high-risk patients.
pmc-13324840:
Daniel Martins and co-authors map brain structure changes in post-COVID syndrome in a 2026 study of patients with lasting fatigue after mild infection. The mapping links tissue patterns to genes, cell types, and brain networks.

Normative modeling compared 20 patients with 20 matched healthy controls on cortical thickness, surface area, and deep brain volumes. Patients showed thinner orbitofrontal cortex and thicker sensory areas, though single-region shifts were uncommon. Changes clustered inside connected circuits, touching up to half of patients. Thickness patterns matched expression of TMPRSS2, the protein the virus uses to enter cells. Network modeling traced likely spread from posterior parietal areas. Serotonin, cannabinoid, and other signaling systems featured in the cell analysis.
pmc-13325440:
Paul Ebersbach and colleagues turn routine stained tissue slides into molecular data sources with a laser method in a 2026 study. Standard H and E slides show shape and color but hide the chemistry that guides modern cancer care.

Broadband coherent anti-Stokes Raman scattering reads both vibrations and dye-linked electronic signals from the stain itself. On breast tissue arrays, maps at each pixel picked out subnuclear zones and shrinkage tied to dead tissue. Retrieved spectra split stain signals from processing chemicals. A pattern workflow then sorted nuclei into ductal in situ, invasive ductal, and invasive lobular cancer classes. The proof of concept could unlock hospital slide archives for molecular study.
pmc-13326940:
Myiah Quach and team set out plain HIPAA rules for today's plastic surgery clinics. Their 2026 focused review takes on a snag of this field. Keeping patient facts safe is the law, yet the field leans hard on patient photos, public ads, and online chats, which makes rule-keeping hard.

The review pulls together rule basics, common slips, and hands-on tactics for clinics that keep to the rules. It covers HIPAA's past, core Privacy and Security Rule needs, and fine points on photos, photo data, online chats, and patient consent, plus daily slips. Slips risk leaks of private facts, lost trust, and steep fines and legal trouble. The team aims for advice that is easy to use and fit for surgery clinic work, guarding privacy with no loss of clinic speed. The paper sums up rules and is no stand-in for legal advice.
pmc-13327540:
Ella H M De Nicola and colleagues study day-length effects on cold tolerance in the yellow fever mosquito in a 2026 article. Aedes aegypti keeps pushing into cooler regions as the climate warms, and seasonal tuning in adults is poorly known compared with eggs. The team varied day length and temperature for adult females.

Long days were introduced at parent, egg, or adult stages, and long-day exposure cut the ability to gain cold tolerance, with timing changing how strong the effect was. Cold treatment also shut down daily cycling in two clock genes and paused blood feeding until warmth returned, without changing levels of dormancy-linked gene messages. Day length early in life thus sets limits on adult cold survival.
pmc-13327940:
Zhi-Yin Lei and colleagues examine quality of life in Chinese patients with neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder in a 2026 survey. The nerve disease burdens daily life heavily, yet its mental and social drivers were little studied in China. A total of 216 patients completed disability checks plus scales for mood, sleep, resilience, support, and social strain.

Physical and mental summary scores sat at medians of 55.5 and 51.0, with role limits hurt most, and women made up 85.2 percent of the group. Older age, depression, social avoidance, and poor sleep independently tracked worse physical scores, while depression weighed heaviest on mental scores and resilience protected them. Care plans should treat mind and social life alongside nerves, the authors say.
pmc-13328240:
Carla Cristina de Sousa and team weighed lactulose making with fixed beta-galactosidase across reactor designs. Their 2026 study notes lactulose, a galactose-fructose sugar pair, feeds good gut bacteria as a prebiotic, and is made from lactose and fructose by beta-galactosidase. The team tried enzymes from Kluyveromyces lactis and Aspergillus oryzae, free and fixed, in turn in a bench-top cone reactor, a stirred-tank reactor, and a fixed-bed reactor. Sugars were gauged by high-performance liquid chromatography.

Only silica-fixed Kluyveromyces lactis enzyme failed to give a strong yield, while all three reactor setups proved fit for making. Lactulose levels ran from 19 to 30 grams per liter, with the stirred-tank reactor with magnetic stirring showing the most promise. The team calls the enzyme route a workable path to prebiotic lactulose making, with lessons for future scale-up studies.
pmc-13328340:
Yong Zeng and co-authors benchmark language models on Chinese dental exams in a 2026 study. GPT-4o, GPT-4.5, and DeepSeek-R1 each answered 300 standardized competency questions from one institution's 2023 to 2025 examinations, and scores were set against a real student cohort taking the same papers. Repeat runs checked each model's consistency.

DeepSeek-R1 scored highest overall at 92.33 percent accuracy on the item set, ahead of both rivals in 2023 and 2024 and level with GPT-4.5 in 2025, and it also answered most consistently. Subject domain did not sway accuracy much, while model choice did. The authors see optimized models as helpers for reviewing curricula, with caution beyond this single Mandarin, text-only setting.
pmc-13330540:
Yuanhui Xiao and team built a conductive MXene hydrogel to restore nerve and vessel repair in infected wounds. Their 2026 paper tackles multidrug-resistant bacterial wounds, which heal poorly from lasting infection, excess inflammation, impaired angiogenesis, and weak skin innervation. The gel, built from flower-shaped MXene microspheres with epsilon-poly-L-lysine in an oxidized pullulan network, goes in by needle, heals itself, and sticks to tissue.

The gel kills methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus biofilms, clears reactive oxygen species, and calms inflammation while boosting autophagy. Its traits shape the wound setting, shift macrophages toward healing, and support cell growth, vessel cell movement, and angiogenesis. The conductive gel helps Schwann cells mature, lifts nerve growth factor levels, and rebuilds the nerve setting. In a mouse full-thickness infected wound model, a single use sped closure, boosted skin nerves, and reduced scarring. It offers a drug-free platform for wound healing.
pmc-13331140:
Milon de Jong and colleagues test whether lenalidomide boosts a dual-target antibody that recruits a special T cell type in a 2026 study. The target cells kill tumours without the usual matching limits. Standard drugs for myeloma and marrow disorders were screened for help or harm beside the antibody in lab tests.

Lenalidomide stood out with synergy, lifting T cell activation, granule release, and growth factor output in the reported assays. Paths involved stronger CD28 signalling, Notch activation, and interleukin-2 release. In marrow samples from syndrome patients, the drug enabled T cell growth that the antibody alone failed to spark. A combined clinical test is justified, the authors argue.
pmc-13332440:
Kristin F Hurst and co-authors tested a discussion exercise in 2026 meant to cool political polarization over climate policy in the United States. Their method, moral perspective-taking, asks people to build moral arguments against their own position, framed in the values of the other side.

Four online experiments covered divisive topics such as moving away from fossil fuels and banning fracking. In all four, the exercise shifted policy support and softened views. The first two studies found it raised cognitive empathy for people holding opposing views. The later studies found it lowered resistance to changing one's mind and increased willingness to act on the issue. The authors present the technique as a flexible, scalable tool that could help unlock the collective action climate policy needs.
pmc-13333140:
Sierra R Parkinson and colleagues report a 2026 case of arteriovenous hemangiomas as a sign of chronic liver disease. Skin abnormalities are common in liver disorders, with the skin a major target for signs outside the liver. Common findings include spider angiomas, palmar redness, caput medusa, plus nail changes. This report covers arteriovenous hemangiomas in a patient with alcohol-induced chronic liver disease.

After an orthotopic liver transplant, follow-up ten weeks later showed a marked shrinkage of the arteriovenous hemangiomas plus clear improvement of spider angiomas. That shrinkage after transplant supports prior evidence that treating the underlying liver disease leads to hemangioma regression. Skin findings can be the first symptoms patients report or doctors spot. Familiarity with common and uncommon skin changes in liver disease aids prompt recognition.
pmc-13333240:
Tom Adomati and co-authors trace an unexpected brake on antiviral immunity in a 2026 mouse study of the lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus. In lasting infection, killer CD8 T cells tire out under inhibitory signals such as PD-1 and IL-10, but what switches those brakes on was unknown.

Early T cell activation, the team found, goes with piles of dead cells. It also goes with fast rises in the calming signals IL-10 and TGF-β from macrophages and dendritic cells, and strong PD-1 display on the T cells. Mice lacking CD8 T cells showed far less of this. The chain runs from T cell killing, which floods tissues with dying cells, to the kinase Mertk on scavenger cells, which drives the calming signals. Mice without Mertk showed weaker brakes, faster antiviral responses, and better virus control. The authors name dead-cell buildup and Mertk as starters of immune suppression in chronic infection.
pmc-13333440:
Ismail Karluka and co-authors report outcomes for a streamlined stent technique in narrowed brain arteries in a 2026 retrospective series. Symptomatic intracranial stenosis of 70 to 99 percent carries a high early stroke risk even on best medical therapy, and the standard balloon-then-stent workflow forces fiddly catheter swaps inside fragile, branch-rich vessels.

Their method skips the swap: after gentle balloon widening, the Neuroform Atlas stent rides straight through the balloon catheter in a single pass. In 57 adults treated between January 2018 and January 2025, technical success was 100 percent, with no dissections, perforations, stray clots, or 30-day strokes or bleeds, and one death from sepsis. Median narrowing fell from 87 percent to 21.5 percent after the procedure and sat at 30 percent at three months. Re-narrowing beyond half within three months hit 7.1 percent, all in basilar artery cases, and rose with lesion complexity. The authors suggest closer watching of back-circulation cases.
pmc-13334440:
Chathura Kumaragamage and colleagues study 2026 reversible changes in brain acetate use linked to alcohol use. Alcohol use raises blood acetate, and prior studies showed acute alcohol lowers brain glucose uptake while raising brain acetate burning. The team earlier showed heavy drinkers have high ability to burn brain acetate. Here they repeat the study, adding people with alcohol use problems.

Four groups were enrolled: light drinkers, at-risk heavy drinkers, alcohol use problem patients in long-term recovery, and a separate group of treatment-seekers who underwent medically supervised detox. Participants received infused labeled acetate during magnetic resonance scans of brain chemicals to measure brain energy rates. Scans at about one week and one month dry in the treatment-seeker group test whether acetate use changes reverse with sobriety.
pmc-13336040:
Jiale Zhang and colleagues study 2026 NAT10-run ac4C tagging of circANKRD12 reshaping the tumor surroundings. Making cancer plans that at once target both tumor growth and tumor surroundings that weaken immunity remains a major challenge. The role of chemical tags in round RNAs in this process remains little known. The authors found circANKRD12 as a key substrate for ac4C tagging, run by NAT10 in multiple myeloma.

This tagging promotes reading of circANKRD12 into a novel 354-amino acid protein. Functionally, this protein links with HDAC2 to steady the cancer protein c-Myc, thereby driving multiple myeloma cell growth. Moreover, circANKRD12 could be moved from multiple myeloma cells to natural killer cells, where it likewise suppressed natural killer cell killing power via the HDAC2/c-Myc axis, aiding immune evasion. In patients, circANKRD12 was raised in multiple myeloma patients and linked with poorer outlook.
pmc-13336740:
Shun Xu and colleagues uncovered a new driver of prostate cancer growth in 2026, centred on fat metabolism. The enzyme fatty acid synthase is abundant in prostate tumours, but what keeps it stable and wired into cancer metabolism was unclear. The team identified the chaperone protein CCT2 as a key promoter of fat synthesis and aggressive tumour behaviour in cells and animals.

A transcription factor called FOXA1 raises CCT2 levels, and CCT2 then joins two partners to form a three part complex. That complex protects fatty acid synthase from breakdown, boosting fat production for tumour growth. Blocking this chain could offer a new treatment angle for prostate cancers driven by disordered lipid metabolism.
pmc-13336840:
Anran Zheng and co-authors present an AI-assisted tracker that watches single enzyme molecules for 15 h in a 2026 methods study. Such enzymes power long-read DNA sequencing, but laser light slowly damages them, and damage is hard to tell apart from natural variation. Their tracker pairs deep learning with chip-based droplets holding thousands of single reactions.

Comparing each polymerase before and after laser exposure revealed a damage pattern they call oxidative scarring. Harm builds on light-sensitive building blocks, leaving a disordered slow group. A reducing, antioxidant buffer eased the damage and restored even behavior. Checks on a real sequencing platform confirmed the tracker's measures set read-length limits. The insight guides tougher enzymes for long sequencing runs.
pmc-13337940:
Haocheng Wang and co-authors map drug resistance in Helicobacter pylori in Nanjing in a 2026 review of hospital data. The stomach bacterium resists antibiotics more each year, threatening cure regimens. Local patterns and agreement between lab growth tests and gene tests had not been summarized recently.

Records covered 7,227 patients from 2018 to 2024, with 5,729 culture-positive cases tested against six antibiotics. Metronidazole resistance reached 84.45 percent as reported, followed by clarithromycin at half of cases. Amoxicillin, furazolidone, and tetracycline stayed rarely resisted. Yearly trends and gene results guide doctors toward drug pairs that still work in this region.
pmc-13338640:
Seung Hee Jeong and In O Sun reviewed in 2026 the role of tiny cell released vesicles in high blood pressure. Hypertension involves the heart, kidneys, arteries, and immune system, yet its full biology remains tangled. Extracellular vesicles, small membrane parcels shed by all cell types, carry signals between cells in health and disease.

The review gathers emerging evidence that these vesicles help drive vascular, inflammatory, and kidney damage in hypertension and may serve as markers or treatment targets. Because they travel in blood and urine, they offer a window on disease activity without invasive sampling. The authors call for work that turns vesicle signals into usable clinical tools.
pmc-13338940: Ke-Qin Yu, Wei-Qiang Zhao, and Ting Zhang published a 2026 correction touching only author affiliations. Their study compared obesity measures for predicting infertility in United States adults. Two hospital name lines were wrong as printed. Zhao was also placed with the wrong unit. The fix gives the right college and department. All findings stand unchanged.
pmc-13339340:
Jeanne Petit and colleagues test full-gene sequencing for the drug-processing gene CYP2D6 in breast cancer care in a 2026 study. The gene handles about 20 percent of common drugs, including tamoxifen, yet targeted tests miss rare and tangled variants. Mismatched cases were rechecked by sequencing.

Sixty-eight patients whose gene result clashed with drug level evidence were sequenced fully as reported. Sequencing refined the gene call in 41 percent and changed metabolism class in 19 percent in the reported recount. Most fixes came from common variants the first test missed. Structural variants drove the remaining gains, supporting sequencing when results disagree.
pmc-13340140:
Molly R. Regan and colleagues survey drug resistance in harmless mouth Neisseria in a 2026 study. These quiet species store resistance traits that can pass to dangerous cousins that cause gonorrhea and meningitis. Samples came from 31 volunteers.

A total of 166 new samples were tested against seven antibiotics as reported. Resistance hit 76 percent for azithromycin and 52 percent for doxycycline in the reported shares. No resistance to gentamicin was found. Set gene changes explained high doxycycline resistance and lowered response to two other drugs. Wide value ranges hint at more unknown factors, warning that mouth flora is a resistance storehouse.
pmc-13341440:

pmc-13382940:

pmc-13383540:

pmc-13391440:

pmc-13392140:

pmc-13392240:

pmc-13392440:

pmc-13392640:

pmc-13392940:

pmc-13393240:

pmc-13393640:

pmc-13394140:

pmc-13395240:

Akash Manes and coauthors review oxygen thresholds used to spot opioid breathing failure in 2026. pmc-13437440:

pmc-13438140:

pmc-13438540:

pmc-13439340:

pmc-13439440:

pmc-13439540:
Zheng-Yu Long and colleagues read ancient lava rocks for signs that surface water reached Earth's deep interior early in its history, reporting in 2026. pmc-13439640:

Coordinated work across specialties is presented as the difference between loss and survival.
pmc-13439840:
Rose McKeon Olson's team mapped barriers in 2026 facing sexual and gender-based violence survivors seeking health care and justice in Sierra Leone. pmc-13439940:
Al-Saadi and colleagues ask how early life shapes mating choices in the roundworm Caenorhabditis elegans. pmc-13441040:

pmc-13441340:

pmc-13443640:

pmc-13443840:

pmc-13445840:

pmc-13446040:

pmc-13447140:

pmc-13447740:

pmc-13447840:

pmc-13448040:

pmc-13448540:

pmc-13448640:

pmc-13448840:

pmc-13449340:

pmc-13450440:

pmc-13450840:

pmc-13451440:

pmc-13451940:

pmc-13452840:

pmc-13453040:

pmc-13454240:

pmc-13454340:

pmc-13457440:

Kanako Ozaki and colleagues uncover a surprising guide in the birth of centrioles, the barrel-shaped structures cells use to organize division. pmc-13458240:
Minnie Au and colleagues follow patients with cirrhosis who were sick enough for intensive care, asking which scoring systems predict who is alive a year later. pmc-13459240:

pmc-13459340:
Norah Mohammed AlZamil and co-authors surveyed Saudi primary care physicians about how well they understand and counsel patients on sexually transmitted infections. pmc-13459440:
Nicole Carrasco-Zambrano and colleagues tracked in 2026 how the bacterial community in raw boar semen changes during cold storage. pmc-13459740:

pmc-13459940:
Guoming Chen and a Hong Kong team set out in 2026 a trial protocol testing herbal formulas meant to strengthen residents against COVID-19. pmc-13460140:
I. István Gecse and colleagues review in 2026 photon-counting computed tomography, a newer scanner type, for planning and checking coronary artery bypass surgery. pmc-13461940:

pmc-13462240:

A new loss function penalises odd shapes and rough edges to sharpen masks under harsh light and shadow. pmc-13462440:

The cancer, oral squamous cell carcinoma, is the main mouth cancer type, and tissue diagnosis guides its care. Attention heat maps highlighted the areas the model leaned on. The authors are careful: without region labels, the maps cannot prove the model looks at the lesion. The pair cost more yet bought over a year of such gains. Its cost per gain sat well below the pay threshold. Sensitivity tests held the result under wide swings.
pmc-13463540:
Martina Marsotto and co-authors study silver chemistry with beta-alkylcorroles, ring-shaped molecules related to porphyrins whose silver complexes are far less developed than their triaryl cousins. pmc-13463640:

pmc-13463740:

The crisis is common where care is scarce and it stretches hospital stays. pmc-13464240:

pmc-13464940:

pmc-13465040:

pmc-13466140:

pmc-13466440:

pmc-13466640:

pmc-13467440:

pmc-13467640:

pmc-13467840:

pmc-13467940:

pmc-13469040:

pmc-13469240:

pmc-13469440:

pmc-13470440:

pmc-13470740:

pmc-13470940:

pmc-13471540:

pmc-13471640:

pmc-13471740:

pmc-13472240:

pmc-13473240:

At the same time, the authors flag risks of treating too broadly, drug harm over long use, and cost strain. Readers get a balanced look at a policy shift that could close a large care gap.
pmc-13473640:
Xingyu Ming and six colleagues evaluated in 2026 a pilot switch from ICD-10 to ICD-11 disease coding in West China. ICD codes underpin morbidity and mortality statistics, billing, and research, yet moving to the richer ICD-11 system can strain coders. The team collected dual coding data over two months at a pilot hospital and surveyed and interviewed 20 coders about accuracy, workload, and obstacles, to judge wider adoption.

After the switch, 92.30 percent of primary disease codes stayed in the same chapter, while 41.10 percent used postcoordination, the linking of extra codes for detail, with up to eight codes joined in one case. Coders felt ICD-11 expressed diagnoses more accurately and found preset postcoordination user-friendly, but many cases still needed manual linking, records often lacked the detail ICD-11 demands, and audits were hard. The authors judge the transition feasible, provided record quality, training, and official Chinese textbooks come first.
pmc-13473940:
Harry Pearce and Chinmay Patvardhan share early experience in 2026 with a single spinal dose of morphine for pain after double lung transplant surgery. The chest cut used in this surgery causes intense pain that can slow recovery. The usual choice, a chest epidural line, brings risks when blood thinners and heart-lung support are in play. Five patients received the spinal dose as their main pain method.

Pain scores stayed low for two full days in all five cases. No one needed rescue with the standard epidural method. Patients rated their comfort as good, and no side effects were blamed on the spinal dose. As the first report of its kind, the series invites larger checks of safety and benefit.
pmc-13474740:
Sakiko Takahashi and colleagues report in 2026 a rare vessel link found ten years after chest surgery in a 56-year-old woman. She had prior surgery for air leaks tied to her cycle, with part of the diaphragm removed. A screening scan raised fear of cancer but instead showed an odd vessel in the lower right lung. Coils placed by catheter closed the feeder fully. Late vessel faults after surgery can hide for years, and time-aware scans can find them.
pmc-13474840:
Jie Pan and co-authors judge a free drug policy in 2026 for older adults with high blood pressure in Quzhou, China. Since mid-2021, residents aged sixty-five and above could get pressure drugs at no cost. Blood pressure records spanned twenty-eight quarters for 1,310 patients. A segmented model split the policy effect from slow drift and seasonal swings.

No instant jump followed the policy, yet long-run paths improved clearly. Systolic pressure swung from a rising path to a falling one after the policy began. By late 2024, systolic pressure sat well below the no-policy forecast. Free supply seems to pay off gradually rather than at once.
pmc-13475240:
Wood and colleagues present a 2026 protocol for a trial testing how to get a modern asthma approach, called SMART, into routine care for children. SMART uses one inhaler for both daily maintenance and symptom relief, and United States guidelines have recommended it since 2020 for children aged five and up on mid-level therapy.

After one year, nurse coordinators and community health workers join to help families with barriers such as insurance approvals and social needs. The team will measure adoption of SMART at visits and its effect on severe asthma attacks, using careful statistical designs.
pmc-13476140:
Sahu and colleagues report in 2026 that pairing two drug classes starves advanced prostate cancer cells into an energy collapse. pmc-13476940:
Brad Sheridan and co-authors review in 2026 how air ambulance teams keep trauma patients asleep with intermittent drug boluses. Records covered 101 blunt trauma patients with fairly preserved alertness scores and stable circulation. Flights ran a median of fifty-six minutes from a United Kingdom helicopter service. Drug doses were adjusted for time and body weight to judge sedation depth.

Fentanyl dosing clustered near a low median rate, with wide spread across patients. Midazolam ran low as well, and ketamine was often unused. Links to starter doses, body traits, and vitals were tested by correlation. Bolus upkeep seems workable in this stable subgroup, though spread was wide.
pmc-13477640:
Bradley Butsch and colleagues present a 2026 single-center study of frailty and body weight in surgical intensive care patients with sepsis. Frailty was scored with a five-item index covering common health deficits. The team compared frailty levels across body mass categories and built four groups by combining obesity status with frailty status.

The cohort covered 766 patients with obesity and 574 without. Severe frailty grew more common as body mass class rose, reaching 37 percent in morbid obesity compared with 19 percent in nonobese patients. Higher body mass independently predicted moderate to severe frailty. The study then sets up comparisons of hospital and 90-day death across the four groups, testing whether obesity changes how strongly frailty predicts death in this surgical sepsis population.
pmc-13478040:
Cody Lo and colleagues present a 2026 retrospective review of acute retinal necrosis care at The Ottawa Hospital in Canada. This rare viral eye infection destroys retinal tissue and often ends in detachment and severe vision loss. The review covers patients newly diagnosed between January 2019 and July 2024.

Fourteen patients covering 16 eyes met the study rules, with an average age of 56 years. Inflammation signs were nearly universal, and fluid testing found varicella-zoster virus in 56 percent of eyes and herpes simplex virus in 40 percent. Eyes received an average of about six antiviral injections, and most patients also got corticosteroids. Preventive laser treatment was rare in the series. The authors use the cohort to describe current practice and the complications that drive poor outcomes.
pmc-13479540:
Ida Marie Stephansen and coauthors published a 2026 biotechnology study teaching an industrial bacterium to eat seaweed sugars it normally cannot use. Corynebacterium glutamicum is a factory workhorse for amino acids and chemicals, yet it ignores rhamnose and fucose, sugars plentiful in green and brown seaweed. Widening its diet could turn abundant marine biomass into feedstock.

The team transplanted gene sets from E. coli that break down each sugar, enabling growth on either sugar alone. Transporter screening found the best import route for each: a borrowed fucose permease moved rhamnose fastest, while a native transporter handled fucose best. A toxic byproduct, lactaldehyde, forms during use of both sugars, and the study shows a native enzyme helps clear it. The work is a step toward seaweed-based bioprocessing.
pmc-13480040:
Ting Li and co-authors describe a 2026 method for sorting lettuce types from leaf traits with the help of a knowledge graph. Lettuce leaves vary a lot in shape, colour, and texture, which makes naming types and guarding new plant lines hard by eye alone. The team drew traits from leaf photos of five lettuce types and built a graph that links traits by shared sense, based on global plant variety rules.

A two-channel network then read both trait values and graph links to assign each leaf to its type. The method reached an accuracy near 0.94 on both overall and balanced scores, beating the best single-channel rival by roughly nine to ten points. Checks on which traits and links mattered most add trust in the output. Growers and testers could use the approach to screen new lines before costly field checks.
pmc-13483340:
Natalie Sadler and co-authors report a 2026 study of how a soil bacterium behaves when fed a cocktail rather than a single food. Natural settings serve mixed fare, yet labs usually test one substrate at a time. Their mix copied the juices that fungal threads leak into soil, matched against single foods at equal carbon and nitrogen for a workhorse strain of Pseudomonas putida.

Growth on the mix woke two hours sooner than on glucose and hit peak mass fastest of all options. One single food, fructose, grew more mass eventually yet dawdled with a lag near fifteen times longer. Uptake tracking showed the cells sipped one acid first, then drank several foods at once. Genome-scale models fed with the uptake data forecast the shifts well. Mixed fare creates a growth style no single food copies.
pmc-13483440:
Yingge Zheng and co-authors describe a 2026 hunt for a drug against a pig-killing gut virus, porcine epidemic diarrhea virus. Vaccines leak as the virus mutates, yet animal drug data stay too thin for normal computer screening. The team borrowed strength from human coronavirus data, training a transfer-learning model to flag hopeful compounds.

Piglets dosed by mouth carried lower gut virus loads, and twice as many survived. Borrowing human drug knowledge may speed cures for farm animals widely.
pmc-13483640:
Mugali Pundalik Kalpana and co-workers test how to breed a better dolichos bean with DNA-based picks. The bean is rich in protein but has seen slow gains from old-style breeding. Their 2026 study checks four math models, two kinds of training group, and young versus later plant lines. All plants were scored for fresh pod yield in field trials.

One model, called RKHS, gave the best yield forecasts of the four. Training on a tight inbred-line group worked best of all. Forecasts held up as well in young lines as in later lines. Breeders can thus pick top plants early from DNA alone. That shortcut saves whole seasons of field work for a crop that needs faster gains.
pmc-13483740:
Zhang and co-authors built a two-stage computer method to reconstruct gene regulatory networks, the wiring diagrams showing which genes switch others on or off. Single-cell data is notoriously sparse, with many true signals missing, which corrupts direct inference. Their 2026 framework, SGMHA, first learns sturdy gene descriptions by hiding and rebuilding parts of the data, then applies an attention mechanism, a way of weighing which genes matter to each other.

Across seven benchmark datasets, SGMHA beat eight established rival methods in most comparisons the authors report. It took the top discrimination score in about 86 percent of the head-to-head tests tallied. Applied to breast cancer that had spread, the method surfaced regulatory links specific to that setting. Zhang argues separating the learning stage from the link-picking stage is what shields the method from sparse-data noise.
pmc-13483840:
John and colleagues tested whether blocking a protein called LGALS1 could make head and neck cancers respond to immunotherapy. Such cancers make up most head and neck tumors, yet only about 10 to 20 percent of patients benefit from checkpoint inhibitor drugs, which release brakes on immune cells. Their 2026 study compared blood and tumor samples from responders and non-responders, then combined LGALS1 blockade with a checkpoint drug in mice.

LGALS1 levels ran higher in tumors in a pattern tied to cancer subtype and stage. Inside tumor cells, rather than outside them, the protein appeared to blunt immune attack. Blocking it changed how myeloid immune cells matured and helped killer T cells activate more strongly. Tumors that resisted the checkpoint drug alone responded better once LGALS1 was blocked in the mouse experiments. John also reports LGALS1 levels may help predict which patients will respond.
pmc-13485040:
Yongmin Shin turns fragile perovskite quantum dots into a printable ink sturdy enough for full-color micro-displays. Published in 2026, the resin gains its manners from fumed silica particles that make the ink thick at rest yet flowing under a blade, while also scattering light usefully. Printed dots self-form tiny lenses that boost light extraction.

pmc-13487240:
Obalalu and team simulated hot fluid rising along a vertical wavy wall under a magnetic field, a setup echoing heat exchangers and cooling surfaces. Wavy walls spread heat better than flat ones, but radiation, internal heating, and magnetic drag tangle the flow in ways designers must predict. Their 2026 study solved the transformed flow equations with a spectral numerical scheme in Mathematica software and checked the results against published work.

The solver matched earlier published results closely, validating the computational approach for this combined problem. The authors charted how each control knob, from the radiation-conduction balance to the wall's waviness amplitude, reshaped velocity and temperature fields. Streamline and temperature-contour maps show where heating concentrates along the wave. Obalalu offers the parameter maps as design guidance for thermal systems that deliberately use magnetic fields and wavy surfaces.
pmc-13487340:
Jing Chen and Shuo Yang decode eye movements during the Epley rolling maneuver to predict which dizzy patients will need a second treatment. Published in 2026, the retrospective study reviews 60 patients with loose crystals in the rear balance canal, all treated under video eye tracking. Eye movement direction and speed are logged at each maneuver position.

Nineteen patients, or 31.7 percent, still tested positive a day or two later and needed repeat repositioning. Clinicians often dismiss reverse movements as noise; quantified properly, they warn during the first session that crystals remain stranded.
pmc-13487940:
Semih Tanriverdi and Selin Yesiltepe compare salivary glands in antidepressant users and healthy controls with ultrasound in a 2026 case-control study. Antidepressants often cause dry mouth, yet little was known about whether the glands themselves look different. Tissue texture, edges, and blood supply looked similar in both groups. A few gland dimensions differed, with some measures larger and others smaller among users, without a consistent pattern. The authors conclude that antidepressant use does not clearly change gland appearance on ultrasound, and they suggest adding flow measures and stiffness imaging in future work.
pmc-13488240:
Koji Miyazaki and colleagues test a rapid DNA-based stewardship program for candidemia, a Candida yeast infection of the bloodstream, in a 2026 before-and-after study at a Japanese hospital. The infection kills often and needs fast, well-chosen antifungal treatment, which is hard in smaller hospitals with few infection specialists. pmc-13488440:
Kloos and colleagues in Germany found in 2026 a new route to europium oxides, prized for their glow, by baking a metal mix in air. The classic route mixes two oxide powders at fierce heat. pmc-13489940:

The team shrank the search space with a reduction step that uses arithmetic rules to cut the qubits and time needed. The authors claim early evidence of scaling advantage.
pmc-13490440:

pmc-13490540:
Xiong and colleagues taught a small model to name medical entities in traditional Chinese medicine texts by distilling knowledge from a bigger teacher model. Recall rose by about five points and the combined F-score by about seven, reaching roughly seventy-seven overall. pmc-13491640:

Interviews echoed strong awareness and a preference for traditional approaches alongside hospital care. Gender was significantly linked to awareness levels in the survey data. The authors suggest health planners should understand this preference rather than ignore it when designing stroke services.
pmc-13491740:
Haifu Sun leads a twelve-author team reviewing in 2026 liposomes, tiny fat bubbles that can ferry drugs and imaging agents, as combined diagnosis-and-treatment tools for bone disease. Radiolabeled and fluorescent versions let clinicians watch where the carriers go. The authors close with the hurdles that remain before routine use, among them manufacturing consistency, stability, safety, and whether animal models truly predict patient benefit.
pmc-13492440:
Melanie Gunawardene and Prashanthan Sanders offer career advice to young heart rhythm specialists. Their field, cardiac electrophysiology, is being remade by new tools. Their core advice is to enter the room early, before feeling ready.
pmc-13493640:

Its advantage showed in worst-itch scores at twenty-four weeks, in the share of patients gaining a meaningful itch drop by twelve weeks, and in a combined skin-plus-itch success measure. pmc-13493840:
Fardin Soltani and others test whether adapting a probiotic to penicillin G strengthens its antimicrobial and anticancer effects. In 2026, the study creates a resistant strain of Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus GG, then compares cell-free supernatants from adapted and normal strains against six pathogenic germs and against HT-29 colorectal cancer cells. Gene and protein analysis showed shifts in death and matrix-degrading markers. The authors propose adapted probiotics as a way to protect gut health during cancer treatment.
pmc-13493940:
Firoj and Afzal simulate how curved breakwaters, the harbour walls that calm incoming waves, handle a solitary wave. It compared a concave arc, a convex arc, and a plain straight wall, tracking surface height, vortices, and reflection.

The concave wall acted like a lens, funnelling energy toward its centre and raising the water surface there. It also bounced back far more energy, with reflected velocity up by well over a quarter against the straight wall. The convex wall did the opposite, spreading energy sideways, lowering reflection near the centre, and sheltering the water behind it better. The authors say curvature should be chosen deliberately.
pmc-13494540:
Jimmy Kim, Halen Kovacs, and Simon Wisnovsky present Lec-MACS in a 2026 methods article, a faster way to hunt for genes that control the sugar coat on cell surfaces. The magnetic setup runs faster, handles several sugars, and works in cells that flow sorting cannot manage. Checking the hits turned up a surprise link between the DNA damage response and sialic acid levels.
pmc-13495440:
Yi Jiang, Juan Du, and Jiajun Luo report a study from two thousand twenty-six on whether a nurse-led frailty check before liver transplant predicts post-surgery confusion. Trained nurse coordinators scored frailty with two standard scales before surgery. Confusion within seven days hit about fifty-two percent of frail patients versus eighteen percent of others. Frailty independently raised the odds more than fourfold. Frail patients also spent longer on breathing machines and in intensive care.
pmc-13495540:
Takato Inoue and colleagues present a 2026 case report of a fast-moving cancer found at the ampulla of Vater during routine watch of a pancreatic cyst. The ampulla is the small opening where bile and pancreatic ducts meet the gut. A 77-year-old woman under surveillance for the cyst showed a newly swollen papilla on scope examination, though scans a year and two months earlier had raised no alarm.

Since the tumor hid beneath the gut surface, a needle biopsy guided by ultrasound from inside the gut secured the diagnosis: neuroendocrine carcinoma, a rare and fierce subtype. Drainage of the bile duct and chemotherapy followed, yet the disease raced ahead and she died four months after diagnosis. The authors urge careful looks at any new ampullary change during cyst follow-up.
pmc-13496240:
Israeli and colleagues studied in 2026 what makes online crowd collaborations stay good over time, using Wikipedia as the test case. Many articles reach top quality status, but some later lose it. About seven percent of those articles were later demoted from high-quality status. For each article the dataset holds over 300 features, covering edit history, editor experience, and team makeup. Machine learning models trained on these features could flag articles at risk of decline. Editor experience emerged as the strongest predictor of lasting quality. Articles that took longer to earn top status were also more likely to keep it, the authors found.
pmc-13499840:
Dharmarajan and colleagues use insurance claims to ask whether three exon-skipping drugs extend life in Duchenne muscular dystrophy, a progressive muscle-wasting disease of boys. Randomised trials of eteplirsen, casimersen, and golodirsen were too small and short to answer the survival question. So the 2026 team emulated a trial from real-world records. Deaths were uncommon in both groups during roughly four and a half years of median follow-up, which makes the comparison delicate. After adjustment, the drug-treated group showed a substantially lower mortality hazard, with the estimate suggesting around a two-thirds reduction in the risk of death over the study window. Most treated patients received eteplirsen, the oldest of the three.
pmc-13499940:

Early education, desensitisation, swelling control, and supervised rehabilitation form the cornerstone, while drugs such as steroids and bone-protecting agents may ease therapy participation in selected patients. Nerve blocks, infusions, and spinal stimulation sit as adjuncts for stubborn cases within a staged, function-first plan.
pmc-13500440:
Jing Liu and co-authors build in 2026 a framework around programmed cell death, the orderly self-destruction pathways of cells, to sort acute myeloid leukaemia into prognostically useful groups. The lower-activity subtype looked immune-active and fared better. Three of its genes were confirmed raised in patient samples and cell lines in the lab.
pmc-13500540:
Guangyong Yu and co-authors improve in 2026 the control of permanent magnet synchronous motors, workhorse motors in vehicles and industry, for settings where loads jump suddenly and parameters drift. Adding the disturbance observer cut peak speed wobble under sudden load further and slashed speed error under parameter drift by a large margin. Control held steady throughout, supporting the combined design for demanding drives.
pmc-13501340:
Thiele and colleagues produced data on bloodstream infection with Serratia bacteria in North Denmark, in a 2026 study. The region holds about 590,000 people, and the data run from 2010 to mid 2024. Such data are scarce because most reports come from single hospitals or intensive care outbreaks. The team combined records with the microbiology database for every case.

Thiele found 188 patients, seventy years old, two thirds men, and nearly half carrying burdens of diseases. Incidence held steady at over two cases per hundred thousand per year, with infection acquired in the community in over a third and in hospital in another third-plus. The urinary tract was the commonest source, followed by the bile system and lungs, though no source was found in over a quarter. Nearly one in four patients died within thirty days, with older age and high comorbidity, not where infection was acquired, driving mortality.
pmc-13501640:
Lingxiao Wang leads a four-author team with a 2026 network toxicology study of whether the insecticide bifenthrin can worsen ulcerative colitis. Bifenthrin is a widely used pyrethroid and a known endocrine disruptor, but its gut effects were unclear. The team mined several poison and disease databases to predict the chemical's targets, overlapped them with colitis-related genes, and built protein networks to find hub genes. Cell tests then confirmed the predicted direction of harm, with exposure lowering the protective genes BCL2 and TP53 while raising the inflammation markers IL6, TNF, and PTGS2. The authors frame the insecticide as a plausible environmental factor in colon inflammation.
pmc-13501940:
Kuhlmann and colleagues asked whether gut bacteria are needed for killer T cells to become exhausted during chronic viral infection. Exhaustion is a state in which stimulation dulls the cells' fighting capacity. Their 2026 study infected germ-free mice, animals raised with no microbiome at all, and ordinary mice with a chronic strain of lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus. It compared their virus-specific CD8 T cells.
