That narrows the search for exhaustion's drivers to antigen load and inflammation.
pmc-13503440:
Nairana Melo leads a team on arsenic trioxide and liver metabolism. Their study from twenty twenty-six uses a lone perfused rat liver. The compound cures one leukemia type but is also a strong poison.

The liver set up keeps blood flow and cell order intact. Sugar making from two food sources fell with the compound. Oxygen use fell only at higher doses than that. Urea making, which clears nitrogen waste, also fell. Sugar break down from stored starch rose at low doses. Fruit sugar paths were changed as well. Energy levels in tissue were also checked.
pmc-13503840:
Mutsumi Kimura and others develop a complete neuromorphic system from amorphous metal-oxide semiconductor thin films. In 2026, the study fabricates and evaluates a thin-film transistor, a neuron built from those transistors, a memristor and Schottky diode, and synapses joining them. It finally builds an integrated system, each step checked by model and experiment. Neuromorphic hardware promises compact, energy-efficient machine minds.

All components come from one family of matter, avoiding the memory wall and von Neumann bottleneck that slow standard chips. Circuit-aware training on MNIST handwritten digits reached 94.1 percent recognition rightness in logic model. The work demonstrates that thin-film neurons, synapses, and systems are feasible for future giant-micro electronics.
pmc-13503940:
Lijuan Ren leads a team that paired single cobalt atoms with a cobalt-palladium alloy to boost zinc-air batteries, in a 2026 study. Such batteries are cheap and safe, but slow oxygen reactions at charging waste energy. Swapping the charge reaction for hydrazine oxidation eases that load.

The catalyst sits in a porous nitrogen-rich carbon frame. Electric coupling between the lone atoms and the alloy shifts both partners' states. That weakens oxygen grip on the lone atoms and strengthens hydrazine grip on the palladium, speeding the slow steps of each reaction. Cells with the catalyst showed a small charge-discharge voltage gap, high peak power, and strong capacity. The values rival or beat standard zinc-air cells.
pmc-13504140:
Argyro Bizaki-Vallaskangas and others search for age- and sex-specific gene risk factors in nerve hearing loss. In 2026, the genome-wide meta-analysis joins FinnGen and Estonian Biobank data covering 531,059 individuals, including 35,960 cases, with subgroups by sex and by onset before or after age fifty-five. Hearing loss is the most common sensory deficit across ages.

Twenty-two loci appeared in the general group analysis, three earlier unreported, and thirty-two loci reached genome-wide significance in at least one subgroup, nine of them novel. Effect sizes differed across subgroups for fourteen lead variants. The findings reinforce inner-ear structure and mechano-transduction genes and open translational research directions.
pmc-13504740:
Erik Laes leads a team asking what fair rule of personal health data would look like in Belgium, in a 2026 study. New European laws push wider reuse of health data while guarding private rights. The authors warn that such laws often treat citizens as passive donors with no real share in gains.

Interviews with institutional stakeholders in Flanders, read through three forms of justice, showed a shared wish for data solidarity. Fair sharing meant gains flowing back into public goods. Fair process meant ongoing citizen voice and oversight, not a single consent click. Fair regard meant valuing varied knowledge and bringing in groups often left out. The team offers design guidance for a Flemish health data space.
pmc-13505040:
Jing Su leads a team building a chart tool to predict heart artery damage in children with Kawasaki disease, in a 2026 study. The disease inflames blood vessels in young children, and artery damage is its gravest harm. Early flags would let doctors treat high-risk children harder from the start.

Records covered 255 children treated across about a year and a half; just under a third developed artery lesions. A shrinking selection method kept four predictors: age, clinical type, platelet count, and a clotting time measure. The chart built on those four sorted risk well in internal checks, and its calls matched observed rates closely. Decision analysis also favored its use. The authors present it as a bedside aid, pending outside testing.
pmc-13505140:
Dilek Sakallı and co-authors tested a Turkish version of a questionnaire that measures how much nurses feel they are thriving at work. Thriving here means feeling energetic while also learning and growing on the job. They surveyed nurses at a hospital between May and July 2025, and 164 nurses with complete answers formed the study group.

Factor analysis supported a revised three-factor structure, and the fit measures fell in the acceptable-to-good range. On that basis the authors judge the Turkish questionnaire valid and reliable for local use. They suggest nurse managers could use it to see which conditions help staff thrive, and to guide efforts to strengthen the nursing workforce. Nurses with under six months at the hospital were left out, which bounds the group the findings describe.
pmc-13505340:
Chih-Hao Liu and ten co-authors study voice problems after thyroid surgery in a 2026 paper. Voice loss after this surgery is usually blamed on nerve damage, but some patients lose voice quality even when nerves are proven intact during surgery. The team asked whether thyroid autoimmunity, measured by antibody levels before surgery, plays a role.

They reviewed two hundred twelve patients whose throat nerves were monitored and confirmed intact. Patients with high antibodies had larger tumors and more two sided surgeries. After adjusting for those traits, high antibodies still predicted abnormal voice measures. A grading analysis hinted the link may not rise in a straight line with antibody level. The authors call the finding exploratory.
pmc-13506240:
Maria López-Brotons, Sergio Javaloy-Ballestero, and José-Manuel Ramos-Rincón evaluated a clinical skills programme at a Spanish university where senior medical students tutor juniors through simulated procedures. Small-group workshops ran under faculty supervision, growing from six topics in the first year to eight in the second, adding spinal tap and basic ultrasound. Altogether 139 students took part across two academic years, generating 440 attendances.

Knowledge scores rose sharply from before to after each workshop, with average marks climbing from about six to nearly nine out of ten. Second-year students gained more than third-years, and men gained slightly more than women. Satisfaction ratings stayed high, averaging above four out of five. With no comparison group, the gains cannot be credited to peer tutoring alone, yet the authors show the model is workable, popular, and able to sustain participation across years.
pmc-13507140:
Olivia Vitale and Maha Haji published a study in 2026 on wave energy converters acting as guardians for offshore wind farms. Offshore turbines face cyclic wave loading that fatigues their structures over time. That wear is a genuine obstacle for durable, reliable clean energy.

The authors built experimentally validated models of how farms of wave energy converters dissipate wave energy. Their key point is methodological: sheltering should be modeled through fluid-structure interaction, not rated power, to avoid biased comparisons. In the system model, small wave height reductions propagated into meaningful savings. A six percent reduction produced nearly a five percent decrease in the wind farm's levelized cost of energy. Co-location also lets the two farms share siting costs, maintenance teams, mooring lines, and transmission cables. The work supports integrated wind and wave systems as a resilient, cost-effective pathway.
pmc-13507240:
Ali Alasiri, Ahmed A Lahiq, and Abdullah A Alshehri develop, in 2026 work, a hybrid AI pipeline for drug solubility. It predicts how drug ingredients dissolve in supercritical carbon dioxide, a green solvent used in drug processing. Solubility there depends on tangled links between heat, pressure, and molecular traits, so lab measurement is slow. Their dataset holds more than 350 published measurements.

Two model types, an attention-based tabular network and a gradient boosting method, were tuned by three nature-inspired optimizers. The best pairing reached a fit score near 0.98 on held-out checks, with narrow uncertainty bands. Statistical tests confirmed real gaps between optimizers. Formulators could screen solvent conditions in software before committing bench time.
pmc-13507540:
Ravi Sarode and six co-authors report a subanalysis of the LEX-209 trial on reversing blood-thinning drugs before urgent surgery, published in 2026. The trial tested a concentrate of four clotting factors in adults taking vitamin K antagonists who faced surgery with high bleeding risk. This report covers only patients whose blood was far too thin, with test values above 6. Those patients received the top permitted dose, set by body weight.

Twenty-three patients met that mark, and their average test value was well above the normal range. Every patient in both treatment groups achieved effective control of bleeding during surgery. Levels of the missing clotting factors rose as expected in both groups. No drug-linked side effects or clots were reported, though the small group size limits how far the result can be stretched.
pmc-13507640:
Mohammad Raza, Farahanaz Irani, and Pranita Kadam examine how job stress relates to thinking skills among trainee doctors at a medical college in Maharashtra, India, in 2026 work. The study ran from April 2024 to March 2026 and enrolled 281 resident doctors aged 25 to 45. Residents came from clinical, para-clinical, and pre-clinical departments. Stress was scored with a standard test, and computer tasks measured attention, perception, planning, and working memory.

Nearly half of the residents showed moderate stress, and a similar share showed high stress. Clinical residents carried the heaviest load, with longer hours, more emergency calls, less sleep, and higher blood pressure than other groups. Their thinking test scores also suffered in the areas the team measured. The authors link heavy ward demands to poorer mental performance, a risk for both doctor health and patient care.
pmc-13507840:
Shael Brown, Nathan Anderson, Jazmin Orozco, and Richard Levenson test a slide-free imaging method for mapping blood vessels in breast cancer tissue, in 2026 work. Routine slides are thin slices that can cut vessels into fragments and hide their layout. Their method, called FIBI, makes slide-like images straight from tissue or wax blocks within minutes. The team paired FIBI images with standard stained slides from the same breast tissue blocks. They then traced vessels in tumors and nearby tissue by hand.

Vessels looked more complete and easier to follow in the FIBI images. Measures of vessel size, length, and branching rose, and gaps between vessels shrank in network maps. A math approach that tracks shape across scales added detail that simple vessel measures did not capture. The work suggests richer images could sharpen computer analysis of tumor blood supply.
pmc-13508240:
Sujitha Sethuramalingam leads an eight-author trial comparing two forms of a key leukemia drug in Indian children, in 2026 work. The drug, asparaginase, starves leukemia cells, and it comes in a plain bacterial form and a coated long-acting form. Fourteen children with newly diagnosed leukemia were assigned to each form, given by muscle injection during early chemotherapy. Blood drug activity was checked on day 33, and body handling of the drug was modeled.

Drug activity on day 33 ran far higher in the long-acting group than in the plain group. Antibody formation, leftover disease, and side effects looked similar between groups. The plain form varied much more from child to child in how the body handled it. Levels also dipped below the useful range in nine of fourteen plain-form patients, but in none on the long-acting form. The authors favor the long-acting version for first-line use.
pmc-13508340:
Gary Duclos and five co-authors lay out the protocol for a trial testing whether low-dose ketamine can cut morphine use in badly injured patients, in 2026 work. Severe trauma brings intense pain, heavy early opioid exposure, and risks of side effects and lasting pain. The single-center trial will assign adult patients with injuries in at least two body regions to ketamine or a saltwater placebo, with neither patients nor staff told which. Treatment starts within twelve hours of intensive care arrival and runs for 48 hours.

All patients also receive standard multi-drug pain care. The trial has twin main goals: proving opioid use falls, and proving pain control is no worse within a set margin. Total opioid dose at 48 hours and average pain scores will settle both questions. The planned size is 140 patients. Results should give the first firm randomized evidence for this use of ketamine.
pmc-13508840:
Hernán Antonio Alzate-Díaz, Samir Julián Calvo-Cardona, and Sandra Clemencia Pardo-Carrasco wrote this research paper, published in 2026. It studies what long transport trips do to the skin barrier of young red tilapia, a farmed fish moved often between hatcheries and grow-out sites.

The team simulated trips of zero, five, twelve, and twenty hours, then checked the fry's skin. They read the activity of ten genes tied to skin sealing, mucus, and defense, and counted mucus-making goblet cells. Eight genes shifted with trip length, in waves rather than straight lines. Some spiked mid-trip and settled later. Goblet cells held steady up to twelve hours but thinned after twenty. The authors conclude that trips of twelve hours or less leave the skin mostly stable, while longer hauls strain it.
pmc-13514140:
Valerie Lankes, Andrea Coldea, John Meinen, and Bogna Stawarczyk test how sandblasting angle and nozzle shape change the surface and strength of a feldspar dental ceramic, in 2026 work. Seventy ceramic plates were split into seven groups. Six groups were blasted with fine alumina at low pressure, from four angles with a standard nozzle or two angles with a cone-shaped trial nozzle. One control group was etched with acid, the standard preparation for bonding.

Treatment clearly moved surface energy and roughness. The shallowest angle with the standard nozzle gave the lowest values on both. At a mid angle the standard nozzle beat the trial nozzle on surface energy, while at a right angle the trial nozzle roughened more. Bending strength sat in a narrow band across all groups with no reliable gap. The authors warn the results alone do not justify swapping acid etching for blasting.
pmc-13515140:
Marko Bašković and six colleagues review, in a 2026 narrative article, when children's fractures can safely heal without surgery. Growing bone differs from adult bone: a thick outer sheath, open growth plates, and a strong power to remodel mean many breaks straighten as the child grows. Yet registries show operations rising, even for fractures with good natural correction. The authors gathered studies from four databases and set out, region by region, the accepted limits for angle, rotation, shortening, and displacement.

Each limit shifts with the child's age and the bone involved, and the review presents the numbers in comparative tables. Genuine reasons for surgery are spelled out just as plainly, so the line between watchful care and the operating room stays sharp. Bašković's team aims to help doctors trust the child's own remodelling where evidence supports it, avoiding both needless operations and missed corrections.
pmc-13516140:
Junyao Ding and eight colleagues test a traditional Chinese formula against fatty liver disease in a 2026 study. The blend, Sanzi Sijun Formula, had shown early promise against the metabolic form of the disease, yet its working route was undefined. Chemical profiling first catalogued seventy-seven active ingredients. The team then fed mice a fat-rich diet with sugary water for ten weeks to build the disease, and treated them for eight weeks.

Treated mice lost body and liver weight, and their blood fats, liver enzymes, and inflammation signals all fell, while a protective hormone rose. Liver tissue showed less fat build-up, swelling, and immune invasion. Gene profiling pointed at lipid handling and one signalling route, AMPK with SIRT1, which lab tests on liver cells confirmed: blocking either switch partly cancelled the formula's benefit.
pmc-13517640:
Sun and co-authors developed in 2026 a single test that detects five respiratory bacteria at once in specific pathogen-free chickens, laboratory birds that must be certified free of listed infections. Checking each bacterium separately is slow and costly, and existing combined assays cover only two to four targets. Their method uses Luminex xTAG liquid array technology, where coded beads each carry a probe for one target gene.

The assay targets a unique gene from each of the five bacteria, which include the mycoplasmas that cause chronic respiratory disease and joint infection in poultry. In validation it showed high sensitivity, specificity, and repeatability, and it did not react with other common bacterial species. When the team tested samples from specific pathogen-free flocks, none of the five bacteria appeared, exactly as expected. They present the assay as a faster routine monitoring tool for laboratory animal quality control.
pmc-13518940:
Hanane Abbou leads an eight-author computational hunt in 2026 for measles antivirals among minor cannabinoids, the lesser-known cannabis compounds. No approved drug treats measles, and the virus's fusion protein, locked in its prefusion shape, is a prime target. Screening pointed to three candidates, with cannabichromevarin, or CBCV, on top.

Docking placed CBCV ahead of the reference inhibitor AS-48, and thousand-nanosecond simulations plus free energy calculations confirmed stronger binding. CBCV compacted the fusion protein and held it in its inactive shape, acting like a conformational lock. Toxicity and drug-likeness predictions also favored CBCV, including possible entry into the brain, which matters for a rare measles brain complication. Real-world testing still lies ahead.
pmc-13519040:
Acerra and colleagues compared sixteen cleaning protocols for flushing debris out of side canals in root canal treatment, in a 2026 laboratory study. It used 176 printed resin blocks with canals. The side canals were filled with a gelatin-based gel mimicking organic debris. Protocols varied the bleach solution used and whether a chelating rinse was added. They also varied how the fluid was activated, from syringe delivery to sonic, ultrasonic, and heated combinations.

Acerra weighed specimens to measure gel loss and checked canals under a microscope. Saline and syringe irrigation produced no loss. Combinations of internal heating with activation removed the most. Two heated protocols topped the table for both weight loss and clearing of the smaller canal near the root tip. Adding the chelating agent made no marked difference over bleach alone, and no protocol fully cleared the small canal, which the authors caution limits clinical translation.
pmc-13519340:
Papasratorn and co-authors test an AI tool that maps gum tissue on cone beam CT scans of the upper jaw. Clean maps of the gum edge and the tissue above it guide dental planning. Their method uses a fluoride tray to separate soft tissue so the scan shows the gum line clearly. The team ran 35 scans through a cloud AI platform and compared results with expert edits. Six scans were also traced by hand, using oral scans as a reference.

The team checked surface match, voxel match, and the time each method took. Expert edits served as the standard for the AI output. The study tests whether tray-based scans make automated gum mapping reliable enough for clinic use.
pmc-13519540:
Hyeonji Choi and four colleagues review recent genetically engineered mouse models of melanoma in 2026 and the signaling pathways they expose. Mouse skin mirrors human skin structure, so these models let researchers watch melanoma begin in pigment cells and their stem cells, then spread from surface to deeper layers.

Beyond the classic MAPK and PI3K pathways, newer models implicate cell-cycle control through Cdk4, Jak-Stat transcriptional signaling, Hippo-Yap/Taz signaling, a p62-Igf2bp1 axis, and the epigenetic regulator Tet2. Each pathway feeds tumor variety and shape-shifting behavior. Choi and co-authors argue the models clarify how melanoma starts, progresses, and diversifies, while nominating fresh therapeutic targets for a cancer whose incidence keeps rising.
pmc-13520140:
Murilo Damasceno Brunet de Freitas and four colleagues field-test other options in 2026 after the standard drug doramectin failed against screwworm maggots in newborn calves. The fly Cochliomyia hominivorax invades the umbilical stump, and its return to cleared regions of the Americas threatens herds. On a Brazilian beef farm, 200 calves were split by lot into four groups during navel care.

Untreated calves developed myiasis at a rate of 26 percent. Doramectin barely helped, at 22 percent, while pour-on fluralaner cut cases to 4 percent, perhaps blunted by mothers licking the treated spot. Oral fluralaner, a trial formulation, blocked every case. Lesion scores matched the pattern, favoring fluralaner groups.
pmc-13520240:
R Sharples leads a team in 2026 tracing how a Canadian community paramedicine program took root across four rural health services in Victoria, Australia. Paramedics ran free drop-in clinics with chronic disease screening, referrals, care guidance, and health education. Notes from 13 monthly meetings of a Community of Practice, where the teams swapped experiences, were mined for what helped and what hindered.

Four themes emerged: workforce development, community engagement, data collection, and program sustainability. Barriers included unclear roles, slow trust-building, heavy paperwork in low-signal areas, and shaky funding. The Community of Practice acted as the engine room, speeding role transitions and practical problem-solving. The authors argue durable change also needs built-in funding for training and the long term.
pmc-13520340:
Zhang and colleagues identify a new escape route that lung cancers use against osimertinib, the targeted pill that initially melts tumours carrying EGFR mutations but almost always stops working. Their suspect is the shed outer piece of a surface protein called GPNMB, which floats free in tissue and blood. In their 2026 study, single-cell and bulk gene profiling of sensitive and resistant tumours, plus protein staining and blood tests, singled out resistant cancers as heavy producers of this fragment.

Adding the fragment to sensitive cancer cells in dishes blunted the drug, reorganising the cells' internal skeleton in ways that favour survival and spread. Mouse models echoed the effect in both under-skin and lung tumours on the reported experiments. Blood levels of the fragment ran substantially higher in patients whose cancers had turned resistant, hinting at a monitoring test.
pmc-13521940:
Linglin Yang and colleagues record in 2026 brain activity inside the anterior insular cortex while epilepsy patients navigate a virtual maze toward rewards. Expecting a reward sharpens attention, while the timing system behind that sharpening was unknown in humans.

Reward-specific patterns switched on before reward arrival, followed by coupling between slow theta waves and fast gamma bursts. Stronger pre-activation meant stronger coupling. Across repeated rounds, gamma peaks crept earlier within each theta cycle, resembling phase precession seen in memory circuits. Patients showing stronger creep improved faster at collecting rewards trial by trial, linking precise timing with learning.
pmc-13522340:
Wubalem Alebachew and Destaw Worku profile in 2026 honey quality from selected districts of South Wollo, Ethiopia, sampling thirty modern-hive lots across two harvest seasons and three altitude zones. Standard measures covered acidity, moisture, ash, pH and a heat-damage marker called HMF.

Average values sat within established quality standards overall. Season effects varied by zone, touching ash and HMF most consistently, while most measures stayed stable across seasons. First-season honey held the highest ash share, whereas second-season honey carried higher HMF. The district-level baseline helps producers and buyers judge Ethiopian honey against international benchmarks.
pmc-13522440:
Nuwan T Attygalle and colleagues address a practical training problem for radar-based gesture recognition in a 2026 study. Radar can sense hand movements through opaque materials, which allows sensors to hide inside everyday objects. The team recorded more than seventeen thousand gestures through seventy-three materials to test how much covering-specific training data is really needed.

Training on a carefully chosen subset of fourteen materials performed almost as well as training on all seventy-three, and far better than training with no such examples. Artificially augmented data did worse than real recordings from selected materials. For builders of hidden radar controls, the finding offers a cheaper path: collect good examples from a representative set instead of every possible covering.
pmc-13522540:
Nathan J Day leads a team that overturns a long-held view of tuberculosis bacteria in a 2026 live-imaging study. Slow growth inside host cells was thought to explain why the bacteria tolerate antibiotics. A new high-throughput imaging method tracked single bacteria replicating inside human immune cells, and a mouse model with a fluorescent growth timer checked the finding in living tissue.

Contrary to expectation, some intracellular bacteria doubled in under ten hours, far faster than the usual day-long estimate. Those fast growers survived treatment with first-line antibiotics. Heavily infected host cells held the most actively replicating bacteria. The authors argue that fast growth, not only dormancy, helps the bacteria evade treatment, which matters for shortening the long tuberculosis drug course.
pmc-13523440:
Dominic N. Facciponte and colleagues describe, in a 2026 technique report, a needle-based repair for femoral artery pseudoaneurysms that follow catheter access. A pseudoaneurysm is a contained leak from an artery wall. Usual options include compression, thrombin injection, a covered stent, or open surgery, yet some patients are poor candidates for those routes or have already failed them.

The team used a suture-mediated closure device, guided only by ultrasound, passing through the neck of the pseudoaneurysm under real-time imaging along its long axis. Five patients with noninfected lesions and suitable opening sizes were treated, and the repair succeeded in three. Two needed other repairs, after access to the neck failed or the suture closure did not hold. The authors present the method as a radiation-free option for selected high-risk patients.
pmc-13525940:
Fernández Arias and a large team ask whether tau, the tangled protein of Alzheimer's disease, damages memory differently depending on which side of the brain it burdens. Textbook neurology assigns verbal memory mostly to the left hemisphere and visual memory more to the right, but tau imaging lets researchers test that map directly. Their 2026 study gave 132 healthy older adults and 44 impaired, amyloid-positive participants both a word-list test and its picture-based twin, alongside tau and amyloid PET scans and MRI.

The map held up. Higher tau in the right hemisphere tracked worse visual memory specifically, surviving models that included verbal scores, while left-hemisphere tau leaned toward verbal memory at stronger statistical thresholds in the voxel-wise maps. Still, the results suggest memory clinics could read side-specific tau as a clue to which kind of forgetting will dominate.
pmc-13527140:
Berk Can Özdemir, Nilay Filoğlu, and Yeşim Yeşil examine, in a 2026 study, how pelvic floor problems and body image relate to sexual desire in late pregnancy. It reshapes a woman's body and sexual life together. The study took in 209 women in their late months, average age about 29.

People filled in standard forms on pelvic floor distress, body image in pregnancy, sexual interest and desire, and attitudes toward sexuality while pregnant. Pelvic floor dysfunction showed no real differences across body mass or parity subgroups. Greater pelvic floor distress tracked with lower sexual desire and worse sexual attitudes. Poorer body image view was, against expectation, linked with slightly higher desire in simple pairings. Models confirmed pelvic floor dysfunction and body image as independent predictors of desire, and the authors urge weaving both into prenatal care.
pmc-13528040:
Lily C. Farrell and six colleagues detail eye imaging in a rare genetic disease in a 2026 case series. Faults in the KIF11 gene cause a retinal disorder with a flat central pit. The series covers two patients, four eyes in all. Scans mapped the macula and the choroid, the blood-rich layer under the retina. Thickness and vessel share were measured and compared with a healthy control.

Both patients had flat foveas in both eyes. The lower retina showed underdeveloped zones with dragged vessels. Choroid thickness under the macula was lower and patchier than in the control. In lower regions the choroid was thick, peaking sharply beside the underdeveloped zone. Vessel share ranged from fifty-eight to sixty-five percent. The authors say choroid changes may help drive the disease. They call the findings early and in need of more cases.
pmc-13528140:
Qianbei Yi and four colleagues present a computer method that reads tumor surroundings with cell talk included in a 2026 paper. Most tools estimate cell mixes in a tumor while treating each cell type alone. Their method, CrosstalkIn, builds a network per patient. It weighs how alike cell types are in function and which proteins touch. A wandering algorithm then scores how much of each cell type is present.

Tests on two checked cohorts beat or matched rival tools for most cell types. In brain glioma the scores named cell types tied to survival. Risk scores split patients into clear outcome groups. Across several gland cancers the score kept its value, mainly in advanced disease. In melanoma it sharpened forecasts of immune therapy response. The authors offer it as a sturdier lens on tumor ecology.
pmc-13528840:
Luigi Fontana and five colleagues report the first three cases of a combined cornea operation in a 2026 paper. The method joins a full cornea transplant with an artificial inner membrane, placed without stitches. All three patients had failed earlier transplants and many prior eye operations. The membrane was tucked into a pocket in the donor cornea before grafting. No gas bubble was needed to hold it.

At six months every graft stayed clear, with the device fully stuck. Corneas thinned markedly in all three eyes as swelling drained. Vision improved from near blindness to hand motion in the weakest eye. The best eye reached twenty over one hundred. No complications appeared. The authors aim the method at eyes too scarred for the membrane alone. Bigger series must confirm the early promise.
pmc-13529840:
Canling An and Soichiro Matsuda study how gaze-triggered distance changes reshape where people look. Their experiment from twenty twenty-six uses animated face approaches and retreats. Social distance is a basic cue in human interaction. Whether gaze itself trains later looking habits was unknown.

Fifty adults completed approach and recede training blocks. Staring at a face triggered its animation during training. Looking time was measured before and after in still phases. Approach training reduced later dwell on that face. Recede training produced a different allocation pattern. Effects depended on condition, not mere exposure time. Eye behaviour learns from social outcomes quickly, it seems.
pmc-13530140:
Lingling Xu and colleagues trace in 2026 how the hormone leptin weakens the calming effect that fat-derived stem cells have on immune cells. In obesity, leptin runs high and these stem cells lose some of their useful control over inflammation. Cell culture work isolated the chain of events behind that loss.

Leptin pushed the stem cells toward self-digestion of their own parts, a process called autophagy, and lowered output of a protective protein named TSG-6. Blocking autophagy restored the protein and the calming effect. A signaling route involving p38 carried the leptin message, marking a possible drug target.
pmc-13530240:
K Saranya and S Ramakrishnan build a 2026 detector for fake position reports in networks of talking vehicles. Cars that lie about location threaten safety in vehicle-to-vehicle communication. Their detector stacks five different learning classifiers and lets a final model weigh the combined verdicts.

A bee-colony search tuned each base classifier toward its best settings before stacking. The tuned ensemble outperformed existing detection methods in the reported comparisons. Strong location honesty matters because braking, merging, and hazard warnings all assume nearby vehicles truly are where they claim to be. The work targets misbehavior detection for safer connected roads.
pmc-13531840:
Halefom Kahsay Haile, Bruck Messele Habte, and Teferi Gedif Fenta run a 2026 randomized trial of peer support groups for diabetes patients in northern Ethiopia. Ninety-seven adults at a tertiary hospital were split between three peer-led sessions and usual care, then followed for six months. Sessions taught self-care, medicine habits, and disease knowledge.

The peer group gained clearly on every measure against controls. Medicine adherence rose by a net one and a half scale points, and self-care added over a day per week of recommended habits. Knowledge gains held for insulin users and non-users alike. Low-cost peer groups fit resource-limited clinics.
pmc-13534440:
Nojoud Abdullah Alrashidi and colleagues survey in 2026 burnout, job satisfaction, and plans to leave among emergency nurses working in Saudi Arabia's Hail region. Emergency nurses carry heavy loads, and their strain affects care quality and staffing. Standard questionnaires reached 370 nurses across seven hospitals through professional chat groups.

Satisfaction fell as burnout rose, and both tied strongly to plans to leave. Mid-career and highly experienced nurses reported lower satisfaction and higher burnout than new graduates. Nurses with master degrees also reported higher burnout, while large hospitals paired lower burnout with lower satisfaction.
pmc-13534740:
Nguyen T N Vo and colleagues work in 2026 toward heart cell production from human stem cells without animal serum. Serum raises ethical and clarity concerns, and policy pushes for animal-free methods. Using marker checks for fibroblast and vessel cell types, the team tuned a defined serum substitute called Panexin.

The substitute supported efficient production of cardiac support cells at high purity without extra sorting steps. Engineered heart tissues built with it contracted poorly, though, while human serum supported strong tissues that beat animal-serum versions. Readers see both progress and a remaining gap for fully animal-free tissue building.
pmc-13535540:
Chen Gao and colleagues tune a copper catalyst for turning plant waste into a plastic building block. Their study from twenty twenty-six targets HMF electrooxidation. The product, FDCA, can replace petroleum-based plastic ingredients. Competing surface reactions usually waste charge and blur selectivity.

Added partner ions change the electron density at copper centres. That change loosens the coupling between two competing adsorbates. Hydroxyl groups and HMF no longer fight on equal terms. The tuned catalyst reached near-perfect charge efficiency in tests. Product selectivity also reached very high levels. Current density stayed strong at the working voltage. Catalyst-level control, not process tweaks, delivered the selectivity here.
pmc-13538540:
Ma and eight co-authors compare first line drug combinations for lung cancer with brain spread, in work from twenty twenty-six. Brain metastases are common in EGFR mutant non small cell lung cancer. Newer targeted drugs reach the brain better, yet the disease stays hard to control.

Direct head to head trials between combination strategies are limited. The systematic review and network meta analysis ranked first line combinations built on EGFR targeted drugs, using indirect evidence across trials. Three oral microbes faced it alone and in mixtures: Streptococcus mutans, Enterococcus faecalis, and the fungus Candida albicans.

F7 never killed free-floating microbes outright at the doses tried. Against settled biofilms it worked by interference. At the top dose it blocked new film formation by 78.8 percent, against Candida, and stripped existing films by three-quarters in a mixed pairing. Microscopy showed membranes and matrix disrupted. The authors describe an anti-stick strategy rather than a poison, suited to gentler oral care.
pmc-13563940:
Hongtao Liu, Ronecca Arjune, and Aini Xie synthesize, in a 2026 systematic review, nine studies of liver dysfunction after emergency surgery. The surgery repairs a torn inner wall of the aorta, the Stanford type A dissection. The nine single-center studies covered 3,234 patients, and definitions of liver problems varied across them.

Pooled results put liver dysfunction in roughly thirty-seven percent of patients after repair. Male sex, higher white cell counts before surgery, longer time on the heart-lung machine, longer clamping of the aorta, and more transfused blood all linked to higher risk. Surgeons and intensive care teams get a clear set of perioperative factors to watch when protecting the liver.
pmc-13565640:
Fabrizio Urraro and eight colleagues compare ultrasound against MRI at spotting the stalk that anchors bladder tumors. A fibrovascular stalk signals a papillary tumor's attachment; MRI shows it as the inchworm sign, while contrast ultrasound can watch the stalk's blood flow arrive before the tumor lights up. Sixty-nine patients had both scans checked against pathology.

Ultrasound found forty-six of forty-eight stalks, a sensitivity near ninety-six percent, against MRI's seventy-five percent. Both agreed strongly between readers. A visible stalk favored non-muscle-invasive cancer but did not rule out invasion. The authors conclude ultrasound adds real perfusion information, while MRI scoring remains central to staging the tumor's depth.
pmc-13568740:
Li and colleagues map a molecular relay in this 2026 study of endometrial adenocarcinoma, the commonest cancer of the uterine lining, centered on the tumor suppressor PTEN, whose loss propels this disease. They examined how a pro-cancer phosphatase called PRL-3 connects to PTEN through its decoy pseudogene and two microRNAs in tumor samples and cell lines.

The logic runs as a double negative. PRL-3 raises levels of miR-21 and miR-17, two small RNAs that directly target both PTEN and its pseudogene PTENP1, a decoy that normally soaks up microRNAs to protect PTEN. With the decoy and the suppressor both suppressed, cancer cells proliferate and migrate faster in dish assays. Forcing PTEN or its pseudogene high, conversely, restrained growth and movement. The authors nominate PRL-3 as the upstream switch worth drugging in this cancer's progression circuitry.
pmc-13569240:
Junho Yoon and Jun-Hyung Tak test, in a 2026 study on house flies, whether fast knockdown by pyrethroid insecticides means the insects will actually die. That link is an assumption built into many household and public-health products. Three insecticide classes were compared, and computer vision tracked symptom patterns in a promising chemical mixture.

For type-I pyrethroids, fast knockdown did not predict death, and early-fallen flies often recovered. Type-II pyrethroids and organophosphates showed the expected link. One mixture unexpectedly shifted symptoms toward the type-II pattern while boosting effect. Regulators and product makers are urged to judge knockdown and killing as separate claims rather than treating one as proof of the other.
pmc-13569440:
Lorenzo Pagano and a large team of co-authors study a gene variant that may delay frontotemporal dementia in work dated two thousand twenty-six. Changes in the granulin gene are a top cause of that dementia, yet age of onset varies a lot, even within one family. Other genes likely tune the course.

A variant in a related gene, TMEM106B, had been tied to lower risk in past work. The team screened one hundred eighty-seven carriers of granulin changes in Italy, the largest such group yet for this variant. They tracked how the variant relates to age at onset, survival, and levels of the granulin protein. Carriers of two copies of the shielding form are a key group in the study.
pmc-13570840:
Annefleur C. Langedijk and colleagues model, in a 2026 cost-effectiveness study, a bivalent vaccine against respiratory syncytial virus for older adults in the Netherlands. National advice backs vaccinating at-risk adults aged sixty to seventy-four and everyone seventy-five and older. A lifetime model for about five million people weighed cases, deaths, quality of life, and medical plus productivity costs.

One dose would prevent roughly eighty-four thousand illness cases and about twenty-three hundred deaths across that population over a lifetime. Quality-adjusted life years gained numbered about eleven thousand against added program costs. Dutch policy makers get numbers tuned to their uptake and price assumptions for judging whether the recommended program earns its cost.
pmc-13571240:
Lukas Eggenberger and colleagues follow, in a 2026 Swiss longitudinal cohort study, 731 young adults whose hair was tested for more than one hundred substances at ages twenty and twenty-four. Hair testing captures real drug exposure better than self-report. Patterns of change were grouped into profiles, then related to thinking tests and mental health symptoms at twenty-four.

Among those with any use, five change profiles emerged, from a large low or decreasing group to smaller groups increasing cannabis, club drugs, medical stimulants, or medical sedatives. Cannabis increasers showed weaker attention and higher anxiety, depression, and attention-deficit symptoms than non-users. The objective timeline helps prevention programs see which escalation paths carry mental health costs.
pmc-13571440:
Dierick and colleagues analysed in 2026 how often a precancerous colon lesion type carries dysplasia, a step toward cancer. Sessile serrated lesions are flat polyps that can progress to bowel cancer through a dysplasia stage. Pathology reports for 3,570 lesions were reviewed and terms standardised to current World Health Organization classes.

Initial reports flagged dysplasia in 102 lesions. After expert meeting review, nine were reclassified as other lesion types or as lacking dysplasia, leaving 93 confirmed cases, about 2.6 percent of lesions. Dysplasia rates did not differ significantly between the right and left sides of the colon, nor at any single site. The authors conclude dysplasia is spread evenly through the colon in this setting, so vigilance cannot focus on one region.
pmc-13572340:
Tahmida Sharmin and eight colleagues published a blood study in two thousand twenty-six on early Alzheimer's disease signals. Amyloid plaques can build up in the brain years before memory fails. The team asked whether fat-like molecules in blood track that silent stage.

They profiled blood from one hundred older adults with normal thinking, split by brain scans into amyloid-positive and amyloid-negative groups. Eighteen molecules differed between the groups, mostly in two fat families. Ratios between those families tracked plaque load, thinking scores, and a blood marker of tau protein. One ceramide also rose with plaque load. The authors say such blood signatures may one day help flag the disease before symptoms.
pmc-13572440:
Muhammed Talha Karadogan, with seven colleagues, reports a 2026 rat study of a plant compound that may shield the liver and kidneys from a cancer drug. The drug, doxorubicin, fights tumours well but harms both organs as the body clears it. The compound, syringic acid, is a natural substance that fights oxidation.

Rats got syringic acid by mouth at 100 milligrams per kilogram for ten days. On day eight, one set got a single shot of doxorubicin at 20 milligrams per kilogram to trigger organ harm. Blood tests tracked liver enzymes, urea, and creatinine, which rise when the organs suffer. Tissue slices from liver and kidney were checked under the microscope, along with a marker of fat damage. The design tests whether pre-treatment can blunt the drug's harm while it does its cancer work.
pmc-13572540:
Roman Radionov and Alla Levina present a 2026 framework that builds new attacks on image classifiers from parts. Neural networks can be fooled by tiny, crafted changes to an image, yet safety tests lean on a small set of hand-built attacks. Whole regions of possible attack designs may sit unexplored.

The framework treats an attack as a kit of blocks: a starter, a loss rule, a schedule, and a new gradient engine. Two search methods, Bayesian optimization and a custom evolutionary search, then hunt for strong combos. Tests used hardened ResNet-18 models on a small image set. The found attacks beat set benchmarks, from PGD to the AutoAttack suite, at the same change limits. The authors say auto-built audits give a tougher, more honest safety check.
pmc-13573340:
Haixia Zhao, with three colleagues, reports a 2026 survey study of students who feel guilt or anxiety when they rest. That unease, called rest intolerance, may push students toward heavy, hard-to-control internet use. The team asked whether self-compassion carries the link and whether self-control changes its strength.

The study drew 7,163 Chinese college students who rated rest unease, internet habits, self-compassion, and self-control. Rest unease rose with problem internet use in a clear positive link. Self-compassion ran the other way against both traits, and part of the path from rest unease to heavy use passed through lower self-compassion. Strong self-control softened both the direct path and the path through self-compassion. The authors offer campus programs two levers: kind self-talk and control skills.
pmc-13573440:
Tianzhao Du, with six colleagues, reviews 2026 work on smart hybrid nanoparticles for breast cancer drug delivery. These particles pair a polymer core with a lipid shell, which mixes sturdy structure with a body-friendly coat. Past carriers reached tumours unevenly and were designed by trial and error, so gains in patients stayed small.

The review weighs how particle size, mix, surface ligands, and release pace can be tuned against the barriers tumours pose. Artificial intelligence tools enter as organisers: they sort the many design choices and rank which ones merit lab tests. Flow-based manufacturing may then make the chosen designs the same way each time. The authors flag thin data, few particle-specific checks, and rule hurdles as the brakes. They frame smart design as a filter, not a cure.
pmc-13575040:
Guo-Liang Lin, Yue Wang, and Bi-Huan Cheng review tiny gene regulators called microRNAs in Parkinson's disease for 2026. Parkinson's has no reliable early test and no treatment that slows its course. MicroRNAs are short molecules that tune which genes stay active inside cells.

The review links faulty microRNA levels to cell death, energy failure in mitochondria, oxidative stress, and clumping of the alpha-synuclein protein. Since microRNAs can be measured with minor sampling, they may serve as early warning markers. The authors also cover therapies that aim to fix or block specific microRNAs. Their summary maps where these molecules might aid diagnosis and where treatment ideas still need proof.
pmc-13576140:
Ahmed Elkashif leads a 2026 mouse study of a nose-delivered vaccine against SARS-CoV-2, the virus behind COVID-19. Shots in the arm mainly target the spike protein and lose ground as variants change. A nasal vaccine that also targets the virus's membrane and nucleocapsid proteins could hold up better, since those parts change less.

Two adenovirus carriers, one from cattle and one from chimpanzees, delivered the spike part plus either full membrane and nucleocapsid proteins or selected fragments of them. The fragment version matched or beat the full version on antibody and cell responses. Vaccinated mice made strong neutralising antibodies against Omicron variants. In a susceptible mouse strain, nasal dosing gave near-complete protection, with no detectable virus in the lungs after challenge. The authors back the multiepitope nasal design.
pmc-13576240:
Muhammad Mudasar leads a 2026 genome study of the ACS gene family in papaya, the genes that drive production of ethylene, the ripening hormone. Knowing these genes helps explain fruit ripening, growth, and stress responses in a crop sold worldwide. Computer analysis of a red hermaphrodite papaya variety found seven family members.

Family trees placed the genes in four groups matching the known scheme from a model plant. Gene shapes, shared motifs, and duplication history were mapped, showing the family grew partly through segment copying. Expression data across ripening showed two genes, CpACS5 and CpACS6, switching on strongly, confirmed by targeted lab tests. A third gene acted late in fruit development. Most family members also tied to stress handling. The authors frame the catalogue as a base for breeding and ripening research.
pmc-13576440:
Michael Anyane-Yeboa and colleagues follow a six-year-old whose rare brain tumor kept coming back, in this case report from twenty twenty-six. The tumor was an intracranial mesenchymal tumor carrying a FET-CREB gene fusion, a locally aggressive growth with a high recurrence rate, worst in children. The boy, who had cerebral palsy, arrived with vomiting, unsteady gait, and headaches.

Scans found a large cystic mass in the cerebellum pressing on the brainstem and blocking fluid flow. Surgeons removed it repeatedly through the back of the skull as it recurred. Each time they faced the same bargain: the tumor hugged the nerves of face and hearing, so a small remnant was left on purpose to spare his function. Adjuvant therapy followed, with long rehabilitation for facial droop and nerve palsy. The authors stress molecular confirmation, team care, and the need for better drugs for this tumor.
pmc-13577540:
Ivan L A Spirandelli leads a 2026 study adding a shape-based guiding force to simulations of proteins assembling themselves. Simulations of molecular building blocks often get stuck in wrong shapes, since the energy landscape is rugged with many dead ends. Their added force is a long-range potential built from topology, the mathematics of shape, scored by a weighted persistence measure.

The new force works alongside an established solvent energy model based on surface geometry. Across four protein systems, the pair raised assembly success rates by up to sixteen times, and rescued cases that otherwise never assembled. Earlier topology tools only described finished structures; this one steers the search while it runs. Since it depends only on atom positions, the authors say the trick should extend to other self-assembling materials beyond proteins.
pmc-13578040:
Mashego Jackson Mamosebo and co-authors hunt natural compounds that jam a bacterial chatter system in a drug-resistant pathogen, in a study from two thousand twenty-six. The germ, Klebsiella pneumoniae, resists more drugs each year. Its LuxS system coordinates group behavior and biofilm growth, making it a tempting target.

Six plant compounds were screened by computer modeling first. Three bound the target well, and one, resveratrol, formed the steadiest complex. Lab tests then showed resveratrol killed the germ and cut its signaling traits. Mixed biofilms with a second pathogen shrank by over half. The authors pitch it as an anti-virulence lead.
pmc-13578240:
Yangyang Yuan and colleagues apply a 2026 planning method to the mix of water and green space in Nanjing, China. Parks, trees, ponds, and wetlands cool a city, store carbon, soak up storm water, and shelter wildlife, yet gains in one service can cost another. A grid of small land units forms the base for their choices.

The team weighed four services at once with an evolution style search method that keeps many good trade-offs rather than one answer. Carbon storage and cooling rose together, while wildlife value and storm water gains pulled against each other. Their final maps give one balanced layout plus four that lean toward a single aim, giving planners options they can defend with numbers.
pmc-13579840:
Jiajing Zhao and colleagues build a scoring chart to forecast liver cancer return after surgery in overweight patients, in a 2026 study. Even with clean margins, this cancer often comes back, and extra body weight may feed the risk. The group followed 259 patients with a body score at or above the overweight line, all operated at one center, and split them into training and test sets.

Two measures stood out as lone predictors: how fit patients were for daily activity, and a nutrition risk score. The chart built on the full risk set sorted future cases fairly in training and held up in the held back group. Its calls beat a standard staging system on decision value. Patients split by the chart into high and low risk groups parted clearly on cancer free time.
pmc-13580440:
Man Li and colleagues test two routine blood values together as a heart failure warning in over sixty thousand adults, in this cohort study from twenty twenty-six. Inflammation, read by high-sensitivity CRP, and low albumin, the blood's main protein, each predict heart failure alone. The Kailuan cohort let the team judge them jointly over eleven years.

One thousand four hundred forty-four participants developed heart failure. The dangerous pairing was exactly as suspected: high inflammation with below-median albumin carried about double the risk of the opposite pairing. The two risks also amplified each other beyond simple addition. A model using the joint classification discriminated best among those tried, beating the fashionable ratio of the two markers. The authors propose the pair as a cheap, everyday risk flag hiding in tests clinics already run.
pmc-13582240:
Yunjing Duan and Wei Li build a framework based on a transformer, to sort laryngeal lesions into classes from contact endoscopy images. Their 2026 study joins data from clinics, radiomic features, and representations from deep learning.

Three hundred patients from three medical centres gave close to eight thousand images. The team joined eighteen clinical variables, more than one hundred radiomic features, and thousands of deep features. They did so through a transformer encoder. More than one way to pick features, and more than one way to sort them into classes, were set side by side. The best set-up used one way to pick features, with a vision transformer classifier. Accuracy stayed high from training, through checks made in the same group, to a test centre that stood on its own. The system aims at sorting of lesions that runs on its own, and that is true.
pmc-13582640:
Valeria Pingue and six co-authors wrote a study in 2026 on rehab for grave brain harm in old adults. Strong live-in rehab can bring back lost skills, but what marks poor gains or death past age sixty-five was not well known.

The team split two hundred fifteen sick people at one site at age sixty-five. In the old group, poor swallow skill and diabetes marked weak skill scores at the time they left. Hard-to-kill germs found on the day they came in, and sepsis that came later, marked worse brain state. Poor swallow skill stood out in the young group too. The team names early flags staff can act on, such as firm care of the swallow and of germ spread. Age by itself was not the key point.
pmc-13582740:
Hailu Geremew Zeleke computes the best proton energy for making scandium-47, a medical isotope that both treats tumors and lights them up on scans, in a 2026 study. The isotope is bred by firing protons at enriched calcium-48 in a cyclotron. A nuclear reaction code simulated three exit channels, and its curves were checked against a world data library, matching well overall.

Energy choice ruled purity. Low energies mostly made the wrong scandium sibling, tanking purity near nine percent. A middle window, roughly sixteen to twenty two million electron volts, gave strong yield at about ninety four percent purity. Higher energies bred a long lived contaminant that spoiled the batch. The paper hands cyclotron teams a clear window to aim at.
pmc-13583340:
Zhaogang Liu and six co-authors published a review in twenty twenty-six on hydrogen, the smallest molecule, as a therapy for diseases of the mouth. Hydrogen selectively mops up damaging oxidants and calms inflammation and cell death in study after study. The review gathers its dental evidence disease by disease.

Caries, gum disease, implant inflammation, mucosal disorders, jaw conditions, oral cancers, and facial nerve pain all get sections. Delivery routes, from hydrogen water to inhaled gas, are compared. The molecule's effects on oral pathogens and on immune, bone, and connective tissue cells are traced through their signaling pathways. Shortcomings in the current evidence are admitted, and the authors map what convincing clinical proof would require.
pmc-13583740:
Jialei Zhang and co-authors set out a trial of an immune drug to stop flares of IgG4-related disease in a protocol from two thousand twenty-six. The disease scars many organs and often returns during maintenance care. Flares are likelier when blood IgG4 climbs again.

The China-wide trial will enroll one hundred eight such patients. Half get the drug mycophenolate mofetil added for fifty-two weeks, and half get a placebo, with neither side knowing which. The main measure is the share flaring by week fifty-two. Time to flare and disease activity are also tracked. Ethics approval and consent steps are in place. Results will go to journals and conferences.
pmc-13584440:
Ariel Pollock Star and colleagues test whether depression changes what people get from social media in this 2026 study. Support once came mostly in person, yet much of it now flows online, and people with depression often have thinner in-person networks. The team recruited 340 adults with no stated mental health diagnosis, then split them by a depression screen into settled and low-mood groups.

Active use of social media, such as posting and replying, went with stronger felt online support in both groups. That support in turn went with less loneliness and higher life satisfaction. The link between online support and lower loneliness ran stronger in the low-mood group. The authors read this as online ties making up, in part, for what depression takes away face to face.
pmc-13584740:
Großjohann and ten co-authors mapped octopamine receptors in fruit fly larvae for this study from twenty twenty-six. Octopamine is a signaling chemical that steers insect behavior and body functions. Six receptors receive its messages in different tissues. The team validated mutant fly lines for all six, each built with the same genetic tool.

The lines both mark where a receptor appears and disable it. Mapping showed all six receptors across the nervous system, central and peripheral. One stood out in the body wall muscles. Three receptors proved needed for hatching and for survival through the pupal stage. Tests also covered smell sensing and crawling. The authors offer the line set as a base for dissecting the system.
pmc-13586040:
Yutaka Miyawaki and colleagues asked how long early gullet cancer surgery can safely wait. Delays sometimes cannot be avoided, and prior studies disagreed, mostly covering late disease. Their multi-hospital look-back study followed 160 patients with early-stage gullet cancer. All had upfront surgery at seven Japanese hospitals between 2008 and 2021. Number analysis found the waiting-time line that best flagged return.

Waiting 67 days or more cut three-year time free of return from 87.9 to 73.5 percent, a hazard ratio of 2.71, while cancer-only survival did not differ clearly. Longer waits, deeper spread, and lymph-node spread flagged return on their own. The authors conclude that surgery beyond about two months raises return risk, and urge prompt booking, pending larger checks.
pmc-13586440:
Ana Paula Santos Oliveira and colleagues test teams of helpful root bacteria on common beans in field plots. Beans are a staple in Brazil, yet they demand rich soil, and heavy fertilizer use costs farmers money and harms the environment. The team built treatments from triples of growth-promoting bacterial strains, 22 mixes in all, and compared them with plain and fertilized controls at flowering and at harvest.

Three mixes stood out, each pairing a Rhizobium strain with Bacillus partners. Plants given those mixes grew stronger roots and shoots and yielded more grain. The winning bacteria fix nitrogen, free up phosphorus, and make growth hormones, which together feed the plant in place of part of the fertilizer bag. The authors offer the mixes as a cheap, greener route suited to family farms across varied soils and weather.
pmc-13587040:
Zhiyu Ma and co-authors close a large, uneven stomach wall hole with crossed purse-string loops after a scope cut, in a case report from two thousand twenty-six. A man aged sixty-three had a growth cut through the full wall, leaving a ragged gap near four centimeters wide. Three nylon loops were clipped around the rim on staggered paths.

Tightening the loops in turn wove a mesh that sealed the hole fully. Air tests showed no leak, and scans found no stray air or fluid. The growth proved a low-risk stromal tumor, and the man left hospital on day seven. Scope checks over a year showed steady healing. Readers get a low-tech fix for hard holes.
pmc-13587440:
Robert Šáhó and colleagues follow every known Czech patient with Morquio A syndrome in this 2026 cohort report. The disease, also called MPS IVA, is a storage disorder that deforms the skeleton, above all the spine and chest, because a missing enzyme lets sugar chains pile up in tissues. Nineteen patients from 17 families were tracked, most with the severe form, and eight received enzyme replacement therapy for years.

First signs appeared near age three on the whole, with firm diagnosis around age five, and every patient had skeletal symptoms at that point. Each child had at least one operation, most often on knees or spine, and neck narrowing was common. In treated patients, breathing tests and walking distance held steady or improved rather than sliding, which matters in a disease that only worsens. The team also reports two gene changes never described before.
pmc-13587540:
Qi Yu and co-authors report a study from two thousand twenty-six on the mouth bacteria of adults with allergies and their link to tooth decay. People with allergic rhinitis or asthma develop cavities more often, and shifts in oral microbes may play a role. The team sampled plaque above the gumline for gene-based profiling.

Eighty-nine people took part: thirty-two with cat-dander rhinitis, forty-six with allergic asthma, and eleven healthy controls. Allergic patients carried more diverse plaque communities than controls. Certain bacterial groups stood out in each allergy type, and one genus ranked as the top signal in the decay model. Regular dental check-ups tied to much lower decay scores among allergic patients. One common genus linked to less decay instead.
pmc-13587640:
Felix Vöhringer and colleagues reported a nickel-catalysed method to join xanthate esters with aryl and alkenyl iodides. Cross-coupling builds carbon-carbon bonds, but many partners are air-sensitive or hard to buy, and alcohols resist direct coupling. Xanthate esters, easily made from alcohols, offer a workaround. Their 2026 study shows reductive coupling of these esters under nickel catalysis, with S-allyl xanthates outperforming the common S-methyl versions.

The reaction tolerated many functional groups and converted drug-derived xanthates into diarylmethanes. Electronic properties of the partners strongly shaped outcomes. Mechanistic tests pointed to a benzylic radical formed from the xanthate, likely by single-electron transfer from nickel(I). The authors present the method as a practical route to complex molecules from simple alcohols.
pmc-13589140:
Xingyue Niu and colleagues estimated genetic links between immunity to Mycoplasma synoviae and egg traits in two laying-hen lines. The bacterium inflames joints and airways, damages eggshells, and cuts production, while vaccines work imperfectly. The team followed 2,375 Rhode Island Red and 2,575 White Leghorn hens, measuring antibodies at one hundred weeks and egg quality through the laying cycle.

Antibody levels varied widely, and heritability of the Mycoplasma-specific titer was low in both lines. Genetic patterns differed sharply by line: the titer correlated positively with eggshell strength, thickness, shape, and weight in White Leghorns, but showed mixed links in Rhode Island Reds. Breeding for disease resistance must therefore be tailored line by line, the authors conclude.
pmc-13589340:
Metin Çınaroğlu studies refugee mothers and their children in Türkiye in a paper from two thousand twenty-six, written alone. Syrian children exposed to war and displacement face high risks for emotional and learning problems. Caregiver mental health and parenting stress may shape how those risks play out.

Two hundred mother-child pairs took part, with children aged six to eleven. Mothers with more trauma symptoms reported more parenting stress and more child behavior problems. Their children also scored worse on a test of attention control. Parenting stress carried part of the link in both cases. Interviews echoed the numbers, showing exhaustion and irritability mirrored in children. Warmth, school support, and faith were protective.
pmc-13589440:
Angelika Masiarz and five colleagues published a review in two thousand twenty-six on treating inherited metabolic disorders before birth. These conditions can damage organs irreversibly starting in the womb. Earlier prenatal diagnosis now opens a window for treating the fetus itself.

Animal studies show transplanted cells can settle, produce missing enzymes, and partly correct defects, helped by fetal immune tolerance. Early human experience in storage diseases and Pompe disease suggests feasibility. Gene therapy in utero achieved lasting correction in animals. Barriers remain: weak cell take, immune reactions, vector safety, ethics, and regulation. The authors judge the field promising but experimental, with proof strongest before the clinic.
pmc-13589940:
Zhuoliang Hu leads a 2026 review of lab models for a fast growing class of cancer drugs. These drugs link a targeting antibody to a potent cell killer, so the poison goes mostly to tumor cells. Newer forms swap in other guides, such as short proteins or gene strands. Testing them in animals often fails to predict what will happen in people, Hu and the team argue.

Their answer is lab grown mini tumors from patient tissue, called organoids, and chips that link such tissue to flow and other cell types. Both keep much of a real tumor's mix of cells. The review weighs how these models could screen drugs, pick doses, and cut late failures. Cost, standards, and scale remain open problems.
pmc-13590240:
Shohei Yamaki and nine co-authors present a case report from twenty twenty-six on a cancer that filled a man's bone marrow. The cancer began in the urinary tract and spread. Such marrow spread is rare and can look like a blood disease. The man, in his mid sixties, came in with back pain and low platelets. A marrow draw came back dry.

A biopsy then showed cancer cells packed through the marrow, which nailed the cause of its failure. Low dose chemo drugs were used first, given the weak marrow. Blood counts came back and scans improved. Full dose care and a maintenance drug followed. He lived just over a year past the diagnosis.
pmc-13590940:
Zhinan Ye and co-authors link an immune balance measure in spinal fluid to memory decline in a study from two thousand twenty-six. The complement system is part of the immune defense, but its role in Alzheimer's disease is murky. The team studied people with mild cognitive impairment.

Spinal fluid from one hundred twenty-three such patients gave a ratio of two complement parts. Memory was tracked over time, along with a blood marker of tau, a protein tied to the disease. Alone, the ratio showed no tie to memory. But when the tau marker ran high, a higher ratio linked to slower memory decline. The authors call the pattern a lead for future work, not a settled fact.
pmc-13591040:
Qiujin Huang, Xiang Huifei, and Liu Qiaoyun report esophageal cancer that resurfaced in the small bowel, in a case report from two thousand twenty-six. Spread of esophageal squamous cancer to the intestine is exceedingly rare. As a rule it is found in the midst of emergency surgery.

Their patient was a fifty-four-year-old woman with stage four disease. She had repeated complete bowel obstruction in her course of care. It struck during chemo-immunotherapy and radiation for her cancer. Emergency surgery found many deposits on the bowel's outer surface. They studded the wall and made the tube narrow. About twenty centimeters of jejunum were taken out and reconnected, with a decompression tube placed. The obstruction resolved smoothly. But her decline kept more cancer therapy out of reach. A review part pulls what little literature there is on this presentation into one place.
pmc-13591340:
Rishabh Deo Singh, Mauro Calvoli, and Kyeong Kyu Kim review a bold repair strategy: turning one mature cell type into another right inside the body. Lab grown replacement cells often arrive immature, land in hostile tissue, and die soon after transplant. Cells converted in place can borrow cues from their home tissue and mature more fully. The review covers how the switch is thrown, which factors drive it, and how those factors are delivered.

Uses span many organ systems, from heart to brain to pancreas, the authors report. Open hurdles include weak delivery, patchy grasp of tissue cues, and thin detail on how the change unfolds. Singh and the team close by weighing fresh tactics meant to lift success rates toward clinic ready repair.
pmc-13592640: An Expression of Concern from the editors of PLOS One warns readers about an earlier article. That article studied health risks from iron in food crops grown with wastewater near Sargodha. The editors say concerns arose over the article's compliance with the journal's authorship policy. They advise readers to treat its findings with caution. The notice also corrects errors in how samples were gathered, in the iron values for water, soil, and crops, and in four figure captions.
pmc-13592840:
Yen-Chun Koh, Chun-che Chang, and Min-Hsiung Pan review how gut microbes sway the body's daily clocks. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-six. Day-night rhythms run much of body and brain work, and their loss tracks with metabolic, heart, and immune ills. Food and gut microbes are two hubs in that clock web.

Fat-heavy diets, excess fruit sugar, and steady drink use jar the clocks of organs and bend metabolism toward weight gain and insulin dullness. Timed feeding and set food mixes can reset clock genes and ward off such ills. Microbes swing by day too, and their acids cue host clocks. A broken microbe rhythm deepens clock drift. Human proof still lags the animal work.
pmc-13594440:

pmc-13594940:

pmc-13595340:

pmc-13595540:

pmc-13597340:

pmc-13598040:

pmc-13600840:

pmc-13605140:

A core of twenty-one mat genes ran high in all four ills. Most lone-ill marks were but thin signs of shared shifts that weak sets missed. In one set where two ills could be set side by side clean, two hundred five mat genes did split them. Shared core stands.
pmc-13605840:

pmc-13607240:

pmc-13608040:

The concentrate grade doubled as well. The authors offer the method for hard oxidised copper ores.
pmc-13608240:

pmc-13609140:

pmc-13610440:

Dose sat at a vast count per mL in the tank feeds. Past one day, no mark showed in tank wet in counts. That hints the mussels cleared the grit from the wet fast. pmc-13611940:

pmc-13613640:

pmc-13616240:

pmc-13616340:

pmc-13616840:

pmc-13616940:

pmc-13623740:

pmc-13624040:

pmc-13624540:

pmc-13624840:

pmc-13626340:

pmc-13627840:

pmc-13628140:

pmc-13628540:

pmc-13628940:

pmc-13635040:

pmc-13635240:

pmc-13635840:

pmc-13637340:

pmc-13638040:

pmc-13641140:

pmc-13642940:

pmc-13643140:

pmc-13643440:

pmc-13643540:
