Artificial tricuspid valves wear out over time, and patients with several past open-heart operations may not survive another. A catheter-delivered valve inside the old one avoids the chest being reopened.

Their forty-two-year-old patient with rheumatic heart disease had already had three sternotomies and failing right heart function with liver congestion. Imaging showed the tissue tricuspid valve severely narrowed while the left-sided valves still worked. The new valve was implanted through a vein, easing symptoms and pressure gradients markedly. The report supports the approach for carefully chosen high-risk patients.
pmc-13643640:
Muscolino and co-authors published a 2026 systematic review on body dissatisfaction in teenagers, meaning unhappiness with how one's body looks. Puberty brings fast physical change and also shifts how teens handle emotions. The review asked how those three threads, puberty, emotion control, and body image, connect during adolescence.

Muscolino searched five databases for English studies from 2000 to 2025 on young people aged six to eighteen. From 3,658 records the team kept 103 studies for detailed extraction after full text screening. The studies linked body dissatisfaction with emotion control, with links that shifted by puberty stage. A positive body image predicted calmer feelings at puberty onset, while early and advanced development carried lasting costs for wellbeing.
pmc-13645240:
Menière's disease, an inner-ear disorder marked by spinning vertigo, fluctuating hearing loss, and ringing, is revisited by Rajpoot and colleagues. The condition has puzzled clinicians since the eighteen hundreds because attacks arrive unpredictably and treatments work unevenly, while lifestyle advice alone often fails to control vertigo. The team assessed a practical oral regimen at a tertiary centre, starting with lifestyle measures and adding betahistine, an antihistamine-like drug, plus two diuretics that reduce fluid pressure in the inner ear.

Lifestyle steps alone did not control vertigo adequately, but combined oral therapy brought marked improvement, with far fewer vertigo episodes and hearing levels that held steady. Only a small share of patients still needed assessment for surgery after maximal medical treatment. Rajpoot and colleagues propose this non-invasive combination as a first-line strategy, reserving operations for patients whose disabling vertigo persists despite full drug therapy.
pmc-13645540:
Teshamae Monteith and nine colleagues report a United States survey study on sex differences in short-term use of the migraine drug rimegepant. Short-term prevention means taking a drug for a limited stretch when attacks are more likely. The team gathered real-world answers online from adults who had used the drug recently. Their focus is how women and men differ in triggers and in reasons for choosing this approach.

Of 425 adults surveyed, 152 used rimegepant for short-term prevention, and most users were women, who more often cited a doctor's advice, attack frequency, and attack severity as reasons. Stress, poor sleep, and noise were the leading triggers for both sexes. Satisfaction ran high across the group, which the authors read as support for this flexible way of preventing attacks.
pmc-13646040:
Tae Hoon Yang and four colleagues review 232 patients who had lumbar spine surgery at one hospital between 2020 and 2024, looking for links with a rare bleeding complication. The complication is a blood collection pressing near the spinal nerves after surgery, which can force a second operation. Four patients developed it, and three of those bleeds sat below the operated level. The team compared surgical and past-treatment factors between groups.

All three patients with the lower-level bleed had earlier received a needle procedure called percutaneous epidural neuroplasty, against about one in six of the other patients. With so few events, the authors treat the link strictly as a lead for further study, not a proven risk. They advise doctors to stay alert when patients with that earlier procedure develop symptoms after surgery. In such cases, scans may need to cover levels below the operation site.
pmc-13646140:
Manyoga Blantina Mathoto and four colleagues interview professional nurses in public hospitals of Mopani District, Limpopo, South Africa, about reporting adverse events, the incidents where care itself harms a patient. Twenty-six nurses took part in in-depth interviews chosen for their experience. The team coded the transcripts for what nurses know about events and about the steps for reporting them. Clear reporting is treated worldwide as a backbone of patient safety.

Most nurses knew the broad idea and process, yet real gaps showed. Some could not say what counts as an adverse event, and several mixed events up with near misses, where harm was barely avoided. Answers also clashed on who should report and how fast. The authors recommend focused teaching and repeated grounding in standard procedures. Their findings give district managers a concrete training agenda for safer wards.
pmc-13648040:
Maruthasalam Pannerselvam and six colleagues made a light-driven cleaner from iron disulfide coated with a plastic called polythiophene. Their goal was to break down two germ drugs, tetracycline and ciprofloxacin, in water under plain visible light. These drugs linger in waste water and can breed drug-proof germs.

The mix was made by a simple brew step, and surface tests showed the two parts touch closely. Under light, the cleaner wiped out about 83 percent of one drug and 85 percent of the other in their runs. It also held up well across repeat use. The team says the work backs green ways to clean drug-tainted water.
pmc-13649440:
Weihua Yang and three colleagues introduce a set of 79 papers on new ideas in eye disease research. Eye disease is a top cause of sight loss worldwide, and the field is shifting fast with new scans, smart tools, and digital health.

The papers fall into six groups, from eye scans and sight tests to gene markers, disease forecasts, and care for whole populations. A shared thread runs through them: the field now measures more, links eye signs to whole-body health, and uses computing to sort complex data. The editors note that the eye can serve as a window on the health of the rest of the body. Their goal is to turn rich data into better care.
pmc-13649740:
Sarah W. Alawadhi and two colleagues report a 13-year-old boy whose immune system has destroyed his own red blood cells since he was 11 months old. He first came to care pale and yellow-skinned with a fever. Tests showed low blood counts, young red cells flooding out, and a positive antibody test that fit the disease.

Gene sequencing found a new change in a gene called PLCG1, which helps steer immune signals. The change had never been reported before. The authors say it may help explain why his immune system turned on his blood, and it widens the known range of harm from this gene. They call for lab work to test how the change acts.
pmc-13650140:
Zeyu Li and seven colleagues, publishing in 2026, release EGID, a dataset of stomach endoscopy images built to train and test artificial intelligence for gastritis classification. Gastritis is stomach lining inflammation, and its shrinking form can precede stomach cancer, yet earlier image collections labeled only part of the picture.

The set holds 5,883 white-light images from 229 patients seen at a Shanghai hospital during 2024. Each patient's images carry labels on four separate dimensions: infection with the H. pylori bacterium, whether tissue shrinkage is present, how that shrinkage is distributed, and the gastritis type. Two experienced endoscopists labeled the image-based dimensions independently, with a senior specialist settling disagreements, and their agreement was very high. The authors describe EGID as the first public multi-label set of its kind, useful both for building diagnostic software and for training clinicians.
pmc-13651440:
Paulo Piluski and seven colleagues review blood clot prevention after reverse total shoulder replacement, an operation with no agreed standard for extended drug prophylaxis after discharge. Clots after this surgery are uncommon but can kill, and three habits coexist in practice: a direct anticoagulant, aspirin, or nothing beyond the hospital stay.

One referral center's cases from January 2021 to April 2024 were reviewed, and 68 patients met the study's rules after screening. No symptomatic deep vein clots occurred in any group. One lung clot struck the no-prophylaxis group and proved fatal, one struck the aspirin group, and none occurred under the anticoagulant, though the small numbers left every comparison far from significance. Three non-clot complications all appeared in the anticoagulant group. The authors present the patterns descriptively and stop short of recommending one strategy over another.
pmc-13651740:
Basma Ali and six co-authors compute, from first principles, how arsenolite cages clump together. Arsenolite is a molecular crystal built from matching cage molecules of arsenic and oxygen. Why the cages clump as a team explains how such molecular solids hold together at all.

Clusters of one through five cages were relaxed and studied with density functional theory, mapping shape, energy balance, electronic structure, charge flow, and electrostatic potential. Movies of the clusters at finite temperature tested their thermal toughness. Each added cage made the whole more stable, a team effect, yet every cage kept its own shape intact. Charge shifted step by step across the growing cluster, knitting a changing electrostatic network between cages, and the clumps survived simulated heating. The authors offer this route as a design basis for cage-based molecular crystals and larger assembled materials.
pmc-13652540:
Christopher Graser and six colleagues study how sudden bursts of mutation, rather than slow steady change, shape the way cancers adapt. Tumors often gain their genetic changes in punctuated jumps, and the team asked what those jumps do to later evolution. Their focus is the fitness valley problem, where a cancer cell needs several mutations at once because each single change hurts on its own but the combination helps.

Modeling and analysis show that bursty mutagenesis makes valley crossing far more likely, since a single burst can deliver the whole winning combination in one step. Steady mutation, by contrast, tends to lose the harmful first step before the rest arrive. The finding reframes punctuated change as an engine of adaptation, not just a pattern in tumor genomes. It may help explain why some cancers evolve resistance and aggression with surprising speed.
pmc-13659540:
Jiashu Han and five colleagues describe an organ-sparing operation for benign tumors of the pancreatic head, planned with photon-counting CT scans. The standard operation for this area removes the pancreatic head with parts of nearby organs and rebuilds the digestive tract, a heavy price for a growth that is not cancer. Precise imaging let the surgeons map the shared blood vessels of the pancreatic head and duodenum before cutting.

The subtotal resection removed the tumor while fully protecting the pancreaticoduodenal arcades, the vessel loops that keep the duodenum alive. Keeping those vessels intact is what makes limited resection safe here instead of reckless. The report shows how a newer scanner, able to show fine vascular detail. Can widen the group of patients who can avoid the full Whipple operation and its long-term digestive costs.
pmc-13674540:
Staszewska and Merecz-Kot review evidence on fit between person and organization and mental health at work, in work from twenty twenty-six. Person organization fit describes how well an employee matches their employer in values, goals, needs, and traits. Research has mostly tied fit to performance.

Attention is shifting to mental health outcomes. The review summarized current evidence on whether good fit protects, and poor fit harms, employee mental health in occupational settings. If fit predicts wellbeing, hiring and onboarding become mental health tools, not just productivity tools. The review also exposes where the evidence is still thin.
pmc-13677440:
Yuria Takamura and five colleagues report a man whose hormone control glands failed decades after childhood cancer care, in a case dated twenty twenty-six. The man had leukemia at age five and received chemotherapy plus whole-brain radiation. At forty-two he came in with bleeding around the brain, which was drained. He then lost appetite and energy, and his blood salt fell low.

Tests showed his pituitary system had failed on several hormone lines, including stress and growth hormones. A scan found a fluid sac pressing on the gland. The gap of thirty-seven years may be among the longest ever reported for this late effect. The authors urge life-long hormone checks for childhood cancer survivors.
pmc-13682840:
Briseida Yáñez and a team of co-authors studied beetles in a Texas pine forest after a wildfire. Their paper, from twenty twenty-six, covers the Lost Pines area, a lone stand at the west edge of this pine's range. Fires have grown more frequent and more severe in recent decades. The team caught flight active beetles two years after a twenty twenty-two fire. They used past data from twenty eleven as a base line.

They asked if fire severity, plant growth, or plain change over time drove the beetle mix. Burned and unburned sites were set side by side. Readers in ecology learn how range edge forests and their insects bounce back from fire. Both time and burn depth shaped the mix they found.
pmc-3021840:
Oostenveld, Fries, Maris, and co-authors describe FieldTrip, open-source software for analysing brain recordings. FieldTrip handles MEG, EEG, and invasive electrical recordings from the brain. It is built as a MATLAB toolbox with a complete set of consistent, user-friendly functions.

Inside, the toolbox covers the full path from raw signals to statistical results. Open code lets labs share analysis steps exactly, so findings can be checked and reused. FieldTrip became a standard environment in cognitive neuroscience, shaping how brain activity data are processed across many labs.  Shared pipelines also make multi-site brain studies far easier to compare directly.
pmc-4320440:
Moher, Shamseer, Clarke, and many colleagues issued the PRISMA-P statement in 2015. Systematic reviews should rest on a protocol that sets out the reason, the hypothesis, and the planned methods in advance. Few reviews at the time reported whether such a protocol even existed.

PRISMA-P lists what a review protocol should describe, item by item. Well described protocols make a review's methods easier to understand and judge. They also limit quiet changes of plan after results are seen. Journals and funders use the checklist to raise the quality of reviews that guide medical practice and policy.
pmc-5139140:
Ouzzani, Hammady, Fedorowicz, and their co-authors presented Rayyan in 2016, a web and mobile app for systematic reviews. A systematic review can summarize the effects found in many randomized trials and give numerical answers on whether a treatment works. Screening search results to find the right trials is slow work.

Rayyan was built to speed up that filtering step. Reviewers can screen titles and abstracts on the web or a phone, alone or as a team. No single earlier method met the priority needs of reviewers, the authors note. Faster screening frees time for the analysis and writing that give a review its value.
pmc-5866840:
Mohammad Saklayen reviewed the global epidemic of metabolic syndrome in 2018. The syndrome groups belly fat, insulin resistance, high blood pressure, and abnormal blood fats. Definitions vary a little between health bodies, but the pattern is the same.

The review traces how this cluster raises the risk of diabetes and heart disease. It links the worldwide rise to urban living, rich diets, and low activity. Rates now climb in poorer countries as well as rich ones. Readers get a clear picture of why doctors treat the cluster as one warning sign rather than separate small problems.
pmc-6602440:
Zefang Tang, Boxi Kang, Chenwei Li, and coauthors launched GEPIA2 in 2019. GEPIA is a web server for studying gene expression in tumors and normal tissue. It draws on the large TCGA cancer and GTEx normal data sets.

The new version adds finer tools, including analysis by cancer subtype and by gene signature. Users can compare survival between high and low expression groups with a few clicks. No programming is needed, which opened cancer data to many clinicians. GEPIA2 became a quick first check for whether a gene behaves oddly in cancer.
pmc-8387240:
Kathryn Tunyasuvunakool and colleagues at DeepMind reported in 2021 that they had predicted structures for nearly the whole human proteome, the full set of human proteins. A protein's shape reveals how it works and where a drug might grip it. After decades of effort, experiments had covered only part of the residues in human protein sequences.

Using the AlphaFold method, the team computed models for the great majority of human proteins and released them openly. The article describes the coverage achieved, how confidence in each model is reported, and the limits users should keep in mind. For medicine, an atlas of human protein shapes offers starting points for drug design and for understanding disease mutations.
ranke-history-popes-vol-1-1840:
Leopold von Ranke's History of the Popes, Volume 1, appears in Sarah Austin's translation of 1840. Ranke is called the father of modern historiography for his use of archives. This volume covers the papacy from its medieval height through the Reformation era. Popes, cardinals, and Italian courts come alive from state papers.

Ranke aimed to show the past as it actually was, in his famous phrase. His calm tone toward Catholic and Protestant alike was new and striking. The work made the seminar method of history famous abroad. Austin's version carried it through the English-speaking world. Volume 1 opens a classic of both church and political history.
regino-prum-de-synodalibus-causis-latin-:
Regino, abbot of Prüm, compiled his two books on synodal cases around 906. Bishops used the collection when judging clergy and laity in their courts. This text follows Wasserschleben's edition of 1840, the standard scholarly printing of Regino's Latin.

Regino's gathering is famous above all as the transmitter of the Canon Episcopi. That canon, set among his cases, taught that witches' night flights were demonic illusions. His books also treat magic and superstition across many headings. The collection is a foundation of canon law on such matters. Through Regino, an early medieval ruling of doubt shaped church courts for the next six hundred years.
savigny-system-heutigen-roem-rechts-1840:
Savigny's System of Modern Roman Law began appearing in German in 1840, the summa of his career. He had led the historical school for a quarter century, and the System gathers its doctrine into one ordered account of private law. Lawyers call the approach pandectist, after the Pandects, the Roman Digest at its core.

The volumes order the whole of private law: persons, property, obligations, and family, each concept defined and placed by historical light. Savigny's method treats law as a system whose parts explain each other, growing from a people's life rather than a legislator's whim. The System became the bible of nineteenth-century jurisprudence in Germany. Its concepts passed into the German Civil Code of 1900, so its fingerprints rest on the private law of many nations today.
shelley-defence-of-poetry-1840:
Percy Bysshe Shelley wrote A Defence of Poetry in 1821, answering a friend's playful claim that poetry was fading in a practical age. Shelley left the essay unfinished, and it stayed in manuscript until 1840. By then Shelley had been dead for eighteen years.

Shelley argues that poets shape the moral and social imagination of their age. Reason counts and measures, he says, but imagination gives knowledge its human worth. Poetry strengthens sympathy, the root of all moral good. The essay closes with the famous claim that poets are the unacknowledged legislators of the world. It became the most quoted defense of poetry of the whole century.
st-martin-s-summer-pg2640: Rafael Sabatini wrote St. Martin's Summer. It was first published in 1921. The contents open with the Seneschal of Dauphiny. Monsieur de Garnache comes next. The dowager's compliance and the chateau de Condillac follow. One chapter shows Garnache losing his temper. The next shows him keeping it. The opening of a trap and its closing frame the middle. The seneschal's advice and a recruit stand there. Valerie's gaoler, a courier, and Florimond's letter lead on. A conference, a surprise, and a night run in Chapter XIX close the list shown.
state-of-the-union-addresses-pg5040:
Dwight D. Eisenhower gives nine yearly addresses, from February 2, 1953, to January 12, 1961, parted by three stars. The first welcomes the honor of speaking before the Eighty-third Congress with his first message. It is plainly the joint aim of the house's leaders and of his team, he says, to bear out the call to duty sent last November by the American people.

He lists the great labors of that lead: to use America's weight in world affairs with such strength and foresight as to check attack and in time win peace. At home, a rule of such clean record and good working that its honor wins respect abroad. Free rein for the drives that spark new work in trade and making, so that its yield may brace freedom in all lands. And care for the well-being of all citizens, with an equal chance for all.
stukeley-stonehenge-temple-restord-1740:
Antiquary William Stukeley surveyed Stonehenge and read it as a Druid temple. His book Stonehenge, A Temple Restor'd to the British Druids came out in 1740. Stukeley was a doctor and cleric who loved old Britain.

He measured the stones and the avenues around them with care. Then he built a grand theory of Druid rites upon the plan. That theory is now doubted, but his records hold real value. Later diggers destroyed much that he drew in place. His dream of Druids shaped how Britain saw the stones for two centuries.
teste-manuel-pratique-magnetisme-1840:
Alphonse Teste wrote his Practical Manual of Animal Magnetism in French in 1840. French healers who used magnetic passes and trance soon treated it as their standard guide. Teste aimed to make a disputed art look calm, skilled, and safe.

Step by step, the manual shows how to induce a trance in a patient. It then explains how to read illness during magnetic sleep and how to treat it. Clear rules, case notes, and warnings fill the pages. The book shows what a trained magnetizer in France was expected to know and do each day.
the-great-round-world-and-what-is-going-: No. 40 of The Great Round World and What Is Going On in It is dated August 12, 1897. The paper is a weekly newspaper for boys and girls. Only front matter is present here: a masthead and the paper's camera premium. Four new subscribers earn the sender a Pocket Kodak, the same premium offered in the numbers around this one. The Kodak comes loaded for twelve exposures. Its slides tell the user which stop stands before the lens, and whether the shutter is set for a time exposure or an instant one.
the-history-of-don-quixote-volume-2-part:
In Ormsby's translation, Don Quixote by Miguel de Cervantes moves on to Volume 2, Part 40. Chapter sixty-seven tells of the resolution Don Quixote formed to turn shepherd and take to a life in the fields while the year of his pledged word runs its course. Reflections crowded on him before his fall; far more crowd on him after it.

Under the shade of a tree, thoughts come stinging like flies on honey. Some turn on the disenchantment of Dulcinea, others on the quiet life ahead. Cervantes lets a beaten knight plan a pastoral year, trading the lance for a shepherd's crook while his promise binds him to stay home.
the-mirror-of-literature-amusement-and-i:
For Saturday, May 30, 1829, the Mirror's No. 372 illustrates Epsom's new race stand ahead of the June races. The Epsom Grand Stand Association raised 20,000 pounds in a thousand twenty-pound shares, patronized by the Jockey Club's stewards. The building, modeled on Doncaster's stand but much larger, will hold four to five thousand persons. Its style is Grecian, and the roof is already on.

The stand measures 156 feet wide including its terrace and sixty feet deep. A portico with Doric columns supports a balcony under a verandah of ornamental iron pillars. Four large refreshment rooms, a spacious hall, and a stone staircase serve the interior. Temporary accommodation will serve the ensuing spring races. Readers receive horse racing's new architecture itemized like a prospectus, because it is one: the engraving advertises the shares' finished product.

The Mirror's number for Saturday, April 4, 1829, No. 364, illustrates the tomb of Gower, the poet, in St. Saviour's, Southwark. Dr. Johnson dignified Gower as the father of English poetry, so no apology is needed for the memorial. The tomb stands in the church's north aisle under three Gothic arches rich with cinquefoil tracery, roses, and carved work. Two rows of trefoil niches line the space behind.

Within three painted niches stand Charity, Mercy, and Pity, entwined with golden scrolls. The scrolls carry French verses begging Jesus to regard Gower with pity and guard his soul, each followed by an English rendering. A square Doric column rises between the arches, crowned with carved pinnacles. Cherubim descend from the interior arches' lower ends. Readers receive a fourteenth-century poet's monument transcribed figure by figure, inscription by inscription.

Volume 19, No. 536, dated March 3, 1832, opens at the entrance to the Botanic Garden in Manchester. The town is introduced as a place where a thirst for knowledge reached every rank. Its Philosophical Society, Royal Institution, philological society, and public libraries all support that claim.

The Botanical and Horticultural Society, organized in the autumn of 1827, stood behind the garden. An earlier floral society already counted six hundred subscribers. Quoted addresses stress that botany around Manchester was not confined to the rich. Working cottagers and mechanics had improved many plants and fruits, yet rare foreign specimens stayed costly and hard to obtain. A shared garden was meant to remove that barrier.
the-moravians-in-georgia-1735-1740:
Adelaide L. Fries's history The Moravians in Georgia, 1735-1740, printed at Winston-Salem, North Carolina, opens with a preface about judging events by their endings. Her example is the Battle of Bunker Hill. British troops quickly drove raw American volunteers from their hill on June 17, 1775, yet descendants of the beaten side raised the monument.

Fries applies that argument to the Moravian Church's first settlement attempt on the American continent. Histories usually pass over the Georgia colony in a few paragraphs, she writes. Yet the story of the Renewed Church, the Unitas Fratrum, would have run wholly differently without it. The Moravian Church might never have rooted in England, Methodism might never have arisen, and no American Moravian provinces might have been planned.
the-playboy-of-the-western-world-a-comed:
J. M. Synge's The Playboy of the Western World, a comedy in three acts, opens with the author's preface. That is the same preface that opens the sibling record of the play. Synge writes that the wildest sayings in the piece are tame beside what may be heard in hillside cabins at Geesala, Carraroe, or Dingle Bay. Anyone who has lived closely with the Irish peasantry, he says, knows their imagination at first hand.

Much of the preface defends the richness of that speech. Synge contrasts Mallarmé and Huysmans, makers of an elaborate town literature, with Ibsen and Zola, who handle real life in joyless words. He recalls writing The Shadow of the Glen in a Wicklow house. Talk overheard through a chink in the floor, from servant girls below, helped him more than learning could. A contents list promises the persons of the play and its three acts.
the-tempest-pg1540: A contents list and cast of characters are what this record gives of Shakespeare's Tempest, with no spoken line included. The contents move from the ship at sea in a tempestuous noise, through Prospero's cell and other parts of the island, to an epilogue. The cast names Alonso of Naples, Prospero the right Duke of Milan, his usurping brother Antonio, Miranda, Ariel the airy spirit, and Caliban the slave. Readers can chart the whole play's setting and company while its poetry waits elsewhere.
tob-0040:
Rob Arndt compiled German Disc Programs and Occult Origins, a research file on the claims of Nazi disc aircraft and their supposed occult roots. It treats the Haunebu and Vril craft of postwar legend and the Thule and Vril societies of early Nazi lore. The work dates from 2016 and circulates as a fringe-history dossier.

Arndt gathers the saucer stories, secret-society genealogies, and wonder-weapon tales into one documented survey of the mythos. No reliable evidence supports the disc programs as real aircraft; historians class them as postwar legend. The compilation's value lies in showing the legend whole: how occult societies, wartime rumor, and flying-saucer culture fused into a lasting story.
tob-10040:
Evelyn Underhill, the scholar who brought mysticism to modern English readers, devoted a full study to Jan van Ruusbroec. Ruusbroec was a fourteenth-century Flemish mystic, among the great voices of medieval Dutch spirituality. Underhill follows him from parish priest to prior of a religious community.

Beyond the life, she explains his vision of the soul's ascent toward God, in language meant for readers outside a monastery. His teaching stressed an active life of love joined to deep contemplation. Underhill treats him not as a curiosity but as a serious guide, and her study remains a short, sympathetic entry into his thought.
tob-13340:
R. H. Charles's classic translation presents the Book of Enoch, an ancient apocalypse attributed to Noah's great-grandfather. Quoted in the New Testament letter of Jude, Enoch was nevertheless left out of most Bibles. Preserved whole only in Ethiopia's canon, the text survived in Ge'ez while its Hebrew and Aramaic forms largely vanished.

Its central story tells of the Watchers, angels who descended for human women, fathered giants, and taught forbidden arts, bringing judgment on heaven and earth. Visions of the end times follow. Enoch shaped early Christian and Jewish ideas of demons, fallen angels, and final judgment more deeply than its excluded status would suggest.
tob-4140:
Elias Ashmole, astrologer and collector, saved England's alchemical verse in the Theatrum Chemicum Britannicum of 1652. He printed the poetic pieces of the famous English philosophers of the hermetic art: George Ripley, Thomas Norton, and masters whose names are lost.

The poems teach the Great Work in allegory and riddle, in the spelling and music of their age. Ashmole, whose gifts founded Oxford's Ashmolean Museum, knew these texts might vanish without him. He was right. Checked from the 1919 printing, his collection remains the great storehouse of English alchemy in verse, and a monument to one collector's foresight.
tob-4240:
William Hone, the radical London printer who beat blasphemy charges in famous trials, published his Apocryphal New Testament in 1820. His collection prints the writings the early church left outside its canon. Infancy gospels of Jesus stand here, and the Gospel of Nicodemus. Letters ascribed to Paul and others fill out the set.

Hone meant the book for freethinkers' shelves, and it stayed in print for that audience all century. The translations are old ones, gathered rather than made fresh. Checked from the 1919 printing, his volume shows how apocrypha reached ordinary readers: cheaply, boldly, and under a fighter's imprint.
townshend-facts-in-mesmerism-1840:
Chauncy Hare Townshend made the literary case for mesmerism in Facts in Mesmerism, printed in 1840. Townshend was a poet and man of letters, not a doctor. His book records cases he witnessed and tested himself. The subtitle pleads for a dispassionate inquiry into the subject.

He asks readers to weigh evidence before they mock or believe. Mesmeric sleep, painless operations, and clairvoyant claims enter his record. The work became the most cited early English defense outside medical journals. It shows mesmerism winning cultured friends in its first British years. Townshend's tone is curious, candid, and measured. His cases still anchor histories of the movement.
traite-de-phrenologie-1840: Traité de phrénologie, 1840. The French treatise. This book preserves that work. The paper lived through the years. Coming generations can find it. It holds its historical place. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later in their work.
un-ga-res-140:
Nauru, a tiny island in the Pacific Ocean, passed from League of Nations rule to UN trusteeship under Resolution 140, adopted on 1 November 1947. Under the old League mandate, Australia had run the island on behalf of itself, New Zealand, and the United Kingdom. The UN Charter of 1945 had since set up a Trusteeship System for just such lands.

The three states agreed to place Nauru under that system and to run it on the terms set out here. The Assembly, acting under Article 85 of the Charter, approves those terms in place of the old mandate. Nauru stayed a trust land for two more decades, until its freedom in 1968.
un-ga-res-40:
Strains over the big-power veto showed up early at the United Nations. Resolution 40 was passed on 13 December 1946. It notes the rows that had grown up around Article 27 of the Charter. That clause gives the five permanent members of the Security Council their veto. Small states feared the veto would slow the Council or block it outright.

The Assembly begs the permanent members to take care, in talks with each other and with fellow members, that the veto not bar swift Council action. It also urges the Council to adopt habits of work, within the Charter, that ease the strain. The veto fight, as this text shows, is as old as the UN itself.
un-ga-res-a-69-40:
Nuclear arms are named the gravest threat to mankind in Resolution A/69/40, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. Any use or threat of such arms, the text holds, would breach the Charter. It argues that the spread of these arms in any form would deepen the risk of nuclear war. Full nuclear disarmament, and the end of such arms for good, are held up as the sole sure guard.

Till that day comes, states with nuclear arms are pressed to shield states without them from use or threat of use. The hair-trigger alert of ready arms is singled out: it carries an unfit risk of a launch by error or without leave, with ruin for all mankind.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
Resolution 140 (II) was approved by the General Assembly on 1 November 1947. It placed the island of Nauru under the United Nations trusteeship system. Nauru is a small island in the Pacific. It had been run by Australia under a League of Nations mandate. Australia ran it on behalf of Australia, New Zealand, and the United Kingdom. The agreement replaced that mandate.

The three governments were named joint administering authority. Australia was to carry out the day-to-day rule, lawmaking, and courts. They promised to guard the rights and land of Nauru's own people. They promised to aid their progress in schooling, health, and public life. They promised to protect free speech, worship, and assembly. All this was under the watch of the Trusteeship Council.

General Assembly Resolution 40, adopted on 13 December 1946, took up the use of the veto in the Security Council. Members disagreed over how Article 27 of the Charter should be read and used. The Assembly earnestly asked the permanent members to work in talks with each other and with the Council's other members. The aim was that their special voting privilege would not hold up prompt decisions.

The Council was urged to adopt habits and ways of working, within the Charter, that would ease the strain around Article 27 and let it act fast and well. In shaping them, it was to weigh the views members had voiced during the session.

Resolution 69/40 of the General Assembly, 'Reducing nuclear danger,' focuses on accident and miscalculation rather than arsenals themselves. It calls for a review of nuclear doctrines. It calls for immediate steps to cut the risk of unintentional or accidental nuclear use. In particular, weapons should be taken off hair-trigger alert and de-targeted. The five nuclear-weapon states are asked to carry out such measures. The Secretary-General is asked to push the Advisory Board on Disarmament Matters' seven recommendations for reducing the risk of nuclear war.
un-sc-res-1040: The official series of Council decisions runs through Resolution 1040, catalogued here for 1996. A resolution may address a conflict, a court vacancy, a new member, or the running of the United Nations itself. Anyone studying UN practice can read the decision itself here, in the Wikisource transcription of the official record. The catalog places it in the DECLASSIFIED group of official public records.
un-sc-res-1340: Council action recorded as Resolution 1340 appears in this catalog under the year 2001. Formal decisions of this sort guide UN staff, peacekeeping forces, and governments in the years that follow. What is preserved is the exact formal wording, transcribed on English Wikisource from the official record of the Council. Its place here reflects the library's aim of keeping primary records readable.
un-sc-res-140: Madagascar, then styled the Malagasy Republic, asked to join the United Nations in 1960. The Council took up the request at its 870th meeting. That meeting fell on 29 June 1960. Members raised no objection. In a single sentence, the Council says it has examined the application. It then recommends admission to the General Assembly. Brief as it is, the text marks the formal UN welcome for a newly independent state.
un-sc-res-1440:
Chechen gunmen held hundreds of hostages in a Moscow theater in October 2002. On 24 October 2002 the Security Council condemned the seizure in the strongest terms. It called the act heinous. It treated it, like all international terrorism, as a threat to peace. The Council acted one day after the attack began. The standoff was still under way as members voted.

The resolution demands the immediate and unconditional release of all hostages. It sends deep sympathy to Russia's people and government. It also goes to the victims and their families. All states must help Russia find and punish those behind the attack. That duty flowed from the counter-terrorism rules set in resolution 1373.
un-sc-res-1540:
Weapons of mass destruction in private hands drove this landmark text of 2004. On 28 April 2004 the Security Council ruled that spreading such weapons threatens world peace. It acted under Chapter VII, so its orders bind every state. The fear was that terrorist or criminal groups might build nuclear, chemical, or biological arms. States had to cut off every path to that outcome.

No state may help non-state actors seek such weapons in any form. Every state must pass laws that bar private work on them. States must also build tight controls over dangerous materials. Stockpiles had to be counted and guarded. A committee would track how states carried the rules out. The text made non-proliferation a duty for all, not just treaty members.
un-sc-res-1640:
Eritrea and Ethiopia faced twin demands over the stalled border peace on 23 November 2005. Eritrea had banned UNMEE helicopter flights on 5 October and tightened other limits since. The move cut the mission's ability to work and put its staff at risk. Ethiopia still refused to accept the Boundary Commission's final ruling without conditions. An envoy had visited both capitals from 6 to 9 November.

The Council deeply deplored Eritrea's continued restrictions on UNMEE. It demanded that Eritrea reverse its steps and give the mission full freedom of movement. Both parties were called to show maximum restraint and to pull their forces back from the border zone. The Council demanded that Ethiopia accept the Boundary Commission's decision fully and without delay, and start the talks needed for marking the border. The Secretary-General would watch both sides' compliance and report. Further measures were held in reserve.
un-sc-res-1740:
Nepal's peace agreement gained a United Nations mission on 23 January 2007. The government and the Communist Party of Nepal (Maoist) had signed a Comprehensive Peace Agreement on 21 November 2006. Both sides asked for United Nations help with arms monitoring and election watching. An advance team of monitors and electoral staff was already going in. The Secretary-General's report of 9 January 2007 set out the plan.

The Council established a United Nations political mission in Nepal, UNMIN. Its mandate covered watching the management of arms and armed personnel of both sides and helping monitor the coming constituent assembly election. The mission was sized to Nepal's special setting and to the parties' own ownership of the peace. The Secretary-General had to keep the Council informed of progress. The parties were asked to guard United Nations staff and keep the process moving.
un-sc-res-1940:
Sierra Leone's sanctions chapter closed on 29 September 2010. The government in Freetown wrote on 9 September asking for the measures to be lifted. Its letter updated the Council on the country's recovery. The Council had long said it would end the measures once the government held full control and all other forces stood disarmed. The peacebuilding office in Sierra Leone drew its praise.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council terminated the measures in paragraphs 2, 4, and 5 of resolution 1171 (1998) with immediate effect. Those terms carried the arms and travel limits left from the war years. The Council also dissolved the sanctions committee set up in 1997 under resolution 1132. States were urged to help the Special Court, or any court taking its cases, bring Johnny Paul Koroma to justice if he lived. Lifting the last measures marked Sierra Leone's formal exit from the Council's sanctions list.
un-sc-res-240: Formal action by the Council in its numbered series produced Resolution 240, which the catalog dates to 1967. These short legal texts often sit at turning points, since the Council acts when peace or security is at stake. The text here follows the English Wikisource transcription of the official record, so readers get the Council's own wording. It sits in this library among other public records in the DECLASSIFIED group.
un-sc-res-340:
Fighting in the October 1973 Middle East war had outrun two ceasefire orders. On 25 October 1973 the Security Council demanded a complete ceasefire at once. It told the parties to return to the positions held on 22 October. United Nations observers still could not reach both sides of the line. The Council wanted more of them, fast.

The resolution also creates a United Nations Emergency Force on the spot. Its troops would come from member states, but not from the permanent members. The Secretary-General had twenty-four hours to report on the first steps. That force, known as UNEF II, then stood between the Egyptian and Israeli armies.
un-sc-res-40: Indonesia's political future in two regions drew the Council's eye in February 1948. On 28 February 1948 it asked its Committee of Good Offices to watch western Java and Madura closely. The committee had to report to the Council at frequent intervals. Political events in those areas were the focus. The whole resolution is a single sentence. It formed part of the Council's close watch on the Dutch-Indonesian dispute.
un-sc-res-540: Entered in the record as Resolution 540, this Security Council text is catalogued at 1949. Behind each numbered text lies a meeting, a draft, and a vote, even when the final wording runs to a few lines. Read in sequence with its neighbours, it helps trace how Council practice grew across the postwar decades. No summary replaces it; the record itself is the content of the entry.
un-sc-res-940:
A Council decision on Haiti took shape as Resolution 940, adopted on 31 July 1994. A military regime held power against the Governors Island Agreement. Rights abuses grew, refugees fled, and the joint civilian mission had been expelled. The elected president, Jean-Bertrand Aristide, asked for help from abroad.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council lets member states form a multinational force under one command. The force may use all necessary means to remove the military leaders and bring Aristide back. A small United Nations advance team of up to sixty will link with the force. After calm returns, the United Nations Mission in Haiti takes over at 6,000 troops. Sanctions will end once Aristide returns.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Security Council resolution 1040, adopted on 29 January 1996, addresses the worsening crisis in Burundi. The Council says it is deeply concerned at the continued deterioration of the situation and the threat to regional stability. It condemns those responsible for the rising violence, including attacks on refugees and aid workers. It stresses Burundi's responsibility for the safety of international personnel.

The Council demands restraint from all concerned. It backs a comprehensive political dialogue in support of the Convention of Government of 10 September 1994. It invites states to help identify and dismantle radio stations that incite hatred and violence. It asks the Secretary-General for contingency planning and a full report by 20 February 1996. It warns that it is ready to consider an arms ban and travel restrictions. Those would target leaders who keep encouraging violence.

Resolution 1140, adopted on 28 November 1997, is a two-line procedural text on the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia. Recalling its Resolution 1110 (1997), the Security Council decides to extend the mandate of the United Nations Preventive Deployment Force, UNPREDEP. The extension is for one additional short period ending on 4 December 1997. The Council also decides to remain actively seized of the matter. The force was the UN's first preventive deployment, stationed to watch the country's northern borders.

Choosing judges for the war crimes tribunal for the former Yugoslavia takes a formal step forward on 8 February 2001. The tribunal, set up in 1993, tried people accused of crimes in the Balkan wars. Its permanent judges are elected by the General Assembly, but only from a list the Security Council forwards.

That forwarding is the whole of this text. It sends the Assembly the nominations the Secretary-General had received by 31 January 2001: 26 candidates put forward by countries across Europe, Africa, Asia, and the Americas. From that list, the Assembly would elect the judges who would hear the tribunal's trials and appeals.

Madagascar's entry into the United Nations begins with this short text of 29 June 1960. Having examined the application of the Malagasy Republic, the Council recommended to the General Assembly that the republic be admitted to membership. That recommendation is the Charter's required first step. Only after it can the General Assembly vote on admission, which makes this brief resolution the formal doorway to the new state's seat in the world body.

A theater full of hostages in Moscow drew the Council's swift word in 2002. On 24 October, it adopted Resolution 1440 without dissent. Chechen gunmen had seized the hall a day before, mid-show. Hundreds of playgoers and cast members were held inside. The seizure came amid a string of terror attacks in many lands.

The text condemns the hostage-taking in the strongest terms. It demands the instant, free release of all hostages, with no conditions. Deep sympathy goes to Russia's people and leaders. It goes to the victims and their families as well. All states must help Russia hunt down those behind the attack. That duty rests on the terror rules of Resolution 1373.

What if a terror band built a gas bomb or stole a nuke? That fear drove one of the Council's boldest texts. Trade in parts for such arms had shown black paths round the law. States had gaps in their books. Resolution 1540 passed with no dissent on 28 April 2004. It speaks to all states at once, with the Charter's teeth.

No state may aid lone groups that seek such arms. Each state must pass laws to bar the work. Goods that could feed such arms must be tracked and locked down. Borders and ports must watch for banned trade. Shipments in and out need strict checks. A team of the whole Council would track the work for two years. First word from each state was due in six months. Few texts reach so deep into each land's own law books.

Resolution 1640, passed on 23 November 2005, takes Eritrea to task for curbs on UN troops. In October, Eritrea had banned all UN flights by air in its skies. Fresh curbs on the UN team's ground moves came on top of that. The team watched the border with Ethiopia. The curbs crippled its work and put its staff at risk. Ethiopia, for its part, still balked at the border ruling in full.

The demands ran to both sides. Eritrea had to lift the flight ban and the ground curbs, with no strings tied. Ethiopia had to take and apply the border panel's ruling, which both had sworn to treat as final. With no line marked on the ground, the Council warned, no real peace could last in the region.

Nepal's peace deal gets a UN mission in Resolution 1740, adopted on 23 January 2007. The government and the Maoist party had signed a comprehensive peace agreement on 21 November 2006, ending a decade of civil war. Both sides asked the UN to help with the trickiest parts: managing the arms and fighters of both armies, and monitoring elections.

Answering that request, the Council established the United Nations Mission in Nepal, UNMIN, for an initial twelve months. Its monitors would watch cantonments and weapons storage, and support the vote for a constituent assembly. The text notes the strong public desire for peace and restored democracy, and calls for attention to women, children, and groups long shut out of power.

Resolution 1940, passed on 29 September 2010, sweeps away the last UN bans on Sierra Leone. The bans dated from 1997, when a junta seized power by force. As elected rule came back, the bans were trimmed year by year. In a letter of 9 September 2010 the state's envoy brought fresh news and asked for the last bans to go. The bans team's final report backed the step.

The Council ended the last bars that same day. It praised the UN peace team's work in the land's revival. It urged all states to keep aiding the war crimes court set up for Sierra Leone. One task named was to bring a key indictee to court if he still lived. A long war file thus closed.

Fighting in the Middle East continued in the autumn of 1967, months after the Six-Day War had ended. The Council had ordered a cease-fire, but its orders were being broken. Reports from the Secretary-General documented the violations one by one. Resolution 240 was adopted unanimously on 25 October 1967.

The Council condemned the cease-fire violations. It expressed regret over the deaths and the damage to property that they caused. It reaffirmed that the cease-fire resolutions had to be strictly obeyed. The member states concerned were told to halt all prohibited military action in the area at once. They also had to work fully and without delay with the United Nations Truce Supervision Organization. That observer body was the United Nations presence on the ground.

A broken ceasefire in the Sinai produced a new kind of UN force in 1973. On 25 October, the Council adopted Resolution 340. Fourteen members voted yes and none voted no. China took no part. The truce ordered by Resolution 338 three days before was being breached again and again. UN observers still could not reach both sides of the line.

The text demands a full and instant ceasefire. Both sides must return to the lines held when Resolution 338 passed. More observers are ordered at once. The big step comes next. A United Nations Emergency Force is set up under the Council's own command. Its troops come from member states, but not from the five permanent members.

Indonesia's independence struggle drew UN mediators after the Second World War. Dutch forces were fighting to restore colonial rule. A Committee of Good Offices tried to broker peace. Resolution 40, adopted on 28 February 1948, gave that committee a specific assignment. Eight members voted in favor. Argentina, the Ukrainian republic, and the Soviet Union abstained.

The committee was told to watch political events closely. Its focus was western Java and Madura, two restive regions. Reports had to reach the Council frequently. The task was fact-finding, not enforcement. Still, steady reporting kept world attention on Indonesia. That pressure helped push the Dutch toward the transfer of sovereignty completed in 1949.

The war between Iran and Iraq was in its third year in the autumn of 1983. A mission sent by the Secretary-General had inspected civilian areas in both countries. Those areas had come under military attack. Resolution 540 was adopted on 31 October 1983.

The Council deplored the conflict and its heavy toll. Civilian lives were being lost, and cities and industry were badly damaged. All violations of international humanitarian law were condemned, above all breaches of the Geneva Conventions. Attacks on civilian targets had to end. The text affirmed the right of free navigation and trade in international waters. Both sides were told to stop hostilities at sea. The Secretary-General was asked to keep mediating toward a full settlement, and to consult both parties on ways to sustain and verify a cease-fire.

Haiti's military regime is ordered out by force if needed in Resolution 940, adopted in July 1994. The de facto regime had defied the Governors Island Agreement, blocked the UN Mission in Haiti, worsened the humanitarian crisis, and expelled the international civilian mission's staff. Letters from Haiti's president and its UN envoy were before the Council.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council authorizes member states to form a force under unified command. The force may use all necessary means to make the military leadership leave, secure the return of the legitimately elected President, Jean-Bertrand Aristide, and restore Haiti's lawful government. A UNMIH advance team of up to 60 goes in with the force. Once a stable environment exists, UNMIH takes over with 6,000 troops, to keep security, professionalize the armed forces, create a separate police force, and help prepare legislative elections. Sanctions are to be lifted on Aristide's return.
uslaw-usc-t2-s640:
Section 640 of Title 2 of the United States Code covers House approval of regular appropriation bills. It sits in Chapter 17A of that title, on the congressional budget process. The section lays down a bar on House business in July. It is not in order in the House to take up a resolution for a break of more than three calendar days in that month too soon.

The bar lifts once the House has approved the yearly appropriation bills. Those bills must give new budget authority under all the subcommittees of the Committee on Appropriations. The bills must cover the fiscal year that begins on October 1 of that year. The text is current through Public Law 119-134, as issued by the Office of the Law Revision Counsel.
uslaw-usc-t2-s6540:
Section 6540 of Title 2 of the United States Code covers changes to rates of pay by the Secretary of the Senate. It sits in Chapter 65 of that title, on Senate officers, in the part on the Secretary of the Senate. A rate of pay set by law for a post under the Secretary is to be taken as the top rate for that post. That holds for the rate as raised, or as it may be raised, by or under law.

On that base, the Secretary is cleared to adjust the rate of pay of a post under his authority. The text goes on to state the terms of that power. The text is current through Public Law 119-134, as issued by the Office of the Law Revision Counsel.
vishnu-purana-wilson-1840: Horace Hayman Wilson rendered the Vishnu Purana from the original Sanskrit for John Murray of London in 1840, as the file header dates it. His title page calls the work a system of Hindu mythology and tradition, with notes drawn chiefly from other Puranas. Wilson's own titles crowd the page: fellow of the Royal Society, member of Asiatic societies in Bengal and Paris, and Boden Professor of Sanskrit at Oxford. Pages present here hold that title page only, so the Purana's myths themselves are not shown.
vivian-grey-pg9840:
A publisher's note fronts this copy of Vivian Grey, Benjamin Disraeli's first novel. A twin record of the same book carries the same note. The note dates the novel to 1826 and 1827. It pairs the book with Sybil of 1845, as the bounds of his creative years. It sets him beside Bulwer, Dickens, Thackeray, and the elder Scott. His life dates stand as 1804 to 1881. This copy adds frontispiece and title page pictures that the twin lacks.

The note goes one step further here. Disraeli, it says, was barely twenty-one when Vivian Grey, his first work of fiction, appeared. The young author won notice at once. The tale of a clever, pushing hero in fashionable and political London made his name before Parliament did. Readers get the novel with an editor's map of where it stands in a long writing life. That life ended with Lothair and Endymion.
vyse-operations-pyramids-gizeh-vol-1-184:
Richard William Howard Vyse blasted his way into the Great Pyramid in 1837, and Vol. 1 of his Operations, out in 1840, tells how. Vyse was a chief of troops with funds and zeal. With the aid of Perring, he forced the hid rooms past the king's hall. There he found the name of Khufu writ in red paint.

That find fixed who built the heap for good. Logs, costs, and tales of the dig crowd the tome. His rough means drew scorn, yet his finds changed the field. This is the first full tale of a dig there.
vyse-operations-pyramids-gizeh-vol-2-184:
Richard William Howard Vyse pushed his dig past the great heap in Vol. 2 of his Operations, out in 1840. The first tome told of the forced rooms and the name of Khufu. Here the work spreads to the next heaps, the Sphinx, and tombs in the sand. Perring's fine plans and cuts fill page past page.

Those plans are the tome's chief worth. Digs since then still cite their sums and lines. The log prose is dry, yet the scale of the work stuns. Read as a pair, the tomes found the dig of the heaps.
whitefield-journals-1740:
George Whitefield was the most famous preacher of the eighteenth century, whose voice could reach crowds in open fields. His Journals, first published in 1740, record his preaching tours across Britain and America in his own words. Whitefield wrote them partly to answer his critics.

He describes packed churches, weeping hearers, journeys by horse and ship, and his break with John Wesley over doctrine. The entries mix frank self-praise with real wonder at the crowds his message drew. Historians of the Great Awakening treat the Journals as a prime source written from the movement's center.
